  "expires_at": "2026-02-19T18:10:00Z",
  "request_id": "3f8b3a2a-9e1f-4e6b-8c2a-3fd0fbfe7e0d"
}
{code}

h2. Constraints and limits

* Max time range: 31 days (server may reject larger ranges with 400).
* Max rows (post-grouping): 2,000,000 (returns 413 or 400 with guidance).
* Export jobs are rate limited per workspace and per user.

h2. Audit logging requirements

Export creation and download MUST emit audit events (see security guidance). Minimum fields:
* actor_user_id
* workspace_id
* export_id
* requested_range
* filters hash (not raw prompt/data)
* created_at / downloaded_at
* client_ip (if available)

h1. GET /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}

Returns export job status, progress, and download link when ready.

h2. Response shape

{code}
{
  "export_id": "exp_01HTY5Q7K2Y0A0N6ZK3Z0K9P0M",
  "status": "ready",
  "created_at": "2026-02-16T18:10:00Z",
  "started_at": "2026-02-16T18:10:05Z",
  "completed_at": "2026-02-16T18:12:44Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-02-19T18:10:00Z",
  "format": "csv",
  "file": {
    "file_name": "usage-insights_ws-123_2026-02-01_2026-02-16_route-model_day.csv",
    "content_type": "text/csv",
    "size_bytes": 18299331
  },
  "download": {
    "url": "https://downloads.redwood.example/signed/....",
    "url_expires_at": "2026-02-16T19:12:44Z"
  },
  "failure": null
}
{code}

Status enum:
* queued
* running
* ready
* failed
* canceled

If failed:

{code}
{
  "export_id": "...",
  "status": "failed",
  "failure": {
    "code": "query_timeout",
    "message": "Export exceeded time limit for the selected range. Try reducing the range or grouping by fewer dimensions."
  }
}
{code}

h1. POST /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}/cancel

Cancels an export job if it is queued or running.

h2. Response

{code}
{
  "export_id": "exp_...",
  "status": "canceled"
}
{code}

h1. Pagination standard (cursor-based)

All list endpoints in Usage Insights use cursor pagination.

Rules:
* *cursor* is opaque; clients must not parse it.
* *page_size* defaults and maximums are endpoint-specific.
* Responses include:
  * page.next_cursor (string|null)
  * page.has_more (boolean)

If the underlying dataset changes between pages (late events/backfill), the API may return slightly inconsistent ordering; clients should treat results as best-effort for interactive exploration.

h1. Filter semantics

h2. Multi-value filters

v1 supports single-valued filters for route/model dimensions. Multi-select may be added later as additive fields (e.g., routes=[...]).

h2. Route matching

* route filter matches the *normalized* route string.
* Unnormalized paths (high-cardinality) are aggregated under the sentinel value: "/__unattributed__/untemplated" when applicable.

h2. Model matching

* model is the stable Redwood model identifier used in metering events.
* model_family/model_version are reporting buckets and may map multiple model identifiers.

h1. Caching and HTTP semantics

* Breakdown and top-drivers endpoints may return:
  * Cache-Control: private, max-age=30
* Exports:
  * Status endpoints are not cached.
  * Signed download URLs are short-lived and must not be stored long-term.

h1. Security and compliance notes

* Exports are subject to retention constraints and workspace restrictions (e.g., restricted workspaces may disallow exports entirely).
* Download URLs must be signed, single-purpose, and time-bound.
* API responses must not include raw prompts, completions, or customer payloads; only aggregated usage/cost metrics.

h1. Open questions / follow-ups

* Multi-select filters for route/model in v1.1 (console UX may require it).
* Optional “shareable link” object for exports/reports (requires expanded security review).
* Standardization of retry vs replay definitions across gateway/runtime telemetry.

h1. Changelog

* 2026-02-16: Clarified tz behavior for bucket boundaries; added export cancellation endpoint; documented billing tolerance expectations.
* 2026-02-06: Added freshness fields (as_of, data_lag_seconds) to all interactive endpoints.
* 2026-01-29: Initial v1 contract published.

title: Handoff Harmony: Eviction and Transfer Playbook
content:
Handoff Harmony: Eviction and Transfer Playbook

Summary:

This playbook codifies a deterministic, observable approach for transferring in-flight requests and gracefully reclaiming runtime resources. It balances user-visible correctness (avoiding aborted responses and consistency loss) with operator needs for fast resource reclamation during scale events, maintenance, or kernel failures.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs on-call for runtime clusters
- Platform owners planning canaries or capacity changes

Goals and guardrails:
- User-visible aborts from planned or forced handoffs should be < 0.05% monthly.
- Typical handoff commit latency: median <= 150 ms; p99 <= 2.5s for short requests.
- Eviction flows must reclaim a node within configured eviction_window while providing final best-effort completion for affected sessions.

Core terminology (short):
- handoff_token: single-use opaque identifier with expiry ISO8601 timestamp. Appears in traces.
- drain_epoch: the short wait after marking sessions to allow running kernels to finish naturally (configurable).
- eviction_window: hard timeout for completing a transfer or executing graceful eviction.
- kv-sync: optional asynchronous synchronization of minimal KV state to target. Marks session degraded if incomplete.
- preempt_credit: a small retry allowance given to callers during transfer to reduce client-visible failures.

Architecture components involved:
- runtime-dispatcher (dispatcher): selects destination node/shard and initiates handoff intents.
- node-agent: per-host service orchestrating local drain, KV exports, kernel lifecycle, and final commit/eviction actions.
- handoff-orchestrator (leader): optional distributed coordinator for multi-shard transfers and conflict resolution. Data store: etcd.
- telemetry-agent: annotates traces with handoff_token and emits events for Handoff:started, Handoff:committed, Handoff:evicted.

Protocol (ordered steps):
1) Dispatcher detects transfer reason: planned drain, OS maintenance, GPU error, preemption, or capacity balancing. It calculates candidate target(s) and issues an Intent to node-agent: {token, targets, reason, ttl}.
2) Node-agent marks sessions in drain set and enters drain_epoch. It sets internal state to DRAINING and begins non-blocking kv-sync for streaming sessions.
3) Handoff-orchestrator (if present) attempts to reserve a receive slot on the target node. Reservation response includes acceptance, backoff recommendation, or alternate node list.
4) Target node verifies compatibility (model variant, quantization profile, KV shard affinity) and responds. If accepted, it returns a receive_handle with a short TTL.
5) Source node streams session metadata and small KV chunks (if supported). Only metadata required to resume decoding is streamed; secrets and raw user payloads are never proxied.
6) Target node writes session metadata to local cache, acknowledges, and telemetry records Handoff:committed. Source node marks session COMPLETE_LOCAL_CLEANUP and releases kernel resources.
7) If the sequence fails to finish before eviction_window, node-agent triggers graceful-eviction: attempt a synthetic completion (fast-fallback generation), then issue final kernel teardown and emit Handoff:evicted.

Configuration reference (defaults):
| key | default | note |
| .handoff.eviction_window_secs | "30" | applies to short non-stream sessions |
| .handoff.stream_eviction_window_secs | "120" | applies to chat/stream sessions |
| .handoff.drain_epoch_ms | "1500" | small wait to let kernels finish naturally |
| .handoff.max_parallel_transfers | "6" | per-node outgoing transfer concurrency |
| .handoff.preempt_credit_tokens | "1" | number of ephemeral retries clients may consume |
| .handoff.kv_sync_enabled | "true" | best-effort; false disables KV transfer attempts |

Observed failure patterns and recommended mitigations:
- reservation_timeouts (common): when requests queue at dispatcher due to oversubscription. Actions: reduce dispatcher weight, scale dedicated capacity, or reroute to compatible fallback variant. Metric: handoff_reserve_timeout_total.
- kernel_stall during drain: identified by kernel.active_ms spikes and no progress markers. Action: extend drain_epoch up to a soft cap once for kernels flagged as idempotent; otherwise escalate to forced eviction. Metric: kernel_blocked_handoff_total.
- kv_sync_partial: KV sync completed partially. Action: mark session degraded; downstream resume will perform token re-priming. Metric: handoff_kv_partial_total.
- oscillation between nodes: rapid flip-flops identified by repeated commits for same session token. Action: insert randomized cooldown (2m) and raise handoff priority to avoid future oscillations.

Operational runbook (triage):
Alert triggers:
- handoff_reserve_timeout_rate > 5/min sustained for 3m
- handoff_evicted.rate spikes > 1/min for 5m
- handoff_kv_partial.rate > baseline by 200%

Initial responder steps (SRE):
1) Confirm alerts and scope: query Prometheus examples:
   - sum(rate(handoff_reserve_timeout_total[5m])) by (cluster)
   - sum(rate(handoff_evicted_total[5m])) by (node)
2) Inspect dispatcher and node-agent dashboards: dispatcher.route_failures, node.queue_depth_p95, node.kv_sync_errors.
3) If a single node is overloaded: cordon it via node-agent API (dry-run first), allow existing handoffs to proceed, and unfavour new routing to it. Example API:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 60, "dry_run": true}' \
     https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon
4) If topology-level saturation: scale up dedicated pools or adjust dispatcher routing policies to prefer fallback variants.
5) If KV sync errors: collect node-agent logs (tag: handoff.kv), and export traces from telemetry-service for the handoff_token.
6) Follow recovery verification checklist: handoff_commit_rate returns to baseline, handoff_evicted_total is flat, and canary synthetic workload p99 latency within expected tolerance.

Profiling and benchmarking guidance:
- Synthetic profiles to include in PRs changing handoff logic:
  * Short-request profile: 100k reqs, seq=64, concurrency=800. Report: handoff_commit_success, handoff_latency_p50/p95/p99.
  * Streamed-session profile: 3k sessions, avg_tokens=1500, concurrency=250. Report: kv_sync_success_rate, stream_handoff_commit_latency_p99.
- Profiling tips:
  - Correlate GPU kernel timeline (Nsight/trace) with handoff telemetry. Capture 2s samples across drain_epoch.
  - Sample node-agent state machine transitions and annotate traces with kernel ids to root-cause blockages.

Benchmark pass criteria for merge (non-exhaustive):
- handoff_success_rate >= 99.5% under 75% traffic;
- handoff_latency_p99 degradation <= 25% vs baseline;
- kv_sync_success_rate >= 98% for streaming workloads.

Release & rollout guidance:
- Any protocol change must publish a compatibility matrix and automated migration plan.
- Use feature-flagged canaries: 1% x24h, then 5% x48h, instrument both v1/v2 events.
- Provide explicit rollback actions: disable feature flag and allow existing tokens to expire over one eviction_window cycle.

Telemetry and SLOs (recommended):
- Metrics to emit: handoff_commit_total, handoff_evicted_total, handoff_reserve_timeout_total, handoff_kv_partial_total, handoff_latency_ms(quantiles), handoff_kv_sync_success_ratio.
- Example SLOs (hosted & dedicated):
  * Handoff commit success >= 99.5% monthly
  * User-visible aborts due to handoff <= 0.05% monthly
  * Handoff median latency <= 150ms, p99 <= 2.5s (non-stream workloads)

Debugging snippets:
- Node status (jq):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/status | jq '.'
- Extract recent handoff traces via telemetry API:
  curl -s "https://telemetry-agent.internal/api/traces?tag=handoff_token&from=-10m" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.samples[] | {token: .token, events: .events}'
- Force a dry-run cordon (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 45, "dry_run": true}' \
    https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon

Owner and contacts:
- Primary owner: runtime-platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.com)
- Primary engineers: Marissa Cheng (author), Andrej Kove1cs (handoff/orchestrator), Priya Raman (SRE lead)

Rollout checklist for protocol changes:
1) Unit tests + integration with simulated drain & blocked kernels.
2) PR-level synthetic benchmark comparisons saved to artifacts.
3) Canary rollout (1% -> 5%) with automated alert gates.
4) Full rollout with 30-minute pause windows between increments.

Related resources:
- Runtime dashboards: "Handoff Overview" (Grafana)
- Tools: tools/runtime-canary, synthetic-benchmark-generator
- See also: session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Created (initial playbook and runbook).
- 2026-07-20: Added kv_sync and profiling guidance.
- 2026-12-14: Updated SLO targets and release guidance.

title: Redwood enterprise procedures kit — company operations (2026)
content:
Redwood enterprise procedures kit — company operations (2026)

Overview

Purpose: This document centralizes company-wide operational policies and ready-to-use process templates covering access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor management, and travel. It is intended as the canonical reference for operational owners, approvers, and team leads.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and suppliers who request access, make changes to production systems, handle company data, engage vendors, or incur business travel/expenses. Exceptions must be approved by the owner_team (finance-legal) and recorded in the exceptions register.

Principles
- Least privilege and auditable approvals for access.
- Risk-proportional controls: higher risk => higher review/fail-safe.
- Single source of truth for templates to speed approvals and audits.
- Clear ownership for every control and handoff.

Owners and escalation
- Policy owner: Finance & Legal (owner: Maya Chen).
- Operational owners: People Ops (travel & people-related expenses), Eng-SRE (change management for infra), Eng-Platform (deployment change policies), Procurement (vendor onboarding), Security (data classification & RBAC design).
- Escalation channel: #ops-escalation (Slack); for regulatory incidents notify security@redwood.com and legal@redwood.com.

1) Access & Permissions
Summary: RBAC-based model with centralized requests through the Access Request Portal (ARP). Temporary elevation via Just-In-Time (JIT) access is encouraged.
Responsibilities:
- Requester: provide justification and duration.
- Approver: manager or service owner depending on resource type.
- IAM admin: perform provisioning and maintain audit logs.

Access categories and approval matrix (summary):
| Resource type | Approver | Max default duration | Escalation threshold |
|---------------|----------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Non-prod cloud project | Team manager | 90 days | Security review if > 30 days or cross-team |
| Prod read-only role | Service owner | 30 days | Security review if > 30 days |
| Prod write / admin role | Service owner + Security | 7 days | Required approval from Eng-SRE for > 7 days |
| Vendor access (limited) | Procurement + Service owner | 14 days | Contract/DPAs required for > 30 days |

Request process (high level):
1. Submit ARP form including business justification, requested resources, and duration.
2. Auto-notify approver(s); if multi-approver, require all approvals.
3. IAM admin provisions account/role and tags request id for audit.
4. Access automatically expires at the requested end date; reminders sent 7 days before expiry.

Temporary elevation/JIT steps:
1. Request JIT via ARP with short justification and immediate timeline.
2. Approver reviews and sets a task window; JIT sessions are logged and session recordings retained for 90 days.

Access review cadence:
- Quarterly reviews for all active Prod admin roles.
- Annual certification for vendor accounts.

2) Change Management
Goal: enable fast, safe, and auditable changes across infra and product services.
Change categories:
- Standard change: pre-authorized, repeatable operational tasks (e.g., routine scaling) — no CAB required but must follow runbook.
- Normal change: requires change ticket, impact assessment, approver sign-off, and scheduled window.
- Emergency change: implemented to remediate incidents. Post-implementation review required within 72 hours.

Change request template (short):
- Title
- Owner/Requester
- Change category (standard/normal/emergency)
- Impact assessment (services/users, rollback plan)
- Scheduled window
- Validation plan / smoke tests

Approval matrix:
- Normal change: Service owner + Eng-SRE (for infra) or Product owner (for API) depending on impact.
- High-impact (customer-facing outage risk): CAB approval required. CAB meets twice weekly; use asynchronous voting for low-latency approvals.

Implementation steps (normal change):
1. Open change ticket in Change Management system (link: /tools/change).
2. Fill template, attach runbook, assign approvers.
3. Complete pre-change checklist (backups, canary, synthetic checks).
4. Execute in maintenance window.
5. Run validation tests.
6. Close ticket with outcomes and metrics (latency, error rate).

Emergency change protocol:
1. Tag ticket as EMERGENCY; notify on-call and #incident.
2. Implement mitigation with minimum scope.
3. After stabilization, conduct a post-implementation review within 72 hours.

Change windows and blackout periods:
- Production major releases blocked on high-traffic holidays (list maintained by Product).
- Routine changes allowed in designated windows: Mon–Fri 02:00–06:00 UTC and Sat 08:00–12:00 UTC (exceptions handled by CAB).

3) Data Management
Classification scheme (three levels):
- PUBLIC: no restrictions.
- INTERNAL: default for business documents.
- RESTRICTED: PII, customer data, proprietary model weights.

Data handling requirements:
- RESTRICTED data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, stored in approved buckets, and access controlled via RBAC with explicit justification.
- Export/egress of RESTRICTED data requires a Data Use Request and DSA review (Data Security & Assurance).

Retention and deletion
- Logs (diagnostic): 180 days by default, extendable to 365 days upon SRE request.
- Backups: retention per service SLA; restore tests quarterly.
- Customer data retention: as per contract or 7 years max unless otherwise specified.

Data breach steps (summary):
1. Contain and preserve evidence.
2. Notify Security and Legal within 24 hours.
3. Conduct forensics; follow regulatory notification timelines.

Data labeling and metadata requirements:
- Every dataset must include: owner, classification, retention policy, last updated, and approved uses.

4) Procurement & Expenses
Procurement lifecycle:
1. Need identification and owner assignment.
2. Create Purchase Request (PR) using Procurement template (see Templates section).
3. Competitive sourcing required for purchases > $50k.
4. Procurement team reviews vendor compliance (security, SOC2, DPAs) and negotiates terms.
5. Purchase Order (PO) issued; vendor onboarding completed.

Approval thresholds (summary):
- Up to $2,500: Team lead approval.
- $2,500–$50,000: Department head + Procurement review.
- > $50,000: VP approval + Procurement + Legal.

Card and travel expenses:
- Use corporate card for approved travel with pre-approval.
- Expense report due within 14 days of trip end.
- Receipts required for any individual expense > $25.
- Per diem model: US domestic $75/day (meals & incidental), international vary by country — check Finance portal.

Reimbursements and audit
- Finance reserves the right to audit expense claims for 12 months.
- Non-compliant claims will be remediated with manager and may lead to revocation of card privileges.

Procurement request example (JSON snippet to paste into PR form):
```
{
  "requester": "Name",
  "department": "Engineering",
  "description": "GPU cloud capacity: 4 x A100 reserved for Q1 experiments",
  "estimated_cost": "48,000",
  "vendor": "CloudCompute Inc.",
  "business_justification": "Prototype + evaluation for Dedicated offering",
  "approval_chain": ["team-lead", "procurement"]
}
```

5) Vendor Management
Vendor onboarding checklist:
1. Complete vendor intake form and risk assessment.
2. Verify security posture (SOC 2, ISO, pen-test results if applicable).
3. Data processing addendum (DPA) and contractual terms signed by Legal.
4. Create vendor record in Vendor Registry with owner and contract dates.
5. Provision necessary access and limit by least privilege.

SLAs and monitoring:
- Key vendors must have a documented SLA and escalations.
- Quarterly vendor review for strategic vendors; annual review for others.

Offboarding:
- Revoke all accounts and access within 48 hours of contract termination.
- Verify data return/destruction per contract.

6) Travel Policy (summary)
Pre-approval: All business travel requires a Travel Request in the Travel Portal and manager pre-approval.
Booking: Use preferred travel vendors for corporate rates; personal arrangements reimbursable only with prior approval.
Safety & compliance: Follow local guidance and travel advisories; register high-risk travel with People Ops.
Expense categories and caps:
- Lodging: reasonable nightly rate per city band (see Finance portal).
- Meals: per diem or itemized receipts.
- Ground transport: ride-share or economy car rental.

Travel emergency support: 24/7 travel assistance is available via travel-support@redwood.com.

7) Internal Templates (canonical templates to use)
- Access Request (ARP) template (fields: requester, resource, duration, justification, approver).
- Change Request template (fields: owner, impact, rollback, validation, stakeholders).
- Procurement Request (PR) template (fields: requester, vendor, cost, justification, approvals).
- Vendor Intake form (fields: vendor, controls checklist, contracts, risk rating).
- Travel Request template (fields: traveler, dates, destination, business purpose, manager approval).

Example Access Request (text):
--Start ARP--
Requester: Jane Doe
Resource: prod-ml-models S3 bucket (RESTRICTED)
Duration: 7 days
Justification: Investigate model drift for customer incident #1234
Approver: Service owner (ML Infra), Security (if > 3 days)
--End ARP--

Governance and audit
- All actions (access grants, change tickets, procurement approvals) must be tagged with policy id and retained per retention rules.
- Internal audit cadence: semi-annual for access controls, quarterly for change management evidence, annual for procurement/vendor compliance.

Amendments and exceptions
- To request an exception, submit an Exception Request with rationale, compensating controls, and expiration date. Exceptions expire automatically unless renewed via the same process.

FAQs (short)
Q: Who signs off on vendor DPAs?
A: Legal in coordination with Procurement.
Q: How long are access request logs retained?
A: 365 days for provisioning logs; session recordings for 90 days.

Contacts
- Policy owner: maya.chen@redwood.com
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.com
- Security: security@redwood.com
- Travel support: travel-support@redwood.com

Related pages and references
- Central policy index: /confluence/policies-and-process/central-policy-index-and-core-processes-2025
- Change management runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/change-management
- Data classification guidelines: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention

Revision history
- 2025-11-15: Created by Maya Chen (finance-legal).
- 2026-02-10: Updated access durations and procurement thresholds; added JIT access section.

End of document

title: Graceful Capacity Degradation: Commercialization and Customer Onboarding Playbook
content:
Graceful Capacity Degradation: Commercialization and Customer Onboarding Playbook

Overview

This playbook defines the product, commercial, and operational approach for "graceful capacity degradation" — an end-to-end feature that lets Redwood continue serving customer traffic under transient capacity pressure by: routing to lower-fidelity model variants, applying short-term batching changes, and issuing customer-facing credits where quality/latency SLOs are impacted. The goal is to keep customer applications online while limiting cost and preserving predictable economics.

Use cases:
- Enterprise customers on Dedicated pools experiencing regional GPU contention.
- Hosted-tier customers during cross-region failover events.
- Migration windows where full-capacity variants are being rolled out.

Who should read this: product managers, solutions engineering, account teams, SRE, billing, and customer success.

Objectives

1) Business: minimize revenue churn from outages by providing a transparent, contractual fallback behavior and straightforward crediting model.
2) Product: expose controls for fidelity vs cost tradeoffs and automated fallback policies per tenant.
3) Ops: give SREs deterministic, observable fallbacks with clear telemetry and rollback procedures.

Scope and Non-Scope

In scope:
- Policy definitions in the control plane for per-tenant fallback sequencing (model variant, quantization, batching).
- Billing credit calculation for short-term fidelity/latency degradations.
- Customer onboarding flows and contract language templates.
- Console UX for visualizing fallback events and credit history.

Out of scope:
- Long-term contract renegotiation (handled by Sales).
- Deep model retraining to recover fidelity (handled by Applied ML).

Product contract and SLO implications

SLO mapping (examples):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% regional for Hosted API (unchanged).
- Latency SLO (TR1 route): p95 < 300ms. During graceful degradation that target may be relaxed to p95 < 700ms per policy.
- Quality SLO: BLEU/ROUGE or embedding distance budget for evaluated prompt sets — a soft guard used to trigger crediting when exceeded.

When a degradation policy is applied, the system will:
1) Record an event in routing-proxy and console (event_id).
2) Flag the tenant for billing-service credit evaluation.
3) Update runtime headers to indicate fallback variant (X-Redwood-Fallback-Variant).

Credit calculation rules (summary):
- Windowed approach: credits are calculated per 5-minute window where observed quality/latency exceeds the configured tenant thresholds.
- Credit basis: fraction of token cost attributable to degraded fidelity + fixed service-level goodwill amount.
- Max credit cap: 20% of the tenant’s billed usage in the affected week unless escalated by CSM.

Operational controls and owner ship

Owners: 
- Product: Aisha Patel (owner for commercial playbook updates)
- Opt-in policy feature flag: eng-platform (feature-flag service)
- Runtime/fallback orchestration: eng-serving-runtime (runtime team)
- Billing & credits engine: finance-and-legal (billing-service team)
- Onboarding & comms: customer-success-and-support (CSM team)

Immediate contacts (escalation):
- Oncall SRE: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations
- Billing escalation: Sana Becker (finance)

Customer onboarding checklist (CSM / Solutions Eng)

1) Pre-signing (Contract/Legal):
   - Insert fallback covenant into Appendix B of the contract (template snippet below).
   - Agree on maximum weekly credit cap and SLA tiers.

2) Initial setup (first 7 days):
   - Enable per-tenant fallback policy default in the Console (DefaultPolicy: standard_fallback_v1).
   - Capture a canonical prompt set (10–20 prompts) for quality monitoring. Add to tenant profile: 'fallback_guard_prompts'.
   - Set tenant-specific thresholds: latency_margin_ms, embedding_distance_threshold.

3) Post-activation (day 7–30):
   - Run a simulated load test using the hosted-sim-runner to validate fallback behavior.
   - Walk through customer Console views showing fallback events and credits.
   - Schedule a QBR within first 30 days to review observed fallbacks and crediting.

Template contract snippet (Appendix B):

"During transient capacity constraints Redwood may route traffic to lower-fidelity model variants or apply batching that can affect latency and output characteristics. Redwood will provide usage credits for material degradations consistent with the Customer’s SLA. The maximum weekly credit is 20% of billed usage for the affected time period unless otherwise negotiated."

Staged rollout plan (recommended)

1) Canary (internal): enable on 10 internal tenants and exercise 3 failure modes (GPU pressure, cross-region network spike, warm-pool exhaustion). Duration: 2 weeks.
2) Beta (select customers): opt-in by invitation to up to 20 paying customers. Monitor for false positives in crediting and UX clarity. Duration: 4 weeks.
3) General availability: automatic opt-in default for new enterprise customers, opt-out for legacy contracts.

Rollout metrics to validate at each stage:
- False positive credit events per 1000 degraded windows < 1.
- Time to detect and apply fallback < 15s from threshold breach.
- Percentage of requests served without failover increased vs baseline (resilience uplift).

Billing and pricing impact examples (table)

| Degradation Level | Runtime change | Billing credit % (windowed) | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Minor | small-quant (int8) | 5% | Quality delta within 3% of baseline on eval prompts |
| Moderate | reduced-fp32-context | 12% | p95 latency > baseline by +300ms OR embedding distance exceedance |
| Major | variant-fallback-to-small | 20% (cap) | Significant quality regression; automatic CSM review triggered |

Example credit calculation (simplified):
- Tenant A had $2,000 billed in the affected week. During a 30-minute incident with moderate degradations affecting 3 five-minute windows, system calculates 12% credit on tokens for those windows: estimated credit = $2,000 * (minutes_affected / total_week_minutes) * 12% (simplified). Final credits are rounded and shown in Console adjustments.

Console UX and telemetry requirements

Required Console elements: 
- Fallback events timeline per-tenant with event_id and reason codes (REASON_GPU_PRESSURE, REASON_COLD_START, REASON_NETWORK_EGRESS).
- Credit calculator preview and audit trail.
- Toggle for opt-in/out and tenant-specific thresholds.

Telemetry and logging:
- routing-proxy: fallback_applied (bool), fallback_variant (string), event_id (uuid).
- runtime-metrics: model_variant, avg_batch_size, effective_qps.
- billing-service: credit_eval_id, credit_amount, reason_code.

Operational runbook (SRE)

Trigger conditions: automated detection when any of the following repeat for N=3 consecutive 1-minute windows:
1) p95 latency > 2x configured latency SLO.
2) evaluated prompt-set quality metric breaches threshold.
3) GPU pool capacity utilization > 92% and queue depth > 50%

Immediate actions (ordered):
1) Confirm detection in routing-proxy and surface to incident channel #fallback-events.
2) If automated policy applied: verify X-Redwood-Fallback-Variant in live requests.
3) Notify oncall and CSM if predicted credit > $5,000 in the next 60 minutes.
4) If false-positive: rollback policy via feature-flag (feature-flag service CLI).

CLI snippets (example):

# Inspect current fallback policy for tenant
redwoodctl tenants get --id tenant_123 --fields fallback_policy

# Force-rollout rollback (engineering only)
redwoodctl feature-flags set graceful_degradation false --scope tenant_123 --reason "false-positive"

Acceptance criteria for GA

- Feature flagged and controllable per-tenant in Console.
- Billing-service integration able to generate provisional credits and surface to Console.
- Automated detection rules validated with < 1% false positives in Beta.
- CSM & Sales trained with playbook and contract template.

Success metrics (product & commercial)

- Reduction in outage-related churn rate by 30% for customers using fallback within 6 months.
- Mean time to apply fallback < 15s.
- Percentage of fallback events with customer-visible credits processed within 24 hours > 95%.

Risks and mitigations

Risk: Customers perceive credits as a license for degraded experience.
Mitigation: Restrict rollout to enterprise customers by default; add explicit contract language and weekly credit caps.

Risk: Over-crediting due to noisy quality signals.
Mitigation: Require N=3 consecutive windows and cross-validate with canonical prompt-set before issuing credits.

Appendix: Implementation notes for eng teams

- routing-proxy should emit structured event payloads to kafka topic: fallback-events (schema v1). Fields: event_id, tenant_id, reason_code, variant, window_start, window_end.
- billing-service will consume fallback-events and join with usage-aggregates to produce provisional credit entries (credit_eval_id).
- Console will render a reversible audit trail entry for each provisional credit and allow CSM to approve final credit posting.

Sample fallback-events kafka payload (human readable):
{
  "event_id": "evt-8f3a2",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_123",
  "reason_code": "REASON_GPU_PRESSURE",
  "variant": "small-variant-quantized-v2",
  "window": "2026-06-09T10:05:00Z/2026-06-09T10:10:00Z",
  "metrics": {"p95_latency_ms": 820, "embedding_distance_delta": 0.12}
}

Note: the actual kafka schema is managed in eng-platform/schemas and must be updated in the schema registry before GA.

Related pages and next steps

- Coordinate with finance-and-legal to finalize crediting algorithm and weekly caps.
- Schedule lab tests with Applied ML to calibrate canonical prompt-sets for Beta tenants.
- Run the Canary starting 2026-07-05 and record validation metrics in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.

Document revision history

- 2026-03-29: initial draft (A. Patel)
- 2026-04-15: added billing calculation examples and SRE runbook (D. Martinez)
- 2026-06-10: post-beta updates, clarified contract language and Console mockups (P. Narayanan)

title: Pitch playbook: compact economics & risk scripts
content:
Pitch playbook: compact economics & risk scripts

Overview

Purpose: This playbook gives field teams a compact, repeatable set of messaging scripts, competitive talking points, pricing heuristics, and a short customer case study to accelerate technical discovery conversations with platform and engineering buyers. It is optimized for 10–25 minute technical deep dives and CISO/Finance readiness checks.

Who this is for
- Sales Engineers: concise scripts for demos and risk conversations.
- Account Executives: framing snippets for exec/C-level briefs.
- Solution Architects: competitive countermeasures and deployment notes.

Positioning pillars (30-second soundbites)
1) Predictable inference economics: "Redwood converts model choices into predictable per-token costs via quantization profiles, smart batching, and autoscaling policies—so you can forecast ML spend like any other infra line item."
2) Production-grade reliability: "We provide SLAs, fallbacks, and dedicated capacity options so user-facing LLM features stay online even under load or model regressions."
3) Deployment flexibility and security: "Host with Redwood, or deploy Redwood Private into your VPC / on-prem—with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs for regulated workloads."
4) Developer-first operations: "Same API, tooling, and rollouts across hosted, dedicated, and private—reduces cognitive load for platform teams."

Competitive brief (quick reference)
- OpenAI / Anthropic (hosted LLM APIs)
  - Strengths: largest model ecosystem, simple API, fast time-to-prototype.
  - Redwood response: Emphasize SLO-backed dedicated capacity, cost controls (batching/quant), and enterprise security for regulated customers. Highlight predictable unit economics and rollout controls.
- Cloud-managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex)
  - Strengths: deep cloud integration, billing consolidation.
  - Redwood response: Stress inference-optimized runtime (KV cache, continuous batching) that typically reduces per-token runtime by 20–40% vs generic endpoint configurations; point to dedicated GPU pool options and multi-cloud routing.
- Self-hosted runtime vendors (open-source runtimes/orchestration)
  - Strengths: control, no vendor lock.
  - Redwood response: Call out the operational burden, ongoing kernel selection, and performance tuning required. Position Redwood as a managed alternative that preserves control (Private deployment) while removing engineering debt.

Quick battlecards (friction points + counters)
- "We can just run this ourselves on EC2/GKE."
  - Counter: For sustained user-facing latency SLOs, the engineering cost of kernel tuning, KV cache correctness, and autoscaling policy development is non-trivial. Offer a 6–8 week pilot that shows unit-cost delta and time-to-market delta.
- "OpenAI has better models / quality."
  - Counter: Redwood supports model rollouts and automatic fallback to tuned variants; for many production workloads model parity is not the primary constraint—latency, cost, and observability are. Offer a side-by-side eval with traffic replay.

Demo scripts: 12-minute technical deep dive (structure)
1) 0:00–1:30 — 30-second product framing & value props (use positioning pillars).
2) 1:30–4:00 — Live trace: show Console call graph, per-token cost breakdown, and latency SLOs for a sample chat workload.
3) 4:00–7:00 — Deployment options: toggle to Dedicated and simulated failover to Private mock (show routing policy UI + audit logs).
4) 7:00–10:00 — Economics toggle: show autoscaling, batching, and quantization profiles and an on-screen estimator for per-10k tokens cost.
5) 10:00–12:00 — Security & compliance quick tour: KMS key rotation demo, RBAC role preview, and a link to compliance evidence pack.

Concise SE scripts (one-liners and short paragraphs)
- For platform engineers: "You can pin model versions and route traffic by latency or cost tiers so your product teams get consistent latency while finance keeps predictable billing."
- For CISO/InfoSec: "We integrate with customer KMS and provide immutable audit logs per request; Private installs run entirely in your VPC and optionally air-gapped environments."
- For Finance: "Our optimizer provides cost-sensitivity controls—scale down quantization for low-risk workloads and reserve Dedicated capacity for high-throughput endpoints to cap spend."

Pricing guidance (heuristic framework)
- Pricing levers to discuss: model class, dedicated capacity vs hosted, latency SLO, caching hit rate, and quantization profile.
- Sample scenarios (illustrative; use the pricing calculator for final quotes):

| Scenario | Model class | Traffic pattern | Key levers | Expected per-10k token cost (est) |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Small chatbot MVP | Llama2-13B quantized | 10 reqs/s bursts | aggressive batching, prefix caching | $1.20 |
| Customer support scale | Llama2-70B trimmed | 50 reqs/s sustained | Dedicated pool, conservative quant | $5.60 |
| Document embeddings | Efficient embed model | batch offline | batch-only, high throughput | $0.08 |

- Pricing talking tips: always include three levers customers can act on immediately (batching, cache, quantization) and show dollarized impact in the demo. Use committed Dedicated capacity to cap unit costs for high-throughput endpoints.

Security FAQ for prospects (top 8 questions)
1) Where are request logs stored and who can access them?
   - Answer: Request logs are stored in the customer’s control plane for Private deployments or in a tenant-isolated storage layer for Hosted; access is RBAC-controlled and recorded in audit logs.
2) How do you handle encryption and key management?
   - Answer: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM; keys are never exported to third parties in Private deployments.
3) Can we run Redwood in a fully air-gapped environment?
   - Answer: Yes — an on-prem package is available with an install guide and cross-checklist.
4) How do you support data residency and retention policies?
   - Answer: Per-route retention settings and legal hold controls are available; we provide exportable evidence for audits.
5) What is your incident notification and SLA for security incidents?
   - Answer: We follow our security incident playbook; affected customers receive email + console notifications within 2 hours and a root-cause summary within 72 hours for P1 security incidents.
6) How are model weights/vulnerable artifacts controlled in Private installs?
   - Answer: Model artifacts are stored in customer-managed artifact stores with provenance metadata; automated checks prevent execution of unsigned artifacts.
7) Do you provide penetration test reports and SOC/compliance evidence?
   - Answer: Yes — we supply SOC2 Type II reports and pen test summaries in the compliance evidence pack; for dedicated/Private customers we provide redacted reports as appropriate.
8) How do you prevent model extraction or prompt-injection leakage?
   - Answer: We recommend a layered approach: response filtering, graduation of quantization for sensitive models, request size and rate limits, and application-layer input validation; we also provide monitoring that detects anomalous query patterns.

Short customer case study (anonymized)
- Customer: "FinScale" (financial SaaS platform, mid-market)
- Problem: Unpredictable inference costs and frequent user-visible latency spikes as demand scaled from 5k to 50k daily queries.
- Solution: Migrated 3 high-volume customer-facing endpoints to Redwood Dedicated, applied prefix caching and conservative quantization profile, and set autoscaling policies with burst capacity.
- Outcome (90 days):
  - 38% reduction in per-token runtime latency (median p50)-> from 230ms to 143ms.
  - 27% reduction in unit inference spend vs their prior cloud endpoint configuration.
  - Zero production incidents during Black Friday-like traffic test.

Objection handling cheat sheet
- "We need to keep everything in-house for compliance." => Offer Private deployment checklist and propose a technical pilot in their lab environment with our SRE support.
- "This is a pricing/ROI conversation." => Use the per-10k demo estimator and propose a 30-day traffic replay pilot to measure delta.
- "Model quality concerns." => Offer traffic-split rollouts and A/B evaluation harness; commit to quality regression alerts tied to their prompt set.

Next steps & pilot template (3-step rapid pilot)
1) Align scope (week 0): Confirm 2 endpoints, traffic replay dataset, and success metrics (latency p50/p95, cost per 10k tokens).
2) Pilot (weeks 1–3): Deploy Redwood in org trial mode or light Private deployment, run traffic replay, and tune batching/cache/quant profiles. Provide daily checkpoint notes.
3) Wrap & decision (week 4): Deliver ROI report, long-term capacity recommendation, and a production rollout checklist.

Owner & contacts
- Playbook owner: Aisha Patel (Go-to-Market)
- Escalation for security questions: Priya Nair (Security & Compliance)
- Technical pilot support: Ethan Brooks (Solutions Engineering)

Related assets & templates

- Pilot onboarding checklist (link: /sales-enablement/pilot-activation-playbook-and-technical-economics-2027)

Revision history

- 2025-11-03: Added demo scripts after SE feedback.
- 2026-01-12: Updated pricing scenarios and security FAQ; moved to in_review.

Appendix: handy CLI snippets and JSON samples

  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H \"Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>\" -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -d '{"model":"redwood-13b-q8", "prompt":"Summarize the invoice", "max_tokens":200}'

- Example rollout policy JSON:
  {
    "routes": [
      {
        "name": "primary-latency",
        "policy": "latency-first",
        "fallbacks": ["cost-saver"]
      }
    ]
  }

End of playbook.

title: SLO-driven automated fallthrough and incident playbook
content:
SLO-driven automated fallthrough and incident playbook

Summary
-------
This document defines an SLO-driven incident response pattern we call the "fallthrough flow": automated detection of SLO boundary crossings, progressive mitigation (automated routing and model fallbacks), and human-run escalation/playbooks where automation cannot resolve the issue. It combines end-to-end runbooks, on-call rotation guidance, game day scenarios, status page and customer communications templates, and a postmortem checklist.

Scope
-----
- Services: model-serving (hosted and dedicated), routing layer, cache services (prefix/KV), and the control plane that performs routing and rollouts.
- Intended for incidents that originate from performance or availability regressions that cause SLO boundary crossings (latency, request error rate, embedding failure rate).
- Not intended for security incidents (see security-and-compliance incident playbooks).

When to apply this playbook
--------------------------
Apply when an automated SLO alert triggers (see SLO table below) or when an on-call detects a customer-impacting degradation. For minor anomalies that do not cross SLOs, follow the local diagnostics flow and file an RCA if recurring.

SLOs and severity mapping
-------------------------
| SLO Category | Target | Alert trigger | Severity |
|--------------|--------|---------------|----------|
| p95 latency (text-gen) | < 300 ms | p95 > 600 ms for 5m | Sev-2 |
| p99 latency (text-gen) | < 900 ms | p99 > 1800 ms for 2m | Sev-1 |
| Request error rate | < 0.5% | 1% sustained for 5m | Sev-1 |
| Embedding failure rate | < 0.2% | 0.5% sustained 10m | Sev-2 |
| Control plane API availability | 99.9% monthly | 5min outage | Sev-1 |

Severity definitions (quick)
- Sev-1: Broad customer impact or production outage (multiple customers/regions failing). Immediate all-hands escalation.
- Sev-2: Significant degradation affecting a subset of customers or elevated error/latency but partial functionality.
- Sev-3: Localized issue, non-critical, triage during office hours.

Automated fallthrough flow (overview)
------------------------------------
1) Detection: SLO alerting triggers via Prometheus/Alertmanager (SLO bridges into Alertmanager rules).
2) Automated mitigation: playbook-runner executes pre-configured actions for the matched service and severity. Typical actions (in order):
   - Activate per-customer model fallback (route to a compatible model variant with lower latency/quantizations).
   - Enable aggressive prefix/KV cache priming for affected route.
   - Apply temporary throttling/burst control to limit new requests (protect downstream).
   - If control-plane unavailable, promote a cached routing policy (local policy file) to avoid dependency calls.
3) Notification: PagerDuty alert to primary on-call, Slack incident channel created, status page incident draft created.
4) Human escalation: If automation resolves within the auto-resolve timeout (default 7 minutes), automation posts a closure note. Otherwise, escalate to Sev-1 runbook.

Automated mitigation examples (commands)
- Promote a fallback model via rcli (Redwood CLI):
  rcli rollout promote --service model-router --from live --to fallback-low-latency --reason "auto-slo-fallthrough"

- Enable KV caching warmup for route:
  rcli cache enable --route /v1/generate --ttl 3600 --mode warmup

- Apply throttling at gateway:
  rcli gateway throttle --route /v1/embeddings --rate 200rps --burst 400

Sev-1 incident runbook: high p99 latency across region
----------------------------------------------------
Immediate actions (first 10 minutes)
1) Acknowledge the alert in PagerDuty and create an incident channel: #incident-<service>-<YYYYMMDD>-<id>.
2) Post the short incident summary to the channel with the SLO breaches and region(s) affected.
3) Run quick health checks (commands):
   - kubectl get pods -n model-serving -l app=model --output wide
   - rcli metrics query --expr "avg_over_time(model_p99_latency[5m])" --service model-serving
   - curl -sS https://status.redwood.example/api/v1/incident-drafts | jq .
4) If automation has already applied fallbacks, confirm fallback status: rcli rollout status --service model-router
5) If error rate also elevated, capture sample failed requests (request ids) and attach to the incident channel.

Diagnostics (5–30 minutes)
- Check resource saturation: nvidia-smi on affected nodes, node CPU/memory, network errors in dmesg.
- Check model runtime logs for OOM, kernel errors, or compilation failures.
- Verify upstream dependencies (S3, control plane, KMS) with synthetic checks.
- If KV cache hit rate dropped, run: rcli cache stats --route /v1/generate

Mitigation options (ordered by risk)
1) Scale up dedicated pool for the model: rcli capacity add --pool model-pool-4x --count 2
2) Reduce model concurrency/sequence length defaults for new requests (config change): update config at /configs/model-serving/runtime.yaml and apply: rcli config apply --file runtime.yaml
3) Rollback to previous model revision: rcli model rollback --service model-serving --to revision-20260201
4) If control-plane dependent routing failing, swap to static routing: rcli routing set-static --service model-router --file static-routes.json

Rollback guidance
- Preconditions: validate that the target revision was healthy (pass smoke tests). Run: rcli model smoke-test --revision revision-20260201 --tests basic-gen,embed
- Rollback steps: 1) Schedule a rolling rollback with canary 10%. 2) Wait 2 minutes, evaluate p95/p99. 3) Ramp to 100% if stable.

Post-incident (within 24–72 hours)
- If automation resolved the incident without human intervention, author must still file a short incident note with cause and what automation did.
- For Sev-1/Sev-2 incidents: file a full postmortem (template below) within 72 hours and declare an owner for action items.
- Runbook update: if an automated action misfired or made the incident worse, immediately add a gated rollback step to the automation and mark the runbook for review.

Runbook: high p99 latency (example)
- Owner: runtime-team@redwood.example
- Primary TLDR: p99 latency > 1800ms across region for 2m. Follow automated fallthrough, then escalate to human if unresolved.
- Dashboard: [Model Serving - Latency] (grafana://dashboards/model-serving-latency)
- Steps:
  1) Confirm SLO and scope.
  2) Execute automated fallthrough (if not already executed).
  3) Capture traces for 5 requests: rcli trace tail --service model-serving --limit 5
  4) If CPU/GPU saturation: add capacity (see mitigation options).
  5) If tracing shows KV cache misses as root cause: warm caches and consider cache policy change.
  6) If third-party dependency (S3, KMS) is slow: engage infra-oncall and consider short-circuiting calls.

On-call rotation and handoff checklist
------------------------------------
- Recommended rotation: primary on-call 7 days, secondary 7 days, SRE duty engineer 1 week; overlap handoff windows of 30 minutes.
- Handoff checklist (to be posted in calendar invite):
  - Current incidents and their status.
  - Outstanding action items and owners.
  - Any scheduled rollouts or canaries in-flight.
  - Paging schedule and escalation policy.
  - Link to rotation roster: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/roster-2026

Game day scenarios and exercises
------------------------------
We run quarterly game days. Scenarios to include:
- Model-wide p99 latency spike caused by new kernel path. Objective: validate fallback automation and rollback steps.
- Control plane API outage simulated for 15 minutes. Objective: validate static routing promotion and degraded-mode behavior.
- Multi-region partial blackout (eg: simulated AZ failure). Objective: validate cross-region routing and customer-safe fallbacks.
- Silent regression: 10% increase in model hallucination rate (quality). Objective: validate quality alerting and rollback to previous model.

Status page and customer communications templates
----------------------------------------------
Status page draft (short form):
- Title: Degraded model-serving latency in us-west-2 - Impact: Some hosted inference requests experience elevated latency or failures.
- Affected Services: Hosted text-generation (model: redwood-llama-13b-quant).
- Start time: 2026-02-10T09:12:00Z
- Next update: 2026-02-10T09:27:00Z
- Mitigation: Automated fallbacks and cache warmups applied. Scaling in progress.

Customer-facing email template (for high-impact incidents):
Subject: Service impact affecting inference latency (region: us-west-2)
Hi <CustomerName>,
We are investigating an incident affecting inference latency in us-west-2 that may impact requests to hosted text-generation models. Our automated mitigation has been applied and we are actively scaling capacity. We will post updates on https://status.redwood.example and notify you as we have a resolution.
If you require assistance or have a critical workload, reply to this email and our customer success team will prioritize you.
Sincerely,
Redwood Inference Support

Slack templates for incident channels
- Initial post (pinned):
  > Summary: p99 latency breach in us-west-2 for model-serving.
  > SLOs: p99 > 1800ms.
  > Immediate actions taken: automated fallback promoted, cache warmup, gateway throttling.
  > Commands to run: rcli rollout status --service model-router
  > Owner: @runtime-oncall

- Ongoing updates: timestamped short notes listing new diagnostics and mitigations. Avoid long paragraphs.

Postmortem template (required for Sev-1/Sev-2)
-----------------------------------------------
- Title:
- Incident ID:
- Status: draft | reviewed | closed
- Timeline (UTC): bullet list with timestamps and short events.
- Impact: systems/customers/regions affected, estimated % of requests impacted.
- Root cause analysis: concise causal chain with evidence.
- Why it wasn't detected earlier: instrumentation gaps.
- Action items: each with owner, due date, risk level.
- Follow-up verification plan: smoke tests, scheduled audit.
- Lessons learned.

Runbook maintenance and governance
--------------------------------
- All runbooks must be reviewed quarterly and after any Sev-1 incident.
- Automation scripts referenced by a runbook must include a canary check and a manual abort flag.
- Ownership: runtime-team owns model-serving runbooks; eng-sre owns oncall rotations and escalation policies.

Appendix A: Example incident log entry (copy into incident channel)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-02-10 09:12:04 UTC] ALERT: p99 latency exceeded threshold in us-west-2 (p99=2.2s). Automation triggered: fallback promoted to fallback-low-latency.
[2026-02-10 09:15:30 UTC] Action: fallback at 100% confirmed; p99 decreased to 980ms.
[2026-02-10 09:35:00 UTC] Action: scaled model pool by 2 instances; p99 stable at 320ms.

Appendix B: Quick reference commands
----------------------------------
- rcli rollout status --service model-router
- rcli model rollback --service model-serving --to <revision>
- rcli cache stats --route /v1/generate
- kubectl logs -n model-serving <pod> --since=10m

Contact matrix (escalation)
--------------------------
- Primary on-call: runtime-oncall@pagerduty (page immediately)
- Secondary on-call: eng-sre@pagerduty
- Incident commander rotation: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/ic-rotation

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-15: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-01-20: Added automated mitigation examples and CLI snippets (reviewers: Ethan Rivera).
- 2026-02-10: Clarified rollback guidance and added game day scenarios (reviewers: Priya Natarajan, Liam O'Connor).

References and related pages
---------------------------
- SLO policy: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-policy-2025
- Runtime runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks
- Routing and control plane playbook: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/routing-playbook

title: Accelerator feature flagging and zero-downtime IaC adapter
content:
Accelerator feature flagging and zero-downtime IaC adapter

A pattern and reusable Terraform adapter that wires runtime accelerator feature flags (kernel/quantization/priority routing) to CI/CD canaries enabling zero-downtime toggles across Dedicated and Private deployments.
Overview

Purpose: provide a standardized, low-risk path to enable or disable accelerator-level features (e.g., mixed-precision kernels, quantized runtime paths, KV-cache prefetching, latency-optimized attention kernels) using feature flags backed by infrastructure as code. This document describes the Terraform adapter pattern, CI gating and rollout procedure, runtime integration points, safety checks, and an on-call runbook for rapid rollback.

Scope and motivation
- Scope: eng-infra Terraform modules, CI/CD pipelines, serving runtime feature gates, and canary rollout runbooks for hosted/dedicated/private environments.
- Motivation: historically enabling kernel-level toggles required manual operator steps, service restarts, or image rollouts. That increases outage risk and long lead times for experiments. The adapter enables:
  - Zero-downtime toggles across fleets by combining runtime dynamic flags with rolling config application.
  - Reproducible IaC for compliance and audit (Terraform-managed flags + versioned state).
  - Safe canary gating in CI that ties to telemetry-based SLO checks before global rollout.

Key concepts and components
1) Feature flag model (infra-first)
- Flag types: runtime-boolean, percent-traffic, config-string, kernel-variant (string).
- Backing store: LaunchDarkly for customer-facing toggles; internal Redis+etcd-backed config-store for infra flags where LaunchDarkly is prohibited (private/onprem).
- Rupture mode: an emergency global off switch owned by Oncall SRE (see runbook).

2) Terraform adapter module (accelerator_feature_flag)
- Purpose: provide a canonical TF module that creates flag metadata, optional provider wiring (launchdarkly flag or k8s ConfigMap + Vault secret), and CI artifact metadata.
- Location: terraform-modules/accelerator_feature_flag
- Interface (module inputs):
  - name (string) - unique flag key, e.g., "runtime.kernel.mixed_precision.v2"
  - description (string)
  - default_state (string) - "enabled" | "disabled"
  - rollout_strategy (string) - "immediate" | "percent" | "canary"
  - canary_targets (list) - list of tenant or node selectors (optional)
  - provider (string) - "launchdarkly" | "k8s_configmap" | "internal_store"
  - owner (string) - pager/team owning the flag
- Outputs:
  - flag_id (string)
  - provider_endpoint (string)
  - ci_gate_metadata (string) - JSON blob used by CI to assert the expected telemetry buckets

3) CI/CD integration patterns
- Pipelines: all feature flag changes must go through a pipeline that:
  1. Validates Terraform plan (tfsec, OPA policies).
  2. Creates a dry-run plan and posts a preview to the PR with expected ci_gate_metadata.
  3. If rollout_strategy == "canary", the pipeline triggers canary gating tasks (see gating checks below).
- Canary orchestration: use Argo workflows step that performs a staged flag enablement:
  - Stage 1: enable flag for internal-eval tenants (5 nodes, 0.1% traffic) for 10 minutes.
  - Stage 2: enable flag for seeded canary tenants (config in canary_targets) for 60 minutes.
  - Stage 3: conditional expand to 10% for 30 minutes, then to 50% pending metrics.
  - Stage 4: full rollout.
- CI gating checks (automated):
  - Latency P50 and P95 delta compared with baseline (reject if P95 increased > 15ms or P95 is > SLO*1.1).
  - Error rate: tokenization or generation errors increased > 0.5% absolute (reject).
  - Cost signal: GPU util per-request significantly increased (reject if average GPU-ms/request > baseline*1.25).
  - Quality signal (optional): eval prompt set regressions >= 2% absolute.

4) Runtime integration
- Serving runtime exposes a stable API to read flags in-process via an SDK (go/java/py) and a hot-reload path for config changes.
- For Private customers where central flag store is unavailable, the module renders a signed config blob into Vault and a node-local agent pulls and hot-applies it.
- Kernel selection example (pseudo-code):
  ```go
  flag := flags.Get("runtime.kernel.mixed_precision.v2")
  if flag.EnabledFor(request.Tenant) {
      executor.UseKernel("mixed_precision_v2")
  } else {
      executor.UseKernel("fp16_fallback")
  }
  ```
- KV-cache/Prefetch toggle: flags must support a "graceful-disable" semantics to drain ongoing sessions before turning off prefetch. The runtime will emit event: "prefetch.drain.started" / "prefetch.drain.completed" to telemetry.

Operational safety and SLOs
- Target SLOs for feature toggles:
  - Canary reaction window: pipeline must evaluate canary metrics within 75% of canary duration (example: 60-min canary -> gate result posted within 45 minutes).
  - Oncall latency blast radius: < 3% of production requests affected for initial canary.
- Telemetry hooks to validate:
  - metric names: inference.latency.p50, inference.latency.p95, inference.errors.tokenize, inference.gpu_ms_per_request, inference.quality.eval_regressions
  - alerting thresholds (examples):
    - inference.latency.p95 > baseline + 15ms -> Pager (severity P2)
    - inference.errors.tokenize > baseline + 0.5% -> Pager (severity P1)

Terraform policy guardrails (examples)
- OPA/Rego snippet (pseudocode): ensure no default_state == "enabled" with rollout_strategy == "immediate" for flags affecting > 10% traffic in production.
- Mandatory review labels: any flag that touches kernel selection must include reviewers: ["eng-serving-runtime", "eng-infra", owner_team].

Rollout and rollback procedure (step-by-step)
1) Author creates a TF change in a branch using accelerator_feature_flag module with rollout_strategy="canary". Include canary_targets.
2) CI runs plan + policy checks and posts PR preview.
3) Merge triggers Argo canary orchestration: Stage 1 -> Stage 2 -> automatic gating.
4) If a gate fails, Argo triggers rollback task: disable flag (or decrease percentage) and emit a rollback ticket into the incident queue.
5) Oncall triage: run the Fault Isolation checklist (see runbook).

Operational runbook (oncall steps for failed canary or emergency)
- Trigger: automated gate failure or customer reported regression correlated to recent flag.
- Immediate actions (within first 5 minutes):
  1. Identify flag_id from CI metadata, PR ID, or tagging in telemetry.
  2. Use the accelerator_feature_flag module outputs (provider_endpoint) to issue an emergency disable:
     - LaunchDarkly: curl -X POST $LD_API/flags/$flag_id/off -H "Authorization: $LD_TOKEN"
     - Internal store: terraform apply with variable force_disable=true (ci-runner account).
  3. Confirm hot-reload events: check service logs for "flag.toggle.received" and "kernel.switch.completed" across 3 representative nodes.
  4. If underlying kernel failed to revert cleanly, follow kernel rollback steps: drain node, restart runtime process, validate health probes.
- Post-incident: create postmortem, capture telemetry slices, and block future immediate rollouts until a retrospective.

Checklist for authors (pre-change)
- Has owner from eng-serving-runtime approved? (required)
- Is rollout_strategy set to canary by default? (required)
- Are canary_targets seeded and reproducible in CI? (recommended)
- Does PR include ci_gate_metadata and expected deltas? (required)

Examples and snippets
1) Terraform usage (example):
```hcl
module "mixed_precision_v2_flag" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/terraform-modules.git//accelerator_feature_flag"
  name = "runtime.kernel.mixed_precision.v2"
  description = "Enable mixed_precision_v2 kernel path for latency experiments"
  default_state = "disabled"
  rollout_strategy = "canary"
  canary_targets = ["canary-tenants/alpha", "node-selector:gpu-type=t4-highmem"]
  provider = "launchdarkly"
  owner = "eng-serving-runtime"
}
```
2) CI gate config (example JSON used by the pipeline):
```json
{
  "flag_id": "runtime.kernel.mixed_precision.v2",
  "expected_deltas": {
    "inference.latency.p95_ms": 10,
    "inference.errors.tokenize_pct": 0.2
  },
  "canary_duration_minutes": 60
}
```

Governance and audit
- All TF changes are captured in the Terraform state and must include a clear change comment. The accelerator_feature_flag module writes an audit annotation (git commit url, PR id, owner).
- Quarterly review: eng-infra and eng-serving-runtime will run a sweep to identify stale flags older than 90 days and recommend removal.

Ownership and contacts
- Module owner: eng-infra (primary: Asha Patel)
- Runtime integration owner: eng-serving-runtime (secondary: Diego Ramos)
- Oncall escalation: SRE Pager rota (page@sre.redwood.ai)

Appendices
A. Example alert queries
- P95 regression query (Prometheus-ish pseudo):
  increase(inference_latency_p95_ms{flag_id="runtime.kernel.mixed_precision.v2"}[30m]) > 15
B. Troubleshooting quick commands
- Check LaunchDarkly flag state: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LD_TOKEN" "https://app.launchdarkly.com/api/v2/flags/$ENV/$flag_id" | jq '.'
