title: Manual traffic shift: Hosted API regional failover (US/EU)
content:
Manual traffic shift: Hosted API regional failover (US/EU)

# Purpose
This runbook describes how to manually shift (fail over) production inference traffic for the Hosted API between regions or clusters during GPU capacity shortages, elevated error rates, or regional degradation.

# Scope
- Applies to: chat + embeddings endpoints served by Redwood API (Hosted).
- Not for: Redwood Dedicated customer-specific pools (see dedicated incident playbooks).

# Triggers (choose one)
- Sustained 5xx > 1% for 10+ minutes in a region
- p95 latency > 2x baseline for 15+ minutes with correlated GPU saturation
- GPU capacity deficit (queue depth increasing; admission control engaged)
- Cloud provider incident impacting a region

# Preconditions
- Incident declared or oncall lead approval
- Status page draft ready (if customer-visible)
- Confirm target region has headroom (GPU free capacity + router capacity)

# Definitions
- "Traffic shift": changing routing weights so new requests land in a different region/cluster
- "Failover": shift to secondary region and disable new traffic to primary

# Procedure (regional traffic shift)
1) Confirm situation
   - Check dashboards: Hosted API error rate, p95 latency, queue depth, GPU utilization
   - Confirm whether issue is model-specific or region-wide

2) Choose target
   - Preferred: same cloud + secondary region (us-west -> us-east; eu-west -> eu-central)
   - If capacity constrained, pick the region with the most available GPU pool headroom

3) Prepare routing override
   - Open the routing override doc: confluence://eng-platform/router-policy-manual-traffic-shift
   - Identify the "hosted-api-prod" policy and the route group for the impacted endpoint(s)

4) Shift traffic gradually
   - Start with 20% weight to target region for new requests
   - Observe for 5–10 minutes: errors, latency, saturation in target
   - Increase to 50%, then 80% if stable

5) Full failover (if needed)
   - Set impacted region weight to 0% for new requests
   - Keep existing in-flight streams running when possible
   - Confirm rate limiting thresholds in target region are compatible

6) Verification
   - Confirm overall system p95 recovers within 15 minutes
   - Confirm token throughput is stable and no sustained 429 spikes
   - Confirm new incidents are not triggered in the target region

7) Rollback
   - Reverse weights in 20% increments
   - If rollback causes immediate degradation, pause and reassess capacity

# Cluster-level alternative
If the issue is isolated to a single cluster (not whole region), use the infra drain + handoff procedure first: confluence://eng-infra/gpu-cluster-drain-and-traffic-shift-handoff

# Communication
- Use the oncall checklist: confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/initiating-regional-traffic-shift-checklist
- Post updates in #incidents and #eng-sre

# Common pitfalls
- Shifting traffic without confirming tokenizer/model compatibility across regions
- Over-shifting too quickly and saturating the target region
- Forgetting to remove overrides after the incident

# Owners
- Primary: Eng SRE
- Routing changes: Eng Platform (Router/Policy)
- Capacity: Eng Infra (GPU fleet)

title: Developer consumption sizing and packaging playbook
content:
Developer consumption sizing and packaging playbook

Overview
--------
This playbook describes recommended approaches to size consumption estimates and package offerings for developer-focused customers using Redwood Inference. It translates observed developer behavior, common integration patterns, and cost/SLO tradeoffs into actionable pricing and packaging guidance for product managers and pricing analysts.

Goals
- Reduce ambiguity for self-serve customers when selecting a package.
- Align packaging units with developer mental models (requests, tokens, embeddings, features).
- Provide reproducible hand-off artifacts for finance and sales engineering.

Intended audience
- Product managers (pricing/packaging)
- Growth and go-to-market engineers
- Solutions engineering and customer success
- Finance and billing engineers

When to use this playbook
- New feature launches (e.g., streaming, fidelity tiers) where consumption patterns are unknown.
- Designing a self-serve bundle or a trial credit allocation.
- Responding to recurring support requests about how to estimate bills.

Key concepts and units
- Token unit: per 1,000 output tokens normalized to a baseline model (e.g., rdx-base-v1).
- Request unit: a single API call for generation/chat, regardless of streaming vs non-streaming; large responses are token-weighted.
- Embedding unit: per 1,024 vector-ops (rounded up).
- Feature flags: premium features (function calling, structured outputs, high-fidelity variants) are metered separately.

High-level sizing flow (quick):
1) Select representative workload (sample prompts, average length, concurrency).
2) Measure per-request token and latency distribution with the developer sandbox.
3) Map to candidate package units (token buckets, request bursts, embedding quotas).
4) Simulate monthly cost under three scenarios: conservative, expected, aggressive.
5) Pick price points and guardrails (rate limits, overage rates, feature throttles).

Detailed steps and templates
----------------------------
1) Choose workload archetype
- Reference archetypes: conversational-agent, document-search, summarization-batch, realtime-autocomplete.
- Template to capture workload:
  - Example payloads (3–5 representative prompts)
  - Desired P95 latency target and required fidelity (e.g., hallucination tolerance)
  - Expected concurrency (sessions per minute)

2) Local measurement (developer sandbox)
- Use Redwood local sandbox or hosted free tier to run the workload for 10k synthetic requests.
- Capture: tokens_in, tokens_out, total_tokens, API_time_ms, streaming_fraction.
- CLI example:
  rdx-bench --model rdx-base-v1 --prompt-file ./sample-prompts.json --requests 10000 --concurrency 16 --out telemetry.json
- Required telemetry columns: request_id, start_ts, end_ts, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, status_code, variant_used

3) Normalize to monthly consumption
- Convert per-request metrics to monthly:
  monthly_tokens = average_total_tokens * projected_monthly_requests
  monthly_requests = projected_monthly_requests
- Include 95th-percentile burst multiplier (default 2x) to provision burst allowance.

4) Pricing candidate generation
- Packaging options to consider (choose 1–2 primary):
  A. Token-bucket subscription + overage per 1k tokens.
  B. Request-bundle (N requests/month) + token soft-cap with throttles.
  C. Feature add-ons (embeddings, streaming, high-fidelity variants) priced per-unit.

5) Simulate cost scenarios (table)
- Create a three-scenario table (samples provided below).

| Scenario | Monthly requests | Avg total tokens/request | Monthly tokens | Recommended package | Expected bill (USD) | Notes |
|---------:|-----------------:|------------------------:|---------------:|---------------------|-------------------:|-------|
| Conservative | 10,000 | 120 | 1,200,000 | Starter: 1.5M tokens @ $5 per 1k = +embeddings 200K @ $0.20 | $6,400 | good for small teams |
| Expected | 100,000 | 240 | 24,000,000 | Growth: 25M tokens + 50k embeddings + streaming flag | $96,000 | requires burst allowance |
| Aggressive | 500,000 | 300 | 150,000,000 | Enterprise: custom reserved quota, dedicated latency contract | $480,000 | recommend Dedicated evaluation |
Note: the dollar figures above are illustrative. Replace with current list prices and reserved discount schedules from finance table (link below).

Guardrails and feature boundaries
- Rate limits: set per-tenant RPS and per-route token rate. Typical defaults: 10 RPS, 5k tokens/s peak for Growth bundle.
- Overage behavior: auto-throttle at soft-cap + email warnings at 80% consumption; overage charging at 1.5x list per-1k token rate.
- Feature gating: streaming and function-calling are off in Starter; available as add-ons for Growth; included in Enterprise.

Billing & metering artifacts (required deliverables)
- Billing spec: CSV row format submitted to billing pipeline with fields: customer_id, billing_period_start, billing_period_end, unit_type, units_consumed, list_price_per_unit, discount_code, net_amount.
- Metering window: UTC monthly (first-of-month to last-of-month).
- Audit log: keep per-request metering for 12 months for disputes.

Packaging playbook decisions (decision matrix)
- Use this matrix to pick packaging approach quickly:
  - Developer-first UX: prefer token-buckets with small starter buckets and clear overage rates.
  - High latency-sensitive workloads: emphasize request-bundle or reserved throughput (Dedicated).
  - Embedding-heavy customers: quantify vector-ops, offer embedding top-ups.

Operational runbook for new package launch
1) Phase 0 — Experiment (2 weeks)
   - Create lab tenant with telemetry capture and synthetic traffic.
   - Publish internal pricing teaser and update sandbox UI.
2) Phase 1 — Soft-launch to selected orgs (4 weeks)
   - Invite 10–15 beta orgs. Monitor consumption, errors, and refunds.
   - Weekly sync with CS and Sales Engineering.
3) Phase 2 — Public launch
   - Enable packaging in Console, update pricing pages, and send email campaigns.
   - 24/7 on-call for first 72 hours for consumption disputes.

Migration path recommendations
- From free-tier -> Starter: auto-suggest when 7-day consumption > 100k tokens; offer trial credit equal to 20% of projected first month.
- From Starter -> Growth: recommend when sustained 30-day average > 60% of bucket for 10 days.
- From Growth -> Enterprise: engagement trigger when expected monthly bill > $50k or latency SLO violations > 2 events/month.

Telemetry & KPIs to track post-launch
- Conversion funnel: sandbox -> paid trial -> paid customer.
- ARPU by archetype (conversational vs batch).
- Churn by overage frequency.
- Disputes per 10k billing events.
- SLO compliance: percentage of requests meeting P95 latency objective per-plan.

Example JSON policy snippets (Console & API configs)
- Sample plan definition used in billing pipeline:
{
  "plan_id": "growth_v2",
  "unit": "token_1k",
  "monthly_quota": "25000000",
  "overage_rate_usd_per_1k": "7.50",
  "features": ["streaming", "high_fidelity_variants"]
}

- Rate limit config example (YAML):
rate_limits:
  - plan: starter
    rps: 10
    token_rate_per_sec: 1000
    burst_multiplier: 1.5

Implementation notes and owners
- Product: define archetype mapping and pricing thresholds (owner: Maya Chen).
- Finance: validate list prices, reserved discounts, and billing CSV contract (owner: Priya Patel).
- Engineering: expose metering API for real-time usage; ensure per-request IDs in logs (owner: Diego Martinez).
- CS/SE: author typical migration email templates and implementation guides (owner: Claire Nguyen).

Open questions (to resolve before GA)
- What is the canonical token-normalization baseline model we should use for pricing (rdx-base-v1 vs rdx-compact-v2)?
- Over what time window should we allow one-time free overages before billing begins?
- Should streaming responses count as full-completion tokens or be billed by bytes/token-delta?

Appendix: pricing reference links and artifacts
- Finance list price canonical table: /internal/finance/pricing-master-table (link)
- Sandbox workload templates: /internal/devtools/sandbox/workloads/developer-onboarding (link)
- Billing schema and CSV spec: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/billing-csv-spec-2026 (link)

Revision history
- 2026-11-30: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-12-18: Added sample billing CSV fields (reviewer Priya Patel).
- 2027-01-12: Finalized launch runbook and owners (published).

Contact
- Primary owner: Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.com)
- Finance: Priya Patel (priya.patel@redwood.com)
- Engineering metering lead: Diego Martinez (diego.martinez@redwood.com)

title: Service boundary evaluation and quantization migration checklist
content:
Service boundary evaluation and quantization migration checklist

Overview

This checklist defines the cross-functional operational playbook for evaluating service boundaries and migrating model serving from floating-point artifacts to quantized artifacts (8-bit, 4-bit, mixed) with minimal user-facing regression risk. The goal is to ensure predictable latency/cost improvements while preserving quality and observability contracts. This document ties together: eval-harness checks, prompt and benchmark selection, model onboarding gates, quality guardrails, quantization profile validation, and regression triage steps.

Scope

- Applies to any model promotion that changes runtime numeric representation (FP16/FP32 -> INT8/PACT/4-bit) for production endpoints (hosted, dedicated, or private).
- Includes single-model migrations and model-variant rollouts where a quantized variant will be routed by policy.
- Excludes research-only artifacts and offline-only embeddings refreshes.

Primary owners and contacts

- Service owner: Priya Natarajan (ML Infra / Applied ML) - priya@redwood.example.com
- SRE/Performance owner: Jamal Carter - jamal@redwood.example.com
- Evaluation lead: Ethan Miller - ethan@redwood.example.com

Priorities and acceptance criteria (summary)

- Safety/Quality: Zero critical semantic regressions on production prompt families; no increase in severity-1 (S1) safety sentinels.
- Latency: P95 token generation latency should not exceed baseline by more than 10% under nominal load.
- Cost: Expected per-token cost reduction (est. 20–60%) must be validated in a 24h shadow run.
- Observability: Traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and eval-sentinels must be active and firing against baseline slices.

Pre-migration checklist (must be satisfied before building quant artifacts)

1) Workload and boundary analysis
   - Identify the service boundary (API route/model key) and all downstream consumers.
   - Produce a baseline workload fingerprint: token length distribution, function-calls ratio, streaming vs batch, cold start rate.
   - Tag the route with a migration candidate label in the config catalog.

2) Prompt & benchmark selection
   - Select a representative probe set (recommended 5k–20k probes) split across: high-traffic slices, safety-sensitive prompts, long-context prompts, multi-turn threads, and rare edgecases.
   - For each probe include: canonical prompt, expected anchor tokens, pass/fail sentinel, and a golden response reference where applicable.

3) Eval harness configuration
   - Configure a dedicated eval job with: deterministic seeds, temperature and max_tokens matching production, and tokenization parity checks.
   - Enable both delta-metrics and qualitative human review queues for slices with >X% regression (X default 5%).

Quant profiling & artifact build checklist

- Quant profile selection: list candidate quant profiles (per-layer or per-kernel) and annotate tradeoffs. Example table: 

  | Candidate | Precision | Notes | Expected cost delta | Owner |
  |-----------|-----------|-------|---------------------|-------|
  | qp-int8   | 8-bit     | Default per-tensor symmetric | -40% | infra-quant |
  | qp-4bit   | 4-bit     | Aggressive, requires KV-cache tuning | -60% | infra-quant |
  | mixed-8-4 | hybrid    | FP16 for attention, 4-bit for FFN | -50% | infra-quant |

- Locally validate tensor parity (per-layer L2 and activation distribution checks) and record artifacts in the quant-catalog location.
- Attach quant metadata to model manifest: quant_profile_id, sample-seed, compressor-version, and build-recipe id.

Shadow/validation stage (golden path)

1) Shadow run (no traffic impact):
   - Run the quantized model in shadow for 24–72 hours against live traffic sampling (recommended 2–10% traffic sample).
   - Capture the following telemetry for both baseline and quantized variant: token-level latency (p50/p95/p99), response-stability-index (RSI), embedding cosine drift on embedding routes, safety sentinel hit-rate, and cost per token.

2) Quality gating using eval harness:
   - Delta metrics to compute: exact-match rate, semantic-similarity delta (BERTScore or proprietary similarity), hallucination proxy (unexpected-entity-rate), and RSI.
   - Gate criteria (default):
     * semantic-similarity delta <= 2.5 absolute points on production slices
     * RSI drop <= 0.03
     * Safety sentinel rate not increased by more than 0.1x absolute
     * Latency p95 regression <= 10%

3) Human-in-the-loop review
   - For slices failing any gate, auto-queue for annotator triage with a sample size of 200 examples or until 95% confidence is reached.

Canary rollout and progressive promotion

1) Micro-canary (1–2% traffic) for 2–4 hours
   - Route a small percentage of traffic via routing policy to quantized variant. Monitor SLOs and quality-sentinels.

2) Macro-canary (5–15% traffic) for 24 hours
   - Increase traffic and run full pipeline (eval harness repeat on live samples + human review of failure samples).

3) Gradual promotion (increments of 10–20% every 12–24h)
   - Stop and roll back if: any S1 sentinels are triggered, semantic-similarity delta exceeds threshold, or latency p95 increases beyond escalation threshold.

Rollback criteria and emergency process

- Immediately rollback if any of the following occur: S1 safety sentinel, customer-facing error-rate > 0.5% absolute increase, or unresolvable semantic regressions on a critical slice.
- Triage steps in rollback event:
  1) Capture failing request IDs and attach full traces + model-side logs.
  2) Run targeted eval-harness replay of failing probes across baseline and candidate quant-artifact.
  3) If root cause is quantization, escalate to infra-quant and model-onboarding owners; prepare hot-fix (less aggressive quant profile or mixed-precision fallback).

Regression triage quickplay (for triage teams)

- Initial assessment (first 30 minutes):
  * Confirm whether regression is reproducible on the eval-harness using the failing probe set.
  * Check KV-cache alignment and tokenization parity for the failing requests.

- Bisect matrix:
  * Axis 1: quant_profile (int8, 4bit, mixed)
  * Axis 2: sequence length bucket (short/medium/long)
  * Axis 3: temperature/decoding settings
  Run a batched grid to isolate when the failure appears.

- Rapid mitigation patterns:
  1) Route failing slices to baseline float model via routing policy.
  2) Enable per-route quant-fallback setting (prefer mixed-precision) for affected model key.
  3) Open a regression incident with title prefixed: [REGRESSION][quant] <service-route> and assign to infra-quant.

Operational dashboards and alerts (minimum required)

- Dashboards:
  * Migration overview: traffic split, P50/P95 latency baseline vs quant, cost per token, safety sentinel delta, RSI trend.
  * Slice heatmap: top 20 slices by volume and quality delta.

- Alerts (recommended thresholds):
  * Quality delta alert: semantic-similarity delta > 2.5 points (severity P2)
  * Safety sentinel increase: absolute increase > 0.1% (severity P1)
  * Latency regression: p95 > baseline * 1.10 (severity P2)
  * Unexpected error-rate: > 0.5% absolute (severity P1)

Post-promotion verification and documentation

- Run a 7-day monitored window where weekly aggregated metrics are reviewed by the service owner and evaluation lead.
- Update model manifest and production catalog with final quant_profile, effective date, and observed cost savings.
- Publish a short post-mortem or migration summary including: decision rationale, measured deltas, any rollback incidents, and recommended next steps for future migrations.

Appendix: example commands and snippets

- Eval harness run (example):
  > ./eval-harness run --manifest manifests/service-xyz.json --probes probes/service-xyz/production-probes.json --seed 42 --compare-to baseline-artifact-id

- Example routing policy (YAML excerpt):

  route: /v1/generate/service-xyz
  variants:
    - id: baseline-fp16
      weight: 80
    - id: quant-qp-int8
      weight: 20
  fallback_policy: route-to-baseline-on-sentinel

- Example quick-check JSON for similarity metric: 
  {
    "probe_id": "12345",
    "baseline_embedding_cos": 0.9234,
    "quant_embedding_cos": 0.8952,
    "similarity_delta": -0.0282
  }

Related policies and references

- See the quantization profile library for approved profiles and binary provenance.
- Follow the eval-harness seeding and determinism rules when building comparison runs.
- Use the regression-triage incident template when opening incidents for production regressions.

Notes and future work

- Next iteration: automate quant-profile A/B scoring via the eval-harness and integrate with rollout policy to support automated gradual promotion when deltas remain within a conservative band.
- Investigate more robust embedding-drift alarms that map directly to downstream retrieval quality impact.

title: SLO-driven fidelity onboarding checklist and playbook
content:
SLO-driven fidelity onboarding checklist and playbook

Overview

This document is a pragmatic playbook for onboarding customers onto SLO-driven fidelity tiers. It describes the mapping between customer SLOs (latency, availability, correctness), recommended fidelity tiers, required telemetry, operational checks, and a step-by-step checklist for commercial and technical leads. Use this when contracting customers for dedicated or private deployments and when migrating high-usage tenants from hosted to dedicated environments.

Audience

- Product managers and solutions engineering
- Customer success and account teams
- Platform and runtime engineers (serving, routing, telemetry)

Goals

1. Provide a repeatable alignment process that converts customer SLAs into recommended fidelity packages.
2. Ensure operational readiness (telemetry, runbooks, rollback) before committing to a fidelity onboarding date.
3. Minimize regressions in perceived quality while keeping unit cost under the negotiated budget.

Principles

- SLOs lead decisioning: fidelity (quantization, model variant, batching) should be chosen to meet the agreed SLO window, not vice versa.
- Measure before change: collect 7 days of representative telemetry prior to finalizing package.
- Guardrails: automated quality checks (sample prompts) must pass before enabling lower-cost fidelity modes.

SLO -> Fidelity mapping (reference matrix)

| Customer SLO Profile | Latency target (P95) | Availability target | Recommended Fidelity Tier | Typical Runtime Configs | Cost impact estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| Ultra-low latency | <= 80ms | 99.99% | High-fidelity stream (A) | no quantization, 8-bit cache warm, aggressive prefetch | +40% unit cost |
| Low-latency transactional | <= 200ms | 99.9% | Balanced fidelity (B) | int8 quant, prefix caching, small batching | +10% unit cost |
| Throughput-first | <= 500ms | 99.5% | Cost-optimized (C) | int8+gptq, larger batching, cold-kv eviction | -35% unit cost |
| Cost-minimum | > 500ms acceptable | 99.0% | Minimal fidelity (D) | heavy quant, lower-context-length, opportunistic caching | -60% unit cost |

Notes: numbers are starting guidelines; individual customer workloads may shift mapping. The product team maintains the fidelity definitions in the model catalog (redwood-console: /catalog/fidelity-defs).

Telemetry and validation signals required

Collect the following at 1m aggregation for a 7–14 day window before and after rollout: 

- redwood-serving: request P50/P95/P99 latency, tokens generated, request size
- redwood-routing: route fallback count, capacity-mismatch events
- console-telemetry: end-to-end success rate, sample response diffs (automated eval capture)
- optimize-advisor: estimated cost per 1k tokens and suggested batch sizes

Quality validation: run a prompt-set (100–500 canonical prompts covering critical intents) through both baseline and candidate fidelity. Required thresholds:

- Semantic delta (automated embedding-based): cosine difference <= 0.06 average
- Task accuracy (when labeled golden outputs exist): delta <= 3% absolute drop
- Regression exceptions: zero critical hallucination rate increases for safety prompts

Operational checklist (numbered)

1. Legal / Commercial alignment
   - Confirm target SLOs, billing model (usage vs reserved), and trial period.
   - Document commitments in CD/contract appendix: include fallback and rollback terms.

2. Pre-rollout telemetry collection (7–14 days)
   - Enable sampling via redwood-routing debug flags: curl -X POST https://console.internal/api/telemetry/sampling -d '{"tenant":"TENANT_ID","rate":0.05}'
   - Ensure optimize-advisor has run the cost scan and attached recommended config.

3. Baseline quality sweep
   - Run canonical prompt-set through current production variant and store golden outputs.
   - Run the same set through candidate fidelity variants using the eval harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness).
   - Produce delta report and sign-off by owner (Product + SRE).

4. Staging rollout and smoke tests
   - Deploy candidate fidelity to a staging pool (redwood-serving/stage-pool).
   - Run 10% of production traffic (traffic-shadowing) for 48 hours.
   - Monitor: P95 latency, error rate, fallback events, and sample diff.

5. Canary and phased ramp (if staging passes)
   - Canary: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% (6–12 hour steps) with automated gates:
     - Gate A: P95 latency within agreed window and error increase < 0.02%
     - Gate B: Semantic delta and labeled accuracy within thresholds
   - Use routing policy: policy=route-by-slo, fallback=previous-variant for N failures.

6. Full transition and billing switchover
   - Coordinate with billing: change tenant plan effective time, toggle metering flags.
   - Post-rollout: retain double telemetry for 72 hours (baseline + new).

7. Rollback plan
   - Immediate rollback if any critical gate fails for >30 minutes.
   - Execute: traffic reassign via redwood-routing: POST /v1/routing/assign {"tenant":"TENANT_ID","variant":"baseline"} and notify stakeholders.

Required configs and templates (table)

| Template name | Location | Purpose | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| fidelity-profile.json | /catalog/fidelity-defs | Defines quant, batch, cache settings | eng-serving-runtime |
| onboarding-checklist.md | /playbooks/onboarding | Customer-facing checklist | customer-success |
| sampling-config | redwood-routing flags | Telemetry sampling for pre-rollout | eng-platform |

Example fidelity-profile.json (excerpt)

```
{
  "name": "balanced-B",
  "quantization": "int8",
  "max_batch_tokens": 2048,
  "kv_cache_policy": "warm-eligible",
  "fallback_variant": "high-fidelity-A"
}
```

Ownership and contacts

- Product owner: Priya Natarajan (product) — overall decision authority
- Runtime owner: Eng-serving-runtime oncall channel (#eng-runtime)
- SRE: contact SRE rotations via oncall-and-incident-response/rota
- Customer success: Account lead and Solutions Engineer (entry in customer record)

Rollout timeline example (4 week plan)

Week 0: Contract sign, sample telemetry enabled
Week 1: Telemetry collection and baseline sweep
Week 2: Staging rollout and smoke tests
Week 3: Canary and phased ramp to 50%
Week 4: Complete transition, billing switchover, 14-day monitoring window

Success metrics and postmortem triggers

Track these for 30 days post-transition:
- SLA compliance: target > 99% of 1-minute windows meeting SLO
- Cost delta: within +/-10% of pre-agreed estimate; product must approve >10% variance
- Quality regressions: any labeled intent accuracy drop >3% triggers a triage
- Customer reported incidents: >1 Sev2 within 7 days triggers formal review

Common edge cases and mitigations

- Burst traffic causing cache thrash: enable conservative kv_cache_policy and increase warm-eligible thresholds.
- Model variant availability shortage: use policy route-by-cost to redirect to alternate region or lower-fidelity variant with explicit consent.
- Regulated workloads: use private deployment checklist (eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library) with encryption key rotation step.

Appendix: Sample sign-off rubric

- Product sign-off: quality delta within thresholds, commercial terms documented
- SRE sign-off: staging smoke tests passed, runbooks updated, oncall briefed
- CS sign-off: customer acceptance test plan executed and customer approves sample outputs

Related pages

- /product-docs/requirements/prd-fidelity-decision-service-and-sdk-2028-04-11
- /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/fidelity-benchmarks-2029-05-10

FAQ

Q: What if customer requests a lower cost than mapping suggests?
A: Offer a staged fidelity reduction with short-term trial and stronger telemetry + rollback windows. Require explicit customer acknowledgment of potential minor regressions.

Q: How do we bill during a canary?
A: Billing remains on baseline until commercial switchover; usage during canary is meta-tagged for reconciliation.

Document maintenance

- Owner: product (Priya Natarajan). Review cadence: quarterly or after any fidelity product release.

End of document

title: Quickstart (2026) Origami hero + step accordion assets (compact quickstart)
content:
Quickstart (2026) Origami hero + step accordion assets (compact quickstart)

h1. Overview
This page documents the final design spec and handoff package for the compact “Origami” hero and paired step accordion pattern used on the Quickstart landing page.

The hero is a space-efficient layout that communicates Redwood Inference’s core value (fast, predictable inference) using a kinetic fold/expand motif. The step accordion provides accessible, keyboard-friendly step-by-step onboarding.

h1. Scope and goals
*Primary goals*
* Reduce above-the-fold height on enterprise consoles where vertical real estate is constrained.
* Communicate “predictable latency” and “fast time-to-first-inference” with a compact, animated visual.
* Provide an onboarding pattern (accordion) that is accessible by default and robust on small screens.

*Out of scope*
* Copywriting beyond final hero headline/subhead and CTA labels (handled by PM/content).
* Net-new onboarding steps content (steps are examples; engineering owns final step content).

h1. Final decisions (updates vs earlier drafts)
* Motion delivery: We are *not shipping Lottie* for the hero. The final spec uses *CSS transforms + opacity* only (engineering preference to minimize JS-driven animation and reduce bundle risk).
* Keyboard shortcut: The optional “press k to jump to steps” enhancement was *removed* to avoid conflicts with existing console shortcuts. Navigation relies on standard focus order and in-page anchor only.
* Accordion animation: Mobile reflow issues observed during spike were resolved by switching to a Web Animations API approach that measures content height once on expand (with a fallback to max-height transition). This reduces layout thrash on narrow screens.
* Performance budget: Hero micro-animations must remain under a *40ms* jank budget on the standard Dedicated demo machine profile (updated from 50ms after perf pass).

h1. Deliverables
h2. Figma
* High-fidelity frames for desktop/tablet/mobile.
* Export-ready artboards with tokens, spacing guides, and component notes.
* Component variants:
** Hero: default, hover CTA, reduced motion.
** Accordion: collapsed, expanding, expanded, error state (timeout), loading/skeleton.

h2. Assets
* SVG/PNG export set for:
** Release notes and marketing snippets (light and dark backgrounds).
** Docs screenshot masters (2x exports for retina).
* Annotated screenshot masters for Docs/Console.

h2. Motion spec
* Documented motion behavior:
** Triggers: initial load (one-time), hover/focus on hero CTA (subtle), accordion expand/collapse.
** Easing: standard “decelerate” for expand; “accelerate” for collapse.
** Durations:
*** Hero fold accent: 160–220ms (staggered), opacity 120ms.
*** Accordion expand: 200–260ms; collapse 160–220ms.
* Reduced motion: if prefers-reduced-motion is set, hero accent becomes static and accordion uses instant state changes (no animated height).

h1. Acceptance criteria (final)
1. Hero compositions (desktop/tablet/mobile) approved by PM and engineering with final copy and CTAs.
2. Figma frames contain export-ready artboards with component tokens and spacing guide.
3. Step accordion states (collapsed, expanding, expanded, error) include screen reader annotations and keyboard interaction notes.
4. Screenshot masters for Docs and Console match pixel guidelines and include 2x exports for retina.
5. Motion spec documented (duration/easing/triggers) and validated by frontend on staging implementation.
6. Performance check: hero animation does not exceed the 40ms jank budget on the standard Dedicated demo machine profile.
7. All assets uploaded to the release folder and linked from the engineering PR; final sign-off by Design Lead and PM.

h1. Implementation notes for engineering
h2. Responsive layout
* Breakpoints: use Console standard breakpoints (mobile ≤ 480, tablet 481–768, desktop ≥ 769).
* Hero height target: keep primary content + CTA visible without scrolling on 768px-tall viewports.
* Avoid layout shift: reserve hero illustration space with a fixed aspect-ratio container.

h2. Accordion interaction
* Header row is a button element.
* aria-expanded toggles with state.
* aria-controls references the region ID.
* Focus ring must be visible and meet contrast requirements.
* Support keyboard:
** Tab/Shift+Tab: normal navigation
** Enter/Space: toggle current item
** Up/Down arrows: move between accordion headers (optional but recommended)

h2. Error state
* If step content cannot load within 6s, show error state with:
** Short message
** Retry action
** Link to troubleshooting docs (if available)

h1. Accessibility requirements
* Color contrast:
** Body text meets 4.5:1
** Focus indicators meet 3:1 against adjacent colors
* Reduced motion support (see Motion spec).
* Screen reader notes:
** The accordion region must announce expanded/collapsed state changes.
** Ensure the hero decorative fold accents are aria-hidden.

h1. Screenshot capture runbook (QA + Docs)
h2. Naming convention
* quickstart-hero-[theme]-[breakpoint]-v2026-04.png
* quickstart-accordion-[state]-[theme]-[breakpoint]-v2026-04.png

h2. Capture guidelines
1. Use deterministic content:
* Use mocked API responses or seeded demo org to avoid flakiness in Docs screenshots.
2. Set viewport sizes:
* Desktop: 1440x900
* Tablet: 768x1024
* Mobile: 390x844
3. Use 2x export for retina.
4. Verify theme variants (light/dark) and ensure the CTA focus ring is visible.

h1. Handoff checklist
* [Design] Final Figma link includes:
** components + tokens
** annotations
** export settings
* [Design] Assets exported (SVG/PNG) and uploaded to the release folder.
* [Eng] Staging build validated for:
** responsive layout
** reduced motion
** keyboard navigation
** screen reader announcements
** performance (no visible jank)
* [PM] Copy and CTA labels approved.

h1. Timeline and release
* Intended release train: console-2026.04 (moved from console-2026.03 due to QA window and token parity checks).
* Final asset freeze: 2026-03-18.
* Doc last verified on staging: 2026-03-20.

h1. Change log
* 2026-02-26 — Kickoff: scoped minimal viable hero + accordion pattern. Prioritized space efficiency for enterprise consoles. (Avery Chen)
* 2026-03-02 — Internal critique: concept B (origami fold) selected; tightened type scale and increased CTA contrast. (Design)
* 2026-03-05 — Motion prototype validated; guidance to avoid JS-heavy animation. (Miguel Ortega)
* 2026-03-07 — Accessibility pass: updated tokens to meet contrast; added aria-expanded + focus ring notes; removed shortcut proposal later. (Priya Singh)
* 2026-03-10 — Engineering spike: resolved mobile reflow by changing accordion animation strategy. (Miguel Ortega)
* 2026-03-12 — PM review: subhead updated to emphasize predictable latency. (Elena Martens)
* 2026-03-21 — Final: removed Lottie deliverable, confirmed reduced-motion behavior, updated perf budget to 40ms, and published release-2026.04 asset set. (Avery Chen)

h1. Owners
* Design: Priya Singh (assignee), Avery Chen (author)
* Engineering: Miguel Ortega
* Product: Elena Martens

title: oncall-rotation-onboarding-and-slo-ownership-runbook-2024
content:
oncall-rotation-onboarding-and-slo-ownership-runbook-2024

Overview:
This runbook describes the standard onboarding flow for engineers joining the SRE on-call rotation and the concrete handoff for SLO ownership and error-budget stewardship. It is written for new rotation members, rotation leads, and managers who need a repeatable checklist to verify readiness to carry SLO responsibilities in production.

Purpose:
- Ensure consistent knowledge transfer for SREs joining or re-joining rotation.
- Reduce time-to-first-independent-incident-handling while protecting customer-facing SLOs.
- Establish a clear sign-off process for SLO ownership and capacity remediation privileges.

Scope:
Applies to: core inference platform services (api-gateway, runtime-router, kv-cache, model-host-pool) and SREs who will be primary or secondary on-call. Does NOT replace service-specific runbooks — those remain authoritative for service-level troubleshooting.

Definitions:
- SLO owner: rotation engineer accountable for monitoring, first-response and initiating mitigation for a target SLO.
- Error budget: rolling 30-day percentage (or per-SLO window) of allowable user-impacting failures.

Before you start (prerequisites):
- GitHub access: read/write to infra/playbooks repo.
- Confluence access to eng-sre space and product SLO matrix.
- PagerDuty and Slack access; add yourself to #sre-oncall and service channels.
- Complete the mandatory SRE training module: "SLO Fundamentals and Incident Triage" in LMS.
- Local dev cluster credentials and sandbox project (for safe drill exercises).

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step):
1) Orientation (Day 0–1)
   - Read the SLO matrix: open the SLO dashboard and export the list for your service(s). Verify thresholds for: p50, p95, p99 latency, availability, and correctness metrics used by product.
   - Join recurring oncall handover: attend next rotation change and shadow the outgoing oncall.

2) Tooling and alerts (Day 1–3)
   - Subscribe to alerts: PagerDuty, OpsGenie (fallback), and Slack alert bridge.
   - Verify alert routing: confirm that critical SLO alerts escalate to your primary channel and that low-severity alerts are rate-limited.
   - Walkthrough the telemetry queries:
     - Example PromQL (tail-latency):
       sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime-router\",le=\\\"0.5\\\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{job=\"runtime-router\"}[5m]))
     - Example traces: open the trace link pattern: https://jaeger.company.local/trace/{{trace_id}}

3) Read and rehearse runbooks (Day 2–4)
   - Read core runbooks: SLO rollback, capacity hedge, model-hotpatch, and circuit-breaker reset.
   - Run a table-top drill: simulate a p95 latency spike caused by a KV cache miss storm. Walk through mitigation steps (enable short-circuit cache warm, apply tiered throttles). Document decisions.

4) Capacity and provisioning basics (Day 3–6)
   - Review capacity model: headroom policy, burst pools, and preemption rules for spot instances.
   - Review tenant fair-share rules: how requests are prioritized across Dedicated and Hosted customers.
   - Practice issuing a safe scale action: CLI example (dry-run):
     rfn-capacity scale --cluster runtime-prod --pool inference-pool --count 4 --reason "oncall-drill" --dry-run

5) Error budget stewardship (Day 4–7)
   - Understand error budget windows and burn-rate alarms. Verify the dashboard shows the rolling window used by the SLO (30d by default).
   - Confirm the automated responses enabled for the service: throttling, model-fallback, cross-region reroute.
   - Practice executing an emergency fallback:
     - Step: trigger model fallback to smaller quantized variant (canary first)
     - Command (internal API):
       curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://console.internal/api/v1/rollouts/fallback" -d '{"service":"runtime-router","action":"fallback-quantized","target":"model-v2-q4"}'

6) Incident communication and post-incident responsibility (Day 4–8)
   - Run the incident comms template: copy and post to #incident-comm when practicing. Include: impact, scope, mitigation, ETA.
   - Ownership: the SLO owner must create the post-incident ticket under ENG-SRE > incident-review and ensure attachments: timeline, telemetry snapshots, and decision log.

Acceptance criteria (sign-off):
- Completed checklist items 1–6 and provided evidence (screenshots / links) in the onboarding folder.
- Passed a recorded tabletop drill assessed by rotation lead.
- Demonstrated ability to run three recovery actions in the sandbox (scale, fallback, throttle).
- Rotation lead signs off in Confluence comment and updates rotation roster.

Escalation matrix (who to call):
- Immediate (pager): oncall-sre-primary -> oncall-sre-secondary -> eng-sre-manager.
- For capacity quorums (if >2-hour impact): capacity-ops@redwood.com and cloud-accounts oncall.

Runbook snippets and templates:
- Incident start checklist (first 10 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty.
  2. Post initial impact message (template):
     - Subject: [INC][service] brief title
     - Body: one-line impact, estimated affected tenants, user-visible effect, immediate mitigation in progress.
  3. Attach top-3 telemetry graphs: p95 latency, request rate, error-rate (per-tenant).

- Quick mitigation decision matrix (summary):
  - If error-rate spike and p95 increased -> look for traffic shift or model regression.
  - If traffic surge without elevated error-rate -> provision temporary capacity or enable burst pool.
  - If sustained burn-rate > 2x baseline for 60m -> initiate throttling and notify product.

Ownership and responsibilities table:
| Role | Responsibility | OK to action without manager approval |
|-----|---------------|---------------------------------------|
| SLO owner (oncall) | Triage, execute mitigations, create incident ticket | Yes (scale, fallback, short-term throttles) |
| Rotation lead | Sign-off postmortem, progressive escalations | No (policy changes are escalated) |
| Capacity oncall | Provisioning, permanent capacity changes | No (requires capacity committee approval) |

SLO-specific quick references (examples):
- API-Gateway availability SLO: 99.95% (30d rolling), error budget 0.05%.
- Runtime-router latency SLO: p95 < 200ms for inference path, p99 < 600ms (window: 7d).
- Embeddings service correctness SLO: 98% similarity threshold pass rate (30d).

Training plan and milestones (first 90 days):
- Week 1–2: Complete checklist above and shadow two full rotations.
- Week 3–4: Run two live drills and participate in a capacity rehearsal.
- Month 1–2: Co-own one minor incident under supervision and produce post-incident notes.
- Month 3: Independently manage an escalation and be eligible for rotation lead consideration.

Continuous improvement notes (what to update in this doc):
- Add new commands when automation tooling changes.
- Update SLO thresholds when product SLOs change (owners to file Confluence change note).
- Add examples of new mitigation patterns (e.g., adaptive throttles) after tabletop validations.

Appendix A — Useful commands and links:
- SLO dashboard: https://metrics.redwood.internal/dashboards/slo-matrix
- PagerDuty playbook: https://pagerduty.com/orgs/redwood/services
- Capacity CLI: rfn-capacity (help: rfn-capacity --help)
- Trace UI: https://jaeger.company.local

Appendix B — Post-oncall checklist for outgoing engineer (handover):
1. Document unresolved actions with owners.
2. Export and link current top telemetry graphs.
3. Confirm any temporary mitigations remain or are part of a long-term plan.
4. Hand off any running audits or tickets to next rotation.

Notes and rationale:
- We require a formal sign-off to reduce silent SLO ownership drift. This runbook emphasizes evidence-based progression (drills, recorded actions) rather than ad-hoc approval.

Contact & ownership:
- Document owner: Maya Thompson (SRE).
- Rotation lead (example): Arjun Patel — contact via Slack @arjun.p.

Last reviewed: 2025-02-10 by Hannah Li.

title: backward-compatibility-strategies-for-streaming-endpoints-2026
content:
backward-compatibility-strategies-for-streaming-endpoints-2026

Summary
-------
This guideline defines our company-standard approach to backward compatibility for streaming inference endpoints (gRPC/HTTP2 server-sent events/HTTP chunked streaming). Streaming endpoints have different compatibility constraints than request/response APIs: long-lived connections, stateful per-request lifecycles (KV cache, partial outputs), and client SDK expectations for chunk framing. The goal is to provide concrete practices that minimize customer disruption while allowing the runtime and model-serving stack to evolve.

Applicability
-----------
- Applies to all public and internal Redwood inference streaming endpoints (hosted API streaming, Dedicated streaming, Private deployments) and any SDKs that surface streaming primitives.
- Applies to protocol-level changes, envelope/metadata changes, chunk framing, and semantic changes to streaming messages.
- Does NOT replace per-model quality change policies (use Optimize & evals to manage generation/regression risks).

Principles
---------
1. Principle of least surprise: preserve existing client parsing semantics for active minor versions.
2. Safe evolution: prefer additive changes; avoid breaking clients during long-lived connections.
3. Observable rollouts: all streaming changes require observability gates (SLOs, error metrics) before serving to >=10% of traffic.
4. SDK-first compatibility: SDKs are the reference implementation of client-side expectations — changes must ship SDK updates and server fallbacks.

Versioning model
---------------
- Major.Minor.Patch for API contracts. Major changes = incompatible protocol or message framing changes. Minor = additive fields, new optional events. Patch = server bugfixes and non-behavior changes.
- Streaming endpoints MUST include an explicit "stream_api_version" string in initial connection metadata/headers and first control message. Example header: "X-Redwood-Stream-Version: 1.4.0".
- Server behavior: if a client presents an unsupported major version, reject the connection with a typed error (see Error model).

Streaming-specific compatibility rules
----------------------------------
1. Framing and chunk semantics:
   - Never change chunk separator characters or byte-encoding without a major version bump.
   - For text-based streams (SSE/HTTP chunking), continue supporting CRLF and LF as delimiters for two minor releases.
2. Envelope and metadata additions:
   - Add fields only under an explicit envelope extension object: "extensions": {"field_name": value}. Clients that ignore unknown keys must continue to operate.
   - If adding required metadata for downstream routing (e.g., tenant-mapping), include it on a separate control event rather than embedding in every chunk.
3. Control events and lifecycle messages:
   - Control events (start, heartbeat, partial-complete, final-complete, error) are part of the stable contract. Add new control event types as optional until a major bump.
4. Binary payloads and serialization:
   - When introducing new serialization (protobuf v2 schema changes, compressed frames), the server must advertise supported encodings in initial handshake and accept negotiated encodings.
5. Behavioral changes (generation semantics):
   - Any change that could alter tokenization, KV cache semantics, or partial completion timing must be accompanied by a compatibility report and a canary plan (see Rollout steps).

Error model for streaming endpoints
--------------------------------
- Use typed control errors encoded as JSON in a control-event envelope: {"type":"stream.error","code":"UNSUPPORTED_VERSION","message":"...","retry_after_secs":30}.
- Map streaming control errors to standard HTTP/gRPC codes when the underlying connection is terminated (e.g., UNSUPPORTED -> 400/INVALID_ARGUMENT or gRPC INVALID_ARGUMENT).

Observability and gating
-----------------------
All streaming contract changes require telemetry to be added to the platform dashboards prior to broad rollout. Minimum telemetry set:
- Connection acceptance rate (per version)
- Control-error-rate (per code)
- Partial-output-latency P50/P95/P99 (ms)
- Token-throughput and per-token CPU/GPU utilization
- Client disconnects and reconnection rates within 60s of control events
- Data-plane cost delta (tokens * cost-per-token delta)

SLOs to protect during rollouts:
- Connection success rate: >= 99.5% for non-heavy workloads
- Partial-output latency (P95) must not regress more than 20% relative to baseline for the first 24h of canary
- Control error rate < 0.1% for the affected traffic slice

Testing and CI gates (mandatory)
-------------------------------
1. Contract tests:
   - Unit and integration contract tests using the server and SDK mocks that validate behavior across advertised versions.
   - Golden-frames test: capture representative long-lived session traces and diff chunk sequences after changes.
2. Load and stability tests:
   - Simulate sustained 10k concurrent long-lived streams for Dedicated and Private serving variants.
   - Measure resource usage and KV cache growth (memory-pressure indicators).
3. Regression evals:
   - If streaming behavior affects generation output, run an automated eval against a blocklist of critical prompt-sets used by customers.
4. Chaos tests:
   - Connection flapping, mid-stream server restarts, and abrupt event drops. Ensure graceful reconnection semantics in >=90% of simulated sessions.

Deployment and rollout checklist
-----------------------------
1. ADR and design sign-off: create or update an ADR for major changes. Minor changes should reference existing ADRs when applicable.
2. SDK release: new SDK must be published with clear migration notes and deprecation warnings 2 weeks before server-enforced changes.
3. Observability: dashboards and alerting added to staging and prod.
4. Canary: start at 1% traffic for 6 hours -> 10% for 24 hours -> 30% for 24 hours -> 100%. Advance only if SLO gates are met.
5. Rollback plan: automated traffic routing rollback and feature flags to disable new control event types.
6. Customer communication: for changes that require client action, send targeted notices at 30/14/3 days before rollout with migration examples.

Performance budgets and infra considerations
----------------------------------------
- Target per-stream memory usage: < 200MB peak for 90% of streams on Dedicated instance classes (r5-gpu-48).
- KV cache growth threshold: if average per-stream KV cache grows > 2x baseline under canary, abort rollout and investigate.
- Burst capacity: streaming endpoints should permit 3x ephemeral bursting for 60s during client reconnection storms; autoscaling must honor burst limits configured in Dedicated.
- Quantization/Kernel changes: changes to runtime kernels that affect per-token latency must be tested with long-lived streaming workloads; measure tail-latency P99 and 99.9.

Developer and SDK guidance (examples)
---------------------------------
- Handshake header example (HTTP2):
  curl -v -H "X-Redwood-Stream-Version: 1.4.0" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
    https://inference.redwood.ai/v1/stream/generate

- Client expectation checklist:
  1) Treat unknown control events as ignorable for two minor versions.
  2) Implement idempotent reconnection: include last-acknowledged-token index in reconnection handshake.
  3) Respect backpressure signals from server control events (e.g., "throttle_hint_ms").

Decision records & history
------------------------
- ADR: stream-versioning-and-handshake-2025 (major model informing header usage).
- ADR: control-event-typing-2024 (defines control event envelope and error model).
- This document supersedes ad-hoc streaming notes and centralizes rollout/gating flow.

Appendix: sample control-event envelope (JSON)
-------------------------------------------
{"event":"control","name":"partial_complete","seq":12,"meta":{"token_index":256}}

Migration examples
-----------------
- Adding an optional confidence field in partial outputs:
  - Server adds: "extensions":{"confidence":0.94}
  - SDKs ignore unknown extension keys; server servers should not make client behavior rely on presence of extensions for two minor versions.

Ownership and contacts
---------------------
- API contract owner: Maya Chen (api-contracts@redwood.ai)
- Runtime lead (canary infra): Rajesh Nair (serving-runtime@redwood.ai)
- SDK owners: client-eng@redwood.ai

Notes and follow-ups
------------------
- Follow-up action: create an automated contract-diff job in CI that flags framing changes. Owner: api-contracts team.
- Quarterly review: this guideline will be revisited Q1 2027 or after two major streaming changes, whichever is earlier.

References
---------
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/api-compatibility-and-deprecation-policy-2026.json
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/streaming-protocols-and-kv-cache-2025
- ADR: control-event-typing-2024

title: Day-2 Automation, Upgrade & Rollback Runbook for Private Deployments
content:
Day-2 Automation, Upgrade & Rollback Runbook for Private Deployments

Summary:

This document is the canonical Day-2 operations runbook for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It combines: the operational checklist for steady-state, automated workflows for common tasks, verified upgrade and rollback procedures for releases, packaging validation for air-gapped installs, and a customer requirements checklist used during sales/onboarding. Target audience: SREs, platform engineers, and solutions engineers executing upgrades or troubleshooting production private deployments.

Goals:
- Ensure upgrades are repeatable, observable, and reversible.
- Minimize customer downtime and manual intervention via automation.
- Provide a single source of truth for safety checks, SLAs, and escalation.

Owner & Contacts:
- Primary owner: Platform SRE (team: eng-private-deployments)
- On-call escalation: private-deployments oncall rotation (pager: #infra-oncall)
- Escalation matrix: Marcus Li (SRE Lead), Priya Nair (Solutions Eng), Daniel Morales (Product).

Prerequisites (preflight):
1) Validated customer topology: list of control-plane endpoints, worker subnets, routing tables, and CIDRs.
2) KMS/HSM configuration verified and accessible (or pre-staged for air-gapped).
3) Current deployment manifest and image digests stored in the release artifact registry.
4) Backups: KV cache snapshot + model artifact snapshot + database backup stored off-host.
5) SLOs & maintenance window agreed with customer and recorded in the SA notes.

Customer Requirements Library (minimum set):
| Requirement | Expected value / action | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------|
| Supported OS | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS or RHEL 8 | Kernel >= 5.15 recommended |
| Network | Static routing for control plane + NAT for egress | BGP optional for large customers |
| Storage | NFS or Ceph for model artifacts, 1 TB per shard baseline | Validate IOPS against perf profile |
| KMS | AWS KMS / CloudHSM / Onprem HSM | Provide key ARN or cert bundle |
| Air-gap | Installer tarball + SHA256 + signed manifest | See packaging section |

Day-2 steady-state checklist (daily/weekly tasks):
- Verify control-plane health: /health endpoint for each service (latency < 200ms p50).
- Check autoscaling events and GPU pool utilization. Target: 60-75% average utilization for efficiency.
- Review error-rate dashboard: requests with 5xx should < 0.05% of total requests over 1h.
- Verify cache hit-rate: prefix/KV cache hit-rate target >= 80% for production traffic.
- Confirm backups completed and verify restore on a staging cluster monthly.
- Rotate TLS certs and KMS keys per customer policy (at least quarterly for test keys, annual for production keys).

Automations & Scripts (examples):
- Preflight automation: terraform plan + custom manifest diffs to detect incompatible changes.
- Canary automation: scripted canary rollout that updates 10% of pods and runs synthetic traffic checks.
- Rollback automation: safe-rollback script that restores previous image digests and replays KV cache warmup.

Example preflight script snippet (bash):

#!/bin/bash
# preflight-check.sh - run from CI or operator machine
set -euo pipefail
RELEASE=$1
# 1. Validate digests
jq -r '.images[] | .name + @"@" + .digest' manifests/$RELEASE.json
# 2. KMS smoke test
curl -sSf "https://kms-check.local/v1/unwrap" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN"
# 3. Run perf profile validation (local binary)
./perf-validate --manifest manifests/$RELEASE.json --thresholds perf_thresholds.yaml

Packaging & air-gapped install notes:
- Distribution: signed .tar.gz with release manifest (manifest.json), SHA256SUMS, and a detached GPG signature.
- Verification steps for customer: verify SHA256, verify GPG signature, compare manifest image digests with internal inventory.
- Example verification commands:
  - sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
  - gpg --verify manifests/$RELEASE.manifest.sig manifests/$RELEASE.manifest
- Offline registries: prior to install, push images to customer local registry and update manifest image URLs. Provide a registry-sync script.

Upgrade procedure (recommended safe path):
0) Schedule: define a maintenance window; notify customer with the runbook and rollback plan.
1) Preflight checks: run the automation from CI and ensure no failing checks.
2) Snapshot: trigger artifact snapshots and DB backup; verify completion.
3) Canary rollout (10%):
   a) Deploy canary using the orchestration tool (Helm or kustomize).
   b) Run the automated synthetic test suite for at least 15 minutes. Key tests: token latency, throughput, correctness on canonical prompts.
   c) If any synthetic test fails or error-rate > 3x baseline, abort and rollback.
4) Staged rollout (50%): expand to 50% and run 1 hour of traffic; monitor heatmaps and P99 latency. Thresholds: P99 < 2x baseline and 5xx < 0.2% absolute.
5) Full rollout: if staged checks pass, complete rollout.
6) Post-upgrade validation: run customer smoke tests and confirm SLAs.
7) Mark release: update inventory and release notes; capture model-variant compatibility matrix if changed.

Rollback procedure (fast revert):
1) Trigger: any of the following triggers rollback:
   - Canary synthetic suite failed
   - Error-rate > configured abort threshold
   - Operator judgement during staged rollout
2) Actions:
   a) Pause trafﬁc to the updated pods (service weight to previous).
   b) Execute rollback automation: restore previous image digests + restart pods. Example Helm command: helm rollback <release> <revision> --namespace redwood-private || kubectl rollout undo deployment/<svc> -n redwood-private
   c) Rehydrate cache: replay cached prefixes from snapshot to minimize cold-start latencies.
   d) Validate health endpoints and synthetic tests before re-opening traffic.
3) Post-rollback: create postmortem, notify customer, and schedule a follow-up patch release.

Observability & SLOs (what to track during upgrades):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 per route; abort if p99 > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes.
- Errors: 5xx absolute threshold and relative increase; abort if 5xx > 0.2% or >3x baseline increment.
- Resource usage: GPU/memory per-pod; abort if OOM or GPU saturation detected.
- Synthetic tests: pass rate must be >= 95% during canary.

Runbook for common Day-2 incidents:
- degraded-control-plane: reduce client timeouts to protect control-plane; scale control-plane out by +1 replica per 10% increase in cpu.
- high-error-rate-after-upgrade: trigger rollback if error-rate persists > 15 minutes; capture traces and core dumps to support debugging.
- model-serving-slowdowns: validate KV cache hit-rates and warm caches using cached-prefix-replay tool.

Templates & customer comms (use these verbatim or adapt):
- Pre-upgrade notice (48h): "We plan to perform a non-disruptive upgrade on <DATE>. Expected impact: brief rolling restarts; no data loss. Contact: <SRE_CONTACT>."
- Post-rollback notification: "An automated rollback to version <REV> was performed on <DATE> due to <REASON>. Incident ticket: <TICKET_ID>. We will follow up with a root-cause analysis within 5 business days."

Change log & audit trail requirements:
- All upgrade actions must be recorded in the deployment audit: operator, timestamp, release manifest digest, preflight result ID, and canary run-id.
- Store artifacts and logs in the customer-specific retention bucket for 90 days (default) or customer-specified retention.

Appendix A: Example Terraform pattern (snippet):

# module: redwood_private_cluster/main.tf
# - uses provider aliases for customer accounts
module "control_plane" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/redwood/terraform//modules/control-plane"
  cluster_name = var.cluster_name
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}

Appendix B: Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Image digest mismatch: abort and verify signed manifest.
- KMS transient failures: fall back to wrapped key cache if available, otherwise pause upgrade.
- Storage I/O degradation: throttle model loading, increase replicas temporarily.

Appendix C: Post-upgrade checklist (within 24h):
- Confirm synthetic test coverage for customer-critical prompts.
- Verify billing/usage counters for anomalies.
- Close the maintenance ticket and attach upgrade artifact digests.

Notes & references:
- See related reference architecture for hybrid-control-plane considerations.
- For air-gapped installs, consult the onprem packaging guide for pre-staging images and KMS cert exchange.

If you find any missing steps or make improvements, update this document and add yourself to the reviewers list.

title: Offline-to-Online Quality Checker and Continuity Spec
content:
Offline-to-Online Quality Checker and Continuity Spec

Overview

This document defines the Offline-to-Online Quality Checker (O2O-QC), a lightweight, production-facing continuity spec that ensures models promoted from offline evals remain within expected quality and resource envelopes once serving traffic begins. The O2O-QC bridges model-onboarding checklists, the eval harness, quantization profiles, and runtime guardrails to reduce regression windows and enable fast, safe rollouts.

Motivation

Despite strong offline metrics, models can exhibit operationally significant changes when exposed to live workloads (prompt distribution shift, embedding drift, KV-cache sensitivity, quantization degradation). O2O-QC establishes:

- A minimal, standardized set of signals to collect at promotion time and continuously afterward.
- Deterministic decision rules and thresholds for automated canary escalation and rollback.
- Integration hooks with the eval harness, rollout manager, and Alerting/Incidents.

Scope

Applies to all model promotions from "staging" -> "canary" -> "production" across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Focus areas include generation quality (semantic fidelity), latency/throughput regressions, token-cost changes, and quantization/kv-cache regressions. This spec intentionally excludes offline-only research metrics (e.g., FLOPs) unless they affect runtime behavior.

Key Concepts and Definitions

- Baseline snapshot: the canonical metric vector captured from the promoted model during offline certification (see "holistic-acceptance-matrix-for-model-promotion").
- Live delta: the rolling-window percentage change between baseline and production signal.
- Canary cohort: a controlled fraction of traffic (default 3%) used for early detection.

Signals to collect (minimum required)

1. Quality and correctness
- Prompt-level BLEU/ROUGE/MAUVE-like proxy where applicable (for structured outputs, use schema-validator failure rate).
- Rerank/semantic-similarity score distributions for retrieval-augmented tasks.

2. Distribution and embeddings
- Embedding population centroid drift (cosine distance) on automated sample of user requests.
- Token distribution shift (unigram/bigram KL divergence).

3. Runtime and economics
- P95 and P99 tail latency (ms).
- Avg tokens-per-request and tokens-per-second.
- Per-token compute cost estimate (normalized to baseline).

4. Cache sensitivity
- KV cache hit-rate and effective tokens saved.

Signal collection frequency and windows

- Baseline capture: Single pre-promotion window of 50k representative prompts (or 24h representative traffic in shadow).
- Live windows: 1m, 1h, 24h rolling aggregates. Canary decisions use 1h windows with 15m sub-windows for early abort heuristics.

Decision rules and thresholds

Table: Primary decision thresholds (defaults; teams may tighten per workload)

| Signal | Trigger condition (canary abort) | Escalation condition (require human review) | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Semantic proxy delta | >= 6% decrease in 1h window | 3%–6% decrease sustained over 24h | preserves user-facing correctness |
| Embedding centroid cosine drift | >= 0.12 (1h) | 0.08–0.12 sustained (24h) | retrieval recall risk |
| P99 latency | >= 2x baseline or >1200ms | 1.3x–2x sustained | user-latency SLO protection |
| Tokens-per-request | >= 25% increase (1h) | 10%–25% increase (24h) | cost blowout guardrail |
| KV-cache hit-rate drop | >= 15% absolute drop | 7%–15% sustained | quant/cache interplay |

Notes: Thresholds are tunable per-customer and per-model class. For latency, absolute ceiling overrides relative change.

Automated canary policy

1. Start canary at 3% traffic for 24 hours by default.
2. Evaluate 1-hour windows at 60-minute mark and 15-minute early-check sub-windows.
3. If any abort trigger fires, automatically scale canary down to 0 traffic and mark the rollout as "failed-canary". Generate an incident (severity S2) with attached artifacts.
4. If only escalation conditions fire (no abort), notify owners and hold rollout for manual review; do not expand canary.

Artifacts to capture when a trigger fires

- Canonical sample of 1k requests that contributed to the signal delta (anonymized/pseudonymized).
- Model input/output pairs, embeddings, and similarity scores.
- Perf traces (p95/p99), allocation telemetry, and kernel selection info if available.
- Baseline snapshot used for comparison and eval harness run-id.

Rollback and mitigation runbook (executed automatically or manually)

1. Automatic actions (triggered by abort):
   a. Stop routing to the canary model variant.
   b. Re-route to prior production model variant immediately.
   c. Create incident in PagerDuty with template "o2o-canary-abort" and attach artifacts.

2. Initial human triage (within 30 minutes):
   a. Owner reviews artifacts, validates anonymization, and reproduces failure with the eval harness in shadow mode.
   b. If failure is due to quantization profile or KV-cache mismatch, attach relevant quant profile and cache stats.

3. Targeted mitigations:
   a. Apply a temporary config that increases batching/limits sequence length or switches to higher-precision path.
   b. If semantic quality degraded, roll back permanently or escalate to research for hotfix.

4. Post-incident follow-up:
   a. Update the onboarding checklist entry that failed and add a dedicated regression test to the eval harness.
   b. Run a 7-day shadow run to assert stability before reattempting canary.

Integration points and examples

- Eval harness: Use eval run metadata keys: run_id, seed_set, quant_profile_id. The O2O controller fetches the baseline using run_id at promotion. Example shim to fetch baseline: 

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ 
  "https://eval-harness.internal/v1/runs/{run_id}/snapshot"

- Rollout manager (canary config snippet):

{ "canary": { "traffic_fraction": 0.03, "monitoring_windows": ["15m","1h","24h"], "abort_criteria": ["semantic_proxy_delta","p99_latency"] } }

- Alert payload example (JSON):

{ "alert_type": "o2o_canary_abort", "model_id": "gptx-7b-q", "canary_fraction": "3%", "trigger": "semantic_proxy_delta", "details": "6.8% decrease in 1h window", "artifacts": ["s3://o2o-artifacts/2025-09-08/run-12345/sample-1000.json"] }

Operational guidance and ownership

- Primary owner: Applied ML (model-onboarding) team. Secondary owners: Serving Runtime and Platform SRE.
- PagerDuty routing: Severity S2 -> model-onboarding escalation; Severity S1 only for catastrophic regressions (widespread production failures).

SLOs and reporting

- Canary abort reaction time: initial triage within 30 minutes, mitigations started within 2 hours.
- Canary false-positive tolerance: <5% of canaries aborted due to transient noise per quarter.

Testing and verification matrix

- Add canonical tests to the eval harness for: adversarial prompt slices, token-inflation probes, and cache-stress scenarios.
- Label new onboarding bundles with quant_profile_id and cache_mode to ensure reproducibility.

Appendix A — Example prompts for stress probes

1. Token inflation probe: repeat patterns that trick autoregressive step-sizing.
2. Cache eviction probe: long-context prompts that simulate shifted KV-cache locality.
3. Retrieval drift probe: queries that exercise obscure domains to surface embedding shifts.

Appendix B — FAQ

Q: Who may relax thresholds for a high-value customer?
A: Only the platform SRE in coordination with model-onboarding and customer-security; document the exception and add compensating tests.

Q: How do we anonymize sample artifacts?
A: Use the internal pseudonymization script at /tools/anonymize-requests with the "--strip-pii" flag before upload.

Related work

- See "holistic-acceptance-matrix-for-model-promotion-2026" for baseline capture format.
- See "kv-cache-quant-stability-audit-playbook-2025" for quantization recovery steps.

Change log

- 2025-03-12: Spec created by Aisha Banerjee.
- 2025-06-02: Added KV-cache specific thresholds after pilot with customer X.
- 2025-09-08: Tuned semantic proxy delta thresholds and clarified artifact retention.

Contact

For questions or exceptions, contact the model-onboarding channel (#model-onboarding) or the doc owner Aisha.Banerjee@redwood.ai.

title: First Week Systems & Badge Onboarding Playbook
content:
First Week Systems & Badge Onboarding Playbook

Overview

This playbook describes the recommended, low-friction process for new hires to obtain systems access, physical badge entry, and the core toolchain needed to be productive in their first week. It is intended for people-ops partners, hiring managers, IT/staff engineers, and hiring-team buddies who coordinate access. The emphasis is on automated flows, clear owners, and fallback runbooks for common failures.

Intended outcomes (by the end of week 1)
- Employee has building badge and primary laptop configured.
- Access to core cloud projects, code repositories, and primary communication tools (Slack, email, calendar).
- Access requests are auditable and issued with minimum-privilege roles.
- New hire is able to run the local dev quickstart and join at least one team-sync.

Owners & escalation
- Primary owner: people-ops (badge logistics, orientation scheduling)
- Systems owner: IT Ops / Staff Engineer on-call (laptop imaging, VPN/KMS)
- Access control and IAM: Security team (RBAC policy exceptions)
- Escalation path: People-ops -> IT Ops -> Security -> CTO on emergent risk items

Before day 0 (People-ops checklist)
1. Confirm start date and work location; schedule badge pickup (if office) and shipping of laptop (if remote).
2. Pre-provision SSO account and temporary Slack invite.
3. Generate onboarding access bundle: initial repo access list, cloud project names, and team-specific infra tickets.
4. Create calendar invites for orientation, manager 1:1, and buddy sessions.

Day 0 / Pre-boarding automated tasks
- Trigger account creation job: run `onboard create-account --email <email> --team <team-slug> --start <YYYY-MM-DD>`
- Auto-approve baseline access role: `roles:employee-basic` (access to internal wiki, Slack, and email).
- Push laptop image to courier or on-site pick-up location.

Day 1 checklist (manager + buddy)
1. Welcome meeting and orientation (walkthrough of this playbook)
2. Badge pickup / building entry verification (if on-site): bring government ID; sign H&S brief.
3. Verify SSO login and MFA enrollment. If failure, escalate to IT Ops (see troubleshooting).
4. Confirm Slack and email deliverability.
5. Validate access to source control and package manager: run the quick test in the `quickstarts/new-hire` repo.
6. Run a smoke test with the team’s canonical dev environment (local or cloud).
7. Confirm calendar and team workspace membership.

Core systems access table (summary)
| System | Typical initial role | Owner | Time to grant (SLA) | Notes |
|--------|----------------------|-------|----------------------|-------|
| Single Sign-On (SSO) | employee-basic | people-ops | 0-4h | MFA mandatory; include recovery options |
| Slack | member | people-ops | 0-2h | Auto-joins primary team channel |
| Email & Calendar | standard mailbox | people-ops | 0-2h | Auto-forward rules for manager |
| Source control (git.redwood) | repo-read | hiring manager | <24h | Managers request additional repos via PR |
| Cloud project (dev) | viewer | infra team | <24h | Bump to editor via infra ticket |
| Internal VPN | vpn-user | IT Ops | 0-8h | Required for private regions; certificate-based |
| Badge / Physical access | building-level | Facilities/People-ops | 1-3 business days | Expedited pickup available with manager note |

Notes about the table: the above is a human-readable summary. Individual repos, cloud projects, and sensitive services require explicit tickets or role approvals. Use least privilege by default.

Common first-week operations (how-to)
- Request additional repository access: open `Access Request` in the IT portal, fill repo name and justification, tag manager and security reviewer. Typical flow: manager approves -> auto-grant script runs -> audit log entry created.
- Request production access: production access requires a documented justification and a security review. Use template in the IT portal and attach the rollout plan.

Troubleshooting checklist (frequent failures)
- SSO login fails: ensure new hire registered authenticator; run `auth-tool verify --user <email>` and check error codes. If `ERR_MFA_NOT_ENROLLED`, instruct to register via SSO URL; if `ERR_USER_NOT_FOUND` escalate to people-ops.
- Laptop imaging failed: escalate to IT Ops; temporary loaner policy applies (loaner devices available for <= 14 days).
- Badge not programmed: verify employee ID in facility system, then request reissue with Facilities ticket `FAC-ISSUE-BADGE` and tag People-ops.

Automations and CLI snippets
- Pre-provision role and repo access (people-ops):
  `onboard preprovision --email maria@example.com --teams infra,eng --repos team-repo,shared-lib`
- Manager grant pattern (for recurring contractors):
  `access-request create --user contractor@example.com --scopes "repo:team-repo:write" --expires 2025-04-30`

Security & compliance guidance
- All initial accounts are created with time-limited default roles; any permanent elevation requires a documented business case.
- Audit logs for access grants are retained for 365 days.
- Physical badge provisioning must be linked to a signed offer and background check clearance for roles that require secure-zone access.

First-week success signals (manager report)
- New hire completed quickstart and opened their first PR.
- New hire is in calendar and Slack, attended at least 3 team events.
- No unresolved access blockers older than 48 hours.

Appendix A: Access request template (copy into IT portal)
- Requester: <manager-name>
- Employee: <employee-name>
- Start date: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Systems required: <list>
- Justification: <short description>
- Expiration: <YYYY-MM-DD or none>

Appendix B: Emergency escalation contacts
- People-ops pager: people-ops@redwood.example.com (watch: 9am-6pm PT)
- IT Ops on-call: it-oncall@redwood.example.com (24/7)
- Security incident inbox: sec-ops@redwood.example.com

Related documentation
- See: /confluence/company-handbook/04_hiring-and-onboarding/manager-first-90-and-career-mobility-playbook-2026 for manager-facing onboarding rhythms.
- See: /confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025 for toolchain-specific deep dives.

Revision history
- 2024-10-20: First draft created by Marisol Chen.
- 2025-06-18: Revised to add CLI snippets and updated badge SLA (Marisol Chen).

title: SLO-driven chaos curriculum and capacity simulation guidelines
content:
SLO-driven chaos curriculum and capacity simulation guidelines

Overview

This document defines a repeatable curriculum and operational guidelines for SLO-driven chaos/gameday exercises and capacity simulations. The goal is to exercise realistic multi-tenant inference failure modes, validate SLOs and error-budget controls, and collect forensic evidence suitable for incident review and actionable remediation. This guide is intentionally lightweight so teams can run 1–2 hour labs or full-day rehearsals with equivalent outcomes.

Goals

- Validate that production SLOs reflect customer-impacting outcomes.
- Confirm autoscale and capacity policies behave under realistic traffic and model-serving degradations.
- Exercise fallback and graceful degradation (model variants, region failover, cache priming).
- Collect structured evidence and metrics for post-event analysis tied to deployments, rollouts, and model changes.
- Train on controlled abort and rollback criteria to avoid customer harm.

Scope and audience

- Audience: SREs, runtime engineers, platform owners, and on-call partners.
- Systems: Redwood inference serving runtime, request router, cache layer, autoscaler, and per-tenant priority controls.
- Not covered: billing/accounting reconciliation (separate finance runbook).

Prerequisites

1. Testbed environment with traffic replay capability (see Tooling).
2. Canary dataset and representative token-length distribution for workload.
3. Owner sign-off and scheduled maintenance window (if exercises touch production).

Key definitions (for this curriculum)

- Target SLOs: 99.9%% p95 latency for short-text generation routes; 99%% p99 for embedding batch jobs; availability SLOs per-tenant remain as defined in SLO registry.
- Error budget window: 30 days rolling; exercise will consume a controlled percentage (target 5–15%%) for tabletop calibration.
- Capacity simulation run: a synthetic traffic injection with stepwise load, introduced faults, and validation windows.

Curriculum overview (modular)

1. Quick warm-up (30–45 minutes)
   - Objective: Ensure team familiarity with telemetry dashboards and evidence collection.
   - Activities: Walk the SLO dashboards, confirm alert subscriptions, run a 10-minute synthetic baseline replay.

2. Mini chaos lab (1 hour)
   - Objective: Simulate a single-fault cascade and validate graceful degradation.
   - Faults injected (choose one): KV cache eviction, model quantization path misconfiguration, or network routing flapping between regions.
   - Expected outcomes: Fallback to smaller model variant, increased token cost but preserved critical responses, clear SLO delta.

3. Capacity simulation (1.5–2 hours)
   - Objective: Measure autoscaler headroom and service tail-latency under increasing concurrency and long-context traffic.
   - Steps: Stepped traffic ramp: 25%%, 50%%, 75%%, 100%% of projected peak; hold intervals 10 minutes. Introduce a 10-minute throttling event at 75%% to validate token-priority arbitration.
