4. Complex multi-tenant scenario (2–4 hours)
   - Objective: Validate tenant isolation, fair-share heuristics, and emergency eviction procedure.
   - Scenario: One tenant spikes with emergent batch embedding jobs while other tenants run steady low-latency requests; test backpressure and eviction policies.

5. Post-exercise tabletop & evidence handoff (45–60 minutes)
   - Objective: Capture lessons, map root causes, and generate remediation tickets with owners and SLO impact.

Tooling and artifacts

- Traffic replay: load-generator with token-length and event-time fidelity (recommended: replayer v2). Example CLI: replayer run --trace sample.json --scale 1.4 --duration 20m
- Failure injection: failctl (network, process, latency, and memory faults). Example: failctl inject --target runtime-node-3 --type socket-delay --ms 250
- Telemetry dashboards: SLO overview, p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, per-tenant error budget burn, request-router traces, KV hit/miss.
- Evidence collection: standardized evidence bundle (see Evidence Matrix). Script: evidence-collector --scope exercise --output /tmp/evidence-<YYYYMMDD>.tgz

SLOs and error budget policy for exercises

- Pre-declare the error budget allocation for the exercise: annotate the SLO registry with an exercise token and approval.
- Target consumption: small labs 1–5%%, full-day rehearsals 10–15%%.
- Hard abort: if cumulative error budget > 25%% for any production tenant without explicit exec approval, abort exercise and roll back injected faults.

Capacity simulation configuration table (recommended baseline)

| Parameter | Recommended value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Baseline multiplier | 1.0 | Normal traffic profile |
| Peak multiplier | 1.5–2.0 | Simulate high demand bursts |
| Ramp step | 25%% increments | Small enough to observe inflection points |
| Hold duration | 10 minutes | Capture steady-state metrics for each step |
| Long context ratio | 10–20%% | Models with KV-cache pressure show different tails |

Runbook: executing a standard simulation (checklist)

1. Pre-checks (15–30 minutes)
   - Confirm owners, communication channel (pager, slack), and maintenance windows.
   - Snapshot current SLO status and evidence baseline.
   - Ensure replay traces and canary keys loaded.

2. Start baseline replay and validate dashboards (10 minutes)

3. Execute traffic ramp (operators: run replayer with step schedule)

4. Inject single-point faults at planned time markers; observe autoscaler and fallback behavior

5. Collect evidence bundle at each stage and tag with step id and timestamp

6. If abort criteria triggered: run abort procedure (see Abort & Rollback)

7. Post-run verification: validate services restored, caches re-primed, and model-variants pinned back if changed.

Abort & Rollback (safety gates)

- Abort triggers (any of the following):
  - Tenant-level error budget > 25%%
  - Uncontrolled memory pressure causing OOM restarts across > 10%% of serving nodes
  - Data-plane errors that corrupt persisted KV cache state
- Immediate steps on abort:
  1. Halt traffic generator and failctl scripts.
  2. Revert injected network/process faults.
  3. Verify core runtime health, then escalate to on-call SRE lead if not recovered within 10 minutes.

Evidence Matrix (minimal fields)

Each evidence bundle must include the following items and be named consistently:
- exercise-id: string (e.g., slo-chaos-20260112-01)
- dashboard-snapshots: list of png/csv exports with timestamps
- trace-exports: tracing spans correlated to exercise windows
- node-metrics: cpu/mem/gpu-utilization CSV
- autoscaler-events: raw events log
- injected-faults-log: failctl output
- sample-requests: 50 raw request/response pairs from each affected tenant (sanitized)

Attachment naming convention: <exercise-id>_<artifact-type>_<YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ>

Post-exercise retro template (minimum required fields)

- Summary (one paragraph): what we set out to test and the outcome.
- SLO impact: quantifiable delta and error-budget consumption.
- Root cause hypothesis: top 1–3 contributors.
- Evidence pointers: artifact filenames and timestamps.
- Action items: owner, priority, due date.

Ownership and run cadence

- Exercise owner: service steward listed in SLO registry (primary contact).
- Recommended cadence: team-level mini-labs quarterly; full cross-functional rehearsals semi-annually.

Measurement and success criteria

- Success: clear mapping from injected faults to SLO telemetry where mitigation patterns performed as designed (fallback invoked, degradation prioritization enforced).
- Secondary success: reproducible remediation steps and closed action items for the top remediation tickets within 30 days.

References and related pages

- See: Chaos exercises library: /confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/chaos-exercises-and-failure-hypothesis-library-2026
- See: Capacity rehearsal runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/capacity-rehearsal-decision-playbook-2026

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call (cheat sheet)

- Before exercise: publish exercise id, start time, and abort thresholds to #sre-gameday.
- During: stream evidence bundle to shared storage every 15 minutes.
- After: file retro within 48 hours and annotate SLO registry with consumed budget.

Contact

For questions or to schedule a cross-team rehearsal, contact Marco Reynolds (marco@redwood.example) or the eng-sre scheduling channel.

title: Traffic shaping and priority fanout standards
content:
Traffic shaping and priority fanout standards

Overview
======

This document defines standards for traffic shaping, request priority fanout, and related operational controls across Redwood’s inference platform. It covers API-level shaping, per-tenant and global priority classes, model fanout rules, backpressure and circuit-breaker behavior, observability and SLOs, plus rollout and testing guidance. The goal is predictable performance and graceful degradation during contention while preserving fairness and cost predictability.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all user-facing inference endpoints (generation, chat, embeddings, rerank) served by Hosted, Dedicated, and Private runtimes.
- Includes per-tenant shaping, global ingress throttles, model-variant fanout, and priority routing used by internal control-plane and per-customer routing policies.
- Excludes low-level GPU kernel scheduling (covered in runtime docs) and network-level QoS applied by cloud provider (see infra network topo).

Motivation & Background
-----------------------
Redwood supports mixed workloads: latency-sensitive interactive traffic and large batch/async requests. Without disciplined shaping and priority-aware fanout, hotspots can:
- Increase tail latency for premium customers
- Cause excessive cache/kv churn across hosts
- Escalate cost by triggering unnecessary model fallbacks or overprovisioned capacity

We adopt a layered approach: lightweight API ingress shaping, tenant-aware scheduling, controlled model-level fanout, and circuit-breakers at the model/instance boundary. This document records the standards and concrete configuration suggested for new services and updates to existing services.

Standards (high level)
----------------------
1) Priority classes
   - class=interactive (highest): short requests, p95 latency SLOs, enterprise customers; preemptible only per policy.
   - class=background: batch jobs and async generation; higher throughput tolerance, lower priority.
   - class=best_effort: free-tier, burst-limited.

2) Ingress shaping (per-route)
   - Rate limit tokens: default 300 req/s per route for interactive; configurable via product plan.
   - Burst window: allow bursts up to 3x sustained for interactive, 1.2x for background.
   - Leaky-bucket queueing with max-queue-depth 200 (interactive) and 1000 (background). Excess is rejected with HTTP 429 and x-retry-after header.

3) Fanout rules (model selection and routing)
   - Primary fanout: when a request requires model-side parallelism (e.g., multi-encoder or split-LLM pipelines), fanout must be limited to at most 4 replicas by default and documented in the model manifest.
   - Overflow fanout: On queue pressure, automatically reduce fanout to 1 and prefer lower-cost quantized variants (see model manifest tags: fallback_candidates).
   - Deterministic ordering: fanout router must try replicas in affinity order to preserve cache locality.

4) Backpressure and circuit-breakers
   - Circuit open threshold: error-rate > 10% or consecutive timeouts > 5 within 1 minute for an instance.
   - Throttle degradation: upon crossing 75% CPU or 80% queue depth, reduce per-tenant concurrency by 25% (configurable).

Concrete configuration table (recommended defaults)
-------------------------------------------------
| scope | key | default | notes |
|-------|-----|---------|-------|
| route | ingress.rate_limit.rps | 300 | interactive routes; override per-tier |
| route | ingress.burst_multiplier | 3.0 | max burst factor |
| route | ingress.max_queue | 200 | requests queued before 429 |
| runtime | fanout.max_replicas | 4 | documented in model manifest |
| runtime | fanout.fallback_variant_order | quantized,fp16,fp32 | router uses this order when reducing fanout |
| instance | circuit.error_rate_pct | 10 | rolling 60s window |
| instance | circuit.consecutive_timeouts | 5 | timeouts in 60s |
| scheduler | tenant.max_concurrency | 50 | soft limit; enforced by scheduler |

Examples (YAML configs)
-----------------------
api_route: 
  name: chat.v1.generate
  ingress: 
    rate_limit: 300
    burst_multiplier: 3.0
    max_queue: 200
  priority_class: interactive
  fanout: 
    max_replicas: 4
    fallback_candidates: ["redwood-7b-q4", "redwood-7b-fp16"]

Router pseudocode (behavioral example)
-------------------------------------
```
receive(request):
  if request.priority==best_effort and global_queue_depth > 10000:
    reject(429)
  route = select_route(request)
  if route.ingress.full():
    return 429 with x-retry-after
  replicas = pick_affine_replicas(route.fanout.max_replicas)
  for r in replicas:
    if r.circuit_open:
      continue
    send(r)
  if all attempts fail:
    fallback_to_variant(route.fanout.fallback_candidates[0])
```

Observability & SLOs
--------------------
- Exported metrics (per route, per model instance, per tenant):
  - request_rate (rps)
  - queue_depth
  - p50/p95/p99_latency_ms
  - error_rate_pct
  - fanout_inflight_replicas
  - circuit_state (open/half/closed)
- Dashboards: new service onboarding must include a traffic-shaping dashboard with: total ingress, queue depth, per-priority latencies, top rejected tenants, fanout distribution.
- Alerts (examples):
  - P95 latency for interactive routes > 120ms sustained for 5m -> P1 alert to oncall (Escalation playbook: increase capacity, enable emergency routing).
  - Queue depth > 80% of max_queue for 3m -> P2 alert to platform team.
  - Circuit open ratio > 10% of instances for 2m -> P2.

Rollout and testing guidance
---------------------------
1) Simulation tests before production change: feed synthetic traffic shaped to mix of priority classes. Validate p95/p99 latency and rejection rate under 1.5x expected peak.
2) Canary phases:
   - Step 1: Apply routing rule to 1% of traffic; run 30m with synthetic burst tests.
   - Step 2: 10% for 2 hours; monitor newly created dashboards.
   - Step 3: 100% after 24h with continuous monitoring.
3) Chaos scenario runbook:
   - Simulate a stuck instance by setting artificially high latency; ensure router respects circuit breaker and reduces fanout.
   - Validate fallback to quantized variant does not drop correctness beyond product-defined regression threshold (see quality-guardrails).

Security & Compliance considerations
----------------------------------
- Rate-limiting headers must be preserved and logged for auditing (x-tenant-id, x-route-id, x-rate-limit, x-retry-after).
- For Private deployments, local network QoS may override cloud ingress limits; document deviations in customer-specific runbooks.

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------
- Platform Networking & Router Team: implement ingress shaping primitives and fanout router (owner).
- Serving Runtime Team: expose circuit state and variant metadata via instance telemetry (collaborator).
- Observability Team: add dashboards and alert rules on onboarding checklist.
- Product: define per-plan defaults and priority class assignment.

Decision record (summary)
------------------------
We chose layered shaping + fanout reduction (instead of global reject-first approach) to: preserve low-latency service for premium users; minimize model-variant thrash; and enable predictable cost behavior. Alternatives considered: strict global queue (rejected for poor tenant isolation) and pure per-instance caps (insufficient for model-level cache locality).

Related pages and references
---------------------------
- Resource QoS and profiling playbook (infra-standards)
- ADR: request segmentation and priority routing (decision-records)
- Quality guardrails and fallback evaluation guidelines (applied-ml-and-evals)

Appendix: quick CLI test recipes
--------------------------------
- Simulate load: `ab -n 10000 -c 50 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat`
- Check queue depth metric: `curl -s https://observability/api/metrics?name=queue_depth&route=chat.v1.generate`
- Force circuit open (dev only): `curl -X POST http://router-admin/instance/1234/simulate-latency -d '{"latency_ms": 10000}'`

Change history
--------------
- 2025-11-15: Draft created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-10: Review and examples added (Miguel Santos).
- 2026-02-10: Updated SLO thresholds and rollout steps after platform load test (Rina Takahashi).

Contact
-------
For questions or suggested updates, contact the Platform Networking & Router Team (router-team@redwood.ai) or the doc owner, Aisha Patel.

title: Scheduled Launch Capacity Safeguard & Post-Event Incident Template
content:
Scheduled Launch Capacity Safeguard & Post-Event Incident Template

Summary
-------
This playbook defines the SRE runbook and post-event incident template for scheduled, high-impact launches (marketing campaigns, partner integrations, large customer migrations). It covers pre-launch SLO/error-budget gating, capacity booking and reservations, operational tooling to validate run readiness, live-day safeguards and escalation paths, and a structured post-event incident review that combines reliability and business impact analysis. Use this when a launch is expected to increase QPS, unique session length, or bursty embedding/chat workloads > 5x baseline for more than 30 minutes.

Goals
-----
- Protect tiered SLOs while maximizing launch throughput and customer experience.
- Provide a repeatable pre-launch checklist that ties capacity pledges to error budget impact.
- Define live-day operational controls and automated throttles to prevent prolonged SLO burn.
- Standardize post-event incident reviews to capture capacity-forensics, model-quality regressions, and customer impact.

Scope and applicability
----------------------
- Applies to any coordinated external launch that will materially change request profile for hosted/Dedicated/private tenants.
- Not intended for routine deployments (< 10% traffic change) or internal A/B experiments below canary threshold.
- Cross-functional stakeholders: Product launch owner, Platform PM, SRE oncall, Model owner, Customer Success.

Pre-launch: decision criteria and gating
--------------------------------------
1) Risk assessment (owner: Product launch owner)
   - Expected peak multiplier (QPS): <value> (example: 6x baseline)
   - Session length shift: median token count change (e.g., +40%)
   - % traffic to new model variant / unvalidated prompt sets
   - Business-critical SLAs during launch window (e.g., 99.9% p50 latency; 99.5% p99)

2) Error-budget gating (owner: SRE lead)
   - For the service(s) affected, compute projected error budget burn over launch window using historical traffic and synthetic canaries.
   - Gating rule: proceed only if projected burn keeps the monthly error-budget consumption <= 60% unless an approved risk waiver is recorded.

3) Capacity reservation and verification (owner: Capacity/Infra)
   - Reserve headroom: min(reserved_gpu_tokens, projected_peak_tokens * 1.25).
   - Reserve a warm-pool of model hot-pools: N warm instances per region (recommended: baseline_hotpool * 0.5 rounded up).
   - Test plan: run synthetic workload with 1.0x, 2.5x, and expected_peak multiplier for at least 15m each and capture latency, KV cache hit rates, GPU memory pressure.

Example capacity reservation request (JSON)
| payload |
{
  "tenant": "marketing-campaign-aug25",
  "start": "2025-08-25T10:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-08-25T14:00:00Z",
  "peak_qps_estimate": "12000",
  "model_profile": "gpt-4x-infer-8k-quant",
  "hot_pool_instances": "12",
  "reserve_reason": "Public launch - campaign"
}

Operational tooling readiness checklist (owner: Platform/Tooling)
- Canary pipelines validated and toggles wired to traffic router (feature flags and routing policies).
- Telemetry retention for launch window: increase sampling to 100% for p95/p99 latency, error types, and tokenized model outputs for 24h post-launch.
- Synthetic canary jobs scheduled and healthy: canary-id, last-success timestamp.
- Automated throttle guard configured: error_budget_controller and traffic_shepherding policy attached to tenant.
- Model shadowing enabled where feasible: mirror 10–20% of traffic to new variant for quality checks without user-facing exposure.

Live-day runbook (owner: SRE oncall / Launch coordinator)
1) T-minus 60m: final readiness check
   - Confirm capacity reservations are active and warm pools at target.
   - Confirm datadog/telemetry dashboards show expected synthetic baseline.
2) T-minus 15m: enable expanded sampling and reduced aggregation windows (1m).
3) Launch start: staged ramp strategy (owner: Traffic Ops)
   - Stage 0 (0–5m): 5% traffic to new route. Verify latency p50/p95 and error-rate.
   - Stage 1 (5–20m): escalate to 25% if no SLO regression and error budget controller reports < 10% incremental burn.
   - Stage 2 (20–60m): escalate to 60–80% depending on business target.
   - Full ramp after 60m if all indicators green.
4) Real-time decision thresholds (automated & manual)
   - Auto-abort if p99 latency > baseline_p99 * 3 OR 5xx rate > baseline_5xx * 4 sustained for 3m.
   - Soft throttle if projected error budget burn rate exceeds 15% of remaining monthly budget within a 30m window.
   - Manual rollback if model-quality alerts detect >3% semantic regression on held prompt set or if customer-impacting errors observed for >10m.
5) Runbook escalation matrix
   - Pager: SRE oncall -> Platform lead -> Model owner -> Product launch owner.
   - Slack channel: #launches-live (pinned runbook link and incident playbook).

Telemetry and alerting specifics (owner: Observability)
- Required metrics (per-route and per-model): qps, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, token consumption, KV cache hit ratio, GPU memory pressure, scheduling latency.
- Alert types and thresholds:
| Metric | Alert | Priority | Action |
| p99 latency | p99 > baseline*2 for 5m | P1 | Auto-throttle + page SRE |
| 5xx rate | 5xx rate > baseline*3 for 3m | P1 | Auto-abort route + page SRE |
| error-budget-burn-rate | projected > 25% remaining in 1h | P2 | Throttle recommendations to traffic ops |
| model-quality-regression | semantic-score drop > 2% vs baseline set | P1 | Mirror traffic to fallback, page model owner |

Automated tooling snippets
- Example CLI to create a temporary traffic gate:
  redwood traffic create-gate --tenant marketing-campaign-aug25 --rule "percent=0.05,condition=metrics.p99<2000" --expires "2025-08-25T11:00:00Z"

- Example alert rule (YAML):
alert: Launch_P99_Throttling
expr: rate_latency_p99{route="marketing-campaign"}[5m] > baseline_p99 * 2
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: critical
annotations:
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/scheduled-launch-capacity-safeguard-and-postmortem-template-2025"

Live forensic capture guidance
- When an alert fires during a launch, immediately enable launch-mode traces for the affected route for at least 30m.
- Capture the following artifacts into the incident evidence bucket:
  - telemetry snapshot (1m resolution) for 30m before and after alert
  - sampled request/response payloads (redacted) for model-quality triage
  - GPU host metrics timeseries and scheduler logs
  - traffic router decisions (which nodes served which tokens)

Post-event incident review: template and required deliverables (owner: SRE/Incident Lead)
1) Executive summary (required)
   - One-paragraph summary: what happened, impact to customers, duration, and resolution.
2) Timeline of key events (required)
   - Structured timeline with timestamps, actor (automation or human), and decision.
3) Data and metrics appendix (required)
   - Include time-series charts and a table of key KPIs: baseline vs observed (QPS, p50/p95/p99, error-rate, token consumption, error budget consumed during window).
   - Example KPI table:
| KPI | Baseline | Peak during launch | % delta |
| QPS | 2,000 | 12,000 | 500% |
| p99 latency | 800ms | 2,400ms | 200% |
| monthly error budget used | 15% | +18% during window | n/a |
4) Root cause hypothesis and validation steps (required)
   - Enumerate hypotheses and evidence supporting or refuting each.
5) Operational actions taken (required)
   - Describe throttles, rollbacks, and config changes performed, with timestamps.
6) Business impact and follow-up (required)
   - Customer tickets created, credits issued, and cost delta for extra capacity.
7) Postmortem remediation plan (required)
   - Owners, priority, expected completion dates, and verification criteria.
   - Example remediation items: optimize KV cache warm-up to reduce cold-start p99 by 30% (owner: runtime team, due: 2025-09-30).
8) Lessons learned for future launches (required)
   - Concrete changes to the pre-launch checklist or tooling.

SLO & capacity change recommendations after a launch
- If launch burned >60% of monthly error budget, schedule a retrospective to reassess monthly SLOs and tenant admission policies.
- Consider temporary SLO relaxations with explicit customer communication only when: business critical and after approval by product + SRE director.
- Update capacity projection model inputs with real observed peak multiplier, session length shift, and quantized-model memory usage.

Ownership matrix (table)
| Role | Responsible | Contact / Pager |
| Product launch owner | Defines business targets and tolerances | product+launch@redwood.ai |
| SRE lead | Error-budget gating, runbook authority | sre-lead@redwood.ai |
| Capacity/Infra | Reservations and hot-pool ops | infra-capacity@redwood.ai |
| Observability | Dashboards, alerts, forensic snapshots | observability@redwood.ai |
| Model owner | Quality regression triage and rollback | model-owner@redwood.ai |

Approval and waiver process
- If pre-launch error-budget gating fails, a waiver may be requested with: justification, compensating controls, and explicit rollback criteria. Approval required from SRE director and Product VP. Record waiver in the launch ticket and link to this playbook.

Runbook maintenance and periodic exercises
- Runbook owner: SRE lead (review cadence: quarterly).
- Mandatory tabletop exercise: run a simulated launch twice per year with synthetic traffic and at least one cross-functional incident drill reproducing an auto-abort scenario.

Appendix: sample postmortem checklist (quick reference)
1) Link incident page and capture evidence artifacts.
2) Produce executive summary and timeline within 48 hours.
3) Complete remediation plan with owners within 7 days.
4) Publish postmortem and schedule follow-up verification within 30 days.

References and related pages
- Capacity reservation API (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/capacity-reservations-api
- Model quality evaluation guide: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails/model-quality-evals

Change history
- 2025-03-18: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-08-26: Added live forensic capture guidance and example CLI by Liam Chen.
- 2026-01-12: Minor edits to auto-abort thresholds and sampling recommendations by Sofia Martinez.

title: Jira Field Guidelines + SLA Timers (SUP Tickets)
content:
Jira Field Guidelines + SLA Timers (SUP Tickets)

## Purpose
This page defines the **required Jira fields, priority/severity rules, SLA timer usage, and linking/closure standards** for customer-facing Support tickets in the **SUP** project.

Goals:
- Reduce time-to-triage and time-to-mitigation with consistent, searchable ticket data.
- Ensure Support **SLAs** are tracked consistently (first response + update cadence) and align with Engineering on-call practices.
- Make escalations auditable: every page/bridge/incident should be linkable from the SUP ticket.

Scope:
- Applies to all SUP tickets (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).
- Applies to Support + CS when creating/updating SUP tickets.

Non-goals:
- Replacing incident process (#incidents + incident commander). Use SUP as the **customer-impact record** and handoff anchor.

---

## Golden rules (read first)
1) **One SUP ticket per customer issue** (even if Engineering work spans multiple teams). Link out to Linear/GitHub as needed.
2) Every SUP must have:
   - **Priority (P0–P4)**
   - **Incident Severity mapping (Sev0–Sev3)** when escalated
   - **Customer/org**, **tier**, **region**, **model**, and **request IDs** (or explicit note that none are available)
   - **SLA timers set** (first response + next update due)
3) If a Slack bridge exists, the ticket must include a **Slack link**, and the Slack bridge must include the **SUP link**.
4) When closing a ticket, write resolution notes so the next on-call can answer: **what happened, what we changed, what the customer should do next**.

---

## Required fields (SUP)
Fill these at creation or during initial triage. Missing fields are the #1 cause of delays.

**Customer & routing**
- **Customer / Org**: Company name and (if applicable) workspace/org identifier.
- **Customer tier** (`customer_tier`): `self_serve` | `dedicated` | `private` | `enterprise`
- **Product area** (`product_area`): Hosted API | Dedicated | Private | Console | Optimize | SDK | Billing
- **Environment** (`environment`): prod | staging | private cluster (name)

**Technical context**
- **Region** (`region`): e.g., `us-east`, `eu-west` (or `N/A` for Private/on-prem where region is not applicable)
- **Model** (`model`): exact model ID + version if known (e.g., `rw-llama-70b@2026-01-31`) or `unknown`
- **SDK + version** (`sdk`): python/ts/go + version, or `HTTP` if direct REST
- **Request IDs** (`request_ids`): at least 1–3 IDs for failing requests (preferred). If unavailable, include timestamp window + client IP hash if provided.
- **Symptoms** (`symptoms`): short, customer-observable description (errors, timeouts, truncation, latency)

**Impact & comms**
- **Impact summary** (`impact_summary`): what’s broken + who is affected + since when.
- **Customer-facing comms owner** (`comms_owner`): Support owner (and CSM for enterprise)
- **Slack link** (`slack_thread_or_channel`): link to Slack thread/bridge if used

**Escalation tracking (when applicable)**
- **Escalation status** (`escalation_status`): Not escalated | Monitoring | Eng engaged | Incident declared | Mitigated | Resolved
- **Incident link** (`incident_channel` / `incident_id`): if moved to #incidents, link the incident channel + incident record if one exists
- **Engineering tracking link(s)** (`linear_link`, `github_pr_link`): links created during escalation

---

## Priority (Support) vs Severity (Incident)
Support uses **P0–P4** to manage urgency and SLA behavior. Engineering incident response uses **Sev0–Sev3**.

Use the published rubric as the source of truth:
- See: *Severity Matrix and Escalation Triggers*

### Quick selection guidance (Support Priority)
**P0 — Critical, active customer outage**
- Production down or near-down for customer(s), no viable workaround.
- Examples: auth outage, widespread 5xx, total inability to stream across a region.

**P1 — Major degradation or high-risk incident**
- Severe performance degradation, partial outage, or failure affecting key flows; workaround may exist but is risky/complex.

**P2 — Significant issue with acceptable workaround**
- Material impact but customers can proceed via documented workaround, or impact is limited in scope.

**P3 — Minor issue / “how-to” with some urgency**
- Small subset affected; minimal business impact.

**P4 — General question / request / non-urgent**

### When to assign Incident Severity
- Assign **Sev** only when escalation/incident process is engaged (or imminent).
- If you set a Sev, also set: `escalation_status`, Slack link, and the on-call/team engaged.

**Rule of thumb:** If you are paging on-call or moving to #incidents, you should have a Sev mapping.

---

## SLA timers: fields and how to use them
We track two time-based fields on SUP tickets:

1) **`first_response_due_at`**
- The deadline for the *first human response* to the customer.
- This is based on **customer tier** and the SLA policy.

2) **`sla_due_at`**
- The deadline for the *next required customer update* (update cadence timer).
- Reset this after every meaningful customer update.

Reference policy:
- See: *SLA Policy by Customer Tier*

### SLA timer rules
- Set both timers at ticket creation (or immediately during initial triage).
- Update `sla_due_at` every time you send a customer update (email, support portal response, or agreed Slack Connect update).
- If you are waiting on the customer, set ticket status to **Waiting on Customer** and follow the “pause” guidance below.

### “Waiting on Customer” and timer behavior
To avoid SLA confusion:
- Only move to **Waiting on Customer** when we have asked a clear question AND provided the next step the customer can take.
- Add a public comment stating what is needed (e.g., request IDs, timestamps, region).
- **Do not silently stop updates** for P0/P1 tickets. If impact persists and we’re actively mitigating, keep updates on the agreed cadence.

(If your Jira configuration supports SLA pausing, the automation will pause update timers in Waiting on Customer. If it does not, explicitly set `sla_due_at` to a reasonable follow-up checkpoint and note the expectation in the ticket.)

---

## Standard workflow by ticket stage

### 1) Intake (first 10 minutes)
1. Set **Priority (P0–P4)**.
2. Confirm **tier, region, model, SDK version, request IDs**.
3. Set **`first_response_due_at`** and **`sla_due_at`**.
4. Respond to customer with acknowledgment + request for missing diagnostics.
5. Add labels:
   - `hosted` / `dedicated` / `private`
   - `streaming` / `quota` / `autoscaling` / `audit-logs` / `sso` etc.

### 2) Triage (first 30–60 minutes)
- Use the *Support Triage Intake Checklist*.
- Link dashboards/runbooks in internal comments.
- If the issue matches a known issue, add `known_issue_link` and use the macro.

### 3) Escalation (when triggers hit)
When escalating:
1. Create (or join) a Slack bridge per *Slack Bridge and Incident Channel Conventions*.
2. Fill:
   - `slack_thread_or_channel`
   - `escalation_status = Eng engaged`
   - incident fields if moved to #incidents
3. Page the correct team via the escalation directory (do not “drive-by DM”).
4. In the ticket, add an internal comment with:
   - Why we escalated (trigger)
   - What we’ve tried
   - What we need from Engineering (specific ask)

### 4) Mitigation / Monitoring
- Keep `sla_due_at` aligned to the customer update cadence.
- For mitigations, document:
  - What changed (config knob, region failover, retry guidance)
  - Customer action required
  - Any risk/rollback plan

### 5) Resolution / Close-out
Close only when one of the following is true:
- Issue is fixed and verified, OR
- Workaround is documented + customer confirms acceptable outcome, OR
- Customer confirms they no longer need help.

Before closing:
- Add a final customer-facing summary.
- Complete the **Resolution Notes** section (template below).
- Link any related Engineering follow-ups (Linear/GitHub) and known-issues article.

---

## Linking standards (make the ticket the system of record)

### Slack
- Always link the Slack artifact used for coordination:
  - Single thread: paste permalink in `slack_thread_or_channel`
  - Bridge channel: paste channel link + pin the SUP link in the channel

### Incidents
- If escalation becomes an incident:
  - Link the #incidents channel in the SUP ticket
  - Add the incident identifier (if your incident tooling generates one)
  - Keep customer updates aligned with the incident comms owner

### Engineering work
- Link at least one of:
  - Linear issue (bug/task)
  - GitHub PR
- In the SUP ticket, add a one-line “why it matters” translation (customer impact) so Engineering doesn’t have to parse the ticket.

### Knowledge base / known issues
- If there is a known issue article:
  - Add the link in `known_issue_link`
  - Use consistent language in customer updates (copy/paste-ready)
- If you discover a repeatable issue without an article:
  - Flag it with label `known-issue-candidate`
  - Add a short draft workaround in an internal comment

---

## Resolution notes standards (required)
Add a final internal section called **Resolution Notes** with the following structure. This is mandatory for P0–P2.

**Resolution Notes (template)**
- **What the customer saw (symptoms):**
- **Customer impact:** (scope, region, tier, timeframe)
- **Root cause (known/likely/unknown):** (be explicit about confidence)
- **Mitigation applied:** (what we changed; include config values if safe)
- **Customer action required:** (if any)
- **Verification:** (how we confirmed recovery; include dashboards/logs at a high level)
- **Follow-ups:** (Linear/GitHub links; doc updates; monitoring gaps)
- **Prevent recurrence:** (if applicable)

Quality bar:
- Write so someone outside the original thread can understand in <2 minutes.
- Avoid customer-sensitive details in broadly visible fields; if needed, put sensitive artifacts in restricted locations and reference them.

---

## Field-by-field guidance (common pitfalls)

### `region`
- Use the region where the request was served (customer’s configured region), not the customer HQ.
- If multi-region: list all affected regions and note primary.

### `model`
- Prefer the exact model ID + pinned version.
- If the issue may involve fallback, explicitly note “fallback suspected” and link relevant routing metrics if available.

### `request_ids`
- Minimum: 1 request ID per failure mode.
- For streaming issues: include both the initial request ID and any reconnect request IDs if client retries.

### `priority`
- Do not “upgrade to P0” just because the customer is loud. Use the rubric + impact.
- Do upgrade to P0/P1 when there is broad/regional impact even if the first ticket is from a single customer.

### `impact_summary`
Good: “~35% of streaming requests reset mid-generation in us-east for Hosted API customers since 14:05 UTC; affected customers report truncated outputs; no workaround confirmed yet.”
Bad: “Streaming is broken.”

---

## Automation expectations (what Jira will do)
(Exact automation names may vary, but expected behaviors are below.)

- On ticket creation in SUP:
  - Prompt for required fields (tier, region, model, request IDs)
  - Set placeholder SLA timers if not set (must be corrected by triager)
- On Priority change:
  - Update escalation prompts (e.g., “Create bridge for P0/P1”)
  - Remind to set/update `sla_due_at`
- On transition to Waiting on Customer:
  - Prompt for a clear customer ask and next follow-up checkpoint
- On transition to Resolved/Closed:
  - Validate Resolution Notes present for P0–P2

If you see the automation misbehaving or blocking legitimate cases, file an internal request and tag **Dylan Brooks** (Jira automation owner).

---

## Examples (what ‘good’ looks like)

### Example A: P0 streaming resets (Hosted)
- Priority: P0
- Tier: enterprise
- Region: us-east
- Model: rw-llama-70b@2026-01-31
- Request IDs: 3 sample IDs from customer
- Slack: bridge channel link
- SLA:
  - `first_response_due_at`: set per enterprise policy
  - `sla_due_at`: set to next scheduled customer update (per cadence)
- Resolution Notes:
  - Includes mitigation (client-side reconnect guidance), verification (error rate drop), and Engineering follow-up PR link.

### Example B: 429 confusion after SDK upgrade (Hosted)
- Priority: P2
- Tier: self_serve
- Request IDs: sample ID + header captures
- Known issue link: rate-limit/headers workaround
- SLA: first response + update checkpoint
- Resolution Notes:
  - Clarifies headers vs quota enforcement and points to corrected SDK configuration.

---

## Compliance and confidentiality
- Do not paste customer secrets (API keys, full payloads with proprietary prompts) in Jira.
- For logs, request IDs are preferred. If payload samples are required, redact and confirm customer consent.
- If you must store sensitive artifacts, use restricted storage and reference location/owner in the ticket.

---

## Changelog
- 2026-02-18: Clarified Waiting on Customer guidance and added mandatory Resolution Notes fields for P0–P2.
- 2026-02-12: Added `first_response_due_at` + `sla_due_at` definitions and reset rules.
- 2026-02-06: Initial publication for escalation playbook refresh.

title: Proration and Price-Protection Guidance for Variable Capacity Contracts
content:
Proration and Price-Protection Guidance for Variable Capacity Contracts

Overview
========

Purpose: This document establishes the policy and operational procedures for proration, price-protection, and billing treatment for variable-capacity and burstable/commitment contracts (multi-tiered dedicated capacity, reserved GPU pools, and usage credits). The guidance ensures consistent accounting, predictable customer experience, and correct revenue recognition across Procurement, Sales, Billing, and RevRec.

Scope
-----
Applies to: Sales (deal desk), Legal, Procurement, Finance (Billing & RevRec), and Customer Success when negotiating or operating contracts that include any of the following:
- Reserved capacity with monthly or annual commit but with variable monthly utilization
- Burst credits or overage tiers tied to committed capacity
- True‑up, downgrade/upgrade windows, or partial-month start/stop behavior

Definitions
-----------
- Commitment Period: Contracted calendar range where the customer is committed (e.g., 12 months).
- Commitment Units: The resource or token units the customer commits to (e.g., GPU-days, throughput hours, token commit).
- Proration Window: The time span used to compute partial charges when capacity starts/stops mid-billing period (default calendar month).
- Price‑Protection Period: Window after an amendment during which the customer is guaranteed not to see a higher unit price for pre-agreed capacity.
- True-up: End-of-period reconciliation where actual usage is compared to committed units and billed or credited.

High-level principles
---------------------
1) Transparent, predictable customer billing: Billing system must show line items for committed capacity, usage, proration, and any price-protection credits.
2) Consistent RevRec treatment: Commitments recognized as deferred revenue and amortized over the committed period when not contingent on performance.
3) Minimize accounting churn: Where possible, prefer monthly smoothing over ad-hoc daily journal adjustments.
4) Contract-first approach: Pricing clauses must map to billing config and RevRec rules during deal ingestion.

Roles & responsibilities
------------------------
- Sales / Deal Desk: Select proration method in negotiation and tag contract with accounting flags (see Contract Ingestion checklist).
- Legal: Approve price-protection clause templates and escalation path.
- Procurement (internal use): Ensure supplier pass-throughs mirror customer pricing windows, if applicable.
- Billing Platform (owner: Finance Ops): Implement proration calculation and generate explicit line-items.
- RevRec Processor (owner: Finance Accounting): Configure amortization schedule and perform true-ups per policy.
- Customer Success: Communicate billing changes and provide proration/explanation during onboarding.

Proration types and when to use them
-----------------------------------
1) Calendar-day proportional proration (DEFAULT)
   - Formula: (Active days in period / Days in billing period) * Monthly committed charge
   - Use when customers start/stop capacity mid-month and contract specifies calendar-month billing.

2) Full-month round-up (CONSERVATIVE)
   - Behavior: Any activation within the month bills the full month price; cancellations do not prorate.
   - Use only when explicitly agreed (e.g., promotional pricing or seat-based licensing).

3) Hourly pro rata for metered infra (PRECISION)
   - Formula: (Active hours / Total hours in billing period) * Monthly committed charge
   - Use for short-lived infrastructure experiments and on-premises start/stop events where precision is required.

4) Smoothing (SMOOTH)
   - Behavior: Convert committed annual amount into equal monthly invoices regardless of monthly usage, with annual true-up.
   - Use for enterprise customers who require predictable monthly spend. Requires clear true-up clause.

Sample proration table (billing configurations)
------------------------------------------------
| Contract Flag | Proration Method | Billing Line Item Name               | Accounting Treatment              | Notes |
|---------------|------------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------|
| PROR:CAL      | Calendar-day     | Reserved Capacity (Prorated)         | Deferred revenue -> monthly ARR  | Default for mid-month changes |
| PROR:FULL     | Full-month       | Reserved Capacity (Full Month)       | Deferred revenue full month      | Only when negotiated |
| PROR:HR       | Hourly           | Reserved Capacity (Hourly)           | Recognize as consumption or def. | For lab/onprem cases |
| SMOOTH:12M    | Smoothing-annual | Fixed Monthly Reserve (Smoothed)     | Deferred -> Amortize monthly     | Annual true-up at year-end |

Example calculations
--------------------
1) Calendar-day proration example
- Monthly committed charge: $120,000 for 1 unit (monthly)
- Start date: 2026-03-11
- Billing month: March 2026 (31 days)
- Active days: 21 (Mar 11–31 inclusive)
- Prorated invoice line: (21/31) * $120,000 = $81,290.32 -> round to cents

2) Smoothing example (12-month commit)
- Annual committed charge: $1,200,000 for 12 months
- Monthly invoice = $1,200,000 / 12 = $100,000
- True-up at contract anniversary adjusts for over/under usage via a single invoice or credit.

Contract clause templates (boilerplate language)
------------------------------------------------
1) Proration clause (calendar-day - default)
"If this agreement commences or terminates partway through a billing period, charges for the portion of the period during which the Service was active will be prorated on a calendar-day basis."

2) Price-protection clause (sample)
"Customer shall receive price protection for a period of 90 days following any price increase or amendment such that the unit rate applicable to committed units at the time of the amendment shall not exceed the rate agreed at signature for the duration of the Price-Protection Period. Any deferred or residual credits will be applied to subsequent invoices in accordance with Billing Platform rules."

Procurement & supplier alignment guidance
----------------------------------------
- When customer pricing includes price-protection or smoothing, Procurement must source equivalent supplier capacity commitments or negotiate pass-through protections to avoid negative gross margin scenarios.
- Include Supplier Clause: "Supplier shall honor contiguous billing schedules and not backdate price increases into customer-protected periods."

Billing system implementation checklist
-------------------------------------
1) Contract ingestion populates these fields: commit_start, commit_end, commit_units, proration_flag (PROR:CAL/PROR:FULL/PROR:HR/SMOOTH:XX), price_protection_window_days.
2) Billing generates discrete line items for: committed_base, prorated_adjustment, usage_overage, price_protection_credit.
3) Invoice UI must display: calculation basis (dates/hours), formula summary, and a link to the signed contract ID.
4) Automated rounding rule: round to cents after line calculation; accumulate rounding differences into a single rounding adjustment line per invoice.
5) Reconciliation: Billing must export a monthly reconciliation CSV to RevRec Processor with columns: invoice_id, contract_id, invoice_date, line_type, amount_cents, deferred_flag.

RevRec accounting rules (summary)
--------------------------------
- Committed non-contingent fees: defer and amortize ratably over the Commitment Period.
- Contingent true-up fees (usage overage billed after month): recognize when billed or when usage is deemed probable and measurable per ASC 606 judgment notes.
- Price-protection credits that are contractual obligations: treat as contra-revenue and reduce recognized revenue in the period the credit is applied.

Sample journal entries (high-level)
----------------------------------
- On invoice for smoothed monthly commitment (deferred):
  DR Accounts Receivable $100,000
  CR Deferred Revenue $100,000

- Monthly amortization (recognize revenue):
  DR Deferred Revenue $100,000
  CR Revenue - Reserved Capacity $100,000

- True-up invoice for overage (usage-based recognized when billed):
  DR Accounts Receivable $20,000
  CR Revenue - Usage $20,000

Operational procedures for end-of-period true-up
------------------------------------------------
1) At T+3 business days after period close, Billing exports usage vs commitment delta for contracts with PROR:CAL or SMOOTH flags.
2) Finance Ops runs validation scripts to ensure sample size and outliers flagged (top 1% of deltas auto-escalate).
3) RevRec Processor posts true-up invoices within 10 business days.
4) Any credits exceeding $50k must be reviewed by Finance Director before issuance.

Monitoring and alerts
---------------------
- KPI: Monthly true-up variance rate (target < 2% of committed revenue).
- Alert: If a single contract true-up delta > $150k or > 25% of monthly invoice, trigger Deal Desk + Finance Ops review.
- Dashboard metrics: committed ARR, monthly smoothed invoiced ARR, month-to-date utilization, pending credits.

Escalation matrix
-----------------
1) Billing discrepancy <= $5k: Billing Ops to handle, customer notified within 5 business days.
2) $5k < discrepancy <= $50k: Finance Ops + Customer Success; issue resolution within 15 business days.
3) > $50k or legal ambiguity: Escalate to Finance Director + Legal + Sales Lead; target resolution 30 business days.

Edge cases and FAQs
-------------------
Q: How do we handle mid-period contract amendments that increase committed units?
A: For increases: newly committed units are prorated from amendment effective date unless smoothing is explicitly chosen. Price-protection windows apply per the amendment language.

Q: Are refunds permitted for early termination?
A: Refunds only if the contract includes an early-termination refund clause. Otherwise, unused commitments remain non-refundable and are recognized per contract terms; provide CRO-approved exceptions via Deal Desk.

Rollout and adoption plan
-------------------------
1) Pilot with three large enterprise customers on smoothing and calendar-day proration (Q2 2026).
2) Update Contract Templates and Sales Playbook to include proration_flag guidance (release to Sales: 2026-04-01).
3) Billing Platform feature deploy: proration_line_items, smoothing_mode, price_protection_window (target 2026-04-15).
4) Full rollout after two billing cycles with pilot customers and sign-off from Finance Accounting (target 2026-06-01).

Appendix A — Sample SQL (pseudocode) to compute calendar-day prorate
-------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT
  contract_id,
  invoice_month,
  ROUND((active_days::decimal / days_in_month) * monthly_charge_cents) AS prorated_amount_cents
FROM (
  SELECT
    c.contract_id,
    date_trunc('month', i.invoice_date) AS invoice_month,
    GREATEST(0, LEAST(c.commit_end, i.month_end) - GREATEST(c.commit_start, i.month_start) + 1) AS active_days,
    EXTRACT(day FROM i.month_end - i.month_start) + 1 AS days_in_month,
    c.monthly_charge_cents
  FROM contract_table c
  JOIN invoice_month_table i ON i.month = date_trunc('month', generate_series(c.commit_start, c.commit_end, '1 month'::interval))
) t;

Appendix B — Suggested negotiation checklist (one-line items)
-------------------------------------------------------------
- Confirm proration method and set proration_flag in CRM;
- Confirm price-protection window length;
- Confirm smoothing requested and true-up cadence;
- Document supplier pass-through risk;
- Tag contract for Finance review if price_protection_window > 180 days;
- Confirm invoice visibility requirements for the customer (line-level detail).

Contacts and owners
-------------------
- Document owner: Aisha Raman (Finance Ops)
- Billing Platform owner: Devon Patel (Finance Ops)
- RevRec owner: Thomas Li (Accounting)
- Legal reviewer: Marina Ortega

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-10: Initial draft by Aisha Raman
- 2026-02-24: Reviewed by Thomas Li and Marina Ortega; added reconciliation exports
- 2026-03-01: Published after Finance Director sign-off

title: Fidelity Budget Scheduler and Sweep Catalog
content:
Fidelity Budget Scheduler and Sweep Catalog

Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the Fidelity Budget Scheduler (FBS) and a canonical sweep catalog used by Applied ML to run reproducible, cost-aware evaluation sweeps across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. FBS translates business/engineering priorities and monetary/token budgets into concrete eval-harness jobs with fidelity profiles, quantization constraints, and scheduling SLAs.

Scope: covers policy, fidelity bands, scheduling heuristics, operational runbook for failed/slow sweeps, CLI examples, and integration notes for the eval-orch and probe-farm services. Does NOT prescribe model-specific metrics or threshold values — those belong in the model onboarding acceptance matrix.

Motivation

- We run many sweep types: smoke checks, stability regressions, quantized regressions, adversarial probes, and large coverage sweeps. Each has different cost and timeliness requirements.
- Teams have limited eval budgets; FBS ensures predictable spend and repeatable coverage by mapping "budget bands" to fidelity profiles and resource classes.
- FBS reduces ad-hoc eval sprawl, decreases wasted compute on low-value probes, and creates repeatable signals for rollouts and regressions.

Definitions

- Sweep: a collection of eval jobs for a given prompt set, split into slices.
- Fidelity Profile: a named set of evaluation knobs (seeds, candidate counts, adversarial augmentation, multi-turn depth).
- Budget Band: a named cost/time envelope (micro, small, full, extended).
- Eval-orch: the internal orchestrator that schedules eval-harness jobs against probe-farm compute pools.

Components

1) Fidelity Profiles (canonical):
   - low-fidelity: single-seed, 1 candidate, deterministic sampling; used for quick smoke checks and CI gating.
   - medium-fidelity: 3 seeds, top-3 candidates, light adversarial probes on high-priority slices.
   - high-fidelity: 5+ seeds, diverse sampling, adversarial/randomized perturbations, multi-turn chaining for stateful workloads.
   - quant-check: medium fidelity but forces quantization profile matrix (int8, int8+KV, float16) and records per-slice degradation metrics.

2) Budget Bands

| Budget Band | Walltime target | Max evals (approx) | Typical use-cases | Default fidelity | Default pool |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| micro | < 1 hour | <= 50 | CI smoke, pre-commit checks | low-fidelity | shared-cpu |
| small | < 6 hours | <= 500 | Quick regression triage, PR-level checks | medium-fidelity | burst-gpu-small |
| full | < 48 hours | <= 10,000 | Release readiness, model promotion, SLA regression | high-fidelity | dedicated-gpu |
| extended | <= 7 days | <= 100k | Large-scale stability scans, multi-model ensembles | high-fidelity + extended adversarial | multi-cluster |

3) Quant Constraints
   - Sweeps that include quant-check must list allowed quant profiles in the sweep manifest and must also register a control non-quantized run.
   - Default quant profiles: int8, int8-kv, float16. For private deployments set via quant-profile-override in onboarding manifest.

Scheduling Policies

- Priority Tiers: low (background), normal (developer-triggered), high (release block). Priority determines preemption and fair-share on probe-farm.
- Admission Control: Eval-orch subjects each sweep to a cost estimate step; if the estimated compute/token cost exceeds the project's monthly budget remainder, the sweep is queued to low-priority or rejected with an explanatory error.
- Prefetching / Warmup: For full/extended bands, probe-farm reserves KV caches for models that benefit from warm-up; the scheduler charges a fixed warmup credit to the sweep budget.
- Adaptive Throttling: If latency SLOs (see Operational SLOs) are at risk, scheduler will throttle medium fidelity sweeps by reducing seeds or candidate counts automatically. This change is recorded and tagged as "fidelity-throttled" in telemetry.

Operational SLOs and Alerts

- Completion SLO: 90% of small-band sweeps should complete within the band walltime; 95% for micro.
- Cost SLO: per-sweep estimated cost should be within ±20% of final billed cost 90% of the time.
- Noise SLO: quant-check sweeps must have per-slice variance < 8% relative to non-quantized baseline or flag for manual review.

Alerting rules (examples):
- alert_eval_sweep_stalled: fired if a sweep reports no job progress for 60 minutes and has > 5 running tasks. Pager to eng-platform team.
- alert_quant_degradation: fired if quant-check variance exceeds Noise SLO on >= 3 high-priority slices. Send email to model-onboarding owners and applied-ml oncall.

Runbook: Common Procedures

1) Submit a new sweep (owner: evaluator / applied-ml engineer)\   
   1.1 Create sweep manifest (YAML) with: name, prompt-set, slices-file (s3://), budget-band, fidelity-profile, quant-profiles (optional), related-release-id.
   1.2 Run local cost estimate: `redwood-eval estimate --manifest sweep.yaml` and confirm.
   1.3 Submit: `redwood-eval run --manifest sweep.yaml` or via eval-orch UI.
\2) Sweep stuck in queued state > 2h (owner: eng-platform oncall)\   
   2.1 Check eval-orch logs: `kubectl logs deploy/eval-orch -n evals --since=2h`.
   2.2 Check probe-farm pool usage: `probe-farmctl pool-status`.
   2.3 If blocked by budget, inform owner and suggest lowering fidelity or scheduling off-peak window.
\3) Quant-check failure (owner: applied-ml / model owner)\   
   3.1 Review per-slice reports in S3 (path printed in sweep metadata).
   3.2 If degradation crosses thresholds, mark the model version as QUANT-RISK and open a regression triage ticket using template `quant-regression-template` with links to artifacts.

Triage Playbook for Regression Signals

- Initial signal: failing slices from high-fidelity sweep or a spike in error-rate in production telemetry mapped to eval slices.
- Fast path: run a targeted small-band sweep using the failing slice set with quant-check and an unquantized baseline; if the failure reproduces, escalate to causal-regression team and attach sweep manifest and job ids.
- Bisect: use the automated-regression-bisect assistant (see related_pages) to isolate commit/manifest changes.

CLI Examples

1) Micro smoke sweep\

```
redwood-eval run --name smoke-latest --prompt-set s3://prompts/smoke.yaml --budget-band micro --fidelity low-fidelity
```

2) Quant-aware small sweep\

```
redwood-eval run --name quant-check-salesbot --prompt-set s3://prompts/salesbot/slices.csv --budget-band small --fidelity quant-check --quant-profiles int8,int8-kv
```

Kubernetes job snippet (simplified)

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: eval-sweep-quant-check
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: eval-runner
        image: registry.redwood.internal/eval-runner:stable
        args: ["--manifest", "/manifests/sweep.yaml"]
      restartPolicy: Never

Integration Notes

- Link to evaluator-sdk adapters: sweeps must use the standard evaluator-interchange-format (see evaluator-interchange-format doc) so downstream analysis and dashboards can aggregate metrics.
- For Private deployments: the sweep manifest must include `data-plane: private` and quant-profile overrides must be declared. Onboarding checklist requires a smoke-run on a staging cluster before production sweeps.

Acceptance Criteria for Promoting a Sweep Template to the Catalog

- Reproducibility: template produces the same top-level slice pass/fail on 3 independent runs within tolerance.
- Cost estimate accuracy: final cost within 20% of estimate for >= 5 historical runs.
- Observability: per-slice telemetry, logging, and artifact retention metadata present in manifest.

Appendix A — Sweep Manifest (example)

```yaml
name: "salesbot-quant-check-2026-02"
prompt_set: "s3://prompts/salesbot/primary.yaml"
slices_file: "s3://prompts/salesbot/slices.csv"
budget_band: "small"
fidelity_profile: "quant-check"
quant_profiles: ["int8","int8-kv"]
related_release: "release-2026-03"
retention_days: 30
```

Appendix B — Mapping to Eval-harness Jobs

- The scheduler expands the manifest into groups of eval-harness jobs by slice shard. Each job is labeled with `sweep=<name>`, `band=<band>`, `fidelity=<profile>` and writes artifacts to `s3://eval-artifacts/<team>/<sweep-name>/<job-id>/`.

Notes and Future Work

- Planned: automated fidelity annealing (start high-fidelity on critical slices, automatically degrade non-orthogonal slices after X% progress to save budget).
- Investigate: per-tenant cost attribution so teams can be auto-billed for extended sweeps.

Ownership

- Product steward: Applied ML (eval orchestration)
- Implementation: eng-platform (eval-orch, probe-farm)
- Oncall / Triage: applied-ml oncall for model regressions; eng-platform oncall for scheduling/infra issues.

Related Pages

- See: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/eval-mesh-and-workload-fingerprinting-2026
- See: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/automated-regression-bisect-and-blame-assistant-2026

Document History

- 2026-02-15: created by Aisha Kapoor
- 2026-03-01: added quant-check band and acceptance criteria

title: Field Evaluation Fast-Path and Rollback Playbook
content:
Field Evaluation Fast-Path and Rollback Playbook

Overview
========
This playbook defines a minimal-latency, low-friction 'fast path' for promoting model candidates to limited field traffic and the precise automated and manual rollback procedures that must be applied when regressions or infrastructure anomalies are detected. It combines evaluation harness checks, prompt-set sampling, quality guardrails, and quantization verification into a single operational flow so teams can ship changes quickly while bounding user impact.

Scope and applicability
----------------------
- Applies to: model promotions for Redwood Hosted and Dedicated flows where a model variant is introduced as a canary (traffic <= 5%).
- Not covered: full-scale (>=50%) rollouts, private air-gapped on-prem packages (see onprem-packaging docs).
- Intended audience: Applied ML engineers, runtime owners, SRE oncall.

Definitions
-----------
- Fast-path: a shortened promotion pipeline intended for low-risk model updates (bug fixes, quant tweaks, minor prompt-template changes).
- Canary cohort: a small, deterministic subset (~1–5%) of live traffic selected by routing policy (user sampling or route-based split).
- Regression: any measured drop below defined quality guardrail thresholds or breach of latency/cost SLOs for the canary cohort.

Prerequisites and gating checks
-------------------------------
Before triggering fast-path promotion, the candidate must have passed all items below:
1) Offline eval harness smoke: unit tests, 3 synthetic slices, and at least one few-shot stress benchmark (see eval-harness checklist).
2) Quantization sanity (if applicable): per-workload quant profile applied and run for 2k in-distribution samples with top-k accuracy delta <= configured budget (default 0.6%).
3) Prompt-set sanity: prioritized prompt subset (N=500) passes coverage/edge checks including tokenization stability and injection-resilience.
4) Telemetry hooks: trace IDs, request provenance, and per-request scoring metadata must be emitted by runtime (see runbook snippet below).
5) Canary config declared in deployment manifest and approved by owning team.

Ownership matrix
----------------
- Model Owner: prepares candidate artifacts, offline eval results, quant profile.
- Runtime Owner: validates tracer and metrics integration; creates canary routing.
- SRE Oncall: watches health dashboards during rollout window; empowered to trigger automated rollback.
- Applied ML (on-call): performs prompt-level triage and quality assessment.

Fast-path rollout procedure (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------------
1) Pre-flight (T-30m):
   - Verify rollout window on calendar and oncall availability.
   - Confirm alerting receiver list and escalation policy.
   - Attach the candidate release notes and quick-check results to the rollout ticket.
2) Canary enable (T0):
   - Update routing policy: add candidate variant with weight 1% (or route by hash to specific user cohort).
   - Start a 15-minute passive monitoring phase before enabling synthetic probing.
3) Probe + score (T+15m):
   - Launch synthetic probe job that replays 1k high-priority prompts sampled from the prioritized prompt-set.
   - Supply probes with annotated golden outputs where available and compute the following metrics: Quality Score (Q), Response Stability Index (RSI), and Safety Flag rate (S).
4) Evaluation windows (T+15m..T+60m):
   - 15 minute early window: if any metric breaches critical thresholds (see thresholds table) trigger immediate rollback.
   - 60 minute extended window: require metrics to remain within warning thresholds for automated promotion to 5% or handoff for broader rollout.
5) Promotion or rollback:
   - If all checks pass for 60 minutes, optionally promote to 5% and repeat observation. If checks fail, execute rollback (automated path preferred).

Automated rollback triggers and thresholds
-----------------------------------------
- These thresholds are minimums; product or compliance teams may impose tighter limits.

| Class | Metric | Immediate rollback threshold | Warning threshold | Notes |
|-------|--------|-----------------------------:|------------------:|-------|
| Quality | Quality Score (Q) delta vs baseline | >= 2.0% absolute drop | 0.8% drop | Q is a weighted F1/semantic-similarity composite for the prompt-set. |
| Safety | Safety Flag rate | > 0.2% absolute increase | > 0.05% increase | Includes toxic/PII/excess-leak flags from guardrail classifiers. |
| Latency | P95 request latency | > 250 ms increase | > 100 ms increase | Measured server-side, region-specific. |
| Error | 5xx rate | > 0.1% absolute | > 0.02% | Includes malformed responses and rejection-rate increases. |
| Cost | Per-token cost | > 20% increase | > 8% | For quantized vs baseline comparison. |

Alerting and observability configuration (examples)
--------------------------------------------------
- Dashboards: canary model panel, per-prompt drift stream, error-by-slice heatmap, latency heatmap by region.
- Prometheus alert examples (PromQL):
  - Quality drop (pseudo):
    sum(rate(quality_failures_total{model="candidate",cohort="canary"}[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total{model="candidate",cohort="canary"}[5m])) > 0.02
  - Latency spike (P95):
    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{model="candidate"}[5m])) by (le)) - histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{model="baseline"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.25

Rollback procedures
-------------------
Automated rollback (preferred):
1) Alert triggers automated rollback lambda which immediately flips routing weight of candidate to 0 and routes traffic back to baseline variant.
2) System creates a rollback incident ticket with prefilled diagnostic context (metrics snapshots, top failing prompts, recent traces).
3) Notification posted to #oncall-alerts and relevant team Slack channels.

Manual rollback (if automation unavailable):
1) Runtime owner runs: 
   rwdctl rollout set-weight --model candidate --variant v42 --weight 0 --reason "fast-path rollback"
2) Confirm traffic normalized and watch for rate/latency stabilization for 10 minutes.
3) SRE records incident and attaches diagnostic artifacts.

Triage checklist after rollback
------------------------------
- Capture the top 200 canary requests (persist to secure bucket) and run them through: baseline, candidate, and offline eval harness.
- Produce a prompt-failure inventory that categorizes failures into: Safety, Coherence, Hallucination, Latency/Timeout, Infrastructure error.
- Run automated blame-assistant bisect if regression appears after a baseline-within-memory window change (see automated-regression-bisect doc).
- If quantization implicated, revert to float variant and re-run the quant sanity job.

Prompt-set and evaluation artifacts to attach to the rollback ticket
------------------------------------------------------------------
- Prioritized prompt set subset (500 samples) used for probes.
- Top 200 live canary requests (scrubbed for PII) and the annotated human labels if available.
- Offline eval harness logs and per-slice metrics.
- Quant profile metadata and tensor-level warnings (if used).

Quantization-specific guardrails
-------------------------------
- If candidate uses an updated quant profile: require a targeted micro-benchmark: 5k tokens replay with token-level divergence tracking, and a top-k token stability metric.
- Rollback if token-stability > 1.0% or hallucination proxies spike.

Runbook snippets and tooling
---------------------------
- Example canary YAML (deployment manifest):
  ---
  canary:
    variant: v42
    weight: 0.01
    sampling: user_hash_mod_100 < 1
    probe_job: probe-scheduler/field-probe-v42
    observability_tags:
      cohort: canary
      owner: sofia-patel

- CLI quick commands:
  - Promote to 1%: rwdctl deploy promote --model my-model --variant v42 --weight 0.01
  - Force rollback: rwdctl deploy promote --model my-model --variant baseline --weight 1.0 --reason "rollback"

Post-incident learnings and permanent actions
---------------------------------------------
1) If rollback was due to model quality: create a remediation PR in the model-onboarding tracker with items: prompt-set gaps, new unit tests, and expanded synthetic probes.
2) If rollback was due to infra: raise an SRE hotfix ticket for runtime or kernel-level failure and schedule a game-day if recurrence >2x/month.
3) If quantization is repeatedly implicated: add the workload to the per-workload quant tuner queue and require a shadow rollout before field fast-path.

Safety and compliance notes
--------------------------
- All captured canary requests used for triage must be scrubbed by the automated PII scrubber before attaching to tickets.
- If customer-sensitive content is present, route materials to the security-and-compliance team and mark the incident as restricted.

Appendix: quick play summary (cheat-sheet)
-----------------------------------------
1) Preconditions: offline smoke ✅, quant sanity ✅, tracer hooks ✅.
2) Start canary: 1% weight, passive monitor 15m.
3) Run probes: 1k prioritized prompts, compute Q/RSI/S.
4) If any critical thresholds breached -> auto rollback.
5) If stable 60m -> promote to 5% and repeat.

Contacts and escalation
----------------------
- Applied ML oncall: #applied-ml-oncall, pager: pageduty/team-applied-ml
- Runtime owner oncall: #runtime-sre, pager: pageduty/runtime-sre
- Product escalation: product-ops@redwood.ai

Related reading and links
------------------------
- Promotion readiness and synthetic safety playbook (internal): /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/promotion-readiness-synthetic-quant-safety-playbook-2026
- Automated regression bisect guide: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/automated-regression-bisect-and-blame-assistant-2026
- Quant profile synthesis notes: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/quant-profile-synthesis-and-safety-playbook-2024

Document revision history
------------------------
- 2025-11-12: Created by Sofia Patel.
- 2025-12-18: Added automated rollback lambda example (review: Ethan Liu).
- 2026-01-09: Tightened thresholds for safety flags and added PII scrubber requirement.

title: NVLink interconnect degradation and remediation playbook
content:
NVLink interconnect degradation and remediation playbook

Summary:
This page describes symptoms, detection signals, triage steps, and remediation actions for NVLink / GPU interconnect degradation observed in the runtime fleet. NVLink issues typically present as increased tail latency and elevated per-request GPU-to-GPU copy times for sharded models or multi-GPU kernels. The goal of this playbook is to provide a repeatable oncall and engineering triage path, automated mitigations where safe, and guidance for permanent fixes or vendor escalation.

Scope and impact:
- Affects multi-GPU model shards, cross-GPU KV cache fills, and kernels that perform peer-to-peer communication (e.g., sharded attention, distributed KV cache updates).
- Typical customer impact: 99.9th percentile generation latency spikes (5x–20x), increased error rates due to kernel timeouts (grpc errors, TPU-like watchdog resets), and occasional node-level GPU panic requiring node restart.
- Known affected subsystems: gpu-dispatcher, shard-orchestrator, kvcache-sync-job, and the runtime kernel layer.

When to use this playbook:
1. Alert fires: "nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 10ms for 5m" or "gpu_p2p_error_rate > 0"
2. Tail latency regressions correlated with multi-GPU allocations in Grafana panel 'Model Shard Latency by Node'
3. Post-deploy increase in intra-node memcpy or nvlink error counters in node exporter

Detection signals (ranked):
1. Telemetry (high confidence):
   - PromQL: sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_count[5m])) > 0.01 // mean > 10ms
   - PromQL alert: increase(gpu_nvlink_link_error_total[10m]) > 0
   - Perf counters: PCIe DMA stall events and increased memcpy latency in per-kernel telemetry
2. Runtime traces:
   - Trace span 'p2p-copy' duration spike on request trace
   - Traces show 'wait-for-peer' subspan dominated in GPU scheduler traces
3. Node metrics:
   - nvlink_utilization / nvlink_throughput drop while local GPU utilization remains high

Immediate oncall triage (0–15 minutes):
1. Confirm alert context and scope:
   - Determine affected node(s) and model(s) using 'alert.labels.node' and 'alert.annotations.models'.
   - Run quick queries: 
     - kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
     - prometheus query: topk(10, rate(nvlink_transfer_time_sum[1m]) / rate(nvlink_transfer_time_count[1m]))
2. If the issue is isolated to a single node and no kernel panics: divert new multi-GPU allocations off the node.
   - Command: curl -X POST https://internal-scheduler/api/v1/drain-node -d '{"node":"<node>","reason":"nvlink_degradation"}'
3. If kernel panics / GPU watchdog resets observed: escalate to SRE and set short maintenance window for node reboot.
   - Oncall runbook: run 'sudo nv_peer_sync_check.sh' (see diagnostics below) before reboot; collect logs to /tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-<timestamp>.tar.gz

Automated mitigations (safe defaults):
- Auto-fallback policy (configured in dispatcher): when nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 10ms for a node for 3m, do not schedule multi-GPU shards to the node; allow single-GPU fallbacks. See 'fallback-routing-config' below.
- KV cache sync throttle: reduce kvcache-sync parallelism from 64 -> 8 for nodes with nvlink anomalies. Controlled by the 'kvcache.sync_parallelism_per_node' feature flag.

Deep triage (15–90 minutes):
1. Reproduce telemetry in isolation: run a synthetic cross-GPU memcpy microbenchmark against the node:
   - test tool: /opt/runtime/tools/p2p_transfer_test --size 256MB --iters 200 --target-node <node>
   - Expected baseline: p2p latency median < 2ms, p95 < 5ms. If p95 > 10ms, then NVLink degradation confirmed.
2. Collect GPU and NVLink counters:
   - nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 -o DUMP > /tmp/gpu-dmon-<ts>.log
   - nvlink error counters (via nvidia-smi nvlink) or vendor tool: nvlink-smi --show-errors > /tmp/nvlink-errors-<ts>.log
3. Kernel-level profiling: capture a short runtime profile (10–30s) with tracing enabled:
   - curl -X POST http://localhost:15000/api/v1/trace/start -d '{"duration_s":30, "include":"p2p-copy,kernel-launch"}'
   - Save trace: /tmp/trace-nvlink-<ts>.json and open in TraceUI. Look for long queues at 'gpu-mem-copy' spans.
4. Check OS-level messages: dmesg, kernel logs may show peer-to-peer DMA errors or nvlink faults.
   - sudo journalctl -u nvidia-node-manager -n 500 | grep -i nvlink

Diagnostics scripts and snippets:
- nv_peer_sync_check.sh (runs basic nvlink and p2p checks):
  #!/bin/bash
  node=$1
  timestamp=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
  nvidia-smi nvlink --query-gpu=all > /tmp/nvlink-summary-${timestamp}.txt
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 -c 10 > /tmp/gpu-dmon-${timestamp}.log
  /opt/runtime/tools/p2p_transfer_test --size 32MB --iters 50 --target-node ${node} > /tmp/p2p-test-${timestamp}.log
  tar -czf /tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-${timestamp}.tar.gz /tmp/nvlink-summary-${timestamp}.txt /tmp/gpu-dmon-${timestamp}.log /tmp/p2p-test-${timestamp}.log
  echo "/tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-${timestamp}.tar.gz"

Recommended alert definitions (Prometheus):
- Alert: NVLink_P2P_Latency_High
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_bucket[5m])) by (le,node)) > 0.01
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page, subsystem: runtime }
  annotations: { runbook: "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/nvlink-interconnect-degradation-and-remediation-2026" }

Fallback routing config (example YAML):
- name: fallback-routing-config
  version: 2
  rules:
    - when: nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 0.01 and nvlink_error_rate > 0
      action: avoid_multi_gpu_on_node
      ttl: 15m
      owner: runtime-scheduler-team

Operational thresholds and SLO impact guidance:
- If a single node exhibits nvlink p95 > 10ms for > 10 minutes, mark node as 'degraded' and avoid new multi-GPU allocations.
- If >= 3 nodes in a single AZ show degradation for 15m, open an incident (sev2).
- SLO impact: a single degraded node hosting large model shards can increase per-request cost by 30% and tail latency by up to 10x for affected customers.

Permanent remediation checklist (owner: hardware-ops / infra-eng):
1. Validate hardware: reseat NVLink bridges, check physical connectors, and run vendor diagnostics.
2. Firmware: ensure GPUs have vendor-recommended firmware revision (vendor_firmware >= 2025.12.1).
3. OS driver: verify NVIDIA driver >= 535.x where known nvlink fixes exist.
4. Replace unit: if nvlink errors persist after reseat + firmware + driver, schedule GPU or node replacement with priority 'P1 hardware' queue.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall SRE (first): notify via #sre-runtime and tag runtime-oncall (pager if sev1).
- Hardware ops: if nvlink error counters persist after reboot/resync, create ECC ticket with vendor and include diagnostics tarball.
- Product/Customer Success: if major customers are affected, inform assigned CSM and prepare a customer-facing incident summary.

Post-incident analysis and permanent mitigations (RCA template):
1. Timeline of detection, mitigations, and service impact.
2. Root cause hypothesis (hardware / firmware / OS driver / workload pattern).
3. Evidence: telemetry graphs, diagnostics tarball, vendor response.
4. Action items with owners and ETA (firmware rollouts, alert tuning, scheduler constraints).

Appendix: Useful queries and dashboards
- Grafana panels: 'NVLink topology and errors', 'Model shard p2p latency by node', 'KVCache cross-gpu sync latency'.
- PromQL quicklist:
  - nvlink_error_total: increase(gpu_nvlink_link_error_total[10m])
  - nvlink_p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_bucket[5m])) by (le,node))
  - p2p_wait_traces: sum(rate(runtime_p2p_wait_seconds_count[5m])) by (node) / sum(rate(runtime_p2p_wait_seconds_sum[5m])) by (node)

Contacts and ownership:
- Primary: runtime-infra (pager: pagerduty runtime-infra)
- Secondary: gpu-hardware-ops (slack: @gpu-hw-ops)
- Documentation owner: Lina Park (lina.park@redwood.ai)

Change history:
- 2026-02-14 (Lina Park): initial draft
- 2026-06-07 (Marcus Chen): added automated fallback policy and alert examples
- 2026-11-03 (Aisha Bello): updated firmware and driver recommended versions, clarified diagnostic commands

Notes and references:
- Vendor NVLink troubleshooting guide (internal link stored in hardware-ops drive)
- See related runbooks: 'gpu-affinity-and-eviction-strategies', 'gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook' for mitigation overlap.

End of document.

title: Session-aware cost tuning playbook
content:
Session-aware cost tuning playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines the product guidance, internal runbook, and pricing heuristics for session-aware cost tuning. It targets teams building conversational or session-based integrations that need predictable per-session economics while preserving latency and quality SLOs. The document covers when to choose session-aware pricing, how to compute per-session effective cost, recommended fidelity presets and discounts, telemetry signals to monitor, and a staged rollout plan for Hosted and Dedicated customers.

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable method to estimate, present, and bill per-session costs for conversational products.
- Give product and sales concrete presets and negotiation levers for customers migrating from pure per-token billing to session-pricing.
- Ensure fidelity and latency SLOs are respected with clear fallback and rollback steps.

Scope:
- Applies to: Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Redwood Optimize cost recommendations when sessions are the primary billing unit.
- Not in scope: One-off batch embedding jobs, pure vector store billing, or marketplace third-party resale.

When to apply session-aware pricing:
1. Customer wants predictable monthly cost for interactive experiences with variable tokens per conversation.
2. High frequency short sessions (e.g., chat widgets) where token variance creates billing unpredictability.
3. Customers requesting fidelity guarantees per session (response consistency SLO).

Key definitions:
- Session: A logical conversational interaction tied to a session_id maintained by the integrator for up to 30 minutes of inactivity.
- Session unit: Billing unit representing an allocated compute & fidelity envelope for the session (includes kv-cache usage, warmup, and reserved micro-burst capacity).
- Fidelity preset: A named profile (low/medium/high) mapping to model variant, quantization, and max token budget.

Pricing model variants (recommended):
- Fixed session price: flat price per session unit (best for small/consistent interactions).
