title: Borealis Health — Data Protections & Training Assurance
content:
Borealis Health — Data Protections & Training Assurance

Focused security review covering SOC 2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO, audit logs, encryption/KMS, data residency and explicit confirmation that customer prompts/content are not used to train models. Action items include sharing certs, KMS diagrams, questionnaire and scheduling pilot VPC test.
SOC 2 Type II evidence; ISO 27001 status; SSO/SAML and Okta integration; RBAC roles and least privilege; audit log retention/export; data residency options and region pinning; encryption at rest and in transit, KMS/BYOK/HSM; prompt retention and 'no training' assurance on customer data; PII/PHI handling and HIPAA/BAA conversation; retention policies and ability to opt-out of analytics/usage logging; legal DPA and contractual controls
[00:00] Alex Mercer: alright folks thanks for joining, we have about 40 minutes, um, quick roll call — Alex from Redwood, Samira and Jin on engineering. Priya, Ethan, Marta and Liam from Borealis — can you hear us okay?
[00:08] Priya Desai: yes loud and clear, thanks. we wanted to focus this session on two things — how data flows, and a hard confirmation that customer content won't be used to train models. also a couple follow up Qs on encryption and audit logs.
[00:18] Samira Khan: great, we'll start with the high-level compliance pack — Redwood has a SOC 2 Type II audit in the last 12 months, and an ISO 27001 certification, both available. i'll drop links after the call.
[00:28] Marta Alvarez: is that full cert or just a gap report? we need evidence for our procurement.
[00:32] Alex Mercer: good call — it's the full Type II report and the ISO cert; we can provide redacted copies and the auditor letter.
[00:38] Ethan Ross: redaction is fine but we need the AICPA attestation page, ok.
[00:42] Jin Wu: on technical controls, i'll cover auth, keys, and logs — on auth we support SAML 2.0 SSO (Okta, OneLogin), SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC with pre-defined roles — admin, developer, observer, billing — and custom roles via the console.
[00:56] Priya Desai: for roles can you do scoped roles to limit HIPA... HIPAA-relevant scopes? we need least privilege for PHI access.
[01:04] Samira Khan: yes you can scope routes per role; for private deployments we can map to customer groups and enforce segregation. there's also field-level redaction in the request/response pipeline if needed.
[01:15] Liam O'Neal: quick q on SSO lifecycles — if a user leaves, how immediate is deprovisioning? we integrate with SCIM so removal is usually TTL under a minute for tokens to expire, active sessions can be revoked from console. there is some lag for long-lived sessions but revocation is available.
[01:33] Alex Mercer: next, encryption and KMS — we encrypt at transit (TLS 1.2/1.3) and at rest using AES-256. customers can use Redwood-managed keys or bring-your-own-key (BYOK) with a KMS integration; for the strictest controls we support HSM-backed keys and customer-managed keys in supported clouds.
[01:49] Marta Alvarez: do we rotate keys automatically? where are the keys stored when BYOK is used?
[01:54] Jin Wu: rotation is supported and auditable. with BYOK the key material stays in your KMS/HSM and we only receive a wrapped key or allow remote crypto operations depending on the integration. that way raw key material isn't stored in Redwood.
[02:07] Priya Desai: can you confirm that customer data is not used to train models? in writing is preferable — we need contractual assurance.
[02:15] Alex Mercer: short version: we do not use customer prompts or content to train or fine-tune models for the hosted product, unless explicit opt-in is agreed and documented. for dedicated/private deployments the customer controls training entirely. we'll include this clause in the DPA and the security artifact bundle.
[02:33] Marta Alvarez: okay we want exact language for our legal team.
[02:36] Alex Mercer: noted — action item: we'll share the exact no-training clause.
[02:40] [00:03] Ethan Ross: you mentioned logs — what's captured in audit logs and retention?
[02:45] Samira Khan: audit logs capture login events, API calls (including route, model, token usage), key management events, and admin actions; we do not log full request/response payloads by default in audit logs for security reasons, but there's a separate request logs option for debug which is configurable and can be routed to a customer's SIEM.
[03:05] Liam O'Neal: retention windows? default vs configurable?
[03:08] Jin Wu: default audit log retention is 90 days on hosted, exportable as compressed JSON/CSV. for Dedicated/Private you can set retention to match your policy and we have a facility to forward logs to your storage or SIEM (S3, Splunk, Datadog).
[03:19] Priya Desai: we need immutable audit trails for 7 years for certain workflows — do you support WORM-style retention or append-only logs?
[03:26] Samira Khan: for hosted it's more limited; for Dedicated/Private we can support write-once storage via your cloud S3 with object lock or by routing into a third-party archive. we'll detail the architecture in the follow-up docs.
[03:38] Marta Alvarez: what about data residency — is there region pinning? we can't send PHI outside the EU for some workloads.
[03:44] Alex Mercer: yes region pinning is supported on Dedicated and Private. Hosted API has regional endpoints and we can pin volumes to EU regions for enterprise plans; for absolute residency guarantees we recommend Private deployment in your VPC.
[03:56] Priya Desai: the big one for us — prompt retention and PII/PHI handling. what retention is applied to raw prompts and responses?
[04:05] Jin Wu: by default, request logs are stored for 30 days for diagnostics; prompts/responses used for telemetry are pseudo-anonymized and aggregated. however, if you enable "no retention" mode on your account or choose Private, we can disable storage of prompts entirely. we also provide a redaction API to mask PII before it leaves your environment.
[04:24] Ethan Ross: pseudo-anonymized — can you clarify? how reversible is that?
[04:27] Samira Khan: pseudo-anonymization removes direct identifiers and hashes unique tokens, but it's not guaranteed irreversible for highly structured PHI; for strict PHI handling you should use redaction + Private deployment or pre-processing on your side.
[04:41] Priya Desai: HIPAA/BBA — will Redwood sign a BAA for the hosted product?
[04:47] Alex Mercer: Redwood can sign a BAA for Dedicated and Private deployments; for hosted we have customers on a per-case basis — we need to take it through legal review. we'll include our standard DPA and then escalate BAA discussion with legal.
[04:58] Marta Alvarez: ok please flag that as high priority.
[05:01] [00:05] Liam O'Neal: on-the-fly question: what about model fallbacks and routing? if a request is routed to a cheaper model, does that change data handling assumptions?
[05:08] Jin Wu: good catch — routing policies are configured per-tenant. all models in the catalog follow the same data handling rules; if you route to external, third-party model providers (not in Redwood) we make that explicit and the contract will reflect their training policies.
[05:22] Priya Desai: are there any telemetry tags that leak PII into ML features?
[05:26] Samira Khan: telemetry is token-level counts and latency metrics; we don't include prompt text in telemetry. that said, we maintain strict controls — but we will add a note about turning off telemetry for your tenant during the pilot.
[05:38] Alex Mercer: quick demo offer — Jin can show a live audit log export to S3 and we'll simulate a redaction rule later. would you want this in the pilot?
[05:46] Ethan Ross: yes, that helps. we want to see the export shape to map to our SIEM.
[05:50] Marta Alvarez: also need the exact legal clause re: no training + DPA language.
[05:54] Alex Mercer: understood. we'll attach the clause and the SOC/ISO artifacts.
[05:59] [00:06] Priya Desai: one final Q — where are backups stored and how are they encrypted?
[06:04] Jin Wu: backups are stored in encrypted object storage, same region as your primary data plane unless you opt for cross-region replication. backups are encrypted with keys under your control if BYOK is enabled.
[06:16] Liam O'Neal: for the pilot we want a VPC private deployment and BYOK with rotation every 90 days, and audit logs exported to our Splunk instance.
[06:25] Alex Mercer: noted — we'll scope that in the pilot plan.
[06:28] Marta Alvarez: legal will review the DPA + BAA possibility, i'll turn around a redline if needed.
[06:33] Alex Mercer: cool, recap and next steps: we'll send SOC2/ISO, KMS diagrams, no-training clause, and set the pilot date. any blockers?
[06:42] Priya Desai: no blockers, just need the docs to close procurement. thanks.
[06:46] Alex Mercer: great, thank you everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments and schedule. bye.
[06:50] [END]
Redwood to share latest SOC 2 Type II report and ISO cert by 2025-06-20
Customer to send completed security questionnaire by 2025-06-24
Schedule hands-on pilot network test in VPC with BOR-Eng on 2025-06-30
Alex Mercer - share SOC2 + ISO artifacts (2025-06-20)
Samira Khan - provide KMS key flow diagram and HSM/BYOK docs (2025-06-20)
Priya Desai - send completed security questionnaire and list of required compliance clauses (2025-06-24)
Jin Wu - set up short demo of audit log export to customer's SIEM (follow-up meeting)

title: Thunderbolt AI - Dedicated surge & isolation intake
content:
Thunderbolt AI - Dedicated surge & isolation intake

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lucas Ramirez (Head of Platform, Thunderbolt AI), Priya Singh (SRE), Owen Park (CTO)

Summary:
Thunderbolt AI is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private for a low-latency real-time recommendation service used in multiplayer games. Primary concerns: reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation, burst-to-4x traffic patterns during events, latency SLOs (95p < 80ms), encryption/KMS (Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 compliance, and on-prem path as contingency. They asked about failover playbooks, warm pools/prewarm behavior, and pricing for reserved nodes + burst credits.

Topics:
- Workload profile and burst patterns
- Isolation and tenancy model (hot pools, tenant fencing)
- Failover and fallback to hosted model
- Prewarm / warm pool strategies and costs
- Compliance: SOC 2, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration
- Timeline and procurement constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros—I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Ravi, our SE focused on Dedicated and Private deployments.
[00:12] Lucas: Hey Maya, hey Ravi. Lucas here, Head of Platform at Thunderbolt AI. Thanks for making time.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, SRE. We'll likely be the ones running the fist fights when things go sideways.
[00:22] Owen: Owen, CTO. I'll listen in; happy to answer higher-level questions.
[00:26] Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your peak patterns and isolation needs so we can recommend reserve sizing and failover options. Roughly 45 minutes, leave some time for next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll jump in.
[00:35] Ravi: Quick note—if it helps later I can pull up the docs for prewarming and our warm-pool cost model.

[02:05] Lucas: To give context: we run a real-time recommendation engine for a live multiplayer title. Typical traffic is low steady-state, then during tournaments/events traffic spikes 3-4x for short bursts (10-40 minutes). We need 95th percentile inference latency under 80ms for player-facing calls.
[02:25] Priya: Most requests are short sequences, 32 tokens or under, but throughput is high. We also can't have noisy neighbors; when one tenant runs training or batch jobs, it breaks our tail latency.
[03:02] Maya: Got it. Sounds like isolation and tail latency are the big ones. Have you considered Dedicated pools vs Hosted fallback model?
[03:12] Lucas: We like the economics of hosted for baseline, but we need guaranteed performance for peaks. Thinking about a dedicated reserved pool (or a warm reserved hot pool) for critical traffic and fallback to hosted API for non-critical flows.
[03:29] Ravi: That's a common pattern—dedicated for SLO-critical traffic, hosted for overflow. We support routing policies that prefer dedicated, with automatic fallback to hosted variants when capacity is exhausted. We also support model variants (quantized or smaller models) as fallbacks.

[04:10] Priya: A couple of concrete questions: how fast can you spin up burst capacity? And how does warm pool prewarm behave—do you keep GPUs hot and is there a prewarm cost?
[04:22] Ravi: Prewarm: you can configure a warm-pool size that maintains kernels and KV states warmed. There's a continuous cost for reserved warm nodes; it's cheaper than full-on spare nodes because they can be smaller or quantized for faster resume. We also offer burst credits for short bursts if you have reserved capacity. For spin-up to fully ready, warm pool to fully warmed serving path is typically under 90s; cold spin from zero can be several minutes depending on model size.
[04:51] Lucas: Ninety seconds is ok but sometimes our spikes are sudden—tournament queue opens and we get hit instantly. Can we do instant failover to hosted and still maintain the same model?
[05:04] Maya: You can. We allow routing to point to hosted model variants with compatible behavior. There will be slight differences if the hosted variant is quantized differently; we can test parity with your eval prompts.

[06:10] Owen: Security: we need KMS integration (we're on Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 Type II, SSO via Okta, and audit logs for every inference. How does Redwood handle that?
[06:24] Ravi: For Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via our KMS integrations; Azure Key Vault is supported. We can enable envelope encryption so keys never leave your control. SOC 2 artifacts and the compliance pack can be shared—I'll add them to the follow-up. Audit logs and per-route tracing are available; you can ship logs to your SIEM or retain in Redwood console.
[06:46] Priya: Do the audit logs include per-token traces or just request-level metadata? We need enough detail to debug tail cases.
[06:54] Ravi: Currently request headers, request/response sizes, latency breakdowns and model selection events are logged. Full token-level traces can be enabled in debug mode but with cost and privacy considerations; we usually advise redacting PII.

[08:12] Lucas: Another operational question—how do you enforce tenancy isolation? We want burst traffic from other tenants, or internal batch jobs from our non-prod tenant, to never impact prod.
[08:26] Ravi: Dedicated Reserved can be configured with soft or hard isolation. Hard isolation pins GPUs to your tenancy (no multi-tenancy). Soft isolation uses fenced hot pools where compute is dedicated but control plane can borrow under emergency. For strict SLAs you want hard isolation. Our hot-pool topology supports tenant fencing at node-level.
[08:50] Priya: What's the blast radius if a hardware failure occurs on a pinned node? Do you prewarm standby nodes or have automatic failover?
[08:58] Ravi: For pinned nodes we recommend N+1 standbys. There is an automated failover into standby nodes, but warm standby reduces time to recovery. If you want near-zero impact you can provision hot-standbys that are warmed and ready. That increases cost, but it's the usual trade-off.

[10:12] Lucas: Cost is a big factor—our finance team will push back on always-on hot standbys. We need guidance on sizing so we don't overcommit.
[10:21] Maya: We can do a sizing exercise. If you share typical QPS and token distribution we can model reserved node counts and warm-pool sizing. We also provide a cost/latency tradeoff sheet.
[10:33] Owen: Quick procurement note—we have a 60-day procurement cycle and prefer 12-month committed pricing for reserved capacity. Do you offer monthly vs annual commits?
[10:44] Maya: Yes, reserved commitments can be monthly or annual; annual has better pricing. We'll include both options in the pricing matrix.

[12:15] Priya: What's the difference between Dedicated and Private here? If we need on-prem later, how big a lift is migrating?
[12:26] Ravi: Private is essentially running Redwood control plane in your VPC or on-prem package. The APIs are consistent but Private brings additional network and install controls. Migration is straightforward if you keep model versions and config consistent, but there is an integration cost: networking, KMS, and potential hardware procurement. We have reference on-prem manifests and a runbook.
[12:50] Lucas: For now we're leaning Dedicated but want Private as a contingency in case regulations tighten.
[12:59] Maya: That's a common path—start on Dedicated, then move to Private if needed.

[14:05] Lucas: One more technical—how does the runtime handle KV cache across sequence continuity? We rely heavily on KV cache for context, and eviction can harm latency.
[14:18] Ravi: We manage KV cache per-session and have configurable cache retention policies. For Dedicated we can tune cache sizes and prioritize your tenant's KV allocations to reduce cache churn. There was a minor note in our docs where KV cache got transcribed as 'KV cash' sometimes in automated notes—sorry for the typo in the docs.
[14:34] Priya: Ha, yes I saw that.

[15:44] Lucas: For burst modeling—our peak bursts historically last 15-30 minutes. We might see a 3.5x spike for the first 10 minutes then taper. If we reserve nodes for average peak it's wasteful. Are there hybrid models—like partial reserved + burst credits?
[15:58] Ravi: Yes, hybrid is typical: reserve a baseline of capacity to cover median peaks and then have either warm-pool sizing to cover the initial spike and fallback to hosted for overflow, or reserve a small hot standbys pool plus burst credits. We can also suggest model quantization and smaller model variants to absorb overflow with less cost.
[16:30] Lucas: Can you run a simulated burst with our sample load so we can see tail latency behavior?
[16:40] Maya: Absolutely. If you can share a representative load generator and a small prompt corpus, we can run a hosted simulation or spin up a small Dedicated trial environment.

[18:10] Priya: Networking—we need VPC peering and strict egress controls. Does Redwood Dedicated allow VPC peering?
[18:19] Ravi: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private networking. For Private deployments you'd have full control. For Dedicated hosted in our cloud region we offer VPC peering and restricted egress with customer NAT. We'll share network diagrams.

[19:45] Owen: I want to call out parity of model behavior—if we route to hosted fallback, we must guarantee minimal semantic drift. How do you evaluate that?
[19:59] Ravi: We recommend running an eval suite—sample prompts, quality checks, and A/B comparisons. Redwood Optimize has a regression alerting feature tied to prompt sets; we can run the same tests across variants and give a delta report.

[22:05] Lucas: Are there any hard limitations on model size for warm pools? We use a 30B model currently, but might move to 70B for specific tournament features.
[22:18] Ravi: Warm pools can handle larger models but cost and warm time grow. For 70B the warm-to-ready time is longer and you may need more reserved memory. Another option is a mixed fleet: keep a smaller 30B tuned variant warmed for the common path and enable a slower 70B path only for high-value calls.

[24:30] Priya: How do you price reserved nodes vs warm pool instances? Is warm pool cheaper because of shared memory or is it just a smaller instance type?
[24:44] Maya: Warm pool pricing is typically lower than fully warmed serving nodes because they can be configured to be smaller or use quantized flavors. But the pricing varies by region and GPU type. We'll include detailed per-GPU SKU pricing in the follow-up.

[26:05] Lucas: Any vendor lock-in concerns? If we wanted to move off after a year, how easy is it?
[26:15] Ravi: We provide model and config exports; the runtime uses standard model formats. Network and infra teardown is the main work. We also support pinned model versions and recommend a data egress plan in the contract.

[28:30] Priya: Regarding SLOs—what's Redwood's SLA for Dedicated? We need specifics for uptime and p95 latency commitments.
[28:40] Maya: Dedicated SLA covers uptime of the control plane and your reserved capacity. For latency SLOs we provide guidance and per-route SLO monitoring; contractual latency SLOs are available on enterprise contracts with accepted guardrails. We'll include template SLA language.

[30:05] Lucas: Competitors—someone internally suggested DeepServe because they have pre-baked gaming optimizations. How do you compare?
[30:14] Maya: DeepServe is focused on model-side optimizations for gaming but we differentiate on unified routing, observability, and enterprise controls. We'll share a competitive brief.

[32:20] Owen: On the timeline—if we decide to move forward, what is a realistic ramp for Reserved dedicated capacity?
[32:31] Ravi: From contract to live varies; typically 4-8 weeks including network setup, model onboarding, and warm-pool tuning. If you want quicker ramp we can do a hybrid start on Hosted then flip routes once Dedicated is ready.

[34:10] Lucas: Let's cover a couple of edge cases: sudden peak plus regional outage—can you failover across regions?
[34:21] Ravi: Yes—cross-region routing and automated fallback policies exist. However, model parity and cold-start times differ. We can replicate model artifacts to a standby region; that's an added cost.

[36:00] Priya: For the technical deep dive, Priya will need details on kernel selection, quantization tradeoffs, and batching behavior at short sequences. Who should lead that?
[36:12] Maya: Ravi can lead the deep dive. He'll walk through batching heuristics, kernel choices, and KV cache tuning.

[38:05] Lucas: Can you include an initial sizing sketch in the follow-up? Even rough numbers help our procurement.
[38:14] Maya: Yes—we'll model multiple scenarios: conservative, balanced, and aggressive (covering 4x short bursts).

[40:20] Owen: We should also consider a canary strategy for rollout. We prefer canary -> phased -> full. Does Redwood Console support canary and A/B routing?
[40:32] Ravi: Yes, canary rollouts, weighted traffic routing, and automatic fallback policies are supported. You can set thresholds to auto-rollback on regression alerts.

[42:05] Lucas: Priya—anything we missed from an SRE perspective?
[42:11] Priya: Just two things: our compliance team will likely ask for network flow logs and KMS proofs; and we want a runbook for incident scenarios involving warm pool exhaustion.
[42:23] Ravi: We'll include a runbook template and network flow guidance in the follow-up.

[45:00] Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing and reserve options, KMS/SOC2 artifacts, schedule the technical 60-min deep dive with Priya and Lucas, and run a hosted burst simulation if you can share the load generator.
[45:17] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll share a load generator and sample prompts by EOB tomorrow.
[45:24] Maya: Great—we'll aim to have materials to you by Friday.

[46:50] Owen: One more thought—if we choose annual commit, is there any enterprise discount for multi-year?
[46:59] Maya: Yes, multi-year discounts are part of enterprise negotiations; we'll flag that to the sales ops team.

[48:30] Priya: Small nit: will test harnesses be able to collect p99 traces? We want to see tail behavior; p95 isn't enough for major tournaments.
[48:41] Ravi: You can enable extended tracing in test mode, but it has overhead. For p99 we usually advise dedicated profiling runs with a small set of traced sessions.

[50:05] Lucas: Ok, I think that's everything for now. Thanks all.
[50:12] Maya: Thank you, we'll follow up with docs and pricing.
[50:20] Owen: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

title: Polaris POC — Quality & Hallucination Evaluation Scope
content:
Polaris POC — Quality & Hallucination Evaluation Scope

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05T16:00:00Z
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Polaris ML), Lena Ortiz (Polaris PM), Rajiv Menon (Polaris SRE), Tasha Nguyen (Polaris Regulatory)

Summary:
A scoping session to finalize the POC quality evaluation plan: define golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination and format checks, scoring approach and load/bench timings. Customer prioritized correctness/format over lowest cost but wants latency SLOs.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and weighting (accuracy, hallucination rate, format compliance, latency, cost)
- Golden prompt set composition and seeding strategy
- Regression test harness and CI gating rules
- Hallucination detection heuristics and patching strategy
- Benchmark load profile (QPS, tokens per request, concurrency) and timeline
- Data privacy, SOC2/SSO, private vs hosted concerns

Action items (discussed): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): OK, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:10] Daniel (Polaris): hi all, Daniel here — head of ML. Lena and Rajiv are with me as well.
[00:14] Lena (Polaris PM): hi, yeah thanks, excited to get this scoped.
[00:17] Arjun (Redwood SE): great, i'll jump into the technical goals after Maya quickly frames the business objectives.
[00:22] Maya: perfect. Polaris told us earlier that the POC success criteria are mostly quality focused — accuracy, low hallucination, and strict response formatting for downstream parsers. cost and latency are secondary but still important. is that right?
[00:36] Daniel: yes that's the short version. we want the model to produce a structured JSON snippet for 95% of queries with less than 3% hallucination on named entities in the finance domain. latency target is 300–500 ms p50 for typical queries.
[00:50] Rajiv: and from infra, we need to validate sustained 40 qps with burst to 120 for 30s windows, so the benchmark plan needs to include load shape.
[01:02] Arjun: ok noted. for the quality eval itself we usually split into automated metrics and human review. automated checks cover schema/format, exact-match fields, fuzzy entity match for named entities, and a hallucination detector; human review covers edge cases and ambiguous prompts.
[01:18] Lena: when you say hallucination detector, is that a heuristic checks, or model-based? how do you measure it?
[01:24] Arjun: good question. we use a mixed approach: rule-based checks (e.g., verifying entities against a provided canonical list), embedding-similarity checks for factual claims against a small knowledge base, and optionally a secondary verification model that flags probable hallucinations. for the POC we can start with rule-based + embedding threshold, then add the verifier if needed.
[01:42] Tasha (Regulatory): will you need any raw customer data to run that? from a compliance perspective we need logs redacted and no PII leaving the VPC if we go private.
[01:50] Sofia (Redwood): we can run both hosted and private sims. for hosted we ask for anonymized examples only, and we keep logs per our SOC2 practices — we'll send the security FAQ.
[01:58] Daniel: ok we'll anonymize, but we also want to test realistic failure modes so we might provide synthetic records for edge cases.
[02:04] Arjun: perfect. partition the dataset into: golden set (200 examples), regression set (1,800 examples), and holdout (200) for final verification — that's a typical split we recommend.
[02:16] Lena: 200 golden seems small; how do you ensure it covers domain variety?
[02:20] Arjun: golden should be curated: 50 canonical positive templates, 30 tricky edge cases, 60 entity-heavy financial tasks, 30 formatting/escape cases, 30 adversarial hallucination examples. we seed golden from your top-traffic intents and historical failures.
[02:33] Daniel: sounds reasonable. for scoring, we want a single composite score to decide pass/fail for the POC, but also component metrics. can you propose a weighting?
[02:40] Maya: typical starting weighting we use is accuracy/format 50%, hallucination penalty 30%, latency/cost 20% combined, with thresholds that must be met for pass. but we can tweak per customer.
[02:50] Lena: we want format compliance to be hard fail: if JSON schema isn't followed, downstream systems break. so even if the score is high, any format schema failure should be a showstopper for that example.
[02:59] Arjun: agree. we'll implement hard gating on schema checks: examples failing schema get flagged and excluded from automated composite score but counted as failures in the report.
[03:09] Rajiv: on hallucination measurement — you mentioned entity canonical lists. we can provide a names/identifier corpus for Polaris securities, tickers, and bank names. would that be sufficient?
[03:19] Arjun: yes, that materially helps. embedding-based checks will compare response claims to the KB and if similarity below threshold we flag it. we'll provide false positive/negative calibration guidance.
[03:29] Daniel: what's a realistic hallucination threshold? 3% across the regression set?
[03:34] Arjun: 3% is aggressive but feasible; depends on prompt engineering and model variant. for early baseline we aim for <=6% then optimize.
[03:41] Lena: ok timeline — how long do you need to run a proper regression?
[03:45] Maya: typical run is one week for initial baseline (hosted) including prompt tuning and one dedicated config run (if you choose Dedicated) the following week for throughput/latency. so about two weeks end-to-end for initial pass.
[03:56] Daniel: do you need a canary or warmup before the dedicated run?
[03:59] Arjun: yes, we'll do warmup sequences and KV cache priming for a 2 hour window and ramp tests for concurrency.
[04:06] Tasha: can you describe what info you capture in logs? i.e., are outputs stored, and how long?
[04:11] Sofia: we'll capture request/response, model id, latency, and scoring signals for the eval; retention policy can be set per agreement. for hosted we retain minimal logs for 30 days by default; for private deployments we follow your retention policy.
[04:24] Daniel: great. on the scoring side, what automated metrics do you produce?
[04:28] Arjun: we produce exact match %, schema pass %, normalized entity F1, embedding-distance hallucination rate, and a cost-per-request metric. we also produce human-review adjustment factors.
[04:38] Lena: do you do BLEU/ROUGE etc? is that useful for us?
[04:42] Arjun: for generative templates BLEU/ROUGE add little value; we prefer exact-match or token-level normalized edit distance for structured outputs. for free-text responses we can compute ROUGE but we'll prioritize human judgments.
[04:55] Daniel: i want to see an example rubric for human review — like severity levels for hallucination and how they map to pass/fail.
[05:01] Maya: we'll include a suggested 3-tier severity: minor (formatting/typo but no factual error), major (incorrect entity values that could cause downstream misprocessing), and critical (materially wrong financial claim). major+critical count as failures in the composite.
[05:15] Lena: ok. regarding golden prompts — who curates them? we expect collaboration.
[05:20] Arjun: Redwood will provide a first-draft golden set curated from your top intents; you review and augment. We iterate until both parties sign off.
[05:28] Rajiv: about the load profile— 40 qps sustained, 120 burst — what hardware footprint do you simulate for dedicated?
[05:34] Arjun: depends on model size and quantization. rough rule: a 7B quantized model can hit that qps on a 2-GPU pool with batching; 13B requires 4 GPUs. we'll propose a baseline config and cost estimate in the bench spreadsheet.
[05:47] Tasha: any privacy concerns for sending the 2k prompts?
[05:50] Maya: redact PII; we also accept synthetic equivalents. if you prefer, we can run on your private deployment image so data never leaves your VPC.
[05:59] Daniel: let's try hosted baseline with anonymized data first, then private if we need on-prem keys.
[06:03] Lena: timeline recap?
[06:05] Maya: plan: Redwood sends draft golden prompts + rubric by 8/10, Polaris provides datasets by 8/12, baseline hosted run week of 8/17, dedicated sim (if requested) week of 8/24, and final report by 8/28.
[06:16] Daniel: that timeline works.
[06:18] Arjun: one more technical note — hallucination detector thresholds will be tuned on your holdout set; we'll share calibration notes and false-positive rate targets.
[06:27] Lena: how will we consume results? dashboard, CSV?
[06:30] Sofia: both. Redwood Console export includes per-example results, summary dashboards, and a regression CSV that you can plug into your CI. we'll share a sample export format.
[06:39] Rajiv: for CI gating, can we set a nightly regression check that fails the build if composite drops 5%?
[06:44] Arjun: yes, we can integrate with your CI (we've done Jenkins/GitLab/GitHub actions hooks) to post pass/fail. we'll document the webhook and payload.
[06:53] Tasha: send over SOC2 cert and SAML SSO setup docs.
[06:56] Maya: will do — action item.
[06:58] Lena: ok thanks everyone, seems actionable.
[07:02] Maya: thanks, i'll follow up with the plan and spreadsheets. bye.

End of transcript.

title: New Windsor Labs — Private VPC Assimilation Kickoff
content:
New Windsor Labs — Private VPC Assimilation Kickoff

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), John Ramirez (CTO - New Windsor), Maria Santos (Infra Lead), Kevin O'Neill (Security), Sara Liu (Network), Tom Park (DevOps)

Summary: quick intake to map New Windsor's private onramp needs. Primary asks: region gating (EU-only), private endpoints vs. transit-gw peering, egress IP stability, KMS/HSM for encryption, and a short Dedicated trial to validate latency/throughput.

Topics: networking topology, private endpoints, transit gateway vs VPC peering, egress IPs/NAT, region restrictions (eu-west-1 + uk-south), audit/logging, pilot plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. testing audio ok?
[00:12] John Ramirez: yeah, can hear you — cheers.
[00:15] Priya Kapoor: great, i'll just run the agenda quick — intake on network, compliance needs, pilot timeline, then next steps.
[00:23] Maria Santos: cool, we've got limited time so i'll be concise. our primary constraint is data residency — must keep inference traffic and model state inside EU (eu-west-1 + maybe london region). also want private-only access, no public internet endpoints.
[00:40] Alex Chen: understood. so you're looking at Redwood Private in a VPC-mode, correct? not hosted API.
[00:48] John Ramirez: yes. we evaluated hosted but the auditors flagged data exfil risk. we'd consider Dedicated if it helps with latency and isolation.
[00:57] Priya Kapoor: ok, two common patterns — private endpoints (PrivateLink style) or transit gateway peering to our VPCs. each has tradeoffs: PrivateLink gives per-subnet ENIs and stable private DNS, transit-gw is better for many-VPC architectures and reduces per-endpoint plumbing. do you currently run transit gateway?
[01:18] Sara Liu: yes, we use TGW across 4 VPCs and two accounts; also have a shared services VPC. we prefer centralized egress through NAT GW in a single egress VPC to keep IPs stable.
[01:30] Tom Park: and the egress IPs are important because our security rules only allow a handful of partner IPs.
[01:36] Priya Kapoor: ok, that maps well to a transit-gw approach with an egress VPC. Redwood can expose private endpoints in the customer VPC or accept traffic over a transit attachment. a couple details to confirm: do you need TLS termination on your side or shall we terminate at our side and present a private endpoint with mTLS?
[01:56] Kevin O'Neill: security preference is mTLS mutual auth, and we'd like HSM-backed KMS for keys. also need full audit logs for prompt content retention policy (we may redact later) — what are the retention controls?
[02:12] Alex Chen: we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations in Private deployments. audit logs are available; retention can be configured but we'll share our security whitepaper. note: prompts can be optionally disabled from retention or redacted via redaction hooks, but that's part of the config during onboarding.
[02:30] John Ramirez: good. on region gating — if we pin to eu-west-1, can Redwood guarantee compute lives in that region for Private?
[02:41] Priya Kapoor: yes, Private deployment can be pinned to specific regions. Dedicated can reserve capacity in eu-west-1. the only caveat is model variants that require specialized hw — we'll surface compatible variants limited to that region.
[02:56] Maria Santos: whats the networking topology you recommend for low latency between our app tier and the model endpoints? we have an app VPC in eu-west-1 too.
[03:07] Priya Kapoor: shortest path is private endpoint in the same region VPC, ideally in the same AZ to avoid cross-AZ hops. if you want centralization for many VPCs, use TGW with route propagation. also consider pinned subnets and placement groups on our side; we'll share a diagram.
[03:25] Sara Liu: any MTU or fragmentation issues we should know about? we already have jumbo frames internally.
[03:31] Priya Kapoor: we typically support standard MTU 1500; jumbo can be supported but must be negotiated because the service ENIs are 1500 default. we'll note that as an action item.
[03:42] Tom Park: about egress: we push outbound calls through a NAT GW with a fixed set of Elastic IPs. can Redwood allow us to present those as allowed egress for callbacks and model downloads?
[03:55] Alex Chen: Redwood's Private nodes can be configured to use customer egress via NAT. But for hosted fallback or external artifact pulls, we may need to route in/out — we can document the exact egress IP set and you can whitelist them. for Dedicated, that list is smaller and more stable.
[04:14] John Ramirez: what about bringing your runtime on-prem? we have a colo in FRA that houses some latency-sensitive services.
[04:23] Priya Kapoor: we do private on-prem packages but it's heavier. two options: run Redwood Private in the cloud with a private interconnect (Direct Connect or ExpressRoute) back to colocation, or an on-prem bundle — both need network workshop. colo needs certain kernel/driver support for GPUs.
[04:40] Maria Santos: our preference is cloud VPC + direct connect — simpler from ops.
[04:44] Kevin O'Neill: compliance question: do you support customer-managed logging to our S3 and meet GDPR deletion requests?
[04:51] Alex Chen: yes, we can forward audit logs to your S3, and we support deletion workflows tied to records. exact SLA for deletion depends on deployment type; we'll include it in the security doc.
[05:03] Priya Kapoor: quick question — how many QPS and token/sec are you expecting for the pilot?
[05:10] John Ramirez: pilot is small — maybe 5-10 rps, peak 60 concurrent requests, median prompt length ~120 tokens, embedding calls lower but continuous. aim is to simulate production with a 2-week burst.
[05:25] Priya Kapoor: cool, that's modest. Dedicated trial will let us reserve a small pool and test cold-starts and KV cache behavior. we can also enable prefix caching to reduce token cost.
[05:36] Tom Park: is prefix caching automatic? how does it handle user prompt variations?
[05:41] Priya Kapoor: its workload-aware; similar prefixes are cached, but it's not semantic — exact token prefixes or KV cache from previous contexts. for chat-like sessions you'll see big benefits.
[05:51] Sara Liu: about endpoint types — PrivateLink vs Private NLB in peered VPC — any recommendations given our TGW architecture?
[06:00] Priya Kapoor: if you prefer minimal route table changes and per-account isolation, use PrivateLink. If you have TGW and want multicast-like access across many VPCs, an NLB + TGW attachment could be simpler. PrivateLink has more ENI overhead.
[06:15] Maria Santos: any cost differences we should be aware of?
[06:18] Alex Chen: PrivateLink has per-GB and per-hour ENI costs on AWS; TGW attachments are charged differently. We'll include rough cost delta in the follow-up. Dedicated pricing vs PrivateLink tradeoffs we'll outline.
[06:30] Kevin O'Neill: what about IP allowlists — can we do client cert pinning or are IPs the only primitive?
[06:36] Priya Kapoor: we support mTLS, and we can do per-token level RBAC as well. For IP allowlists, we provide a fixed set for Dedicated; for hosted it's larger. We'll provide the list.
[06:47] John Ramirez: network ACLs — we want to restrict egress to only certain S3 buckets for model weights. is there a way to ensure downloads only happen from your signed buckets?
[06:58] Alex Chen: yes, we can sign artifact URLs and optionally host model weights in your S3 via replication. there's a secure artifact fetch flow; we'll show the sequence diagram.
[07:09] Sara Liu: latency question — what's typical RTT for eu-west-1 in a dedicated deployment?
[07:15] Priya Kapoor: cold start time depends on model and quantization. For a 13B model with fast kernels in our runtime, token latency is ~25–45ms steady-state when co-located in same AZ. We'll include benchmark numbers.
[07:29] Tom Park: if we pin model quantization (int8) does that change the network requirements?
[07:34] Priya Kapoor: mostly affects compute, not networking. smaller memory footprint may reduce cache spills but networking same.
[07:41] Maria Santos: regarding DNS, we use split-horizon internal DNS. can your private endpoints honor our internal DNS names?
[07:48] Alex Chen: yes, via private hosted zones and endpoint DNS configuration we can map service names to private IPs. we'll include DNS config notes.
[07:58] John Ramirez: ok, let's talk failure modes — if your cluster in eu-west-1 is overloaded, do you fail open to hosted multi-region? we can't allow cross-border failover automatically.
[08:11] Priya Kapoor: we have routing policies: you can set strict region-only or allow automatic fallback to a designated region. given your compliance constraints, we'd set strict region-only and then configure on-call alerts and capacity escalation. fallback to other region would be manual and requires your sign-off.
[08:29] Kevin O'Neill: are there SLA credits tied to latency or availability?
[08:33] Alex Chen: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers. Private (on prem) gets enterprise SLAs — we'll include the doc.
[08:42] Maria Santos: network path MTU — you mentioned default 1500. we use 9001 internally. can the Redwood ENIs be jumbo-aware?
[08:51] Priya Kapoor: it's not enabled by default. we can work with AWS settings but it's a multi-party change; we'll put that in the workshop.
[08:58] Tom Park: who on Redwood will run the network workshop?
[09:02] Alex Chen: Priya will lead the technical side; i'll coordinate logistics and pricing items.
[09:07] Priya Kapoor: action item list — i'll collect your TGW attachments, route tables, and NAT EIP list. also we'll sketch two proposed topologies: PrivateLink and TGW+NLB.
[09:18] John Ramirez: sounds good. timeline — we'd like pilot running early Jan; is that realistic?
[09:23] Alex Chen: yes — if we get your infra details by Jan 4 we can spin a minimal Dedicated trial the week of Jan 9.
[09:30] Maria Santos: one more — audit and redaction. we have legal asking for selective prompt redaction before any log leaves region. can Redwood do inline redaction?
[09:40] Priya Kapoor: yes, we have redaction hooks that run pre-ingest; they can be customer-provided regex or a server-side plugin. performance impact is minimal but we should test it in pilot.
[09:51] Kevin O'Neill: encryption in transit — do you support TLS 1.3?
[09:54] Alex Chen: yes, TLS 1.3 supported and mTLS for private endpoints.
[09:59] Sara Liu: regarding IPs again — we want the smallest possible allowlist. for dedicated trial what's the size?
[10:05] Priya Kapoor: dedicated trial can give you a /28-ish stable set depending on deployment; we'll confirm exact count.
[10:12] Tom Park: can we get a sample Terraform module for peering + route table changes?
[10:18] Alex Chen: yes, we'll attach a starter TF module and routing snippets.
[10:22] John Ramirez: any blockers from our side? we need to validate budget and schedule security review.
[10:28] Alex Chen: understood. we'll send pricing bands and the SOC2/ISO docs.
[10:32] Maria Santos: ok thanks. let's capture the follow-ups.
[10:36] Alex Chen: recap: Priya will run network workshop early Jan; Alex to send diagrams, pricing, security docs; customer to provide CIDRs, TGW attachments, NAT EIPs by Jan 4. Dedicated trial proposed week of Jan 9.
[10:52] John Ramirez: perfect, appreciate it.
[10:55] Kevin O'Neill: thanks all.
[10:58] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, talk soon. bye.

Note: transcript contains natural filler, occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "multicast-like access" used colloquially), and some proper nouns slightly garbled.

title: Argo Bio — Retainer top-up & EU on-prem pilot sync
content:
Argo Bio — Retainer top-up & EU on-prem pilot sync

Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-05-06 14:30 UTC
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Voss (Argo CTO), Markus Klein (Argo Head of Infra), Sana Iqbal (Argo Procurement)

Summary:
High-level: Argo wants to top-up their retainer and run a small EU on-prem pilot to validate latency and data residency for regulatory pipelines. Agreed to run dedicated throughput tests and to exchange an amendment to extend the contract term with committed capacity. Discussed tradeoffs between hosted fallback vs full private deployment, SOC2 and KMS needs plus pilot success criteria.

Topics covered:
- Retainer top-up mechanics and term extension
- EU on-prem pilot scope and constraints (data residency, network/firewall requirements)
- Dedicated capacity sizing and latency targets
- Security controls: SSO, KMS, audit logs, SOC2 evidence
- Next steps and owners

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya: alright folks we can get started, thanks for joining, i know we have a pretty packed agenda today to go over the retainer top up and the eu on prem pilot
[00:00:15] Elena: yep thanks maya, we wanted a tight sync — main ask is: can we get predictable latency for our clinical inference pipelines while keeping data inside eu, and also figure out committed pricing for the next 12 months as usage is spiky
[00:00:36] Jonah: cool, quick ask from our side, do you expect most inference to be batch (scheduled) or real time? that changes the dedicated sizing and the cache strategy
[00:00:45] Markus: it's a mix: 70% batch overnight but the 30% realtime matters — the clinician dashboard needs sub-300ms tail latency for short prompts (~256 tokens)
[00:01:05] Speaker 3: (mumble) sub 300? 
[00:01:07] Jonah: got it, sub-300ms for 256 tokens is doable with a dedicated pool if we tune batching and keep kv warm; we'll demo the difference in the benchmark runs
[00:01:25] Maya: on the contract side, you're looking at top-up retainer vs a full capacity shift, are you thinking a 6 month or 12 month commitment?
[00:01:35] Sana: procurement here, short term we prefer 6 months but if pricing looks favorable we can do 12. we need clear break clauses and an SLA for throughput/latency in the amendment
[00:01:50] Jonah: we can propose tiers for 6/12/24 months — pricing delta comes from committed units and reserved GPU pool sizes; dedicated vs hosted fallback paths affect cost too because hosted bursting is charged differently
[00:02:07] Elena: also we need to lock down security — SOC 2 evidence, SSO via SAML/Okta, KMS integration for key control, and audit logs accessible for our compliance team
[00:02:24] Maya: yes we'll attach our SOC2 report and a KMS integration guide, okta SAML is supported, and we can surface audit logs in the console. for on-prem we provide a private control plane option plus an on-prem runtime package but of course that requires network setup and an NDA
[00:02:42] Markus: about the on-prem pilot, this is where some of the nuance is — we want to keep data on-prem, but still use Redwood's control plane for rollouts if possible. are there examples of customers doing hybrid control plane?
[00:02:55] Jonah: yeah a number of customers run the private control plane in their VPC; the runtime talks back to control plane endpoints over a tunnel — we can show the network diagram. caveat: metrics and tracing sometimes need explicit allow-lists and we redacted a few hostnames in earlier docs, transcription sorry — (laughs)
[00:03:18] Elena: haha noted. what's the expected lead time for standing up a 4-GPU dedicated pool in eu-west?
[00:03:25] Maya: provisioning to reserved is typically 2–4 weeks depending on capacity in the region; a pilot using your on-prem appliances could be shorter if infra is ready — depends on firewall rules and cert provisioning
[00:03:40] Markus: our security team also asked about HSM/KMS for key custody. we can't have keys stored in a multi-tenant vault for certain datasets
[00:03:49] Jonah: we support customer-managed keys via KMS and HSM integrations for private deployments; for hosted we can do envelope encryption with customer KMS in some cloud providers — but for the strictest control you want the private on-prem runtime and customer KMS/HSM
[00:04:05] Sana: procurement note — we need a pricing worksheet that shows base retainer, committed units, and unit price for bursting vs hosted fallbacks; also cancellation terms
[00:04:18] Maya: understood, i'll prepare an amendment + pricing scenarios. also we discussed pilot success criteria — maybe we should codify them now?
[00:04:29] Elena: success = 1) median latency under 120ms for 64-token inferences, 2) 95th percentile under 300ms for 256 tokens, 3) no exfiltration risk and KMS in place, 4) ability to route degraded traffic to hosted fallback under cost/time thresholds
[00:04:49] Jonah: that's a good set; for the latency numbers we'll need to run both cold-cache and warmed-cache scenarios, and include continuous batching behavior; i'll include quantized model runs since you plan to use smaller variants in prod
[00:05:05] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) quick question about models — are you planning to use open weights or an enterprise model?
[00:05:12] Elena: we'll use an open foundation model fine-tuned in-house; need to validate quantized 4-bit performance for cost reasons
[00:05:20] Jonah: okay good, quantization will help; one callout about accuracy degradation — we'll run a prompt set you provide and create a small eval harness so we can measure regressions between full-precision and quantized runs
[00:05:34] Maya: on the fallback story, we recommend a policy: primary private runtime, fallback to Redwood-hosted identical model family with traffic shaping after X% queue or Yms latency — that reduces downtime risk but does increase egress/hosting costs
[00:05:52] Markus: what's the uplift on cost if we keep hosted fallback enabled? ballpark?
[00:05:59] Jonah: ballpark depends on burst frequency; if you reserve a 4-GPU pool and use fallback for rare spikes (<5% traffic) uplift is ~15–25% on unit cost in our example worksheet; if you rely on hosted for 30% of traffic uplift becomes large ~2x cost on that portion
[00:06:21] Sana: that's helpful, procurement will need the worksheet to model those scenarios. also need an SLA addendum for 99.9% uptime and an escalation path
[00:06:31] Maya: we'll provide draft SLA text and escalation contacts.
[00:06:36] Elena: timeline — we want pilot to start in June, run 6 weeks, and then decide on committed top-up by mid July. is that feasible?
[00:06:45] Jonah: timeline feasible if we get on-prem readiness and NDA done in two weeks; benchmarks to be shared within one week after runs
[00:06:53] Maya: ok action owners: jonah runs benchmarks; maya sends amendment; elena to share compliance checklist and sample prompts.
[00:07:05] Speaker 1: (short silence)
[00:07:10] Jonah: small technical note — for the throughput test i'll run a 1k token and 256 token workload, measure p50/p95, cold starts, kv warm, and also run a quantized 4-bit model variant; i'll include config for batch size and max latency SLO
[00:07:26] Markus: for the network, we'll need a list of egress IP ranges and the control-plane FQDNs so our firewall team can whitelist them; can you share that?
[00:07:35] Maya: yes, i'll include a security checklist and the CIDR list; note some hostnames rotate per deployment but we'll give the canonical endpoints
[00:07:45] Sana: and pricing — can you include an example monthly amortized cost for the 6 month vs 12 month committed tiers? we want to justify a 12 month if it saves >20%
[00:07:56] Maya: yes, we'll model it.
[00:07:59] Elena: any blockers on Redwood side about the hybrid control-plane?
[00:08:05] Jonah: none technical, just network and cert provisioning; operationally we do need an SRE contact on your side for cert rotation and troubleshooting during pilot
[00:08:14] Markus: that we can pair on, i'll assign an engineer.
[00:08:18] Maya: great. do we want a follow-up demo of the control-plane UI and audit logs for your security team?
[00:08:24] Elena: yes, please. security wants to see audit log retention and role based access controls in the console
[00:08:32] Maya: ok i'll schedule a 30 minute deep dive with our CSM and product security next week — suggest May 11th at 15:00 UTC?
[00:08:41] Sana: that works for us.
[00:08:45] Jonah: last technical note: please include a small prompt set (10–20 prompts) that represent clinical vs admin traffic so our evals match production signals
[00:08:55] Elena: will do.
[00:09:00] Maya: thanks everyone — quick recap of next steps then we'll close: jonah to run and share benchmark spreadsheet; maya to send amendment and cidr/security checklist; elena to share prompts and compliance checklist; schedule control-plane demo with security on May 11th; target pilot start early June.
[00:09:20] Markus: good recap. thanks.
[00:09:24] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in CRM and slack.

title: Novaplane Tech - Security & Hosting Intake
content:
Novaplane Tech - Security & Hosting Intake

Intro discovery on Novaplane's security gates and hosting preferences. Focus on SOC2/ISO posture, SSO/SAML, RBAC model, audit log retention, and customer-managed KMS. Agreed to a follow-up technical deep-dive and a short Dedicated trial for latency/cost validation.
SOC2 / ISO scope and artifacts
SSO/SAML and IdP integration
RBAC and least-privilege model
Audit logs & retention (90/365-day scenarios)
Encryption and KMS: CMK vs Redwood-managed keys
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs
Next steps: docs + trial
Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II redacted report and ISO 27001 scope
Schedule 60-min technical deep-dive with Diego and Maya (week of 11/20)
Provision trial Dedicated environment for benchmarking (2 weeks)
Confirm data residency options and KMS integration model
Alex Chen - email SOC2 summary + security whitepaper by 2028-11-17
Maya Patel - prepare Dedicated vs Hosted perf/cost matrix and share by 2028-11-19
Tom Evans - share Novaplane's data residency and retention policy doc by 2028-11-18
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Evans (Novaplane Head of Security), Sara Li (CTO), Diego Ramirez (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick intake, fairly noisy on one end, some transcription mistakes, but captured main asks.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, i'm the AE on this account, quick round robin?
00:07 Tom Evans: tom evans here yep head of security at novaplane, thanks for making time, sorry if there's a bit of background noise on my side
00:13 Sara Li: sara li, cto, i've got diego on the conn— 
00:16 Diego Ramirez: yo hey, diego, platform eng, we'll mostly listen for the infra bits
00:22 Maya Patel: maya, solutions engineer, i'll cover the technical side, perf, keys, all that.

02:05 Alex Chen: high level, where are you today with inference hosting? are you self-hosting or using public endpoints?
02:13 Tom Evans: currently a mix, core models are private on prem for PII parts, but a lot of experimental endpoints hit mega cloud managed services, cost is creeping up, and we need a clear path for SOC2 and auditability for the customer data flows
02:34 Alex Chen: got it, and what are the non-negotiables for you security-wise?
02:37 Tom Evans: SOC2 Type II is required, ISO 27001 desirable but not immediate, SSO via corporate IdP with SAML, RBAC for separation of duties, strong audit logs with retention we can set, and the ability to use our KMS for CMK, we can't have plain text keys outside our control, also data residency - certain workloads must remain in eu-west-1
03:12 Maya Patel: okay that aligns with typical enterprise asks. quick clarifier — when you say CMK, do you mean customer-managed keys in your cloud KMS, HSM backed?
03:22 Tom Evans: yes, HSM backed, we want envelope encryption where tokens and any logs are encrypted with our key when at rest
03:35 Sara Li: and for latency-critical endpoints we may want dedicated capacity, but we'd like a hosted path for lower throughput features — curious about routing, fallback if dedicated misses capacity
03:49 Maya Patel: yep so redwood supports three modes — hosted api, dedicated reserved gpu pools, and private vpc/on-prem. routing policies can fallback to a compatible variant, we'll auto-failover region-wise, we can also configure model variants for cost vs latency.

06:10 Diego Ramirez: question on SAML: we enforce SCIM-based provisioning and Okta as idp, need group membership mapping into roles. how granular can the RBAC be?
06:24 Maya Patel: we support SAML SSO + optional SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with resource scoping — you can map groups from idp to roles in redwood, and we have audit events tied to tokens and API keys, though sometimes the transcription shows 'token list' as 'tonk' — ignore that.
06:45 Tom Evans: audit logs — retention windows, can we store logs for 12 months and export to our splunk? also need immutable audit trails for compliance
06:58 Maya Patel: yes, we stream audit logs to customer destinations (s3, splunk, bigquery) with signed manifests. retention is configurable per-tenant; immutable trails supported via object lock or WORM on s3. we can also push to your SIEM via forwarders.
07:25 Alex Chen: on SOC2 artifacts — we can share a redacted SOC2 Type II report, our ISO attestation details, encryption whitepaper, and a network diagram for the private control plane, will send those after the call
07:38 Tom Evans: great, do you have a list of controls mapped to customers' purple team checks? like a control-mapping spreadsheet?
07:45 Alex Chen: yes, we have a compliance matrix mapping to common frameworks (SOC2, ISO, HIPAA notes), i'll include that.

09:10 Sara Li: for KMS, can customers bring their key into your hosted offering or only for Dedicated/Private? we prefer bring-your-own-key (BYOK) even for hosted if possible
09:22 Maya Patel: current hosted product supports customer-managed keys in the sense of envelope encryption with root-of-trust in cloud KMS for specific customers — for full BYOK hardware-backed CMK we typically recommend Dedicated or Private, because you need the key material to be under your control end-to-end. but we can engage to scope a hosted BYOK path if it's a hard requirement
09:49 Diego Ramirez: ok that matters, we need HSM-backed CMKs for some pipelines so likely we'll want Dedicated or Private for those models, but maybe host sandbox for non-PII features
10:03 Maya Patel: makes sense, we also have token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards so you can split traffic and cost across hosted and dedicated routes

12:40 Tom Evans: another question, what about pen tests and vulnerability scans? we need third-party pentest reports and annual scans, and we require notification windows for incident response
12:56 Alex Chen: we run internal pen tests annually and vendor scans, and we can provide a summary of third-party engagements; incident response SLA main points: notification within 24 hours for confirmed breaches, and we have playbooks and forensics support on enterprise tiers
13:21 Tom Evans: SLA for uptime and latency for Dedicated? we might need SLOs pinned for customer contracts
13:30 Maya Patel: Dedicated comes with contractual SLAs for throughput and latency tiers; we can pin SLOs in the reserved capacity contract. Hosted offers best-effort with published performance profiles but not the same contractual throughput guarantees

15:02 Diego Ramirez: on the logs again, are system-level logs separated from application logs? we need clear separation and different access controls
15:15 Maya Patel: yes system logs and application logs are separated. system logs are retained in the control plane with restricted access; application logs (your inference request/response traces) can be routed to your storage with the retention you choose. RBAC can gate access to those exports.
15:46 Tom Evans: about data residency — if a region is required, can you guarantee single-region hosting, and what about backups? backups must remain in-region or in a specified set of regions
15:58 Alex Chen: we can pin workloads to regions and control backup replication policies; for Dedicated and Private it's straightforward to limit cross-region replication, hosted can be configured per-account to limit to a region though multi-region failover is an opt-in.

18:30 Sara Li: curious about telemetry — we need obfuscated metrics to be shared with our product team but not contain raw prompts; can you redact or mask PII in logs before exporting?
18:44 Maya Patel: we have built-in redaction filters and tokenization hooks; additionally we recommend a prefix-KV cache to reduce exposure of raw prompts, and we can enable on-prem pre-processing for PII scrub before hitting hosted endpoints
19:06 Tom Evans: that sounds promising. can you show how redaction is configured? we might want to see a sample config and the scrubber rules
19:14 Maya Patel: i'll include sample scrubber config and docs in the follow-up bundle.

22:05 Alex Chen: any blockers to running a two-week dedicated trial for a small model set? what's your internal procurement cadence?
22:20 Tom Evans: procurement is 2-3 weeks but security sign-off is the gating factor, if we get the SOC2 artifacts and a short architecture diagram we can spin up a sandbox approval quickly. cost approvals are easier for a short eval
22:38 Alex Chen: good — we'll aim to deliver docs by friday and propose a trial start the next monday, assuming ok from your security team

28:10 Diego Ramirez: technical nit — how do you handle KV cache and warm starts for latency? we run high qps so cache efficiency matters
28:21 Maya Patel: runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management; we can tune cache TTLs and shard placement for your workload. note sometimes the transcript will convert 'KV' to 'k v' or 'k v cache', ignore that

31:00 Tom Evans: compliance question — do you provide evidence for keys rotation and access logs to satisfy audits? auditors want a chain of custody for keys
31:12 Maya Patel: yes for Dedicated we can provide rotation logs, KMS access logs, and who/when API calls were made. For hosted, we can provide redacted KMS event logs and access records but full key material audit trails are available when you control the CMK in your cloud provider

34:40 Sara Li: any known integration issues with okta/scim? our provisioning is fairly heavy with nested groups
34:51 Maya Patel: we have customers with large scim deployments, we sometimes hit mapping limits with deeply nested groups; our config guide has patterns for flattening or mapping to role-sets — we'll share that guidance.

38:05 Alex Chen: wrap up — recap: you need SOC2 Type II + ISO docs, sample architecture, KMS integration options, RBAC mapping guide, audit log retention details, and a Dedicated trial proposal. Next step deep technical sync with diego and maya. agreed?
38:26 Tom Evans: yep agreed. please include any known limitations for hosted BYOK in the notes.
38:33 Maya Patel: will do, i'll add clear recommended pathways: hosted sandbox for non-PII, Dedicated for HSM-CMK workloads, Private for full air-gap/on-prem needs

41:00 Sara Li: timeline — security review to complete by end of month? we are aiming to put this into vendor shortlist by early december
41:12 Alex Chen: we'll try to get docs to you by 11/17 which gives you two weeks for review before your shortlist deadline
41:22 Diego Ramirez: also let's add a perf benchmark plan — small throughput tests first then 95th pct latency runs
41:30 Maya Patel: noted, i'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet and runbook.

50:05 Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the bundle and invite for the technical deep-dive, talk soon
50:15 Tom Evans: thanks all
50:18 Sara Li: thanks
50:20 Diego Ramirez: great, bye

End of transcript.

Notes: occasional mis-attributions and minor transcription errors (e.g., 'Sam L' for 'SAML', 'K-M-S' spelled out). Document links referenced during call: SOC2 redacted report (link to be emailed), compliance matrix (link), Dedicated trial proposal (link).

title: Private VPC egress & runtime interop deep dive - OrionHealthTech
content:
Private VPC egress & runtime interop deep dive - OrionHealthTech

Deep technical session focused on private VPC egress patterns for Redwood Private. Covered NAT hairpin issues, PrivateLink binding options, DNS resolver design, KV cache coherence across AZs, batching windows and quantization tradeoffs; agreed to run a staging benchmark and exchange network diagrams.
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lila Cho (Redwood SE), Damien Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jared Molina (Orion - Platform), Priya Narayan (Orion - Lead SRE), Evan Brooks (Orion - Security)

Summary: quick recap at top, but full transcript below. Note: auto-transcription has small errors (K V cache sometimes written K V cache, PrivateLink sometimes 'private link').

[00:00] Samir: hey everybody, thanks for carving time today. I think agenda is VPC egress, private connectivity, runtime impacts like KV cache and batching. we'll call out known hairpins.
[00:22] Jared: cool, yeah we wanted to understand the network patterns, especially because our regulatory folks want no public egress for PHI. so the question is, can Redwood Private run in our isolated subnets without hitting the internet for model serving?
[00:37] Lila: short answer yes, with caveats. you can either use PrivateLink to expose the inference API into your VPC, or you can deploy Redwood Private inside your VPC‍—in which case egress only needed for optional telemetry or to pull model artifacts. if telemetry is restricted, we support an airgap package.
[01:05] Priya: if we go PrivateLink, how do we handle egress for downloading container images or pulling checkpoints? our current plan is to use an internal artifact repo but some ops still rely on s3 endpoints.
[01:25] Damien: for model onboarding we recommend either a pre-staged S3 in the same region with VPC endpoint or scp transfer into the node. PrivateLink doesn't magically give you S3 access; it's about ingress to the service endpoints. so, commonly customers put a NAT gateway in a controlled egress subnet with tight route tables and egress-only rules.
[01:48] Evan: we have a strict policy - no outbound to public S3, only VPC endpoints allowed. any NAT hairpin or egress path has to be auditable.
[02:02] Samir: understood. one pattern we've used is dedicated isolated subnets for runtime nodes with no Internet gateway. then a separate managed egress subnet with NAT Gateway and a proxy that whitelists IPs for model fetch or telemetry. for PrivateLink specifically, you set up interface endpoints in your VPC and allow traffic to Redwood's private dns.
[02:27] Jared: there's the hairpin issue though — when nodes try to reach PrivateLink-bound endpoints in the same VPC, we saw packets leaving the subnet and failing source/destination checks. any tips?
[02:40] Lila: yeah, that's the classic source/dest check problem. you need to make sure the ENI for the PrivateLink acceptance is in the right AZ and the route tables point to the interface endpoint. if you're using NAT in the same subnet, disable source/dest check on the ENI and ensure the security groups allow the internal CIDR. sometimes Linux host routing also needs policy routing rules so return packets flow correctly.
[03:06] Priya: so is that something Redwood manages on the PrivateLink side, or we have to do infra changes?
[03:12] Samir: Redwood can provide the CloudFormation/Terraform templates that create the endpoint service and show the accept/attach steps. for PrivateLink the customer must accept and attach the interface endpoint; we can automate some of it via our onboarding script but infra changes are typically on the customer side.
[03:28] Jared: got it. moving into DNS — if we enable private DNS, what's the recommended resolver config? split-horizon?
[03:37] Lila: we recommend enabling private DNS for the interface endpoint so your calls to api.redwood.example (our example host) resolve to the interface IPs. for customers with split-horizon, point the VPC resolver to a centralized forwarding resolver — that way internal hostnames still resolve. beware TTLs and our SDK's connection pooling which caches IPs; if endpoint ENIs failover across AZs you might need to flush connections.
[04:03] Damien: small note — our runtime keeps persistent HTTP2 or GRPC connections to reduce cold-start token overhead. if DNS updates mid-stream, existing connections won't pick up new IPs, so we have keepalives and a periodic reconnect policy (default 10s graceful drain) but you can tune that.
[04:23] Evan: that reconnect window concerns us, because we have latency SLOs. if an AZ goes down, we don't want a 10s blackhole. can we shorten that?
[04:32] Lila: yes, we can lower the drain to 2–3s, but you trade off transient increased CPU while reconnecting. for strict SLOs we recommend multi-AZ clients + per-AZ endpoint binding and health checks in the routing policy.
[04:55] Jared: switching to KV cache — our inference workload is chat-like with long context. we rely on KV caching to avoid re-encoding prefix tokens. how do you keep KV cache coherent across nodes in different AZs?
[05:10] Damien: Redwood runtime uses local KV cache with optional remote invalidation messages. simplest pattern: pin requests to the same AZ (session affinity) so the hot KV cache stays warm. if you need cross-AZ resiliency we do a pub/sub invalidation via the control plane; you'll see a slightly higher tail latency on cold miss if the remote cache needs to fetch.
[05:31] Priya: session affinity sounds fine but our traffic is behind an internal load balancer that balances by round-robin. can we do sticky routing?
[05:40] Samir: yep we can set the LB to use least-conn or a cookie-based stickiness. another pattern: use a small shared redis/kv-store for frequently-mutated prefixes, but that adds network latency — usually 1–4ms extra.
[05:53] Jared: any recomms on TTL/eviction? we have variable prompt lengths, sometimes the prefix is huge.
[06:00] Lila: TTL should reflect typical conversation warm period; for chat apps, 30–90s is common before eviction, but memory pressure and KV slot count matter. we provide telemetry to show cache hit ratio and eviction churn so you can size nodes.
[06:12] Evan: are these KV caches encrypted at rest or in transit?
[06:16] Damien: in transit always TLS, at rest depends on deployment — for Redwood Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM or managed volume encryption.
[06:24] Jared: batching — our P99 for token latency needs to be sub-200ms. how much batching can we do without blowing that SLA?
[06:33] Lila: batching is a knob. smaller batching windows (5–15ms) get you decent throughput benefit for short queries without adding too much tail. for strict tail latency we recommend adaptive batching: batch up to N tokens or T ms whichever triggers first. Redwood Optimize can suggest initial N and T based on your token distribution.
[06:55] Priya: what's the CPU/GC impact of very short windows? we've seen JVM-like runtimes thrash if the load is spiky.
[07:02] Damien: true for some runtimes — our engine is largely C++ with controlled memory allocs; still, very small windows increase scheduling overhead. there's a sweet spot at 10–30ms for most conversational workloads. we'll share benchmark graphs.
[07:18] Jared: quantization — Orion is considering int8 quantized models to reduce memory. how does quantization affect latency and batching?
[07:28] Lila: quantization reduces memory footprint so you can fit larger batches on the same GPU, improving throughput. however, quantized kernels sometimes change per-token latency slightly — especially for attention kernel reorderings. expect 5–15% improvement in throughput but tail latency variance may increase slightly. we recommend testing both int8 and int4 profiles.
[07:48] Samir: and note, quantization interacts with KV cache sizes — smaller checkpoints mean faster KV cache restore on cold start.
[07:57] Evan: what about warmup? if we spin new nodes in an AZ, how long to warm the KV and model artifacts?
[08:05] Damien: depends on model size. for a 13B model with quantized weights on NVMe local storage, artifact load is ~20–45s; KV warmup for chat prefixes depends on traffic — we often run synthetic warmers that ping typical prefixes to pre-populate the KV. we can provide a warmup script.
[08:23] Priya: can that warmup traffic be internal-only? we don't want warmed-up data going to telemetry collectors in Redwood.
[08:30] Samir: yes, that can be configured to stay internal. telemetry opt-out is possible for Private deployments; you can either forward metrics to your own collector or allow Redwood to collect anonymized telemetry only.
[08:45] Jared: security check — our InfoSec wants RBAC and audit logs for inference requests. is there request-level logging for who invoked what model?
[08:55] Lila: yes, we support token-level audit logs, request metadata, and can integrate with your SIEM. logs can be stored in your S3 bucket with server-side encryption and an optional redaction layer to avoid storing PHI content.
[09:09] Evan: about network policies: if we put nodes in isolated subnets, what NAT or egress rules are required for model rollouts?
[09:19] Damien: you only need outbound for artifact fetches, optional license verifications, and updates. those can be limited to specific IPs or VPC endpoints. our recommended pattern is a minimal egress host that proxies to allowed endpoints, combined with strict route tables and security group rules.
[09:34] Priya: are there any known issues when using an egress proxy + PrivateLink and DNS resolver forwarding?
[09:42] Lila: proxying can complicate TLS mutual-auth if the proxy rewrites SNI. make sure the proxy preserves SNI and does TCP passthrough for TLS connections unless you intend to terminate TLS at the proxy. for HTTP traffic we support mTLS to Redwood if required.
[09:58] Jared: we are worried about IP churn when we scale nodes up/down, will that break long-lived streams (websockets / streaming outputs)?
[10:08] Damien: long-lived streams are bound to an instance until you drain. our draining policy is graceful — we finish inflight streams and then shutdown, but if the node loses connectivity you'll transiently re-route to another instance and the client may need to reconnect. best practice: client-side reconnect logic with exponential backoff; also use session affinity to reduce mid-stream reassignment.
[10:30] Samir: quick architecture sketch — three subnet tiers: management (api plane for control), runtime (isolated nodes), egress (NAT + proxy). PrivateLink interface endpoints bound into management subnet for control-plane calls. runtime nodes talk to management plane over internal-only paths.
[10:50] Priya: does Redwood require specific MTU settings? we have jumbo MTU and sometimes packet fragmentation messes up GRPC streams.
[10:58] Lila: we recommend standard 1500 MTU on the data plane unless you have tuned your infra. jumbo frames are ok but ensure all hops support it; otherwise you'll get path MTU issues. also watch for AWS ENI limits per instance when you have many network interfaces for PrivateLink.
[11:16] Jared: any guidance on monitoring — how to correlate network-level drops with KV cache misses and inference error rates?
[11:25] Damien: our console exposes per-route latencies, cache hit ratios, and pod-level health. we also ship tracing hooks that emit spans for cache hit/miss, batching windows and egress time. you can send traces to your Jaeger/Zipkin or to our console. correlating via trace IDs makes debugging easy.
[11:43] Evan: we need the SOC2 artifact and any penetration tests for your private deployment package.
[11:50] Samir: we'll attach our SOC2 packaging and the penetration test summary. for Private deployments we also provide an architecture security checklist.
[11:58] Priya: last thing — can we do a quick experiment: mid-call run a tiny benchmark that simulates 200rps, 8 tokens avg, session-affinity vs no affinity, to see cache hit ratio?
[12:09] Lila: we can show a sample script but we shouldn't run heavy loads on your prod account. we can set it up in your staging VPC and run tomorrow.
[12:18] Jared: that works. can Redwood also provide a target config for batch window and KV sizes to start with?
[12:24] Damien: yes, we'll include a suggested config as part of the onboarding bundle — it's what we normally give to other healthcare customers.
[12:31] Samir: ok recap of action items — Samir: share network diagram and security pack; Lila: share warmup script and batching experiment; Jared: provision staging VPC and accept PrivateLink; set meeting to run benchmark next week.
[12:48] Jared: thanks everyone. anything else?
[12:50] Evan: one tiny note — encryption key lifecycle: we want rotation capability without service disruption.
[12:56] Damien: supported — we rotate keys with rolling restarts and you can bring-your-own-KMS. we'll share the rotation playbook.
[13:06] Samir: great, we'll follow up with docs and the templates. thanks all.

End of transcript.
