title: POC weekly: latency diagnostics & rollout plan
content:
POC weekly: latency diagnostics & rollout plan

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood CSM), Jordan, Priya, Liam, Anika (CrestEdge)

Summary:
Quick sync on results from last week's microburst/TTFT experiments, discuss kernel tradeoffs for streaming first token, sequence length tuning, and agreement on next steps for a 3-hour soak and security follow-up. Some noisy audio; a couple names fuzzy in the transcription.

Topics:
- TTFT regressions observed on the 08/14 cluster patch
- Streaming handshake latency and early-byte path
- Sequence length distribution and KV cache sizing
- Kernel choices (fast-gemm vs attention-chunk) and quantization impact
- Rollout plan for canary + soak

Action items (recorded in notes above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Okay folks, hi thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Evan and I from Redwood, Samira on the CSM side. CrestEdge team?
[00:07] Jordan: Yeah Jordan here. Priya is on, Liam and Anika as well.
[00:12] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda: results recap, kernel tuning, seqlen, and canary plan. Evan you wanna kick off with the numbers?
[00:20] Evan (SE): Sure. So we re-ran the fastpath with the attention-chunk change and the microburst hedging enabled. Baseline before the change — median TTFT around 220ms, 95th at 620ms. After patch we saw median drop to ~135ms, 95th to ~370ms on the synthetic load, but real traffic shows a tail at ~480ms when bursts align. There's some jitter in the KV cache hits, we saw hit-rate down to 68% on one run which amplified tail.
[01:02] Priya: Sorry can you repeat the 95th numbers? They— I missed the first one.
[01:06] Evan (SE): Yeah baseline 95th ~620ms, patched 95th ~370ms synthetic, but on production-like traces we still measure ~480ms tail depending on seqlen distribution.
[01:18] Jordan: That 68% KV hit— is that because the cache size was too small or because request prefixes are more diverse?
[01:24] Evan (SE): Good question. It looks like two factors: prefix diversity and some requests with longer effective context that push older keys out. We also noticed our default KV shard sizing put hot prefixes across nodes causing extra cross-shard lookups.
[01:38] Anika (SRE): On our side we saw spiky cross-node latency spikes when big seq requests hit.
[01:42] Evan (SE): Right. One mitigation is increasing per-worker KV capacity and switching to sticky routing for hot prefixes, but that increases memory footprint. Another is a small sequence-length clamp for streaming first-byte path to reduce cache churn.
[01:55] Maya (AE): Can you explain the clamp tradeoff in plain terms?
[01:58] Evan (SE): Sure — for the early-response fastpath we can cap the effective seqlen we consider for KV caching to, say, 512 tokens even if the client sends 1024. That reduces cache pressure and improves TTFT for most requests, but long-context queries will get slightly degraded rerun cost or fall back to the slower path which increases end-to-end for those rare requests. It's a latency v cost/accuracy tradeoff.
[02:25] Priya: If we clamp at 512, what percent of our traffic would be affected? I can share distribution but off the top — maybe 7–9% over 512.
[02:32] Maya (AE): Helpful. Priya can you upload the seqlen percentiles after the call? Evan will use that to recommend clamp threshold.
[02:40] Liam (CTO): Also curious: the attention-chunk kernel — is that something you'll ship in hosted immediately or do we need dedicated?
[02:48] Evan (SE): We can push it to hosted experimental instances but for guaranteed SLOs we'd recommend a dedicated pool for the pilot end-state. The kernel change touches some assembly-fast paths and needs a more conservative rollout on shared infra.
[02:58] Jordan: Is there a measurable accuracy difference with attention-chunk vs fast-gemm?
[03:03] Evan (SE): In our evals we saw no deterministic output deltas for float32 but quantized INT4/INT8 paths show tiny token-level diffs — within acceptable ranges for most assistant workloads. If your use-case is low hallucination tolerance, we should run the prompt set through both kernels.
[03:20] Priya: Okay we'll need that prompt set run.
[03:23] Maya (AE): We'll run Redwood's eval harness and share the CSV.
[03:27] Samira (CSM): Quick note — CrestEdge had asked about SOC2 scope and audit logs earlier, do we need to align that with the dedicated ask?
[03:35] Liam: Yes, dedicated helpful for our compliance team. We also need KMS integration for payload encryption at rest.
[03:42] Maya (AE): Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated; we'll attach the security docs.
[03:47] Jordan: Thank you. Back to microburst— what about hedging parameters? You mentioned microburst hedging earlier.
[03:53] Evan (SE): Right— we enabled a 20ms early-hedge for the streaming handshake which reduces first-byte variance. It gives a small extra compute cost for hedged requests but drops the 99th by ~120ms in our tests. The cost/benefit depends on your SLOs.
[04:12] Anika (SRE): Does hedging interact with batching? We batch at the runtime layer, right?
[04:16] Evan (SE): Yes, continuous batching is in play. Hedging is coordinated with the router; when a request exceeds the hedge threshold without response we issue a hedged request to a warm path. It can increase token-level compute due to duplicate work but we have de-dup caches for final outputs.
[04:33] Priya: Any impact on KV cache coherence with hedged duplicates?
[04:36] Evan (SE): Minimal — hedged requests typically hit the same KV version. If they diverge we have a reconciliation path but shouldn't be common.
[04:42] Jordan: Can you walk through the proposed canary/soak plan?
[04:46] Evan (SE): Sure. Proposed: 1) push attention-chunk + hedging to a canary dedicated pool (10% traffic) for 24 hours, 2) run a 3-hour soak at 100% with synthetic blended load capturing your seqlen histogram, 3) if soak passes 95th/T target we roll to 50% then full. We'll also run the evals in parallel to check output diffs.
[05:07] Priya: For the 3-hour soak, do we need a separate host or can we do it in hosted?
[05:11] Evan (SE): Dedicated is safer because of kernel variability. Hosted experimental may be acceptable for an initial smoke, but for soak we recommend dedicated reserved nodes.
[05:19] Maya (AE): Cost implications— we'll include a reserved 6-week trial pricing and delta vs hosted in the doc.
[05:25] Liam: For auditing, can we capture token-level latency traces? Our compliance team will want per-token histograms.
[05:31] Samira (CSM): Yes, we can enable per-token tracing for the pilot with retention limited to the trial. We'll coordinate retention window.
[05:39] Jordan: One weird data point: on 08/16 we saw an odd bump in TTFT correlating with a model version change — could model params be affecting kernel performance?
[05:47] Evan (SE): Model topology can change memory layout and kernel coverage; a model with different attention bias or more heads can change kernel heuristics. We track model build tags and recommend pinning a model artifact for the soak.
[05:58] Priya: We'll pin to the v2026-07-30 artifact used in the synthetic runs.
[06:02] Evan (SE): Great. Also we have a small optimization: switching the matmul path to fast-gemm on layers 1..6 only, leaving later layers on attention-chunk, that hybrid approach reduced CPU-to-GPU memcpy overhead in our internal tests and trimmed ~10–15ms from median.
[06:22] Anika (SRE): That sounds promising but is it stable?
[06:25] Evan (SE): It's been stable in infra tests but we still want soak runs.
[06:29] Jordan: Any changes to model quantization planned? We saw INT8 gave 2x speed but some odd token probability shifts on our LLM.
[06:37] Evan (SE): Quantization is a big lever. INT8/INT4 can change logits and downstream behavior. For this pilot we recommend keeping float32 for safety and run quant evals separately. If you accept small output variance we can explore INT8 on a narrow set.
[06:53] Maya (AE): Ok the plan then — dedicate a canary pool, run 24h canary then 3h soak, eval outputs, and if passes proceed roll. Priya to share request histograms, Evan to push kernel, Maya to send cost + SLO docs. Samira to set up security artifact share.
[07:11] Priya: I'll send the histogram and a sanitized sample of requests by tomorrow.
[07:15] Evan (SE): I'll push the attention-chunk build to the test cluster by Friday and attach a simple runbook.
[07:21] Maya (AE): We'll also include a short runbook for sticky routing and KV shard sizing changes.
[07:25] Liam: How do we revert if we see tail regressions in canary?
[07:29] Evan (SE): Instant rollback to the previous kernel + routing config. We keep canary traffic split and route a small % to fallback. Also we have automatic fallback rules if 95th exceeds threshold for 15 minutes.
[07:41] Jordan: Good. A couple of quick clarifying questions — do you have a recommended hedging threshold for our workload?
[07:47] Evan (SE): Given your seqlen mix, I'd start with a 20ms hedge and iterate to 10ms if compute cost too high; we'll measure 99th reduction and delta cost.
[07:58] Priya: About KV memory footprint: what's the estimated increase if we double per-worker KV capacity?
[08:03] Evan (SE): Ballpark +18–22% RAM per worker depending on sharding config. We'll provide exact numbers after we see your histogram.
[08:12] Anika (SRE): Any network implications for sticky routing? More cross-zone affinity?
[08:17] Evan (SE): It can increase intra-cluster affinity and reduce some cross-node traffic; overall network should be neutral or slightly improved because we avoid cross-shard lookups.
[08:26] Maya (AE): Samira, do we have the security doc link handy?
[08:29] Samira (CSM): Yes — I'll paste it in the follow-up email; it's the SOC2 + KMS integration doc.
[08:34] Jordan: One more: can Redwood produce a short CSV of run metrics we can ingest into our internal dashboard?
[08:39] Evan (SE): Yep we can provide per-request latency CSV with token-level times and kernel tag, anonymized.
[08:45] Priya: That will help our SRE to correlate spikes.
[08:49] Maya (AE): Great. Any other concerns from CrestEdge?
[08:53] Liam: No, sounds like a solid plan. We'll expect the docs and the kernel by EOD Friday.
[08:59] Maya (AE): Perfect — Samira will own the calendar invite for the canary kickoff; target Monday 2026-08-23 for canary push.
[09:07] Samira (CSM): I'll send invites and the security artifact link.
[09:10] Jordan: Thanks everyone.
[09:12] Priya: Thanks.
[09:14] (transcription noise, overlapping voices)
[09:20] End of recording.

Notes on audio quality: brief crosstalk at 09:14, a couple of names transcribed imperfectly (Anika sometimes appears as 'Annika'); some numeric decimals fuzzy but cross-checked in follow-ups.

References shared during call:
- internal: link to runbook (shared later)
- Redwood eval harness CSV (will be attached)
- Security/KMS doc (to be attached by Samira)


Redwood to share updated kernel recommendation matrix and curated benchmark CSV
Customer to run 3-hour soak with updated fastpath and report 95th pct TTFT
Schedule security review follow-up with SRE + Redwood engineering (target 2026-08-26)
Maya Patel - send dedicated vs hosted cost comparison and sample SLO configs - due 2026-08-24
Evan Cho - push new 'attention-chunk' kernel build to test cluster and share runbook - due 2026-08-21
Priya Nair - provide anonymized request distribution histogram (seqlen percentiles) - due 2026-08-22

title: Proxy + SDK + Observability Onramp - Meridian BioAnalytics Discovery
content:
Proxy + SDK + Observability Onramp - Meridian BioAnalytics Discovery

Exploratory discovery to understand Meridian's constraints for onramp to Redwood: deciding between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; integration via SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex; gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks. Customer wants pilot with predictable throughput and audit logs; has strict KMS/HSM requirement for keys used in embeddings. Action: SE to send sample connectors and run a short benchmark; AE to send security docs and pricing.
Current stack and traffic patterns
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
SDKs, LangChain & LlamaIndex compatibility
Gateway/proxy vs sidecar deployment
Rate limits, quotas, burst handling
Observability and telemetry hooks (OpenTelemetry, traces, token-level cost)
Security: KMS/HSM, SSO, audit logs
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros? We have Maya and Carlos from Redwood - Maya is AE, Carlos lead SE. Could you share roles at Meridian?
[00:18] Noah (CTO): Hey, I'm Noah - CTO. Aisha is platform, Derek does SRE. We're evaluating options to run inference for our clinical summaries and search embeddings. Latency matters but cost is also big, so we want to see Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs.
[00:35] Maya: Great, that'll help. Briefly, Redwood offers Hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private VPC or on-prem. Carlos will cover integration patterns - SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy options.
[00:48] Carlos (SE): Hi all. Before we deep dive, quick qual: what's your expected QPS and typical sequence lengths? Also do you need data to stay in your VPC?
[01:04] Aisha: Good question. For search and summarization, avg prompt length ~200 tokens, peaks to 1.5k. Baseline is 15 QPS with occasional spikes to 80 QPS for short bursts. Data needs to stay in our VPC for PHI — so Private or a VPC-hosted option is preferred. We also have HSM-backed keys for encryption.
[01:30] Derek: And we need audit logs and per-request tracing, plus role-based access — SSO/SAML. SOC2 compliance is table stakes.
[01:44] Maya: Understood. Private deployment supports customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations. Dedicated can be in our cloud with private networking; Hosted has some VPC peering options but you'd need to check the data residency flow. We'll send SOC2 and KMS notes.
[02:02] Noah: Okay. For integration, our app uses LangChain and some bespoke orchestration. We also have a LlamaIndex-based vector store. How smooth is integration?
[02:15] Carlos: We have SDKs in Python/Node, plus examples for LangChain agents and LlamaIndex connectors. For LlamaIndex, the vectorstore adapter needs just a small shim; we've seen customers swap the API key for a Redwood client and it works. We'll share a sample repo. Note: some customers use the Redwood gateway sidecar pattern to centralize retries and rate limiting.
[02:45] Aisha: That sidecar idea — can it live in our cluster? We prefer not to run SDKs directly from many microservices.
[02:54] Carlos: Yes, sidecar or gateway. Two main patterns: 1) SDK direct calls inside app, 2) centralized gateway/proxy that handles batching, caching, auth, and quotas. Gateway gives you single place for observability and consistent retries. Sidecar scales with pods but can be heavier operationally.
[03:18] Derek: For quotas and rate limits: we need per-tenant and per-route quotas. Bursting up to 4x baseline is okay but should be throttled gracefully. Any built-in quota enforcement?
[03:33] Maya: Redwood has per-token and route quotas, and per-api-key limits. For Dedicated you can configure reserved throughput and burst policies. Gateway/proxy can enforce tenant-level quotas before hitting the runtime. We'll demonstrate policy configs in the pilot.
[03:50] Noah: Observability — we use OpenTelemetry and DataDog. We want token-level cost attribution, latency percentiles, traces, and KV cache hit rates. Can Redwood emit open spans and telemetry?
[04:05] Carlos: Yes, we support exporting traces via OTLP, plus webhook traces into DataDog. The Console exposes token-level breakdown and per-model tracing. Small caveat: some internal metric names might differ; we can map them. Also there's a sampling option for high-QPS routes to control telemetry volume.
[04:32] Aisha: You mentioned caching — prefix caching or KV cache — how transparent is that to the app? Could it change semantics?
[04:42] Carlos: Automatic prefix/KV caching is opt-in per-route. It preserves response consistency for deterministic prompts, but for non-deterministic sampling you'll want to disable. We'll review your prompt patterns in the pilot. There's also a cache invalidation TTL you can set.
[05:01] Noah: On models, do you support both open models and Redwood-verified variants? We plan to evaluate smaller quantized models to cut cost.
[05:11] Maya: Yes. Hosted includes curated models, Dedicated and Private can host compatible variants. We also provide recommendations for quantization and kernel selection per workload. Our Optimize toolkit gives batch/caching suggestions.
[05:26] Derek: Is model fallback supported? If a Dedicated node is full can calls route to Hosted? We need graceful degradation.
[05:35] Carlos: Yes, smart routing policies allow fallback to compatible model variants or other regions — configurable per-route. For strict offline/on-prem needs you can disable fallback.
[05:46] Aisha: Security — HSM: we manage customer keys via KMS/HSM. How does Redwood integrate?
[05:57] Maya: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSMs. For Dedicated we can set up a KMS integration (cloud KMS or HSM appliances). We'll include specifics in the security pack. Also SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are all available for Enterprise plans.
[06:14] Noah: Great. Practical question: we use LangChain chains with multiple LLM calls per user request; we'd like routing decisions to be policy-driven — e.g., cheap model for embeddings, higher-quality for final summarization. Can Redwood support per-call model selection?
[06:31] Carlos: Absolutely — you can route by route name, header, or cost threshold. The gateway can rewrite requests to route to different model variants and keep the rest of the app unchanged. Many teams use the gateway to inject a 'routing hint' header.
[06:47] Maya: Maybe a quick demo in the pilot: LangChain example showing embeddings on a quantized model and summarization on a larger model in one workflow.
[06:55] Aisha: That would be ideal. Also, what about token accounting across a chain of calls? We need aggregated cost per user action for billing and audit.
[07:06] Carlos: The Console can aggregate per-transaction when you provide a transaction-id header. We also export per-token logs to your S3/URI if you want offline cost recon. There's a small ingestion fee for long-term retention.
[07:22] Noah: On performance — for our 80 QPS spikes we need sub-200ms tail latency on short prompts. What SLAs can you provide?
[07:34] Maya: SLA varies by product. Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime guarantees; Hosted has best-effort but predictable performance for common configs. We'll propose Dedicated for predictable 99th pct latency. Carlos can walk benchmark results from similar customers.
[07:50] Carlos: We have a benchmark sheet we can share. For short prompts we've sustained 120ms p50 and 220ms p99 in a similar setup with batching and KV caching disabled for low latency. I'll attach the sheet.
[08:06] Aisha: About the gateway/proxy — we prefer the gateway approach to centralize telemetry and quotas. What deployment options exist? A single managed gateway in Redwood vs running their gateway in customer VPC?
[08:20] Carlos: Both. Managed gateway is easiest (Hosted) but requires some network peering. You can also deploy our gateway as a sidecar or a central ingress appliance in your VPC. For PHI, customers often run the gateway on-prem or in their VPC so requests never leave their network — then we only provide control plane access.
[08:41] Derek: If we run gateway in our VPC, can we still use Redwood Console for traces and rollouts?
[08:48] Maya: Yes, the control plane can be hybrid: telemetry and rollouts are reported to the Console while preserving PII in your VPC. We can limit what telemetry leaves your network and provide filtered metrics. We'll document telemetry fields and PII redaction options.
[09:05] Noah: Licensing and pricing — how do pilots work? We'd like a 6-8 week pilot with a Dedicated pool and ability to test burst policies. Any minimum commitment?
[09:17] Maya: Pilots are flexible. For Dedicated we typically ask for a 3-month reserved capacity for predictability, but we can do a scoped pilot for 6-8 weeks with capped usage. We'll send a pricing sketch for a small Dedicated pool plus ingress burst credits.
[09:34] Aisha: On the SDKs, does Redwood provide a LangChain Agent integration or do we need to write adapters?
[09:41] Carlos: We provide code samples: a LangChain LLM wrapper, an embeddings client for vectorstores, and a LlamaIndex connector. Most customers copy/paste the wrapper and replace the key. For more complex chains we recommend using the gateway to centralize logic.
[09:57] Derek: Some words get mis-typed by our infra — like KV cache being called 'K V cash' in earlier docs — just flagging we'll want the exact implementation details.
[10:05] Carlos: Haha, noted. We'll make sure to include accurate docs and a short runbook for cache semantics.
[10:12] Maya: Quick pivot — a security question from procurement: can we support audit logs going to their SIEM?
[10:20] Noah: Yes, we need to push logs to Splunk and also have tamper-evident audit trails.
[10:26] Maya: We support log forwarding to Splunk/S3 and have append-only audit logs in Private deployments. We'll include SIEM integration steps.
[10:35] Aisha: Can you talk about data retention and deletion? For compliance we need data purged after 30 days unless flagged for review.
[10:43] Carlos: Retention windows are configurable per-tenant. For Hosted we retain minimal request metadata by default but can set custom retention and deletion via API. For Private, it's under your control.
[10:56] Noah: One more technical: we have an in-house optimizer that does batching across requests — will Redwood's batching add on top of ours and cause unexpected delays?
[11:07] Carlos: Redwood does continuous batching in the runtime; if you already batch upstream, you can set the runtime to bypass additional batching. We have parameters for max-latency windows and batch size to tune for low-latency workloads.
[11:24] Derek: On quotas again — we need per-team, per-route, and per-user quotas, with alerting when thresholds are near. Does Redwood support webhooks for quota breach alerts?
[11:36] Maya: Yes, quota alerts via webhook, email, and Console dashboards. You can configure soft and hard limits and set pre-threshold alarms.
[11:48] Aisha: For the pilot, what do you need from us to get started?
[11:54] Carlos: Ideally: a small sample prompt set, a TM for expected QPS profile, an example LangChain chain you want to run, and confirmation on network pattern (peered vs in-VPC gateway). We'll run a micro-benchmark and demo the LangChain example.
[12:08] Noah: We'll prepare sample payloads and a dev VPC for the gateway. Also we'll need the LangChain sample earlier you mentioned.
[12:16] Maya: Action recap: Carlos will share the LangChain/LlamaIndex repo and benchmark sheet; Maya sends security docs and pricing; Noah confirms stakeholders and VPC details. Schedule pilot kickoff for week of July 6th. Any blockers?
[12:32] Derek: Only internal legal sign-off; procurement may ask for SOC2 and encryption details but should be standard.
[12:38] Maya: We'll add that to the packet. Any other product questions?
[12:42] Aisha: One thing — metrics naming. We use strict tags (team, env, tenant) in OTEL. Will Redwood mapping support custom attributes?
[12:52] Carlos: Yes, you can map your OTEL attributes to Redwood Console fields. We'll include mapping examples in the integration checklist.
[13:02] Noah: Regarding LlamaIndex vectorstore, we store vectors in our managed store. Do we need to rehydrate embeddings in Redwood?
[13:10] Carlos: You can either call embeddings from Redwood and store vectors back in your store, or send precomputed embeddings. For latency-sensitive retrieval, many customers compute locally and only call the LLM for ranking/augmentation.
[13:25] Aisha: Pricing clarity: how granular is per-token billing, and can we get a forecast for cost if we run at average 15 QPS?
[13:36] Maya: Billing is per-token for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings. We'll run a cost projection in the pricing doc; include your prompt distribution and QPS and we'll model quantized vs full models.
[13:50] Derek: Any experimental features we should be aware of? Like automatic re-try logic that could double-charge?
[13:58] Carlos: Retries are idempotent-aware if you pass an idempotency key. Console will attribute retries separately unless it's deduped by the runtime; we'll explain best practices.
[14:10] Aisha: For audit, we want a binary proof of who called what model when — is that available?
[14:18] Maya: We have append-only request logs with identity and model version. For Private you can host the logs and we can provide a signed manifest if needed.
[14:28] Noah: Any red flags from your side on our architecture?
[14:31] Carlos: Nothing major. Main area: ensure gateway in-VPC has low-latency path to your vectorstore. Also validate HSM connectivity for KMS early in the pilot.
[14:44] Noah: Good to know. Let's talk pilot specifics now: timeline and success criteria. Our success metrics: p99 <300ms for short prompts, cost per user action under X, and secure handling of PHI (auditable).
[14:58] Maya: We'll propose pilot success criteria aligned with that: p99 target, cost modeling, integration completeness (LangChain + LlamaIndex working), and security checklist completion.
[15:08] Aisha: Sounds good. Any dependencies on their side? We'll need RBAC mappings and sample transaction-id header to test aggregated billing.
[15:18] Carlos: We'll provide a small integration test harness that emits transaction-id and demonstrates aggregator in Console. We'll run a short load test to validate quotas and burst behavior.
[15:28] Derek: One last thing — we integrate with an API gateway (Kong). Will that sit in front of Redwood gateway or will Redwood gateway sit behind Kong?
[15:36] Carlos: Either. Common pattern: Kong in edge, Redwood gateway behind for LLM-specific routing and observability. We'll include an example deployment diagram.
[15:47] Maya: Great. Recap of next steps and I'll follow up via email. Thanks everyone, we'll send docs and schedule the kickoff.
[15:56] Noah: Thanks all. Bye.
[16:00] (call ends)

title: POC weekly - quality drift & guardrail investigation with Cliffside Care
content:
POC weekly - quality drift & guardrail investigation with Cliffside Care

Weekly POC sync to investigate recent quality drift on triage prompts. We reviewed scorecard deltas, identified 3 prompt permutations that regressed after a model swap, discussed guardrail tightening and monitoring thresholds, and agreed on next steps: run isolation A/B for model variants, share security artifacts, and schedule a focused evaluation run with 5k prompts.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-11
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM), Nina (Cliffside Head of Data), Marcus (ML Eng), Aisha (PM), Tom (Security)
---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick roll call. we got nina, marcus, aisha, tom on the cusp?
[00:06] Nina: yep here, hi.
[00:07] Marcus: here.
[00:08] Aisha: hi all.
[00:10] Maya: great. ok quick objective for today is to walk through the scorecard deltas you saw yesterday and dig into a couple of prompt regressions, and then decide whether to tighten the guardrails or roll back to the earlier model variant.
[00:22] Diego: i'll share my screen, i pulled the batch eval from friday — you'll see baseline v12 vs v13, and there's a clear dip in Recall@top1 for the diagnosis prompts. weirdly precision held up.
[00:35] Nina: yeah our ops alert fired, about a 6.8% drop in top-1 accuracy on the triage set. not catastrophic but it's above our threshold.
[00:43] Marcus: quick context — we switched to a quantized variant last week to save token cost, that was supposed to be nearly indistinguishable.
[00:52] Diego: right, and the quantization profile used reduced FP bits and a different kernel which may affect conditional probabilities for short completions. the KV cache behavior looked fine, though — or at least the logs don't show cache misses. app logs say some answer truncation happened, odd.
[01:10] Aisha: do we have an example prompt that regressed? we want something we can point product at.
[01:14] Maya: yes, diego — can you read through the 3 failing prompts?
[01:18] Diego: sure. first one: "Patient presents with chest pain, ECG normal, what next?" baseline answer was stepwise — order troponin and monitor for four hours; new model gave a general reassurance and suggested outpatient follow-up which is wrong for our triage bar.
[01:35] Marcus: that is exactly the case we flagged. it's dangerous because the user-facing assistant may under-escalate.
[01:41] Tom: and from sec standpoint, we need deterministic guardrails to prevent under-escalation. if the model variance increases risk, we must mitigate.
[01:50] Nina: side question — did the model swap also change temperature or stopping heuristics? our config shows temperature 0.0 but maybe the token stop sequence handling changed?
[01:59] Diego: good point, we did disable some stop-sequence postprocessing in the runtime to test streaming behavior. that could be related. i should add that to the matrix.
[02:08] Maya: ok so potential causes on the table: quantization effect, kernel selection differences, and stop-sequence/streaming config.
[02:16] Priya: also noting the eval scoring — the heatmap shows drift concentrated in short-answer clinical prompts rather than long narrative ones. so prompts that expect a single recommendation are more sensitive.
[02:28] [02:28] Marcus: can we run an isolation A/B — pin baseline weights on 50% of traffic for 24 hours? we want to compare real traffic not just synthetic.
[02:36] Maya: yes we can do a traffic split. for the POC we can do rollout policy canary with 10/90 up to 50/50, but we need to discuss capacity if you're worried about latencies.
[02:46] Nina: latencies are fine; our concern is correctness. cost savings were attractive, but not at patient-safety risk.
[02:53] Diego: i'll flag one more thing — the internal reranker that we added for answer selection might behave differently post-quant. it's small but could change top-1 picks.
[03:03] Aisha: is the reranker part of Redwood's managed pipeline or our side? it's in our pipeline right now but uses embeddings from the Redwood endpoint.
[03:11] Maya: correct, you're using our embed endpoint then doing a rerank client-side. we did see an embedding cosine shift of 0.02 on average between the variants. small but could cause reorderings.
[03:22] Tom: security question — if we roll back the model will we incur extra cost or is there versioning penalties? also need to get KMS logs for the traffic in question.
[03:32] Diego: no versioning penalty; we keep model variants available. regarding KMS logs, we can export key usage, but remember if you're on the hosted plan some logs are redacted; for Private VPC we provide more detailed HSM/KMS audit trails.
[03:46] Nina: cliffside is evaluating private vs dedicated — what was the recommended path again?
[03:50] Maya: for production patient-data sensitive flows we usually recommend Redwood Private (VPC) if you need full control and unredacted audit logs; Dedicated works for high throughput with predictable latency and is SLA-backed. there was a small stutter in the transcript where people called it Redwood Privy — that's a common transcription hiccup.
[04:06] [04:06] Marcus: back to scoring, we noticed the scorer's threshold for safety flagging didn't fire for those regressed examples. the threshold was set at 0.7 but the new model produced an answer with 0.65 safety score — just below.
[04:20] Diego: we can adjust the scorer to be more conservative — move threshold to 0.75 — but that'll increase false positives. tradeoff between recall of unsafe answers and user friction.
[04:30] Aisha: product-wise we'd prefer higher recall on safety flags, we can tune UI to provide escalation steps rather than block users entirely.
[04:37] Priya: operationally, if we tighten guardrails we should add a monitoring alert for false-positive rate so we don't degrade UX unnoticed.
[04:45] Maya: agree. action plan proposal: 1) run 24h A/B with baseline pinned at 50% to measure real traffic regression, 2) run offline isolation eval on 5k recent prompts with both models, 3) increase safety threshold to 0.75 in a canary to measure FP rate, 4) share security artifacts.
[05:05] Nina: that sounds good. what about timeline for the 5k run? can you do it by end of week?
[05:10] Diego: yes i can spin it up tomorrow; should finish within 36 hours given our batch infrastructure. i'll push results to the shared spreadsheet and link in slack.
[05:19] Maya: ok i'll send a small email to confirm the rollout window for the canary.
[05:23] Marcus: also a note, some prompts show hallucinated recommendations referencing tools we don't integrate. it's subtle, probably because of the model variant's broader completion distribution.
[05:33] Priya: we've also got one regression where the model truncates the last token on streaming — transcript shows 'monitor for four hour' missing trailing s — likely stop-seq/streaming mismatch.
[05:44] Diego: yep that's the stop-sequence thing i mentioned; i'll re-enable the post-processing stop handler for streaming and test.
[05:51] Tom: for security, we'll need the SOC2 package and key rotation logs before we move to dedicated or private. can you share those docs?
[05:59] Maya: yes i will upload the SOC2 attestation and the KMS integration guide to the shared drive. note that the hosted plan redacts some parts, but for Dedicated/Private we can supply the full package.
[06:12] Aisha: what's the impact on latency if we bump safety scoring or add extra reranking?
[06:17] Diego: extra reranking adds 20-40ms on average per request if it's local, if you run it as an additional call to the embed endpoint it could add 80-120ms. for patient triage we still meet sub-400ms SLO in Dedicated; hosted can be higher variance.
[06:34] Nina: ok we need to see a cost estimate for the 50/50 canary and for keeping quantized variant in production vs baseline weights.
[06:41] Maya: i'll include a cost delta in the follow-up email — approximate numbers for token cost difference and the Dedicated delta if relevant.
[06:47] Priya: quick note on evaluation metrics — let's also look at Rouge-L for narrative prompts and exact-match for triage answers so we capture both flavors.
[06:57] Diego: noted. i'll add those metrics to the spreadsheet.
[07:02] Maya: any other blockers?
[07:05] Marcus: none from eng, just want the A/B and the 5k offline run.
[07:09] Nina: same.
[07:11] Maya: ok recap and owners now.
[07:15] [07:15] Diego: (owner) run 5k offline eval and post results to sheet (due 2025-06-13).
[07:22] Maya: (owner) send rollout window and cost delta + SOC2/KMS docs (due 2025-06-12).
[07:28] Priya: (owner) add FP/TP alert to monitoring for safety flags and baseline metrics (due 2025-06-16).
[07:34] Marcus: (owner) confirm client-side reranker logs and share a small sample for debugging (due 2025-06-13).
[07:41] Tom: (owner) send list of required audit logs we need for Private evaluation (due 2025-06-14).
[07:46] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll reconvene after the offline run and the first 24h canary. any final Qs?
[07:52] Aisha: none, thanks.
[07:54] Maya: bye everyone.
[07:56] [end]
Diego Alvarez (SE): run 5k offline eval and post results to shared spreadsheet (due 2025-06-13)
Maya Chen (AE): send rollout window, cost delta, and SOC2/KMS docs (due 2025-06-12)

title: Auriga MLOps - model selection & tool-calling discovery
content:
Auriga MLOps - model selection & tool-calling discovery

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Auriga - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Auriga - Platform Eng), Marisol Vega (Auriga - PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):
- Auriga is evaluating model selection for multilingual, long-context customer-facing assistant; they have strict latency targets for chat and require function/tool calling to enrich responses from internal systems.
- Key decision factors: context length (up to 65k in some use cases), multilingual quality (EN/ES/DE), cost/latency tradeoffs, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2).
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to share pricing sheet and run dedicated benchmarks on Auriga sample data; customer to share redacted dataset and schedule security deep dive.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, private vs dedicated hosting, benchmarking, security/compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining—I'm Alex, AE at Redwood. Samira, do you want to intro?
[00:12] Samira Patel: Hey all, Samira here, solutions engineer. We'll probably do 45 to 55 minutes, talk through Auriga's use cases, latency/cost constraints, and then map model candidates and deployment modes.
[00:25] Priya Rao: Hi, thanks. I'm Priya, Head of ML at Auriga. Quick context: we run a customer-facing assistant and an internal search/chat for docs. Currently on prem K8s, vector db is Faiss-ish managed in house, retrieval pipeline is our own microservices. Key asks: long context (sometimes 60k tokens of transcript + docs), multilingual support (EN/ES/DE), and ability to call our internal tools for account lookups.
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: Platform notes — we are sensitive about data residency and keys, prefer VPC or private. We also need predictable p99 latency for chat flows (ideally < 350ms) and clear cost numbers.
[01:12] Alex Chen: Great, that's super helpful. Two big axes we'll discuss: model family and deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private). For models, given long context and multilingual, we typically look at 32k and 64k context LLMs — there are open weights like Llama-3 variants, Mistral mixtral, and also some quantized flavors. We've got Redwood-verified profiles for throughput and token-cost.
[01:36] Priya Rao: When you say Redwood-verified profiles, is that publicly available? And how often do those profiles change based on kernel selection?
[01:44] Samira Patel: We publish benchmarks in the console and docs — they show typical latency/cost on GPU types. Kernel selection is automatic in the runtime; it picks optimized kernels and quantization settings based on the model arch and the request shape. That can change effective perf a bit per model.
[02:05] Priya Rao: Our ML team cares about hallucination rates across languages. Any model recommendations for EN/ES/DE parity?
[02:13] Samira Patel: In our experience, Mistral-family and Llama-3 derivatives with instruction-tuning tend to be stronger for high-quality multilingual outputs. If you need parity, the 64k context Llama-3 variant tuned for multilingual data is a strong candidate, but it's heavier on infra. For cost-sensitive paths, a quantized 32k variant plus retrieval augmentation can be much cheaper and still meet quality targets.
[02:41] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood support function/tool calling like OpenAI-style function calls? We need structured outputs to trigger downstream services.
[02:50] Alex Chen: Yes — we support tool/function calling patterns and structured output. We also provide webhooks and a light-weight reformatting layer in the console. Note that function calling adds some latency depending on the number of round trips and whether you embed tools in the generation loop or post-process.
[03:10] Priya Rao: For our flows we prefer single-shot tool calling: model returns a JSON payload and we trigger APIs. Any constraints around size of tool descriptions or number of tools?
[03:19] Samira Patel: You can register multiple tools; the runtime will include tool schemas as needed. The practical limit is token budget — large tool schemas consume context. We recommend compact schemas and using retrieval for tool docs.
[03:33] Marisol Vega: On deployment mode: what pushes customers to Dedicated vs Private? We want both predictable latency and to keep control of keys.
[03:42] Alex Chen: Good question. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our infra with SLA-backed latency/throughput and data isolation — you bring your workload but it's hosted. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency or air-gapped needs; you run a customer-controlled control plane and we support KMS integrations. Dedicated has faster time-to-value; Private has more control and compliance overhead.
[04:05] Priya Rao: Does Private support on-prem GPUs?
[04:08] Samira Patel: Yes, we have an on-prem package. For on-prem you'll coordinate image versions and kernel builds; our team supports onboarding. There's some Ops lift but it's a fit for regulated workloads.
[04:21] Liam O'Connor: Latency — you mentioned kernel selection. If we pick a 64k context model, do we expect p50/p95 to blow up versus 32k?
[04:29] Samira Patel: Generally, cost and latency scale with context length. 64k sequences will show higher per-token latency and memory pressure; you can mitigate with KV cache strategies, prefix caching for static context, and retrieval to keep the prompt size smaller. For chat p95 targets under 350ms, many customers pick 32k or use hybrid: 64k for batch/document tasks and 32k for chat.
[04:55] Priya Rao: Are there examples of customers who do 65k plus retrieval?
[04:59] Alex Chen: Yeah, a couple verticals — legal and clinical — use long-context models with heavy retrieval and prefix caching. We have published an example case study on our docs where they shard the context and only include top-K passages into the prompt. We'll share that link after.
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: Security — SOC 2? How does Dedicated vs Hosted affect audit logs and SSO?
[05:24] Samira Patel: Hosted can be SOC 2 compliant (we provide audit logs and enterprise SSO). Dedicated also includes enhanced logging and per-customer telemetry. Private gives you full control of logs and SSO integrations. We support SAML/Okta and integrate with customer KMS for key control.
[05:42] Priya Rao: For encryption at rest in Dedicated, do we have customer-managed keys or do you manage them?
[05:48] Alex Chen: We support both. For the highest control you can use customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or Private. We'll note that in the pricing sheet options.
[05:58] Marisol Vega: For benchmarking, what do you need from us to run realistic tests?
[06:03] Samira Patel: Ideally: a redacted sample dataset that mirrors your longest contexts, a retrieval sample (top K), and the typical prompt templates. Also your latency SLO targets and expected concurrency. With that we can run a 5-10 run latency benchmark across candidate models and deployment shapes.
[06:21] Priya Rao: We can provide that. We'll need NDA considerations for sample data — do you have a secure upload?
[06:27] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll share secure upload links and an S3 presigned flow tied to the deal. Also we'll mask PII on our side during testing. We'll include that in the security doc.
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: A technical question — how does Redwood handle KV cache persistence across restarts? We want to avoid cold-start thrash.
[06:46] Samira Patel: The runtime supports persistent KV caching and warm-up policies. In Dedicated you can configure instance warm pools; for Private you control the persistence layer. Note transcription might say KV cash sometimes — it's KV cache.
[06:59] Priya Rao: Tooling: we plan to expose a small set of internal tools (account_lookup, billing_history, policy_fetch). We need type-safety on the outputs. How do you recommend we implement that?
[07:13] Samira Patel: Use strongly-typed function schemas and post-call validators. Our runtime can enforce schema validation on function outputs and reject mismatches. Also consider end-to-end tests in your CI that assert contract expectations.
[07:26] Marisol Vega: Cost — any rough numbers for 32k vs 64k on Dedicated? Ballpark to justify PoC sizing.
[07:33] Alex Chen: Ballpark is tricky without exact workload, but roughly 64k can be 2-3x token-cost compared to 32k for equivalent generated tokens because of memory and compute overhead. Dedicated commitments can reduce unit cost substantially compared to hosted on-demand; we'll include sample SKU pricing in the sheet.
[07:55] Priya Rao: Can you do adaptive serving — route heavy-context requests to cheaper variants if quality threshold met?
[08:02] Samira Patel: Yes, smart routing policy is available: you can route by latency, cost, or region. We also support fallbacks to smaller models with a quality gate — useful for keeping service available under load.
[08:16] Liam O'Connor: How about multilingual evals? We want a reproducible eval harness.
[08:21] Samira Patel: We can run automated evals on your test slices across EN/ES/DE and return BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity metrics plus human evaluation samples. We also recommend running a small human eval on critical intents.
[08:39] Priya Rao: Will you run those evals as part of the benchmark?
[08:41] Alex Chen: We can include a basic multilingual quality run; for deeper human evals we'd collaborate on the rubric and scope.
[08:48] Marisol Vega: Any red flags we should be aware of in the onboarding?
[08:51] Samira Patel: Biggest ops stuff is if you go Private/on-prem — that has more lift. Also large context models need careful batching and memory tuning; we'll help tune batching policy to meet p95 SLOs.
[09:04] Alex Chen: Ok quick recap before Qs: Redwood will send pricing sheet and Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, Samira will run benchmarks with redacted sample data, Auriga to share dataset and schedule security session.
[09:16] Priya Rao: Sounds good. A few quick Qs — how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks?
[09:21] Samira Patel: We have model version pins and rollout controls: canary, A/B, automatic fallback to older pinned versions if error rates spike. Everything is per-route and per-customer.
[09:32] Liam O'Connor: Is there a way to get telemetry into our existing Datadog stack?
[09:36] Alex Chen: Yes, we provide traces and metrics exports; Datadog + OpenTelemetry integrations are supported. We'll share the dashboard JSON for a sample route.
[09:47] Priya Rao: Any common misconfigurations you see?
[09:50] Samira Patel: Too-large prompt templates and not using retrieval — that blows up token cost. Also forgetting to compact tool schemas and over-fetching context.
[09:59] Marisol Vega: Can we see an example of a function-schema and how Redwood validates it?
[10:03] Samira Patel: We'll send an example in the follow-up email; it's a small JSON schema and the runtime enforces types.
[10:12] Priya Rao: One more on data retention — how long are logs kept in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[10:17] Alex Chen: Hosted defaults to 30 days, Dedicated can be configured up to 365 days for enterprise packages, Private you control retention. We'll include these defaults in the security doc.
[10:29] Priya Rao: Perfect.
[10:31] Alex Chen: Anything else from the Auriga side?
[10:33] Liam O'Connor: Not from me.
[10:35] Marisol Vega: No.
[10:36] Priya Rao: One ask — can you include a sample autopilot config for routing heavy-context docs to batch jobs?
[10:42] Samira Patel: Yes, we'll include a snippet of autoscaling and routing policies.
[10:46] Alex Chen: Great. We'll follow-up with the spreadsheet, secure upload link, benchmark plan, and security docs. Thanks everyone.
[10:55] Priya Rao: Thank you.

Auto action items (end of transcript):
- Alex: pricing & SKU sheet, Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, retention/keys options.
- Samira: benchmark plan + run with Auriga's sample data.
- Auriga: share redacted sample dataset, schedule security deep dive.

References/links mentioned (to be attached after call):
- Redwood benchmark doc (console link placeholder)
- Example prefix caching case study (legal vertical)
- Secure upload link (will be emailed)

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some proper nouns and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache rendered as KV cash), occasional overlap on speakers, minor punctuation issues.

title: Ignite Labs — Developer Onboard: SDK + Auth Runbook
content:
Ignite Labs — Developer Onboard: SDK + Auth Runbook

Intro + live walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, auth patterns for CI and multiple environments, demo of Console sandbox, and Optimize suggestions for latency/cost tradeoffs. Agreed to follow-up poc scoping and get a sandbox API key and sample repo.
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-16 14:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Desai, Daniel Park, Sofia Martinez, Lina Zhou

00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, Alex from Redwood — thanks for making time. Um, we'll do a quick agenda, then dive into a hands-on SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, cover auth patterns and the Console sandbox, and end with Optimize tips and next steps. Sound good?

00:14 Daniel Park: Yeah that sounds great. Quick note — Sofia's joining for the first 20 minutes and then she has another meeting.

00:21 Sofia Martinez: Hi all — jumping in. We're really keen to understand how this will fit into our CI/CD workflows and data residency stuff.

00:30 Priya Desai: Awesome — we'll call out the CI secrets patterns and the VPC/private options too. Um, for the demo I'll share my screen and run both the Python quickstart and a small TypeScript example.

00:45 Alex Chen: Quick qualification — can you remind us where you're planning to run inference today? Hosted, on-prem, or hybrid?

00:53 Daniel Park: Right now it's all in-house, we run a kube cluster and an internal model-serving layer. We're evaluating whether to keep serving models ourselves or move to managed inference. Main constraints are latency under 120ms p95 for short prompts and tight cost control.

01:10 Priya Desai: Got it. That latency target is reasonable — we'll show how batching and cache policies can be tuned so you don't lose that SLO. Also we'll discuss Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs.

01:28 Lina Zhou: Question — we have strict secrets policies, CI can't see long-lived API keys. How do you recommend rotating keys and integrating with our Vault?

01:36 Priya Desai: Good question. Typical pattern is to use short-lived tokens via our sandbox or exchange tokens from your KMS. We support KMS/HSM integration and recommend storing long-lived credentials in the Vault, then issuing ephemeral tokens in CI using the Redwood token exchange API. We'll share an example GitHub Actions step.

01:58 Alex Chen: Ok jumping into the code. I'm going to paste the Python quickstart command in chat: pip install redwood-sdk (note: the package name here might be a placeholder in transcript).

02:10 Priya Desai: I'm running a tiny script: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY')); resp = client.generate('Write a one-sentence summary of product usage'); print(resp.text)

02:28 Daniel Park: Cool. Does the SDK stream events? We need streaming for our chat UI.

02:35 Priya Desai: Yes, the SDK supports streaming. In Python you can iterate over client.stream_generate(...) and in TypeScript it's event-based with async iterators. Streaming works with our Console so you can debug token timing too.

02:45 Sofia Martinez: I saw in the docs something about function calling and structured outputs — is that stable? We're going to rely on a schema to fill forms.

02:54 Priya Desai: Function/tool calling is supported — we call it tool-calls in some older places in the docs, so you might see variant names. It lets you return JSON and map to your schema. There's also a validation layer in the Console for outputs.

03:10 Alex Chen: Switching to the TypeScript example; I'll open a basic node project. npm install @redwood/sdk (again package name fuzzy in transcribe) and here's a snippet: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY }); const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'rwd-3-small', input: 'Summarize...' });

03:38 Daniel Park: That model name — rwd-3-small — is that a hosted Redwood model? We plan to bring our own model sometimes.

03:44 Priya Desai: Yes rwd-3-small is one of the verified catalog models. You can also point the SDK at a private model in your Dedicated or Private deployment. There's a model alias layer so you can switch models without changing code.

04:02 Lina Zhou: For private deployments, do you manage the control plane or is it customer-managed?

04:08 Alex Chen: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane option. You get the Console and telemetry but you host the runtime in your VPC or on-prem; we integrate with your KMS and audit logs.

04:22 Daniel Park: Good. Walk us through the auth example for CI.

04:27 Priya Desai: Sure. Typical pattern: store long-lived credential in HashiCorp Vault; CI job requests an ephemeral token via an internal service or via Redwood's token exchange endpoint; that token is short-lived (e.g., 1 hour) and injected as REDWOOD_KEY into the job. For local dev, devs can use a local short-lived key from the Console or a developer sandbox key. We'll attach a sample GitHub Actions snippet in the follow-up.

04:55 Sofia Martinez: Any RBAC? We need to limit which services can call generation endpoints and which can only create embeddings.

05:02 Priya Desai: Yes we support token scoping and role-based policies. In the Console you can create route-level permissions, and tokens can be limited to only embeddings, or only certain models, and you can also scope to rate limits.

05:18 Alex Chen: Okay, next I'm going to bring up the Redwood Console sandbox we provisioned for Ignite. One moment — sharing screen.

05:30 [screen share noise]

05:36 Priya Desai: Here in the Console you can see the Sandbox project: Activity, API keys, Quickstart links. I'm clicking the Quickstart repo which contains a mono-repo with py and ts examples and a GitHub Actions workflow. That repo link will be in the follow-up email.

06:02 Daniel Park: Nice — I see usage limits and a token breakdown. Does the Console show per-route latency percentiles?

06:09 Priya Desai: Yes, per-route dashboards with p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and you can correlate with request tracing IDs. We also surface KV cache hit rates when enabled.

06:22 Lina Zhou: About caching — can prefix caching be used without violating user privacy with PII? We need to ensure we don't cache any user-identifying strings across tenants.

06:33 Priya Desai: Absolutely — caching policies are configurable by route and you can redact sensitive fields before caching. For multi-tenant setups we'd recommend tenant-scoped caches or disabling prefix caching for PII routes.

06:48 Sofia Martinez: We have a questions about model rollouts. If a new quantized model is cheaper but lower quality, can Redwood do canary rollouts?

06:57 Alex Chen: Yes, rollouts are built-in: you can do traffic splits per model version or fallbacks to a higher-quality variant if quality degrades. The Console will alert regressions tied to a prompt set.

07:10 Daniel Park: Great. Let's talk about Optimize — you're recommending batching/caching — any heuristics for our chat-like workload?

07:20 Priya Desai: For chat where latency is important, use small micro-batches (e.g., 8-16) and aggressive KV caching for repeated context. For embedding-heavy pipelines, batch larger with async pools. We'll give a recommended profile based on the sample traffic you provide.

07:38 Alex Chen: Quick demo of a small benchmark script I run in the repo: it uses the SDK and hits the sandbox with a tokenized payload distribution that matches a 3-turn chat. Results show 95ms median, 140ms p95 with default settings — we can tune batching to hit your 120ms p95.

07:58 Lina Zhou: You've mentioned quantization — do you handle quantized models in Hosted? Any lock-in?

08:06 Priya Desai: We support quantized variants in both Hosted and Dedicated; quantized models are model variants so it's easy to switch. There's no lock-in — you can export model configs and run them in your private infra if you choose.

08:22 Daniel Park: Ok, stopping screen share. For the code samples, what about telemetry and logging? We need request IDs to tie back to our logs.

08:30 Priya Desai: The SDK automatically returns a request_id header and you can attach custom metadata. The Console ingest shows traces and lets you search by request_id and user token. We'll show an example log snippet: RequestID: rwd-abc123, model: rwd-3-small, latency_ms: 118

08:50 Sofia Martinez: (overlap) also audit logs for admin actions — we need them to go into our SIEM.

08:55 Alex Chen: Audit logs can be exported via syslog or S3 and you can plug them into your SIEM. For Private deployments you have full control.

09:05 Daniel Park: Let's talk about limits — sandbox vs prod. If we start with sandbox and then move to Dedicated, what is the onboarding time?

09:12 Priya Desai: Sandbox is immediate. Dedicated provisioning is typically 2-4 weeks depending on region and GPU availability; Dedicated also includes reserved capacity and SLA. We'll put a timeline in the follow-up.

09:25 Lina Zhou: Are there any compliance certs we should be aware of? SOC2? ISO?

09:30 Alex Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and are working on ISO 27001 for certain regions; we'll share our security package.

09:36 Daniel Park: (note of transition) okay Sofia needs to drop now — thanks for joining.

09:40 Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone — follow-up with the security packet would be great. Bye.

09:45 [Sofia leaves]

09:50 Alex Chen: Back to the demo — Priya, can you run the TypeScript streaming example to show how message-by-message comes through?

09:58 Priya Desai: Sure — running node stream-demo.js. This will stream tokens for a 50-token response. (background typing) You'll see in the console it prints partial chunks, then final event. There's also a callback hook so you can send partial render events to your UI.

10:25 Daniel Park: Looks good. One more question — do you have limits on max context length and how to handle long documents?

10:32 Priya Desai: Max context varies by model family. For long documents we recommend chunking + retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Redwood has built-in embeddings endpoints and you can use our reranker to filter candidate passages. For very long context we also support model-specific streaming of KV cache to disk in Dedicated environments.

10:55 Daniel Park: Let's cover billing. How granular is usage reporting? We need per-team cost chargeback.

11:03 Alex Chen: The Console has token-level billing and you can tag routes and API keys to map usage to teams. We also expose an API for exports so you can run chargeback scripts nightly.

11:18 Lina Zhou: Quick follow — are there example policies for redaction we can apply?

11:24 Priya Desai: Yes, the repo includes a small redaction middleware for Node + Python that strips PII patterns before sending. We'll attach it.

11:35 Daniel Park: Ok, I think that's a solid demo. For the follow-up POC scoping, we'll share expected qps, typical prompt lengths, and required compliance items.

11:45 Alex Chen: Great. Recap of next steps: Priya will send sandbox key and repo; Alex will draft a pilot price; Ignite will provide traffic profile; we'll schedule POC scoping the week of 10/27. Any final questions?

11:58 Lina Zhou: No, thanks — this was helpful.

12:05 Priya Desai: I'll also include the GitHub Actions snippet and the token exchange example.

12:12 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the email.

12:18 [meeting ends]

title: Vanguard Tech - Inference Deployment Discovery
content:
Vanguard Tech - Inference Deployment Discovery

Discovery focused on Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private for Vanguard Tech's inference platform. Key constraints: strict data isolation, bursty nightly traffic, 99th pct latency SLOs for 2s at p99, need for on-prem option for regulated clients. Agreed next steps include pricing, benchmark, and security doc share.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Liam Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Head of ML, Vanguard Tech), Ethan Cole (Platform Eng), Ruth Delgado (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto gen): Vanguard evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted/Private. Primary drivers: isolation for regulated customers, predictable throughput for nightly batch and daytime interactive burst, and the ability to run on-prem for a subset of customers.

[00:00] Liam Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. quick intros on our side, i'm liam park, account exec. Sofia's our solutions eng, she'll do the technical lift.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hi all, priya here — head of ml. We run inference for personalized recommendations and a new assistant product. We have some regulatory customers who require data not leave their VPC, so that's driving interest in private/dedicated options.
[00:31] Sofia Ramirez: Great, thanks priya. quick question — is the VPC requirement per-customer (tenant) or just for specific regulated flows?
[00:40] Priya Nair: It's a subset. about ~15% of our enterprise customers need full isolation and proof of data residency. The rest are fine with cloud-hosted as long as it's encrypted and auditable.
[00:55] Ethan Cole: And on traffic patterns: we have pretty spiky QPS. daytime baseline is 80–120 qps, then we have nightly jobs that push 4–6k qps for short bursts, like 20–30 minutes, for batch enrichment. That's what we're worried about for capacity and costs.
[01:15] Liam Park: Alright that's helpful. high level, Redwood supports three modes — Hosted API for quick ramp, Dedicated reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation, and Private for VPC/on-prem. For your use case sounds like a hybrid could fit — Dedicated for the regular traffic plus a plan for controlled burst capacity or fallback to Hosted for overflow.
[01:35] Ruth Delgado: Can you explain how Redwood's burst model works? We can't have long cold starts for dedicated nodes, and we need guarantees around p99 latency.
[01:45] Sofia Ramirez: sure. for dedicated, customers reserve a pool of GPU capacity. we support autoscaling within the pool and also burst policies — you can configure burst to use either unallocated cloud capacity or pre-assigned burst credit. important: bursts are subject to region availability and we've got rules for fallbacks to compatible model variants to preserve latency.
[02:05] Priya Nair: what about the cost? bursting to hosted sounds cheaper in some cases but then data leaves the private pool, which is an issue for those 15% customers.
[02:16] Liam Park: Exactly — that's the tradeoff. Many teams use a mixed routing policy: route regulated tenants to Dedicated/Private always, and others to Hosted during extreme bursts. If you need absolute on-prem isolation for some customers, we can support Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane — no egress.
[02:36] Ethan Cole: if we go Private for those 15%, can the same model versions be served across Dedicated and Private so we don't have divergence?
[02:45] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, the deployment abstraction lets you pin model versions and rollout policies. The same artifact can be deployed to hosted, dedicated, or private clusters; the runtime handles kernel selection and quantization variants. There can be small differences in latency depending on hardware and quantization, but functionally it's the same model.
[03:06] [background noise, slight crosstalk]
[03:20] Priya Nair: On latency, our target is p99 < 2s for interactive inference. Nightly batch jobs can be relaxed. Will dedicated get us there?
[03:30] Sofia Ramirez: With properly sized pools and kernel/sequence tuning we often hit sub-second p99 on Llama2-ish workloads at typical token lengths. The big knobs are batching, KV cache locality for chat-like workloads, and quantization. For deterministic p99 we recommend dedicated capacity pinned to a commit and a small headroom buffer (10–20%) to absorb spikes.
[03:57] Ruth Delgado: What about lifecycle — model rollouts, canarying? we need to be able to rollback quickly if a new model regresses.
[04:08] Liam Park: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You can set rollout percentages and have automatic fallback to a prior model or a smaller variant if latency or error rate increases.
[04:25] Ethan Cole: On the ops side, what SLA do you offer for Dedicated? We need uptime and latency guarantees for our SLAs to customers.
[04:33] Sofia Ramirez: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets on our reserved tiers. specifics depend on contract level — we can share typical SLA numbers in the doc pack.
[04:45] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk about burst sizing. Our nightly surge is 4–6k qps for ~25 minutes. Do you typically recommend over-provisioning or using burst credits?
[04:57] Sofia Ramirez: There's two common patterns: 1) reserve enough GPUs to handle baseline and moderate spikes and use burst credits for rare extremes; or 2) reserve more aggressive dedicated pools to keep everything internal. The first reduces cost but needs careful routing to ensure regulated tenants aren't routed off-prem. If those bursts are frequent (e.g., daily), reserved capacity is usually more predictable and can be cheaper than repeated burst consumption.
[05:25] Priya Nair: They're nightly and predictable, so maybe reserved makes sense. but cost is still a concern. can you provide some cost modeling?
[05:33] Liam Park: absolutely, we'll send a cost model. we'll ask for your workload traces so Sofia can model token distribution, sequence length, and concurrency to estimate GPU-hours and recommended reservation.
[05:44] Ruth Delgado: Security — we need SOC 2, SSO, audit logs, KMS. How mature is Redwood on that?
[05:52] Liam Park: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integrations (customer-managed KMS for private). We have SOC 2 reports and can share compliance artifacts. For on-prem Private, you can keep the control plane private and integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[06:10] Ethan Cole: For VPC peering, what networking requirements exist? Do we need BGP or specific route setups?
[06:18] Sofia Ramirez: For Private we typically use VPC peering or private link options. There's a network design doc we'll share — it covers IP ranges, peering, firewall rules, and NAT options for restricted environments.
[06:32] [00:06:32 — pause while sharing doc link in chat]
[06:40] Priya Nair: Can you describe the benchmark process? we'd like to run a two-hour benchmark with our payloads.
[06:45] Sofia Ramirez: Sure. Typical benchmark steps: 1) customer provides representative traces and sample prompts; 2) we produce a job that replays traffic at desired QPS and distribution; 3) run on both Dedicated candidate config and Hosted fallback; 4) collect token-level latency, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, and cost per token. We can also test quantization/compile variants.
[07:12] Ruth Delgado: How do you handle cold-start effects for model weights and KV cache? Our chat workloads are sensitive to first-token latency spikes.
[07:22] Sofia Ramirez: Good point. We have pre-warming options, and we maintain warm pools that keep model artifacts resident. For chat, KV cache locality is important — continuous batching and small headroom help avoid those p99 spikes. Cold starts typically affect the very first request after scale-up; we can configure keep-alive to mitigate.
[07:45] Ethan Cole: If we need on-prem, what's the installation footprint? GPU requirements, kube versions?
[07:53] Sofia Ramirez: For on-prem/private deployments we support common distributions Kubernetes 1.25+ typically, NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA 12+ recommended. We'll share an architecture guide with exact node sizing guidance.
[08:07] Priya Nair: Do you provide managed services for Private? We may not have a big infra team.
[08:14] Liam Park: Yes, enterprise plans often include a managed offering where Redwood supports control plane ops and patching. Alternatively, teams can self-manage with our install bundle and we provide remote support.
[08:28] [08:28 — brief crosstalk]
[08:37] Priya Nair: Quick question — what about multitenancy? we want per-tenant isolation for the regulated set but also consolidated models for easier updates.
[08:45] Sofia Ramirez: You can do logical isolation (namespace, RBAC, per-tenant routing) and physical isolation (separate Dedicated pools or Private clusters). Many teams use logical isolation for non-regulated tenants and physical isolation for regulated ones.
[09:00] Priya Nair: Any caveats with model variants and quantization across different hardware? we want consistent outputs for A/B testing.
[09:10] Sofia Ramirez: Quantization and different kernel implementations can introduce tiny numeric differences, but we try to match float32 behavior with debug builds for eval. For strict A/B you can pin the same runtime config or keep a single deployment and route.
[09:30] Ethan Cole: On auditing, do you capture token-level logs? That could be sensitive.
[09:36] Liam Park: We capture metadata and optionally token-level logs depending on config and retention. For regulated data we recommend redacting or using on-prem Private where logs can be kept entirely in customer control.
[09:55] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk timeframe — we're aiming to pilot in Q1. what's a realistic timeline to go from contract to pilot?
[10:05] Liam Park: For Dedicated hosted pilot with reserved pools typically 4–6 weeks — that includes sizing, contract, and a benchmark run. For Private/on-prem it's 6–12 weeks depending on approvals and infra readiness.
[10:18] Ruth Delgado: Do you support heterogeneous GPU fleets? e.g., mix of H100 and A100? We have some older infra.
[10:27] Sofia Ramirez: We support heterogeneous fleets but runtime kernel selection matters — we can route workloads to compatible instances for latency-critical paths. Mixing GPUs is fine but you should expect different perf characteristics.
[10:40] Priya Nair: What's the typical headroom you recommend for p99 guarantees?
[10:45] Sofia Ramirez: 10–25% buffer depending on burst predictability. For highly bursty daily jobs, we recommend a higher buffer or scheduling batch windows to smooth load.
[10:55] Ethan Cole: If we wanted autoscaling on Dedicated, how fast can it scale? seconds? minutes?
[11:02] Sofia Ramirez: Scaling is in the order of minutes for new GPUs to be attached in cloud environments; if you need sub-minute response you should keep warm capacity or use pre-warmed burst pools.
[11:16] [11:16 — short pause while Liam types a note]
[11:25] Priya Nair: Let's get into some concrete numbers — i'll share a 7-day trace with token lengths and concurrency tomorrow. can you take a swing at recommended reserved GPUs?
[11:35] Liam Park: Absolutely. once we have those traces Sofia will run a cost/perf model and propose a recommendation: baseline reserved pool + suggested burst sizing.
[11:44] Ruth Delgado: Any legal hurdles around data residency if we use Hosted for non-regulated tenants?
[11:50] Liam Park: We support region pinning and data residency controls; legal team can review the DPA and addendum for regulated accounts.
[12:00] Priya Nair: ok great. one last question — how do you handle regressions detection? we need alerts when model quality drops after rollout.
[12:08] Sofia Ramirez: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tie-ins to prompt sets and evals. You can set regression alerts on specific prompt sets and automatically halt rollouts.
[12:20] Ethan Cole: I'm curious about caching — can we do prefix caching across tenants to reduce load?
[12:27] Sofia Ramirez: yes, prefix and KV caching are supported. be careful with privacy boundaries — don't share across regulated tenants unless allowed.
[12:36] [12:36 — soft laughter]
[12:40] Liam Park: ok to recap — action items: we'll send pricing/ cost model, Sofia will draft a benchmark plan and we need the traces from Priya. we'll also share SOC2 and the network architecture doc. Pilot timeline targeted Q1.
[12:56] Priya Nair: That sounds good. we'll get traces and schedule the benchmark in the next week. thanks for the clear options.
[13:06] Ruth Delgado: thanks liam and sofia. this was productive.
[13:12] Liam Park: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the doc bundle and scheduling links.

End of transcript.

Shared links and references mentioned in chat: [Security pack (SOC2, DPA) link], [Network architecture guide link], [Dedicated pricing spreadsheet link], [Benchmark plan template link].
