title: IvyGrid - Redwood API credits & hosting options (quickstart discussion)
content:
IvyGrid - Redwood API credits & hosting options (quickstart discussion)

Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-08-27 16:00 PT
- Duration: 47 minutes (recording)
- Attendees: Jordan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (CTO, IvyGrid), Marta Lopez (Head of ML), Samir Patel (SRE), Nina Rivera (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
IvyGrid is evaluating Redwood for an initial PLG-style quickstart (time-to-first-token, free credits) with the possibility of Dedicated or Private later. Key concerns: latency vs cost, data residency and VPC, SOC2 and KMS integration, and pilot success criteria. Redwood to provide credits, security docs, and a follow-up SE benchmark run.

Topics: quickstart credits, time-to-first-token, hosted vs dedicated vs private, VPC/KMS/SAML, throughput/latency tradeoffs, pilot success metrics, next steps and owners.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Miller: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. we have priya, our solutions engineer, too. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Alex Chen: good, thanks. i'm alex. we try to keep this tight, we have like 45 minutes. want to understand quickstart path and what tradeoffs we should be thinking about — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:14] Marta Lopez: yes, and also, how quickly can we get to first token? we have a small demo for investors in two weeks so timeline matters.
[00:19] Priya Shah: absolutely. high level — hosted is fastest to get started, we give free credits and an API key so you can be up in hours. dedicated is reserved GPU capacity for predictable throughput, and private gives the VPC/on-prem control for compliance.
[00:30] Samir Patel: quick question, when you say "free credits" — are there heavy rate limits or warmup penalties? our traffic spikes can be pretty bursty.
[00:37] Jordan Miller: great question. for PLG quickstarts we do throttle to protect the cluster but it's super generous for proofs — and you can request burst increases. the quickstart credit flow is designed to get you to a demo with realistic samples.
[00:48] Nina Rivera: also curious about log retention and audit, we have internal audit teams that ask for long term logs.
[00:52] Priya Shah: hosted has configurable retention tiers; for enterprise we can increase retention or export to your S3. for Private, audit logs stay in your VPC and you control retention via your infra.
[01:01] Alex Chen: ok, on security — do you support SSO/SAML? and KMS integration for key management?
[01:07] Jordan Miller: yes to both. SSO with SAML and SCIM for provisioning. KMS/HSM integrations are available for Dedicated and Private, hosted supports customer-managed keys via our KMS bridge for enterprise customers.
[01:18] Marta Lopez: and SOC2? we need attestation for vendor review.
[01:22] Priya Shah: we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO certs — i'll drop the attestation and the security pack after the call.
[01:28] Alex Chen: lovely. now performance: our workload is short chat completions ~200 tokens with context, p95 latency needs to be sub-300ms for UX reasons, cost target is mid-range — we don't want premium GPU pricing if avoidable. can Redwood meet that on hosted?
[01:44] Priya Shah: p95 <300ms for 200 tokens is aggressive on some models, depends on model family. we have optimized kernels and prefix-KV caching to reduce latency, but the common pattern is: hosted lowest friction, Dedicated gives you tighter latency SLOs (reserved GPU pools), and Private removes network hops if on-prem.
[02:00] Samir Patel: what about the K-V cash? sorry, K-V cash? i saw that in docs — how does that affect latency?
[02:07] Priya Shah: haha, K-V cache — sometimes transcribed as cash — K-V cache stores key-value states of the attention cache so for multi-turn chat we avoid re-computing. it improves latency significantly for repeated context.
[02:18] Alex Chen: and what about cost optimization? we've looked at quantized runtimes and batching.
[02:23] Priya Shah: we recommend a mix: for latency-sensitive calls keep smaller batch sizes and lower quantization aggressiveness; for background embeddings or async tasks use higher batching and 4-bit quantization. Redwood Optimize will suggest batching configs and quant profiles based on your observed workload.
[02:36] Marta Lopez: if we start with hosted and then move to dedicated, how seamless is the routing and rollout?
[02:41] Jordan Miller: seamless — same API and model catalog. you can pin model versions and set rollout policies; traffic can be routed by latency or cost policy. also automatic fallback to compatible variants if capacity is constrained.
[02:52] Alex Chen: we might need private deployment later for EU data residency. what are typical lead times?
[02:57] Jordan Miller: for Private VPC it's usually 4–8 weeks depending on region and networking approvals; on-prem is longer because of air-gapped packaging, typically 8–12 weeks. Dedicated is faster — provisioning reserved pools in a couple of weeks once contract signed.
[03:12] Nina Rivera: what about encryption at rest and in transit?
[03:15] Priya Shah: TLS in transit, and encryption at rest with customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we can enable CMEK via our KMS bridge with customer keys.
[03:24] Samir Patel: curious about limits for streaming responses and function calling — we use tool calls a lot.
[03:29] Priya Shah: streaming is supported on hosted and Dedicated; function/tool calling patterns work the same. large streaming throughput benefits from Dedicated since you can reserve capacity to avoid preemption.
[03:39] Alex Chen: ok, let's talk pilot success criteria. what do you recommend?
[03:42] Jordan Miller: milestones: 1) TTFT — get to first token with your sample app within 48 hours using quickstart credits. 2) Perf baseline — Redwood SE runs a perf test against a realistic payload to measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. 3) Integration checklist — SSO, logging, KMS validation. 4) Go/no-go criteria: p95 under target and cost within expected budget.
[04:03] Marta Lopez: sample app is react based, calls streaming chat for suggestions. maybe we can share the demo code.
[04:07] Priya Shah: perfect — if you share a sample request shape and concurrency, we can do a baseline.
[04:11] Alex Chen: our concurrency is unpredictable; typical baseline is 50 rps with spikes to 250 for short bursts.
[04:16] Priya Shah: that's helpful; we'll propose batching/caching configs. Dedicated autoscaling and burst capacity options can handle spikes better.
[04:25] Jordan Miller: one practical question — time-to-first-token for quickstart: usually under 2 hours if you follow the quickstart and we provide credits. that's accounts for API key, sample app wiring, and initial warmup.
[04:36] Samir Patel: two hours sounds good. any gotchas with rate limits that can block the investor demo?
[04:41] Jordan Miller: for demos we can bump limits for that timeframe. we'll include instructions on how to request a temporary increase in the quickstart docs.
[04:48] Nina Rivera: about billing — can we get a cost projection for expected traffic? we need to justify to finance.
[04:53] Jordan Miller: yes, i'll include a modeled run rate using your shared traffic profile. we'll show hosted vs dedicated unit economics so you can see break-even points.
[05:01] Alex Chen: one more — compliance: do you have an audit log export for SIEM integration (we use Splunk)?
[05:06] Priya Shah: yes, audit logs can be exported to your S3 or pushed to a SIEM endpoint for hosted enterprise; for Private it's native.
[05:13] Marta Lopez: ok great. thanks, this is helpful.
[05:16] Jordan Miller: to recap and close, we'll: send security pack and SOC2 attestation, issue a trial credit code and quickstart guide, and schedule an SE perf call next week to run baseline tests.
[05:27] Alex Chen: sounds good. we'll share sample request shapes and the demo code by Friday.
[05:31] Jordan Miller: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the notes and links.

End of transcript. Some automatic speaker labeling and timestamps may be imperfect.

title: POC Weekly - Synthesis Network Heatmap & Routing Decisions
content:
POC Weekly - Synthesis Network Heatmap & Routing Decisions

Weekly POC sync focussed on newly generated network heatmap, intermittent egress latency spikes during canary, kernel upgrade impact, and risk tradeoffs between hosted fallback and dedicated on-prem capacity. Team agreed to run a controlled rollback rehearsal and to capture traceroutes and firewall rules for deeper analysis.
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-10
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Liu (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM), Ethan Park (Solutions) — Lina Park (Aurelian PM), Tom Reynolds (Aurelian Infra), Jasper Cole (Aurelian CTO), Rita Menon (Aurelian Security), Mike O'Neill (Aurelian Dev)

Summary: quick walk through of network heatmap artifacts, three observed latency spikes on canary routes at 02:14/02:37/03:05 UTC, discussion about MTU and jumbo frames, suggestion of kernel-backed optimization rollback, and next steps to collect traceroutes and firewall/export logs.

[00:00] Sarah Liu: okay everyone, thanks for joining, we got a packed sync — Marco will run the heatmap and then we can triage the spikes, Lina you had flagged the first spike?
[00:12] Lina Park: yeah thanks Sarah, quick thing — we saw the first big tail at 02:14 during our load window, it looked like packet fragmentation maybe? but the team wasn't 100% sure.
[00:22] Marco Diaz: right, we generated the heatmap this morning, it overlays p50/p95/p99 latency per egress hop. i pulled the canary traces and there's a repeated 8-12ms bump before the transit gateway hop, which points to either MTU mismatch or microbursts on the firewall.
[00:40] Tom Reynolds: we did change the firewall ACLs last week, also bumped up anti-ddos signature scanning. that coincides with the timing. could be inspection pause.
[00:50] Jasper Cole: just to be clear, the infrastructure path is our VPC -> TGW -> partner transit -> redwood private peering. if any of those inspect packets with deep packet inspection there's CPU context switches, yeah it adds latency.
[01:05] Marco Diaz: one weird thing — the KV cache warmup on the Redwood side shows an extra 15–20ms on first token for some sessions, but subsequent tokens are fine. so initial handshake + egress queuing compound.
[01:24] Mike O'Neill: are we sure handshake is not TLS renegotiation? we saw a few TLS alerts in the logs but couldn't tie them.
[01:33] Rita Menon: security here — TLS renegotiation would be a red flag for us, but logs were inconclusive. we'll export the full TLS session logs after the call.
[01:45] Sarah Liu: good. Marco, on the kernel upgrade you rolled last week — did you observe any link flapping or offload changes?
[01:53] Marco Diaz: yes small change — we enabled GRO/LRO offload tweaks on a subset of nodes to reduce CPU per packet; in testing this reduced throughput CPU but it can interact badly with jumbo frames when MTU isn't matched. i suspect an offload mismatch.
[02:12] Tom Reynolds: we don't use jumbo frames broadly, only on some racks. maybe that mismatch is the root cause.
[02:21] Ethan Park: i worry more about the fallback routing — we saw a test where traffic shifted to the hosted fallback and p99 jumped by 60ms for a subset. we should quantify cost vs latency for keeping fallback turned on during spikes.
[02:33] Lina Park: cost is definitely a factor. our SRE lead wants predictable SLAs, they'd consider dedicated capacity if cost delta is manageable.
[02:42] Sarah Liu: noted. Marco — can you put together a small paper that shows expected token-cost delta for a dedicated fallback kept for 12 hours/day vs ad-hoc?
[02:50] Marco Diaz: yes, i'll include batching/kv cache effects and note quantization changes.
[02:58] [03:00] Speaker 6: (muffled) also want to call out BGP flap detected earlier — might be noise in traceroute
[03:08] Marco Diaz: good catch, that was a short BGP withdraw at 02:37, the heatmap shows a simultaneous spike — likely route churn. we need the partner transit logs to confirm.
[03:22] Jasper Cole: we're pushing for multi-path to avoid single transit dependency, but partner doesn't support ECMP reliably on that leg.
[03:31] Sarah Liu: okay action: Tom will collect partner contact and traceroutes for the 02:37 window.
[03:35] Tom Reynolds: yes i'll pull traceroutes and netflow and send by Friday.
[03:40] Lina Park: and we'll also share the updated firewall rule set, there are some lingering legacy NAT rules.
[03:45] Rita Menon: security will also export audit logs and the KMS rotation schedule. Jasper, remind — are we comfortable sharing KMS metadata with Redwood?
[03:54] Jasper Cole: we will share metadata and key IDs, not the raw keys. Redwood's KMS integration was in the docs, right Sarah?
[04:02] Sarah Liu: yes we support KMS/HSM integrations and we never ask for customer private keys. we'll accept wrapped keys and audit logs. we'll share the security package link after the call.
[04:12] Marco Diaz: back to perf — i propose a controlled kernel rollback on a canary pool during off-peak. revert the GRO/LRO tweaks and run the same synthetic test with jumbo frames disabled. that should prove/disprove the offload mismatch hypothesis.
[04:27] Tom Reynolds: fine, but we need a rehearsal runbook because our infra team got surprised last time and it caused a brief compaction event.
[04:36] Sarah Liu: yes we'll provide a rollback rehearsal plan. Ethan, can Redwood run the rehearsal and allow customer to shadow?
[04:42] Ethan Park: absolutely, we'll run in a mirrored canary and provide live logs and metrics.
[04:47] Marco Diaz: also i'll produce a heatmap delta comparing pre-upgrade, post-upgrade, and today so the team can visually inspect where latencies clustered.
[04:57] Lina Park: that visual diff would be super helpful. can you annotate which hops are owned by us vs partner vs redwood?
[05:05] Marco Diaz: yes i'll annotate ownership where we have it and mark unknowns.
[05:12] Mike O'Neill: one more dev note — we noticed a tokenization variance between quantized model and float model in internal evals, not related to routing but affects fallback quality. if traffic moves to a smaller quantized fallback, we need to track quality regressions.
[05:27] Sarah Liu: perfect segue — we'll add a small eval harness to capture model output diffs at canary sample rates. Priya will own that with your dev team.
[05:36] Priya Rao: noted, i'll share a template eval set by end of week so you can plug it in.
[05:42] Jasper Cole: regarding compliance, we need proof that audit logs will be retained in-country for certain datasets. Rita will coordinate specific datasets.
[05:51] Rita Menon: yes, i'll send an annotated list of regulated data categories; expect that Monday.
[05:58] Sarah Liu: walk-through of next steps: Marco to generate annotated heatmap and token-cost delta, Tom to provide traceroute/netflow and partner contact, Rita to share regulated dataset list and TLS logs, Redwood to share security docs and KMS integration guide, and schedule kernel rollback rehearsal week of Jan 24.
[06:18] Tom Reynolds: quick Q — what's the recommended default MTU from Redwood side for private peering?
[06:24] Marco Diaz: we recommend 1500 unless you're using jumbo end-to-end and have confirmed MTU on all transit hops; otherwise stick to 1500 to avoid fragmentation.
[06:31] (crosstalk)
[06:40] Sarah Liu: okay everyone, we'll capture these in the ticket and share artifacts. any blockers?
[06:45] Lina Park: non-blocker, timeline is fine as long as rehearsal is scheduled before Feb 1.
[06:50] Jasper Cole: same, if we can have rehearsal and postmortem within two weeks that's good.
[06:55] Sarah Liu: great thanks — we'll circle back in the next weekly unless anything urgent pops up.

End of transcript.

title: Hosted API sandbox lab — chat & text-gen basics + retry scenarios
content:
Hosted API sandbox lab — chat & text-gen basics + retry scenarios

Intro demo of Redwood hosted inference for chat/text generation. Walked through streaming behavior, key request params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop tokens), retry/backoff and idempotency considerations, and a short Console tour for per-route latency/cost. Discussed Optimize recommendations (batching, KV cache reuse, quantization) and enterprise concerns (SAML SSO, SOC2, audit logs). Agreed to sandbox access and smoke tests.
Meeting header: 2026-04-09 15:00 UTC — duration 47m. Attendees listed above.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone — thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. We've got Priya, our SE, and Sam who will jump in with the console demo. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Lena: Good thanks, Jordan. Excited — we just want a short hands-on of the hosted API for chat gen, mainly streaming, params and what to do when things error out.
[00:18] Jordan: Perfect that's exactly what we'll show. Priya, you want to intro the lab?
[00:21] Priya: Yeah hi all — real quick plan: 10 minutes on core streaming behavior and request params, 15 minutes live sandbox runs (I'll paste curl and SDK calls), then 15 on retry/backoff, idempotency and Console/Optimize tips and finally Q&A. Sound ok?
[00:33] Marco: Sounds great. We're especially worried about tail latency and cost per token.
[00:37] Priya: Totally. We'll show the console traces so you can see token breakdown and how batching/kv cache affects unit cost.
[00:45] Jordan: One quick administrative note — are there any security or compliance blockers up front? SAML / SSO, SOC2?
[00:50] Aisha: We need SOC2 certificate and we use SAML SSO internally. Also KMS for keys ideally.
[00:55] Jordan: Great — we will share security pack after the call. Redwood supports SSO and KMS/HSM integrations and SOC2. I'll follow up with the docs.

[05:00] Priya: Ok, starting the demo — this is the hosted chat endpoint in the sandbox. First behavior: streaming. When you open a stream you'll get incremental partial chunks — useful for UI latency. Note partials are not final predictions; in speech it's like interim captions.
[05:20] Jordan: One common gotcha — streaming shows partial tokens and can be restarted on retries; your frontend should handle deduping partials vs final.
[05:35] Kenji: If we reconnect and resume, does the service replay the entire context or just deltas?
[05:40] Priya: We replay deltas where possible, but to be safe you should send a conversation snapshot up to the last confirmed user message. We also support KV cache reuse if you're pinning model variants. Some transcriptions will show "K V cache" spelled out in places.

[10:00] Priya: Live curl example: POST to /v1/chat with messages array, set stream=true for SSE. Key params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop tokens. We'll paste this in chat.
[10:20] (Priya pastes curl)
[10:30] Marco: Quick question — which param most affects hallucinations?
[10:33] Priya: Temperature and top_p. Lower temperature reduces randomness; top_p controls nucleus sampling. Also good prompt engineering and stop tokens cut off generation where applicable. For deterministic outputs set temperature ~0 and top_p ~0.0-0.1.

[15:00] Priya: Now a small failure mode — we purposely induced a partial drop mid-stream. Watch how the stream emits a 5xx and then our SDK triggers exponential backoff.
[15:18] Sam: The SDK includes automatic retry for idempotent requests. For non-idempotent generation (streams that have side effects) we recommend client-controlled retries with idempotency keys. We usually attach a client_message_id to each user turn.
[15:40] Aisha: So idempotency key is our responsibility?
[15:42] Priya: Yes — you supply an idempotency_key header. For simple text generation where you can tolerate duplicates, the SDK retry policy is fine; for billing and dedupe we recommend explicit keys.

[20:00] Priya: Backoff: use jittered exponential backoff. Example: base 500ms, multiplier 2x, max 8s, with full jitter. Avoid tight retry loops because they inflate load and cost.
[20:20] Kenji: Any rate limit headers we can read to adaptively backoff?
[20:24] Priya: Yes the API returns x-rate-limit-remaining and a Retry-After when throttled. Console traces also show per-route QPS metrics.

[25:00] Priya: Now let's look at the Console — Sam, can you show the token breakdown?
[25:10] Sam: Sure. Here is a sample route — per-token cost, P95 latency and token counts. The Console groups by model variant so you can see the cost impact if you switch to a quantized variant.
[25:30] Sam: Also we surface prefix cache hits — which we call KV cache reuse — that reduces model work when you've repeated prompts or system instructions.
[25:45] Marco: If we use dedicated capacity versus hosted, how different are the SLOs?
[25:50] Jordan: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and private pools with higher SLAs, hosted is multi-tenant but we still publish performance profiles. For strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated or pinning to a lower-latency model variant.

[30:00] Priya: Optimize suggestions: 1) batch short messages to amortize GPU overhead, 2) enable prefix KV caching for repeated system messages, 3) use a quantized variant (8-bit or 4-bit) if high throughput with slightly lower quality is acceptable, 4) tune max_tokens per user turn to the minimum needed.
[30:25] Lena: For batching — how does that affect user perceived latency?
[30:28] Priya: Batching is tradeoff — it improves throughput and lowers cost per token but you increase queuing latency. We recommend adaptive batching: small immediate responses for interactive UI, larger batches for background tasks (summaries).

[35:00] Priya: Quick note on safety: if you use stop tokens, model guarentees for truncation are best-effort. Also we recommend server-side safety filters or a secondary reranker to catch edge cases.

[36:00] Marco: For retries, do we get chargedback for partially generated tokens that then fail?
[36:05] Jordan: You get billed for tokens processed by the model. If a stream fails mid-generation you are charged for tokens consumed. That's why idempotency + conservative retry logic matters. We'll include guidance in the follow-up doc.

[40:00] Priya: Wrapping up — we pushed a small guided exercise: run the sandbox curl we pasted, try toggling temperature and stream=true/false, trigger an intentional error and observe console traces.
[40:15] Lena: We'll run that and get back to you.
[40:20] Aisha: And we'll need the SOC2 and SAML docs.
[40:25] Jordan: Yep I'll send the security pack. Priya will share the Optimize spreadsheet and sample SDK snippets.

[45:00] Jordan: Any other questions?
[45:05] Kenji: One last — can Redwood run a short perf benchmark with our typical token mix?
[45:10] Jordan: Yes we can — that would be a scoped POC. We'll propose a runbook after your smoke test.
[46:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and snippets.

End transcript.

Notes: occasional transcript artifacts e.g., misheard acronyms ("K V cache" spelled occasionally), filler words and overlapping talk. References shared: sandbox curl (link sent in chat), console screenshot (link), security pack (link to drive).

title: ElkShore throughput & latency characterization call
content:
ElkShore throughput & latency characterization call

First discovery focused on p95 latency and throughput needs for ElkShore's real-time summarization product. Customer is weighing Redwood hosted for speed of onboarding vs Dedicated/Private for data residency and consistent p95. Agreed to run a short token/sec benchmark and follow up with dedicated sizing worksheet and security docs.
Redwood: share dedicated capacity worksheet and rough pricing (Alice) - by 2029-08-15
Customer: provide representative prompt set and traffic profile (Maya) - by 2029-08-16
Redwood/Customer: schedule 2-hour token/sec benchmark window (Marco + Owen) - target week of 2029-08-19
Redwood: share SOC2 and VPC packaging docs (Alice) - by 2029-08-16
Alice Chen (AE) | Send dedicated capacity worksheet + hosted pricing assumptions | 2029-08-15
Marco Ruiz (SE) | Propose benchmark harness and sample scripts, coordinate run | 2029-08-16
Maya Li (Customer) | Upload 3 representative prompts + avg reply length to share link | 2029-08-16
Owen R. (Customer) | Provision test VPC peering details if we run private pilot | 2029-08-19
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-08-13
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (CTO - ElkShore), Maya Li (Lead ML Eng), Owen R. (Infra)

Auto-summary: Quick discovery to map p95 targets and throughput for a streaming summarization use-case. Heavy focus on p95 at tail, fallback policies, and whether hosted can meet SLOs or if they need Dedicated/Private for predictable tail latency and KMS integration.

[00:00] Alice Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, on today's agenda we want to understand your latency SLOs, concurrency patterns, and what kind of streaming or token/sec behavior you have. Sanjay, do you want to kick off with a little context?

[00:17] Sanjay Patel: Sure, yep, thanks Alice. So ElkShore runs a real-time meeting summarization product embedded in our web client. Typical sessions are 10 to 60 minutes, but we do incremental summaries every 5-10 seconds of new transcript. So it's very streaming-y, like token bursts. Our SLA is customer-facing: p95 end-to-end summary update under 250 ms ideally, but we know that includes network and client processing. The core ask is can Redwood meet p95 generation under 120-150 ms at our expected concurrency.

[00:48] Marco Ruiz: Quick clarification — is the 120-150 ms target purely for server gen time (inference) or end-to-end?

[00:53] Maya Li: It's really server-side. We instrumented our current stack, and network/client takes roughly 80 to 100 ms, so we want inference not to blow out the p95.

[01:10] Alice Chen: Got it. And volume-wise, what's peak concurrent requests per region?

[01:15] Maya Li: Peak concurrency is about 600 concurrent users in US-East during lunch hour, each producing a burst of short prompts every 5-8s. Average tokens per prompt is 30, average tokens generated ~60. So tokens/sec is spiky — like short bursts of 3k to 6k tokens/sec sustained over a few seconds.

[01:40] Owen R.: And the customer data is PII, so we'll need encryption at rest and KMS integration, also SOC2 and audit logs; may need a private deployment if we can't get those guarantees in hosted.

[01:52] Marco Ruiz: Understood. So couple of axes: latency SLO at p95, steady-state throughput, and cold start/kind of KV cache behavior for streaming with KV cache/prefix caching. For streaming, we can keep KV cache warm for a session, which really helps tail for incremental tokens.

[02:10] Sanjay Patel: Can you explain the KV cache bit more? We've seen people talk about KV cache but not sure how it translates to our per-session summaries.

[02:18] Marco Ruiz: Yeah. So when you do iterative summaries of a conversation, the model keeps a KV cache of previous context so subsequent tokens don't need to recompute full attention on the full prefix. That reduces per-token latency as session grows. On Redwood hosted, we have session affinity options and prefix caching to keep that state cached in memory; on Dedicated we can pin sessions to GPUs for even lower tail latency. On Private you manage the cache, so it's super predictable but needs ops work.

[02:50] Maya Li: Do you have numbers for how much p95 drops with warm KV cache vs cold?

[02:55] Marco Ruiz: Ballpark: warm token latency can be 20-40% lower than cold for the same model and batch size, because we avoid recomputing prefix. But it depends on seqlen and model architecture. We'll need to measure with your prompt distribution.

[03:09] Sanjay Patel: Ok. Another question: how do you handle batching for short prompts? Batching helps throughput but hurts latency.

[03:15] Alice Chen: Right, so our runtime does continuous batching and you can configure latency SLOs so the router will trade off batching vs single-request latency. For strict p95 we can set a tight latency budget and the router will prioritise immediate dispatch to avoid waiting for batch fill. That means higher cost per token but lower tail.

[03:33] Owen R.: If we go Dedicated, do we get stricter controls over batching thresholds?

[03:36] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Dedicated gives you more control — and you can size GPU pools to match concurrency so batching behavior becomes predictable. Also Dedicated supports reserving warm pools and pre-warmed models which reduces cold starts.

[03:49] Maya Li: We also want to minimize jitter at p95 across multi-region. We plan to route users to us-east primarily, with failover to us-west. How's multi-region routing handled?

[03:59] Alice Chen: We support region routing by policy, and you can configure fallback policies. For strict p95 we usually recommend keeping active capacity in your primary region and a readied failover in secondaries. If you need guaranteed cross-region p95, Dedicated or Private with multi-region deployment is safer. Hosted can do it but there's more variability during spikes.

[04:27] Sanjay Patel: What about model choice — are you suggesting a smaller model for latency? We're currently on an in-house tuned LLaMA-ish variant but might consider Redwood-curated models.

[04:36] Marco Ruiz: Model choice matters a lot — smaller, int8/4-bit quantized models reduce per-token latency. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles. There's a tradeoff between quality and latency; for short summary updates you might tolerate a smaller decoder and then run a higher-quality recap less frequently.

[04:56] Maya Li: Hmm might be an interesting hybrid: low-latency incremental summaries with a high-quality batch recap every minute. That could reduce overall cost and p95 pressure.

[05:05] Owen R.: On Private, can we integrate our HSM/KMS for key management? We need envelope encryption keys in our HSM.

[05:12] Alice Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. Dedicated supports KMS integrations too but for HSM-level custody we recommend Private. We'll share the KMS integration doc.

[05:26] Sanjay Patel: Let's talk numbers — can Redwood hit 120-150ms server-side p95 for token generation for ~600 concurrency with those short token bursts?

[05:36] Marco Ruiz: Short answer: probably not on hosted at scale without specialized tuning and warm pools; hosted may hit it for lighter loads but for 600 concurrent bursty sessions Dedicated with pinned warm pools or Private are much more predictable. But we should run a benchmark. Proposed test: we spin up a dedicated bench harness simulating 600 concurrent sessions, average prompt 30 tokens, generate 60 tokens, repeat bursts every 6s for a 10-minute window and measure p50/p95/p99.

[06:03] Maya Li: That sounds good. What hardware do you plan to run on? We have cost limits and want a realistic estimate for GS/RTX class.

[06:11] Marco Ruiz: For initial profiling we suggest testing on a few instance types — e.g., A100-class and an accelerated inference config (like 80GB and quantized 8-bit on cost-optimized Ampere). For Dedicated we can propose a mix. We'll include Redwood's performance profiles per model+hardware so you can see tokens/sec and p95 numbers.

[06:37] Sanjay Patel: For the benchmark, can we also see impact of batch sizes and router latency budgets — like run three runs: aggressive batching, balanced, and low-latency mode?

[06:46] Alice Chen: Absolutely. We'll run multi-config tests and provide the CSV with p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.

[06:52] Owen R.: One more infra question — do you manage GPU preemption or eviction? If a node is evicted, how graceful is fallover for in-flight streaming sessions?

[07:02] Marco Ruiz: For Dedicated and Private we have controlled eviction policies — Dedicated has SLA-backed capacity so evictions are rare. The runtime supports graceful fallback: we checkpoint KV cache periodically and have automatic retries to a fallback model variant in another pool. For hosted we have multi-tenant constraints and fallbacks to smaller model variants if capacity is constrained. We can show our fallback policy diagram.

[07:25] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Any compliance gaps we should be worried about?

[07:30] Alice Chen: We are SOC2 Type II, and we can provide detailed audit/logging for Dedicated and Private. Hosted includes audit logs but for some audit requirements customers want Private to own the logs. We'll attach the security pack.

[07:43] Maya Li: On telemetry — we need token-level latency traces. Does Redwood expose per-token latency or just per-request?

[07:49] Marco Ruiz: We expose detailed token-level traces in Redwood Console for Dedicated and can push traces to your tracing backend via traces hooks. Hosted exposes summarized metrics but we can enable more detailed debug traces during benchmark windows.

[08:05] Sanjay Patel: Ok next let's lock down the benchmark window. We want to minimize user disruption but need realistic load. Owen, can your infra team give a couple of windows next week?

[08:14] Owen R.: Yes, I'll ping ops and propose Thu/Fri next week mornings. I'll share a calendar invite after.

[08:20] Alice Chen: Great. We'll draft the harness and send it to Marco and Owen for sign-off.

[08:25] Maya Li: Slight tangent — cost sensitivity. If we go low-latency mode with tight latency budgets and low batching, cost per token may spike. Can you provide rough cost tradeoff numbers?

[08:35] Marco Ruiz: We'll include a cost-vs-latency spreadsheet — two axes: cost per 1k tokens vs achieved p95 for each model/hardware/config. Historically, reducing batching to hit sub-150ms p95 increases cost 1.8-2.3x compared to optimized batching. We'll provide more precise estimates after the benchmark.

[08:56] Sanjay Patel: Also want to know runbook for on-call when p95 spikes. How do fallbacks and alerts work?

[09:04] Alice Chen: Redwood Console supports per-route SLO alerts, and you can configure automatic fallback to a lower-cost model or different region. We'll demo the runbook and escalation paths in the next call.

[09:18] Marco Ruiz: Quick note on quantization — some of the earlier generation quant tools can change output distribution; we recommend running quality regressions tied to your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can automate those evals and tie them to rollout policies.

[09:35] Maya Li: Ok that is helpful. Any blockers for starting a pilot?

[09:38] Alice Chen: Only thing we need from you is the prompt set and permission to run a 10-20 minute benchmark. We'll use a separate bench account and neutral data handling, then delete logs as per your retention policy.

[09:50] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Could you also include a sketch of expected Dedicated sizing for 600 users targeting 150ms p95? Even a rough ballpark will help justify to finance.

[09:58] Marco Ruiz: We'll include a sizing sketch — likely a mix of several GPU nodes with pre-warmed pools; we'll put ranges. We'll be explicit about assumptions (prompt length, model, quant).

[10:12] Owen R.: Final question — any differences in error budgets when streaming partial tokens vs full response streaming? We sometimes send partial deltas to client.

[10:22] Marco Ruiz: Partial streaming increases surface area for transient errors — but our streaming runtime supports resumable streams and tokenized ACKs so the client can re-request missing token ranges. This is more robust in Dedicated/Private where session affinity is guaranteed.

[10:40] Alice Chen: Ok, we've got good alignment. Recap of next steps: Alice shares pricing & security docs; Marco shares benchmark harness and coordinate runs with Owen; Maya shares prompt set; Owen schedules infra window.

[10:55] Sanjay Patel: Appreciate the time. If the benchmark looks good, we'll likely pilot Dedicated capacity for the US-East region and consider Private for EU data residency.

[11:05] Alice Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with an email thread and get the invites on the calendar. Thanks everyone.

[11:12] -- end meeting --

Notes on transcript quality: intermittent mis-attribution of speakers in the live notes, a few filler words, some technical acronyms may be slightly garbled (e.g., HSM spelled out or heard as H S M).

title: BridgeScale — streaming liveness & burst simulator demo
content:
BridgeScale — streaming liveness & burst simulator demo

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-21
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 66 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Jason Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Product), Alex Chen (BridgeScale CTO), Maya Patel (Eng Manager), Samir Rao (SRE), Erin Lee (Security)

Summary:
Quick demo focused on streaming liveness under burst traffic, long-context behavior (50k token-ish use case), and how Redwood's Console/Optimize suggestions interact with throughput and backpressure. Customer wanted to validate Hosted vs Dedicated tradeoffs and confirm telemetry for audit/SOC2.

Topics covered:
- Burst simulator run and how it triggers streaming backpressure fallback
- Long context KV-cache hit/miss effects on latency and memory
- TTLs and session eviction policies in Console
- Quantization and batching recommendations from Optimize
- Security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO) and data residency

Action items (recorded in call):
- Run extended burst sim with their prompt set
- Share SOC2 + KMS integration doc and private deployment options
- Pricing for a month-long Dedicated pilot with burst buffer capacity

Transcript:
[00:00] Jason: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm Jason, AE on the account, and Priya is our SE who'll walk through the simulator and the console.
[00:12] Alex: hey Jason, hi Priya, thanks. we got a packed agenda. we're most worried about the voice assistant's 40k–60k context windows and then sudden spikes at holiday launches.
[00:22] Priya: cool, yeah we'll show both long context behavior and a synthetic burst we run from the Console. we'll also point out what Optimize recommends for batching and quant profiles.
[00:31] Maya: quick qual question — are you expecting us to go Dedicated for the pilot or can we do Hosted with burst buffer?
[00:38] Jason: good question. short answer: you can start Hosted but with predictable bursts Dedicated gives better latency SLOs and isolation. there are tradeoffs on cost.
[00:48] Samir: cost and SLOs — do you have real numbers? like p50/p95 for hosted under a 5000 rps burst for a 4k token response vs dedicated?
[01:03] Priya: i have an example — it's in the Console demo. but high-level: Hosted uses smart routing and fallback to a smaller quantized variant when queues fill, so p95 can climb. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools so tail latency stays stable, we can show numbers.
[01:18] Erin: and from security, SAML SSO and KMS — can you confirm where keys live for Hosted?
[01:25] Jason: Hosted can integrate customer KMS via our keywrap flow, but for full control Private deployment/VPC keeps keys entirely customer-managed. we'll attach the KMS doc after.
[01:36] [00:60] Priya: ok i'm sharing my screen — Console > Experiments > Burst simulator. i'm going to load BridgeScale's anonymized prompt profile (sample) and run the 10-minute burst at 5k rps to show the state transitions.
[02:10] Alex: slight audio delay here, but i'm seeing the graph. what's that orange line?
[02:17] Priya: that's queue depth. blue is throughput, green is avg latency. notice at minute 2 the KV cache starts getting evictions, we have a spike to 1.2s avg — that correlates to cold kv hits.
[02:32] Maya: the KV cash — excuse me — kv cache — are those per-session or global?
[02:36] Priya: they're shard-local but we present them as logical per-customer caches. we can tune TTLs per route in the Console; Optimize will recommend a TTL based on access patterns.
[02:49] Samir: when the KV cache evicts and latency spikes, what fallback happens for streaming? do you buffer or chunk tokens?
[02:58] Priya: Redwood's streaming runtime does continuous batching and if the backpressure exceeds the burst buffer threshold, we switch to chunked generation with per-chunk ACKs. that keeps connections alive but increases perceived latency.
[03:12] Alex: so chunked generation will still stream tokens but slower, right? we worry about liveness — users disconnecting if tokens lag for >2s.
[03:20] Priya: correct, that's why we demoed the liveness policy. you can set a minimal token heartbeat and fallback to a shorter model variant to keep token heartbeat under 200ms.
[03:32] [03:45] Jason: quick interruption — previously you mentioned smaller quantized variants — do those change output quality? we have regression sensitivity tests.
[03:52] Priya: they can. Optimize will suggest when to use a quantized variant and surface evaluation deltas on your prompt set. for BridgeScale's QA set we expect negligible drop for templated responses but could see regression on long-form narratives.
[04:07] Maya: hmm, for our product the narrative style matters. we won't accept hallucinations increasing. what's the rollback story?
[04:14] Priya: rollouts are canary/A-B with automatic rollback based on your eval hooks and quality thresholds in the Console. also you can pin a model version per route.
[04:26] [05:00] Priya: i'm toggling the burst buffer to simulate saturation — notice the system moves requests to a fallback pool. that triggers the Console alert and creates a replay log you can download.
[05:16] Samir: logs — do those include raw prompts?
[05:19] Priya: by default logs are redacted; we support full-text if you opt-in and sign the data policy. there's also field-level redaction and PII masking hooks.
[05:30] Erin: ok, audit logs for SOC2 evidence — are they immutable? can we forward to our SIEM?
[05:36] Jason: yes, audit trails are append-only and we have integrations to forward to Splunk/Datadog and S3 for long-term retention.
[05:43] [06:00] Priya: now i'll run the long-context run. this is a 50k token conversational session that keeps growing. watch memory usage and kv-hit rate.
[06:15] Maya: timeline on memory — what happens when session exceeds the GPU KV capacity? does Redwood truncate history?
[06:21] Priya: default is soft-truncate based on relevance scoring; we maintain a sliding window and score chunks, but you can opt-in for full-history offloading to cheap storage with prefetch. that's part of the private deployment play.
[06:35] Alex: would that prefetch add cold-start latency for old segments?
[06:40] Priya: yes, slightly — Optimize can recommend a prefetch horizon to balance hit-rates vs latency.
[06:46] [07:00] Jason: can we pause — deep question on telemetry: we need token-level billing and per-route latency histograms for our finance/ops. is that available?
[07:09] Liam: yes, Console exposes token counts, model choices, and per-api-key cost breakdowns. there's an API export for billing pipelines.
[07:19] Maya: how about per-tenant throttling? we have multi-tenant customers with different SLAs.
[07:25] Priya: you can set per-api-key quotas and priority classes. we also support routing policies so high-priority traffic goes to dedicated pools.
[07:35] [08:00] Priya: i'm toggling to the Optimize tab — it shows recommendations: increase batch window to 15ms for throughput vs p95, consider q4_8 quant for the encoder, and TTL 30m for KV for this profile.
[08:19] Samir: q4_8 — does that require model conversion time? how disruptive is a quant swap?
[08:25] Priya: conversion is a one-time step for a model variant. we host multiple quant variants and can route to them. switching in production is via rollout policy. downtime is zero.
[08:36] [09:00] Alex: you mentioned routing fallbacks across regions — if a whole region loses capacity do you failover? what's the cross-region latency penalty?
[09:10] Priya: we do cross-region failover, we prefer warm standbys, but cross-region adds RTT so p95 will increase. Console shows simulated failover impact for your region-to-region RTT.
[09:24] Maya: are there costs for cross-region egress?
[09:27] Jason: yes, egress is billed; we'll show a pricing matrix. for mission-critical apps many customers accept the trade-off.
[09:36] [10:00] Priya: time for a rough live simulation: i'm initiating a 10-minute synthetic burst with mixed long-session and new session traffic. watch the streaming connections and token heartbeats.
[10:13] Alex: seeing a spike, the stream delta widens at t+90s. can you scroll console to the trace?
[10:19] Priya: mmh let me pull traces — here's a few request traces showing chunked fallback at 1:32. notice the connection stayed open even though throughput dropped.
[10:34] Samir: okay, but what about connection churn? do you have auto-reconnect hints for clients?
[10:39] Priya: we surface retry hints and recommended client-side backoff. also we provide SDK patterns for streaming reconnection to re-establish KV context.
[10:50] [11:00] Jason: question for Priya: for our POC can you run this exact profile for 2 hours and export the raw traces and the Optimize suggestions?
[11:08] Priya: yes, we can. i'll include timestamps and the console replay logs.
[11:12] [12:00] Maya: what about end-to-end latency SLOs in SLA? we need a 99th under 800ms for 4k token responses — is that achievable?
[11:24] Priya: on Dedicated with pinned model versions and pre-warmed KV caches it's achievable. Hosted is trickier unless we provision burst buffers and reserved capacity.
[11:34] Erin: on security again — if we go Dedicated in our VPC, do you still see any PII in logs?
[11:41] Jason: Dedicated in VPC with customer-managed KMS keeps logs in your tenancy, but debug-level logs may still contain tokens unless you enable PII scrubbing. we'll provide config.
[11:52] [13:00] Alex: competitive question — have you run similar demos for other vendors? we looked at OpenAI's streaming behavior and it would drop connections without chunked fallback.
[13:09] Priya: yes, we've done comparative tests. Redwood emphasizes graceful degradation rather than hard drops; Optimize helps choose the right fallback that minimizes quality loss.
[13:20] [14:00] Priya: i'm toggling replay — here's an example where Optimize suggests switching to a different batching profile mid-burst which reduced p95 by 30% at cost +12%.
[14:13] Samir: can we tune the cost/latency knob per route?
[14:18] Priya: yes, per-route policy allows you to set cost sensitivity and latency targets. Console will then surface explicit tradeoffs.
[14:27] [15:00] Liam: small aside — Liam from Product here — how reproducible are these sims in customer's environment vs ours?
[15:35] Priya: sims approximate customer patterns but we always recommend a pilot with real traffic; that's why we do a pilot for a week with live traffic shaping.
[15:44] Alex: timeline — we want to pilot before our summer release in mid-May. is that feasible?
[15:50] Jason: yes, feasible. we can kickoff pilot in early April.
[16:00] [16:30] Priya: running through the last part — TTL tuning, eviction thresholds, and fallback model config. i'm adding an example of a canary rollout policy and how Console automates rollback when evals degrade by >2%.
[16:45] Maya: two concerns: our QA team will run long narrative prompts and will fail any change that alters style. will Optimize give us the delta matrix per prompt?
[16:59] Priya: yes, we can attach per-prompt delta in the Optimize report. it's a key feature for your use-case.
[17:10] [17:30] Jason: Security followup — Erin, anything else?
[17:33] Erin: just to confirm: will you provide a KMS integration runbook and SOC2 evidence? also we want example audit logs for a month retention.
[17:45] Jason: will do, we'll attach to the follow up email.
[17:50] [18:00] Alex: ok, last set of items — pricing appetite and pilot size. we think 200k monthly active users, avg 3k tokens, and peaks up to 8k rps over minutes.
[18:09] Jason: noted. we'll produce a Dedicated pilot quote with burst buffer and a Hosted pilot alternative.
[18:16] [19:00] Priya: i'll note that Optimize suggested q4_8 for enc and TTL 30m, but for your narrative alerts we'll pin the full fp16 variant in the pilot.
[19:27] Samir: do you have SDK guidance for streaming reconnection that preserves KV context? we need Node + mobile examples.
[19:34] Priya: yes, we have client SDK patterns for rehydration and we'll share links.
[19:39] [20:00] Jason: wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners. Priya will run 2hr sim, Alex to send prompt set, Jason to send pricing, and Erin to get SOC/KMS docs.
[20:12] Alex: sounds good. one last question — will we get live support during the pilot?
[20:18] Jason: pilot includes SE support and a warroom for the initial 72 hours of the pilot.
[20:24] Maya: ok thanks everyone.
[20:30] [END]

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional mis-typed terms (KV cash, Red wood) and minor speaker mislabels. The Console demo produced export artifacts (burst-sim replay, trace logs) referenced above.

References shared: https://redwood.ai/docs/kms-integration (link placeholder), https://redwood.ai/console/burst-simulator (link placeholder)

Explicit next steps (verbatim):
- Priya to run 2hr simulated burst with BridgeScale prompt set and share raw traces and Optimize report (due 2027-03-24)
- Jason to provide pilot contract template and two pricing options (Hosted burst + Dedicated pilot) (due 2027-03-23)
- Alex to share anonymized prompt set and 90-day traffic histogram (due 2027-03-22)

title: Pilot latency sizing and benchmarking kickoff
content:
Pilot latency sizing and benchmarking kickoff

Meeting header: 2027-11-24 16:00 PT | Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Cobalt Head of ML), Tom Reed (Cobalt SRE), Priya Shah (Cobalt Product), Ethan Cole (Cobalt DevOps)

Summary:
- Kickoff to define POC success criteria for latency/throughput (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, and an initial measurement plan.
- Agreement to collect representative traces and run a hands-on benchmark early December.
- Action items: Redwood to produce benchmark matrix; Cobalt to share traffic samples and infra constraints.

Topics:
- Clarify TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total per-token) SLO intent
- Define target percentiles (p95/p99) and acceptable tails
- Workload composition (short Q&A vs long generation) and sampling plan
- Measurement harness, environment (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and cost/runtime tradeoffs
- Security and on-prem constraints for routing/fallback

00:00 Maya: "All right, folks, thanks for joining. I'll give a quick agenda: scope success criteria, figure out the workload mix, set p95/p99 goals for TTFT and TPOT, and then align on next steps. Diego will walk the benchmark approach."
00:28 Lena: "Sounds good. For context, our app is a clinical summarization assistant. Mixed traffic — about 70% short requests (single-paragraph summaries), 30% long notes generation, and occasional batch embeddings. Latency is user-visible for triage flows."
00:45 Tom: "We also have constraints on PII handling and a private VPC requirement for any pilot that touches PHI. We'll try to keep data anonymized for the initial run, but we need to know if Redwood can support a VPC or on-prem path later."
01:10 Diego: "Understood. For the POC we can run in Redwood hosted infra with sanitized traces; after we validate SLOs we can move to Dedicated or Private. Quick question: is the primacy TTFT — i.e., time to first token for a user-facing typing experience — or TPOT/cost per token?"
01:31 Priya: "TTFT is most important for the triage UI — users expect answers quickly. For nightly batch jobs, TPOT and cost matter more. We need both, but TTFT gets top priority for acceptance."
02:05 Noah: "Just to set terms: TTFT is time-to-first-token (measured at the API ingress to the first byte returned). TPOT we'll treat as total per-token latency (or the wallclock to stream the entire response) — and we'll also report per-token throughput (tokens/sec)."
02:28 Lena: "Can we align on percentiles? We're thinking p95 for TTFT should be 150-200ms, p99 under 400ms for short prompts. Is that realistic?"
02:45 Diego: "Depends on model, sequence length, and batching. For a 7B quantized model on a dedicated GPU pool, p95 TTFT ~80-120ms is achievable; p99 can spike higher. On hosted multi-tenant we typically budget higher. For long generations TPOT p95 is more like 200-600ms per k tokens depending on context. We should map targets per workload class."
03:10 Tom: "We can't accept p99 > 1s on our triage flow. That will look bad to clinicians."
03:20 Maya: "Okay, let's capture hard acceptance criteria vs stretch goals. How about we propose: triage short (<=64 tokens) TTFT p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 450ms as acceptance; stretch p95 <= 120ms p99 <= 300ms. Long generation (<=1024 tokens) TPOT p95 <= 1.2s per 100 tokens, p99 <= 2.5s per 100 tokens? We can iterate."
03:55 Priya: "The per-100-token metric is fine, we just need a consistent normalization. We'll model costs against TPOT eventually."
04:10 Diego: "Great. For benchmarking we recommend a matrix: workload class (short/medium/long), token distributions, concurrency levels, cold vs warm cache, routing fallback scenarios, and sample percentiles (p50/p95/p99/stddev). We'll also capture throughput (tokens/sec) at steady state."
04:40 Lena: "What about KV cache / prefix reuse? Our triage uses common prompt prefixes and we expect cache hits to reduce TTFT. Should we simulate different hit rates?"
04:55 Diego: "Yes — include cache hit tiers: 0%, 50%, 90% to show impact. Redwood supports prefix / KV caching. We'll instrument the runs to show delta. Also show batching effects at various concurrency points."
05:20 Ethan: "One constraint: our test environment has egress bandwidth caps and no GPU bursting for the private option. We'll document that so the benchmark matches realistic constraints."
05:40 Maya: "We'll need those infra details — Tom/Ethan can supply them. Next, measurement harness: we can provide a reproducible test runner (locally-run load runner + Redwood benchmark harness) and a template for traffic replay. Does that work?"
06:00 Tom: "Yes. We'll need instructions to anonymize PHI. Also, we may prefer to run the final acceptance benchmark in our staging VPC with Redwood Private if the hosted results are promising."
06:20 Diego: "That's fine. For the POC we'll do a two-phase run: 1) Redwood-hosted synthetic + sanitized trace replay to validate SLOs and tune config; 2) Staging replay in the customer's VPC/Private to validate network and egress behavior. Phase 2 only after we lock configs and sanity metrics."
06:45 Priya: "Timeline? We want results before end of Q4. Is that realistic?"
07:00 Maya: "If we get traces by Dec 1, Redwood can run phase 1 during the week of Dec 6 and share a results deck by Dec 10. Phase 2 (staging) could be the following week if needed. So timeline is tight but feasible."
07:20 Lena: "OK. Can you walk through an example benchmark plan now — what we'll see in the spreadsheet?"
07:35 Diego: "We'll have rows for workload class, sample prompt, median tokens, token variance, cache hit rate, concurrency sweep (1, 5, 10, 25, 50), ramp duration, measurement window, and steady-state token/sec. Columns for metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens estimate, and notes (warm vs cold)."
08:10 Noah: "We'll also capture error rates, HTTP 429/5xx counts, GPU utilization, and token generation variance. That helps correlate tail latency with resource saturation."
08:35 Tom: "A question on measuring TTFT — do you measure from our load generator to first byte or from Redwood's ingress?"
08:48 Diego: "We instrument both. We'll ask you to run the client-side replay (local to your VPC) and Redwood will log server-side ingress timestamps. We diff them to show network vs server latency. For acceptance we use server-side ingress to first byte to avoid network noise, but we'll show both."
09:10 Priya: "How do we handle model fallbacks? If the primary model can't meet latency, can we route to a smaller quantized variant?"
09:22 Maya: "Yes — Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible variants. We'll include a scenario where we intentionally constrain capacity to trigger fallback and measure user-visible TTFT impact."
09:45 Lena: "Cost tradeoff: we'd like suggestions — quantization, batching, dedicated capacity vs hosted. Can Redwood provide a recommended config for our workload mix?"
09:58 Diego: "Absolutely. After baseline runs we'll produce a recommendation sheet: model family + quantization level + batching target + caching policy + estimated cost per 1M tokens and latency profile."
10:20 Tom: "On the security side: SOC2 docs and SSO integration are gating items. We need to know if Redwood can do SAML SSO and KMS integration for private deployments."
10:35 Maya: "Yes — Redwood supports SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private. I'll send the security pack after the call. For hosted during the pilot we'll use sanitized data and limit retention as agreed."
10:52 Ethan: "Also want to flag that our compliance team requires audit logs at the request level for any run we do in production-like environments."
11:05 Noah: "We can enable request-level audit logs in Private and Dedicated; in hosted we'll provide request sampling and enhanced logs for the pilot. We'll document retention and access controls."
11:25 Priya: "One more: sample size for p99 — how much traffic do you need?"
11:33 Diego: "To get stable p99 estimates we prefer at least 10k requests per workload class during the steady window. If that's not feasible, we run more iterations and bootstrap confidence intervals. We'll also show running tails across multiple runs."
12:00 Lena: "Ok that's helpful. Anything else we should capture?"
12:08 Maya: "Recap: Acceptance criteria proposal — triage short TTFT p95 <= 200ms p99 <= 450ms; stretch p95 <= 120ms p99 <= 300ms. Long gen TPOT per-100-token p95 <= 1.2s p99 <= 2.5s. We'll formalize in the benchmark spreadsheet. Actions: Diego will draft benchmark matrix; Lena will provide traces; Maya will send security docs and pricing ballpark."
12:45 Tom: "Agree. We'll try to get the traces to you by Dec 1 and flag any network/egress limits in the same payload."
12:55 Maya: "Great. We'll set the hands-on slot for Dec 6. I'll send calendar invite and the benchmark template. Thanks everyone."

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcript contains minor transcription errors and speaker timing approximations typical of automated call capture. References: "TTFT" (time-to-first-token), "TPOT" (total per-token/time per token metric), KV cache/prefix cache, VPC/private deployment, SOC2/KMS, p95/p99 target discussion.

title: Helix strategy and ops deconflict
content:
Helix strategy and ops deconflict

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-18
Start: 10:00 PT
Duration: ~74 minutes
Location: Zoom - company all-hands
Attendees: Elena Park, Marco Alvarez, Priya Desai, Samir Khan, Lina Torres, plus open Q&A from company

Summary:
- Leadership reviewed "helix" initiative (cross-functional push to tighten product/ops cadence).
- Discussed recent incident, reliability mitigations, and tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted routing.
- Agreed on hiring priorities and a conservative rollout plan for canary/traffic shaping.
- Next steps: prioritized action items for product, infra, and people.

Topics covered:
- Helix initiative overview and desired outcomes
- Incident review highlights and short/medium term mitigations
- Cost control: batching, quantization, region routing, dedicated pools
- Hiring cadence and org resourcing
- Customer & enterprise posture: SOC 2 timing, audit log retention

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Elena Park (CEO): Hey everybody, good morning, thanks for joining our helix update, we'll keep it tight, we got a lot to cover and then open q and a. um Marco, quick microstate of infra?
[00:18] Marco Alvarez (CTO): yeah, morning. so we've been tracking that spike last week, the incident, turns out it was a combo of an autoscaler bug and a kernel selection mismatch on the newest gpu nodes, uh, and that caused very uneven tail latency, and then a the fallback routing didn't kick fast enough.
[00:35] Speaker 4 (Engineering lead - Samir): to add, the KV cash — sorry, KV cache priming logic was racing with the cold starts, so lots of cache misses when we hit long sequences, so token costs spiked.
[00:50] Elena: ok, that's the gist. i'm hoping we can walk through short-term mitigations first, then product priorities. Priya?
[01:02] Priya Desai (Head of Product): yeael, so helix is meant to be the cross-team cadence — product builds, infra optimizations, and ops guardrails. high level targets: reduce P99 latency by 20%, keep per-token costs flat, and cut incident recovery time in half by Q3. those are our north stars.
[01:25] [01:25] Lina Torres (Head of People): and tangentially hiring: we need to line up three infra senior ICs and two SREs by end of Q2 to hit these numbers, otherwise we won't make the throughput work without cost overruns.
[01:40] Marco: yea the capacity plan is tight, and our vendor quotes for extra reserved capacity are... not great, so we need to balance dedicated pools versus smarter routing.
[01:54] [01:54] Audience Question (Speaker X): hi could you clarify what dedicated pools mean for existing hosted customers, any pricing changes?
[02:03] Elena: good question — in short, dedicated is reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput, it's opt-in for enterprise customers, pricing considered as a monthly commit. won't change hosted pricing for existing users. we'll send a short FAQ later.
[02:20] Priya: also important, for helix we want more canary control: traffic shaping by region, by tenant tier, and automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if latency SLOs break.
[02:38] Marco: the automatic fallback needs to be model-aware though; not every variant has the same function-calling or structured-output behavior, so we'll need compatibility checks. some of the autogen tests failed because of that.
[02:56] Samir: yes and there's a product-quality tradeoff — fallback to a quantized 8-bit variant gives cost savings but sometimes the hallucination rate nudges up, which our evals catch but customers might see.
[03:13] Elena: we need to balance unit economics with trust metrics. Priya, keep eval thresholds tight.
[03:21] Priya: noted.
[03:24] [03:24] Marco: quick point on the incident root cause: the new kernel selector we pushed assumes consistent sequence length distribution. during a customer experiment, sequence lengths skewed long and that pushed a codepath we hadn't exercised in staging. staging datasets didn't cover the churn.
[03:42] Speaker 7 (Product PM): so we should expand staging replay and add stress tests for long sequence tails, yes?
[03:48] Marco: exactly. we'll add a sequence-tail stress harness.
[03:51] [04:00] Audience (Volunteer): will this affect the private deploys and VPC customers?
[04:06] Samir: private customers are on a different upgrade cadence, but the same runtime code flows. for private we can schedule staggered upgrades and extra canaries since they control their infra. the main worry is the private on-prem customers that are air-gapped — their kernel backports take longer.
[04:25] Elena: we'll capture those timelines separately with CSMs.
[04:28] [04:30] Lina: hiring note — compensation for the infra hires is tight, we've got to move offers by May 3rd to meet joiners in June. otherwise Q3 headcount will slip.
[04:43] Priya: on product roadmap, the helix MVP is three features: 1) traffic shaping UI in console, 2) explicit model-variant compatibility checks, 3) improved rollout telemetry and tracing per request. those are our first deliverables.
[05:03] Marco: on telemetry, we need token-level tracing that ties back to route config and to the KV priming state. right now traces are coarse.
[05:13] Samir: that telemetry will also let us tune batching better — we can identify request shapes that benefit from bigger batch windows. bigger batches reduce cost but up latency for short requests; so routing rules need to be aware.
[05:30] [05:30] Audience (Q): do we have new SOC 2 timelines?
[05:35] Elena: good timing — audit kickoff is next month, target completion end of Q3. Lina and security will share specifics. we'll publish an FAQ.
[05:44] Lina: security readiness is in parallel; we have two key gaps: long-term log retention policy and more formal RBAC in the console. both are on the board for May sprints.
[05:57] [05:57] Priya: quick product concern — if we enforce stricter RBAC it may change how we do customer-level rollouts for early access features. need product and security handshake.
[06:09] Marco: yes, and for the canary we need a fallback policy that prioritizes continuity over feature parity — meaning if a canary fails we keep customers online on last-known-good model variant.
[06:22] Samir: on the ops side, the short term mitigation is to revert the autoscaler change for the hot path and add safer thresholds; medium term is to revamp our kernel selector testing and expand mix of real traffic in staging.
[06:36] [06:36] Audience: any customer impact notices sent?
[06:40] Elena: we sent a brief to affected customers with a high-level postmortem and said we were executing mitigations. follow-up will include a more detailed postmortem and timelines.
[06:50] [07:00] Priya: ok timeline for helix: sprints 1-2 (2 weeks) finish telemetry and canary control, sprints 3-4 (4 more weeks) ship console UI and rollout compatibility checks. we want an internal canary by mid-May and public canary in late May if hiring and infra align.
[07:18] Marco: about cost optimization — two levers: smarter batching and model quantization recommendations surfaced in console. the Optimize toolkit will suggest quantization profiles and batching windows per route. we should be careful: not all models are safe at 4-bit, and we need evals for each customer workload.
[07:36] Samir: that said, we can start with non-critical tenants for aggressive quantization to get baseline numbers.
[07:45] [07:50] Audience (Question): are we changing pricing for embeddings?
[07:55] Elena: not today. any pricing adjustments would come with clear customer comms; our priority is stability and predictable unit economics.
[08:05] [08:10] Priya: a small but important ask: product will need example prompts and eval criteria from sales and solutions so our regression alerts are meaningful — please send the top 10 prompt sets by next Tuesday.
[08:24] Lina: people update — org health looks good in most teams but infra is stretched. hiring freeze lifted for critical roles; recruiters will prioritize infra and SRE. also we want to remind managers about offer flexibility for counteroffers.
[08:42] [08:45] Audience: are we going to centralize the benchmark sheets?
[08:49] Marco: yes, a single benchmark spreadsheet will be the source of truth; infra will own it with read perms broadly but edit perms limited. we'll put it in the shared drive and link in the console docs.
[08:59] Samir: action on incident owner mapping: we'll publish a runbook with clear owners for autoscale, kernel selection, and KV priming.
[09:10] [09:10] Priya: ok let's take live questions.
[09:15] Audience Q1: will this change our roadmap for Dedicated customers?
[09:20] Marco: Dedicated still gets priority for capacity; any region routing changes will be backwards compatible. Dedicated customers can still pin versions and we will offer a rollback window.
[09:31] Audience Q2: what's the customer-facing SLA change?
[09:35] Elena: no SLA change today; we will only adjust SLAs with clear product and infra readiness and after legal signs off.
[09:44] Audience Q3: can we get an incident dashboard?
[09:50] Samir: yes, we will publish an internal incident dashboard and a high-level customer-facing timeline for affected customers.
[10:00] [10:00] Elena: brief recap — Priya product plan and eval thresholds; Samir postmortem and runbook; Marco hardware/cost review; Lina hiring and offers. big ask: leaders to empower their teams to escalate when telemetry shows odd tails.
[10:18] Marco: last thing, competitor note: BigCloudAI rolled out a cheaper dedicated option last month; their fallback behavior isn't as mature as ours but their price looks aggressive. watch for sales objections and we'll prepare battlecards.
[10:33] Priya: and FastServe is pushing a private-edge pitch in EMEA, we should coordinate partner messaging.
[10:40] Elena: alright, thanks everyone. we'll post slides and the canary plan. meeting closed.

Post-meeting notes:
- Slides: link (internal) - "Helix initiative overview and canary plan"
- Shared artifacts: incident summary (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link), hiring slate (link).
- Tone: constructive, operationally focused, few tense questions about cost and hiring but consensus on next steps.

End of transcript.

title: Kestrel Ventures Tokenflow & p95 Throughput Discovery
content:
Kestrel Ventures Tokenflow & p95 Throughput Discovery

Discovery call focused on p95 latency targets and token/sec throughput for streaming chat workloads. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private due to compliance and burst traffic. Agreed to run benchmark and share pricing + security docs.
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-04-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Reilly (CTO, Kestrel), Sana Patel (Platform Lead), Markus Li (SRE), Ana Gomez (Product)

Auto-summary (auto): Customer wants p95 under 600ms for streaming token flow during peak, tolerates slightly higher during cold starts; interested in Dedicated for burst windows but wants private for regulated pipelines.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros, then we'll dive into traffic shapes and p95 goals.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Liam): Hey, thanks. Our primary thing is realtime summarization in the product, so streaming latency is the big one. We're trying to get p95 of, like, under 500ms for user visible tokens, otherwise the UX feels laggy.
00:35 Speaker 3 (Maya): Got it. When you say "user visible tokens" do you mean partial token flushes per streaming chunk or end-to-end response p95?
00:42 Speaker 2 (Liam): Partial streaming. We stream as the model generates. So p95 per token chunk is the key number.
00:50 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Okay, good. Can you share expected concurrency? tokens/sec peaks?
01:02 Speaker 4 (Sana): We see about 250 concurrent active sessions in the EU region during peak; average request length is 120 tokens prompt + 300 tokens response historically. Burst can go up to ~700 concurrent for a marketing campaign.
01:20 Speaker 3 (Maya): Quick note: that response length is substantial. For 300 tokens response, sustained token/sec and KV cache reuse matter a lot. Do you have any prefix reuse across requests?
01:34 Speaker 4 (Sana): Yes, lots of repetition—system prompt and a few contextual turns are similar across sessions. So KV cache should help.
01:42 Speaker 5 (Markus): Our constraints: infra is hybrid — primary in-cloud but some workflows must run on-prem for regulated customers. Also strict key management, we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs.
01:55 Speaker 3 (Maya): That's fine. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs; Dedicated has isolated capacity but still managed control plane, and Hosted is the fastest to get started. We can walk through lat/throughput tradeoffs.
02:10 Speaker 1 (Jordan): For p95 goals, are you targeting single-digit token latency or end-to-end?
02:16 Speaker 2 (Liam): Realistically we want p95 per partial chunk under 400–600ms during non-burst, and under 800–1,000ms acceptable during big bursts as long as we don't drop sessions.
02:28 Speaker 3 (Maya): Good benchmark to aim at. For a 300 token response streamed, you'll hit token/sec limits depending on model size and GPU type. What model families are you planning to run?
02:40 Speaker 2 (Liam): We're evaluating open models right now; want something high-quality but quantized for cost. Probably an LLaMA-derivative, 34B-ish.
02:52 Speaker 3 (Maya): Okay, that maps well to Redwood Dedicated profiles. We typically recommend 8xA100-equivalent for heavy streaming, but with quantization and kernel selection we can increase throughput. With prefix caching you can reduce effective compute per request.
03:07 Speaker 5 (Markus): Network jitter is a big factor for us; sometimes inter-region routing adds spikes. Do you do region pinning or fallback?
03:16 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes — smart routing can pin traffic to a region and we have automatic fallback to adjacent region/model-variant to preserve availability. But that adds a little latency on failover.
03:26 Speaker 6 (Ana): Question on KV cache: how much does it actually buy us in real traffic?
03:32 Speaker 3 (Maya): In our experience with similar customers, when there's high prefix reuse you can see 30–60% reduction in consumed tokens and 20–40% latency improvement on p95, depending on model and batch sizes. But depends on hit rates.
03:48 Speaker 2 (Liam): Important for us: we can't accept any logs being stored in a shared control plane for regulated flows. Private offering needs to support air-gapped or VPC-only control.
03:58 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Understood. For Private we do offer on-prem packages; control plane can be customer-managed and logs kept behind your VPC. We'll share the security pack after this call.
04:10 Speaker 3 (Maya): Back to numbers — can I confirm your p95 target: 400–600ms per streaming chunk at 250 concurrency typical, with 700 concurrency burst up to 1,000ms p95 acceptable?
04:22 Speaker 2 (Liam): Yes that's right. Also want to look at token/sec throughput per GPU and cost.
04:29 Speaker 3 (Maya): For a 34B quantized model on an 8-GPU Dedicated pool, rough rule of thumb: sustained aggregate throughput ~6k–10k tokens/sec depending on kernel/quantization. With a single request producing 300 tokens, that implies X concurrency before you saturate — we can run a precise token/sec run with your prompt set.
04:50 Speaker 4 (Sana): Can you also test streaming tail-latency (first-token vs steady-state)? Our UI is sensitive to first-token latency.
04:58 Speaker 3 (Maya): Absolutely, we capture first-token latency and p95 for stream chunks. We'll include that in the benchmark.
05:05 Speaker 5 (Markus): For Dedicated, what's the autoscaling behavior during bursts? We don't want cold-starts that make p95 spike.
05:14 Speaker 3 (Maya): We have configurable autoscale with warm pool and burst capacity. You can keep a minimum number of instances warm to meet p95 SLOs; During sudden spike we have fallback policies to smaller model variants to keep latency bounded.
05:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Pricing note: Dedicated commits give you reserved capacity with lower per-token cost but you pay for baseline. Hosted is usage-based, higher unit cost but zero management. Private is a license plus ops. I'll send a cost model.
05:45 Speaker 6 (Ana): How do you measure p95 in streaming scenarios? Token boundaries vs chunk boundaries?
05:53 Speaker 3 (Maya): We measure both: first-byte latency, chunk p95 (n tokens), and end-to-end response p95. For dashboards we break them down per route/model.
06:06 Speaker 4 (Sana): Network: our egress limits may mean we need to colocate inference near customers. Do you support regional deployments?
06:13 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes, Hosted has multiple regions; Dedicated can be provisioned in a chosen region; Private can obviously be on-prem. We'll document region options in the follow-up.
06:22 Speaker 2 (Liam): Can Redwood run a mixed strategy: Hosted for general traffic, Dedicated reserved for peak sessions, and Private for regulated customers?
06:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Absolutely — hybrid routing is a core pattern. You can route by policy: percent to Dedicated, failover to Hosted, and direct-regulated flows to Private.
06:39 Speaker 5 (Markus): Curious on observability — can we get token-level cost breakdown and per-token latency?
06:45 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route p95, and trace hooks; you can export logs to your SIEM.
06:55 Speaker 4 (Sana): Anything about model fallbacks — is content and safety preserved when you downgrade to a smaller model during burst?
07:04 Speaker 3 (Maya): We recommend a canary test and quality gating; fallbacks preserve prompt context but quality will vary. We can set rollback thresholds based on evals.
07:13 Speaker 2 (Liam): Okay, high-level makes sense. Next, can you run that benchmark you mentioned with our prompt set? We want numbers: first token p95, streaming chunk p95, aggregate tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens on Dedicated vs Hosted.
07:31 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes. We'll need sample prompts and a small dataset of representative sessions. Also, network conditions are important — if you can replicate jitter we'll do it in the run.
07:42 Speaker 4 (Sana): We'll provide a subset of 500 sessions and a synthetic burst plan.
07:49 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Great. I'll attach the cost model and SLA comparatives. Also sharing SOC 2 / ISO docs and PKI/KMS notes.
07:58 Speaker 6 (Ana): One last ask — can you show P95 drift over time? We need to know how p95 behaves under model updates.
08:06 Speaker 3 (Maya): We can set up quality monitoring tied to eval prompt sets and alert on regressions. That's part of Redwood Optimize.
08:15 Speaker 2 (Liam): Cool. Timing: we want to make a decision in two weeks if benchmarks show we can meet p95 at peak with reasonable cost.
08:23 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Sounds achievable. We'll aim to deliver benchmark results and pricing within 5 business days.
08:30 Speaker 5 (Markus): Small note: encryption in transit and at rest must conform to our compliance list — we'll email legal.
08:40 Speaker 3 (Maya): We'll include the compliance checklist.
08:45 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Recap — Jordan shares pricing + security pack, Maya runs benchmark with Kestrel prompts, Kestrel provides prompts + network profile, schedule Private architecture deep-dive if needed.
08:59 Speaker 2 (Liam): Thanks everyone, talk soon.
09:05 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Thanks, bye.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions where product names heard as "Redwood Privatee" or "KV cash". Speakers sometimes labeled generically. There was overlap at 03:30 with cross talk.

Customer is risk-averse on data residency. Strong candidate for hybrid approach: Dedicated for cost-sensitive steady-state and Private for regulated pipelines. Benchmarks will drive final commit.
Jordan to send Dedicated vs Hosted cost model spreadsheet (by 2028-04-21)
Maya to run a 1-hour token/sec benchmark with Kestrel sample prompt set (target week of 2028-04-24)
Liam to share SSO/SAML requirements and data residency note (by 2028-04-20)
Schedule on-prem/private deployment architecture review (tentative 2028-04-28)
Jordan Park | Share pricing spreadsheet and example SLA language | 2028-04-21
Maya Singh | Run 1hr benchmark on Dedicated 8-GPU pool with Kestrel prompts | 2028-04-26
Liam O'Reilly | Provide network egress limits & expected peak concurrency | 2028-04-20
