title: Galehound - Streaming SLA & Hosting Assessment
content:
Galehound - Streaming SLA & Hosting Assessment

Discovery focused on p95 streaming targets, when to choose Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and what benchmarks Galehound needs to commit to a pilot. Customer cares about sub-200ms p95 for short chats and steady 4000 tokens/sec throughput across concurrent streams. Security (VPC, KMS) and audit logs are gating for Private option.
Meeting header: 2026-05-07 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya Patel, Ryan Chen (Redwood); Tom Keane, Priya Sharma, Marcus Lee (Galehound)

[00:00:02] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick intro from redwood side then jump into your latency and throughput goals.
[00:00:12] Tom: thanks Maya. quick note — we had a brief sync earlier, so Priya and Marcus are here to dig into perf details.
[00:00:20] Ryan: great, i'm ryan, i'm the se. i'll own the microbench and p95 tests. 
[00:00:28] Tom: quick context: Galehound is moving from a CPU-based in-house solution to a GPU-backed streaming pipeline. target is conversational assistants, short prompts ~30-80 tokens and longer completions up to 2k tokens. primary SLAs: 95th percentile latency under 200ms for short-turn responses and sustainable token/sec for sustained bursts.
[00:00:52] Priya: and we expect spikes — our front-end can fanout 1k concurrent users with ~2 requests/sec each during peak. so concurrency math matters.
[00:01:05] Maya: ok that's helpful. curious — are you more focused on single-request p95 or end-to-end UX p95 including frontend and networking?
[00:01:14] Tom: the former, server-side p95 is the gating number. we can tune frontend separately.
[00:01:20] Marcus: Also want to confirm data flows — we're allowed to send prompts to hosted services as long as PII is removed. For PHI or regulated flows we'll need Private with VPC and KMS.
[00:01:33] Ryan: makes sense. quick to the benchmarking plan: we'll measure p95 under 5 concurrency scenarios: 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024. streaming enabled for the chat path, and we'll capture tokens/sec and end-to-end server p95.
[00:01:52] Priya: when you say streaming enabled, do you mean chunked response streaming or true server side incremental tokens? we care about reconnects/resume.
[00:02:03] Ryan: yes chunked streaming, like SSE/WebSocket streaming. Redwood's streaming path keeps KV cache between calls if pinned, and we can simulate reconnect behavior.
[00:02:15] Tom: good. a few tradeoffs we worry about: Hosted is easiest but worried about noisy neighbors and unpredictable p95 during token storms. Dedicated solves that but costs more. Private is our preferred for regulated customers but ops overhead increases.
[00:02:30] Maya: that's the classic tradeoff. we usually recommend Hosted for pilots where data residency isn't required, Dedicated for predictable p95 and throughput, and Private for strict compliance. but there are tactical options — Dedicated with VPC peering is possible.
[00:02:44] Marcus: peering latency — what's typical? if our app sits in GCP us-central and Dedicated is in AWS us-west-2 that adds unpredictability.
[00:02:53] Ryan: yep, network hop matters. in our experience <5ms intra-region peering, cross-region can be 20-50ms. we recommend aligning region with your app.
[00:03:03] Priya: ok can we talk numbers: for a 3B quantized model, what throughput can we expect per GPU for streaming?
[00:03:11] Ryan: rough ballpark: with continuous batching disabled, streaming overhead lowers throughput relative to pure batch. for a 3B quant model on an A100 class node we often see 800-1500 tokens/sec single-stream baseline; with optimized kernels and prefix KV cache, sustained aggregate can be 4k-6k tokens/sec per GPU depending on sequence length distribution.
[00:03:35] Tom: that aligns with some vendor numbers we've seen, though ModelHoster advertised higher numbers but with caveats.
[00:03:43] Maya: can i ask about p95 numbers under multiplexed streaming?
[00:03:48] Ryan: sure — p95 depends heavily on queueing and batching. with continuous batching and SLO for 200ms p95 on short responses, you'd want reserved Dedicated slices sized to keep queue depth low. we can hit sub-200ms p95 for 16-32 concurrent streams per GPU for short 40-token responses. when you scale to 256-1024 concurrent streams, you'll need multiple GPUs and routing to maintain p95.
[00:04:15] Priya: what's the impact of KV-cache hits?
[00:04:20] Ryan: KV-cache hits reduce decoder compute — if you can cache prefixes across the conversation, p95 improves significantly, often cutting p95 by 20-40% for repeated context patterns. there's complexity in cache warmup on cold starts which we'll test.
[00:04:36] Marcus: what about tokenization variance? sometimes our prompts expand to 1.5x tokens in model space which changes token/sec math.
[00:04:44] Ryan: yes account for tokenizer overhead; we'll include token inflation tests in the microbench.
[00:04:50] Tom: security question — for Dedicated can we have customer-managed KMS and audit logs?
[00:04:56] Maya: yes, Dedicated supports KMS integration and audit logs; Private adds more controls like air-gapped and HSM if needed.
[00:05:04] Priya: any documented SLOs for streaming p95? we saw a doc but it was general.
[00:05:10] Maya: i'll send the streaming SLO doc, it has measured p50/p95/p99 for a bunch of model families, plus our Recommended Batch sizes. link: https://redwood.example/docs/streaming-slos (note: placeholder).
[00:05:22] Tom: perfect. can you walk through an example test scenario so our infra team can map it?
[00:05:27] Ryan: sure. test plan sketch: 1) baseline single-stream latency with warm KV-cache; 2) ramp to concurrency target following your real-world curve (we'll use the 1k concurrent users example); 3) run sustained token/sec for 5-10 minutes to detect thermal or GC effects; 4) inject reconnects and partial messages to validate resume and caching behavior; 5) measure p95/p99 and tokens/sec across phases.
[00:05:57] Marcus: for step 2 how do you route traffic? sticky sessions?
[00:06:01] Ryan: Redwood can route by session affinity to keep KV-cache local to the worker pool; for high availability we have automatic routing fallback to other pools but that invalidates cache. we'll test both sticky and stateless routing.
[00:06:14] Priya: about quantization — we use 4-bit in prod experiments. does Redwood support int4 inference and how does that affect p95?
[00:06:22] Ryan: yes we support quantized execution paths. int4 reduces memory and can increase throughput but kernel-level inaccuracies can cause mild quality regressions. performance-wise you often gain 1.5-2x tokens/sec; we'll include a quality/regression check in the pilot.
[00:06:37] Tom: and what about warmup patterns for cold starts? if a pod restarts, how long to warm KV-cache and cold pipeline?
[00:06:45] Ryan: cold start is primarily model load time + cache rebuild. with warm model pinned on Dedicated, model load time is amortized; typical cold start for large models can be 10-30s if model isn't preloaded. we recommend preloading pools for strict SLOs.
[00:06:58] Maya: ok let's lock some acceptance criteria you mentioned: server-side p95 <200ms for short-turns at 16-32 concurrent streams per GPU, aggregate tokens/sec 4k sustained per GPU, and predictable p95 behavior under 5-minute sustained bursts. any additions?
[00:07:16] Priya: add cache-warmup time and reconnection handling must be <=2x normal latency.
[00:07:21] Tom: also audit log retention of 90 days for compliance.
[00:07:26] Maya: noted.
[00:07:28] [00:07:30] Speaker 2 (transcription noise): um -- sorry background noise --
[00:07:34] Marcus: slight crosstalk, sorry.
[00:07:37] Ryan: no worries. jumping to pricing: Dedicated reserved pools come with commit tiers and burst capacity. Maya can share the sheet after.
[00:07:46] Maya: yes i'll share tiers. Pilot usually runs on a small Dedicated pool, we do the tests, then propose a commit to match sustained needs.
[00:07:55] Tom: about fallback policies — if a Dedicated pool is saturated during an unexpected surge can you fall back to Hosted cheaper variants automatically?
[00:08:04] Ryan: yes we support smart routing and fallbacks by policy — you can define graceful degradation to a smaller model variant or to Hosted, with weighted routing. we can test failover scenarios too.
[00:08:16] Priya: do you have instrumentation we can push to our tracing? can we correlate trace IDs?
[00:08:21] Maya: Redwood Console exposes per-request IDs and supports tracing hooks; we can provide a small tracing adapter to forward spans.
[00:08:29] Tom: great. on legal/compliance: can you share a sample DPA and SOC2 cert?
[00:08:33] Maya: yes, i'll attach SOC2 report and DPA in the follow-up.
[00:08:38] Ryan: last technical nit: for reconnects we emulate partial-chunk lost and reconnection behavior; some vendors mishandle seq numbers which causes duplicate tokens. we'll validate correctness as part of tests.
[00:08:52] Priya: any gotchas for caching when users multi-device? session affinity could be problematic.
[00:08:58] Ryan: for multi-device you either centralize cache or rebuild context per device; there's tradeoff between memory and latency. we'll test a multi-device workflow in the pilot.
[00:09:09] Tom: ok, what's the minimal pilot to prove this?
[00:09:12] Maya: a 2-week pilot: provision 2-4 Dedicated GPUs with your model, run the microbench and streaming scenarios, provide logs and Console access, and review quality/regression. if successful, move to commit.
[00:09:25] Marcus: timeline wise we want results in 2 weeks.
[00:09:28] Maya: we'll aim for a May 18 pilot kickoff as mentioned. Ryan will run preflight microbench next week.
[00:09:36] Ryan: i'll need prompt set and expected concurrency curve.
[00:09:40] Tom: we'll send those by May 12.
[00:09:44] [00:09:46] Speaker 3: um.. small audio glitch earlier, sorry if we missed anything.
[00:09:49] Maya: no problem. quick recap: deliverables — Ryan runs microbench and shares results; Maya shares pricing, SOC2, and streaming SLO doc; Galehound provides prompts and traffic curve. Pilot kickoff May 18.
[00:10:04] Tom: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:10:08] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.

Note: Transcription includes occasional speaker mislabels and filler words; some technical terms may be slightly garbled (e.g., KV-cache sometimes transcribed as "K V cache").

title: Cranemere Systems - Commitment, Sovereignty & Burst Plan
content:
Cranemere Systems - Commitment, Sovereignty & Burst Plan

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min (recorded)
Attendees: Lena Torres (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (Redwood CSM), Oliver Kemp (Cranemere Head of Platform), Priya Shah (DevOps), Markus Vogel (CTO), Hannah Lee (PM)

Summary:
Quick renewal/expansion check-in focused on: committed capacity uplift, adding EU region (data sovereignty), burst/overage pricing, and pilot timeline for private VPC option. Customer brought new compliance timeline (Q4 audit) and wants clarity on SLA, audit logs and key management. Redwood to provide benchmark run and updated pricing amendment.

Topics:
- Committed capacity increase (baseline + burst)
- EU private VPC / data residency path
- Latency SLOs and canary strategy for multi-region traffic
- Security docs: SOC2, SSO, KMS integration
- Contract amendment process and procurement timeline

[00:00] Lena Torres: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um just to set the agenda, quick renewal check-in, we have a couple items on committed capacity and then Marcus will talk through the performance benchmark plan. then we'll go into sovereignty and private vpc options. sound good?

[00:18] Oliver Kemp: yeah that works for us, thanks Lena. quick context: we are coming up on our contract renewal window in september and we need to lock in an uplift for the holiday season, and we also have a q4 data residency audit so the eu region is a hard requirement for some customers.

[00:34] Marcus Li: great, hi everyone. i'll keep the benchmark plan brief — objective is to validate token-level latency at your typical prompt mix and measure cost per 1k tokens under both hosted and private scenarios. we'll run 3 workloads: short chat queries (~32 tokens), mixed QA (~120 tokens), and long generation (~600 tokens) to simulate your support and transcript generation flows.

[00:57] Priya Shah: just to flag, our traffic is spiky — we do big batches at midnight in timezone eu-west and then a daytime chat peak in us-east. how does Redwood handle burst beyond committed pools? do we get throttled?

[01:12] Lena Torres: good question. so you have two levers: reserved capacity (committed) and burst capacity we can attach to the plan. if burst is used we bill at the burst rate — we can add a cap/overage policy so you don't go unlimited. also automatic fallback to a lower-cost compatible model is possible if latency SLOs are flexible.

[01:35] Markus Vogel: okay, what about routing? we can't have eu data leaving region, some of our compliance tests check that tokens are processed inside eu.

[01:44] Marcus Li: for that we recommend Redwood Private with a VPC control plane in eu-west. you can pin the model and route traffic locally. we maintain the same API surface so minimal app changes. there's an onprem option if you need air-gap, but that's heavier.

[02:05] Hannah Lee: timeline question — procurement asked whether we can have the private vpc provisioned before Oct 15, because audit is mid-Oct. is that realistic?

[02:14] Lena Torres: provision time depends on contract and infra sizing. for a standard private VPC we typically do a 4-6 week lead time once terms are signed and capacity is committed. given today's date, that puts provisioning mid-September if contract is signed by Aug 18. we should try to aim for that.

[02:36] Oliver Kemp: procurement will need a concrete contract amendment. can you send a commitment amendment with explicit start date, committed GPUs, and burst caps? and also the pricing tiers so our finance can model it.

[02:51] Lena Torres: yes — i'll send the amendment draft and updated pricing sheet today.

[03:00] Priya Shah: another technical point — we use an older transformer model internally; will Redwood's runtime support the kv cache and token streaming we rely on? i've had issues with other vendors dropping the stream after 2k tokens.

[03:16] Marcus Li: Redwood's runtime supports continuous KV cache and streaming; there are a couple knobs — max prefix, session pooling — we'll surface the default config and also run your benchmark to exercise long sessions so you can see any degradation. some transcriptions might have slight errors in names but core behavior should be solid.

[03:42] Markus Vogel: in terms of cost, how does dedicated compare to hosted? we are trying to decide if purchasing a dedicated pool with reserved capacity makes sense versus staying hosted and paying higher per-token price with burst.

[03:54] Lena Torres: typically for sustained throughput — if you have predictable monthly token volumes — dedicated/reserved is 30-55% cheaper vs pure hosted; exact depends on model family and quantization. Redwood Optimize will provide suggestions like lighter quantization for batch jobs and batching config to lower per-token cost. we'll include cost modeling in the spreadsheet.

[04:18] Hannah Lee: can you also include examples of automatic fallbacks? we need documented behaviour if eu capacity is saturated during peak.

[04:26] Marcus Li: yes — fallback policies are configurable: region-fallback (route to another eu cluster), model-fallback (drop to smaller quantized variant), or rate-limiting with 503 and retry headers. we'll show config snippets in the playbook.

[04:44] Priya Shah: security — we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, audit logs shipped to our splunk. do you support customer-managed KMS with HSM?

[04:56] Lena Torres: short answer yes: SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning, RBAC at token/route level, and audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM. for encryption we support customer-managed KMS for private deployments — HSM is an enterprise add-on. i'll attach the security pack link after the call: https://redwood.ai/security-pack (note: link for reference).

[05:20] Oliver Kemp: can we get a copy of SOC2 and penetration test reports?

[05:26] Jared Kim: absolutely — i'll drop SOC2 Type II summary and the latest pen test redacted artifacts, plus architecture diagrams.

[05:35] Markus Vogel: about benchmarks — Marcus, what metrics will you return? p50/p95/p99 latencies, token throughput, and cost-per-1k?

[05:44] Marcus Li: yes p50/p95/p99, tail latencies on long prompts, throughput in tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens under both hosted and private configs. we'll also provide a CSV with request-by-request timings so you can plug into your dashboards.

[06:02] Priya Shah: got it. also, please include a test that simulates our midnight batch job, because that one hits 4x the daytime load.

[06:09] Marcus Li: yep we'll add a spiky workload. question for you: do you have any hard latency SLOs for interactive chat?

[06:17] Oliver Kemp: under 250ms p95 for the short chat path; for long gen we are ok up to 2s p95 but we want predictable tails.

[06:26] Lena Torres: we can tune pooling, batching, and model choice to hit 250ms p95 on short queries; we'll validate in the benchmark. if not we can propose a dedicated reserved slice sized for your peak.

[06:40] Hannah Lee: procurement will probably ask about termination clauses and credit for downtime. what's Redwood's SLA?

[06:47] Lena Torres: hosted offers 99.9% uptime SLA, dedicated private plans have higher SLAs available as enterprise add-on. credits depend on incident severity and are spelled out in the TOS. we'll include SLA section in the amendment draft.

[07:05] Markus Vogel: any chance to pilot EU private cluster before commit? we'd prefer a short validation run with sample traffic before signing a long-term reserved contract.

[07:14] Jared Kim: yes, we can do a 14-day pilot with limited capacity, or a paid PoC that converts to committed capacity. Marcus can stand up a sandbox in eu-west for you.

[07:26] Marcus Li: process: we provision sandbox with limited nodes, run the benchmark, and then iterate. it'll surface any network egress or config changes you need.

[07:36] Priya Shah: do you support customer-side NAT for egress? our infra team needs to control egress IPs for allowlists.

[07:43] Marcus Li: yes for private VPC we can use customer-controlled NAT and IP whitelisting. we'll document the network diagram and firewall rules.

[07:57] Oliver Kemp: a concern — Anthropic offered us a short-term discount to lock in now; how flexible is Redwood on term length and ramped billing? we might want a 6-month ramp to avoid committing full capacity immediately.

[08:12] Lena Torres: we can do stepped commitments (ramped capacity) with a defined ramp schedule in the amendment. pricing will reflect the ramp. if you need a short-term discount we can also propose a limited pilot discount to bridge procurement.

[08:28] Hannah Lee: thanks — that's helpful. one more — can we schedule a deep-dive with networking team to discuss VPC peering and routing specifics?

[08:35] Lena Torres: yes — Marcus and Jared can meet your network folks. i'll let Jared coordinate calendar invites.

[08:44] [Slight crosstalk / someone types in chat]

[08:50] Marcus Li: we'll run the benchmark next Tuesday (Aug 12) unless you prefer a different date. we need a small sample dataset and a list of endpoints to emulate.

[08:59] Priya Shah: Aug 12 works. i'll upload a sanitized sample dataset and a short prompt set by Aug 11.

[09:07] Lena Torres: perfect. recap quick: 1) Redwood to send amendment + pricing (Lena) 2) SE to run benchmarks and share CSV + results (Marcus) 3) CSM to share security docs and SOC2 (Jared) 4) Cranemere to confirm procurement timeline and upload sample dataset (Oliver/Priya). we will reconvene Sept 2 to review amendment.

[09:31] Oliver Kemp: that aligns. any blockers on your side?

[09:36] Lena Torres: none. we'll aim to get materials out today and have the benchmark results by Aug 13.

[09:45] Markus Vogel: thanks everyone — looking forward to results.

[09:51] Jared Kim: i'll create the sandbox project and send invites; expect the security pack link and SOC2 within the hour.

[10:00] [Meeting ends]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional word swaps (e g 'kv' transcribed as 'k v'), some speaker label slippage in a few short segments; overall medium quality.

References / Links mentioned:
- pricing spreadsheet (shared via drive)
- security pack: https://redwood.ai/security-pack
- benchmark template: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/template

Recap / Next steps (repeat):
- Lena: amendment draft + pricing (due 2025-08-10)
- Marcus: benchmark and CSV (due 2025-08-12)
- Jared: SOC2 + pen test artifacts + sandbox invites (due 2025-08-08)

End of transcript.

title: Skyline Systems telemetry & resiliency workshop
content:
Skyline Systems telemetry & resiliency workshop

Technical sync to align on marketplace listing constraints, telemetry/observability integration for Redwood Private deployment, and resiliency patterns (failover, canary, regional fallback). Action items: share listing checklist, network diagram, and run a short flood test against staging deployment.
marketplace listing requirements
VPC/network topology options
OpenTelemetry vs Prometheus integration
KMS & key management for private deployments
failover and canary strategies
observability retention and cost tradeoffs
Header:
- Date: 2026-09-09
- Start: 15:00 PDT
- Duration: ~72 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ford (Redwood PM); Alex Rivera, Priya Desai, Omar Khalid, Jenny Park (Skyline)
- Recording link: https://redwood.share/example (placeholder)

Summary (auto): Short workshop to reconcile security/network requirements for Skyline's planned Private deployment and to specify telemetry ingestion and retention for marketplace listing.

--- Transcript body ---
[15:00] Maya Chen: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh i'm Maya from Redwood, i'll kick things off. can we do a quick round?
[15:02] Alex Rivera: Alex here, CTO at Skyline. excited to get this mapped out, we've got some tight windows for compliance.
[15:04] Priya Desai: Priya, lead SRE. main asks are: 1) how telemetry flows from Redwood Private to our observability stack, 2) cost/retention, and 3) isolation for PII sensitive traces.
[15:06] Ravi Patel: ravi here, i'll be the technical owner on the integration side. i can walk through the runtime telemetry hooks and where you can scrape metrics or ingest OTLP.
[15:07] Omar Khalid: omar, platform engineering. network and peering questions up front, we have a hub-and-spoke VPC architecture.
[15:09] Jenny Park: jenny from security, i'll be focused on keys and audit logs.

[15:10] Maya Chen: great. alex, can you summarize the desired deployment mode? you mentioned earlier you want private but also a marketplace listing. how are you picturing them?
[15:11] Alex Rivera: yes, we want a private managed control plane, with the inference nodes in our VPC — so kind of Redwood Private on-prem in cloud. marketplace listing is for our internal procurement, it needs an official listing and an approved ref arch doc. we also want the option to fall back to Redwood hosted if our region has capacity problems.
[15:13] Lena Ford: quick note — for marketplace listing we need a network topology diagram, KMS compatibility statement, and a short performance profile. we'll capture what gaps need docs.

[15:15] Ravi Patel: on telemetry: the runtime emits internal metrics via prometheus exposition and also supports OTLP/OTEL collector push. two common patterns: 1) allow Skyline to scrape Prom endpoints from within the VPC (we expose metrics on localhost or loopback with bind in sidecar), or 2) push OTLP via TLS to your ingest gateway. both are supported, but each has tradeoffs.
[15:17] Priya Desai: scraping is easier for us, we already have prometheus federation. question: does Redwood tag traces with model/version metadata and user-defined tenancy ids? we need to link traces to customer tenancy for audits.
[15:18] Ravi Patel: yes we add model/version, shard id, and tenant id if provided. small caveat — sometimes transcription of metadata names may change depending on the runtime plugin, but we can stabilize field names for the marketplace refarch.

[15:20] Omar Khalid: network question — if we expose a scrape endpoint, that requires peering or a private link. we prefer using a VPC endpoint that your agents push to, to avoid opening inbound. what does Redwood support for VPC connectivity?
[15:21] Maya Chen: we support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and static NAT egress with IP allow-listing. for on-prem we also support an outbound-only connector that tunnels to a customer-managed ingress.
[15:23] Jenny Park: for KMS: we need to bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and HSM-level assurances. can logs/audit trails be encrypted with keys we control?
[15:24] Ravi Patel: yes, for Private deployments you can integrate with your KMS; Redwood uses envelope encryption and can be configured to use CMKs. note: there are different UX flows for rotating keys — we'll document them for the refarch.

[15:26] Alex Rivera: can you also enumerate what gets into audit logs vs only short-lived telemetry? auditors will want user prompts, model version, api key id, and anomalies.
[15:27] Maya Chen: good point. out-of-the-box we capture request metadata for audit logs: request id, timestamp, model id, token counts, user id (if provided). PII content does not go into audit logs if you opt-in to filter — but we need to discuss retention windows.

[15:29] Priya Desai: retention: we want 90 days for traces and 1 year for audit events. what's feasible without exploding cost?
[15:30] Ravi Patel: retention is configurable; for high-cardinality traces the ingest cost is the big driver. we recommend sampling: 100% for errors + 1-5% baseline. that reduces cost while keeping error coverage.

[15:32] Omar Khalid: resiliency — if a zone goes down, can your runtime failover to a model in another region with minimal token loss? how does cache/KV behave across failover?
[15:33] Ravi Patel: currently KV cache is local per node to keep latency low; cross-region KV replication is possible but adds complexity. our recommended pattern is: 1) regional model variants with prefix cache warmers, 2) fast fallback to smaller model to sustain availability, and 3) multi-region canary with sticky routing. there is some cold-start cost when warming a new region.

[15:36] Alex Rivera: are there size / model constraints for the marketplace listing? we need to include quantization/throughput numbers in the listing doc.
[15:36] Lena Ford: we'll collect a short performance profile from you. our default is to include p50/p95 latencies at a standard prompt distribution and token rate. we can run a short benchmark on your staging to produce a one-page perf sheet.

[15:38] Priya Desai: security: SSO and RBAC for operators — we need SAML integration and fine-grained role mapping. can we map roles to specific deployment capabilities (scale, rollback, view-only)?
[15:39] Ravi Patel: yes SAML/SSO is supported for the control plane, and we expose RBAC roles that can be mapped to groups. mapping to specific ops actions is possible; we should draft a mapping matrix for the refarch.

[15:41] Jenny Park: also need tamper-evident audit logs and export to our SIEM (splunk). do you support streaming audit logs to an endpoint?
[15:42] Maya Chen: yes streaming to syslog/S3/Splunk via Kinesis is supported for Private. we can provide a lambda/collector example.

[15:44] Maya Chen: okay let me walk through a proposed network pattern on screen — (shared diagram link) — but verbally: hub VPC hosts shared services, spoke VPCs host workloads and our inference nodes in a private subnet, access via PrivateLink to control plane. metrics either pushed from sidecar to OTLP gateway (preferred) or scraped if you open a peering.

[15:46] Omar Khalid: (inaudible) — sorry, did you say sidecar or agent? we prefer a lightweight sidecar we control.
[15:47] Ravi Patel: sidecar — the sidecar runs the collector and can offload enrichment and batching. it also supports local sampling decisions. note: sidecar increases pod resources but gives more predictable telemetry.

[15:49] Alex Rivera: runbook question: during upgrades can we keep a canary and fallback? we require <2% error spike during canary. what are your rollback timings?
[15:50] Ravi Patel: typical canary windows 10-30 minutes depending on traffic; we support automatic rollback on error thresholds. rollout speed depends on model size and whether the cache is warm. we'll include recommended thresholds in the refarch.

[15:52] Priya Desai: testing — we want a flood test that simulates 200% normal token volume for 10 minutes on staging. will that damage the service?
[15:53] Maya Chen: we can coordinate a controlled flood on staging; we'll throttle if it threatens shared infra. recommended is to run the test against your dedicated staging capacity. we'll provide a test plan.

[15:55] Lena Ford: for the marketplace listing doc we'll need: short refarch (network + keys), perf profile (p50/p95), telemetry integration guide (prom/otlp examples), and security checklist (saml, kms, audit retention).

[15:57] Omar Khalid: data residency: some tenants will require EU-only storage. can we pin model inference and logs to region?
[15:58] Ravi Patel: yes we support region pinning for both runtime and logs. for cross-region replication we mark data categories and can restrict replication.

[16:00] Jenny Park: minor note — ensure the KMS key rotation flow doesn't break live connections. we've seen some vendors with a 2-hour outage during rotation.
[16:01] Ravi Patel: we have rolling key rotation that uses double-encryption during rotation, but we will include explicit runbook steps for your security team to validate.

[16:03] Alex Rivera: any competitor wonky behaviors we should watch for while we choose a vendor?
[16:03] Maya Chen: quick note — some vendors only support plaintext scrape endpoints which can cause compliance issues; others force all telemetry to hosted ingestion which breaks offline/on-prem needs. we'll highlight the differences in the doc.

[16:05] Priya Desai: do you have an agent for flamegraphs and slow traces for model execution? we need visibility into token generation time per-token.
[16:06] Ravi Patel: we export fine-grained latencies with per-token breakdown as an optional debug mode — that can be gated behind RBAC and sample only on failure to avoid cost.

[16:08] Maya Chen: okay, let's recap next steps and owners.
[16:09] Alex Rivera: sounds good.

[16:10] Maya Chen: recap: 1) we'll send a draft refarch and marketplace checklist, 2) we'll share a sample OTLP collector config and a prometheus scrape example, 3) schedule a short staging flood test, 4) produce a perf profile from a short benchmark.

[16:12] Omar Khalid: can we get the network diagram in editable form?
[16:13] Lena Ford: yes, we'll share a visio/diagrams.net link.

[16:15] Jenny Park: we'll send a security constraints doc for KMS/HSM requirements and retention windows.

[16:17] Maya Chen: great. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the action items.

--- End transcript ---

Redwood to send draft refarch + marketplace checklist (link to editable diagram)
Redwood to share sample OTLP collector config and Prometheus scrape example
Schedule staging flood test for week of 2026-09-13
Run short perf benchmark on Skyline staging and deliver p50/p95 sheet
Maya Chen - Send marketplace listing checklist and editable network diagram (due 2026-09-13)
Ravi Patel - Provide OTLP collector config, prom scrape example, and RBAC mapping template (due 2026-09-12)
Skyline (Priya/Omar) - Share security constraints doc for KMS, rotation, and data residency (due 2026-09-11)
Lena Ford - Schedule benchmark run and coordinate staging flood test window (due 2026-09-14)

title: Edge proxy & observability for LLM onramp - exploratory
content:
Edge proxy & observability for LLM onramp - exploratory

Exploratory discovery focused on integrating Redwood for NyxWorks' LLM features. Discussion covered hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, SDK adapters (Python/Node), LangChain and LlamaIndex integration patterns, gateway/proxy topology and where to surface rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks (token-level metrics, traces, and KV cache visibility). Customer is leaning toward a hybrid proof-of-concept: hosted for early rollout, dedicated/private for PII-sensitive flows. Action items and pilot plan agreed.
Deployment modes: hosted vs dedicated vs private
SDK integration: Python/Node and server-side SDKs
LangChain & LlamaIndex adapters and prompt templating
Gateway/proxy patterns and sidecar vs centralized gateway
Rate limiting and quota enforcement details
Observability: token-level metrics, tracing, dashboards, audit logs
Security controls: SSO/SAML, KMS, SOC2, data residency
Pilot scope and benchmarking
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego is our SE. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Erin: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in. We wanted to talk through how Redwood would fit into our stack, esp with our edge proxy setup.
00:14 Diego: Great — quick intro from us, we typically help customers pick between hosted, dedicated and private and then align integration patterns with their gateway and LLM orchestration. We'll ask about traffic, SLAs, security, etc.
00:30 Samir: Quick context: NyxWorks runs a global microservice mesh, edge proxies in front of region clusters. We have a central API gateway but also run sidecars for latency-sensitive paths. Typical 95th p99 latency goals for user-facing LLM features are around 250ms. We do about 120 requests/sec during peaks, avg token lengths moderate, and spikes in mornings.
00:52 Maya: Thanks — that helps. Two immediate questions: 1) Do you expect PII/data residency constraints that would push you to private/dedicated right away? 2) How tightly coupled do you want the inference runtime to be to your gateway?
01:08 Erin: For initial pilot, we can use hosted for non-PII. But for our support product we may need a private deployment or VPC. We'll need audit logs and KMS integration for secrets on the private flows.
01:22 Rita: Security side — we'll need SOC2, SSO/SAML for console access, and the ability to push audit logs to our SIEM. Also encryption at rest with customer-managed keys ideally.
01:33 Diego: Understood. We have SOC2 and options for KMS/HSM integrations on Private, and for Dedicated we can support customer-owned VPC peering. Audit log export to Seq/Datadog/Splunk is common — we can push structured logs. I'll upload the security pack after this call.
01:52 Leo: On integration — we use LangChain in the app layer and sometimes LlamaIndex for retrieval augmented generation. How do your SDKs play with these? Any adapter code to avoid reinventing?
02:03 Maya: Yes, great question. Diego: can you speak to the LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors?
02:08 Diego: Sure — we provide Python and Node SDKs that behave like a drop-in transport. For LangChain we have an examples repo with a RedwoodLLM wrapper that implements the chain interface; for LlamaIndex we show how to use embeddings and store vectors, plus config for streaming and chunking. We'll share the repo link. The adapter handles tokenization differences and streaming callbacks.
02:37 Erin: How does streaming work if we route through our own gateway? We're worried about timeouts and partial responses being dropped by proxies.
02:47 Diego: Two approaches: 1) Keep a direct connection from client to Redwood streaming endpoint (less hops) or 2) proxy with websockets or chunked responses through your gateway. If you have sidecars, the sidecar can maintain the connection and stream to client. We recommend configuring long-lived connections at the gateway and increasing proxy read timeouts for streamed endpoints. There's a sample nginx config in our docs.
03:12 Samir: For us, sidecar streaming seems cleaner since we already have that pattern. We'll need examples for nginx and envoy timeouts though. Also how does prefix/KV cache work across restarts?
03:25 Diego: KV cache is per-inference process by default; for Dedicated/Private you can configure persistent KV cache backed by Redis to survive restarts. For hosted customers we handle caching in the runtime and can expose metrics like cache hit rates. We'll show you cache metrics and suggestions to tune TTLs.
03:44 Erin: Rate limits — we want per-route quotas and per-tenant quotas. Where should enforcement live? Upstream gateway or Redwood?
03:52 Maya: Great point — both options valid. If you enforce at the gateway you save on tokens/calls to Redwood but you need to mirror billing quotas. Redwood supports token-level rate limits and per-key quotas, and you can also propagate headers from your gateway for tenant identification. Many customers do a hybrid: gateway blocks obviously malicious floods, Redwood enforces billing and fine-grained quota per API key.
04:18 Samir: If we push enforcement to our gateway, how do we get accurate token counts for billing? We want to reconcile usage for internal chargeback.
04:27 Diego: We expose per-request token metadata in response headers and through our usage API. You can pull aggregated token usage from the API and import into your billing systems. If gateway blocks a request before it hits Redwood, it won't be billed — so we recommend emitting a consistent token-estimate header from gateway using your tokenizer libs so internal accounting matches post-factum billing from Redwood.
04:55 Rita: About observability — we need traces end-to-end, and token-level cost breakdown per route. Does Redwood provide tracing spans usable with OpenTelemetry?
05:04 Diego: Yes, we emit spans and can integrate with OpenTelemetry. For tracing we include span context tags for model, sequence length, KV cache hits, and batching latencies. Token-level cost is available per request in the telemetry payload and ingestible by your metrics backend. There's also a per-route dashboard in Redwood Console that maps tokens, latency P95/99, and errors.
05:28 Erin: Excellent. Can the console export dashboards or webhook alerts for regressions? We want to alert on model output quality drop and latency spikes.
05:36 Maya: You can set monitors and alerts with webhook sinks; we also support regressions tied to eval sets so you can get notified when a prompt set drops below a threshold. Diego, maybe mention eval hooks?
05:45 Diego: Right — Redwood Optimize can run periodic evals against pinned prompts and send alerts if accuracy or hallucination metrics change. Integration is via an API to push prompt sets and reference outputs. Many customers wire this into their CI to gate rollouts.
06:02 Leo: On rollout strategy — we want canary and automatic fallback if latency SLOs are missed. Can Redwood do model variant fallback?
06:09 Diego: Yes. Smart routing can fallback to a lower-cost variant or a region-specific replica if latency or capacity thresholds are hit. For Dedicated you can configure reserved capacity and fallback routes to hosted for overflow. We can demo routing rules in the console.
06:28 Samir: Latency SLOs: p99 under 250ms. Can we get benchmarks for your runtime with our token lengths?
06:35 Maya: We should schedule a benchmarking session. For that we'll need a representative prompt set and traffic profile. Diego can run microbenchmarks and we can run an end-to-end pilot using our dedicated pool or hosted endpoints, depending on what you want to validate.
06:51 Erin: Pilot scope question — we'd like to test: 1) LangChain integration + streaming, 2) Observability hooks into Datadog, 3) Rate-limits mapping, and 4) Private deploy feasibility for PII path. Is that reasonable for a 4-week pilot?
07:05 Maya: Yes, that's a realistic pilot. Typically week 1 onboarding and security review, week 2 SDK + adapter integration, week 3 run benchmarks and iterate, week 4 evaluate and decide on Dedicated vs Private. We'll capture that in the next steps.
07:18 Rita: Security gating — we'll require a pen test coordination and remote attestation for Private installs. Also a question: where are customer logs stored and how long are they retained?
07:28 Diego: For Hosted, logs are retained per your plan and can be exported; retention is configurable and you can opt for zero retention for sensitive flows. For Dedicated/Private you control retention and can forward logs to your SIEM. We'll include log retention examples in the security pack.
07:45 Jules (NyxWorks): note — Erin asked about zero retention option for specific tenants, flagged for action item.
07:51 Maya: Noted. Diego: quick demo idea — show LangChain snippet and proxy config?
07:56 Diego: Yeah I'll share a short example now verbally and then upload the code. Basic flow: install redwood-sdk, instantiate Redwood client with streaming callback, wrap in a LangChain LLM wrapper implementing generate/stream methods, and configure LlamaIndex data connector to call the embeddings endpoint. For gateways, we include an envoy filter example to forward chunked responses and preserve streaming semantics.
08:22 Leo: Does the SDK implement token counting or do we need a separate tokenizer to estimate tokens before gateway enforcement?
08:30 Diego: SDK returns token usage after the call, but we also have a lightweight tokenizer in the SDK for pre-call estimates. Many customers embed that at the gateway for quota enforcement approximations.
08:45 Erin: On pricing — we need an estimate for the pilot (approx 100k tokens/day). Also pricing differences hosted vs dedicated contracts?
08:54 Maya: We'll send a pilot quote. Hosted has pay-as-you-go pricing, Dedicated is a reserved capacity model with a monthly commit and lower per-token rate. Private adds platform fee and some professional services for on-prem. I'll attach the pricing sheet to the follow-up email.
09:08 Samir: One more thing: our observability team wants to correlate user request IDs across our gateway, the Redwood request, and downstream vector DB calls. How best to pass trace ids?
09:18 Diego: Pass the trace/span context headers; we honor W3C tracecontext headers and add them into our spans. We'll include an example where you forward x-request-id and traceparent headers through the proxy and Redwood surfaces them in the logs and traces so you can join across systems.
09:35 Rita: Are there RBAC controls for who can deploy new model versions via the console? We want separation of duties.
09:41 Maya: Yes, RBAC with SSO/SAML, role definitions, and audit trails for rollout operations. For Dedicated/Private you can enforce restrictions via your identity provider.
09:52 Erin: Curious about quantization/accelerators — if we go Dedicated, can you recommend optimized model variants or quantized versions to hit cost targets?
09:59 Diego: Absolutely — part of Redwood Optimize we provide quantization and kernel-selection recommendations based on your sequence length distributions. We can recommend INT8 or mixed-precision variants and show estimated cost savings and latency tradeoffs.
10:14 Samir: On the proxy topology: we're evaluating two patterns — a centralized gateway that forwards to Redwood and a per-service sidecar that handles retries/streaming. Which do you see customers picking?
10:25 Diego: Both exist. Sidecars reduce hop count and are easier for streaming. Centralized gateways simplify policy enforcement (auth, quotas). If you need strong tenant isolation and token-level billing accuracy, sidecar + internal auth header propagation is a good compromise. We'll provide both patterns in the integration doc.
10:45 Leo: For quotas, if we do per-tenant keys, are there tooling APIs for changing quotas dynamically?
10:51 Maya: Yes, quota APIs and admin endpoints allow programmatic updates. We also expose usage webhooks so you can auto-scale quotas based on internal signals.
11:02 Erin: Let's talk risk scenarios — what happens if Redwood has an incident, how do we fail gracefully?
11:07 Diego: We recommend defining fallback strategies: client-side degrade to cached answers, a cheaper hosted fallback model, or queueing. Redwood supports automated fallback to pinned variants and to regional replicas. For Dedicated contracts we have SLA and optional standby capacity.
11:22 Samir: SLA numbers? Uptime and latency guarantees for Dedicated?
11:26 Maya: Dedicated SLAs include 99.9% uptime and latency SLO targets based on instance types. We'll share the SLA doc. Private deployments can have a custom SLA as negotiated in the enterprise agreement.
11:40 Rita: Data residency — we need EU-only for some customers. Can you restrict hosting region?
11:45 Maya: Yes, you can pin workloads to regions. For Private you operate in your DC. For Hosted we offer region selection for endpoints so data doesn't leave region.
11:58 Jules: note — region pinning and EU-only requirement captured as constraint.
12:03 Diego: A small technical caveat: if you do cross-region fallbacks, you'll want to consider latency and compliance implications. For leaked PII you should use Private or Dedicated with strict routing policies.
12:18 Erin: Ok — on the POC can you show an example where we send a prompt through our gateway, Redwood streams the response, and Datadog receives traces/metrics?
12:27 Diego: Yes — that's the baseline POC. We'll prepare a step-by-step runbook: 1) Create sandbox API key, 2) Hook SDK in a LangChain test app, 3) Configure gateway timeouts and streaming proxy, 4) Enable Datadog exporter in Redwood Console, 5) Run load with your traffic profile. We'll demo trace maps and token cost charts.
12:52 Samir: About authentication between our gateway and Redwood — prefer mTLS or API keys?
12:58 Maya: API keys are simplest for Hosted. For Dedicated/Private, mutual TLS is supported and often used for stronger identity. We also support short-lived creds via token exchange if you want ephemeral keys.
13:12 Leo: Any gotchas with LlamaIndex when using managed embeddings? We use local vector DB but need embedding consistency.
13:19 Diego: Ensure you pin embedding model version and replicate normalization steps. We include an example showing how to store embedding metadata and hashing to detect drift. Also we surface embedding logs to help debug mismatch.
13:36 Erin: One more product question — do you support function/tool-calling or structured outputs?
13:41 Diego: Yes, Redwood supports function calling and structured output with enforced schema validation. That can be integrated into LangChain flows too.
13:50 Samir: Great. Any references or docs we should read now?
13:55 Maya: I'll drop links: SDK quickstart, LangChain adapter repo, security pack, and a sample benchmarking plan. Also the price sheet.
14:03 Rita: On pen test coordination — who do we contact?
14:06 Maya: I'll include the security contact in the follow-up email and cc Diego for technical coordination.
14:12 Jules: note — pen test contact to be added.
14:17 Diego: Quick question for you Samir — can you send over token distribution and a representative prompt set after the call? That will make benchmarks realistic.
14:25 Samir: Yep, we'll share that. Expect to send a sample by 2028-11-22.
14:30 Maya: Great — so recapping: we'll send security pack and SOC2, Diego will share LangChain/LlamaIndex example repo and proxy configs, we'll propose pilot pricing and infra diagram, Samir will share traffic/prompt data, and we'll schedule a benchmarking session week of 2028-11-29. Anything else?
14:47 Erin: Nope that's it from us. Thanks Maya/Diego — this was helpful.
14:52 Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts. Bye.
14:55 Diego: Thanks, bye.

title: Zenith Insurance - Evidence delivery playbook & log-lineage review
content:
Zenith Insurance - Evidence delivery playbook & log-lineage review

Redwood ran through a SOC 2 / ISO 27001 posture review focusing on how evidence is delivered, audit log lineage, RBAC/SSO access for the Trust Center, and KMS/encryption options. Customer asked clarifying questions on data residency and log retention; SE committed to a hands-on demo of audit export and key rotation. Next steps agreed: share reports, customer to map control owners, schedule demo and follow-up legal checks.
SOC 2 Type II report access
Trust Center read-only access and RBAC
Audit logs: retention, lineage, and export
Encryption and KMS integration options
Data residency for EU/US PII
Evidence delivery playbook and timelines
Lena Ortiz | Share Trust Center link + SOC 2 redacted PDF | 2026-12-02
Marcus Kim | Demo: audit log export, log-lineage CSV, and KMS key rotation workflow | 2026-12-08
Sarah Patel | Provide control owners list and retention SLA requirements | 2026-12-07
Diego Fuentes | Grant read-only test account for trust portal demo or provide screenshots if blocked | 2026-12-04
Priya Rao | Confirm whether Zenith requires HSM-backed keys for production | 2026-12-03
Redwood to share redacted SOC 2 Type II report link and Trust Center access (Lena) - by 2026-12-02
Customer to provide list of 8 critical controls and evidence owners (Sarah) - by 2026-12-07
SE to run a short log-lineage demo of audit export to S3 and KMS envelope flow (Marcus) - schedule w/ Diego week of 2026-12-06
Legal to confirm residency constraints for EU PII in policy (Priya) - by 2026-12-03
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: okay uh hey everyone thanks for joining, we we have about 50 minutes, we want to run through the posture review and the evidence delivery playbook. um Marcus will cover audit logs and KMS flow.
[00:12] Sarah Patel: thanks lena, appreciate it. to kick off — our timeline is end of Q1 for cert, so the big asks are access to reports, RBAC patterns for trust center, and how logs get exported for audits.
[00:28] Marcus Kim: great, i'll keep it practical. quick agenda: (1) trust center access and RBAC, (2) evidence delivery options and playbook, (3) audit log lineage and retention, (4) encryption/KMS model and key rotation.
[00:42] Tom Ellis: small note — we run in eu-west and us-central, residency is a hard requirement for some PII assets.
[00:50] Lena Ortiz: yup noted. so first, trust center access. lena: we provide read-only Trust Center urls and can create role-based accounts. typically AE creates an org-level view and SE can create a read-only security reviewer role.
[01:04] Priya Rao: when you say role-based, is it SAML SSO integrated or do we need separate credentials?
[01:10] Marcus Kim: we support SAML 2.0 SSO, Okta/ADFS. for partners without SSO we can provision scoped accounts and enforce MFA. sometimes the auto-import of group membership can be imperfect, so we advise a one-time sync and manual mapping.
[01:26] Sarah Patel: ok good. and audit logs — how long are they kept? we need 12 months for certain controls, and some financial artifacts need 7 years.
[01:36] Marcus Kim: default retention for high-fidelity audit logs is 3 months in hot storage, then archived to cold object storage for up to 7 years, configurable per customer. export is via signed S3 export with envelope encryption.
[01:50] Diego Fuentes: envelope encryption meaning our KMS or Redwood-managed key?
[01:54] Marcus Kim: both options. envelope uses a data key encrypted by a master key. customers can use their own AWS KMS or bring-your-own-HSM via our Private deployment integrations — there is an extra ops step for rotation and audit.
[02:08] Sarah Patel: rotation cadence? we prefer 90-day rotation for data keys and annual for master keys.
[02:13] Marcus Kim: yes we can configure data-key rotation at 90 days; master key rotation needs coordination — we have runbooks for key rollover to avoid re-encrypt storms, it's in the trust center docs.
[02:24] Tom Ellis: about evidence delivery playbook — what are the ways we can get evidence? direct portal download, s3 pickup, or pull via API?
[02:33] Lena Ortiz: exactly those three. we typically do: (A) Trust Center direct download (read-only roles), (B) automated scheduled S3 export with signed URLs + envelope encryption, (C) API-backed pull for integrations into ticketing systems. we recommend S3 export for high-volume artifacts.
[02:50] Priya Rao: any PII redaction? can we get redacted copies for external auditors?
[02:55] Marcus Kim: we have redaction filters for certain logs and we can provide redacted report variants in the trust center. full raw logs are available via S3 with appropriate roles. there have been cases where names get transcribed incorrectly in logs, so we do a quick review step when requested — but that's manual.
[03:12] Sarah Patel: okay good. one thing: log-lineage — auditors always ask for chain-of-custody. how do you show that?
[03:20] Marcus Kim: we add immutable markers in the log metadata (UUIDs, origin service, sequence) and every export is signed; the trust center shows export history and checksums. for extra assurance we can add an external signature step — e.g., sign manifests with your KMS key.
[03:36] Diego Fuentes: is the manifest human readable? we'd like to ingest it into our CMDB.
[03:40] Marcus Kim: yes CSV or JSON manifest options, with columns for artifact id, sha256, timestamp, service, control mapping tag.
[03:47] Sarah Patel: control mapping tag — can you map logs to SOC 2 controls?
[03:51] Lena Ortiz: we include control tags per artifact. we also provide a controls matrix export — it's a mapping between Redwood controls and SOC 2/ISO 27001 clauses. we'll share the spreadsheet.
[04:02] Tom Ellis: on RBAC, we need separation of duties, i.e., auditors shouldn't be able to initiate exports. is that supported?
[04:08] Marcus Kim: yes role-based permissions are granular. read-only roles can view and download, but export scheduling and key management require a higher privilege role. these roles can be mapped to SAML groups.
[04:20] Priya Rao: legal question — if we request raw logs for an audit and they contain EU PII, what's the transfer mechanism?
[04:27] Marcus Kim: for EU-resident PII we recommend running export to an EU S3 bucket under your account; if we host the bucket we can restrict region and apply data residency controls. transfers are over TLS and artifacts are encrypted at rest with your KMS.
[04:43] Sarah Patel: can you walk us through a sample evidence delivery timeline? say auditor requests logs today, how long until we can hand over?
[04:52] Lena Ortiz: typical timeline: if artifacts exist in hot store it's minutes to hours (generate manifest, sign, share link). if in cold archive, rehydration may be hours. we can provide SLA options for expedited retrieval.
[05:04] Tom Ellis: any gotchas around re-encryption during key rotation? we've had outages before.
[05:10] Marcus Kim: we avoid full re-encrypts by doing envelope rewraps and background rekeying with a rolling window. the runbook includes a preflight check and staged cutover. Diego, we'll demo that.
[05:22] Sarah Patel: on reports — do you share full SOC 2 Type II report or a redacted version?
[05:27] Lena Ortiz: we share a redacted copy for initial review and provide the full report under an NDA if needed. the Trust Center has a section for compliance artifacts and you can request evidence packages scoped to specific controls.
[05:40] Priya Rao: NDA process — timeline?
[05:43] Lena Ortiz: 24-48 hours typically once legal accepts the template. we'll send our NDA and the redacted report link.
[05:50] Marcus Kim: quick note: for Private deployment customers we can provide SOC attestations for the deployed package as part of the contract; there's an extra step for on-prem evidence collection.
[05:59] Diego Fuentes: for the demo, can you show the manifest CSV and a KMS key rotation example?
[06:04] Marcus Kim: yes we'll set up a short SE session. Diego, what's your timezone preferred window?
[06:08] Diego Fuentes: mornings CET are best.
[06:10] Lena Ortiz: ok we'll propose slots next week.
[06:14] Sarah Patel: one more — retention policy and legal hold. auditors may ask to preserve artifacts beyond retention, can you support a hold flag?
[06:23] Marcus Kim: yes there's an archival hold feature in Trust Center; we can tag artifacts as legal-hold which prevents deletion and preserves manifests.
[06:31] Tom Ellis: nice. small nit — we've seen misspelled service names in metadata before, it's minor but makes mapping messy. can we standardize tags?
[06:39] Marcus Kim: good point. we enforce canonical service ids in the manifest (service_id) and recommend customers map to their internal catalog via our exported fields.
[06:49] Priya Rao: last legal item — KMS audit trail. does Redwood surface key usage logs?
[06:55] Marcus Kim: yes access to key usage events is available. if using your KMS, you can pull CloudTrail logs; if using Redwood-managed KMS, we provide a key-usage report in the Trust Center.
[07:06] Lena Ortiz: ok wrap-up. action items and owners captured. we'll share the redacted SOC 2 and controls matrix, schedule demo for log-lineage and key rotation. any objections?
[07:16] Sarah Patel: no objections. thanks everyone.
[07:20] Tom Ellis: thanks.
[07:22] Priya Rao: thanks all.
[07:25] Lena Ortiz: bye folks.
[07:30] [meeting end — 52 minutes total — further discussion moved to email about NDA details and demo scheduling]

title: POC: open-model prioritization and workload sizing - Lakemount Health
content:
POC: open-model prioritization and workload sizing - Lakemount Health

Discovery + POC scoping for Lakemount Health focused on open-model shortlist, workload sizing, benchmarks and timeline. Agreement to run 2-week bench on dedicated pool, share security docs and sample traffic.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Mark Reyes (CTO - Lakemount), Nina Park (Product), Jorge Alvarez (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto): quick notes captured: prioritize quality for triage UX, latency SLOs for live chat, Spanish/Portuguese support is required, HIPAA + SOC2 compliance non-negotiable.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros — I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Priya, our systems engineer.
[00:18] Mark (Lakemount): Hey thanks, Mark here, CTO. Nina and Jorge are with me. We're trying to scope a proof-of-concept for triage/chat automation across English and Spanish, possibly Portuguese in phase two.
[00:35] Priya: Great — can you outline success criteria briefly? What does a win look like for Lakemount?
[00:48] Nina: Uh, yeah; three things. First, answer accuracy on triage intents above 88% on our eval set. Second, average latency under 350ms p50 for short sessions, p95 under 700ms. Third, cost target — must be less than 0.02 USD per convo on average. And, of course, data residency and HIPAA controls.
[01:05] Alex: Solid. Those are helpful. For models we're proposing an open-model shortlist to keep licensing flexible — thinking of Llama-derived variants and a couple of Mistral-ish models — low-level note: we will provide concrete perf profiles.
[01:20] Jorge: Quick Q — when you say Llama variants, are we talking quantized 4-bit runs on dedicated GPUs or hosted? Our infra team prefers VPC/private but we want Redwood to host initial runs.
[01:37] Priya: We recommend a staged approach: hosted for early iteration, then a small Redwood Dedicated pool inside your VPC for latency and data isolation. For quantization we can test 4-bit and nf4 profiles — there will be a quality vs cost tradeoff.
[01:55] Mark: Yeah cost-quality tradeoffs are key. We're willing to sacrifice some small bit of quality if latency and cost are right, but not for core clinical triage flows.
[02:10] Nina: Also multilingual quality — Spanish evaluations historically drop ~5-7% relative to English. We'll need to see model-specific multilingual benchmarks.
[02:22] Alex: Absolutely. Priya, I'll ask you to walk through the benchmark plan in a bit.

[05:00] Priya: Ok so proposed bench: 2-week run, three model variants: (A) LlamaX-13B (fp16), (B) MistralLike-7B (nf4), (C) Open-Instruct-30B (quantized). We'll perf and quality test on your sample prompts, measure QPS, latency, memory footprint and token cost. We'll run both English and Spanish eval suites.
[05:25] Mark: That sounds about right but can you add a cold-start and KV-cache-heavy scenario? Our bots have long context threads, KV cash — sorry, KV cache — is important.
[05:40] Priya: Yes we'll include long-context tests (up to 8k tokens) and KV/cache warm vs cold. We'll capture tokenization differences too.

[08:10] Speaker 1 (auto): small transcription garble here, but they're confirming timeline
[08:25] Alex: Timeline we propose: baseline bench plan and security docs this week, Lakemount shares traffic sample by Monday next week, Redwood provisions dedicated pool by 01/22, bench runs 01/24-02/06, follow-up results review week of 02/09. Is that viable?
[08:47] Mark: Yes that timeline looks okay if we can get the security/compliance paper trail early.

[11:00] Nina: On the security side, we need to see SOC2 Type II report and HIPAA BAAs. Also can Redwood support HSM-based KMS integration for key management inside our VPC?
[11:20] Alex: We can — Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations for enterprise customers. For the POC we'll provide a scoped HIPAA addendum and SOC2 artifacts. We'll also provide our runbook for VPC peering and logs export.
[11:40] Jorge: Logs export is important. We need audit trails with token-level cost and redaction controls. Can you redact PHI automatically before any logs leave our env?
[12:02] Priya: We have configurable redaction hooks and can run a pre-ingest filter. For the initial bench, best if you anonymize samples; we'll also show redaction in the pipeline.

[15:30] Mark: Another constraint — throughput profile during business hours spikes to 120 RPS sustained for short bursts. Our current peak sessions have long tails with heavy prompt reuse. We need batching to be smart; synchronous latencies still matter.
[15:52] Priya: We'll capture throughput shape and set batching policies that respect latency SLOs; Redwood Optimize will suggest batch sizes and caching TTLs. Expect a 20-35% token cost reduction for workload-aware batching in many cases.

[18:00] Alex: On model selection tradeoffs — smaller models (7B) are cheaper and fast but may lose ~4-9% on the triage eval. Larger models cost more but give higher accuracy and better multilingual coverage. We'll present per-model quality vs token-cost curves.
[18:25] Nina: For safety/regulatory reasons, we may want to route high-risk intents to human-in-the-loop or a larger model even if it's costlier. Can Redwood support hybrid routing?
[18:40] Priya: Yes, policy routing by intent is supported. You can pin certain intents to a higher-capacity model or to a fallback route that goes to a rep.

[22:10] Speaker 2 (auto): brief cross-talk on API keys
[22:30] Alex: For the POC we'll provide a temporary API key scoped to the test pool with RBAC so only your SRE and product folks have access.

[25:00] Mark: Benchmark metrics — please include p50/p95 latency, tokens per request, GPU utilization, cost per 1k tokens, and quality metrics (F1/accuracy) per intent and per language.
[25:20] Priya: Noted. We'll submit a bench spreadsheet with columns for each metric and a column for recommended production config.

[28:40] Nina: On multilingual — our Spanish prompts include regional terms (Mexico, Argentina) which confuse models. Do you have experience fine-tuning or prompt engineering for regional variants?
[29:00] Priya: For the POC we'll do prompt engineering and eval slices by locale. If fine-tuning is needed later, Redwood can host model variants and manage versions but fine-tune Ops aren't part of this initial bench unless you want to add it.

[32:15] Jorge: Question about private deployment — if we go Redwood Private later, what are the differences for latency and observability?
[32:30] Alex: Private/on-prem reduces network hops and can cut latency by ~50ms in many setups. Observability pipelines are the same; you'll retain full audit logs and it's easier to meet data residency. Pricing is different — enterprise license + infra.

[36:00] Mark: Are there any known gotchas with long-context keys and memory when using 4-bit quantization?
[36:15] Priya: Yes, KV cache memory patterns change; some kernels are less optimized for certain quant formats which can increase latency at high token lengths. We'll include memory vs latency charts in the bench report.

[40:10] Alex: Competitors — quick note: some teams use hosted OpenAI for simplicity, but for our use case (HIPAA, VPC, model control) Redwood gives more deployment options. We also compete with Anthropic-ish models for safety-focused workflows and Vertex for cloud-native shops.

[43:00] Nina: Pricing model question — how granular is token billing for a dedicated pool? We need predictable monthly costs.
[43:15] Alex: Dedicated is reserved capacity with commit tiers. We'll show estimated monthly cost based on your projected QPS and the bench numbers; bench will help you pick the right commit.

[46:50] Mark: Ok let's talk acceptance criteria for the POC — minimum accuracy 88% as mentioned, no more than 10% latency regressions under load, and clear evidence of redaction working. If model falls short on Spanish, we'll consider a two-week fine-tune as a next step.
[47:15] Priya: We'll flag regression alerts and provide per-prompt failure cases.

[50:00] Alex: To recap next steps: I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet + pricing template + security pack. Priya will provision the dedicated test pool and share access. Mark will provide anonymized traffic samples and success metric file. We'll run the bench 01/24-02/06 and meet to review results week of 02/09.
[50:30] Mark: That works. One ask — can you include a quick runbook for redaction and PHI handling so our compliance people can sign off faster?
[50:45] Alex: Yes — we'll include the redaction runbook and a contact for our compliance team.

[53:10] Nina: Thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity.
[53:20] Alex: Thanks all — we'll follow up with materials.

End of transcript.

title: Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate
content:
Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate

Title: Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate

Summary
We’ve had a few early beta reports that “console totals don’t match invoice” (see SUP-24811) and a recurring internal concern that aggregation lag + rounding will cause subtle drift. This PR adds a reconciliation suite that compares Usage Insights rollups (route/model aggregates) against billing totals (metering hooks → invoice preview) within a defined tolerance, and wires it into CI + a nightly scheduled run with alert hooks.

Key goals
- Catch drift early (instrumentation regressions, bucketing/alias issues, timezone boundary mistakes, rounding deltas).
- Define and document a tolerance policy that is strict enough to catch real issues but robust to expected effects (late events, FX rounding, minimum billable units).
- Provide a runbook-friendly output: workspace/project, day/hour, route/model slices that contribute most to drift.

What’s included
1) Reconciliation job + report format
- New job: services/telemetry/reconciliation/usage_insights_vs_billing
- Compares totals for a given workspace_id + time range across:
  - usage_insights.route_model_agg (the dataset powering console breakdown tables)
  - billing.usage_totals (billing hook rollups used for invoice preview)
- Outputs both:
  - a single “gate” metric per workspace/time window (pass/fail)
  - a ranked list of top contributing slices (route/model/region/deployment_mode where present)

2) Tolerance policy (documented + implemented)
We gate on both absolute and relative drift, and we avoid evaluating windows likely to be incomplete.
- Windows evaluated:
  - Hourly buckets for last 24 hours (excluding most recent 2 hours)
  - Daily buckets for last 7 days (excluding current day)
- Late-event buffer:
  - Ignore the most recent 2 hours entirely to avoid normal ingestion lag.
  - For daily checks, only evaluate days older than 26 hours.
- Tolerance thresholds:
  - Absolute drift allowed: max($2.00, 2000 tokens worth of cost at the workspace’s effective blended rate) per evaluated window
  - Relative drift allowed: <= 0.50% per evaluated window
  - Gate fails if BOTH absolute and relative drift exceed thresholds (prevents false positives on small totals)
- Currency handling:
  - Compare in USD using billing’s canonical conversion for the period.
  - Usage insights cost uses the same price book snapshot key as billing (price_book_version) to avoid rate drift.
- Rounding:
  - Compare on unrounded micros (int64) where available; rounding only applied in the human report.

Tolerance helper (illustrative snippet):

function isDriftAcceptable({ expectedMicros, actualMicros }) {
  const driftMicros = Math.abs(actualMicros - expectedMicros);
  const rel = expectedMicros === 0 ? (actualMicros === 0 ? 0 : 1) : driftMicros / expectedMicros;
  const absOk = driftMicros <= ABS_TOLERANCE_MICROS;
  const relOk = rel <= 0.005;
  return absOk || relOk; // fail only if BOTH are violated
}

3) CI + scheduled runs
- Adds a Buildkite step (non-blocking in PRs, blocking in main nightly):
  - PR builds: runs reconciliation unit tests + one small integration fixture
  - Nightly: runs full reconciliation across allowlisted beta workspaces with paging
- New pipeline: .buildkite/pipelines/usage-insights-reconciliation.yml
- Artifacts:
  - Uploads a CSV and JSON summary for each run
  - Posts a summary comment to #eng-platform on failures with a link to artifacts

4) Alert hooks + runbook pointers
- On gate failure, the nightly job:
  - Emits metric: usage_insights.reconciliation.drift_exceeded{workspace_id, window_type}
  - Logs structured payload with top slices and suspected causes
  - Posts to Slack: #usage-insights-alerts
  - Creates a lightweight incident event (non-page) unless drift persists 2 consecutive runs, then page the on-call (aligns with SRE feedback from earlier threads)

5) Guardrails to avoid noisy failures
- Workspace allowlist for beta reconciliation (config in services/telemetry/reconciliation/config/beta_allowlist.yml)
- Suppression for known exceptions:
  - If billing is missing a price_book_version for the period (rare), mark “skipped” not “failed”
  - If insights freshness lag > threshold (uses existing freshness metadata), mark “skipped”

Why this approach
- We compare at the same conceptual level as customers: “what billing says you owe” vs “what console says you spent”.
- We still include drill-down slices to make debugging actionable (route/model/region).
- Late-event handling is explicit and conservative; we don’t want to treat expected lag as correctness drift.

Files / areas changed (high level)
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/usage_insights_vs_billing/*
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/lib/tolerance.ts
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/lib/report.ts
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/config/beta_allowlist.yml
- .buildkite/pipelines/usage-insights-reconciliation.yml
- docs/internal/runbooks/usage-insights-reconciliation.md
- libs/billing/pricebook/resolve_pricebook_version.ts (small helper to align snapshots)

Test plan
- Unit tests:
  - tolerance calculations (edge cases: 0 totals, tiny totals, large totals)
  - rounding behavior (micros vs displayed dollars)
  - skip logic (freshness lag, missing pricebook)
- Integration tests:
  - fixture dataset with:
    - retries + fallbacks
    - model alias → version bucketing
    - streaming endpoints
  - verifies:
    - aggregation totals match billing totals within tolerance
    - top-slices ranking is stable/deterministic
- Manual:
  - Ran job for HelioChat staging workspace on 2026-02-16 (7d window) and validated output against invoice preview totals.

Rollout notes
- Nightly reconciliation initially scoped to beta allowlist only.
- If the nightly job is noisy, we can widen the late-event buffer or adjust absolute tolerance; prefer changing absolute tolerance first.
- No change to customer-visible console behavior.

Links
- Linear: ENG-3817
- Related PRs: pr-23114 (aggregation job), pr-23135 (query API)
- Support: SUP-24811

Reviewer notes / questions to focus on
- Tolerance policy: are we comfortable gating on “abs OR rel” instead of “abs AND rel”? (current implementation is intentionally forgiving on small totals)
- Skip windows: is 2 hours sufficient buffer for late events in all regions?
- Alerting: does the ‘2 consecutive runs before paging’ rule match SRE expectations?

---
