title: cross-SDK stream resume + graceful token refresh bridge (python/ts/go)
content:
cross-SDK stream resume + graceful token refresh bridge (python/ts/go)

Motivation: long-lived streaming sessions occasionally encounter mid-stream 401/403 during token expiry/rotation. Clients either dropped the stream (losing partial results) or had to re-establish and reparse responses, causing UX roughness and higher error rates for interactive apps. This PR introduces a cross-SDK compatibility layer and ergonomics improvements to allow graceful token refresh and optional in-band resume semantics so higher-level applications can recover without full restart. Summary of changes: 1) wire-level: introduce an opt-in resume_token header and an optional resume handshake message for streaming transports. The contract is backward-compatible: servers not advertising resume support simply ignore the header. 2) auth: implement a LeakyTokenRefresh shim that transparently handles 401/reauth during an active stream and attempts a resume when the server supports it. 3) SDK ergonomics: Python adds Stream.as_context() to get automatic refresh + cleanup; TypeScript exposes AsyncIterable.withResume({timeout}) helper; Go adds StreamResumer interface and a small helper in the connection pool to retry with jittered backoff. 4) tests: new integrational mocks that simulate mid-stream expiry and validate exactly-once resume semantics for client-visible events. 5) versions: minor bumps to sdk packages to publish compatibility patches (python 1.8.0, typescript 2.4.3, go 0.9.2). Compatibility notes: the new resume header is optional, and servers must explicitly opt into resume behaviour. Existing SDKs will continue to work unchanged if not using the new helpers. Rollout plan: feature gated behind server-side flag for the first two weeks; telemetry added to monitor resume success/failure and any duplicated events. Checklist: - [x] design doc and sequences (linked) - [x] implementation across python/ts/go - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] e2e harness against mock token rotation - [x] docs snippets for SDKs - [x] version bumps and changelogs - [x] telemetry dashboards and alerts (QA)
Liam O'Connor: Can we ensure resume_token can't be replayed? Suggest tying resume_token to connection-id and short TTL.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: added connection-id binding and enforce 5s TTL server-side in design; client includes connection checksum in header to reduce replay risk.
Priya Raman: Question: how does this interact with function-calling / structured responses mid-stream? We need to ensure partial structured frames are re-emitted exactly once.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: shrunk atomic frame unit boundary in transport; integration tests validate dedupe by frame-sequence id. Added note in docs.
Diego Alvarez: CI flaked on linux/py3.11 matrix; re-run fixed it. Please add a small test that asserts no .close() leak when resuming fails.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: added test and resource cleanup in Stream.as_context() implementation.
SDKs: add optional graceful streaming resume and transparent token-refresh helpers across Python/TypeScript/Go. Backward compatible; opt-in resume header required. Minor version bumps: python 1.8.0, typescript 2.4.3, go 0.9.2. See docs/sdk/streaming-resume.md for migration guide.

title: Add cross-stage cost flare visualization and observability playbook
content:
Add cross-stage cost flare visualization and observability playbook

Motivation: When investigating cost spikes we frequently saw noisy, stage-local metrics (tokenization, model_forward, kv_fetch, decode) that were individually unhelpful. This PR introduces a cross-stage visualization ('Cost Flare') that aligns per-stage token-cost and latency signals to surface correlated flares across the inference pipeline and provides an SRE playbook with automated alert suggestions to speed triage. What changed: 1) A new dashboard JSON for the Cost Flare visualization that aggregates rollups from per-stage telemetry and renders a radial heat/flare view to highlight stages with simultaneous cost/latency deviations; 2) A lightweight cost-annotation agent (telemetry/cost_annotator.go) that tags spans with stage_cost_breakdown and emits compact provenance keys so the dashboard can do low-cardinality joins; 3) An auto-suggester (telemetry/thresholds/auto_suggester.py) that examines correlated anomalies across stages and proposes an alerting bundle (thresholds + priority) in the console; 4) A playbook runbook (observability/playbooks/cost_flare_playbook.md) with reproducible triage steps and recommended SLO actions. Backwards compatibility: All new fields are optional and safely ignored by older dashboards; the annotator falls back to emitting legacy token-cost labels if per-stage data is unavailable. Testing & rollout: Unit tests and integration tests added; deployed to staging with a 24h synthetic replay; gradual canary rollout to production with a kill-switch metric. Security & perf: The annotator operates asynchronously and adds a bounded amount of metadata (<= 128 bytes per invocation) to avoid increasing downstream costs. title: Handshake escrow and client-abort semantics for streaming sessions (OpenAI compatibility)
content:
Handshake escrow and client-abort semantics for streaming sessions (OpenAI compatibility)

Motivation: intermittent client disconnects during long-running streaming responses cause two classes of problems: 1) clients that reconnect within a short window are unable to resume because the server immediately tears down session state; 2) client-initiated cancels (or network-triggered resets) have ambiguous semantics with respect to tool/function call idempotency and structured output flushing. This PR introduces a handshake escrow token and clarified client-abort semantics to make resume/reconnect and abort behavior deterministic and OpenAI-compatible. Key changes: - Introduce a short-lived session escrow ticket (Escrow-Token) retained server-side for a configurable grace window to support reconnect-and-resume for active stream sessions. The token is returned in initial stream response headers and via the OpenAI-compat protocol extension. - Define deterministic semantics for client-initiated aborts: a cancelling client sends a terminal CANCEL event; server replies with a 499-equivalent closure in the OpenAI adapter and marks the session state as aborted but keeps an abort-marker for the escrow window to allow idempotent retries for in-flight tool calls. - On reconnect-with-ticket, runtime replays the last stable checkpointed structured-output frame (if any) and resumes token emission; if the abort-marker is present the reconnect is rejected unless the reconnect explicitly requests idempotent-retry scope. - Add explicit flush semantics for structured outputs and tool-call boundaries: runtime now ensures a terminal JSON frame is emitted and persisted before freeing durable KV for that session. This reduces split-output and truncation cases seen in production. - Compatibility mapping: map client cancel to HTTP/499 in our OpenAI adapter and document the header-based Escrow-Token workflow for clients migrating from the legacy resume token. - Safety: by default escrow window is 30s, configurable per-tenant; escrow tickets are single-use and rotated on successful resume. - Tests and docs: unit tests for handshake lifecycle, integration streaming smoke tests for reconnect/resume, updated API docs and SDK examples (Python/TS) showing Escrow-Token usage and abort/retry patterns. The description below includes a short migration checklist and operational knobs.
Amir Shah: Nice isolation of escrow lifecycle. A few questions: how do we avoid unbounded memory retention if many clients disconnect?
Diego Morales: The escrow manager uses a TTL job with small in-memory index + backing in Redis. Default TTL 30s and per-tenant cap on concurrent escrows. Added infra config file to tune.
Leah Chen: We need to be explicit about SDK surface—are we returning a header only, or also emitting a JSON control frame?
Diego Morales: We return both: Escrow-Token header for simple HTTP clients and a control frame for streaming websocket/grpc flows. Added examples in both Python and TS SDKs.
Priya Natarajan: Edge case: what happens if a tool-call had side effects and client cancels mid-call? Should we default to retry or surface a nondeterministic error?
Diego Morales: We surface an abort-marker and allow explicit idempotent-retry on reconnect. We also added guidance in docs: recommend using idempotency tokens for tool calls where side effects matter; we do not auto-retry side-effectful calls without explicit retry intent.
Improves streaming session resilience: adds Escrow-Token for reconnect-and-resume, clarifies client-cancel semantics and OpenAI compatibility mapping (client cancel -> HTTP 499). Default escrow window 30s. SDK examples updated.
Clients that rely on resume should: 1) read Escrow-Token from initial response headers or control frame; 2) on reconnect include Escrow-Token in Resume-Request header/frame; 3) handle 499 as a cancel signal and consult docs for idempotent-retry flow. Server admins can tune escrow_window and per-tenant caps in infra config.
Default escrow retention is short (30s). High-scale tenants should increase Redis eviction capacity or lower per-tenant escrow caps. Metrics exposed: streaming.escrow.created, streaming.escrow.expired, streaming.abort.marked. Alerts recommended: rate of escrow creations spiking without resumes.

title: add-traffic-curation-probe-scaling-and-staged-throttle-guard
content:
add-traffic-curation-probe-scaling-and-staged-throttle-guard

Motivation: Our existing canary probes surface regressions but noisy traffic and transient microbursts cause false positives and unnecessary rollbacks. This PR introduces a traffic curation layer and probe-scaling levers that reduce noise while preserving sensitivity for real regressions. It also adds a staged throttle rollout guard that gracefully applies backpressure during sustained degradation instead of immediate failover.

What this changes (high level):
- perf-canary/orchestrator: new TrafficCurator component that stratifies live traffic into cohorts by request shape (seq_len buckets), origin, and synthetic probe budget. It exposes a lightweight API used by the probe scheduler to decide which traffic to sample for canary comparisons.
- perf-canary/probes: probe-scaling configuration (probe_credit_budget, burst_resilience, temporal_strata) and logic for adaptive probe placement across replicas. Probes now use reservoir sampling with per-cohort weights so low-volume but important slices still get coverage.
- perf-canary/guards: StagedThrottleGuard implements a three-stage response to detected throughput/latency deltas: 1) soft-attenuation (reduce new canary traffic by fraction), 2) adaptive backpressure (increase probe density + throttle non-critical background routes), 3) circuit-escrow (hold critical traffic on safe model variant while rollouts pause). Each stage has configurable thresholds and cooldown windows.
- metrics/tracing: additional tags emitted for curator decisions (cohort, reason, probe_id) and guard decisions (stage, anchor_metric, confidence). These feed into console dashboards and the canary-runbook.
- tests: unit + integration harness: synthetic microburst generator, cohort replay tests, and a new e2e canary scenario that simulates slow memory-pressure-induced tail latency plus throughput drop.

Implementation notes:
- Baselines are estimated via an online quantile sketch per cohort (T-Digest variant) to keep memory bounded for high cardinality slices. The curator periodically compacts sketches and computes delta z-scores used by the guard.
- Probe scaling respects a global probe_credit_budget. Credits accrue on a per-window basis and are consumed by probes; when budget is low the curator prioritizes high-SLO cohorts using a priority function.
- StagedThrottleGuard uses a hysteresis-aware cooldown: each escalation stage has a soft deadline; if metrics recover within deadline the guard de-escalates without rollback.
- Safety: defaults are conservative to avoid customer-visible impact; the guard is opt-in per deployment until one week of canary metrics collection after rollout.

Related work: replaces ad-hoc heuristics from ENG-1920 and complements the rollout-sentinel in ENG-1805 by focusing on sample quality and controlled throttling rather than immediate cutoff.

Checklist:
- [x] Traffic curation algorithm and API
- [x] Probe scaling config + scheduler integration
- [x] StagedThrottleGuard implementation + unit tests
- [x] E2E harness scenario and CI jobs
- [x] Metrics/tags wired to console panels

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: misprioritization of cohorts could under-sample important traffic. Mitigation: default priority function favors low-volume auth/enterprise routes; manual overrides per-tenant are supported.
- Risk: sketch drift during traffic shifts. Mitigation: periodic full-window compaction and a fallback to rolling-window histograms when drift detected.

Rollout plan:
1) merge to main behind feature flag off
2) enable on perf-canary staging for two days, collect telemetry
3) smoke enable on 10% of canaries, monitor for false positives
4) full opt-in for all perf-canary runs after 7 days if stable

This PR is focused on production safety and reducing noisy rollbacks; it does not change model routing logic or model artifacts.
Miguel Santos: Nice approach to cohorting — can we add a simple regression test that verifies prioritization under extreme cardinality?
Aisha Patel: Added a priority stress test in perf-canary/tests/test_curator.py and a comment describing the priority function
Jordan Lee: The T-Digest compaction frequency looks like it may add CPU overhead at high QPS; can we make compaction adaptive?
Aisha Patel: Made compaction adaptive based on QPS and sketch error threshold; added benchmarks to the unit tests
Priya Desai: CI shows a flaky e2e failure on the first run; seems related to test timing — can we stabilize?

Introduce traffic curation and staged throttle rollout guard for perf canaries; opt-in behind feature flag. Reduces false-positive rollbacks by improving probe sampling and adding a gradual backpressure policy.

title: Introduce onboard policy engine and changelog batcher
content:
Introduce onboard policy engine and changelog batcher

Motivation: onboarding playlists and ad-hoc uploads had inconsistent release notes and missing policy checks (licenses, export controls, signature consistency). This PR adds a lightweight onboard policy engine (declarative DSL + runnable validator) and a changelog batcher that synthesizes release notes for grouped onboard events. Goals: 1) provide deterministic pre-merge validation for model metadata and artifact provenance, 2) generate compact, human-readable changelog entries for a given onboard run, and 3) enable batched publication to the registry release stream to reduce noise during large onboarding waves.

What changed (high level): added a policy DSL with a small set of built-in rules (license_allowlist, model_size_threshold, provenance_signature), wired the DSL into the existing onboard pipeline as a pre-commit validator, implemented a changelog batching worker that consumes onboard events and emits aggregated release notes with a sampling summary and impact hints. The batcher groups by time-window and affinity tags (hardware, use-case), and synthesizes a short summary + bullets of material changes.

Key design notes: the policy engine is intentionally minimal — rules are JSON/YAML first-class and validate against the registry schema. Policy evaluation runs in a sandboxed process with strict timeouts (200ms per evaluation) and returns deterministic pass/warn/fail verdicts. The changelog batcher uses a windowed aggregator (default 30m) and uses heuristics to collapse similar updates (semantically equivalent profile deltas) to avoid duplicate notes. The batcher also records provenance links to the original upload and attaches confidence scores for automatic release blurb drafting.

Acceptance criteria / checklist:
- [x] Policy DSL implemented and documented
- [x] Pre-onboard validation hook added to onboarding pipeline
- [x] Batcher worker implemented with idempotent output
- [x] Unit/integration tests for common policy rules and collating behavior
- [x] CI green on all supported platforms
- [x] Feature guarded behind feature flag (registry.onboard.policy_enabled)

Backward compatibility and rollout: feature is opt-in. By default policy_enabled=false in main; infra can flip the flag for select workspaces. The changelog batcher publishes to a new topic (registry.changelog.batched) and does not replace the existing immediate events; downstream consumers can subscribe to either stream. We will roll out in two phases: pilot workspace cohort (~3 teams) for 2 weeks, then global opt-in by config.

Related: Linear ENG-4122 for policy ruleset, PM-134 for changelog UX. See design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4122/onboard-policy-draft and internal spec at /docs/onboarding/policy_spec.md.

Notes on safety and audit: All policy evaluations and generated changelogs include an audit blob (policy_id, evaluator_version, timestamp, evaluation_trace) and are stored in the registry audit ledger so security/compliance can replay validators. The sandboxed evaluator writes only a compact trace to limit PII exposure.

Risks and mitigation: rule misconfiguration could block valid uploads — mitigated by warn-vs-fail semantics, an emergency bypass (admin override) with audit trail, and a clear rollback mechanism. Changelog batcher could delay visibility; default window is conservative and pilot will evaluate UX; immediate verbose events remain available for critical notifications.
Jasper Nguyen: Overall direction LGTM. Please add a benchmark for the evaluator to ensure 200ms budget across typical profiles.
Sofia Patel: Added micro-benchmarks and tuned the parser to avoid allocations. Numbers attached in the CI run artifacts.
Owen Li: Suggest switching the default batch window to 15m for the pilot to surface regressions faster; otherwise good.
Maya Rivera: Approved after minor nits fixed in docs and adding admin bypass logging (requested change addressed).
- Introduced a declarative onboard policy engine (opt-in) for metadata and provenance validation.
- Added a changelog batcher that synthesizes compact release notes from grouped onboard events.
- Policy evaluations and generated changelogs include audit traces for compliance.
- Feature behind feature flag: registry.onboard.policy_enabled (default: off).

title: Cooperative prefill throttler and lazy-decode trigger to reduce KV-cache stalls
content:
Cooperative prefill throttler and lazy-decode trigger to reduce KV-cache stalls

Motivation: In high-concurrency workloads we observed tail latency regressions caused by aggressive prefill batching that floods KV cache and forces frequent soft-evictions; this PR introduces a cooperative prefill throttler plus a lazy-decode trigger to reduce KV churn and smooth kernel utilization. Design summary: (1) Prefill throttler: token-window based admission that coordinates across worker threads using a light-weight sequence ring so simultaneous prefill bursts are spread over a configurable jitter window. (2) Backpressure signal: prefills that detect elevated KV miss ratio emit a transient backpressure mark propagated to the router to preferentially route new requests to decode-first lanes or lower concurrency workers. (3) Lazy-decode trigger: small speculative decode activation that waits for a short micro-window before kicking off full decode kernels if prefill progress stalls; this reduces wasted prefill work when requests are likely to be followed by immediate decode activity. (4) Kernel steering hints: dispatch includes a kernel hint flag (latency-optimized vs throughput-optimized) inferred from throttler state to select the best convolution/attention kernel. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for throttler logic - [x] integration test with kv-cache simulator - [x] new metrics (prefill_window_ms, prefill_backpressure_ratio) - [x] dry-run telemetry enabled behind flag - [x] e2e perf run across small, medium, burst traffic. Impact: 10-18% p99 latency reduction on synth burst workloads and 6% token-cost reduction from fewer reissued prefill ops. Rollout plan: behind feature flag pref_coop_throttle_v1 -> canary in eu-west-1 -> ramp to 30% traffic -> monitor kv eviction rate and cost-per-token. Related linear: ENG-2894 ENG-3010. This description contains implementation notes, high-level algorithm, and rollout instructions in a single contiguous string as required.
Ethan Cole: Can we make the jitter window adaptive to observed inter-arrival times? Suggest adding a config path to tie it to percentiles.
Anya Petrov: Added adaptive window config; default still 25ms, can be tuned via runtime flag.
Marina Alvarez: Need to ensure lazy-decode doesn't increase GPU warmup overhead for cold requests. Request adding a quick test measuring kernel startup counts.
Anya Petrov: Added micro-benchmark measuring decode kernel activations; numbers look stable within noise.
Jasper Liu: Approve after CI green and one more perf run on heavy kv-eviction scenario.

title: Resumable init workers and proactive network validation probes
content:
Resumable init workers and proactive network validation probes

Motivation: long-running init jobs in private installs were failing on transient network errors or node reboots, leaving tenant installs partially seeded and causing confusing rollback behavior. This PR adds a resumable init worker pattern and proactive network validation probes so installs can self-heal and upgrades can resume without manual intervention. Design summary: 1) Init resumer controller: a lightweight templated Job + sidecar pattern that persists step-state into a ConfigMap named redwood-init-resume-{{ .Release.Namespace }} and respects an exponential backoff TTL. Jobs include a compact resume protocol that reads the last successful step id and resumes from the next checkpoint. 2) Hook-level resume flag: values.private.init.resume.enabled and values.private.init.resume.ttlSeconds allow operators to opt-in and tune retention. 3) Network preflight probe: a templated preflight Job and probe helper that performs normalization checks (DNS resolution for control-plane endpoints, TCP connect to customer gateway IPs/CIDRs, cloud metadata reachability for onprem) and writes a structured result to a preflight ConfigMap used by the installer to gate long-running init jobs. 4) Template helpers: helpers added for templating lock ConfigMap names, backoff annotations, and idempotent job command wrappers. 5) Upgrade path: upgrade and rollback tooling will now detect resume-enabled releases and, if a previous init job failed, will schedule a fast-retry resume job instead of a full reinstall. Backwards compatibility: resume feature is opt-in and disabled by default; when disabled, behavior is identical to current hooks. Migration: operators can opt-in by setting values.private.init.resume.enabled=true and optionally configure values.private.init.networkPreflight.{enabled,targets,timeout}. Security considerations: ConfigMaps used for resume metadata are cluster-scoped within the namespace and do not contain secrets; we added RBAC rules scoped to the release ServiceAccount. Testing: included unit tests for template rendering and a small integration harness that simulates a transient network failure and demonstrates resume across a node reboot. Rollout plan: feature will be behind the values flag for one release and monitored via a new alert redwood.install.resume-failures in the SLO toolkit. See release_notes below for operator steps and caveats.
Arjun: The backoff TTL default seems aggressive for air-gapped installs, can we make it longer by default? Author: Raised default to 86400s and added values.private.init.resume.ttlSeconds for tuning.
Lisa: Need to ensure resume ConfigMap can't be abused to inject commands. Author: The resume payload is a small JSON with step ids and checksums, we validated we never store scripts or commands. Added a schema validator in the resumer sidecar.
Tomas: Helm template lint failed on indentation for _helpers.tpl, please run helm template lint locally. Author: Fixed indentation and added unit test to cover helper rendering.
CI: integration e2e failed on first run due to flakey cloud metadata access, reran and all checks passed.
- Added opt-in resumable init worker pattern to reduce manual intervention after transient failures. Enable with values.private.init.resume.enabled=true.
- Added network preflight checks customizable via values.private.init.networkPreflight.targets and timeout.
- No breaking changes when disabled. Operators should test resume in a staging environment before enabling in production.
Enable with helm upgrade --set private.init.resume.enabled=true --set private.init.networkPreflight.enabled=true. Recommended to start with ttlSeconds=86400 and targets set to control-plane IPs and gateway CIDRs. Watch alert redwood.install.resume-failures and preflight metrics under installer.preflight.*.

title: Consolidate pre-install probe templates and introduce tenant-scoped init-rate profiles
content:
Consolidate pre-install probe templates and introduce tenant-scoped init-rate profiles

Context: Private installer customers run into protracted cluster preflight phases when multi-tenant on-prem installs execute large numbers of tenant init jobs concurrently. This causes API server saturation and sporadic timeouts during pre-install health checks.

Motivation: provide a safer, opt-in default for helm charts that (1) centralizes pre-install and readiness probe templates to reduce duplication, (2) exposes tenant-scoped init-rate profiles (concurrency + burst) so operators can trade install speed for API stability, and (3) add a lightweight migration path so existing values are not broken.

Checklist:
- [x] Add unified probe template library for preflight and init jobs
- [x] Introduce tenant.initRateProfiles map in values.yaml with profiles (low/medium/high)
- [x] Implement values merging precedence and deprecation warnings
- [x] Add integration tests for staggered init behavior and preflight liveness
- [x] Documentation: update values.example and migration guide
- [x] CI: lint, unit tests, helm template, and an e2e job that runs a 6-tenant dry-run

Changes (high level):
- chart/templates/_probes.tpl: new consolidated probe helper (preflightProbe, initLiveness, initReadiness) that takes profile and overrides
- chart/values.schema.json: extended schema for tenant.initRateProfiles and probeOverrides with strict types and examples
- chart/values.example.yaml: new examples showing per-tenant overrides and recommended profiles
- chart/templates/init-job.yaml: wiring to read initRateProfile and apply rate controller annotations (init.kubernetes.io/concurrency, init.kubernetes.io/burst)
- chart/templates/preflight-hook.yaml: use preflightProbe helper and dynamically compute timeouts based on profile
- scripts/migrate-values.sh: helper that rewrites deprecated top-level initRate fields into the new tenant-scoped map (used in upgrade notes)
- tests/helm/staggered-init.test.yaml: unit-style helm template test showing annotation presence for each profile

Commits:
- 9c3f7d8 Add probe template helpers and initial tests
- b14a0fe Add tenant.initRateProfiles schema and example values
- e2f4c1a Wire init-job and preflight-hook to profile annotations and timeouts; add migrate-values script
- 4f5b2d0 Fix: revert flaky e2e timeout and tune medium profile
- d3a71b2 Docs: write migration guide and values examples

Files touched (selective):
- chart/templates/_probes.tpl (new)
- chart/templates/init-job.yaml (modified)
- chart/templates/preflight-hook.yaml (modified)
- chart/values.schema.json (modified)
- chart/values.example.yaml (new examples added)
- scripts/migrate-values.sh (new)
- tests/helm/staggered-init.test.yaml (new)

Small snippet (probe helper usage): {{"{{- include \"redwood._preflightProbe\" (dict \"profile\" \"medium\" \"overrides\" .Values.probeOverrides) -}}"}}

Testing & CI:
- Local lint + helm template passed
- Unit-style Helm tests (kubeval + schema checks) added and passed in CI
- E2E job initially failed due to tight timeouts; fixed by adjusting medium profile defaults and rerunning.

Final CI: all checks green (lint, unit, helm-template, e2e-dryrun).

Review conversation (high level):
- Marco Chen (reviewer): "Nice consolidation. Two asks: 1) make sure default medium profile is conservative for older clusters, 2) add a clear deprecation message in values.schema.json for the old initRate keys."
- Author (Aisha): "Addressed both: medium profile defaults dialed back (see commit b14a0fe) and deprecation warnings added in schema and migration script."
- Lena Fischer (reviewer): "Can we add a knob to completely opt-out of the rate controller annotations for customers who use external init orchestration?"
- Author: "Added tenant.initRateProfiles.<profile>.enabled boolean and documented opt-out in values.example.yaml."
- Diego Alvarez (approver): "Verified on internal testbed with 8 tenants, medium profile helps prevent apiserver saturation. Approving for merge."

Migration notes for operators:
- This change is backwards-compatible: existing top-level initRate fields are still supported but deprecated. Use scripts/migrate-values.sh to automatically convert to the new tenant.initRateProfiles map during upgrades.
- Default behavior: if tenant-specific profile not supplied, chart falls back to global initRate profile, then to 'medium' safe defaults.
- If you previously relied on aggressive concurrency, review new 'high' profile and adjust quotas accordingly.

Observability:
- Added two new Helm chart metrics labels for init profile (chart.k8s.redwood/init_profile) so Console dashboards can correlate init-phase latency with configured profiles.

Security and compliance:
- No secrets introduced. Rate-control annotations are purely metadata; no RBAC changes required.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged via GitHub web UI after approvals (merge method: squash).

Post-merge follow-ups:
- ENG-1248 follow-up created to evaluate adaptive-init autoscaler in next sprint
- Documentation PR queued to redwood-docs that imports values.example snippets and upgrade instructions

Notes: kept changes intentionally conservative to avoid surprises for Private customers running in constrained air-gapped environments. The migration script is minimal and prints a dry-run by default.
Add tenant-scoped init-rate profiles and unified pre-install probe templates. Backwards-compatible values; adds migration guide and example values for Private installs.

Subject: Mendrix pilot — traffic simulation & temporary rate exception request

Team,

Mendrix (pilot customer, DEAL-7842) has finalized their pilot start window: 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-18. They expect a concentrated ramp for two hours/day during the morning peak (US PST) and are asking for a temporary increase in per-minute rate limits for that window.

Attached: mendrix_traffic_sim_v2.csv — this contains our Monte Carlo traffic simulation (1000 runs) and the 95th/99th percentile token QPS per minute. Summary: median burst = 420 TPS, 95th = 820 TPS, 99th = 1,200 TPS for the peak 120 minute window. Their current assigned quota would throttle them heavily at 250 TPS.

Asking for:
- Product: confirm if a per-customer temporary rate bump (policy-based, time-limited) is okay and what guardrails we should require (max 1.5x billing multiplier, canary ramp minutes).
- Infra: feasibility of enabling a routing override to our dedicated pool for Mendrix for the two-hour windows (even if capacity needs a short-lived burst). Estimate of any pre-warm or capacity pinning lead time?
- CS (Marissa): confirm we have the signed amendment (I have a doc link) and whether Mendrix will accept automatic fallback to the hosted model if Dedicated becomes saturated.

Next steps suggested:
1) Infra run a quick preflight: can we absorb 1,200 TPS for 2h on 11/10 without impacting SLAs for other tenants? If not, provide mitigation options (routing to dedicated, temporary soft-quota, graceful 429 policy).
2) Product define exact exception entry (duration, multiplier, billing flag).
3) Sales/CS finalize payment security and amendment text.

I will forward Mendrix's ask below.

Thanks,
Jonas

--
Jonas Weber
Head of Sales Engineering, Redwood Inference
jonas.weber@redwood.ai

- Fast mitigations we can do before 11/10: pre-warm routing rules (needs 36–48 hours to shift cold-start profiles), and enable prefix caching for Mendrix prompt templates (we can ship a config change within 8 hours).

If Product wants a user-visible rollback plan, we can implement automatic fallback to the hosted smaller model but we'd need the customer's sign-off for the change in model quality.

Neha

Alex — thanks for the clear responses and the policy excerpt. High-level answers below; Ben/Marissa will add technical details and residency notes.

User-visible purge (30 days):
- Hosted: we can remove all tenant/customer data from active stores within 30 days. We will return an attestation indicating the request id and timestamp of completion.
- Dedicated/Private: we can support accelerated timelines (7–14 days) because we can change snapshot/retention policies on the customer pool.

Backups:
- Hosted offering: our standard backup rotation creates immutable snapshots that we keep per policy. Practically we cannot instantly edit an immutable snapshot; instead we guarantee logical deletion from the service and we schedule scrub-on-rotation. For example, if our rotation is 90 days, after the next rotation the data will no longer be present. We can also provide a signed attestation that the item was marked deleted on X date and removed from active indices.
- For customers needing a contractual 90-day scrub window, we can either: (a) move to a Dedicated pool with a modified retention schedule, or (b) agree to a documented process for hosted that provides the attestation plus a timeline tied to snapshot retention.

Logs:
- We can redact request/response text from logs on request, and we can optionally keep aggregated, non-reversible telemetry for metrics. Raw request logs are retained for debugging for 30 days by default; we can shorten that window for Dedicated/Private offerings.

Subject: Technical appendix: retention, backups, and logs (short)

Alex — adding the technical view you asked for so procurement has concrete steps. TL;DR: active removal is fast; backups and low-level storage depend on the retention window.

Operational sequence when an RTBF request is received (high level):
- Inbound: request submitted to Privacy Ops portal (or via API) -> ticket created.
- Active store deletion: service executes a deletion job that removes references from primary indices and KV stores (T+0 to T+48h depending on load).
- Cache & in-memory: KV caches and node-local stores are invalidated immediately after job completion.
- Snapshots/backups: snapshots are immutable; logical deletion flags are applied to the customer namespace immediately. Actual binary removal occurs on the next snapshot rotation/GC pass. Typical rotation window for hosted snapshots is 60–120 days depending on region — default is 90 days.
- For Dedicated/Private: we can change snapshot/backup rotation to meet contractual windows (e.g., 30/45/90 days) and run a targeted purge during a maintenance window if required.

Logging specifics:
- Request/response logs retained in plaintext for 30 days; after 30 days we either purge or aggregate (per contract).
- Audit logs (who/when) are kept for 365 days by default; those can be shortened but we keep an immutable record of the deletion action for compliance evidence.

Subject: Redwood MSA - IP indemnity carveouts and claims process

Neha —

Thanks again for walking through the MSA today. Our legal team had a couple of follow-ups specifically on the indemnity sections that we wanted to get ahead of before we move to signatures. High level: Acme needs clarity around (1) third-party IP claims procedure (notice, control of defense, settlement approvals) and (2) limits around indemnity for claims arising from derivative or bad-faith use of our data — we do not want to inadvertently assume liability for downstream misuse.

Attached is a short summary from our procurement counsel noting the changes they want to see and a proposed process doc for managing IP claims (who notifies whom, evidence we expect, and timeline for assuming defense). The core asks are:
- Customer must retain right to approve any settlement that imposes obligations on us or admits fault.
- Exceptions for claims resulting from customer modifications or misuse (bad-faith or negligent alteration) — language that excludes Redwood for those.
- A 30-day cure/notice period and a coordination clause (we do not want Redwood to unilaterally settle major IP claims).

Can you loop in your legal and confirm whether Redwood can accept these or propose point edits? We are driving to get signatures by the end of next week.

Samantha / Neha —

Thanks for the clear note and the process doc. I attached a short set of proposed redlines to the MSA (Redwood_MSA_Proposed_Redlines.pdf) and a complementary template that spells out the claims handling flow we are comfortable with (Mutual-Indemnity-draft.rtf). High-level positions below:

1) Control of defense: Redwood is willing to assume defense of third-party IP claims alleging that our delivered model/service infringes provided we have the right to select counsel and control defense, subject to Customer approval of settlements that would (i) require payment by Customer or (ii) impose material operational changes. We will accept a Customer approval right for settlements that impose obligations on Customer; we request that approval not be unreasonably withheld and propose a 15-business-day review window.

2) Bad-faith and modification carveouts: Redwood agrees that claims arising solely from Customer modification, combination with third-party content, or Customer's bad-faith use should not be the responsibility of Redwood. We propose specific examples in section 4 of the draft. Note: the key is defining the standard ("resulting solely from" vs "in part from"); we propose "primarily resulting from" to avoid giving customers a blanket escape for mixed-cause claims.

3) Notice and cure: we can accept a 30-day notice and cure period for non-IP claims; for IP claims we request prompt notice "as soon as reasonably practicable" and reserve the right to move to court if claim handling is unreasonably delayed.

4) Mitigation evidence: we ask that Customer provide contemporaneous records and copies of the demand/claim and representative examples. Our counterparty has to be able to investigate; we cannot accept vague notice.

5) Cap and indemnity allocation: our standard MSA ties indemnity to direct damages and deducts offsets for third-party recoveries. If Acme wants broader unlimited indemnity for IP, we'll need to escalate commercially.

I've highlighted precise edits in the PDF. Happy to hop on a call with Ben and Samantha Thurs 2/12 or Fri 2/13; otherwise we can exchange a short, clean set of strike-and-insert edits for DocuSign.

Rishi Malhotra
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference

From: Ben Atkinson <ben.atkinson@atkinsonlaw.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
Cc: Samantha Holt <samantha.holt@acmehealth.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom.das@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 12 Feb 2026 10:05:00 -08:00
Subject: RE: Redwood MSA - IP indemnity carveouts and claims process

Rishi / Neha —

Appreciate the thoughtful response. A few points from our side:

- The customer approval right is non-negotiable for us when a settlement would require our organization to pay monies or change its operations. Saying approvals cannot be "unreasonably withheld" is a good start but we need a binding approval step (e.g., written approval within 15 business days) — otherwise the seller could effectively force a settlement.

- On the "primarily resulting from" standard: we prefer a clearer bright-line where Redwood remains liable unless the claim "arises solely from Customer's modification, combination, or use in a manner not contemplated in the agreement." We understand Redwood's concern about mixed-cause claims; our compromise suggestion would be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the Customer if the Customer provides prima facie evidence of modification/bad faith.

- Notice timing: we will accept "as soon as reasonably practicable" but request a specified maximum (e.g., within 10 business days of receiving an initial demand), to avoid open-ended delays.

- Finally, the customer is not asking for unlimited IP indemnity across the board — primarily protection for direct claims that allege Redwood's model infringes a third party patent or copyright when used unmodified. We are open to a limited cap tied to the Order Form value but need a clear path to recover defense costs.

If Redwood can provide a clean redline that: (i) preserves Customer approval for settlements that impose payments/obligations; (ii) tightens notice timing; and (iii) clarifies the modification carveout standard — we can take that internally and aim to sign.

Ben Atkinson

Stephanie — quick technical writeup below you can paste into procurement. Happy to expand if they ask for raw traces or schema.

1) Exact SLO definitions (publishable wording):
- Availability: "Successful request rate (HTTP 2xx) >= 99.9% measured over a rolling 30-day window, aggregated in 1-minute intervals. Failed requests include 5xx and timeouts; client re-tries are de-duplicated using request IDs for measurement."
- Latency: "p95 end-to-end response latency < 300ms for standard text-generation single-turn requests, measured over a rolling 30-day window. Latency is measured at egress (time when the first token is returned to the client)."

2) Collection & aggregation:
- Server-side instrumentation at ingress/egress using deterministic counters; per-request metadata (request_id, model_variant, region) is recorded.
- Aggregation frequency: 1-minute rollups, retained for 90 days for dashboarding; 13 months for SLA attestation exports.
- Sampling: full request counts for SLO computation; traces and payloads are sampled (configurable) to minimize PII exposure — default 1% for full traces, higher under debugging.

3) Alerting policy:
- Transient breach: system creates a customer notification (email + Slack) for p95 or availability deviation lasting 1 minute; no paging.
- Sustained breach: if a breach persists beyond a configured window (default 10 minutes), on-call is paged (PagerDuty), and a bridge is opened. Customers can opt into paging for faster escalation.

4) Customer access:
- Read-only dashboard link (links use SSO; can be whitelisted per account).
- CSV exports: selectable windows (1h/1d/30d) and raw 1-minute buckets available as CSV.
- Raw traces: available under NDA & audit request; we provide redacted traces by default.

5) Audit evidence:

- Request process: customer submits request 5 business days prior with start/end times and expected impact; Redwood reviews technical feasibility.
- Approval: engineering & sales sign-off; variance is timeboxed (max 72 hours standard; extensions by exception).
- Credits: if agreed variance results in measurable breach, credit is pro-rated for the timeboxed period per the SLA addendum.

3) Full customer-controlled operator (on-prem handoff): Redwood performs initial install support, then we hand over operator credentials to customer SOC; Redwood commits to a support SLA but not continuous access. Evidence: delivery confirmation + runbook and support tickets.

I think option 2 maps to what you're describing. I'll loop in Legal to get concrete redline language for the MSA/addendum and a narrow set of commitments for the Order Form. Proposed timeline: we prepare a redline draft by EOD Thu and a short summary page for your auditors.

Subject: Re: Fwd: Clarify operator rights and audit evidence for on-prem pilot — need legal wording

Jonas — good summary. Quick legal guidance below; I've kept the options and added specific limited-language you can propose to the customer.

1) License scope language (MSA addendum bullet):
  - "During the Pilot, Redwood will retain title to the Model and grants the Customer a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable license to operate the Model within Customer-controlled infrastructure strictly for evaluation purposes. Operator capabilities are limited to those expressly enumerated in the Order Form (monitoring, health checks, incident remediation) and exclude any capability to exfiltrate training data or to run arbitrary code against customer datasets without explicit prior written consent."

2) Evidence delivery (Order Form annex):
  - "Evidence Package: For the purposes of customer audits, Redwood will deliver an Evidence Package consisting of: (i) a cryptographically signed snapshot (sha256 hash) of the runtime image and configuration; (ii) operator access logs covering the period requested; and (iii) a signed Attestation Letter confirming key rotation following snapshot delivery. Delivery will be to a Customer‑controlled secure storage endpoint (e.g., S3) or to a mutually agreed third party archive. Redwood's obligation is limited to delivery and attestation; Redwood is not responsible for Customer's archival or custodial controls post-delivery."

3) Narrowing custody/escrow exposure:
  - Avoid language that transfers custody beyond delivery and attestation. If Customer insists on third-party escrow, treat that as a separate SOW with fees and an explicit escrow agreement.

4) Operational controls and auditability:
  - Require documented, time-bound admin accounts for any handover and mandatory key rotation within 24 hours of handover. Include a support SLA for any handover window.

5) Redlines and approvals:
  - I'm attaching a tracked redline (proposed_addendum_redlines.docx) that implements the above. Laura — please sanity check the indemnity/limitation crossrefs; Aditya — can you confirm the operational feasibility of snapshot + signed hash and the key rotation timeline?

Kevin — thanks for the clear list. High-level answers inline below; I'm attaching a proposed DPA with redlines and a SOC2 excerpt for your security team to review. I copied Monica (Customer Success) and Lauren (Legal) to help with any contract language.

1) Training opt-out (no-train): Short answer: yes — we offer a contractual commitment to exclude customer content from model improvement. Technically we support this two ways: a tenant-level account setting (for enterprise accounts) and an API-level request flag (DoNotTrain: true) that prevents content from being included in training pipelines. We will include the clause in the DPA.

2) Prompt/response ownership: We do not claim ownership of customer prompts or model outputs. Our standard DPA will state that customers retain rights to their content; Redwood receives a limited license to process the content for the purpose of providing the service only (and we will exclude it from improvement if the opt-out is set).

3) Subprocessors: See attached subprocessor list (and SOC2 excerpt). We provide 30 days' notice for new subprocessors and an opt-out path for material changes. For regulated customers we also offer Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) so data never leaves customer-controlled networks.

4) Cross-border transfers: For hosted customers we use SCCs for EU transfers and participate in the Data Privacy Framework where applicable. For US-only residency (PHI-adjacent) we recommend Redwood Private (or a Dedicated instance) to ensure all processing remains in US regions; we'll reflect transfer safeguards in the DPA.

5) Evidence: SOC 2 Type II excerpt attached. Security questionnaires can be routed to security@redwood.com; we can sign an NDA to share more detailed evidence if needed.

6) Developer experience: If you select opt-out the developer flow is one of these options: tenant-level toggle (console + API) or per-request header (DoNotTrain: true). The header is honored immediately; the tenant toggle applies account-wide. Opting out does not affect latency materially and we do not charge an extra fee for the opt-out on Hosted accounts. Note: some advanced features that rely on aggregated usage signals (e.g., adaptive quantization suggestions) may not be available if you opt out of telemetry required for those features.

I'll follow up with proposed DPA redlines and the subprocessor list as attachments. Let us know if you want a short call with Lauren to walk the wording.

Hi Jane —

Thanks, really helpful list. High-level answers here and I'm attaching a concise "evidence map" that maps each SLA/SLO line item to the telemetry we can provide. Quick summary: 

- Uptime definition: For hosted API we measure "service availability" based on the control-plane and dataplane success rate on the public REST endpoints used by customers (/v1/generate, /v1/chat, /v1/embed). We report a weighted availability metric per region based on successful 2xx responses over total production requests (excluding client-side 4xx). Health-checks are used for internal routing, but they are not the primary contractual signal.

- Latency measurement: We compute p50/p95/p99 on server-side response time from request-accept to final token emission (server processing + model time). Percentiles are computed on a rolling 24h window by default and on contract windows (monthly calendar) for SLA evaluation. We also provide a 1-minute and 5-minute rolling series for on-call debugging.

- Evidence set for crediting: For each incident we can provide: timeline (UTC), raw request ids (up to 1000 sample ids), per-request traces (latency buckets), backend kernel and model version, autoscale/queue metrics, and synthetic probe logs for the same time window. We will redact customer payloads unless a CDA is in place.

- Synthetic vs real traffic: Our standard approach is to correlate synthetic probe signals with sampled production traffic. For credit calculation we weight production traffic at 80% and synthetic probes at 20% by default; we can negotiate different weights or a rule that triggers 100% production-only evaluation if production sampling density crosses a threshold (e.g., >5 requests/sec aggregated over the region during the incident).

Attached: redwood_sla_evidence_map.pdf (mapping + example incident package) and a short SOC2 attestation summary. Turnaround for evidence: we commit to acknowledging requests within 1 business day and delivering a packaged evidence set within 5 business days for standard incidents. For complex multi-region incidents we propose a 10-business-day window (we'll flag those in our initial ack).

I'll loop in our internal SRE and legal reviewers to make sure we can provide the exact artifacts you need without exposing sensitive customer data. Do you have any preferred formats for the evidence bundle (e.g., CSV request list, zipped JSON traces, or a shared Drive folder)?

Subject: Re: Questions on Dedicated commit definitions and remedy ladder

Kyle — thanks for the precise asks. I've attached a short SKU mapping and a worked example (redwood_capacity_mapping.xlsx) — sending high-level answers below and happy to jump on a 30m call if you prefer.

High-level proposed definitions (working draft):
- Capacity Unit (CU): 1 CU = 1 vram-hour on an A100-80GB equivalent instance. For contract language we can also define as "1 CU = 1 GPU-PU (A100-80GB performance profile)" to avoid ambiguity across hardware families.
- Commitment accounting: Monthly commitment is expressed in CU-hours (e.g., 4 A100 equivalents reserved continuously for a 30-day month = 4 CUs * 24 * 30 = 2880 CU-hours/month).
- Throughput guarantee: Measured as two dimensions — (A) Sustained capacity: CU-hours available per monthly billing period; (B) Latency SLO: p50/p95 inference latency measured against a defined synthetic workload (seq len 256 chat mix) routed to the dedicated pool.
- Burst policy: Customers retain short-term burst allowance (up to 2x committed CU for up to 3 hours/day) as billable overage at the committed discount rate; we can offer an optional burst buffer (pre-purchased pool of CU-hours) to smooth billing.
- Service credits (draft ladder): See spreadsheet, summary below. Credits are applied prorata to monthly commit value and capped at a negotiated percentage.

I'll follow up with internal notes to align on credit ladders and discount table then send a redline-friendly clause set.

Best,

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.ai>

Subject: Fwd: Questions on Dedicated commit definitions and remedy ladder — internal proposed redlines

Internal notes / proposed redline items (please comment):

--- Forwarded message ---
From: Kyle Peters <kyle@neurovista.io>
Subject: Questions on Dedicated commit definitions and remedy ladder

1) Capacity Unit (CU): propose we define CU as "1 vram-hour of A100-80GB performance". This avoids vendor-specific model names but ties to perf profile. +1 to include exact micro-bench numbers in appendix.
2) Throughput: measure committed CU as capacity pool; SLA attaches to p50 latency on a defined synthetic profile. If p50 exceeds target for >X% of measured minutes, triggers credit.
3) Ladder: customer prefers a cap. Proposed ladder we should offer: 
   - Monthly uptime >= 99.9% --> 0% credit
   - 99.0% <= uptime < 99.9% --> 5% of monthly commit value
   - 95.0% <= uptime < 99.0% --> 15% credit
   - uptime < 95.0% --> 30% credit cap — propose we cap aggregate credits at 50% of monthly commit (internal concession to customer request).
4) Burst: allow 2x burst for up to 3 hours/day; bill as overage at committed unit price or allow pre-purchased burst pool at 60% of on-demand.

Open items for legal: explicit measurement window (we use rolling 5-minute measurement aggregated to daily), definition of "downtime" vs "degraded performance", and auditability (customers will ask for metric export and root cause write-ups).

Please weigh in on the following before I send to Kyle: 1) cap at 50% vs 100%; 2) 3-hour burst window vs 1-hour; 3) pre-purchase burst pool discounting (60% vs 75%).

--Marcus

Monica — recommend we push for 50% cap and 3-hour burst (improves our flexibility). Aditya — if pricing wants 60% for pre-purchase burst pool we might need to mark special pricing for >12mo commit. Lauren — confirm marketing/packaging language for "CU" and sample math is consistent with docs.

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.ai>
To: Kyle Peters <kyle@neurovista.io>
Cc: NeuroVista Procurement <procurement@neurovista.io>, Contracts Team <contracts@neurovista.io>
Date: 2027-05-20T14:22:00-07:00
Subject: Proposed definitions and example math for NeuroVista commit

Kyle — thanks for the patience. Below is a concise, redline-friendly set of definitions and an example calculation based on your stated profile (4 A100-equivalent appliances reserved; 2x burst allowance). If this matches your intent we can turn it into contract clauses and circulate for signature.

Proposed definitions (final candidate wording):
- "Capacity Unit (CU)": a unit of reserved capacity equal to one vram-hour on a performance profile equivalent to NVIDIA A100-80GB. For clarity: one CU corresponds to the compute capacity required to serve the defined synthetic workload at p50 latency target on an A100-80GB equivalent device for one hour.
- "CU-hour": one Capacity Unit consumed for one hour. Monthly commitments are measured in CU-hours.
- "Committed CU-hours": the CU-hours the customer has prepaid/reserved for the monthly billing period.
- "Burst Allowance": a short duration allowance permitting the customer to exceed the Committed CU-hours rate by up to 2x for up to 3 hours per calendar day; overage beyond the Burst Allowance will be billed as described in the pricing schedule.
- "Throughput & Latency SLO": Redwood will measure p50 and p95 latency for a defined synthetic workload (seq len 256 chat mix). The p50 latency SLO applies to 95% of the measured samples in the monthly aggregation window.

Service credit ladder (measurement & remedy):
- Measurement window: rolling 5-minute intervals aggregated across the monthly period; incidents are reported with timestamped metrics and RCA within 5 business days.
- Ladder (applies to monthly invoice amount for the committed CU-hours portion):
   * Monthly availability >= 99.9%: 0% credit
   * 99.0% <= availability < 99.9%: 5% credit
   * 95.0% <= availability < 99.0%: 15% credit
   * availability < 95.0%: 30% credit
- Credit cap: aggregate credits for a single monthly billing period are capped at 50% of the monthly committed CU-hours value (negotiable).

Example commit math (worked example):
- Customer target: reserve 4 A100-equivalent devices continuously.
- Monthly CU-hour calculation: 4 CUs * 24 hours * 30 days = 2880 CU-hours/month.
- If NeuroVista uses additional burst beyond the Burst Allowance, overage billed at committed unit price (no surcharge) unless pre-purchased burst pool is used.
- If availability for the month measured at 98.4%: credit = 15% of monthly committed CU-hours value (per ladder). If the credit calculation would exceed 50% cap we apply the cap.

Attachments: redwood_capacity_mapping.xlsx contains mapping of common GPU classes to CU equivalents and sample pricing rows for 12/24/36 month commits.

Next steps: 1) confirm the 50% credit cap is acceptable; 2) confirm burst window (we suggested 3 hours/day); 3) we can produce contract-ready language for section: "Definitions — Capacity & Remedies" and attach as an amendment to your draft.

If convenient, I can book a 30m call today to walk through the example with procurement and contracts.

title: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets
content:
Session-cache sizing & target unit economics for Integron pilot

From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Clark <sara.clark@integronhealth.com>, Tom Ellis <t.ellis@integronhealth.com>
Cc: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 21 May 2027 17:05:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets

Hi Sara / Tom — thanks for taking time today. Quick recap from our discovery and proposed next steps so we can get a realistic costing model together: 

Key inputs we captured on the call:
- Expected pilot scope: ~12k unique end-user sessions/day, roughly 2.5M tokens/session on peak flows (some sessions are short, median ~120 tokens).
- Session pattern: ~70% of sessions start with a 1–2 message prompt series that is highly repetitive across users (templates + guidance text).
- SLA needs: p95 latency target ~450ms for interactive flows; availability: standard hosted SLA.

Caching assumptions to validate (what we used for the first-pass economics):
- Session-prefix caching (warm prefixes / reusable instruction text) coverage: we modeled a 35% prefix cache hit rate across tokens — this assumes we can capture the common opening blocks and sticky templates.
- Cold tokens (misses) still incur full inference cost; hit tokens are served from cached KV/prefetch and reduce effective per-token GPU work by ~75% in our model.

First-pass unit economics (ballpark, to align expectations):
- Nominal list price used: $120 / 1M tokens (model variant X quantized path).
- With 35% cache hit & batching/quantization recommendations applied, effective cost range we modeled: $48–$70 / 1M effective tokens (depends on sequence length distribution and batching).

Asks / next steps: 
1) Can you share a 24–72 hour sample of anonymized session telemetry (timestamps, session id, prompt token counts, whether templates were used)? I attached a tiny CSV template to make this easier. [Attachment: session_telemetry_template.csv]
2) If the pilot budget has a target effective price, please flag it — you mentioned a rough target in the call; I want to make sure our modeling converges on your acceptable band.
3) We'll run three hit-rate scenarios (25% / 40% / 60%) and return a spreadsheet showing per-1M token effective costs plus sensitivity to batching and quantization.

I'll also include a short mutual action plan draft for timelines and approvals. 

Best,
Aditya Rao
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference
aditya@redwood.ai | +1 415-555-0182

[Attachment: Integron_MA_plan_draft.pdf]

From: Sara Clark <sara.clark@integronhealth.com>
To: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>, Tom Ellis <t.ellis@integronhealth.com>
Cc: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 21 May 2027 19:43:12 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets

Thanks Aditya — helpful recap. A couple quick clarifications from our side before we send telemetry: 

1) Pilot scale: the initial pilot will be constrained to 3k sessions/day (out of the 12k eventual target) for a 4-week run. Can you show numbers pro-rated for 3k/day as well?
2) Cache hit expectations: our internal engineering lead flagged that the shared templates only cover roughly 20–30% of tokens today (they're working to formalize templates but aren't there yet). Can you run the 25% / 40% / 60% scenarios you mentioned — 25% is the conservative baseline we expect if we don't change prompt design.
3) Budget context: for the pilot, procurement has allocated $18k–$40k for production inference costs over the month (not including Redwood platform/enterprise fees). Converted to effective token terms, our target for the pilot is closer to $45 / 1M effective tokens. If your model shows we're above that at realistic hit rates, we may need to look at a constrained feature set or different model sizing.

I'll attach a small export tonight and aim to send by EOD tomorrow. Also please include the assumptions around quantization and batching in the spreadsheet so our infra team can vet operational feasibility.

Thanks — Sara
Sara Clark
Head of Product | Integron Health
sara.clark@integronhealth.com | +1 415-555-0707

From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 22 May 2027 09:10:00 -0700
Subject: Fwd: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets (internal)

Team — quick internal ask before I send the costing sheet back to Integron: 

Summary: client is likely to start pilot at 3k sessions/day; they expect conservative cache hit ~25% and target $45 / 1M effective tokens for pilot. Need our recommended configuration to hit ~ $45 / 1M at 25% and at 40% hit. Please focus on: 
- Model variant (float16 vs int8/4): which quantization path gets us nearest to target while keeping p95 latency under 500ms.
- Batching policy: recommended batch sizes / policy for interactive (we typically use continuous batching with max latency cap 50ms).
- Storage/eviction for session-prefix cache: how many KB per simultaneous session do we need to assume, and ops cost.

I'll attach the client CSV template to the HubSpot record and ask for the telemetry tonight. Can you turn around a quick XLS with the three scenarios (25/40/60%) and a short note on risk (quality regressions, latency tradeoffs)?

Thanks — appreciate a fast run on this.
Aditya

From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Clark <sara.clark@integronhealth.com>, Tom Ellis <t.ellis@integronhealth.com>
Cc: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 22 May 2027 15:33:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets

Hi Sara / Tom — thanks for the quick reply and the budget transparency. Attached is the costing workbook with the three hit-rate scenarios you requested plus notes on the runtime configuration that underpins each row. Highlights below: 

What we modeled (attached: costing_scenarios_25-40-60_hit.xlsx):
- Conservative baseline (25% hit): effective cost ~ $62 / 1M tokens (assumes int8 quantization, conservative batching due to interactive tail, and 75% reduction in token work on cache hits).
- Mid scenario (40% hit): effective cost ~ $48 / 1M tokens (same runtime, better prefix coverage).
- Aggressive optimization (60% hit + aggressive batching / int4 path): effective cost ~ $35 / 1M tokens but this requires prompt standardization and an A/B run to monitor quality drift.

Recommendations / next steps:
1) Pilot configuration: run the pilot on the int8 path with prefix cache enabled and a 48-hour telemetry feed. That gets us close to your $45 / 1M target if we can push hit toward 40% during the pilot.
2) Short workstream: we propose a 1-week prompt-standardization sprint (we'll provide specs) to increase prefix coverage — aim to move from 25% → 40% hit inside pilot window.
3) Deliverables from us: costing workbook + small mutual action plan (attached). From you: 72-hour telemetry export and a named infra reviewer.

I've attached the MA plan and the costing workbook. Let me know if you want a short follow-up call Monday to walk the spreadsheet with Stephanie (she can answer the runtime tradeoffs).

Best,
Aditya Rao
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference
aditya@redwood.ai | +1 415-555-0182

Attachments: costing_scenarios_25-40-60_hit.xlsx, Integron_MA_plan_draft.pdf, session_telemetry_template.csv

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment: 

Call highlights
- FinTechCo is evaluating Redwood for customer-facing transaction analytics (sensitive PII redaction in-pipeline).
- Primary procurement path today is AP/PO for vendor SaaS, but the team is interested in whether AWS Marketplace would speed approval for a pilot.
- Commercial ask: sample invoice and clarity on PO-via-marketplace vs direct invoicing, and any startup/PO discounts.

Proposed next steps

Thanks for the context — good questions. Short answers and recommended next steps below.

Short answers:
- PulseMetrics: conditionally acceptable. Require signed subprocessor addendum, SOC 2 Type II report, and a commitment they will not persist raw prompts or unredacted PII.
- Retention: propose we aim for a product compromise: 30 days raw traces for product debugging (encrypted at rest) with a legal-approved 90-day incident retention option that requires escalation and justification. Aggregated metrics at 2 years is fine if they’re non-identifiable.
- Residency/Marketplace: require contractual clause that request/response logs for EU customers are processed and stored in EU regions only. For marketplace onboarding, enforce region pinning or use a regional pod for EU customers. No automatic egress to us-east for EU-marked tenants.
- Encryption/KMS: require TLS in transit and KMS-managed encryption at rest. HSM/KMS recommended for telemetry vendors storing any user-identifiable logs; if vendor refuses, we gate them.

3) Confirmation on fields being sent (we should get a sample event schema and a promise to mask/strip PII fields).

- Data plane constraint: payloads include structured payment metadata (~1–2KB) and must not be retained by vendor.

As discussed, we'd like a focused Dedicated capacity validation that compares H100 vs A100 equivalent configs and gives a recommended reserved throughput, plus a cost estimate for a three-month pilot. Forwarding Northridge's asks — their procurement is pushing hard on data-residency-in-VPC and a right to audit (onsite/remote once per year). They also want a clause preventing any PII telemetry without consent. Attached are their scope and our current SOW.

Why I'm escalating: their audit request as written gives them broad access (runtime, logs, personnel interviews) and no constraints on frequency or third-party auditors. Legal is concerned. They are also asking for absolute residency inside their VPC which we can do technically, but it changes our support/incident processes and may require a private deployment SKU.

Proposed trade: we can accept a scoped audit (defined windows, narrow log subsets, 2-week notice for onsite, Redwood personnel present) + a 10% concession on list pricing for a 12-month committed term. Need leadership signoff on the audit carveout and discount cap.

Please reply with firm approvals or suggested alternate guardrails — we need to respond to Northridge by Friday EOD.

From: laura_bennett@redwood.ai

Cc: neha_kapoor@redwood.ai, rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 27 Nov 2025 08:22:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Fwd: RE: Statement of Work + deployment model questions

Alex — thanks for the flag and the docs. I reviewed their redlines. Summary of legal concerns:

- "Audit rights" as written are too broad: they request access to runtime internals, arbitrary personnel interviews, and unlimited third-party auditors.
- "No egress" language for backups & logs inside their account is acceptable technically but we need a clause that still allows Redwood to run monitoring agents for safety & support, and a carveout for incident response that can cross-account with explicit notice.
- Telemetry/PII: we should add explicit opt-in language and a technical appendix describing what telemetry is collected by default and how to disable it.

My recommended compromise (to present to Northridge):
1) Audit: one remote audit per 12 months + optional onsite once in the first contract year with 30 days' notice; audits are scope-limited to configuration, access controls, and archival procedures — no arbitrary runtime interrogation. Third-party auditors allowed only if pre-approved by Redwood and limited to approved scope.

Business ask: if we accept those concessions, recommend approving a one-time 12% commercial concession (discount) and require a minimum 12-month commitment + accelerated support add-on. If leadership won't permit 12%, we can cap at 10% and add a customer-funded SOC2 readiness assessment as a compromise.

I'm seeking leadership approval on the audit carveouts and the discount cap.

Urgent: SummitWorks renewal strategy & capacity uplift

From: Alyssa Turner <alyssa.turner@summitworks.com>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
Cc: Evan Li <evan.li@summitworks.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:22:00 -0800
Subject: Renewal, capacity needs, and a new vendor at the table

Monica,

Thanks for the check-in earlier this week. We are approaching our platform renewal (contract end 2026-12-31) and I wanted to flag two things on our side:

1) Usage growth: Q4 forecasts now show a potential 60% increase in peak concurrent tokens due to a planned personalization rollout. We need guidance on whether our current Dedicated pool can scale to meet that without re-architecting.

2) Competitive pressure: Our infra team ran a short benchmark with Altai AI; they surfaced a managed offer that promises similar latency at ~20% lower unit cost if we commit 12 months. They also propose a migration assistance package.

We value the stability Redwood has provided, but the procurement team is asking for a concrete upsell/price-capacity proposal and a short remediation plan if performance gaps appear. Can you put together an operational playbook and a delta-cost model this week? Evan is looping procurement on next steps.

—Alyssa
Director, Platform Engineering
SummitWorks Inc

Attachments: none

From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
To: Alyssa Turner <alyssa.turner@summitworks.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:08:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Renewal, capacity needs, and a new vendor at the table

Alyssa — thank you for the heads up and for sharing the context. High level response below; we'll follow with a short playbook doc and cost scenarios by Thursday EOD.

- Capacity: you can scale your Dedicated pool to handle +60% peak with a targeted uplift and autoscale policy; no app rewrite needed in most cases. We will propose a pre-warm/burst configuration to avoid cold-start latency for peak windows.
- Benchmark comparatives: we will run a 48h side-by-side with your representative workload (same prompts, sequence lengths, and concurrency) — Redwood will cover the testing fees.
- Commercial: we can present a capacity + term bundle with a scoped discount if you commit to a 12-month uplift and a 30% reserved commit.

Dev and Laura — can you own a short ops playbook (runbook for pre-warm, caching settings, and rollback policy) and a cost model that compares: current committed spend, 12-month uplift w/ reserved commit, and Altai-style managed alternative? Alyssa — want to schedule a 30-min call after we run the tests; what times work for you Thursday?

Thanks,
Monica
Enterprise AE, Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>

Date: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 10:12:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Renewal, capacity needs, and a new vendor at the table

Folks — taking the lead on the technical side. Initial plan:

1) Test harness: Laura and I will deploy a synthetic load mirroring SummitWorks' anonymized prompt set. We'll collect p50/p95/p99 latencies, token cost, and KV-cache hit rates.
2) Pre-warm approach: propose a short-lived warmed pool timed to expected peaks with predictive scaling based on their telemetry (we'll outline required metrics and a webhook).
3) Fallbacks: recommend a read-only fallback variant (size-reduced model) for non-critical requests to preserve SLAs during overload.
4) Timeline: 48h benchmark starting Thu 18:00 PST; deliverables: benchmark PDF and cost_model_scenarios.xlsx by Sat 12:00 PST.

Laura — please include a short ops-runbook (1-2 pages) that the SummitWorks SREs can follow.

Date: Thu, 13 Nov 2026 07:45:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Renewal, capacity needs, and a new vendor at the table

Thanks — Thursday works. We can provide a 24h anonymized production trace for the benchmark. Two asks for the bakeoff:

- Can Redwood demonstrate the pre-warm plan without impacting our live traffic? We need to know rollback steps explicitly.
- Procurement is sensitive to termination clauses and migration assistance in case we decide to switch. Please include a migration-runbook or at least an exportable KV snapshot procedure.

Also, Ben from Altai reached out to outline their offer; I'm attaching their proposal so you can see their scope and pricing. Procurement will be on the call.

Alyssa

Attachment: altai_competitor_proposal.pdf

From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
To: Alyssa Turner <alyssa.turner@summitworks.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 15 Nov 2026 12:03:00 -0800
Subject: SummitWorks benchmark & recommended operational playbook (draft)

Alyssa — attaching the draft benchmark report and the ops playbook highlights below. Full PDFs delivered via Drive link. Quick summary:

- Benchmark results (48h synthetic): Redwood default model configs matched Altai p50 latency within 5% and outperformed p95 by ~8% on the same GPU family. Token-unit cost under our default burst settings was ~12% lower than Altai's listed managed rate in their proposal.

- Key operational recommendations:
  * Pre-warm pool sized to +75% of your current peak with a 15-minute warm window before business-critical events.
  * KV/Prefix caching: enable prefix cache for common personalization prompts — expected 22% reduction in token throughput during peak.
  * Autoscale: predictive autoscaler with a 1.5x headroom setting and an emergency burst lane on Dedicated.
  * Rollback: immediate traffic split back to steady-state (pre-warm off) + auto-fail to a smaller quantized model if p95 > SLO for >120s.

- Migration/export: we provide a validated KV snapshot procedure and an export of model artifacts consistent with industry standard checkpoints; full doc attached.

Commercial notes (Rishi copied): to achieve price parity with Altai's 12-month managed offer, we can structure a 12-month uplift with a 25% reserved commit and a performance credit schedule for missed p95 targets. The credit schedule is contingent on observed traffic shape.

Deliverables: summit_benchmark_report.pdf, cost_model_scenarios.xlsx, ops_runbook.pdf (links below).

Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1SummitWorksRenewal
HubSpot: https://app.hubspot.com/deals/1234567/DEAL-SW-2026-11
DocuSign: https://www.docusign.com/contract/ABC-123-SW-Renewal

Laura Bennett
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments: summit_benchmark_report.pdf, cost_model_scenarios.xlsx, ops_runbook.pdf

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Alyssa Turner <alyssa.turner@summitworks.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@summitworks.com, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 01 Dec 2026 16:05:00 -0800
Subject: Final proposal: renewal term + capacity uplift (next steps)

Alyssa / Evan / procurement team — thanks for the collaborative test. Based on the benchmark and ops runbook, here is Redwood's final commercial proposal and recommended next steps:

1) Offer: 12-month term with a 25% reserved-capacity commit on your Dedicated pool, plus a 60% temporary uplift during Q1 launch windows.
2) Pricing: blended unit rate that yields ~15% cost advantage vs Altai's published managed rate when the 25% commit is accepted. Detailed numbers are in cost_model_scenarios.xlsx.
3) SLA & credits: formal p95 latency SLO with stepwise credits for missed targets (details in DocuSign).
4) Migration protection: export/runbook included and one week of white-glove migration assistance if you elect to terminate within the first 90 days — ensures data portability.

Next steps:
- Procurement: confirm final legal terms and accept or send redlines within 5 business days.
- Technical: Laura/Dev to schedule an on-call run for pre-warm activation during your launch window.
- Commercial: Monica to prepare an executive summary and a short one-pager for your CFO.

We believe this structure balances performance, cost, and operational safety. Let us know if you want a 1:1 with Rishi and Monica to walk the finance team through the numbers.

—Rishi
Head of Strategic Accounts, Redwood Inference

title: Packetized Response Envelopes & Tool Bridge — PRD
content:
Packetized Response Envelopes & Tool Bridge — PRD

Purpose: This document proposes a packetized envelope model for hosted streaming responses and a companion lightweight tool-bridge handshake to support robust tool calling and structured output. The goal is to make streaming predictable for client SDKs and enable safe, resumable tool integrations with strong observability and graceful degradation.

Context and problem statement:
- Current incremental streaming in Hosted API is optimized for free-form token streaming, but lacks first-class primitives for client-visible checkpoints, structured events (tool call / tool result), and resumption semantics.
- SDK authors and integrators repeatedly implement ad-hoc delimiters and heuristics. This causes fragile client implementations, inconsistent telemetry, and poor error recovery for real-world mobile/edge networks.
- Tool calling requires synchronous-looking semantics (request->invoke->result) but must tolerate asynchronous execution, retries, out-of-band results, and security boundaries.

Design principles:
1) Small, composable primitives — an envelope layer on top of the token stream with a minimal set of event types.
