- “What evidence supports this selection? (dashboard link required for Sev0/Sev1)”
- “Is this impacting Dedicated/Private customers? If yes, do NOT name customers; use ‘Dedicated control plane’ component if applicable + coordinate with Support.”
- “Confirm next update time (default 30m for ongoing Sev1+, 60m for Sev2).”

Concerns
- Drafts can sound too confident. Add explicit uncertainty language for low confidence (“We are investigating reports of…”, “Some requests may…”).
- Avoid internal jargon: scheduler, KV cache, shard, etc.

Idea bucket C — Signal-driven suggestions (NOT full automation)
Suggestion mode (recommended)
- Bot posts in #incidents thread:
  - “Suggested impacted component(s): Streaming / US-East (confidence: medium) based on disconnect rate > threshold and p95 time-to-first-token > threshold.”
  - Provide a one-click button to apply on Statuspage (with human approval).

Full automation mode (maybe later, scary)
- Automatically set component to “Degraded Performance” if:
  - error burn rate breaches AND persists beyond anti-flap window
  - AND at least two independent signals agree (e.g., gateway errors + client disconnects)
  - AND a human has opened an incident or acknowledged alert

Anti-flap / false positive controls (must-have)
- Hysteresis: degrade threshold is stricter than recover threshold.
- Minimum duration: require 10–15m sustained breach before marking public degrade.
- Multi-window check: 5m + 30m windows to catch both spikes and sustained issues.
- “Manual override wins” with a cooling-off period (don’t immediately re-mark degraded if human just set operational).

Edge cases to explicitly handle
- Latency-only incidents: when do we publish? (Customers do care; but we need consistent criteria.)
  - Proposal: publish if p95 latency exceeds X for Y minutes AND error budget burn indicates meaningful impact.
- Partial routing impact: only a subset of models/routes failing.
  - Public component is coarse; message should mention “some requests” or “subset of routes” (avoid listing specific customer routes if sensitive).
- Capacity constraints / throttling: can look like errors.
  - Risk of revealing supply/capacity issues. Phrase as “elevated errors/timeouts” and avoid “out of capacity” language.

Idea bucket D — Approval workflow (lightweight)
- For Sev0/Sv1:
  - Add optional approval step before publishing update:
    - approver: IC or designated Comms Lead; Support lead approval if customer comms risk (Dedicated/Private visibility)
  - Timebox approvals (e.g., auto-expire in 5 min, falls back to IC) to avoid blocking urgent updates.
- For Sev2+:
  - Comms Lead can publish without additional approval.

Operational details
- Audit log should capture:
  - who approved
  - what changed (component, status, text diff)
  - when
  - associated incident id
- Statuspage API client needs retries/backoff + idempotency keys to prevent dupes.

Idea bucket E — Auto-generate post-incident summary (publishable)
- Generate a draft summary immediately at resolve time using:
  - incident timeline events (state changes, mitigation actions)
  - impact window (start/end)
  - affected components/regions
  - symptom metrics (peak error %, peak p95 latency)
  - root cause classification (dropdown taxonomy; free text optional)
- Then require human edit + quick legal/security pass only if it touches Dedicated/Private or anything potentially sensitive.

Confidentiality filters (draft tool should warn)
- Red flags in text: customer names, specific tenant ids, specific cluster names, exact capacity numbers (“we had N GPUs”), vendor incident details under NDA.
- Replace with safe phrasing suggestions.

Idea bucket F — Accuracy audits + feedback loop
- Weekly job compares:
  - incident tags (component/region) vs statuspage component updates
  - whether updates were timely (TTFU) and whether we over-scoped
- Output:
  - mismatch report by component
  - top 5 “misclassification patterns” (e.g., embeddings errors tagged as API)
  - recommended instrumentation changes

Failure modes / “how this goes wrong” list
1) False positive degrade => customer panic / trust hit.
2) Flapping statuses => looks chaotic, creates support load.
3) Under-scoping => customers experiencing impact but status shows green.
4) Over-scoping => implies global impact when only one region/capability.
5) Sensitive disclosure => “capacity exhausted” / mentions of specific customers.
6) Slowed comms due to too many required fields.

Mitigations
- Suggestion mode first (no automated publishing).
- Mandatory dashboard link for high severity.
- Anti-flap + confidence score displayed internally.
- Templates that are safe even when wrong (use cautious language).

Quick checklist for what to build first (MVP)
- [ ] Incident intake: add structured component/region/capability fields + validation
- [ ] Draft generator for Investigating + Identified (most time-critical)
- [ ] One-click “apply component selection to statuspage incident draft”
- [ ] Statuspage API client wrapper + audit log
- [ ] Add links to correct dashboards/runbooks per component

Open questions (bring to Rafael/Christine)
- What is the exact component registry source-of-truth? (repo vs Confluence; review process)
- Dedicated/Private: do we ever show regional components publicly, or only generic “Dedicated control plane signals”?
- Who is final approver for Sev0 wording if Legal/Security is asleep? (fallback rule)
- How do we avoid bot drafts becoming the de facto official comms without proper review?

Notes to self
- Watch out for “automation creep”: every optional feature adds new failure modes. Keep the initial flow dead simple.
- Biggest value is not fancy ML; it’s getting the right structured fields + safe templates + links that reduce writing time.

title: Traffic orchestration fallbacks and runbook notes
content:
Traffic orchestration fallbacks and runbook notes

Purpose and scope:

This working note documents pragmatic fallback patterns and embedded operational runbooks for the control plane and routing layer in multi-region deployments. It’s intended for platform engineers, on-call SREs, and anyone troubleshooting routing/control-plane incidents. The focus is on actionable steps (detect, mitigate, verify, escalate) and safe defaults for cross-region traffic orchestration.

Context and goals:
- Problem space: partial region outages, control-plane API instability, traffic routing loops, model-variant regressions, and noisy-neighbor saturation that impact inference availability or latency.
- Goal: Provide low-friction, repeatable mitigation steps that minimize blast radius and provide clear verification criteria.
- Non-goal: This is not a full postmortem or root-cause analysis; those live in Confluence and Jira (linked artifacts).

Quick architecture recap (operational lens):
- Control plane: central API for route rules, traffic weights, rollout orchestration, and policy evaluation. It writes desired state to per-region agents and metrics collectors.
- Data plane (regional): inference pods, autoscaling groups, local cache (KV/prefix), and request proxies.
- Routing policies: latency-priority, cost-priority, affinity-by-customer, capacity-tiered (Dedicated vs Hosted fallback), and canary/gradual rollouts.
- Safeguards: circuit-breakers, per-route rate limits, automatic fallback to compatible model variants, and region-fallback (policy precedence).

Key operational primitives we rely on:
- Traffic weights: distribution percentages per route variant/region.
- Fallback rules: ordered list where the control plane will try next compatible variant/region on failure.
- Circuit breaker thresholds: consecutive errors, p95 latency, and token loss rate.
- Health probes: control-plane agent health, model-liveness, and KV cache readiness.

Observability checklist (dashboards & metrics to inspect first):
- Per-route: request_rate, error_rate (5xx, model-validation-failures), p50/p95/p99 latency, token_rate.
- Control plane: api_latency_ms, reconciliation_lag_seconds, config_errors, last_successful_sync.
- Region health: region_cpu_utilization, gpu_utilization, queue_backlog, cache_hit_ratio.
- Autoscaling: active_replicas, scaling_events, pod_restart_count.
- Traces: recent traces for failed requests (look for long retries, timeout cascades).

Runbook pattern: severity, trigger, immediate mitigation, durable mitigation, verify, post-incident notes.

Runbook A: Control-plane API degraded / write failures
- Typical triggers:
  - alert: control_plane_api_error_rate > 1% for 2m OR reconciliation_lag_seconds > 45s
  - users report inability to roll out canaries or changes not propagating to regions
- Severity: P1 if reconciliation_lag > 5m and traffic policies are changing frequently; else P2.
- Immediate mitigation (first 5 minutes):
  1) Announce incident in #platform-oncall and tag on-call.
  2) Switch to read-only mode for non-essential control-plane writes (disable automated CI/PR-driven updates).
  3) If the API frontend is overloaded, scale API frontend pods (k8s autoscale override) or enable an emergency replica pool behind the load balancer. Command examples: kubectl scale deployment controlplane-api --replicas=6 -n platform || trigger autoscaler override.
  4) Check persistent store (etcd/postgres) health: pg_isready / etcdctl endpoint health. If datastore is the issue, fail open to cached desired state (agents keep last good config).
- Durable mitigation (10–60 minutes):
  1) Roll back the last control-plane release if the problem started after a deploy: github PR check and revert.
  2) If queues back up, temporarily increase reconciliation interval on agents to reduce write pressure. Example: set agent.reconcile_interval=30s -> 120s via emergency flag.
  3) Throttle non-critical automated flows (CI/CD, infra jobs) by applying a feature-flag to pause them.
- Verification:
  - reconciliation_lag_seconds returns to baseline; last_successful_sync updated for all regions.
  - manual config change applied and observed in target region within expected propagation window.
- Post-incident:
  - Run retrospective to determine whether circuit breaker thresholds need tuning and whether read-only mode should be automated earlier.

Runbook B: Regional GPU saturation / noisy neighbor causing high latencies
- Typical triggers:
  - High gpu_utilization > 90% + p95 latency spike for region X
  - Autoscaler failing to add capacity or pods stuck pending for > 2m
- Severity: P1 for customer-impacting sustained errors; P2 if transient.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Shift non-affinity traffic off the impacted region by adjusting traffic weights on the route to 0% for region X and add capacity in another region. Quick control-plane API call example: PATCH /routes/{route_id}/weights {"region_x":0,"region_y":100}.
  2) If weight changes are blocked by control-plane issues, apply local proxy-level traffic deny or return 503 to force clients to retry elsewhere.
  3) If a single tenant is responsible (identified by high token-rate on tenant_id), apply per-tenant rate limit to throttle.
- Durable mitigation:
  1) Spin up dedicated reserved capacity if noisy-neighbor is recurring (escalate to sales for Dedicated offering).
  2) Investigate autoscaler logs and pod events; fix scheduling constraints (taints/tolerations) or increase GPU quota in cloud account.
- Verification:
  - p95 latency in region X drops to baseline and queue_backlog reduces.
  - No increase in error_rate after reroute.

Runbook C: Model variant regression (new model variant returns higher error or hallucination rate)
- Typical triggers:
  - Regression alert from quality monitor or customer-reported regressions; sudden spike in model-validation-failures metric.
- Severity: P1 if production traffic is impacted or quality SLAs violated.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Stop the rollout: set variant weight -> 0% (control-plane traffic-weight update).
  2) Automatically fail back to previously known-good variant (we keep the last stable pinned).
  3) Pin inference calls for affected tenant(s) to hosted stable variant via per-tenant override.
- Durable mitigation:
  1) Run targeted evals and compare prompts that triggered regressions. Add failing prompt set to regression suite.
  2) Restrict future rollouts by increasing canary duration and reducing initial weight.
- Verification:
  - quality_monitoring.alerts clear, customer-reports stop, compare score delta to acceptance threshold.

Runbook D: Routing policy misconfiguration (rules cause unintended amplification or loops)
- Typical triggers:
  - sudden increase in internal retries, duplicated requests, or unexpected traffic spikes between regions
  - config linter produced warnings, or config change recently merged
- Severity: P1 if causes broader outage or cost surge.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Revert offending control-plane config change. Use: controlplane rollback-config --to=commit_id.
  2) If rollback is not possible, apply emergency guard rule at ingress proxies: drop requests matching offending headers or route-patterns.
  3) Reduce retry counts and increase retry jitter globally until stable.
- Durable mitigation:
  1) Add stronger schema validation to control-plane API and a pre-deploy simulator that checks for loops and amplification patterns.
  2) Establish automated cost-guard alerting (budget burn %).
- Verification:
  - duplication/loop metrics return to baseline; cost-rate normalizes.

Runbook E: Multi-region failover test gone wrong (canary rollout created cross-region chase)
- Scenario: a gradual canary unintentionally routes small percentage to region with cold caches causing high tail latency and then control-plane retries chase that region.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Pause or pause-and-rewind the rollout: set canary weight -> 0%.
  2) Warm caches in target region via synthetic traffic at low priority (cache-warm job) before resuming.
  3) If synthetic warmup is not possible, redirect traffic to warm region until cache hit ratio > threshold.
- Verification:
  - cache_hit_ratio increases; p99 latency decreases.

Operational knobs and safe values (starting defaults that should be tuned per workload):
- circuit_breaker: consecutive_errors=5, reset_interval=30s, half_open_attempts=3.
- default_retry: 1 retry with exponential backoff starting 100ms up to 1s.
- canary_policy: initial_weight=2%, step_size=5% every 10m, abort_on_error_threshold=1% error_rate above baseline.
- region_failover_delay: 30s (short to avoid user-visible errors but long enough to avoid flapping).

Automation helpers (cheat-sheet commands and API examples):
- Query reconciliation lag: curl -sS https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/health | jq .reconciliation_lag_seconds
- Set route weights (example): curl -X PATCH https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/routes/route-abc/weights -d '{"weights":{"us-east-1":0,"us-west-2":100}}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CP_TOKEN'
- Pause rollout: curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/rollouts/rollout-123/pause
- Force agent to re-sync (per-region): ssh agent-host && sudo systemctl restart controlplane-agent

Escalation contacts (on-call primary then platform leads):
- On-call: #platform-oncall (rotation info in PagerDuty)
- Platform lead: Daniel Park (pager)
- Serving runtime: Priya Nair
- Applied ML: Miguel Santos

Post-incident checklist (to attach to Jira postmortem):
1) Timeline of events with exact control-plane commands and who executed them.
2) Metric dump for before/during/after windows (store as CSV).
3) Root cause hypothesis and supporting evidence.
4) Action items: config changes, automation, tests, alerts tuning.
5) Owner and target date for each action.

Small experiments and TODOs (open items for platform team):
- TODO: Implement a "safe-mode" that automatically lowers non-critical traffic weights when reconciliation_lag > threshold. (Jira PLAT-4321)
- TODO: Add a simulation harness that replays production RPS against new routing rules in a sandbox to detect loops.
- Experiment: Evaluate using quantified request scoring to route by expected token cost rather than pure latency for cost-sensitive customers.

Notes and open questions:
- How often should read-only mode be auto-triggered? Tradeoff: false positives block legitimate config changes. Need threshold tuning.
- Can we provide tenants an API to opt out of cross-region failover for latency-sensitive applications? (privacy/data residency concerns)

Appendix: quick reference
- emergency steps (1-line): announce -> pause rollouts -> reduce weights on impacted region -> verify metrics -> execute durable mitigation -> open postmortem.
- critical dashboards: Console > Observability > Per-route | Console > Platform > Control Plane Health | Console > Regions > GPU Utilization
- important metrics: reconciliation_lag_seconds, control_plane_api_error_rate, per_route_error_rate, region_gpu_utilization, cache_hit_ratio

This is a working document. If you update any operational steps here, please add a changelog entry at the top and ping #platform-oncall.

End of doc.

title: Progressive Tool Fusion and Client Surface — Lab Notes
content:
Progressive Tool Fusion and Client Surface — Lab Notes

Exploratory PRD-like lab notes proposing a streaming-first approach where tool calls and tool results are progressively fused into the client-visible stream. Focus is on ergonomics for SDKs, lightweight typed frames, resume semantics, and observability required to iterate safely in production.
Context:

This doc captures an ideation run for 'progressive tool fusion' — an approach where hosted inference can emit interleaved partial text, tool-call intents, and tool results in a single stream and the client-side SDK performs deterministic fusion of those pieces into a final structured output. The hypothesis: pushing a small, well-documented amount of fusion logic into SDKs (instead of heavy server-side transactions) produces lower tail latency, better incremental UX, and more deterministic developer ergonomics for tool-heavy workflows (e.g., multi-tool data enrichment, stepwise actions).

Why now:
- Increasing demand for tool-calling workflows with low-latency interactive UX (chatbots that call search, calculators, code-run, db lookups)
- Customers want structured, typed outputs to be accessible incrementally (partial lists, progressive tables)
- Platform has mature streaming primitives; next step is a well-scoped contract for tool-call interleaving and client fusion that scales across mobile/desktop/server SDKs.

Goals:
- Define a minimal streaming frame vocabulary for partial_text, tool_call, tool_result, fusion_marker, and typed_blob that SDKs can implement easily.
- Specify an SDK-facing API contract for deterministic fusion that is resilient to reconnects and duplicate tool results.
- Define telemetry and SLOs to safely roll out fusion-enabled streams (observe per-tool latency, fusion-completion time, and reconstruction mismatch rates).
- Deliver migration guidance for existing non-interleaved hosted-api customers and a toggle/flag-based rollout plan.

Non-goals:
- Full server-side orchestration of multi-tool transactions with ACID semantics (we aim for best-effort correctness with idempotency tokens, not distributed two-phase commits).
- Replacing existing typed-output endpoints (we provide a complementary streaming surface).

User personas and flows:
1) Product engineer embedding a chat assistant in a web app: wants partial answers quickly, and a single final card containing aggregated tool outputs (search snippets + db rows).
2) Platform integrator on mobile: must support intermittent connectivity and resume semantics without duplicating tool side effects (e.g., avoid double-run of a code execution tool).
3) SRE/ops: cares about per-request cost, tool invocation counts and partial-stream error modes.

Streaming frame vocabulary (proposal):
- partial_text: raw incremental tokens (string) with sequence_id and offset.
- tool_call: metadata describing the intended tool (tool_id, invocation_id, schema_hint, input_preview). Sent when model decides to call a tool.
- tool_result: result payload produced by tool (invocation_id, result_id, checksum, maybe typed_blob). May be streamed itself if large.
- fusion_marker: annotation that signals a stable boundary where the SDK should emit a fused output to the app (fusion_id, expected_parts).
- typed_blob: compact typed payload (schema_id, json_schema_version, base64 payload) for high-confidence structured outputs.

Each frame includes minimal routing metadata: request_id, session_id, sequence_number, timestamp, and optional resume_token. Tool frames MUST carry an invocation_id to correlate calls and results across reconnects.

SDK ergonomics (guiding principles):
- Determinism: SDKs should implement a deterministic fusion algorithm given the ordered stream of frames; meaning two identical frame sequences yield identical fused outputs.
- Progressive delivery: SDK surfaces incremental fused candidates (non-blocking) and a final fused commit event when fusion_marker is received or a timeout elapses.
- Safety: SDK must expose hooks for the host app to control 'materialization' of tool side effects (e.g., provide onToolMaterialize callback; default: do not auto-materialize in mobile low-bandwidth mode).
- Resume-friendly: SDK must persist a lightweight resume token map (invocation_id -> result_id/checksum) to avoid duplicate tool replays after reconnect.
- Configurable heuristics: provide tunables for buffer_size, fusion_timeout_ms, allow_partial_on_disconnect (default: true for UX).

SDK API sketch (for JS-like pseudocode):
- createStream({requestId, sessionId, options}) -> stream
- stream.on('frame', (f) => {}) // raw frames
- stream.on('fusionCandidate', (candidate) => {}) // candidate fused partial
- stream.on('fusionCommit', (commit) => {}) // final fused output
- stream.materializeToolResult(invocation_id) // optional manual materialize for idempotency control
- stream.resumeFromToken(token)

Behavioral examples:
- Model emits partial_text x3, then tool_call(invA), then partial_text x2, then fusion_marker expecting invA. SDK should: show progressive text; when tool_result for invA arrives, incorporate into fused structure and emit fusionCommit. If tool_result doesn't arrive before deadline, SDK emits fusionCommit with placeholder and a post-hoc update when result arrives.

Low-bandwidth and offline heuristics:
- If connection degrades, SDK should prefer progressive partial_text deliveries and suppress heavy typed_blob auto-materialization (e.g., large images, file attachments).
- allow_partial_on_disconnect setting controls whether SDK exposes incomplete fused outputs to the app.

Observability and telemetry needs:
- Per request: time_to_first_token, time_to_fusion_commit, number_of_tool_calls, number_of_tool_results_missing, fusion_mismatch_rate (cases where server produces a final authoritative structure different from SDK-fused final after reconciliation).
- Per tool: mean_latency, p95_latency, error_rate, duplicate_invocations_detected.
- SDK-instrumented counters: local_resume_successes, local_resume_failures, pending_invocations_at_disconnect.

SLOs and acceptance criteria:
- Under normal network: median time_to_fusion_commit <= baseline + 120ms (baseline is plain streaming text commit).
- Fusion mismatch rate < 0.3% in canary window.
- Duplicate tool invocation rate (post-resume) < 0.1% in canary.
- SDK must provide a deterministic rehydration flow that passes unit/integration tests included in the SDK test harness.

Migration and backward compatibility:
- Default behavior: streams without fusion_marker are treated as plain streaming text (no fusion).
- Provide an API flag on requests: enable_progressive_fusion=true. Start with invite-only canary customers and an SDK opt-in.

Rollout plan (proposal):
- Phase 0: internal lab tests with simulated tool latencies and reconnect patterns.
- Phase 1: Alpha release to internal Redwood apps + 3 trusted customers (feature flagged). Monitor telemetry.
- Phase 2: Public SDK beta for JS + mobile with opt-in toggle; collect mismatch metrics and developer feedback.
- Phase 3: Gradual default-on for new request workflows with migration docs and 'compat' header to request original stable-only behavior.

Open implementation risks and questions:
- Tool side-effects: we must guarantee an idempotency story for tools where replays can cause side-effects (webhooks, chargeable actions). Recommendation: tool integrations must advertise idempotency_token support and SDK must prefer 'do-not-replay' default unless tool confirms idempotent semantics.
- Contract evolution: will typed_blob schema changes require version negotiation? We propose including schema_version in frames and refusing to auto-parse unknown majors.
- Server authoritative reconciliation: if server later decides to rewrite fused output (e.g., correct hallucinated tool_call), how are SDKs expected to reconcile? We propose final authoritative fusion frames with authoritative=true; SDK should emit a correction event and the app can reconcile.

Testing and validation plan:
- SDK unit tests for fusion determinism across permutations of frame interleavings.
- Integration harness that simulates: lost frames, delayed tool results, duplicate tool_result with different checksums, reordered partial_text chunks.
- E2E with a mock tool that has both idempotent and non-idempotent modes to validate resume heuristics.

Developer docs and UX examples to produce:
- Quickstart: enabling progressive fusion in a single line and sample code to display incremental fused cards.
- Troubleshooting guide: common mismatch causes and how to instrument.
- Migration checklist: what to do before turning on fusion for production traffic.

Next steps (concrete):
1) Team alignment session (product + applied-ml + SDK + platform) to validate vocabulary and heuristics (target week of 2025-02-17).
2) Prototype JS SDK fusion algorithm and a simple mock server within 2 sprints.
3) Build telemetry dashboards (fusion mismatch, per-tool latency) and a canary alert.
4) Draft integration guide and safe defaults for mobile clients.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a lab-level PRD sketch: please challenge the assumptions about pushing fusion to clients vs doing more server-side commit logic.
- Look for edge cases where deterministic recomposition cannot be guaranteed due to lossy network or intentionally lossy model behavior.

References and inspiration:
- Internal hosted-api streaming patterns (see linked artifacts)
- Typical idempotency design patterns from payment gateways (applicability for tool integrations)

End of notes.

title: Cust VPC Change Simulator and Sample Audit Corpus
content:
Cust VPC Change Simulator and Sample Audit Corpus

Purpose and scope:

This is a working PRD / engineering sketch for a lightweight customer VPC change simulator and a curated sample audit corpus intended to: (1) exercise our approval gate logic, sampling and retention heuristics, and attestation bundling; (2) validate telemetry shape and queryability for forensic playback; (3) produce realistic rejection/rollback/rollback-recovery scenarios for SRE and support drills.

Why this exists (problem statement):
- Customers performing private deployments manage their own networks and will occasionally make configuration changes (SG, route, peering, NAT). These changes must flow through our approval gates or be captured fully in audit evidence when done out-of-band.
- We need a reproducible test harness that can generate varied, realistic change traces (benign changes, configuration drift, misapplied firewall rules, partial peering failures) and an associated audit corpus that represents evidence bundles (logs, netflow, sha-signed change manifests).
- Current PRDs focus on policy and retention; we lack a repeatable way to validate operator experience, failure modes, and query patterns for downstream tooling (search, timeline, forensics).

Goals (what success looks like):
- Deliver a CLI-driven simulator that can synthesize change events with parameters (change_type, scope, operator_role, approval_path, evidence_quality).
- Produce a set of 120 sample audit bundles across 6 classes (approved, auto-approved, rejected, emergency-bypass, partial-apply, rollback) that cover our expected query surface (by tenant, by operator, by timeframe, by change hash).
- Ensure each bundle contains a compact set of artifacts: change-manifest.json, operator-assertion.sig (simulated HSM signature), agent-syslog tail, network-trace (pcap-lite), and a compact summary.json with canonical fields for quick indexing.
- Define compatibility tests for Console playback, SIEM-forwarder ingestion, and on-prem observability export.

Non-Goals:
- This project will not implement a hardened HSM signing pipeline — signatures are simulated but schema-compatible with future KMS-backed receipts.
- We are not building a full traffic generator; pcap-lite will be synthetic, small, and focused on metadata that our parsers exercise.

Key definitions and canonical fields (summary.json schema):
- tenant_id: string (redwood tenant namespace id)
- change_id: string (uuid v4)
- change_type: string (route_update | security_group_update | peering_add | peering_remove | nat_delta)
- operator: string (email)
- operator_role: string (tenant-admin | delegated-operator | support-bridge)
- request_time: iso8601
- approval_path: string (console-canary | api-reserved | delegated-approval | emergency-bypass)
- approval_result: string (approved | rejected | timed_out | bypassed)
- manifest_hash: sha256
- evidence_quality: string (complete | partial | truncated)
- forensic_tags: list of short strings (we will store as comma-separated string in the corpus)

Simulator design (CLI + engine):
- Entry: rd-vpc-simulate run --profile PROFILE --seed SEED --count N --outdir /tmp/corpus
- Profiles (examples):
  - small-change-fast: single SG rule add, operator role delegated-operator, expected approval path console-canary
  - cross-region-peering-failure: peering_add with simulated partial propagation and route-ads update; evidence_quality=partial
  - emergency-rollback: nat_delta that triggers emergency-bypass; approval_result=bypassed, with post-facto attestation bundle
- Engine components:
  - event-synthesizer: creates change-manifest.json and deterministic operator actions from seed
  - evidence-generator: emits artifacts (syslog snippets, pcap-lite, manifest.sig) and synthesizes manifest_hash
  - timeline-builder: produces chronological event stream (request -> approval request -> approval decision -> apply steps -> monitoring alerts -> rollback)
  - corpus-packager: zips each scenario into an evidence bundle and writes summary.json (index-friendly)

Sample audit bundle (human-readable example for review):
- summary.json
  {
    "tenant_id": "tenant-82f3",
    "change_id": "9f2c8b4a-3a1d-4e2e-9a0b-1111111",
    "change_type": "security_group_update",
    "operator": "ops+alice@acme.example",
    "operator_role": "delegated-operator",
    "request_time": "2024-10-28T18:22:40Z",
    "approval_path": "console-canary",
    "approval_result": "approved",
    "manifest_hash": "sha256:...",
    "evidence_quality": "complete",
    "forensic_tags": "sg-change,login-from-nonprod"
  }

(above is stored inside each bundle; real JSON in artifact file — here we show for reviewers)

Acceptance criteria for product and infra teams:
- Simulator binary (or Python script) runs in CI producing deterministic bundles when a seed is provided; artifacts are small (<5MB each bundle) and stored under s3://redwood-evidence-dev/sim-corpus/<release> for retrieval.
- Console can ingest a bundle and render a playback timeline (request -> approval -> apply -> alerts -> rollback) without schema changes to the Console timeline UI.
- SIEM-forwarder can index summary.json and extract manifest_hash, tenant_id, and approval_result into a test index.
- A small test harness exists that asserts queries: counts by approval_result, counts by operator_role, and latencies from request_time to approval decision.

Test matrix and scenarios (high level):
- Categories: approval_behaviour (approved/rejected/timeout/bypass), evidence_integrity (complete/partial/truncated), application_impact (no-service-impact, partial-failure, outage), operator_timeline (single-op, multi-op-handoff), scale (single change, bulk 50 changes).
- For each scenario we define EXPECTED_CONSOLE_STATE and EXPECTED_SIEM_EVENTS (documented in test matrix CSV in repo).

Operational considerations and retention experiments:
- Bundles will be compact (summary + minimal binary artifacts). We will evaluate retention and S3 cost for 6 months of generated corpus at scale 10k bundles/day.
- Propose a TTL experiment: store full bundles for 30 days, archive compact summary-only records for 365 days. Evaluate usefulness to support during a simulated incident.

Security and privacy notes:
- All simulator-generated tenant IDs and operator emails are synthetic and labeled "sim" to avoid accidental cross-contamination with customer data.
- Signature artifacts are simulated. Avoid using this simulator as a certifying tool; it is only for UX/telemetry/forensics testing.

Console / UX playback requirements (short):
- Timeline view should be able to accept a bundle endpoint (local file or s3 path) and step through events. Improve timeline to show "evidence_quality" indicator and link to artifacts (view syslog snippet, download pcap-lite).
- Provide a compact summary card in rollouts page that highlights approval_path and approval_result and links to bundle manifest_hash.

Open questions and decisions needed:
- Do we standardize the compact summary JSON schema now (breaking change for Console)? Proposal: adopt the schema above and version it as v1.0-summary. Decision due by 2024-12-05.
- Where to publish simulator artifacts for reuse? Proposal: s3://redwood-evidence-dev/sim-corpus/<branch> + a simple index endpoint maintained by infra.
- What are acceptable sizes for pcap-lite? Proposal: cap at 200KB per event to keep bundles small.

Implementation plan (quarterly roadmap):
- Week 1-2: prototype CLI and simple profile templates (Marcus, Jules)
- Week 3-4: produce first 30 bundles and run Console ingest smoke tests (Aisha, product)
- Week 5-6: integrate SIEM-forwarder test harness and prepare test matrix (Priya)
- Week 7-8: iterate on schema and produce acceptance test coverage in CI (all)

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: simulated evidence might accidentally differ from customer artifact shapes. Mitigation: collect anonymized example shapes from recent support tickets (security review) and incorporate into profile templates.
- Risk: corpus grows and costs escalate. Mitigation: TTL policy and compact-summary archival.

Next steps / action items:
- [Aisha] PR the initial repo with CLI skeleton and one profile (due 2024-11-25) — PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/pull/312
- [Marcus] Draft schema proposal and VersionedSummary RFC (due 2024-12-01) — link to confluence: confluence:PD-4321-cust-vpc-simulations
- [Priya] Draft SIEM ingestion test cases and expected mapping to logs pipeline (due 2024-12-10)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and intended to land quickly as a test harness that improves our ability to validate approval gates and forensic UX. Expect several follow-ups: schema tightening, larger corpus generation, and integration with the attestation service.

Raw brainstorming snippets (notes-to-self preserved):
- consider embedding deterministic anomaly triggers so one can fire a "silent-misapply" where manifest says success but netflow shows block
- simulate operator-network-latency for distributed approvals (two-step OK flow)
- think about a tiny DSL for profiles: change:sg add {cidr} -> approval:console-canary -> monitor:flow-drops

References and related docs:
- Confluence: PD-4321-cust-vpc-simulations (design notes)
- Jira: PD-789-change-sim (epic)
- GH: private-deploy PR 312 (starter)

End of doc.

title: Error Budget Orchestration & Cutover Plan — Q3 2026
content:
Error Budget Orchestration & Cutover Plan — Q3 2026

Executive summary:

This doc lays out a cross-functional program to operationalize error budget orchestration across Redwood services and execute a coordinated cutover from the existing ad-hoc oncall/incident reaction model to an SLO-driven reliability regime. The plan covers policy, runbooks, automation, pilot, and org-wide cutover. Core outcome: teams treat error budget as a first-class signal (deploy gating, routing, and engagement) with automated enforcement where appropriate, and a simple, low-friction escalation model during budget exhaustion.

Why now:
- Growing customer use of low-latency endpoints requires predictable availability and defined tradeoffs (cost vs. latency).
- We lack a consistent, cross-team way to translate SLO violations into operational actions (e.g., slow rollouts, traffic shedding, prioritized bug fixes).
- Incidents are still handled largely by tribal knowledge; we need standardized runbooks and automation to reduce MTTD/MTTR.

Goals (measurable):
- Within 12 weeks, 80% of critical public-facing services have formal SLOs and associated runbooks documented in Confluence.
- Reduce mean incident-to-first-response time for SLO-related alerts by 50% in pilot teams.
- Implement error-budget-aware deployment gating for 3 high-traffic services and demonstrate reduced post-deploy regressions.
- Establish a cadence: weekly error-budget review digest + monthly reliability scorecard per service.

Scope (what's in / out):
In scope:
- Public API services (hosted-api) and the serving runtime control plane (serving-runtime).
- Observability pipelines (Datadog + internal metrics ingestion) and PagerDuty integration.
- Runbook templates, enforcement automation, deployment gating logic, and communication playbooks.
Out of scope:
- Deep instrumentation work that requires model-internal tracing (to be scheduled separately).
- Long-term SLA commercial changes (legal/product will handle later).

Stakeholders and roles:
- Program lead: Aisha Patel (eng-sre) — owns timeline, cross-team coordination, cutover decision.
- Observability lead: Marcus Lin (observability) — metrics ingestion, dashboards, alerting rules.
- Serving runtime: Sofia Martinez (serving-runtime) — SLO definitions for generation and chat endpoints, KV cache considerations.
- Hosted API product: Priya Nair (product-hosted-api) — prioritization of customer-impact services and communication to customers.
- Platform infra: Ethan Cole (infrastructure) — deployment gating hooks, circuit breakers at routing layer.
- Oncall and tooling: Benji Park (site-reliability-engineering) — PagerDuty taxonomy, escalation flows.

High-level timeline (12-week plan):
Phase 0 — Prep (week 0–1): assemble team, finalize pilot services, baseline metrics.
Phase 1 — Policy & SLO drafting (week 2–3): define SLI sources, SLO windows (30d/7d), error budget math, burn thresholds.
Phase 2 — Runbooks & Playbooks (week 4–5): author runbooks, create incident-to-action mapping for burn states.
Phase 3 — Automation & Integrations (week 6–8): implement alert hooks, PagerDuty playbooks, deployment gating in CI/CD.
Phase 4 — Pilot & Iterate (week 9–10): run 3-week pilot on selected services, capture metrics, tweak thresholds.
Phase 5 — Org cutover (week 11–12): expand to other teams, training sessions, formal handoff and retrospective.

Milestones and deliverables (per phase):
- Prep: pilot roster, baseline dashboards, inventory of SLIs for each pilot service.
- Policy & SLOs: SLO document per service (owner, SLI definition, target, window), policy matrix that maps burn to actions.
- Runbooks: templated runbooks in Confluence, runbook for error-budget exhaustion with specific scripts and contact points.
- Automation: alert rules in Datadog, PagerDuty escalation playbooks, CI/CD gate PR templates, traffic routing playbooks.
- Pilot review: quantitative pilot report (deploy regression rate, response times, false positives).
- Cutover package: training slides, quick reference cards, oncall rotation updates.

Detailed tasks by team:
- Observability (Marcus):
  - Map existing metrics to canonical SLIs (latency p95/p99, error-rate by error-class, availability).
  - Create Datadog composite SLO objects where possible, export to internal metrics index.
  - Build SLO dashboards and weekly digest email templates.
- Serving Runtime (Sofia):
  - Propose SLOs for generation endpoints (token-level vs request-level decisions).
  - Document how prefix/KV cache behavior affects SLI calculations and add tags to metrics for cache-hit vs miss.
  - Add optional debug flags to emit per-request SLO attribution for first pilot.
- Hosted API Product (Priya):
  - Select three pilot routes (high traffic, prototypical failure modes).
  - Define customer communication templates for when we engage in mitigation (rate limits, degraded mode).
- Platform Infra (Ethan):
  - Implement a lightweight deployment gate hook: block canary promotion when error budget < X% (configurable).
  - Implement traffic-weighted fallback policy that can route to a lower-capacity but higher-stability model variant.
- Oncall/Tools (Benji):
  - Design PagerDuty service categories and escalation policies tied to SLO burn levels.
  - Create runbook-triggered automation (e.g., slack notify + runbook link + ephemeral incident channel).

Runbook: Error Budget Exhaustion (template snippet)
- Trigger: composite SLO alert (7d burn > 20% or 1h instantaneous burn > 5%).
- Immediate actions (first 15 mins):
  1) PagerDuty page owner for the SLO.
  2) Post ephemeral incident channel in #sre-reliability and tag product owner.
  3) Check Datadog dashboard for recent deploys (last 60m), traffic spikes, and external dependencies.
- Mitigations (first 60 mins):
  - If recent deploy suspected: initiate rollback or pause the pipeline (CI gate).
  - If traffic spike: engage routing team to apply traffic shaping or priority queues.
  - If external dependency: engage vendor/partner and enable degrade mode per product guidance.
- Restore and postmortem:
  - When SLO recovers (below warning threshold for 1h), close incident and create a short postmortem, tag "SLO-impact".

Automation & CI/CD gating specifics:
- Implementation pattern: a lightweight API from infra exposes current error budget percentage per service. CI/CD pipeline can query this API before promoting canary. Default allow threshold = 30% (configurable by service owner).
- Rollout plan: pilot services set threshold to 20% for testing, logs written to audit stream.
- Safety: gating should only block auto-promotions; manual overrides allowed with mandatory incident log entry.

Pilot selection criteria and chosen services:
- Criteria: high traffic, clear SLI instrumentation, active oncall owner, different failure modes (latency vs error-rate).
- Chosen pilots:
  1) hosted-api/v1/generate (latency-affected, high qps) — owner: Priya Nair
  2) serving-runtime/control-plane (route and model selection latency) — owner: Sofia Martinez
  3) embeddings-service (lower latency but sensitive to OOMs) — owner: Ethan Cole

Metrics and KPIs to track during pilot:
- Incident-to-first-response (minutes)
- Mean time to mitigation (minutes)
- Post-deploy regression rate (percent of deploys with SLO blips)
- False positive alert rate (alerts not leading to actionable state)
- Error budget consumption rate (daily burn %)

Communication plan:
- Weekly: short reliability digest to eng-all with top 5 services and their burn status.
- Ad-hoc: when any service crosses critical burn threshold, auto post to #sre-reliability and an email to product stakeholders.
- Training: two 60-minute training sessions for pilot teams on runbooks and CI gating; office hours for broader teams.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Alert fatigue if thresholds too low -> Mitigation: tune thresholds in pilot, adjust alert severity and suppress noisy signals at SLI level.
- Risk: Teams bypass gating via manual overrides -> Mitigation: require incident ticket and post-override review.
- Risk: Ownership ambiguity across platform/product -> Mitigation: signed owner list and SLA for corrective actions in the policy document.

Open decisions (for program council):
- Should we enforce gating on all internal deploys or only auto-promotions? (proposal: auto-promotions only)
- Burn threshold defaults: 20% vs 30% — pilot will use 20% and we will evaluate.
- Which SLO window should be primary: 7d rolling for burn sensitivity vs 30d for contractual view? (proposal: use both; 7d for ops, 30d for reporting)

Acceptance criteria for org cutover:
- >= 80% of services with SLOs have an associated runbook and PagerDuty category.
- CI gating implemented for at least 3 services with audit logs enabled.
- Oncall teams demonstrate <50% of current incident-to-first-response time in pilot.

Next steps (week-by-week immediate):
Week 0: finalize pilot roster, create baseline dashboards (Marcus).
Week 1: host cross-team kickoff, distribute owner responsibilities (Aisha).
Week 2–3: SLO drafting workshops with service owners (Sofia + Priya).
Week 4: runbook pairing sessions, Confluence templates finalized (Benji).
Week 5–7: engineering sprints for gating + alerting (Ethan + Marcus).
Week 8–10: pilot monitoring, threshold tuning, runbook dry runs.
Week 11–12: training, cutover, retrospective and org-wide roll plan.

Appendix A — Quick policy matrix (summary):
- Green (budget > 50%): normal ops.
- Yellow (budget 20%–50%): reduced risk deploys only, increase monitoring cadence.
- Red (budget < 20%): block auto-promotions, notify product and oncall, consider traffic shaping.

Appendix B — Useful links and templates:
- SLO template: confluence.redwood.local/reliability/slo-template
- Runbook template: confluence.redwood.local/reliability/runbook-template
- PagerDuty taxonomy doc: confluence.redwood.local/tools/pagerduty-taxonomy

Notes to reviewers:
- Please comment inline on the SLO thresholds and the CI gating proposal.
- If your team wants to be added to the pilot, ping me (Aisha) with owner name and SLI coverage by EOD next Friday.

title: KMS access governance and audit pipeline design notes
content:
KMS access governance and audit pipeline design notes

Purpose

This note collects design decisions and operational patterns for KMS access governance, RBAC v2 integration, audit log schema, evidence automation for forensics, and SIEM ingestion mapping. Goal: produce an implementable pipeline that makes key access provenance auditable, supports BYOK/HSM flows, and provides timely alerts for suspicious key activity while preserving privacy and performance for production traffic.

Scope

- Key classes: tenant customer-managed keys (BYOK), platform-managed keys, HSM-wrapped root keys, ephemeral request keys used by inference runtime.
- Integrations: RBAC v2 entitlement system, KMS (cloud-managed + HSM appliance), audit-log pipeline, SIEM (ECS-compatible), retention and evidence archival system.

Background and constraints

- We operate across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments; design must work for cloud KMS and on-prem HSMs.
- Low-latency inference paths require minimal per-request cryptographic overhead. Audit metadata should capture access decisions and provenance without adding contention to hot paths.
- Regulatory requirements: retain cryptographic access logs for at least 3 years for enterprise customers opting into compliance add-on; retain high-fidelity forensic artifacts for 90 days for platform incidents.

High-level model: access provenance first-class

1) Principal identity: RBAC v2 issues short-lived principal tokens that include role bindings and region/tenant claims. 2) KMS access decision: KMS enforces policy; it must log decision outcome and token reference. 3) Envelope metadata: every envelope encryption/decryption operation emits a lightweight audit record with request id, principal id hash, key id, operation, justification tag, and latency. 4) Evidence bundle: on-demand or periodic archival of signed manifests + key metadata for forensic reconstruction.

RBAC v2 integration patterns

- Role to key binding table: maintain canonical mapping in the security control plane: role -> allowed key actions (wrap/unwrap, decrypt, generate). Changes go through audited PR flow.
- Attribute-based checks: use attributes (tenant_id, environment, model_family) passed as claims in principal tokens. KMS validates attribute constraints before allowing key use.
- Ephemeral delegation: for high-throughput inference, runtime requests a short-lived key-wrapping token from the control plane which the KMS accepts as delegation; delegation issuance is logged and policy-scoped.
- Escalation and Justification: CLI/API actions that request long-lived key access must include a justification token and optionally an approval id; log both.

Audit log schema (single flat event record)

We standardize on one audit event type for KMS operations to simplify ingestion. Field names below are ECS-friendly, but keys are lower_snake_case to match existing pipeline parsers. All fields are strings unless noted.

- event_type: kms_operation
- timestamp: ISO-8601 UTC
- event_id: uuid
- outcome: success | failure | denied
- principal_id: <stable-principal-id> (we store hash in SIEM; full id retained in evidence store)
- principal_token_kid: token key id (for tracing token version)
- principal_attributes: comma-separated list (tenant:123,role:reader,env:prod)
- key_id: kms://region/keyname or hsm://serial/keyname
- key_version: string
- operation: encrypt | decrypt | sign | verify | wrap | unwrap | generate_key
- operation_context: short JSON string (max 2KB) with non-sensitive fields: request_path, model_family, sequence_length_hint
- request_id: id used across services to correlate
- latency_ms: integer string
- service_node: host id or service role
- decision_source: rbac_v2 | kms_policy | manual_approval
- justification_id: optional approval id
- audit_signature: base64(signed_digest) — used to verify record integrity when pulled into evidence store

Note: sensitive fields (full principal identity, raw request payloads, plaintext tokens) MUST NOT be shipped to SIEM. Only hashes/ids and non-sensitive context go to SIEM. Full artifacts are stored in the evidence archive with strict access controls.

SIEM mapping and ingestion guide

- Indexing: Ingest events into ecs-compliant index: log.kms_access. Use event.dataset = "kms.access" and event.module = "kms". Map outcome to event.outcome and key_id to host.id for searchability.
- ECS tags: add service.name = "redwood-kms", cloud.region, tenant.id (hashed), and deployment.mode (hosted|dedicated|private).
- Enrichment: SIEM pipeline performs geoip on service_node if external, and resolves role names from a cached mapping for dashboards.
- Parsers: implement strict JSON schema validation at ingestion to reject malformed operation_context > 2KB.

Evidence automation and forensics workflow

- Evidence package composition: for a given time window (ad-hoc or incident-driven), build a signed bundle containing: manifest.json (list of event_ids + hashes), raw secured audit blobs (signed by KMS), principal token snapshots (redacted), policy versions, and key metadata (non-secret). All bundle parts are signed by the security control plane key and checksumed.
- Chain of custody: each bundle receives a custody_id, S3 path, and retention tag. Movement between storage classes is auditable.
- Access controls: evidence retrieval requires multi-party approval (security + platform lead) and is logged to a separate immutable store.

Rotation coordination patterns

- Rotation types: soft rotation (create new key version and update metadata), hard rotation (create new key + re-encrypt persisted blobs), emergency rotation (revoke and generate new root).
- Coordination steps for tenant BYOK soft rotation: 1) Create new key version in HSM/KMS. 2) Update control-plane binding to accept new version. 3) Allow dual-use period where both versions are valid. 4) Schedule background rewrap job (best-effort) for persistent stores and update manifests when rewrap completes. 5) Revoke old version when rewrap completes and SLA window passed.
- Rotation SLOs: for soft rotations aim for 72 hours dual-use window; background rewrap throughput must be rate-limited per-tenant to avoid inference impact. Emergency rotations have a documented incident playbook with rollback steps.

Operational runbook (quick checklist)

- Daily: verify audit pipeline lag < 60s for critical events; check SIEM ingestion errors; ensure signing key rotation for audit_signature not older than 90 days.
- Weekly: reconcile key inventory vs role bindings; review any denied key operations with >10 retries.
- After rotation: validate sample decryption on a 1% tenant sample; verify evidence bundle integrity for the rotation window.

Alerting and detection examples

- High-confidence alert: repeated denied unwrap operations on a single key by different principals within 1 minute -> create P1 ticket.
- Medium: key_version used from two different regions in unrealistic pattern (compare against expected region list).
- Low: late audit records (lag > 10 minutes) for decryption operations on dedicated clusters.

Implementation notes and optimizations

- Non-blocking audit: KMS returns result immediately and emits audit event asynchronously to audit pipeline. The KMS includes a persistent event_id in response; downstream systems can query evidence store for full artifact if needed.
- Batching: for high-throughput inference, aggregate per-request low-signal telemetry (cache hits, prefix usage) into 1s batches to reduce noise in SIEM; still emit one authoritative KMS audit event per key operation.
- Token hash rotation: to preserve traceability, use stable principal_id mapping for 90 days, then rotate hash salt monthly and maintain mapping in evidence archive.

Open questions / TODOs

- Decide canonical retention tiers across customer classes (default 1 year, enterprise 3 years, eDiscovery 7 years) and add to SLA appendix.
- Define exact approval flow for evidence retrieval (UI vs API, whitelisting for EDR).
- Performance budget for background rewrap jobs on Dedicated clusters; need SRE runbook to limit IO/CPU impact.

Appendix: example SIEM query snippets

- Detect repeated denied unwraps: 
  event.dataset: "kms.access" and outcome: "denied" | stats count by key_id, principal_id | where count > 5

- One-off suspicious immediate rotation followed by access: 
  event.dataset: "kms.access" and operation: "generate_key" and timestamp > now-1h | join (event.dataset: "kms.access" operation: "decrypt" ) by request_id

- Verify signature validity for recent bundles (offline check): list bundles where manifest signature verification failed -> alert security team.

Notes for reviewers

This is an operational-first draft meant to be implementation guidance for infra, SRE, and security teams. Feedback requested on retention tiers, evidence access policy, and allowed fields in operation_context. Particularly interested in SRE input on rewrap throttling constraints.

title: Feature-gated traffic shift — internal announce + Q&A (notes)
content:
Feature-gated traffic shift — internal announce + Q&A (notes)

Purpose: quick internal announce and Q&A scaffold for the staged traffic shift to the 'latency-optim' model variant behind a feature gate. This is my working notes — rough, intentionally choppy.

Audience: ENG (serving/runtime, infra, sres), Product ops, CS triage leads, Support L2, Growth (for feature-flag targeting), Execs (brief line). Tailor messaging for each group.

High-level ask: we will enable the new model variant (quantized, smaller KV footprint) behind a feature flag for 10% of host-api requests starting Fri 10/11 18:00 PT. Goal: validate latency improvements and error mode behavior at scale while keeping ability to rollback to stable model within 2 minutes.

What I want to land in the short announce (one-paragraph):
- Why: expected median p50 token latency improvement ~12–18% on p3/gh200 families for common seq lengths (64–256). Also expected token-cost reduction ~8% with negligible quality regression for short-respone queries.
- When: Fri 10/11 18:00 PT, ramp to 10% over 30m.
- Who: monitored by infra SRE and the release owner (Asha).
- Rollback: instant toggle, fallback to stable routing if error rate >1% or latency tail > +40% vs baseline for 5m.

Quick Q&A (draft responses):
Q: How are we defining success?
A: Primary: no regression in end-to-end error rate (API 5xx + model errors) and <10% increase in p99 latency. Secondary: token-cost per request reduction and stability of output (sampled prompts show no hallucination spike on our eval set).

Q: Will this affect enterprise/tiered customers?
A: Not initially. Feature gate excludes dedicated and private deployments; flag applied only to hosted-api free-tier & standard routes. Enterprise customer tokens are pinned to stable model variants.

Q: Who can flip the flag?
A: Asha (release owner) + SRE on-call (primary) + me as fallback. We will use the feature-control service (audit logs enabled).

Q: What monitoring is in place?
A: Dashboard: latency by route/model-variant, error-rate by route, model-quality sampling (prompt subset), alerting: page on 5xx increase >0.5pp or p99 increase >30% sustained 5m. Synthetic golden prompts hit every 2m. Logs: correlation ids for sampled traces.

Q: How do we communicate rollback to customers?
A: No customer-facing change planned. If we rollback due to regressions, ops will send a short post-mortem to #ops-notices and customer-success if any customers were impacted.

Talking points for SRE/infra sync (bullet list for standup):
- Preflight checklist: kernel flags, inference node pool autoscale policies reviewed, canary sample size validated, golden prompt runbook ready.
- Resource check: ensure at least 2 spare p3/gh200 nodes in pool for rollouts.
- KV cache warm-up: schedule pre-warm of top 1000 prefixes for the 2h window prior to shift.
- Emergency rollback procedure: feature-control toggle + routing table restore + drain in-flight tokens to avoid partial outputs.

Open/unknowns (notes to self):
- Need exact query set for the "golden prompts" — coordinate with Applied ML (Benji) to ensure it captures long-tail failure modes.
- Confirm cost accounting tag will surface on billing exports (so finance can see delta for the experiment).
- Double-check that the feature-flag audit includes actor, timestamp, reason, and pre/post-state.
- Validate that hosted-api quota enforcement won't inadvertently block partial rollouts (some customers have route-specific rate limits).

Draft Slack announce copy (short):
"Heads-up: Fri 10/11 18:00 PT we’ll enable the latency-optim model variant behind a feature flag for 10% of hosted-api traffic (30m ramp). Goal: validate p50/p90 improvements and stability. Monitored by infra SRE + Asha. Rollback criteria set; will post updates in #ops-notices. Ping me or Asha for concerns"

Extended internal email / standup note (longer):
- One-paragraph summary (what/why/when) + link to playbook + who to call for rollback.
- Include the preflight checklist and quick runbook steps (attach Confluence playbook link).

Post-launch follow-ups (what I want to collect):
- 1h: sanity check p50/p90 and errors on targeted routes.
- 4h: sampling of outputs for quality review (Benji).
- 24h: cost delta and aggregate error/latency metrics + decision: keep ramping to 25% or roll back.

Fallback language for execs (one-liner):
"Running a limited, monitored test of a latency-optim model variant to validate production performance. No expected customer-visible changes; rollback is immediate if any stability signals show up"

Tasks before send (todo list):
- [ ] Finalize golden prompt set (Benji).
- [ ] Confirm billing tag (Luis).
- [ ] Dry-run toggle with SRE staging (Asha + SRE).
- [ ] Draft Slack + Standup lines and get a quick +1 from Product leadership.

Notes to self (tone/style):
- Keep public-facing lines minimal and low-risk. Avoid technical caveats in initial announce; route those into a follow-up runbook for ENG.
- Make sure CS triage gets an FAQ snippet (3 bullets) so they can answer common questions quickly.

Recent edits / context:
- 10/02: initial idea after bench-run improvements on 64-token median.
- 10/03: added rollback thresholds after SRE feedback.
- 10/04: tightened ramp window to 30m and added cost-tag ask.

Questions I need help closing (assignments):
- Benji: final golden prompts by 10/07.
- Luis: confirm billing tag + finance contact by 10/08.
- Asha: schedule staging dry-run 10/09.

If anyone reads — feedback welcome. If you want to be on the notify list DM me and I'll add you to the release watchlist.

title: Tidecrest dispatch assistant integration journal
content:
Tidecrest dispatch assistant integration journal

Call: Tidecrest Logistics — Dispatch Assistant integration (initial technical capture)
Date: 2025-01-12 10:00 PT
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SRE), Anita Rao (Redwood Solutions), Rajiv Menon (Tidecrest CTO), Priya Kapoor (Tidecrest Product), Luis Ortega (Tidecrest Platform)

High level ask
- Replace current rules engine for short text suggestions and driver instructions with an LLM-backed assistant to summarize incident context and propose routing adjustments. Must be realtime-ish (human-in-the-loop, <200ms p95 preferred for suggestion latency).
- On-prem/VPC-first: Tidecrest wants private deployment inside their AWS account (VPC) for sensitive telematics + PII. Dedicated/private deployment preferred; they may start with Dedicated before migrating to Private.

Key constraints (from Rajiv + Luis)
- Intermittent connectivity: some edge hubs (rural terminals) are behind flaky links. Need offline resilience or graceful degradation.
- Small GPU footprint at edge: can't run large 70B models on-site. Looking for a hybrid: small quantized local model for immediate suggestions, and larger hosted model fallback for complex summarization.
- Data residency: trip logs/driver notes considered PII under their policy — must be encrypted at rest and in transit; need KMS/HSM integration and retention controls (default 14 days, configurable).
- Audit trails: compliance wants per-request audit logs with raw prompt and model response for 30 days (log retention + ability to export for audits).

What Redwood can offer / initial recommendations
- Deployment: Recommend Redwood Private (VPC) so control plane can be in their account; if they want lighter ramp, Redwood Dedicated with private network peering is an interim approach.
- Model routing policy: run a quantized 8-bit ~7B local model for latency-critical suggestions on edge caches, route complex summarization (end-of-day consolidation, incident synthesis) to larger hosted model (e.g., 13B/33B) in Redwood Dedicated. Automatic fallback rules if local inference fails.
- Streaming + partial results: use streaming responses for the driver suggestion UI so partial text appears as tokens are generated (improves perceived latency).
- KV/prefix caching: for repeated route templates and driver-specific prompts, enable KV cache on the driver/session id to avoid recomputing context. Watch out for state drift on frequent TTL updates.
- Embeddings for recall: store embeddings of recent incidents to surface similar past cases. Use per-tenant namespace and encrypted vector store.

Technical gotchas / open risks
- Token accounting for telemetry: telematics JSON blobs (gps traces, events) are large. We need a pre-processing filter to extract salient fields; avoid sending raw telemetry as prompt. Otherwise token cost spikes.
- KV cache invalidation: dispatch state updates are frequent (every few seconds). If we cache too aggressively we serve stale suggestions. Need TTLs or event-driven invalidation from their event bus.
- Partial context vs hallucination: small local models hallucinate more on policy/guidance questions. Must add guardrails and deterministic rule checks before recommending route changes.
- Websocket vs REST: their UI uses websockets for live driver status. Need connector to map websocket events -> Redwood request stream; session affinity is required for KV cache reuse.

Integration requirements (explicit asks from Priya)
- Endpoint: a streaming API endpoint that accepts: {tenant_id, session_id (driver_id), event_summary, recent_telemetry_digest, exigency_level}. Returns tokens as a streaming suggestion and a confidence score.
- Real-time webhook: when suggestion is accepted, Redwood should POST a signed webhook to their /dispatch/apply endpoint including model_id, prompt_id, and delta actions for audit + idempotency.
- Per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and token usage dashboards exposed in console and via telemetry webhooks for billing reconciliation.
- Encryption: integrate with Tidecrest KMS (AWS KMS) for model input/output encryption at rest; support customer-managed keys.

Prompts & eval notes (quick, informal)
- Draft prompt (short): "Driver incident: {one-line summary}. Last 2 events: {e1}, {e2}. Constraints: arrival <= 15m, avoid heavy traffic. Suggest 1 concise instruction and confidence."
- Test scenarios to include: broken down routes (lots of reroutes), long-running congestion (preserve patience in suggestions), privacy redaction (ensure phone numbers/IDs stripped).
- Metrics for acceptance: suggestion usefulness (human accept rate) > 85% after 4-week tuning, p95 suggestion latency < 250ms for edge model, fallbacks < 1% of requests in steady state.

Action items / next steps (owners & rough dates)
- Marcus: prototype websocket -> Redwood streaming bridge (POC) and latency bench (target 1/2 week) — due 2025-01-20.
- Anita: design KV cache TTL strategy + inconsistency mitigation doc (include event-driven invalidation patterns) — due 2025-01-24.
- Sofia (me): build sample prompt set (20 examples) and lightweight eval harness for manual labeling; coordinate baseline accept-rate target with Priya — due 2025-01-18.
- Rajiv/Luis: provide sanitized sample telemetry dataset (anonymized traces, <1000 sessions) and KMS contact for integration — asked by 2025-01-17.
- Joint: schedule technical deep-dive for infra & security with Tidecrest infra team (2 hours) — set for 2025-01-22 (tentative).

Questions to resolve (TBD)
- Will Tidecrest allow outbound connections from edge hubs for fallback to Redwood Dedicated? If not, need an on-prem-only architecture.
- What SLA for suggestion availability do they want? Is occasional delay acceptable if correctness improves?
- Audit log retention: can we meet 30-day raw-prompt retention given their company policy and cost implications?

Quick notes / voice-of-customer snippets captured in call
- Priya: "We want suggestions to feel like a senior dispatcher — short, actionable, not long paragraphs."
- Rajiv: concerned about token bills if we naively send traces: "If you charge per token for every ping, it's untenable."
- Luis: strongly prefers KMS integration before any PII leaves account.

Random scratch ideas for future phases (brainstorm)
- Model personalization: lightweight per-driver context embeddings (driving style, preferred phrasing) to tune tone. Keep vector keys encrypted and per-tenant.
- Cost-control ML agent: suggest when to route to local vs hosted model based on cost/latency prediction and current spend budget.
- Offline summarizer: nightly batch summarization of incidents to reduce need for long-term model queries.

End of capture — keep this as working doc. Will iterate after POC latency numbers and once we get sanitized telemetry.

title: Control plane decomposition & regional routing playbook
content:
Control plane decomposition & regional routing playbook

Purpose:
This is a working playbook sketch to clarify service boundaries for the control plane components we own, and to capture a regional routing decision model people can copy into RFCs and runbooks. Focus: API gateway responsibilities, orchestration (control-plane core), runtime adapters (GPU/CPU pools), and how ownership shifts when we run multi-region.

High-level service decomposition (intended):
- API gateway (edge team): ingress, auth, tenant scoping, initial request validation, short-circuiting (rate limits, quota), and primary routing hints (region preference, model / variant selector). Not responsible for model compatibility checks beyond surface level (e.g., model id exists).
- Orchestration / Control-plane core (platform-engineering): policy evaluation, placement decision, global state (capacity map), rollout policies, deployment metadata, canary logic, route fallbacks and A/B selection. Exposes policy API consumed by gateway and autoscaler.
- Runtime adapters (serving-runtime interface): translate placement decisions into concrete fleet operations (allocate GPU slot, pin model binary, configure quantization profile). Responsible for per-cluster capacity accounting and local health signals.
- SRE / Observability: owns incident runbooks, cross-region outage detection, and the tracing/metric dashboards; collaborates on SLA targets for each component.

Routing decision model (step-by-step):
1) Gateway receives request -> extracts tenant & model intent + optional region hint. Apply auth & quota.
2) Gateway requests placement from orchestration service with (tenant, model, region_hint, latency_slo, cost_tier).
3) Orchestration evaluates:
   - Preferred region availability (capacity map)
   - Latency SLO vs estimated p99 for candidate clusters
   - Cost tier (e.g., on-demand vs reserved)
   - Canary/rollout policy binding for tenant/model
   - Model compatibility (via model metadata cached from model catalog service)
   - Fallback rules (force cross-region if no compatible capacity)
4) Orchestration returns route: {target_cluster, adapter_endpoint, expected_latency_ms, fallback_list}.
5) Gateway forwards request to runtime adapter endpoint. If adapter rejects (capacity/health), gateway retries orchestration for next fallback.

Region-aware ownership rules (practical callouts):
- Gateway must be region-aware but stateless in terms of global policy (does not hold authoritative capacity map).
- Orchestration is authoritative for capacity/rollout but must tolerate eventual consistency; ownership includes sharding logic for regional caches and a single leader for write operations (per-region leader + global coordinator).
- Runtime adapters own local health + exact placement operations; they must expose a stable contract (health, tokenized lease, eviction reasons).

Failure scenarios & responsibilities (who acts first):
- Regional control-plane control-loss (leader unresponsive): orchestration should promote standby leader; gateway should consult regional fallback list and route to next region. SRE triggers incident and capacity borrowing.
- Adapter-level eviction (OOM / model crash): adapter emits structured event -> orchestration marks slot unhealthy and triggers reschedule; gateway retries with adapter-suggested fallback.
- Model rollout causing regression across region: orchestration can globally pause rollout and trigger global rollback; rollback owner: product + platform-engineering to coordinate.

Operational boundaries (TL;DR ownership matrix):
- Auth & quotas: API gateway (policy enforcement), but quota counters replicated to orchestration for global quotas.
- Routing decision (final): Orchestration returns canonical route; gateway executes.
- Telemetry ownership: adapters emit raw metrics; orchestration normalizes and tags; observability owns storage/alerts.

Design constraints & rationale (why split this way):
- Keep gateway lightweight & horizontally scalable; avoid embedding long-running policy logic to minimize cold-start surface.
- Centralize policy in orchestration so we can evolve rollout semantics without changing gateway code across many languages.
- Let adapters be the narrow hardware-specific translation layer so new hardware types (e.g., future accelerators) only need adapter changes.

Practical runbook snippets (to copy into ops docs):
- "If region X reports >30% slot error rate for >5m, mark as degraded, remove from primary routing, and notify SRE. Orchestration will drain canary traffic automatically"
- "When promoting regional leader: validate global state snapshot is less than 2m behind; otherwise run snapshot catchup job."

Open questions / TODOs (working list):
- How much policy should live in gateway for fast failover vs. central orchestration latency? (tradeoff: fail-fast vs single source of truth)
- Exact schema for orchestration's fallback_list (should include cost delta and estimated added latency).
- Lease TTL semantics between orchestration and adapters (currently prototyped in PLAT-4121).
- Cross-region data compliance hooks: add a flag in routing response that the gateway logs for audit (GDPR/Paid-region tenants).

Action items (next 3 sprints):
- Sprint A: finalize fallback_list schema + update gateway client (Ethan).
- Sprint B: implement adapter lease TTL enforcement and eviction reason codes (Raj).
- Sprint C: run chaos experiment that kills regional leader and validate fallback behavior (SRE + Platform).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally informal; please annotate sections you want formalized into an RFC. Link any relevant Jira tickets into the TODOs above.

Slack refs / historical context:
- See slack thread: #platform-arch "regional routing sketch" (Nov 2025) for early whiteboard screenshots.
- Prototype work lives in repo: control-plane/placement-v2 (PR linked above).

End.

title: evaluative-hire-sandpit-guide-and-skill-sequencing
content:
evaluative-hire-sandpit-guide-and-skill-sequencing

A compact, experiment-oriented playbook for running a short hiring "sandpit" to surface high-signal evidence quickly and sequence skill evaluations so hiring decisions are faster and lower friction.
Purpose:
This note defines a lightweight, repeatable process we call the 'hire sandpit'—a bounded 7–21 day experimental pipeline that blends micro-takehomes, time-boxed pairing, and short ramp tasks to generate comparable evidence across candidates. Designed for roles where hands-on demonstration + collaborative communication are the strongest predictors of early impact (platform, infra, SRE, and small-feature engineering).

Principles (why this differs from traditional loops):
- Evidence-first: prioritize artifacts you can grade consistently (small demos, PR drafts, infra runbooks) rather than long interviews.
- Time-boxed velocity: keep active evaluation to max 3 weeks to reduce candidate drop-off.
- Symmetry of value: every exercise should give the candidate insight into the job and give us a usable artifact.
- Low-friction conversion signals: make it easy to move a contractor or bench-hire to offer when evidence aligns.

When to use the sandpit:
- Mid-to-senior IC where paired work matters; candidate has already cleared culture screen and basic matching.
- Hiring velocity is important and multiple strong candidates are expected within window.
- Role requires cross-team collaboration (we need to see communication and handoff).

Sandpit structure (recommended template):
1) Day 0: Intake + sandbox setup (1 business day)
   - Send repo/test harness + onboarding readme.
   - Candidate signs NDA / confirms schedule.
2) Days 1–3: Micro-takehome (48–72h)
   - Small scoped task (~3–6 hours) with clear acceptance criteria.
   - Deliverable: PR or gist + short design note (max 1 page).
3) Day 4: Paired session (60–90 minutes)
   - Focus: debugging/extension of takehome artifact or a short design problem.
   - Use structured prompts and recording (with permission).
4) Days 5–7: Ramp mini-task (optional for multi-week loops)
   - Simulate first-week onboarding: document a quick runbook or automate a small routine.
   - Deliverable: README/runbook + example test run log.
5) Decision and evidence synthesis (end of week 1 or week 3 for extended loops)
   - Panel reviews artifacts against rubric and votes.

Scoring rubric (micro-matrix, score 1–5 each):
- Problem decomposition: can they break a problem into testable pieces?
- Code clarity & correctness: is the micro-PR readable, has basic tests, and meets acceptance?
- System thinking: demonstrates tradeoffs, monitoring, and failure modes.
- Collaboration: clarity in async notes, responsiveness in pairing.
- Ownership & follow-through: finishes committed scope and communicates blockers.

Rubric guidance (anchor examples):
- 5 on Problem decomposition: divides problem to components, writes short tests per component, outlines next steps.
- 3 on Collaboration: engaged in pairing but needed repeated prompts; async notes ok but terse.
- 1 on Ownership: missed deadlines without proactive updates.

Interviewer prompts and probe bank (paired session):
- Walk me through the first 2 commits you would do in a production migration of X.
- If the change causes a 10% CPU regression, how would you detect and mitigate without rollback?
- Show a short debugging process for a flaky job: where do you look first?

Asynchronous interview flow (templates):
- Candidate instructions email (concise): objective, scope, success criteria, what repo/files to submit, how to raise questions.
- Auto-checks we run: linter, basic unit test, simple perf smoke (script included).
- Communication windows: we promise response within 24 business hours for clarifications.

Onboarding-lite checklist (for converted hires or contractors):
- Day 0: access request + environment script executed by candidate with logs attached.
- Day 1: shadow pairing with assigned buddy for 2 hours; list of three observation tasks.
- Day 3: candidate owns a small triage or fix and documents the runbook.
- End of week 1: 15-minute sync with hiring manager with evidence summary.

Signals to accelerate conversion (contractor → perm):
- Completed 2 independent artifacts that match rubric 4+/5 across core skills.
- Positive cross-team notes from pairing sessions (2+ reviewers).
- Demonstrated ramp: completed a mini-ramp task that required reading platform docs and producing a safe deploy.

Decision timeline and evidence ledger (panel process):
- Panel: 3 reviewers (1 peer, 1 manager, 1 cross-team) each submit short votes + 3-line rationale.
- Convert to offer if majority >= 2 reviewers and no critical fail in rubric.
- Tie-breaker: hiring manager synthesizes evidence and may request a focussed follow-up (30–60 minute deep-dive).

Templates (copy/paste placeholders below):
- Candidate instruction blurb: 'You have 48 hours to implement feature X in repo Y. Keep changes focused; write a brief design note. We care about clarity and rationale more than lines of code.'
- Panel evidence note: 'Candidate: [name]. Artifacts: PR #, runbook link. Scores: PD 4, CC 4, ST 5, Collab 4, Own 5. Recommend: convert.'

Operational notes for people ops / hiring coordinators:
- Use a single tracking sheet per role with one row per candidate and columns for artifact links, rubric scores, panel vote, and final decision date.
- Pre-book pairing slots before issuing takehome to reduce scheduling lag.
- Allocate reviewer time: 45m artifact review + 30m panel synthesis per candidate.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: candidate non-completion. Mitigation: make takehome incrementally valuable and give partial-credit scoring for incomplete submissions.
- Risk: uneven reviewer calibration. Mitigation: run biweekly calibration sessions with 5 example artifacts and discuss scoring anchors.

Open questions / items for iteration:
- How to adapt for managerial hires (we need longer live design exercises).
