- Experiment: measure time-to-offer and candidate NPS for sandpit vs. baseline over next 6 hires.

Appendix: Example micro-takehome (Infra SRE variant)
- Goal: add a feature flag to rollout a config change safely and write a small smoke-check that verifies behavior.
- Acceptance: feature flag is togglable in staging, smoke-check passes, short runbook documenting rollback.
- Estimated candidate effort: 3–5 hours.

Notes-to-self: keep candidate-facing language friendly; reduce legal friction on recordings; drop ambiguous grading language; sync with hiring managers monthly to refine acceptance criteria.

Authors / review history:
- Drafted by: Aisha Chen (people ops)
- Reviewed: Marcus Alvarez (eng-platform), Priya Singh (talent)
- Last review: 2025-03-02

title: Release Conservatory Runpad — 24hr Stabilization Log & Compact Checklist
content:
Release Conservatory Runpad — 24hr Stabilization Log & Compact Checklist

Context / goal:
This is a compact runpad for the Jun release (codename: conservatory). Primary goal: move traffic to v2 routing with staged canary while preserving 99th percentile latency SLO and keeping per-token unit cost within projection. Use this doc as the single-source quick checklist + 24h stabilization log for on-call and release stewards.

Summary of change:
- Routing layer change: traffic-aware fallback to quantized-compat model when Dedicated pool is saturated.
- Small model upgrade: model-v2 (attention perf patches + kv-cache improvement).
- Operator-visible flags: route.weight, batch.max_tokens and cache.prefetch.

Quick runpad (hour-by-hour highlights)
- T-2h: final preflight (smoke tests, bench against staging, notify CS + infra-watch). Check: smoke/generate endpoint, embeddings sample, auth tokens.
- T-1h: apply route.weight=0.05 for cohort A (10 hosts), open watch channels (#release-conservatory and #sre-nightwatch).
- T+0m: increase cohort A -> 5% global traffic for 15m, verify success criteria (p95 latency <= 180ms, error rate <0.2%).
- T+15m: cohort A -> 20% if green, else abort and revert to previous route config.
- T+45m: cohort B rollout ramp (20% -> 50% over 30m) with telemetry sampling increased.
- T+90m: full ramp to 100% if all gates pass. Begin 24h stabilization log.

Preflight checklist (must be green before any traffic shift)
- [ ] Canary config checked in Git and validated: linear INF-4122 status = ready.
- [ ] Deployment artifact SHA verified and pinned in release manifest.
- [ ] Staging smoke matrix run: basic LLM generation, streaming, embeddings, tool-calling samples.
- [ ] Bench script executed: median and p95 token/sec within 10% of baseline.
- [ ] Observability hooks active: tracing, token-level cost metrics, KV cache hit rate instrumentation.
- [ ] Rate-limit backstop configured for safety-lane and windowing.
- [ ] Pager rotation and guardrails briefed; primary steward (Asha), secondary (Diego), SRE (Maya).
- [ ] Customer success pre-notice sent to top-10 accounts with SLA triggers.

Canary schedule (compact calendar)
- Window: 2026-06-12 18:00–20:00 PT (quiet window, low release collision).
- 18:00 PT: cohort A 5% for 15m -> validate telemetry.
- 18:15 PT: cohort A 20% for 30m -> validate.
- 18:45 PT: cohort B gradual ramp 20% -> 50% over 30m.
- 19:15 PT: pause 15m to inspect signal.
- 19:30 PT: ramp to 80% -> 100% between 19:30–19:45 PT if green.
- 19:45 PT: final commit and mark release-flag active.

Success criteria / gating signals (explicit)
- Latency: p95 request-to-first-byte <= 220ms for Hosted API and <= 350ms for Dedicated in worst-case region.
- Errors: 5xx rate < 0.5% of requests, user-facing API error rate < 0.2%.
- Cost: per-token unit cost delta <= 12% against projection.
- Quality: automated prompt-set eval regressions <= 2% on BLEU-like metric and prompt fidelity checks.
- Observability: KV cache hit-rate not falling > 10% vs baseline.

Telemetry / dashboards to watch (primary widgets)
- api.latency.p95 by region and model variant (hosted vs dedicated).
- infra.gpu.utilization by pod and pool (watch for hot spots).
- token_cost.per_request and token_cost.daily_rate.
- gen.error_rate and gen.exception.classifications (top-10 stack traces).
- kv_cache.hit_rate and kv_cache.evictions/min.
- Traces: sampling for slow requests (p99 > 1s).

Immediate mitigation & rollback criteria (if any of these happen -> trigger rollback)
- Any sustained p95 above threshold for > 10m configured alarm -> immediate pause and scale down new route weight.
- Error spike: 5xx rate > 1% for 5m -> rollback to previous manifest.
- Cost runaway: token_cost running 30% above projection for 2 consecutive 1h windows -> rollback and open postmortem.

Rollback steps (fast path)
1) Revert route config to pinned manifest (git rollback command in infra/runbooks).
2) If rollback fails: trigger hotpatch with global route override (ops emergency toggle).
3) Notify slack: #release-conservatory, escalate to SRE Lead and Product.
4) Keep rollback annotated in ticket INF-4122 and fill the stabilization log with timestamps and signals.

24h stabilization log (template for entries)
- Timestamp | Operator | Action | Signal observed | Notes
- Example: 2026-06-12T18:07Z | Asha | increased A to 20% | p95=172ms, 5xx=0.06% | green
- Keep concise entries; prefer timestamped bullets.

Post-rollout checks (first 24h priorities)
- Hourly snapshot of p95/p99 for first 6h, then 3h cadence until 24h.
- After 4h: run mini-eval suite against our canonical prompt set (regression detection).
- After 12h: verify cost runtimes vs projected model/quantization benefit.
- 24h: finalize release notes and switch status from draft->final in release manifest.

Compact release notes (draft - to be expanded for external changelog)
Title: model-v2 routing upgrade (conservatory) — staged rollout
Short blurb: We rolled out model-v2 with improved attention kernels and routing fallbacks to optimize for latency and cost. This release uses staged canaries and monitored rollouts; no action required for most customers.
Key changes:
- Routing: traffic-aware fallback to quantized model-compat variants when Dedicated pool saturates.
- Model: v2 improves long-sequence KV cache hits and reduces tail latency on typical prompts.
- Ops: improved telemetry for token-level costing.
Known limitations / notes:
- There is a small expected cost delta for heavy prefix workloads; we are monitoring and will publish guidance if we adjust batching defaults.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self)
- Q: Should we pre-warm dedicated pools for accounts with heavy context length? (Maya to advise)
- Q: Do we enable auto-fallback based on predicted latency per-request or keep the deterministic routing policy? (product decision)
- TODO: add a short demo snippet for CS to explain fallbacks in customer-facing notes. (Jonah)
- TODO: check PR #1783 for an optional telemetry tag that isn't merged yet — defer if not in manifest.

Postmortem trigger policy (quick)
- Any rollback causes automatic postmortem with SLO review. Owner: release steward.

Appendix: quick commands & references (cheat)
- Rollback manifest: infra/deployments/releases/2026-06-12/manifest.yaml
- Canary toggle CLI: infra/cli route set-weight --route conservatory --weight 0.2 --cohort A
- Smoke run: scripts/release_smoke.sh --model v2 --sample 50
- Pager oncall: https://oncall.redwood/rota (primary: Asha, secondary: Diego)

Notes: rough, expect edits. This is intentionally compact — put details into the main runbook if we need extended debugging steps.

-- end of runpad --

title: embeddings-rerank-debug-scratchpad
content:
embeddings-rerank-debug-scratchpad

Context:
Small personal scratchpad while I triage the rerank+embeddings endpoint anomalies. This is messy notes-to-self: commands tried, raw snippets, timelines, quick hypotheses.

Summary of issue observed:
- Starting 2025-09-20 ~10:30 UTC we saw intermittent 500s from /v1/embeddings and downstream rerank timeouts.
- Two classes of symptoms: (A) dimension mismatch errors surfaced in the reranker: ValueError about vector shape; (B) latency spikes ~3–8s for otherwise <200ms requests.
- Affects customers using the hosted embeddings -> rerank pipeline that pins model to "open-embed-768" variant.

Quick timeline (rough):
- 2025-09-20 10:28 UTC: first error spike from synthetic probe (alerts).
- 2025-09-20 10:32–10:45 UTC: repeated 500s; many are dimension mismatch.
- 2025-09-20 11:10 UTC: roll-back to previous routing policy for a subset of traffic -> partial recovery.
- 2025-09-21: added extra logging on embedding worker, observed occasional different embedding_dim values.

Commands/requests I reproduced locally (minimal):
1) curl to hosted embeddings endpoint (anonymized):
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.test/v1/embeddings \n  -H 'Authorization: Bearer xxxxx' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n  -d '{"model":"open-embed-768","input":["foo","bar"]}' | jq .

Observed output (one of the failing responses):
{
  "error": "internal server error",
  "message": "embedding dimension mismatch: expected 768 but got 512"
}

2) Python probe to inspect numpy shapes (local):
--- file: quick_probe.py ---
import requests, numpy as np
resp = requests.post('https://api.redwood.test/v1/embeddings', json={"model":"open-embed-768","input":["x"]}, headers={'Authorization':'Bearer x'})
print('status', resp.status_code)
try:
    j = resp.json()
    print('keys', j.keys())
    print('shape', np.array(j['data'][0]['embedding']).shape)
except Exception as e:
    print('json err', e, resp.text)
---
When good: status 200, shape (768,)
When bad: status 500, body contains 'embedding_dim mismatch', or occasionally returns embedding length 512 -> shape (512,) which breaks rerank.

Server logs (redacted snippets):
[2025-09-20T10:33:12Z] worker-7 WARN embeddings: model open-embed-768 reported output_dim=512 (expected 768)
[2025-09-20T10:33:12Z] worker-7 ERROR rerank: failed to construct matrix: shapes (N,512) vs (N,768)
[2025-09-20T10:34:45Z] router INFO routing: fallback to compatible-embed-512 for tenant=acme-corp
[2025-09-20T10:36:01Z] infra WARN batching: large-batch delay=3.2s (queue length 24)

Observed patterns / notes:
- Dimension mismatch is not constant; same model id sometimes returns 768 dim and sometimes 512.
- Latency spikes correlate with a period where a portion of traffic was routed to a quantized variant (open-embed-768-4bit) and a separate instance serving open-embed-512.
- Autoscaler bounced some pods around 10:30 — possible during rollout of a node image that included a new model artifact mapping.
- Rerank code is strict about dims (np.dot assumes same last dim). We see re-rank failures bubble up as 500s & slow retries.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Model artifact mislabelling: model id "open-embed-768" points to two different artifacts on two pools (one actually produces 512-dim). Likely bad release that updated artifact registry without changing name.
2) Runtime model-quantization compatibility: quantized kernel returns reduced-dim compressed vectors (512) when run with certain kernel selection heuristics.
3) Dynamic model routing bug: routing policy fallback incorrectly maps model id to a different canonical model (compatible-embed-512) under capacity pressure.
4) Memory corruption / packing bug: KV cache or memcopy truncation in the inference pipeline leading to 512-length slices returned.
5) Upstream client changed prompt shape causing model to return different projection head (less likely).

Things I tried (and results):
- Forced model pin to a single worker pool (pinning to pool-A with image v1.4.1): shape stabilized -> 768. Good signal for hypothesis #1.
- Pulled recent artifact manifests on worker nodes and compared checksums between pool-A and pool-B: found mismatched artifact id for the same model tag (open-embed-768 -> artifact-abc123 vs artifact-def456).
- Replayed traffic with header X-Debug-Model: true to force logs: observed worker pool-B reporting model_version: artifact-def456 metadata: {embedding_dim:512}.
- Temporarily updated rerank to do a soft-check (pad/truncate) to avoid 500s for emergency mitigation (PR 278). This prevented 500s but produced poor rerank quality; rolled back after artifact rollback.

Quick reproduction steps for eng-sre:
1) Send 1000 concurrent small embedding requests pinned to model=open-embed-768 across multiple zones.
2) Watch worker logs for message 'reported output_dim=512'.
3) Check /artifacts/manifest on the worker node and compare model tag -> artifact id.

Mitigations applied so far:
- Rollback artifact mapping on pool-B to artifact-abc123 (rev from 2025-09-10) -> decreased mismatch reports dramatically.
- Short-term rerank guard: if embedding length != expected, return 424 to caller (so caller can decide). This was later changed to 503/traceable error in the hosted API to preserve semantics.

Next steps (open):
- Incident postmortem draft: collect all manifests, router routing logs, autoscaler events between 10:00–12:00 UTC. (I will start a Confluence page).
- Strongly recommend adding an artifact->model tag immutability check in deployment pipeline: CI should fail if two pools claim different artifact checksums for same model tag.
- Add model metadata enforcement at serving side: when worker loads model, emit metric gauge model_expected_dim and model_reported_dim and fire an alert if mismatch.
- Add automated integration test in canary rollout that sends a few embedding probes and verifies dimension.
- Consider allowing soft-compatibility (pad/truncate) as opt-in with QA on rerank quality; but default should be strict.

Notes to self (todo):
- Email ops with timeline + suggested CI gating.
- Add Jira updates to JIRA-ML-1428 with artifacts and logs.
- Follow up with infra on autoscaler churn around 10:30 — is that normal for that release window?
- Check if any recent PRs touched model-tagging scripts (deploy/manifest-sync).

Scratch/old commands (kept in case useful):
- grep -R "output_dim" /var/log/redwood/serving/* | sed -n '1,200p'
- kubectl get pods -l app=embeddings -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
- kubectl exec -it pod/emb-worker-7 -- cat /artifacts/manifest | jq .

Final quick note: root cause looks like an artifact-tag mismatch across pools (human release/manifest-sync mistake). The immediate production fix (rollback on pool-B) removed the bulk of errors. Still need CI + serving-side guard to prevent recurrence.

End of scratchpad.

-- Maya

title: Pool fallbacks and tenant throttle investigation — nightshift tactical slate
content:
Pool fallbacks and tenant throttle investigation — nightshift tactical slate

Purpose
- Capture the on-call notes and quick runbook for the 2024-10-29 evening GPU pool disruption that cascaded into route fallbacks and tenant-level throttling. This is a lightweight, tactical doc for SRE night crews; follow-up postmortem to be authored in Confluence once root cause final.

TL;DR
- 2024-10-29 ~20:40 UTC: p95 token latency for dedicated-pool-east-1 increased from 120ms -> 2.2s; internal autoscaler triggered multiple replenishments but pool offered degraded capacity (GPU kernel stalls). Traffic routing system paged fallbacks to compatible pools; fallback rate exceeded safe quota and triggered tenant-throttle rules, causing sustained client errors for some customers.
- Immediate mitigation: scaled affected pool manually to 0.8x (drain low-priority slots), disabled cross-pool fallback for 10m window, and applied short-term tenant throttle relaxation for high-SLA customers. Visible recovery by 21:12 UTC.

Impact summary
- Affected: Dedicated capacity customers on pool gamma-east-1 (approx 12 tenants).
- Symptoms: elevated request queue length, increase in model-infer errors and timeouts, surge in KV-cache miss amplification.
- Client visible: timeouts (504), transient 5xx spikes in hosted routing logs, and slowdown in streaming responses.

Detection and alerting
- First signal: p95 latency alert from /metrics/route/p95 (threshold 800ms) at 20:39:48 UTC.
- Secondary signals: allocator eviction spikes, GPU driver interrupt counts, autoscaler thrash events.
- Dashboards: gpu-pair-health, route-fallbacks, tenant-errors (see linked Grafana).

Timeline (concise)
- 20:39:48 UTC: p95 latency alert fired (oncall dispatcher -> SRE pager).
- 20:41:10 UTC: Oncall (Maya) confirmed increased queue depth and 90%+ kernel wait in pod logs.
- 20:42:05 UTC: Autoscaler attempted two scale-ups; new pods failed readiness due to driver timeouts.
- 20:45:30 UTC: Routing service started cascading fallback assignments to beta/pool-west-2. Fallback rate jumped to 320/min (normal < 30/min).
- 20:48:02 UTC: Tenant-throttle engine applied backpressure — rules triggered due to high fallback error rate. Customer support tickets begin.
- 20:50:00 UTC: Manual mitigation: disabled inter-pool fallback for gamma-east-1 -> recovery of routing state.
- 20:55:00 UTC: Began manual eviction of confirmed noisy tenant (suspected tenant id T-3401) from pool.
- 21:08:30 UTC: Queue depth falling, p95 back to ~180ms.
- 21:12:00 UTC: Traffic normalizing; keep watch for recurrence.

Initial hypotheses considered (notes)
- hypothesis A: GPU driver/firmware glitch causing stalls under specific kernel patterns. Evidence: driver interrupts spiked, and new pods failed readiness with driver timeouts.
- hypothesis B: A single tenant started heavy KV-cache-miss pattern causing cache amplification and forcing kernel work leading to eviction/thrashing. Evidence: tenant T-3401 showed 8x normal token throughput and repeated model-cache flushes.
- hypothesis C: Autoscaler hysteresis misconfiguration combined with fallback aggressiveness created a feedback loop where fallback assignments overloaded target pools. Evidence: fallback rate metric high and autoscaler logs show repeated scale events without adequate cool-down.

Triage checklist (quick, for night crews)
1) Confirm scope
   - run: curl -s "https://grafana.redwood.com/api/annotations?panelId=..." (or open gpu-pools dashboard)
   - check p95 and queue length for affected pool (gamma-east-1) and target pools.
2) Look at pod-level GPU signals
   - kubectl -n inference logs <pod> | grep -E "driver timeout|stall|KERNEL_WAIT"
   - nvidia-smi dmon (if accessible) or check prometheus: node_gpu_kernel_wait_seconds_total
   - note GPU util vs kernel-wait ratio; kernel wait > 40% is red flag.
3) Evaluate autoscaler behavior
   - check autoscaler events: kubectl -n infra describe hpa/pool-gamma-autoscaler
   - look for rapid scale in/out and short cool-down violations.
4) Routing & fallback checks
   - query route-fallback-rate metric: sum(rate(route_fallbacks_total[1m])) by pool
   - if >100/min, consider temporary fallback disable for affected pool.
5) Tenant isolation
   - identify tenants with >3x baseline request rate (metric: tenant_request_rate)
   - if identified, note tenant ID and consider immediate eviction/soft-throttle.

Immediate remediation playbook (fast-mode)
- Priority order: (1) stabilize routing and avoid amplifying fallback loops, (2) isolate candidate noisy tenants, (3) reduce pool pressure by draining lower-priority workloads.
Steps: 
1) Disable inter-pool fallback for impacted pool (one-liner):
   - curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN" https://routing.internal/api/v1/pools/gamma-east-1/fallbacks/disable
   - (This prevents cascade until pool health restored)
2) Relax tenant-throttle for high-SLA tenants only (temporary):
   - POST to throttle config with safe window and revert timer 15m.
3) Evict identified noisy tenant(s):
   - mark tenant T-XXXX as low-priority -> drain from pool via placement-api
   - run: placementctl evict --tenant T-3401 --pool gamma-east-1 --reason "noisy-amplification-night"
4) If driver stalls persist, cordon affected nodes and rotate GPU nodes through maintenance image rollback (see infra runbook).

Actions taken during incident (what we did)
- Disabled inter-pool fallback at 20:50 UTC.
- Evicted tenant T-3401 at 20:55 UTC and observed immediate queue depth improvement.
- Relaxed throttle for top 3 SLA tenants for 15m to avoid customer impact.
- Opened emergency support ticket with GPU host vendor (case #VND-112233) due to driver interrupt patterns.

Data collected / artifacts
- pod logs archived: s3://redwood-ops/incident-2024-10-29/gamma-logs.tar.gz
- grafana snapshots linked in linked_artifacts above
- coredumps (if any) uploaded to artifacts bucket and referenced in JIRA-RED-9876

Follow-ups / remediation backlog (short-term)
- Revisit autoscaler cool-down and hysteresis: increase stabilization window from 30s -> 120s for dedicated pools (owner: Omar).
- Adjust fallback aggressiveness: cap fallback-rate per-minute to 50 and add exponential backoff (owner: Priya).
- Add an automated detection for kernel-wait > 30% triggers temporary routing quarantine (owner: SRE-runbook team).
- Confirm driver/firmware upgrade plan with infra and vendor and schedule a canary (owner: Alex).

Longer-term ideas to prevent recurrence
- Implement tenant scoring for KV-cache miss amplification and proactively throttle before eviction.
- Build a routing-simulator to validate fallback policies under noisy-tenant scenarios.
- Create an autoscaler simulator that runs against recorded traffic traces to reveal hysteresis misconfigurations.

Open questions (need engineering input)
- Exact root cause of driver interrupts: firmware bug vs load pattern. Vendor input pending.
- Was eviction of T-3401 an appropriate mitigation or would soft-throttle been sufficient? (data needed: request replay & model call profile).
- Do fallback limits break expected multi-region failover SLAs for Dedicated customers? Need product alignment.

Retrospective quick notes (for the eventual postmortem)
- The outage was a compound event: hardware/driver instability amplified by aggressive fallback policy + autoscaler hysteresis. Single fix likely insufficient; need layered mitigations.
- Night crew response: > good, manual mitigations applied quickly but several actions lacked automation (disable-fallback, tenant-evict) that could be scripted.

Immediate next steps (this doc owner)
- Draft formal postmortem on Confluence (link placeholder) — due 2024-11-09.
- Assign autoscaler and fallback follow-ups in JIRA-RED-9876 before end of week.
- Schedule vendor call (Alex) to review driver logs and coordinate canary.

Notes to self / shorthand (nightshift)
- If you see kernel-wait spike + fallback rate rising -> hit fallback disable early.
- Evict only when you have telemetry showing tenant >3x baseline sustained >2m.
- After mitigation, leave a 30m watch window and capture histograms at 1s resolution.

Appendix: quick command cheats
- Check fallback rate: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(route_fallbacks_total[1m])) by (pool)" | jq
- Identify hot tenants: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=topk(10, sum(rate(tenant_requests_total[1m])) by (tenant))"
- Evict: placementctl evict --tenant T-3401 --pool gamma-east-1 --force --reason "noisy-night-evict"

-- end of notes --

title: Capacity signal debrief — regional demand variance and next steps
content:
Capacity signal debrief — regional demand variance and next steps

Meeting: Capacity signal debrief — weekly infra sync
Date: 2026-04-20
Lead: Maya Chen (Infrastructure capacity lead)
Attendees: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel, Sofia Ruiz, Liam O'Neill, Greta Andersen, on-call SRE rotation

TL;DR:
- Last week we observed a 22% demand spike in APAC (asia-southeast) tied to an unanticipated enterprise customer test run plus higher PLG trial traffic in eu-west. Net fleet utilization rose from 68% to 84% during peak windows.
- Patching the autoscaler hysteresis reduced oscillation in US regions but revealed slot contention in the eu-west pod group (slot starvation between 03:00–06:00 UTC).
- Immediate mitigations: temp reservation of 20 GPUs in asia-southeast and manual ramp of burst pool in eu-west. Mid-term actions focus on improving demand signals and automated hedging rules.

Snapshot metrics (rolling 7 days ending 2026-04-20):
- Global GPU utilization (weighted): 72% avg, 95th percentile 89% during peak hours.
- APAC (asia-southeast): 78% avg, 95th 95% (spike window 13:00–16:00 local) — increased by +22% week-over-week.
- EU (eu-west): 81% avg during UTC overnight window; p95 latency for small-chat endpoints rose by ~120ms correlating with slot contention.
- US (us-west/us-east): stable utilization 60–70%; autoscaler smoothing reduced thrash by ~40%.

Incidents & observations:
- Slot leak hypothesis (INF-4223): observed tasks not releasing allocated slots after failed container pulls; correlated with eu-west contention. Logs indicate intermittent Docker image pull errors after node kernel update.
- Autoscaler tuning: reducing scale-down aggressiveness fixed thrash but makes temporary over-provisioning costlier; need cost-bound safety nets.
- Prefix cache pressure: higher PLG trials increased cache miss-rate on large-context jobs; increased tail latencies for dedicated customers running long sequences.

Actions taken this week (what we did):
- Temporarily reserved 20 GPUs in asia-southeast for customer test traffic (Sofia, done).
- Manually increased burst pool in eu-west by 15% for 48 hours (Arjun, done).
- Rolled back the problematic kernel patch on 7 nodes where image pulls failed (Liam, done).
- Enabled extra logging and a short-lived debug mode on the slot allocator for one eu-west pod (Greta, in progress).

Open action items (owners and due dates):
1) Investigate and fix slot leak root cause (JIRA-INF-4223). Steps: reproduce with failing image pull, add guard to free slots on terminal failure, add integration test. Owner: Liam O'Neill. Due: 2026-04-27.
2) Implement hedging rule prototype: if regional demand variance > 15% vs baseline and sustained for > 30m, preposition 10% of burst capacity from global pool. Owner: Arjun Patel. Due: 2026-05-04.
3) Autoscaler safety-net: add cost cap circuit that prefers cheaper-quantized variants before scaling GPU count beyond threshold. Owner: Maya Chen + Product (consult). Due: 2026-05-11.
4) Prefix/KV cache telemetry: add per-tenant cache-hit heatmaps and alert when miss-rate increases > 8% within a 1h window. Owner: Greta Andersen. Due: 2026-04-30.
5) Customer communication: CS to notify affected dedicated customers about transient latency windows and mitigations applied. Owner: Sofia Ruiz (CS partner). Due: 2026-04-22.

Risks & tradeoffs:
- Prepositioning capacity reduces cold-start latency but increases committed utilization and potential cost. Need an ROI signal tied to customer SLAs and expected QPS.
- Conservative autoscaler reduces thrash but increases tail risk during large spikes; hedging rules must be conservative initially and staged via canary.
- Fixing slot leak may require transient node restarts; coordinate with on-call windows and Dedicated customers to minimize impact.

Data & instrumentation gaps identified:
- Lack of a single region-level demand variance signal — currently derived from multiple dashboards. Priority to build a unified metric (variance-over-baseline) exposed to autoscaler.
- No per-customer cache-hit alerts; hampers root cause for tail latency on long-seq workloads.

Plan for next 7 days:
- Triage and patch INF-4223 (slot leak) and run a small canary in eu-west.
- Ship hedging prototype config to staging and run chaos test with synthetic spikes.
- Instrument unified demand-variance metric and surface it in Console (basic chart + alert).
- Evaluate cost impact of current manual reservations and propose a short-term credit/billing offset for the enterprise test customer.

Notes / miscellaneous:
- Observed that PLG trial traffic tends to cluster on weekdays 13:00–17:00 UTC — we should consider time-of-day-aware hedging for eu-west and asia-southeast.
- Suggested short-term runbook addition: "when regional demand variance > 20% and p95 latency spike > 50ms, reserve N GPUs and notify CS". Drafted a runbook stub and linked above.

Next sync: 2026-04-27 11:00 UTC (weekly capacity sync).

Appendix: quick links
- INF-4223: slot leak ticket
- INF-4298: hedging rules RFC
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/318 (autoscaler smoothing changes)

Document author: Maya Chen
Reviewed by: Arjun Patel, Greta Andersen

title: Throughput & Latency Scaling Playbook — Brainstorm
content:
Throughput & Latency Scaling Playbook — Brainstorm

Meeting: Ad-hoc architecture brainstorm to synthesize RFC proposals into an operational playbook for throughput/latency scaling
Date: 2024-02-12 (notes updated 2024-02-20)
Attendees: Priya Nair (chair), Liam O'Connor, Jasmin Park, Marco Silva, Elena Ivanova, Samir Patel
Purpose: Decide a pragmatic, testable playbook for how the serving runtime reacts to changing load and tail-latency incidents. Bring together recent RFC fragments (dynamic batching knobs, autoscaler sizing, cold-start mitigations, fallback routing) and record decisions and next steps for an RFC that can be published.

TL;DR decisions (high level)
- Adopt a two-tier autoscaling policy: "stable" (predictive, slower scale up/down) + "burst" (fast scale-up with short TTL) to handle sudden spikes while limiting churn.
- Make batching window adaptive by per-tenant sequence-length histogram and per-slot vacancy; default target latency SLA is 150ms p50 for small-req workflows and 300ms p95 across mixed workloads.
- Implement a cold-start warmers subsystem for private/de-dicated deployments (warmers + KV prefetch) and a conservative fallback to smaller model-variants for hosted tier during hard cold-starts.
- Introduce a lightweight routing policy for cost-tiered fallbacks that prefers cheaper quantized variants on background/batch workloads but keeps full-precision variants for interactive SLOs.

Context & motivation
- Multiple postmortems and monitoring spikes show recurring tail-latency events when sudden load changes coincide with cold pods and fragmented KV cache hit rates. Current autoscaler reacts too slowly in some cases and causes head-of-line amplification in batching windows.
- Teams have partially-complete RFCs: adaptive batching strategy (Jasmin), two-stage autoscaler (Liam), warmers & kv-prefetch (Marco), quantized fallback routing (Elena). This meeting stitches them into operational steps.

Detailed discussion notes
1) Autoscaling (Liam + Priya)
   - Two-tier approach: predictive stable pool sized by rolling 24h quantiles for each tenancy class + burst pool that can accept requests for a short TTL (configurable, default 90s).
   - Burst pool should use pre-warmed instances if available. If not, requests are allowed to queue behind the existing serving slots but subject to request-queue length limits to avoid unbounded head-of-line blocking.
   - Metrics to monitor: scale-up latency, scale-down aggression, and request drop rate. Add health check for model load completion (not just container readiness).

2) Adaptive batching (Jasmin)
   - Make per-slot batching window a function of three signals: observed seq-length distribution, target latency budget for that model/route, and current concurrency per-slot.
   - Heuristic: if p50 seq < 64 and target p50 latency < 200ms -> small-window (4-8ms). Otherwise increase window up to 40ms for throughput.
   - Need an initial rollout experiment: A/B route where 10% of production traffic uses adaptive window with conservative knobs. Track token cost/unit, tail latency, and throughput.

3) Cold-start & warmers (Marco)
   - Warmers approach: maintain a warm pool for hot models (user-configurable TTL). Warmers should populate KV cache for expected prefixes (startup prompts, common system tokens).
   - For private deployments we can offer scheduled warm periods tied to customer traffic patterns. For hosted tier, run a cheap sampler to keep a small fraction of pods warm during predicted peaks.
   - Action: prototype an on-demand KV-prefetch API and an internal warmers controller that triggers after scale actions.

4) Model-variant fallback & routing (Elena)
   - Define semantics for fallback: trivial fallback chain is {full-fp -> quantized-4bit -> smaller-arch}. Routing decision uses SLO, cost budget, and tenant policy.
   - Must preserve determinism for critical business workflows (customer can pin no-fallback). Default should be safe: try quantized variant with quality monitor and auto-rollback on regression.
   - Add observable: per-request variant-used metadata in traces for downstream eval.

5) Safety & QoS considerations (Samir)
   - Rate-limit combined with budget tokens per-tenant. Define hard and soft thresholds; soft threshold triggers best-effort fallbacks, hard threshold returns 429 or prioritizes higher-tier customers.
   - Graceful error semantics: when variant fallback fails quality checks, perform automatic rollback and route to a lower-latency region if available.

Experiments & acceptance criteria
- Experiment A (adaptive batching): 2-week A/B test on mixed-chat route. Acceptance: p95 latency does not regress >10% while token-throughput improves >8% and cost/token decreases by >=3% for the test group.
- Experiment B (two-tier autoscaler): synthetic spike tests + shadowing on production traffic for 48h. Acceptance: median scale-up time for burst pool < 30s and request-drop rate < 0.1% under spike profile.
- Experiment C (warmers): simulate cold-start profile for top-10 models; acceptance: cold-start tail (p99) latency improvement >= 2x for warmed pods vs baseline.
- Experiment D (fallback routing): run controlled canary that shifts 5% of traffic to quantized variant. Success if quality regression (measured via eval prompts) < 1% and downstream error rate unaffected.

Open questions / risks
- KV cache consistency across slot migration: if sessions move between pods, we need a clear contract on whether we rebuild the cache or fetch from shared hotstore. Tradeoff: rebuild latency vs cross-node transfer cost.
- Billing and telemetry: tagging fallback variant use has cost implications and must be surfaced on invoices — need finance input (create INF-4305).
- Cross-region fallback complexity: latency of fallback to another region may negate benefits. Need region-aware policies.
- Quantization regressions: require pre-defined eval suites per model; who owns the suites? Research/Applied ML needs a central registry.

Action items (owner, ticket / ETA)
- Priya: Draft RFC combining these decisions into a playbook doc + rollout plan (INF-4316) — ETA 2024-02-23.
- Jasmin: Implement adaptive-batching prototype and set up A/B test harness (GH: runtime#814) — ETA 2024-03-08.
- Liam: Autoscaler bump & burst pool controller prototype (JIRA INF-4322) — ETA 2024-03-01.
- Marco: Warmers prototype + KV-prefetch API spec (JIRA INF-4331) — ETA 2024-03-10.
- Elena: Define variant fallback policy schema and telemetry fields (INF-4340) — ETA 2024-02-28.
- Samir: Draft QoS token model and billing impact note (work with finance) (INF-4305) — ETA 2024-03-05.

Notes to reviewers (informal)
- This doc is intentionally a synthesis — not all concrete knobs are finalized. The goal is to get alignment on the playbook and run narrow experiments. Expect further follow-ups where we pin exact latency windows and numeric thresholds.
- If you have existing benchmarks or customer cases that contradict the acceptance criteria above, drop links in the Confluence page before the RFC deadline.

Next meeting
- 2024-02-26 10:00am PT (sync to review RFC draft and experiment instrumentation checklist).

Raw snippets / ideas captured in jam session
- "burst TTL should be configurable per infra pool, default 90s, but allow 300s for long-running batch windows"
- "consider slot affinity hints to reduce kv-cache thrash when migrating sessions"
- "we could expose an operator-mode: pre-warm for scheduled events (customer-led) vs autonomous warmers"
- "instrumentation: variant_used tag should be searchable in logs and trace sampling prioritized for fallback incidents"

References (quick)
- Adaptive batching RFC (draft): GH issue runtime#789
- Autoscaler two-stage notes: slack thread /infra-runtime Feb 7
- Cold-start postmortem: INF-postmortem-2024-01-coldstart (Confluence)

End of notes.

title: Localized SLO decomposition and notify-gating proposal
content:
Localized SLO decomposition and notify-gating proposal

Draft proposal for splitting global SLOs into localized component SLOs and gating pager notifications with lightweight correlation rules to reduce noisy SLO-burn pages while preserving true incident visibility.
Context and motivation:

- We continue to get a significant fraction of paging noise from global SLO burn alerts that originate from a narrow class of dependency regressions (eg: instrumenter exporters, k/v cache metric drops, and downstream telemetry stalls). These pages often wake the on-call but do not require service-level mitigations (often operator actions at the telemetry layer).
- Our current approach: single global SLOs per product surface (api-latency-slo, generation-success-slo) and immediate pager for burn > 2% sustained over 5m. This is easy to reason about but amplifies noisy upstream signals.

Goals for this proposal:

1) Reduce pager volume by only paging when the SLO burn indicates a probable customer impact vs telemetry-only failures.
2) Improve signal locality so engineers can take fast, scoped actions rather than broad rollbacks.
3) Keep overall error budget accounting unchanged (we still measure global SLOs) but decompose ownership for faster remediation and less interruption.

High-level idea:

- Decompose selected global SLOs into localized component SLOs that represent the health of critical internal subsystems and their contribution to the global SLO. Example component SLOs: kvcache-hit-stability, prefix-cache-kv-exporter-availability, request-serializer-success-rate, region-egress-latency.
- Add a notify-gating layer for pager rules: an SLO-burn alert will escalate to page only when the global SLO burn is accompanied by either (A) at least one component SLO breaching AND a customer-facing metric (p50/p95 latency or error rate) crossing a preconfigured threshold, or (B) multiple component SLOs in the same failure domain breaching simultaneously.
- If only a single telemetry/exporter component SLO is degraded while customer-facing metrics remain within tolerance, route the alert to a lower-severity channel (team slack, ops queue) with automated diagnostic captures and suggested remediation playbooks.

Why this is different from simple suppression:

- We are not muting alerts; we are adding a correlation layer that aims to match alerts to probable customer impact. The global SLO measurement and burn remain unchanged for reporting and product decisions. The gating only affects the paging lifecycle and human routing.

Practical decomposition (initial rollout candidates):

- Hosted API global latency SLO -> decompose into: regional-inference-latency, kvcache-latency-contribution, exporter-metrics-availability, autoscaler-throttle-events.
- Embeddings ingestion success SLO -> decompose into: batch-queue-accept-rate, model-serve-availability, storage-writes-success-rate.

Heuristics for gating rules (first-pass):

- Gate A (customer-impact required): Page if global SLO burn > 2% for 5m AND (p95 latency increase > 30% OR user-facing error-rate increase > 1% absolute) AND any component SLO breach.
- Gate B (multi-component burst): Page if > 2 component SLOs in same domain (eg: telemetry exporters) breach within 3m window regardless of immediate customer metric change. Rationale: multi-component failures often indicate systemic regressions requiring broader action.
- Lower tier routing: If only a single telemetry/exporter component SLO breaches but customer metrics stable, create an Ops ticket and post in #sre-ops with attached diagnostic snapshot, suggested quick checks, and a 30m auto-escalation timer if the component SLO does not recover or customer metrics degrade.

Required telemetry and dashboards:

- New component SLO dashboards (per subsystem): time-series, burn heatmap, correlated traces, top-10 affected request routes.
- A correlation engine dashboard showing active gates, which gate triggered, and the diagnostic snapshot used to make routing decisions.
- Automated diagnostic snapshots to include: last 10 exporter logs, recent histogram of prefix lengths, kv-cache hit/miss rates, top 5 host latencies.

Experiment plan (6 weeks):

Week 0-1: Instrumentation
- Define and implement component SLOs as derived metrics (avoid adding new instrumentation where possible; use existing exporter metrics and labels).
- Add ephemeral dashboards and alert rules in the test (staging) environment.

Week 2: Canary routing
- Deploy gating logic for a subset of services (one product line: hosted-api region-us-west) in monitor-only mode (no pages, just logs of what would have paged). Collect sample for 7 days.

Week 3-4: Review and tune
- Review false negatives/positives from canary. Refine thresholds and which components count as customer-impacting. Prioritize simplicity: prefer a few well-understood components over many brittle signals.

Week 5: Gradual rollout
- Enable lower-tier routing for all regions and enable paging for Gate A/B where canary behaved as expected. Maintain quick rollback path (toggle per-product gating in config).

Week 6: Post-rollout evaluation
- Compare page counts, mean time to acknowledge (MTTA), mean time to restore (MTTR) for affected SLOs vs baseline. Evaluate error budget accounting for global SLO and confirm no silent burn leakage.

On-call playbook (for gated alerts routed to ops queue):

1) Read automated diagnostic snapshot attached. Look for immediate indicators: exporter crash, 5xx spike on ingress, throttling events.
2) Run the three quick checks: (a) exporter process status on collectors, (b) recent prometheus scrape success rate for the exporter, (c) check k/v cache eviction lag.
3) If the snapshot shows telemetry-only issues (exporter errors, scrape failure), follow the telemetry restart checklist attached (restart exporter, validate scrape, confirm metrics flow). Mark ticket with steps taken.
4) If customer-facing metrics degrade while gate suppressed paging, escalate immediately to primary on-call and disable gating for that SLO until root cause is found.

Risks and mitigations:

- Risk: Gate rules might introduce false negatives that suppress pages for real customer impact.
  Mitigation: conservative initial thresholds, canary mode, and automatic escalation if any customer-facing metric worsens even after gating.

- Risk: Increased complexity makes SLO ownership blurry.
  Mitigation: clear owner mapping per component SLO and a simple runbook that lists who to call for each component failure.

- Risk: Diagnostic snapshot generation adds load to monitoring pipelines.
  Mitigation: sample-based generation (only for alerts) and capped snapshot size.

Open questions (to resolve during design phase):

- Which specific component SLOs should be first-class (we want to avoid proliferation)? Proposal: start with telemetry/exporter availability, kvcache hit-stability, model-serving-availability, and autoscaler-throttle-rate.
- How to encode domain grouping (eg telemetry layer vs compute vs network) robustly in our metrics? Tagging conventions and stricter label hygiene will be required.
- How to present gating state to on-call in the console (clear UI affordance needed so paging status is obvious)?

Next actions (owners):

- Aisha: draft component SLO definitions and labels (due 2025-02-17).
- Marco: prototype a correlation rule in staging and run monitor-only sample collection (due 2025-02-24).
- Jin: design diagnostic snapshot schema and storage limits (due 2025-02-21).
- Ellen: prepare communication plan and SRE training doc for new gating behavior (due 2025-02-28).

Notes to reviewers:

- This is a safety-first proposal: if in doubt we page. The intention is to reduce fatigue from noisy telemetry-only pages and route low-impact work to an ops queue with helpful automated context.
- Please annotate the component SLO suggestions with concrete metric names when commenting (eg apply prometheus metric name and label set).

Appendix: example alert flow (short):

1) Global SLO burn triggers an evaluation rule.
2) Correlation engine queries component SLOs and customer metrics (p95/p50/5xx).
3) If Gate A or Gate B matches -> escalate to pager. Else -> create ops ticket + post snapshot to #sre-ops.

Observability TODOs (technical):

- Add prometheus derived rules for component SLOs (ex: kvcache_hit_stability = 1 - rate(kvcache_miss_total[5m]) with target 0.98).
- Add a small lambda service (or extend current alertmanager webhook) that implements the gating decisions and can be toggled per-namespace.
- Add labels to scraped metrics to identify domain (domain=telemetry|compute|network|storage).

End.

title: canary-failure-rootcause-scrapbook
content:
canary-failure-rootcause-scrapbook

Context:
- Quick brain dump after a rough canary this morning. Personal scratchpad for steps tried, observations, and next actions. Not a runbook yet.

Timeline / high-level:
- 2026-03-09 03:12 UTC: Canary deploy started (pipeline #872). Canary subset = 3% traffic to cluster region-us-west2.
- 03:25 UTC: Error spike: 5xx rate from canary pods rose from 0.7% -> 6.8% over ~5 min window. Latency P95 doubled.
- 03:32 UTC: Autoscaler for canary group added 2 pods, but errors persisted.
- 03:40 UTC: We attempted a fast revert by pinning traffic back to stable (see commands below) but rollback didn't fully reduce errors — some stable traffic still impacted.

What I saw (raw):
- Pod logs (canary): several exceptions: "KVCacheMiss: unexpected null for key" coming from runtime client, stack shows model-serving-layer -> token-cache -> transport layer.
- Error sample from app logs:
  ERROR 2026-03-09T03:26:12Z service.go:142 "handler panic" trace="runtime.go:..." msg="KVCacheMiss: unexpected null for key user:session:abc123"
- Kube events: OOMKilled reported for 1 canary pod at 03:27 UTC, memory footprint spiked to ~3.2GB vs usual 1.1GB for same model/seqLen.
- Downstream: small correlation with Redis latency jump (client observed 200ms -> 1.2s) around same time, but not all errors reference cache lookup.

Artifacts / versions involved:
- Canary image: gcr.io/redwood/canary-inference:2026-03-09-7f3a2b (image digest sha256:aa3f4d...).
- Stable image: gcr.io/redwood/inference:2026-02-26-9d1c8f (sha256:9b2c7e...).
- Model variant: v2-quant-8bit (on canary) vs v2-quant-8bit (stable) — same model, but runtime flags differ (canary had KV_CACHE=true, BATCHER=adaptive).
- Helm chart: release/producer v1.14.2 (no change from previous), but rollout controller logs show "featureFlag.kvEviction=experimental" enabled for canary label.

Commands I ran (copied from terminal):
- routed 100% back to stable (quick):
  # kubectl patch svc inference-route -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"canary":"false"}}}'
  -> svc updated, but ingress LB had cached routes for ~30s, verified using curl -I X-Canary header

- manual scale down
  kubectl scale deployment/inference-canary --replicas=0 -n prod
  -> terminated canary pods, but a few requests still hitting canary pods (stale endpoints in envoy), I ran envoy admin /clusters refresh on each node.

- garbage collection / purge local caches on redis client used by runtime:
  redis-cli -h redis-prod-01 BGREWRITEAOF
  redis-cli -h redis-prod-01 INFO memory
  -> memory high but not exhausted; no major evictions logged.

- inspected node metrics where OOM occurred:
  ssh into node node-usw2-45, checked dmesg -> saw OOM killer: PID 12345 (inference-process) killed after allocation failure.

Immediate hypotheses (ordered by likelihood in my head):
1) Canary runtime flags enabled KV_CACHE and experimental eviction algorithm -> caused memory leak under specific request shape (long sequences), leading to OOM and mid-request failures -> 5xx.
2) Indirect cascade: Redis latency spike caused runtime to retry/block, increasing memory pressure and KV cache growth -> OOM.
3) Model change? (unlikely, model artifact same tag) but maybe quantization path takes more transient memory in combination with BATCHER=adaptive -> larger batch windows -> memory spike.
4) Envoy routing stale endpoints caused some requests to hit half-dead pods -> 502 + 5xx noise, but doesn't explain memory usage.

Why rollback didn't fix everything immediately:
- Envoy/ingress caches endpoints for 20-30s; some nodes still had endpoints in warm pool.
- A few canary pods got into a crashloop and left partial state in Redis (locks) causing subsequent requests to block on slow redis ops.
- The autoscaler had created extra canary pods that inherited experimental flag; when we scaled down, some nodes continued to replay queued work (work-queue persisted to disk?) -> not fully sure.

Next immediate actions (short):
- Reproduce locally with high seqLen synthetic traffic and KV_CACHE enabled, reproduce memory growth trace. (Link: repro harness on my laptop: ./tools/repro/canary_kv_leak.sh)
- Disable featureFlag.kvEviction for rollout controller and rerun canary with controlled traffic (1% -> monitor for 30m).
- Patch runtime to add more logging around KV cache insert/size; deploy to staging and run load test.

Longer-term / follow-ups:
- Add a canary-gating step in CI: any runtime flag changes that touch cache/eviction require staging load test with long sequence traces.
- Add a kill-switch annotation to quickly force all nodes to refresh envoy config (or use service annotation to reduce TTL).
- Investigate if adaptive batcher increases transient memory beyond node resource limits; update resource requests to account for worst-case.

Quick checklist for postmortem entry (things to capture):
- exact image digests, runtime flag diffs, helm values diff (can get from release tags).
- timeline of autoscaler rep count, OOM events (kube node dmesg), envoy route cache delays.
- correlation graph of redis latency vs 5xx rate (30s bins).
- snippet of failing stacktrace + approximate line numbers for devs.

Notes-to-self:
- When doing fast revert next time: 1) drain canary pods from LB first (kubectl annotate svc ingress-proxy refresh=true) -> wait 45s -> scale down; 2) run envoy cluster refresh; 3) then heal redis if needed.
- Document the reproducer script path and make it executable for on-call.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Why did one node see memory spike while others didn't? Need to check request affinity / sticky sessions.
- Did the canary get a different config from central config store? (check configmap revision used in canary pods)
- Are there pending PRs that flip kvEviction flag? (cross-check linked PRs).

Scratch CLI snippets I want to save (for replay):
- get pod logs between times:
  kubectl logs -n prod inference-canary-7f3a2b --since=30m | sed -n '1,200p' > /tmp/canary-logs.txt
- collect stack traces if available:
  curl http://inference-canary-7f3a2b.prod:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 > /tmp/gors.txt
- quick heap dump (if process alive):
  kill -SIGUSR1 <pid> && scp node:/var/log/heapdump-*.prof ~/heapdumps/

Final quick mind-map (one liner):
- Probable: experimental KV eviction + adaptive batcher -> memory amplification on long seqLen -> OOM -> request failures; Redis latency likely amplified effect.

If anyone else reading: ping Marco/Jen if you see anything off in CI or the linked PR. Will convert to a proper incident timeline and postmortem after reproducer verified.

-- Aisha

title: Customer Governance Milestone Logbook - inference rollout
content:
Customer Governance Milestone Logbook - inference rollout

Working logbook that centralizes milestones, owners, risk scores, and active blockers for customer inference rollouts. Designed for QBR prep, renewal signal tracking, and fast escalation. Not final — this is the CS team's collaborative snapshot used to brief Solutions and Sales for go/no-go conversations.
M1 | Account kickoff & network scoping | owner: Daniel Rios | due: 2025-11-18 | status: complete | pct: 100 | risk: low | dependent: JIRA-CS-482
M2 | Private VPC peering and firewall rules validated | owner: Priya Kapoor | due: 2025-12-03 | status: complete | pct: 100 | risk: low | dependent: JIRA-INF-1203
M3 | Dedicated capacity sizing & cost estimate sign-off | owner: Maya Chen | due: 2025-12-15 | status: complete | pct: 100 | risk: medium | dependent: FIN-quote-189
M4 | Eval harness run (latency/throughput baselines) | owner: Leah O'Connor | due: 2026-01-12 | status: in_progress | pct: 65 | risk: medium | dependent: PERF-221
M5 | Prompt safety checks & PII extraction review | owner: Security SME (contract) | due: 2026-01-25 | status: in_review | pct: 50 | risk: high | dependent: SEC-33
M6 | Canary traffic ramp & feature flag gating | owner: Daniel Rios | due: 2026-02-10 | status: planned | pct: 0 | risk: medium | dependent: PL-88
M7 | Full production cutover checklist (ops runbook) | owner: Priya Kapoor | due: 2026-02-22 | status: planned | pct: 0 | risk: high | dependent: RUN-404
M8 | Post-cutover QBR and renewal-readiness review | owner: Maya Chen | due: 2026-03-01 | status: planned | pct: 0 | risk: medium | dependent: SALES-512
B-1 | Missing HSM key access to customer KMS in staging | impacted: M5, M6 | owner: Security SME (contract) | blocker_since: 2026-01-14 | mitigation: escalate to infra partner and DM to customer security; temporary signer cert in place until HSM access granted
B-2 | Inconsistent tokenization between customer preprocessing and model tokenizer causing reranking delta | impacted: M4 | owner: Leah O'Connor | blocker_since: 2026-01-08 | mitigation: patch preprocessor to use model-tokenizer lib; small data migration scheduled
