title: Event Log Mapping Playbook (v0.7 exploratory)
content:
Event Log Mapping Playbook (v0.7 exploratory)

Purpose:
This playbook captures a working approach to mapping runtime events into a compact, SIEM-friendly audit log schema and to surface a minimal evidence set for automated compliance workflows. It is intentionally pragmatic: close-to-runtime fields, conservative growth of the schema, and clear migration steps.

Context & constraints (quick):
- Need one canonical event model used by hosted API, Dedicated control plane, and Private deployment tooling.
- RBAC v2 introduces resource-scoped roles and ephemeral role bindings; logs must record enough to reconstruct authorization decisions without leaking PII.
- SIEM exports should align with common ECS-like conventions to ease ingestion by Splunk/Elastic/QRadar.
- Evidence automation (for audits) will pull a deterministic subset of fields per event-class.

Scope for this doc:
- Event naming conventions, core field set, severity mapping, and basic SIEM export map.
- RBAC v2 field guidance (what to log vs what to redact).
- Versioning and migration strategy v0.7 -> v1.0 candidate steps.
- Implementation checklist and open questions.

1) Event naming and taxonomy (short):
- Use dotted, lower-case nouns: auth.login.success, auth.login.failure, resource.access.denied, model.request.start, model.request.complete, model.fallback.
- Prefixes: auth.*, resource.*, model.*, deployment.*, system.*. Keep verbs to the rightmost segment.
- Event families should be broad; fine-grain detail lives in attributes map to keep index cost predictable.

2) Core audit schema (flat, SIEM-friendly):
- event_id: unique UUID for the event (string)
- event_ts: ISO8601 UTC timestamp (string)
- event_type: taxonomy name (string)
- severity: info|notice|warning|error|critical (string)
- outcome: success|failure|unknown (string)
- actor_id: opaque user id (redactable) (string)
- actor_role_ids: list of role ids applied during decision (list of strings)
- actor_role_names: OPTIONAL human-friendly names, redaction recommended in high-sensitivity customers (string)
- resource_type: e.g., model, dataset, project (string)
- resource_id: canonical resource identifier (string)
- request_id: request correlation id (string)
- service: product surface (hosted-api|dedicated|private-controlplane) (string)
- host_region: region tag (string)
- client_ip: IP or proxy tag (redact per policy) (string)
- user_agent: client user-agent (string)
- duration_ms: numeric-ish as string for indexing (string)
- payload_summary: small JSON blob-as-string summarizing request (trim to 1024 chars) (string)
- error_code: canonical error code if any (string)
- linked_evidence_ids: list of evidence artifact ids (list of strings)
- schema_version: semantic-ish v0.7 (string)

Notes: keep top-level fields flat. Extra diagnostic detail should be stored in an attached evidence artifact rather than in the main event body to reduce event size.

3) Event severity & outcome mapping guidance (examples):
- auth.login.failure: severity=warning, outcome=failure
- auth.login.success: severity=info, outcome=success
- model.request.start: severity=info, outcome=unknown
- model.request.complete (with fallback): severity=notice, outcome=success and set attribute fallback=true
- model.request.error (OOM, inference failure): severity=error, outcome=failure, attach stacktrace evidence id

4) SIEM export mapping (ECS-like suggested fields)
Purpose: a straightforward one-to-one mapping to accelerate ingestion. We recommend shipping both the raw event and the mapped ECS envelope. Minimal mapping:
- ecs.timestamp <- event_ts
- ecs.event.id <- event_id
- ecs.event.type <- event_type
- ecs.event.outcome <- outcome
- ecs.event.severity <- severity
- ecs.user.id <- actor_id
- ecs.user.name <- actor_role_names (only if permitted)
- ecs.network.client.ip <- client_ip (apply redaction rule)
- ecs.url.path <- resource_id (when resource is an API endpoint)
- ecs.service.name <- service
- ecs.duration.ms <- duration_ms
- ecs.stack_trace <- error evidence artifact (link)

Implementation note: produce a lightweight flattened ECS view for high-throughput consumers and store the full raw event for internal investigations.

5) RBAC v2 considerations (what to log):
- Log role ids and the binding id used for the decision. Role bindings are often ephemeral; record binding_ts to make the audit reconstructable.
- DO NOT log token values, full credentials, or private keys. Replace with token_hash if needed for correlation.
- For high-sensitivity customers (HIPAA/PII), default to recording role ids only, not role names. Provide a retrieval API (audit-only) to resolve role names via require-auth.
- Record policy version or policy-check-id to tie a decision to a policy revision.

6) Evidence automation (how events trigger evidence collection):
- Evidence levels: minimal, diagnostic, full. Each event_type maps to a required evidence level. Example mapping:
  - auth.login.failure -> minimal (auth headers sans tokens, timestamp, actor_id) + diagnostic on repeated failures
  - model.request.error -> diagnostic (request payload summary + model logs + stack trace)
  - deployment.rollout.failed -> full (deployment manifest, rollout diff, operator id)
- Evidence artifacts should be stored in a tamper-evident store (S3 versioned + KMS + immutable tags) and referenced by linked_evidence_ids.
- Evidence TTLs: evidence level drives retention class. Minimal: 90d; Diagnostic: 365d; Full: 7 years (enterprise customers may override).

7) Schema versioning and migration strategy (v0.7 -> v1.0):
- Semantic intent: vX.Y where X increments for breaking changes, Y for additive backwards-compatible fields. v0.7 is exploratory. v1.0 freeze planned when: RBAC v2 fields approved, evidence taxonomy stabilized, and SIEM mapping vetted by 2 customers.
- Backwards compatibility rules: always accept older schema_version values when reading. New fields must be optional and default to null/empty.
- Migration steps:
  1) Deploy ingestion that accepts both v0.7 and v1.0.
  2) Start emitting v0.8 with authoritative actor_role_ids list and binding_id.
  3) After 60 days of dual-emit, flip default to v1.0.
  4) Deprecate old fields with 90-day notice and maintain a translation layer for SIEM exports.

8) Performance & cost tradeoffs (practical):
- Keep event payload < 2KiB for high-traffic endpoints. Move large artifacts to evidence store.
- Index only the small subset of fields used in SLOs/alerts (event_ts, event_type, actor_id, outcome, severity).
- Batch-export to SIEM — use compressed NDJSON and incremental checkpoints.

9) Implementation checklist (short-term work items):
- [ ] Add schema_version to all event emitters (API surface, runtime, control plane).
- [ ] Implement actor_role_ids logging in auth middleware and include binding_id.
- [ ] Build evidence artifact API with put/get and immutability markers.
- [ ] Produce an ECS-mapped export transformer and integration test with SIEM partner.
- [ ] Draft RBAC v2 logging policy for customers (redaction defaults).
- [ ] Run load test on event sizes and SIEM export throughput.

10) Open questions / unresolved decisions (for sync):
- Should we include anonymous session tags (session_id) by default for model requests? Pros: easier correlation. Cons: increases PII surface.
- How aggressively do we redact user_agent and client_ip for on-prem customers vs hosted? Policy needed.
- Do we require immutable storage for evidence by default or opt-in per customer?

Appendix: Example event (flattened v0.7)
{"event_id":"6f7a8e2c-3b2a-4b0a-9c45-1a2b3c4d5e6f","event_ts":"2024-09-16T17:03:21Z","event_type":"model.request.complete","severity":"notice","outcome":"success","actor_id":"usr_8a3f","actor_role_ids":["role:reader:project-123"],"resource_type":"model","resource_id":"m:gpt-xxl:2024-09-10","request_id":"req_0019","service":"hosted-api","host_region":"us-west-2","duration_ms":"211","payload_summary":"prompt_length=532,answer_tokens=120","linked_evidence_ids":["evid_20240916_0001"],"schema_version":"v0.7"}

------
Notes to self: add suggested log size limits to SDK docs; coordinate with SRE on batching defaults. Come back to archive policy for evidence TTLs with legal.

End of playbook (work-in-progress).

title: Feature Sprocket Sketchbook
content:
Feature Sprocket Sketchbook

Purpose / elevator:
Quick personal sketch for a tiny feature I think could help small product teams prototype response templates and evaluate inference tradeoffs before full integration. Working name: Feature Sprocket (placeholder).

Problem we see:
- Engineers and PMs keep building one-off prompt wrappers and local fixtures to test LLM outputs. Hard to consistently compare latency/cost for variants (e.g., quantized model vs full fp16) and to preview user-facing templates.
- Console UX today exposes models + deployment config but not a lightweight composer that outputs: candidate responses, token/cost preview, and simple rollout gating.

Proposed micro-solution:
- A small in-console sandbox called Sprocket that lets you:
  * Author a response template (instruction + system + few-shot)
  * Add params/variables and example inputs (table-like rows)
  * Select 2-3 model variants and see side-by-side generated outputs
  * Show estimated tokens, estimated cost, and measured latency (from canary bench runs)
  * Save a template and pin it to a feature flag / route as a canary (10% traffic) with an easy rollback

Why this helps:
- Lowers friction to experiment with fallback strategies (cheap model + rerank) and to preview UX copy.
- Gives product folks a repeatable artifact (template + baseline metrics) they can attach to rollouts.
- Encourages cost-aware decisions earlier.

Core UX flows (very rough):
1) Create template: name, description, instruction box, variables list (key + example).
2) Add examples: upload CSV or paste rows. Each row becomes a test case.
3) Pick variants: dropdown to pick model variants (e.g., redwood/gptx-8b-qat, redwood/gptx-8b-fp16, open/model-lite-3b-q4).
4) Run preview: spins up warm mini-bench for each variant, returns sample outputs for first N rows, plus: avg latency, tokens consumed, estimated per-1k cost.
5) Snapshot & Save: store outputs + metrics as a named snapshot. Snapshots are immutable and can be used to create a rollout.
6) Lightweight rollout: from snapshot, choose route (api route id), percentage, and fallback policy (e.g., fallback to cheaper if latency>300ms).

Minimal API / CLI (notes):
- POST /sprocket/templates -> {name, instruction, variables, examples}
- POST /sprocket/templates/:id/preview -> {model_variants: [..], sample_limit: 5}
- POST /sprocket/snapshots -> snapshotId returned
- POST /sprocket/snapshots/:id/rollout -> {route, percent, fallback_policy}

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Authoring UI that accepts templates and example rows (CSV paste)
- Preview across at least 2 model variants with measured latency (synthetic bench) and token estimate
- Ability to save a snapshot and attach it to a simple rollout for a single API route with percentage and rollback toggle
- Snapshot + rollout are visible in Console under a new "Sprocket" list

Metrics to care about (early):
- Time to create a snapshot (median)
- # of snapshots created per team / week
- Snapshot-to-rollout conversion rate (how many snapshots become rollouts)
- Average per-request cost reduction when teams adopt a cheaper variant
- Rollback rate (signals instability or bad UX)

Edge cases & constraints: (brain dump)
- Preview accuracy vs production: bench runs need to be representative; risk of misleading numbers for cold-start heavy models.
- Security: templates may contain customer PII in examples — need redaction guidance and maybe opt-out from retention.
- Permissions: snapshots should respect org/team scoping and not leak between projects.
- Cost: running previews for many variants could be expensive — throttle or quota previews per user.

Open questions / decisions needed: (TODO)
- Is Sprocket a console-only feature or do we expose the API for programmatic tests? (Would be useful for CI.)
- What pricing/accounting model for preview runs? Free credits? chargeable as normal tokens?
- Snapshot retention policy: 90 days or user-configurable?
- Integration with Optimize: can we suggest quantization or batching knobs based on the sample inputs?

Implementation sketch / dev notes:
- Backend: lightweight preview runner that launches small ephemeral pods with selected model variant; warm up with prompt template + examples, run N samples; collect avg latency + token counts. Store metrics in telemetry table + snapshot blob.
- Data model: Template (id, owner, text, variables), Snapshot (templateId, variantResults[] as references to bench runs), Rollout (snapshotId, route, percent, fallback)
- Permissions: reuse console org/route RBAC
- SRE: limit concurrent previews per org to avoid overload during internal hackdays

Risks:
- Users will over-trust preview numbers and deploy incorrectly; need explicit caveats on variance and sample sizes.
- Operational cost may spike if preview is abused; enforce cost guardrails.

Next actions (personal TODO):
- Quick wireframe: two panes (editor / preview table). Sketch on Miro. (task: create Miro board)
- Slack poll to get product & DX vibes: is this useful? (ask @mateo, @sana, @rhea)
- Draft a short RFC for product review (1 page) and link to JIRA-PI-4821.

Notes-to-self:
- Keep scope narrow for MVP: no complex rerank orchestration, just compare model outputs + metrics.
- Consider exporting snapshots as JSON for attaching to PRs so engineers can run the same snapshot locally.

Example user story (for backlog):
- As a PM, I want to create a response template and compare outputs between the default hosted model and a quantized cheaper variant so I can choose a model that balances cost and quality for an assistant feature.
  Acceptance: PM can save a snapshot that shows side-by-side outputs for 3 examples, and the console shows estimated cost delta and avg latency for each variant.

Closing thought:
- This feels like a very high-ROI lean feature that maps to the company thesis (making inference decisions predictable and economical). Build something that nudges teams to measure costs early without forcing infra changes.

Scratchy brainstorm phrases: 
- "snapshot-as-contract" idea (immutable test artifact)
- local->cloud parity: export snapshot to run against local private deployment for parity checks
- quick-rollout templates for marketing experiments (non-dev PMs like simple toggle UI)

End of sketch.

title: Handoff Journeyboard Weekly Inspection
content:
Handoff Journeyboard Weekly Inspection

Purpose: informal weekly inspection of oncall handoffs, two small incidents, and SLO drift that surfaced during night shifts. This is a working note — gaps, TODOs, and hypothesis sections intentionally left half-formed for the next shift to pick up.

TL;DR:
- Two short incidents this week; both mitigated quickly. No customer-visible downtime, but recurring tail latency spikes for model shards.
- SLO snapshot: 99.7% p99 within target (target 99.9%) for the 7-day window; drift correlates with KV cache eviction storms during long-sequence workloads.
- Immediate handoff checklist updated with new KV cache knob to try during noisy auto-scale events.

Summary of events (timeline):
- 2029-04-16 03:22 UTC — Incident RW-INC-2029-1145: p99 latency spike in hosted inference route /v1/chat for region: eu-west-1. Triggered pager, bridge opened. Initial symptom: steady stream of slow requests (p95->p99), worker metrics show abrupt KV cache miss rate jump and increased memory churn on infer-g1 pods.
  - Mitigation steps taken: scaled infer-g1 pool + applied temporary throttle on long-sequence requests (seq > 1200) via routing rule. Brought p99 back under threshold in ~9 minutes.
  - Root-cause hypothesis (interim): a)) background housekeeping job on storage node S3-sync triggered large object re-reads causing network congestion to GPU hosts OR b)) a quantized model variant fallback caused larger-than-usual KV entries and increased cache pressure. Need trace logs to confirm.
  - Notes: applied manual eviction policy (ttl 20s) to secondary kv namespace to relieve memory pressure; removal flagged as a temporary emergency config.

- 2029-04-16 18:05 UTC — Ops noise: autoscaler misfired during a short but intense synthetic traffic spike from customer test harness RW-OPS-3456. Resulted in 2x cold starts and a transient spike in tail latency for dedupe route. No page. Followed by a billing spike alert (billing-warn) that flagged heavy retry traffic.
  - Action: reached out to Solutions Eng to contain rogue test, added rate limit exception and noted to add a guard in the autoscaler to ignore synthetic-signed test tokens.

SLO / metrics snapshot (7d rolling):
- p50: 26ms (target 30ms)
- p95: 138ms (target 150ms)
- p99: 910ms (target 700ms) -> current shortfall driven by cache-eviction episodes and cold-starts
- error rate: 0.03% (well below 0.2% threshold)
- availability: 99.996%

Observed signals and correlations:
- KV cache miss-rate correlates strongly with p99 latency spikes when sequence length distribution shifts right (customers sending longer contexts). See attached metrics (linked below).
- Memory churn and kernel context-switches on infer-g1 hosts appear to co-occur with network egress bursts to object storage (varnish-like behaviour).
- Autoscaler thresholding currently uses 60s lookback; short synthetic bursts create flapping.

Immediate mitigations and config changes applied (ephemeral):
- Temporary route-level throttle for sequences >1200 for eu-west-1 (rollback planned after 48h observation). Ticket: RW-OPS-3489.
- Reduced secondary KV namespace TTL to 20s to limit memory accumulation during high churn windows. (Reverted if regressions).
- Manual bump of infer-g1 pool by +25% for 3 hours during peak maintenance window.

Handoff checklist updates (what next on Monday AM shift):
- Verify rollback hooks: ensure TTL change is recorded in config audit and Revert playbook (runbook ref RW-runbook-kv-evictions).
- Start trace-sampling at 100% for /v1/chat in eu-west-1 for 1 hour to capture full KV cache lifecycle for impacted requests.
- Verify whether the storage housekeeping job overlapped the incident window (check infra-scheduler logs, job id possibly: infra-hs-20290416-02).
- Add autoscaler guard to ignore tokens matching test harness signature (Pattern: RW-TEST-*). Put as a quick patch: autoscale-ignore-list.
- Add a simple sequencelength-aware routing rule to separate long-context requests to a lower-cost variant with pre-warmed instances. (Design spike required).

Longer-term follow-ups and owners: (estimate / backlog prioritization)
- Investigate root cause of KV cache pressure (owner: Luca) — collect trace-level artifacts and map object sizes in kv store. Target: next week deep-dive.
- Autoscaler resilience improvements (owner: Samira) — add debounce window and synthetic-token exclusion. Feasibility spike: 3 days.
- Pre-warm strategy for long-sequence inference (owner: Omar) — experiment with mini-pools pinned to quantized variants. Prototype by EoQ.
- Add regression alert tied to per-route KV miss-rate that fires before p99 breach (owner: Maya)

Notes to next oncall (direct):
- If you see repeated p99 spikes after a TTL rollback, re-enable full-sampled tracing and escalate to infra-networking (channel #infra-egress).
- Avoid broad TTL changes during EU peak hours; prefer targeted namespace adjustments.
- If autoscaler triggers >3 times in 10 minutes, open a P1 and start bridge immediately — flapping autoscale correlates with client retry storms.

Open questions / hypothesis bank (for investigation):
- Did a model fall-back to a different quantized kernel increase KV footprint per request? Confirm with model-catalog logs and variant rollouts around 2029-04-16 03:00–04:00 UTC.
- Is object-store re-read latency causing kernel stall on GPU host? Likely if network queues fill. Need netstat/ifconfig dumps correlated with kernel logs.
- Could a GC/compaction in the secondary kv backend be scheduled during EU night windows? Check maintenance windows.

Meeting notes / sync items for Friday triage (2029-04-19):
- Deep-dive scheduled 2029-04-19 16:00 UTC (30m) — agenda: attach traces, compare kv sizes, review autoscaler logs, decisions on pre-warm prototype. Invites to include: eng-sre, serving-runtime, infra-networking, solutions-eng.
- Deliverable: prioritized action list and an A/B test plan for sequencelength-aware routing.

Appendix (quick links):
- Incident ticket RW-INC-2029-1145 (pager notes and timeline)
- Autoscaler history RW-OPS-3456
- KV runbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/kv-cache-runbook
- Slack: #sre-eu oncall, #infra-egress

Quick raw logs excerpts (copied here for convenience):
- "2029-04-16T03:21:57Z infer-g1-7f4b: kv-miss-rate increased from 4.2% -> 37.9% within 90s"
- "2029-04-16T03:23:12Z network-egress host-120: retransmits spike 12x baseline"

Scratch / notes-to-self:
- Try a controlled run with synthetic long sequences but with cold cache to reproduce. Use small subset of EU infra to avoid broader noise.
- Add a monitoring dashboard tile for per-namespace cache size and eviction rate.

Action items (short):
- [Luca] Collect full trace dump + model variant logs (due 2029-04-18).
- [Samira] Autoscaler debounce patch PR and quick test (due 2029-04-22).
- [Omar] Design doc stub for pre-warm pool and sequencelength routing (due 2029-04-30).
- [Maya] Create regression alert for KV-miss -> p99 coupling (due 2029-04-19).

End of notes.

-- Maya (oncall)

title: candidate-shadow-week-summary-team-health-feb28-2026
content:
candidate-shadow-week-summary-team-health-feb28-2026

Context and purpose:
- This doc captures notes from the candidate "shadow" week (Feb 23–27) where three finalists were paired with eng-platform teams for short rotations. Also includes a snapshot of onboarding friction items and an ad-hoc team health pulse from the week.

Attendees (shadow sessions + debrief):
- Sophie Chen (owner, shadow coordinator)
- Aisha Patel (hiring lead, interviews)
- Ben Huang (senior infra eng, buddy for candidate C)
- Marco Alvarez (sre/ops buddy for candidate B)
- Riley Thompson (platform eng PM)
- Interviewer rotation: Dana, Kurt, Melissa (notes consolidated below)

High-level outcomes:
- We observed good systems thinking across all three candidates; each showed strength in debugging complex infra issues but varied on production tradeoffs (cost vs latency).
- Candidate A (backend infra) recommended for hire with a condition: needs more exposure to Redwood’s serving runtime internals (approx 4–6 weeks ramp).
- Candidate B (sre leaning) is a strong cultural fit but slower on our internal orchestration patterns; recommend follow-up take-home on autoscaler scenarios before final offer.
- Candidate C (embedded infra/ops) performed well on runbook creation and incident postmortem; flagged for potential senior IC track but pinged for leadership readiness check.

Detailed candidate notes:
- Candidate A (id: cand-A):
  - Shadowed Ben on a KV-cache mismatch debug (ticket JIRA-3421). Candidate quickly formulated hypothesis about stale cache shards and suggested a non-invasive canary to validate.
  - Strengths: clear runbook-first mindset, good telemetry reading, comfortable with flamegraph traces and kernel-level noise.
  - Risks: limited exposure to Triton-style batching internals. Onboarding plan: pair with runtime team for 2 sessions/week for first month.
  - Hiring recommendation: Offer (IC3) with 30-day technical mentorship goals.

- Candidate B (id: cand-B):
  - Paired with Marco on autoscaler simulation (JIRA-3499). Showed solid chaos engineering instincts but initially missed our CPU vs GPU scheduling nuances.
  - Strengths: incident response ownership, calm under noisy alerts, empathy with product owners.
  - Risks: needs deeper familiarity with our custom scheduler heuristics and cost-aware routing policies.
  - Action: assign a 48-hour take-home modeling exercise focused on rate-based autoscaling; revisit by Mar 10.

- Candidate C (id: cand-C):
  - Worked with team on runbook and postmortem draft for a recent rate-limiting regression. Draft was pragmatic and prioritized rollback/mitigation.
  - Strengths: strong documentation and on-call hygiene; good cross-team communication.
  - Risks: ambiguous around mentoring junior engineers (leadership signals weaker).
  - Hiring recommendation: Hire (IC2–IC3 flex) pending reference check and an org-fit conversation on mentorship expectations.

Onboarding friction log (items surfaced during shadow week):
- Dev laptop imaging delay: two hires last week waited ~3 days for GPU-enabled VM access. Ticketed as internal ops backlog (JIRA-ops-1120).
- VPN/KMS onboarding: one candidate couldn’t access staging KMS due to stale SSO mapping; follow-up needed with security to streamline service-account onboarding (assigned to Aisha).
- Local debugging: missing local replica datasets (~20GB) for runtime profiling — short-term fix: provide a lightweight sampled dataset and a documented profiling checklist. Owner: Ben.
- Documentation gaps: runtime-contrib onboarding doc is out of date (mentions old quantization flags). Action: create a living checklist for first-30-days tasks. Owner: Riley & Sophie.

Buddy-rotation feedback (from new hires / candidates):
- Positive: buddy rotations helped candidates get realistic on-call context within 24h. Specific shoutout to Ben for practical debugging walkthroughs.
- Improvement: shorten rotation notes to a 1-pager ‘what I learned’ for quicker handoffs.
- Suggestion: formalize a 2-week buddy schedule that maps to concrete milestones (access, local run, first PR).

Team health snapshot (quick pulse from Feb 27 standup + ad-hoc check-ins):
- Hiring sentiment: 2 hires expected to close in March (pending offers), which should temporarily relieve bus factor on runtime infra tasks.
- Burn indicators: a couple of ICs reported >50% context-switching last week due to incident triage; SRE rotation bandwidth is tight.
- Morale: generally positive; small frustration about PR review latency (avg 3.7 days for platform PRs last sprint).
- Signals to watch: onboarding time-to-first-PR metric (goal: <=10 calendar days). Current baseline: 14 days. Owner: Riley to propose process changes.

Unresolved questions / decisions needed:
- Do we require a take-home for all SRE-ish candidates? (Pros: better signal; Cons: slows hiring funnel). Proposal: keep take-home optional but required for senior roles. Vote needed from hiring committee by Mar 5.
- What’s acceptable ramp plan for Candidate A if we hire (mentor capacity)? Need mentor assignment before offer.
- Should we prioritize automating GPU VM provisioning to reduce imaging time to <24h? Cost/benefit analysis needed.

Action items (owners + tentative due dates):
- Aisha: finalize interview feedback rubric for SRE candidates (due Mar 5).
- Ben: provide sampled profiling dataset + quickstart doc (due Mar 6).
- Riley: draft 2-week buddy schedule + propose PR review SLAs (due Mar 9).
- Sophie: run reference checks for Candidate C and schedule mentorship-readiness quick chat for Candidate A (due Mar 6).
- Security contact (cc Aisha): resolve SSO/KMS mapping edge-case; status update by Mar 4.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep candidate shadow week — high signal, worth the scheduling pain. More structure next round (explicit checklist).
- Consider a short postmortem template for candidate-led runbooks to compare across candidates.

References and links:
- JIRA-3421: KV-cache mismatch debug (internal ticket)
- JIRA-3499: Autoscaler simulation worklog
- CONFLUENCE-PLAT-281: Onboarding checklist (needs update)

title: Annotation curation daybook — edge cleanup notes
content: Annotation curation daybook — edge cleanup notes Personal daybook for ad-hoc heuristics, quick adjudication notes, and small triage decisions. Mostly shorthand. Goal: capture instincts + examples so future rounds can flip into a short rules doc later. Top-level goals (reminder): - Keep label set conservative: prefer fewer but higher-precision spans for first-pass. - Flag ambiguous examples with helpful example-based guidance rather than blanket rules. - When in doubt, capture canonical / normalized form as additional metadata field (if pipeline allows) rather than changing span boundaries. Quick heuristics (operational): 1) Overlapping company/person spans - If one span is clearly an honorific + last name ("Dr. Patel") and the other is full name ("Dr. Sameer Patel"), prefer full-name span. - If short span is an acronym contained in long span ("OpenAI" inside "OpenAI Research Lab"), label the longer span but add alias=\"OpenAI\" as metadata where possible. 2) Currency + unit noise - Preserve original token sequence for token-level audits, but normalize separate fields: amount_numeric, currency_code. - Samples: Raw: "€1.200,50" -> amount_numeric: "1200.50", currency_code: "EUR" Raw: "$1,234.00 (USD)" -> amount_numeric: "1234.00", currency_code: "USD" - Heuristic: detect locale separators (".," vs ",.") heuristically by presence of currency symbol and digit groups; fall back to human review for ambiguous formats. 3) Noisy transcripts / filler words - Remove filler tokens from entity spans ("uh", "um", repeated dashes) unless they change meaning. - Example: "um John Smith" -> span: "John Smith". Keep a "raw_span" field for provenance. 4) Partial-label policy (when annotator marks partial overlaps) - If a candidate span overlaps >= 70% token coverage of a canonical entity, accept and mark as "partial_confirmed". - <70% -> send to adjudication queue with 3 sample neighbors for context. Example adjudication entries (copy into triage queue): - ID: daybook-001 Raw: "Sent from support-team@acme.co on 2023-05-09" Candidate labels: EMAIL: "support-team@acme.co" OR ORG: "acme.co" Decision: prefer EMAIL for single token with @; add ORG alias by domain extraction. - ID: daybook-002 Raw: "When we say 'the bank', which org? Wells or First National?" Candidate labels: ORG ambiguous -> require doc-level resolution, mark as 'ambiguous-org' until doc metadata supplied. Span examples (bad -> better): - Bad: label COMPANY: "Acme" when context requires "Acme, Inc." Better: COMPANY: "Acme, Inc." with alias: ["Acme"] - Bad: label ADDRESS: "5th Ave" when full address is present across tokens with PO box nearby Better: capture full address span, mark subspan "5th Ave" as LOCATION_SUBPART. HTML / markup noise - Strip obvious HTML tags from spans but capture them in raw_text. Eg: "Acme" -> span: "Acme". If tags convey semantics (like or ) keep a note in metadata: markup_tag=["a"] Multilingual partials - If entity split across language boundaries (EN/ES): keep single contiguous span if tokens are adjacent and represent same logical entity. Add lang_hint if script differs. Adjudicator quick checklist (for messy items): - Is the span semantically self-contained? - Does normalization fix the issue (currency/date canonicalization)? If yes, prefer normalization + keep span. - Would adding an alias / metadata preserve downstream behavior better than changing span? Prefer metadata when safe. Open questions / TODOs (prioritized): - Q1: How do we treat abbreviated legal suffixes in another language ("S.A.", "GmbH") when annotators vary on inclusion? Proposed: default include if token adjacent to name, but add rule to collapse common suffix variants in normalization step. - Q2: Should we add a "confidence_hint" token-level tag when an annotator marks uncertain? (Useful for active learning sampling). - Q3: Edgecase: timestamps lacking year. Many logs have dates like "Mar 3 10:21"; for annotation, we currently leave as literal. Consider heuristics to infer year from doc metadata. Micro examples for sanity-check training set (copy-paste friendly): 1) "Refund issued: GBP 45.00 to kevin.o'reilly@example.com" Labels: AMOUNT: "GBP 45.00" -> amount_numeric: "45.00", currency_code: "GBP"; EMAIL: "kevin.o'reilly@example.com" 2) "Call with Dr. S. Kwon—rescheduled" Labels: PERSON: "Dr. S. Kwon"; prefer including honorific when present. 3) "Order #4567 (Acme Corp.) shipped" Labels: ORDER_ID: "#4567"; ORG: "Acme Corp." (include parenthesis cleanup) Short-term tags to add to pipeline: ["partial_confirmed","ambiguous-org","markup_stripped","locale_amount"] (these are adhoc — will be formalized later). Notes to self: keep this daybook minimal; move stable heuristics to a living doc in shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml/labeling-guides once we have consensus. When moving, include representative examples and failure cases (with ticket refs). Random thought: build a tiny CLI that given raw token sequence suggests canonicalization + a "why" explanation (rule id + sample match). Would speed up adjudication. End of entry for 2025-02-11.

title: Colocation rack power & cooling planning — on-prem GPU pools (Q2 2026)
content:
Colocation rack power & cooling planning — on-prem GPU pools (Q2 2026)

Purpose:
Plan for next-phase on-prem / colo GPU pool growth: define per-rack power and cooling budgets, physical U-space layouts, PDU/amperage constraints, and rollout checklist for Q2 2026. This is an operational planning sheet — rough numbers and open questions are intentionally included.

Summary / goals:
- Add 48 x A800-equivalent GPUs across two colo sites (site A + site B) to support Dedicated surge capacity and private-customer pools.
- Target average rack PUE and cooling capacity so we don’t exceed facility power draw and can keep inlet temps <= 30C under 95th percentile load.
- Prefer 1:1 cold-aisle containment where feasible; evaluate water-cooled trays if density > 40 GPUs/rack.

High-level assumptions (call these out):
- GPU model used for baseline calculations: NVIDIA Hopper-class A800 (nominal max TDP 350W).
- Typical node: 8x A800 per 2U chassis (8 GPUs per node), with dual PSUs and 3U networking overhead for dense configs.
- Node idle draw: ~120W per GPU-equivalent (includes CPU, NVMe, fans under light load).
- Service overhead per rack: 1 top-of-rack switch (800W), KVM, management 200W.
- Facility power deliverable per rack: negotiable; baseline target is 20kW per rack (208V, 3-phase with 80A PDUs), can push to 30kW with water-cooling/engineering signoff.
- Target operating margin: reserve 15% headroom below facility PDU limit for transient spikes.

Detailed capacity math (baseline):
- Per GPU sustained draw estimate: 300W (conservative for mixed inference workloads).
- For 8 GPUs/node, node draw = 8 * 300W + 200W (CPUs/SSD/fans) = 2,600W ≈ 2.6kW.
- With 42U rack and conservative spacing (account for 3U network + PDUs), we can fit 16 nodes (32U used) => total compute draw = 16 * 2.6kW = 41.6kW (too high for simple air-cooled rack).
- Air-cooled safe configuration (20kW per rack): back-calc nodes supported = floor((20kW - 1.0kW overhead) / 2.6kW) = floor(19kW / 2.6kW) = 7 nodes => 56 GPUs/rack at ~300W/GPU seems inconsistent with earlier density numbers because node size assumption must be rechecked.
- Alternative realistic packing: 4 nodes per rack (2U nodes) would be 8 GPUs/node => 16 GPUs/rack? That’s low density but fits 20kW budget.

Candidate rack profiles (quick variants):
- Profile A — Air-cooled standard (priority: simplicity, lower colo cost)
  - Power budget: 20kW per rack (80A 3-phase); usable ~17kW after 15% headroom.
  - Node config: 2U, 4 nodes/rack (8 GPUs/node) = 32 GPUs/rack.
  - Estimated draw: 32 * 300W + 1.2kW overhead = 10.8kW => comfortably under budget; leaves room for bursty workloads or denser nodes later.
  - Pros: widely supported by colo, cheaper. Cons: lower density, higher rack count.

- Profile B — High-density air + enhanced airflow (containment)
  - Power budget: 24kW per rack (requires colo approval).
  - Node config: 2U, 8 nodes/rack = 64 GPUs/rack (if mechanical layout allows).
  - Estimated draw: 64 * 300W + 1.5kW overhead = 20.7kW => within 24kW.
  - Cons: requires cold-aisle containment and higher fan noise/maintenance; risk if cooling fails.

- Profile C — Liquid-assisted high-density
  - Power budget: 30kW+ per rack, water-cooled rear-door or direct-to-chip allowed.
  - Node config: 4U or specialized trays, 128 GPUs/rack feasible with D2C.
  - Use when we need minimal floor space (e.g., enterprise private racks).
  - Draw: depends on vendor; ensure leak-detection and redundancy.

Site-by-site initial plan (two colo sites):
- Site A (primary): 12 racks available; initial commit: 6 racks. Choose mix: 4 x Profile A, 2 x Profile B to balance density.
  - Compute capacity estimate (approx): (4 * 32) + (2 * 64) = 128 + 128 = 256 GPUs initial.
- Site B (secondary / DR): 8 racks available; initial commit: 4 racks of Profile A for predictable cooling.
  - Capacity: 4 * 32 = 128 GPUs.
- Combined initial on-prem/colo pool: ~384 GPUs across sites. Scaling plan: add 6 racks over 6 months as demand grows.

Power & electrical notes (actionable):
- PDUs: prefer 2x 63A 3-phase PDUs per rack (A+B) on separate feeds. Specify monitoring PDUs with per-outlet metering (Vendor quote VC-3321 covers metered PDUs).
- Breaker requirements: ensure dedicated 3-phase breakers; confirm site wiring (is it 208V vs 400V?) — open question for Site B.
- Generator/UPS: target N+1 UPS for racks serving production Dedicated customers; confirm UPS runtime at expected draw (e.g., 10 racks at 20kW each -> 200kW draw).

Cooling & mechanical notes:
- Baseline air-cooled racks: ensure cold-aisle containment and Aisle-Inlet temp sensors at multiple heights (bottom, mid, top).
- Recommend vendor-supplied airflow management hardware (blanking panels, baffles) for dense racks.
- If any rack > 22kW, require cold-door/water cooling conversation. Obtain quote for Rear Door Heat Exchanger (RDHx) for two candidate racks at Site A.
- Facility PUE target: negotiate for <1.6 at site level for racks consumed by GPU fleet.

Space planning (U count):
- Reserve 3U per rack for networking and management (not counted in GPU capacity).
- Cable management: plan 2U front and rear for cable trays in Profile B/C.
- Weight: approximate 80kg per 2U node (incl rails), ensure floor loading > 1500kg per rack. Confirm with colo.

Network and I/O constraints:
- To avoid top-of-rack bottlenecks, provision 2 x 100GbE uplinks per rack (LACP) and optional 1 x 400Gb spine links later.
- Topology: flat fabric for dedicated clusters; per-tenant VLAN segmentation for private pools.

Cost drivers (rough estimates to include in procurement):
- Colo power premium for >20kW racks: +$2,500 / rack/month vs standard 10kW baseline.
- RDHx retrofit: ~$6k–10k per rack + maintenance.
- Metered PDU (2x63A): ~$2k–3k per rack.
- Installation / commissioning labor: ~16–24 hours per rack.

Open questions / risks (to resolve before ordering):
- Confirm Site B phase/wiring and PDU amperage availability (ticket to colo ops).
- Confirm regulatory/compliance requirements for any customer data in private racks (KMS/HSM proximity).
- Failure modes for RDHx: plan for bypass if water cooling offline — automatic fallback to lower-power mode with GPU shedding policy.
- Spare parts: how many spare nodes and spare PSUs to stock per site? Suggest 2 spare nodes per 12 racks.

Immediate next steps (owner / ETA):
- [Sana] Draft vendor RFQ for PDUs and RDHx (ETA 2026-03-08) — link: GH PR above.
- [Ethan] Verify Site B electrical specs with colo rep and upload power diagram (ETA 2026-03-05).
- [Priya] Cost model update for colo tiers and expected monthly burn; incorporate into Dedicated pricing sheet (ETA 2026-03-12).
- [Luca] Run thermal simulation for Profile B racks using baseline workload traces (ETA 2026-03-15).

Appendix: example per-rack quick checklist for install day
- Confirm 3-phase feeds present and separate PDUs installed (A/B).
- Verify rack grounding and bonding.
- Measure floor loading and confirm seismic/anchoring as required.
- Install blanking panels and airflow management hardware before powering nodes.
- Connect and configure metered PDU and integrate with DCIM alerting.
- Run load tests to 95th percentile expected token throughput for 2 hours and confirm inlet temps < 30C.

Notes to self (raw):
- Might need to standardize on a slightly lower-GPU TDP profile (e.g., 260W) for some private customer racks to avoid costly watercooling.
- Check with legal about language for colo contracts referencing liquid-cooling equipment.
- Keep a two-week buffer between receiving racks and provisioning GPUs (cable/PDUs/testing).

End of sheet — comments welcome.

title: Sentinel Thera Archivist
content:
Sentinel Thera Archivist

Enterprise health system evaluating Redwood Private/Dedicated for PHI-safe RAG search. POC running on de-identified subset; main risks are Epic connector sign-off and PHI data transfer approvals. Strong chance if POC meets latency/cost targets and security attestation provided.
Goal: build RAG search for 25-40M clinical documents (notes, imaging reports, messages). Plan: 1536-dim dense embeddings + BM25 hybrid retrieval; thin-client reranker with cross-encoder for top-100 -> top-5. Target p95 end-to-end query latency <= 200ms (aim 120-150ms) for rerank path; QPS expected 8-12 steady with bursts to 60. Cost target < $0.03 per user query after batching/caching. title: Lodestar Retail AI
content:
Lodestar Retail AI

▶ Summary: POC completed (month-long): integrated personalization model, latency target ~150ms p50 across NA. Results met functional QoE but economics gap large.

▶ What happened:
- AE/SE ran model variants (ffhq-open-65B quantized + 8-bit int8 on dedicated droplet) during POC. Token usage tracked at ~18M tokens/wk for personalization pipelines.
- Finance pushed back: projected monthly GPU burn + per-token costs leave payback >18 months given current ARR profile.
- Procurement flagged minimum commit as too high (preferred smaller commit or spot/usage).
- Internal champion (Dir. ML Ops, Priya Rao) moved to a new role; no replacement champion identified.

▶ Customer quotes / paraphrase:
- "Tech works — latency is excellent. But numbers don't close for us; model runtime costs are the killer." — Priya Rao (during wrap call)
- "Competitor offered dedicated instance with steep commit discount — procurement liked the guaranteed unit cost."

▶ Economics details discussed:
- Redwood proposal: 2x V100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated) reserved, expected token cost $0.0025/token for generation profile.

title: Elm Avenue Bistro AI
content:
Elm Avenue Bistro AI

Lead source: inbound self-serve signup (trial credits used). Small regional cafe chain exploring chat/reservation bot to reduce phone hold times. Currently front-end chat widget (React) calls Redwood hosted API in us-east-1.

Initial problem: customers report the bot feels slow during busy lunch hours. CX measured page-level timings ~800ms median but p95 spikes 2.2s. Elm's internal threshold for 'acceptable' is p95 < 1s for short assistant replies (one-line confirmations), and <2s for multi-turn reservation flows.

Observed behavior and clues:
- Trial account created 2026-02-19, integration via fetch POST to /v1/complete with streaming disabled.
- They are sending full menu + user message in every prompt (avg prompt size ~1.2k tokens), which spikes latency and cost.
- Widget sets client-side timeout to 3s; users see "service unavailable" before Redwood finishes generation on p95.
- Geo: majority of customers in West Coast NA; AE noted they used default us-east-1 region on accident (cheap tutorial).
- No SE-level security gating; require SSO later for enterprise customers but not for current pilot.

Meetings / timeline:
- 2026-02-20: 15m intro call (Ava) — walked through trial usage, live demo of site. Fireflies id ff_20260302_elm-01
- 2026-03-02: 45m technical sync (Marc + dev lead Priya) — captured logs, agreed to test us-west-2 latency, try streaming, and reduce prompt size by moving menu to hosted embedding + retrieval.
- 2026-03-05: Quick follow-up email with sample prompt templates and recommended timeouts (thread-1732-elmbistro-trial).

Key requirements / notes for Redwood ops:
- Workload: chat + short confirmations, occasional reservation flow that needs slot-filling (multi-turn). Estimated traffic ~60-200 requests/hour peak (weekdays lunch). Concurrency low but spikes matter during lunch rush.
- Targets: p50 < 400ms, p95 < 1.0s for one-turn replies; p95 < 1.8s acceptable for multi-turn flows.
- Cost sensitivity: high — SMB budget, looking for hosted credits then entry plan; wants to keep model choice below $/k-token thresholds.
- Model preferences: open to small/medium open models (ggml/quantized) but prioritizes latency and cost. Wants automatic region routing if possible.

Perf tuning suggestions discussed (AE/SE notes):
- Region choice: recommend moving primary endpoints to us-west-2 or us-west-1 for majority-of-users West Coast traffic; run A/B: us-east-1 vs us-west-2 over 48h, measure p50/p95.
- Prompt guidance: separate static menu (embed + retrieval or vector DB) instead of including full menu in every turn; use short system prompts and structured few-shot examples; aim for <300 token prompts for common queries.
- Timeout settings: advise client timeout >= 10s for reservation flows, and keep optimistic 3-4s for one-line confirmations but degrade gracefully (show still-typing state). Suggest server-side idle/response timeout set to 30s.
- Streaming: enable streaming (chunked) to improve perceived latency for user facing UI; will reduce apparent wait even if model token time similar.
- Batching/caching: enable prefix KV caching for repeated small confirmations; recommend caching common responses for menu items.
- Model/routing: try smaller, faster model for confirmations; route multi-turn reservation flows to higher-capacity model variant.

Open items / next actions:
- AE (Ava) to send perf tuning checklist + region test script (by 2026-03-10) — ACTION: pending
- SE (Marc) to provide sample embedding pipeline + cost estimate for embedding-hosted menu (by 2026-03-12)

Customer quotes and attitudes:

- Very price conscious: asked "how much will this cost if we keep it in production for 6 months?"

Data residency: US-only for certain datasets.\n- POC scope agreed: 10M doc ingest (subset of contracts + communications), build index, run baseline embeddings + simple cosine, then compare with learned reranker. POC success metrics: 10-15% nDCG improvement vs baseline and p95 rerank latency <120ms.\n- Commercial: leaning enterprise reserved capacity or Private deployment. title: Teal Ink Studio
content:
Teal Ink Studio

Inbound self-serve signup on 2026-02-18, signed up with company email; tested quickstart and hit parsing issues when enabling streaming + json mode. Wants small POC for chat-based structured responses (order forms, appointment JSON output). AE reached out 2026-02-20, discovery call 2026-03-02. Key quote from CTO: "We need reliable JSON-only outputs; our front-end will fail if the assistant emits stray text."

Current technical summary (from SE triage):
- Customer uses hosted API, streaming=true, json_mode=enabled (front-end parses by incrementally concatenating stream chunks).
- Symptoms: occasional partial payloads with trailing commas, or helper text like "Note:" inserted before the JSON start when the model is uncertain. Sometimes the "function_call" payload arrives but then plain text follows causing parser errors.
- Repro steps captured in meeting recording (ff-2026-03-04-02): provided sample prompt that asks for function-like object (name, args) and requested strict schema with required fields id, type, payload. Parser fails ~15% of calls under burst load (50 rps PoC).
- SE repro: ran 200 requests against hosted model "redwood-medium-1" with streaming; observed non-deterministic extra text in ~12/200 streams; without streaming (non-streaming mode) outputs are consistently valid JSON. Suspect streaming event framing + model fallback behavior when uncertain about schema.
- Temporary workaround: use non-streaming responses and post-parse with a strict JSON sanitizer (loses latency benefit). Another mitigation: instruct model with very strict system prompt and wrap JSON in triple-backticks but still saw edge cases.

Security/compliance notes: Teal Ink prefers public cloud (no VPC requirement right now). Ask for SOC2 attestation; they requested audit logging details for hosted API. CTO flagged GDPR retention questions for message logs but not a blocker to continue trial.

Commercial: SMB price sensitivity; likely to start at low-usage monthly plan and scale if reliability is proven. Expect decision after a short PoC (2-4 weeks).

Next actions logged:

SLA / contract specifics requested by HelixCare (summary of asks):
- Uptime target: 99.99% for prod endpoints; want calendar-year measurement with monthly reporting.
- Credit schedule: prefer graduated credits: 10% monthly service credit for monthly uptime 99.90%–99.99%, 30% credit for 99.0%–99.90%, and termination rights if <99.0% for two consecutive months. Pushback: Redwood proposed 5% / 15% bands.
- Maintenance windows: HelixCare requires planned maintenance to be scheduled in a 2-hour window between 02:00–05:00 local (customer-hosted region); emergency maintenance requires 12‑hour notice and joint rollback plan.
- Support SLAs: P1 initial response < 15 minutes (phone + Slack), P1 mitigation plan within 4 hours, P2 response within 1 business hour, followed by 24‑72h resolution targets. HelixCare requests a named escalation path and monthly incident review.
- Throughput & Latency SLOs: p95 latency for 128-token chat generation < 200ms on committed capacity; sustained throughput target = 400k tokens/min across the pool. Redwood suggested burst to hosted for overcommit.
- Capacity guarantees: committed pool = 8 GPUs reserved, with contractual burst add-on of up to +4 GPUs within 30 minutes notice for traffic spikes; autoscaling policy and on-call capacity windows to be defined.
- Data residency & security: all inference logs stored in-region; KMS envelope encryption required for model keys; audit logs retained 7 years for compliance team.

- Estimated ARR range $300k-$750k depending on final commit length (12 vs 36 months) and burst pricing.
- Procurement wants firm penalty schedule for SLA misses; Redwood legal pushing back on termination thresholds.

title: Archipelago MedData Solutions
content:
Archipelago MedData Solutions

High-level: want private VPC deployment for PHI workflows. Very strict residency + audit requirements.
Encryption posture is primary ask — detailed notes from SecDeepDive:
- In-transit: require mutual TLS between customer LB and Redwood ingress. TLS 1.3 preferred, TLS1.2 acceptable with strong cipher suites.
- mTLS: customer will provision client certs; Redwood to validate client certs against customer CA OR offer mutual-auth with customer-managed certs via ACM in customer's account.
- Service-to-service: internal mTLS between runtime components for zero-trust, cert rotation handled by control plane with cert expiry <90 days.
- At-rest: AES-256-GCM envelope encryption for model KV cache and user data; per-tenant data keys wrapped by customer CMK when BYOK selected.
- Key rotation: recommend two-tier rotation: data-key rotation every 90 days, CMK rotation policy annually (customer can trigger rotation). Rewrap flow documented; no downtime for POC.
- KMS integration: support for AWS KMS (cross-account), AWS CloudHSM, and external HSM via PKCS#11 (enterprise package). BYOK model preferred.
- Secrets management: recommend HashiCorp Vault in customer VPC (auto-unseal with KMS) or AWS Secrets Manager; Redwood control plane will not persist plaintext keys for private VPC.
- Audit logging: immutable write-once logs forwarded to customer SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/Elastic). Retention policy requested: 7 years for audit trails; must include request metadata + token usage (redacted PII).
- Data residency: all inference inputs/outputs must remain in us-east-1; no cross-region backups without explicit consent.
- Network topology: private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) only; no NAT egress for inference traffic. Customer will provide VPC peering/VPN terms.
- Operational controls: RBAC via SSO/SAML, granular route-level policies, per-route key binding (bind a CMK to a model route).
- Compliance asks: provide SOC2 Type II evidence, ISO27001 cert, results of recent pen test + remediation plan.
Customer quotes / call fragments:
- 'We cannot have keys managed by a vendor control plane unless wrapped by our CMK.'
- 'Audit logs must be tamper-evident and stored in our SIEM; we will supply log ingestion credentials.'
POC scope notes: sample dataset de-identification pipeline + RAG with customer KMS BYOK; latency target 200ms P50 for short prompts; throughput 60 QPS burstable to 200 for evaluation.
Cost sensitivity: medium — willing to pay for isolation and BYOK HSM but want clear unit economics for heavy embedding batches.

- Targets: p95 chat <= 50ms; p99 scoring <= 10ms; sustained 500 rps scoring peak, burst to 1k rps for 60s windows.
- Cost constraints: target TCO reduction vs current prototype >= 40% for steady-state; open to reserved capacity commit.
- Model preferences: prefer open weights (LLM family X-style) that quantize well; want Redwood-verified perf profiles and fallback to smaller low-latency variant.
- Routing/fallback: automatic fallback to CPU-backed cheaper model unacceptable for scoring; can fallback for chat but must be labeled and monitored.
- Observability: token-level cost/latency breakdowns, tracing hooks, and rollbacks for bad quality.
- Security: SSO (SAML), SOC2 compliance evidence, KMS integration, audit logs, and retention controls; data must stay in NA.

Redwood-specific asks and POC plan:
- Shortlist model variants and quantization profile suggestions (Optimize).
- 48-hour dedicated benchmarking run with real traffic replay (we'll supply traces). Measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU utilization, and per-token cost.

- Cost scenarios: hosted vs dedicated vs reserved pricing with committed ARR levels.

SE notes (Diego):
- Traffic histogram suggests many short sequences for scoring (<16 tokens) and long tail for chat. Good candidate for separate route: small low-latency quantized scoring model on dedicated pool + separate chat model with dynamic batching.
- KV/prefix caching likely high value for chat continuity; need to tune batch size cap for scoring route to prevent tail blow-ups.

title: Python SDK: streaming requests appear to ignore configured timeouts (hangs indefinitely on slow/stalled stream)
content:
Python SDK: streaming requests appear to ignore configured timeouts (hangs indefinitely on slow/stalled stream)

Issue summary:
Customer reports Python SDK streaming calls do not respect configured timeouts. Non-streaming requests time out as expected, but streaming can hang indefinitely when the connection stalls mid-stream (no bytes received) or when the proxy buffers.

Customer impact:
- Production worker processes hang, consuming concurrency slots.
- Customer sees elevated end-to-end latency and occasional request pileups.
- They are hesitant to enable streaming broadly until timeouts are reliable.

Customer context:
- Company: Northwind AI (enterprise)
- Networking: behind corporate egress proxy (TLS intercept) + occasionally slow upstream
- Observed: most frequently when stream starts but then stops emitting chunks for >60s

SDK / environment:
- redwood-sdk-python version: 0.17.2 (per customer)
- Python: 3.11
- HTTP client: httpx (via SDK)
- Deployment: k8s, us-east

Expected behavior:
When user configures a timeout (e.g., 10s overall), streaming generator should raise a timeout exception and abort underlying connection when no data is received within the configured window (or when overall timeout elapses).

Actual behavior:
Streaming generator continues waiting for bytes (appears to block indefinitely) even though `timeout` was passed to the client.

Steps to reproduce (customer repro, adapted):
1) Configure the SDK with a short timeout.
2) Initiate a streaming chat completion.
3) Simulate a stalled stream (customer sees this behind proxy; we reproduced with a local proxy that accepts upstream, sends initial headers + a partial chunk, then stops sending bytes).
4) Observe Python iterator blocks without raising a timeout.

Repro snippet (customer-provided, sanitized):
```python
from redwood import Redwood

client = Redwood(api_key="<redacted>", timeout=10)  # seconds

with client.chat.completions.stream(
    model="rw.chat.v1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a long answer about caching."}],
) as stream:
    for event in stream:
        print(event)
```

What customer sees:
- In certain cases, iteration blocks on `for event in stream:` and never returns.
- No exception is raised.
- Killing the process is the only way to reclaim capacity.

Logs / evidence:
- Customer supplied request IDs where available (they often cannot get request_id when stuck because no terminal event):
  - request_id: rwreq_01HRQJ9Z2W6J6M7KEXAMPLE
- When it does fail, they occasionally see `httpx.ReadTimeout` on non-streaming endpoints, but not on streaming.

Initial hypothesis:
Timeout is being applied to initial connect / request send, but streaming read loop is not enforcing read/overall timeouts consistently. Potentially an httpx streaming iterator path where read timeouts aren’t triggered if the socket is kept open but yields no bytes, or the SDK isn’t passing the timeout config into the streaming context / iter loop.

Requested outcome:
- Confirm whether this is a known issue/regression.
- Provide a workaround (customer needs something they can deploy this week).
- Provide an ETA for a fix release and link to the PR(s) for tracking.
2026-01-17 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Thanks for the detailed repro. A couple of quick questions so we can reproduce precisely:
1) Can you confirm whether you set `timeout` on the Redwood client vs per-request?
2) Do you see the hang after *any* tokens are streamed, or can it also hang before the first event?
3) If you can share, do you have a proxy vendor/name (Zscaler, Netskope, etc.)?

In the meantime, as a mitigation, can you wrap the streaming loop in your own overall timeout (thread/alarm/async cancellation depending on your setup) so you can abort the worker if it stalls? We’ll look for an SDK-level fix so you don’t need to maintain that long-term.
2026-01-17 10:03 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
1) We set `timeout=10` on the client (constructor). Not per-request.
2) Mostly after some tokens. It starts streaming, then stalls and never resumes.
3) Zscaler (TLS inspection enabled). We can’t change this.

We already have a crude watchdog that kills the pod if a request exceeds 120s, but that’s disruptive (drops in-flight jobs). We need the SDK to throw a timeout so we can retry or fail gracefully.
2026-01-17 11:28 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Got it. Looping in the Python SDK owner (Sabrina) + SDK parity TL (Ibrahim). We’ve seen a few proxy-related streaming stalls; we’ll confirm whether our configured timeout is enforced during the streaming read.

Next update by EOD Monday with either workaround guidance or an identified fix path.
2026-01-20 09:41 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed repro internally using a local “stalling proxy” (accepts connection, sends headers + first SSE event, then stops sending bytes).

Findings (0.17.x):
- The client-level `timeout` is mapped to httpx request timeout for request setup.
- In the streaming path, we were not consistently applying an overall timeout guard around the event iterator.
- With certain proxy/socket behaviors, httpx doesn’t raise `ReadTimeout` in our loop because we’re effectively waiting on the streaming response iterator without a bounded read window in a way that triggers the configured timeout.

Plan:
- Implement the standardized timeout model for Python (connect/read/overall) and enforce overall timeout for streaming iteration.
- Ensure cancellation closes the underlying response and surfaces a typed SDK timeout error that includes `request_id` when available.

Tracking PRs:
- PR-850 (timeout model plumbing)
- PR-854 (streaming disconnect handling + error typing)

Workaround (immediate):
Until the fix ships, wrap the stream consumption in an application-level overall timeout and explicitly close the stream on timeout. If you’re using sync code, you can do this with a watchdog thread that calls `stream.close()` and aborts the request; for async, use `anyio.fail_after` / `asyncio.wait_for` around the stream consumption.

We’ll provide a concrete snippet once we confirm the best pattern with minimal side effects.
2026-01-20 14:12 PT — Ibrahim Khan (SDK parity TL)
Adding: this is in-scope for the cross-language timeout standard. The new default model is:
- connect timeout
- read timeout (max time between bytes/events)
- overall timeout

Streaming will primarily enforce read + overall. We’ll also add a conformance fixture so TS/Go/Python all fail fast on stalled streams the same way (and with consistent error fields).
2026-01-21 08:37 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Customer-facing workaround snippet (sync) proposal — please confirm, Sabrina:

```python
import time
import threading

MAX_SECONDS = 30

with client.chat.completions.stream(...) as stream:
    deadline = time.time() + MAX_SECONDS

    def watchdog():
        while time.time() < deadline and not stream.closed:
            time.sleep(0.25)
        if not stream.closed:
            stream.close()

    t = threading.Thread(target=watchdog, daemon=True)
    t.start()

    for event in stream:
        # handle event
        pass
```

This is not perfect but better than killing the pod.
2026-01-21 10:05 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Confirmed the snippet is directionally OK. Two notes:
1) Encourage customers to set MAX_SECONDS > their expected generation time, and treat this as “overall timeout”.
2) After `stream.close()`, the iterator should exit; some environments may raise an exception depending on where the underlying socket is. They should catch and treat as timeout.

Fix status:
- PR-850 updated to support an explicit overall timeout wrapper for streaming consumption.
- We’ll surface a `RedwoodTimeoutError` (typed) with fields: `request_id` (if known), `timeout_ms`, and `phase` (connect/read/overall).

ETA:
Targeting python sdk 0.18.0 early next week pending CI + review.
2026-01-27 16:22 PT — Sabrina James (Python SDK)
Fix merged and released in redwood-sdk-python 0.18.0.

Release notes (high level):
- Streaming now enforces overall timeout consistently.
- Read timeout is applied to stalled streams (no bytes) where possible.
- Streaming timeout errors are typed and include request_id when available.

PRs:
- pr-850-timeout-model-connect-read-overall
- pr-854-streaming-disconnect-handling-and-errors

Also added conformance fixtures coverage in pr-857 (includes a stalled-stream test).

Docs:
Migration notes updated to clarify the timeout behavior and config names.
2026-01-28 09:02 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Sent customer upgrade guidance:
- Upgrade to redwood-sdk-python >= 0.18.0
- Set explicit overall timeout (example: `timeout={"overall": 30, "read": 10, "connect": 5}` depending on their config format)
- Log `request_id` from errors/events for Support triage

Asked them to confirm behavior in their Zscaler environment.
2026-02-03 15:18 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
We upgraded to 0.18.0 and deployed to a subset.

Results:
- Previously hanging streams now terminate with a timeout exception around ~30s as expected.
- We can catch and retry safely in our job runner.

One note: when it stalls after tokens, the exception doesn’t always include request_id (makes sense because it’s mid-stream and we don’t always have it). But this is still a big improvement.

You can close this ticket.
2026-02-04 09:11 PT — Owen Phillips (Support)
Closing as resolved. Follow-up: we should ensure request_id is emitted in the initial streaming response headers/events consistently to maximize chance of capturing it before a stall (linking to INT-1182 request_id visibility work).
Resolved by shipping redwood-sdk-python v0.18.0 with standardized timeout model and explicit enforcement of overall/read timeouts for streaming consumption. Provided workaround (application-level watchdog + stream.close()) for pre-upgrade mitigation. Customer confirmed fix in production subset and requested closure.

title: On-prem restore fails during manifest apply: missing CRDs / resource ordering causes "no matches for kind" errors
content:
On-prem restore fails during manifest apply: missing CRDs / resource ordering causes "no matches for kind" errors

Issue summary
- Customer attempted a control-plane restore for Redwood Private in an air-gapped on-prem environment.
- `restore apply` fails when applying Kubernetes resources from the backup artifact.
- Errors indicate missing CRDs and/or incorrect ordering (CustomResources applied before CRDs are installed).

Impact
- Customer blocked from completing restore validation for internal DR readiness review.
- No production outage (this was a planned restore drill into a new cluster), but DR timeline at risk.

Customer context
- Customer: MedData Systems
- Deployment: Redwood Private (on-prem, air-gapped)
- Restore target: new Kubernetes cluster (fresh install)
- Backup artifact source: previous cluster (same environment) created via installer `backup create`.

What the customer expected
- Restore should bootstrap required components in a deterministic order and fail fast with clear remediation steps if prerequisites are missing.

What happened
- Restore job attempts to apply Kubernetes manifests (including CRs for cert-manager / external-secrets / redwood control-plane CRs) before the corresponding CRDs exist on the target cluster.

Steps to reproduce (as reported)
1) Stand up a fresh Kubernetes cluster (air-gapped, no external repos).
2) Install Redwood Private base prerequisites (customer believed CRDs would be included in restore bundle).
3) Run: `redwood-private restore apply --from /mnt/backup/backup_2025-02-17T0312Z`.
4) Restore fails during "Apply Kubernetes objects" stage.

Observed errors (snippets)
- kubectl apply output from restore logs:
  - "error: resource mapping not found for name: \"redwood-control-plane\" namespace: \"redwood-system\" from \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"RedwoodTenant\" in version \"platform.redwood.ai/v1\" ensure CRDs are installed first"
  - "error: unable to recognize \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"ExternalSecret\" in version \"external-secrets.io/v1beta1\""
  - "error: unable to recognize \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"Certificate\" in version \"cert-manager.io/v1\""
- Restore summary:
  - "stage=apply_k8s_objects status=failed applied=214 failed=17 skipped=0"
  - "hint: install required CRDs and re-run restore"

Notes
- The customer’s baseline cluster did not have cert-manager and external-secrets CRDs preinstalled in the restore target.
- In air-gapped mode, the customer is using the offline bundle and does not have access to pull charts/images during restore.

Request
- Provide a clear supported workaround for installing required CRDs (and in what order) prior to re-running restore.
- Confirm whether Redwood’s restore workflow should install CRDs automatically (from bundle) or explicitly require them as prerequisites.
- Update customer-facing runbook to prevent recurrence.
2025-02-18 09:14 PT — Fatima Noor (Reporter): Created from customer escalation in #support. Customer blocked on restore drill; attaching initial error snippets and requesting logs + exact installer version.
2025-02-18 10:02 PT — Support (Fatima Noor): Requested: (1) installer version (`redwood-private version`), (2) backup manifest header (format/version), (3) full restore log, (4) list of preinstalled CRDs on target cluster (`kubectl get crd | wc -l` plus grep for cert-manager/external-secrets/platform.redwood.ai).
2025-02-18 13:37 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Provided logs. Installer: 1.9.3-private (offline bundle). Backup created 2025-02-17. Target cluster has no cert-manager CRDs. Error repeats for ExternalSecret and RedwoodTenant kinds. They assumed restore would include everything required.
2025-02-18 14:10 PT — Sean Gallagher (Assignee, SRE): Confirmed symptom aligns with ordering: restore applying CRs before CRDs are present. In air-gapped mode, CRDs must come from the offline bundle (not fetched). Looping in Ethan Park for control-plane restore sequencing expectations.
2025-02-18 15:03 PT — Ethan Park (Control plane eng lead): Restore workflow currently assumes prerequisite operators/CRDs exist (cert-manager, external-secrets, and Redwood platform CRDs via helm install of control-plane chart). If customer ran restore on a completely fresh cluster without running the "bootstrap" step, CRDs will be missing. We should improve preflight to detect and provide a deterministic checklist, and optionally extract CRDs from bundle for install-first.
2025-02-18 16:22 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Sent interim workaround to customer: install prerequisite CRDs first (from offline bundle) then re-run restore. Asked customer to confirm whether they can run helm from bundle and whether images are already loaded into their registry.
2025-02-19 09:05 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): They can run helm from the bundle; images are preloaded. They need exact commands and ordering. Also asked whether Redwood secrets are restored or only references.
2025-02-19 10:18 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE): Provided ordered workaround (below). Also clarified secrets handling: restore rehydrates secret references/config; secret material depends on customer’s secret manager and must be available post-restore (no raw secret export).
2025-02-19 10:20 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE) — Workaround details shared:
1) Verify CRDs missing:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager|external-secrets|platform.redwood.ai)' || true`
2) From the offline bundle, install prereq charts WITH CRDs enabled (do not use `--skip-crds`):
   - cert-manager: `helm upgrade --install cert-manager ./charts/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set installCRDs=true`
   - external-secrets: `helm upgrade --install external-secrets ./charts/external-secrets -n external-secrets --create-namespace`
3) Install Redwood control-plane chart to lay down Redwood CRDs before applying CR instances:
   - `helm upgrade --install redwood-control-plane ./charts/redwood-control-plane -n redwood-system --create-namespace`
4) Confirm CRDs exist:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager.io|external-secrets.io|platform.redwood.ai)'`
5) Re-run restore:
   - `redwood-private restore apply --from /mnt/backup/backup_2025-02-17T0312Z --continue-on-preflight=false`
6) Validation:
   - `kubectl -n redwood-system get pods`
   - run the post-restore health check in the runbook (control-plane API ready, tenant config present, routing policy objects present).

Notes: If the cluster has partially-applied CRs, delete the failed CRs before re-run to avoid immutable field conflicts.
2025-02-19 13:44 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Workaround succeeded after installing CRDs/operators first. Restore completed, but they noted the installer error message was generic and the runbook didn’t emphasize CRD prerequisites for a brand new cluster.
2025-02-20 08:55 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Requested customer confirm final validation checklist results (tenant config restored, routing policies present, control-plane endpoints healthy).
2025-02-20 12:11 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Validation looks good. They asked Redwood to document "fresh cluster" prerequisites and add a preflight check that fails with specific missing CRDs listed.
2025-02-21 09:32 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE): Logged follow-up requests for Eng: add explicit preflight CRD checks + improve ordering (CRDs before CRs). Referencing ongoing restore workflow improvements and helm hook work. Linking internal work to ENG-9822/ENG-9830/ENG-9828.
2025-02-22 10:05 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Marking Resolved. Customer unblocked with documented workaround; awaiting doc patch in next runbook refresh.
Restore failure was due to missing prerequisite CRDs (cert-manager, external-secrets, Redwood platform CRDs) on a fresh on-prem cluster, causing "no matches for kind" during manifest apply. Workaround: install prerequisite charts/CRDs from the offline bundle first, then re-run `restore apply`. Follow-ups filed to improve restore preflight and documentation to explicitly cover fresh-cluster ordering.
Install prerequisite CRDs/operators from the offline bundle (cert-manager with installCRDs=true, external-secrets, then Redwood control-plane chart to install Redwood CRDs) before running `redwood-private restore apply`. If partial CRs were applied, delete failed CR objects prior to re-run to avoid conflicts.
Redwood will update the customer-facing restore runbook to add a "fresh cluster prerequisites" section and enhance installer preflight to list missing CRDs explicitly (targeting the next Private installer + docs release).
This ticket is consistent with recent restore drill feedback: restore should (a) detect missing CRDs and stop early with actionable output, and (b) optionally offer a "bootstrap prerequisites" step in air-gapped mode using bundle-contained CRD manifests. Coordinate with docs owner (Elliot Price / Kira Thompson) and control-plane eng (Ethan Park).
Slack: #support escalation (see internal thread linked from SUP-18421)
Confluence: runbook-control-plane-restore (add prereq CRD section; emphasize ordering for fresh clusters)
GitHub: pr-489 (restore workflow + validation), pr-138 (restore job template/hooks), pr-512 (compatibility/versioning messaging)

title: Streaming disconnects behind enterprise proxy; SDK retry guidance + better error surfaces needed (request_id, partial output)
content:
Streaming disconnects behind enterprise proxy; SDK retry guidance + better error surfaces needed (request_id, partial output)

Issue summary:
Acorn Financial reports frequent disconnects when using streaming responses from Redwood (SSE) from within their corporate network. They are behind an enterprise HTTP proxy (Zscaler-like) and observe the stream terminating mid-response (partial output) with different error messages depending on SDK/language. They request explicit guidance on safe retry behavior for streaming and want request_id surfaced consistently for triage.

Impact:
- Production feature degraded: customers see truncated model outputs or UI hangs when stream ends unexpectedly.
- Retries are currently ad-hoc; customer concerned about duplicate side effects / duplicate billing when reissuing requests.
- Support unable to quickly correlate failures because request_id is not always present in SDK exceptions for streaming disconnects.

Environment:
- Customer tier: enterprise
- Region: us-east
- Network: corporate outbound proxy with TLS interception and idle connection policy
- Observed in: TypeScript SDK (Node 18), Python SDK (3.11), Go SDK (1.21)
- Endpoint: /v1/chat.completions with stream=true (SSE)

Customer-reported behavior:
- Stream runs for ~10–40 seconds then disconnects (no explicit error from API); client receives one of:
  - Node: "TypeError: fetch failed" / "ECONNRESET" or "socket hang up"
  - Python: "httpx.ReadError: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer" or "RemoteProtocolError: Server disconnected"
  - Go: "unexpected EOF" while reading event stream
- Partial text is sometimes available in the UI, but the SDK throws and caller is unsure whether to display partial output or treat as failure.
- Customer notes that non-streaming requests are more reliable (but latency is worse).

Steps to reproduce (as provided by customer):
1) Route outbound traffic through corporate proxy (CONNECT).
2) Run streaming chat completion with longer responses (max_tokens >= 800) and low temperature.
3) Observe intermittent disconnects; rate increases during peak proxy load.

Evidence/log snippets (redacted):
- Customer TS log:
  - "stream error: ECONNRESET" after receiving ~1200 chars; no request_id available in the exception.
- Customer Python log:
  - "httpx.RemoteProtocolError: Server disconnected"; request_id not printed.
- Customer captured response headers from successful calls show x-request-id present, but failures do not surface it.

Initial hypothesis:
- Proxy closes idle/long-lived connections or buffers SSE chunks; may terminate mid-chunk causing client-side protocol errors.
- SDK streaming implementations differ in how they parse SSE and how they attach request_id to raised errors.

What we need:
1) Clear docs guidance for streaming disconnects behind proxies (recommended timeouts, keepalive, proxy settings, partial output handling).
2) SDK behavior: on streaming disconnect, raise typed error containing request_id (if known), status_code if available, and include partial_output (or guidance on how to capture it).
3) Conservative retry guidance (streaming retries should not be automatic; document idempotency keys + request_id logging).

Success criteria:
- Customer can log request_id and provide it to Support for any failure.
- Docs provide recommended patterns: retry policy for non-streaming vs streaming; show safe resume/retry patterns.
- SDKs align on an error taxonomy so customers see consistent fields across languages.
2026-01-29 09:22 (Dev Patel): Ticket opened after CS escalation. Customer reports 5–15% of streamed responses end abruptly behind corporate proxy. Asking for guidance + request_id surfacing. Assigning to Owen for repro + coordination with SDK team.
2026-01-29 10:05 (Owen Phillips): Acknowledged. Requesting: (1) which proxy vendor/policy (idle timeout?), (2) whether they can bypass proxy to confirm correlation, (3) SDK versions + minimal repro, (4) confirm they can capture response headers for successful stream start (x-request-id).
2026-01-29 14:18 (Customer - Acorn Financial): Proxy is managed by IT; appears to terminate long-lived connections. Cannot fully bypass in prod, but can test in a separate network where issue disappears. SDK versions: TS 0.18.2, Python 0.14.7, Go 0.9.1. They can capture x-request-id on successful responses but failures throw before they can access it.
2026-01-30 09:02 (Owen Phillips): Repro attempt internally using a proxy simulator that cuts connections mid-chunk; observed similar errors: Node fetch fails with ECONNRESET; Python httpx raises RemoteProtocolError; Go returns unexpected EOF. Confirms we do not consistently attach request_id for streaming disconnects because headers are read at stream start but not retained/propagated in error path in some SDKs.
2026-01-30 10:21 (Allison Grant): From SRE perspective: do NOT auto-retry streaming by default. Encourage idempotency keys for non-streaming retries; for streaming, recommend application-level retry with explicit user confirmation or safe idempotent semantics. Also recommend exposing disconnect_reason and retry_count fields where possible for debugging.
2026-01-31 11:44 (Sabrina James): Python SDK: we can retain response headers at stream start and include request_id in any downstream stream iterator exception. Also can include a StreamingError that optionally carries partial_text collected so far (opt-in due to memory). Tracking under SDK parity work; will reference this ticket in PR.
