Eng (Priya Nair) 2025-02-18T09:30Z: Reproduced locally. Root cause: orchestrator treat_suppressed_as_abort flag default true; change would be to treat suppression as 'defer' and schedule commit after suppression clears. Drafting PR to adjust logic and add metric for suppressed-commits.
Support (Maya Chen) 2025-02-19T14:22Z: Customer approved manual snapshot write at 2025-02-19 15:00 UTC. Applied forced commit; customer confirms traffic now reaches pf-3b-v2 for pinned requests.
Customer (Alex Rivera) 2025-02-19T15:30Z: Verified outputs normalized; thanked team and asked for postmortem and permanent fix timeline.
Manual snapshot commit applied 2025-02-19 15:00 UTC for tenant pf-tenant-88; pinned routing restored. Engineering merged PR to change suppression handling (orchestrator PR #1223) which treats adaptive-throttle suppression as defer instead of abort and schedules a follow-up commit when suppression clears. Patch scheduled for rollout to prod-us-east on 2025-02-21 during maintenance window.
1) Postmortem doc: create Confluence page documenting root cause, timeline, and customer impact (owner: Priya Nair, due 2025-02-24)
2) Add telemetry: metric suppressed_pin_commits and alert if rate > 1/min for any tenant (owner: SRE team)
3) QA: add regression test to rollout controller simulating adaptive throttle suppression to ensure defer-path commits succeed after suppression clears (owner: rollout-controller team)
4) Customer comms: send summary and offered credit for elevated token cost during incident (owner: CS manager)
5) Monitor: keep a 72-hour watch on pf-tenant-88 routing logs and suppressed-commit metric after patch rollout.

title: Cross-account assume-role failures due to role-tag assertion policy mismatch after provisioner change
content:
Cross-account assume-role failures due to role-tag assertion policy mismatch after provisioner change

Issue summary: Several internal services (provisioner, account-broker) started receiving AccessDenied when calling sts:AssumeRole for cross-account operations. This began immediately after a change to the provisioner that started asserting a role attribute tag 'redwood-env' on newly created roles. Impact: cross-account debug runs, Dedicated provisioning jobs, and scheduled maintenance workflows are failing intermittently; some customer onboards delayed. Environment: production, us-east-1. Observed behavior: sts:AssumeRole calls return AccessDenied with Condition mismatch in CloudTrail logs; role exists and trust relationship is valid. Expectation: assume-role should succeed when principal session tags match policy conditions or when tag assertion is not required.
1) Create a new role in account B with provisioner v2.3.1 which sets tag 'redwood-env=prod'.
2) From account A, call sts:AssumeRole with session tags 'redwoodEnv=prod' (legacy agent).
3) Observe AccessDenied in the response and 'Condition Key mismatch' entries in CloudTrail for sts:AssumeRole.
CloudTrail event (sts:AssumeRole) shows: errorCode=AccessDenied, errorMessage=Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole, condition: StringEquals:aws:PrincipalTag/redwood-env != 'prod'
Relevant IAM role tag list: [ {Key: 'RedwoodEnv', Value: 'prod'}, {Key: 'owner', Value: 'infra-team'} ]
Initial findings: After comparing the provisioner change (PR #2156) we confirmed it started writing 'redwood-env' as a tag on roles. Org policy enforcement layer normalizes tags to PascalCase ('RedwoodEnv') and strips dashes for legacy compatibility. AssumeRole calls from older agents still send session tags using camelCase 'redwoodEnv'. The trust policy uses Condition: StringEquals: aws:PrincipalTag/redwood-env = 'prod' which does not match the normalized tag key. CloudTrail and STS deny message corroborate a tag-key mismatch rather than missing trust. GCP service accounts observed no change; impact is limited to AWS cross-account role flows. Hypothesis: tag key normalization during role creation caused discrepancy between tag keys referenced in the Condition and actual principal tags presented during AssumeRole, causing denies.
Temporary mitigation applied 2026-03-11: updated the provisioner to set both normalized and legacy tag keys when creating roles (RedwoodEnv and redwood-env). Rolled this change to prod in us-east-1 provisioner fleet. Added a short-lived fallback in the account-broker to rewrite session tags to include both camelCase and dashed keys. This restored most failing workflows within 90 minutes.
1) Engineering: update org-policy normalization doc and provisioner so tags are written in three canonical forms (redwood-env, redwoodEnv, RedwoodEnv) where allowed. (owner: infra-provisioning)
2) Security: review trust policies that reference tag keys and migrate them to use aws:RequestTag/TaggedCondition where possible, or use TagKey alias mapping. (owner: secops)
3) SRE: schedule a canary rollout of the provisioner 2.3.2 with the canonical tag strategy and monitor STS deny rate for 48h. (owner: oncall)
4) Postmortem: prepare incident write-up and update runbook with tag-key compatibility guidance. (owner: postmortem-team)
Provisioner dual-writes both 'redwood-env' and 'RedwoodEnv' tags; account-broker rewrites session tags before AssumeRole. Use direct cross-account assume with explicit sts:TagSession calls for critical job reruns while fix is rolling out.
In progress: temporary dual-write mitigation applied; most workflows restored. Permanent fix requires coordinated policy migration and a provisioner update to write canonical tag forms. Security review scheduled. Full resolution target: backfill existing role tags and update trust policies to reference canonical keys or support aliases.

title: Elevated time-to-first-token for short-chat payloads after runtime 2.3.1 + model repin
content:
Elevated time-to-first-token for short-chat payloads after runtime 2.3.1 + model repin

Issue summary:
Elevated time-to-first-token (TTFB) observed for short chat prompts (<32 tokens) from LuminaApps on the Hosted API after the runtime 2.3.1 deploy and model repin performed 2026-03-09 22:00 UTC.

Impact:
- A subset of customer chat sessions see 1.0–3.5s additional delay to first token.
- Affects primarily small prompts and bursty traffic patterns; medium/long prompts show normal tail latency.
- Customer reports degraded UX for chat snippets used in search/autocomplete flows.

Environment:
- Hosted API (prod) in us-east-1, customer using dedicated pool with session-affinity.
- Runtime: 2.3.1 (rolled 2026-03-09), Model repin to redwood-2.0 (quantized variant) at same window.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Send short chat completion request (system + single-turn user prompt ~8–16 tokens) via Hosted API with session affinity header.
2) Observe websocket/HTTP streaming start time and time-to-first-token metric.
3) Repeat at scale (50–200 qps) to reproduce bursty behavior.

Observed logs / metrics snippets:
- api-gw logs: upstream_connect_time spike correlated with 504s early, but most requests return 200 with delayed first-token.
- edge-proxy: TLS handshake durations stable; occasional renegotiation entries for connections with affinity to pool-a.
- serving-runtime: increased per-request setup time before KV cache warm path (~800ms per affected request).
- session-manager: affinity mapping shows 18% of user sessions sent to a new runtime shard (shard-7) after repin.

Temporary workaround attempted by Support:
- Forced customer traffic to a stable pool via temporary routing override (re-routed to pool-b). Observed immediate reduction in TTFB for affected sessions.
- Scoped rate-limit on pool-a to reduce burst pressure; partial improvement.

Notes: This is not a full outage and does not generate widespread 5xxs. Reproducible via short prompts + session affinity and burst pattern.

title: TTL inheritance broken for routing profiles after template bulk-import causing missed P1 escalations
content:
TTL inheritance broken for routing profiles after template bulk-import causing missed P1 escalations

Issue summary: After importing a large batch of routing/macro templates via the new bulk-import tool, several routing profiles lost TTL (time-to-live) inheritance from their parent templates. Impact: Multiple support tickets that should have escalated to P1 after their SLA TTL expired were not promoted; instead they remained in their base queue for up to 6 hours before manual intervention. This affects internal escalation automation and increases time-to-first-response for critical customer issues.

Observed behavior: Templates imported in bulk (CSV + ZIP payload) appear to create routing profiles with an explicit TTL value of 'null' rather than inheriting the parent's TTL policy. The SLA engine treats null as 'do not escalate' for the affected priority lane.

Expected behavior: Newly created routing profiles should inherit TTL/escalation windows from the referenced template unless an explicit TTL override is provided in the import payload.

Scope: Preliminary audit shows ~120 routing profiles affected across 3 namespaces (support, escalation, infra). Initial impact window: 2026-03-09 02:00 - 2026-03-09 09:45 UTC.

Client-facing impact: No external API downtime. Customer incidents that rely on internal automated escalation may have had delayed response; notified CS leadership and Customer Reliability Managers for customers with active P1s during the window.
1) Create a parent template with explicit SLA TTL 30m for P1 escalation and save.
2) Prepare bulk-import package referencing that parent template for 200 child routing profiles, leaving TTL column empty to indicate inheritance.
3) Run support-tooling bulk-import endpoint (UI or CLI) in prod us-east with dry-run disabled.
4) Verify created profiles: expected TTL=inherit -> 30m, observed TTL=null on ~60% of created profiles.
5) Trigger a test P1 ticket against one of the affected profiles and watch SLA engine; escalation does not occur after 30m.
Attached logs from import job: bulk-import-2026-03-09-02.log (S3), routing-engine trace ids: re-trace-8a4f, re-trace-8a5b, sample ticket id: SUP-19921 (test repro). Exported CSV of affected profiles: s3://redwood-support-exports/ttl-null-affected.csv. Console capture of import response: '201 Created' with payload showing template_id mapping but TTL omitted.
Initial triage by support-tooling team (Jonas): replicated in staging with smaller batch; root cause narrows to deserialization path in bulk-import v1.4.2 where TTL column omitted -> code path sets ttlField = parsedValue OR null; however code incorrectly treats null as explicit 'null' marker and persists that to DB rather than leaving TTL unset so inheritance runs.

Debug notes:
- routing-engine schema expects ttl IS NULL -> inheritance logic applied at write-time; current DB rows show ttl = 'NULL_STRING' for affected rows in 34 records, indicating string coerced instead of SQL NULL.
- Regression introduced by commit 9c4a2f (bulk-import): changed CSV parser to coerce empty fields to explicit null-string to avoid empty-string vs null ambiguity; overlooked downstream ORM mapping.
- Quick grep found identical parsing code in import library used by batch job and UI importer.

Temporary mitigation: Ran ad-hoc migration to convert 'NULL_STRING' and empty-string TTLs to SQL NULL for affected profiles (job id: migration-38912-fix). That restored inheritance for 98 profiles; remaining profiles are pending due to lock conflicts.

Next steps recommended:
- Patch: change CSV parser to return None/absent field and update ORM mapping to map absence -> SQL NULL; add unit tests for empty TTL column. (PR drafted: github.com/redwood-inference/support-tooling/pull/842)
- Backfill: run safe migration for all environments to replace invalid TTL sentinel values with SQL NULL.
- Add monitoring: alert when >1% of created routing profiles have explicit ttl-value equal to sentinel string.
- Postmortem: author a short RCA and notify CS leadership and on-call rotation leads.

title: Provision scoped cross-cloud roles and tag-based guardrails for Data Science experimentation
content:
Provision scoped cross-cloud roles and tag-based guardrails for Data Science experimentation

Issue summary:
Customer/internal team: Data Science (DS) wants temporary, constrained access across both AWS and GCP to run experimental pipelines and short-lived model training jobs. They requested a single access pattern that uses attribute-based constraints (resource tags / labels) and enforces timebound use with automated cleanup.

Impact:
- Current process requires multiple ad-hoc long-lived creds or broad roles (e.g., devops-aggregated), which increases blast radius and audit burden.
- DS cannot run end-to-end experiments that touch S3 buckets and BigQuery tables without manual ticketing, slowing iteration.

Requested deliverables (high level):
1) An AWS AssumeRole that 1) can be assumed by staff in the DS group via SSO/OIDC, 2) limits access to S3 prefixes and SageMaker resources tagged with team:ds-experiments, and 3) enforces conditions for MFA and source IP ranges for prod.
2) A GCP service account mapping (Workload Identity Pool or bound SA) that grants BigQuery read/write on datasets with label ds_experiment=true and limited compute (GCE/GKE) quota.
3) Automated lifecycle: roles/assignments expire after 30 days and are automatically revoked unless renewed through the JIT self-service UI.
4) Terraform manifests in infra-access repo + a small operator runbook for SRE to approve emergency extensions.

Specific policy examples (requested by DS):
- AWS IAM policy should allow s3:GetObject/PutObject, s3:ListBucket but only when "s3:prefix" matches "experiments/teams/ds/*" and bucket has tag team=ds-experiments. Also allow SageMaker CreateTrainingJob only when resource tag experiment_owner is present.
- GCP IAM binding to roles/bigquery.dataEditor scoped to datasets with label ds_experiment=true via conditional bindings where possible; otherwise use custom role with explicit dataset allow-list maintained by infra.

Risk and audit considerations:
- Must avoid accidentally granting write to production datasets/buckets. Add explicit deny on any resource tagged prod=true.
- All assume/impersonation events must be logged to CloudTrail and Cloud Audit Logs and forwarded to Splunk/Datadog with a correlation tag 'access_request_id:INT-224530'.

Proposed implementation steps:
1) Infra to author Terraform modules (aws_iam_role, aws_iam_policy, google_service_account, google_project_iam_binding) with tag/label conditions parameterized.
2) Create an SSO/OIDC mapping for the DS AD group (redwood:ds-experiments) to the AWS role and GCP workload identity.
3) Build short-lived credentials glue: AWS STS tokens with max duration 1 hour; GCP OAuth2 ephemeral tokens via Workload Identity Federation.
4) Add lifecycle automation: an infra Lambda / Cloud Scheduler job that revokes bindings older than 30 days and files a renewal request to JIRA slack #infra-approval.
5) Submit a pull request: infra-access/terraform/modules/experiment-access and link here.

Acceptance criteria:
- DS engineers can assume role and operate on test experiment resources without manual ops intervention.
- No user can write to resources with prod=true tag.
- All events show up in central logs with correlation id.
- Terraform PR merged and QAed in staging, with a canary rollout to one dev project.

Notes/constraints:
- GCP conditional role bindings are limited; we may need a short-lived allowlist of dataset IDs managed by a small automation that reads dataset labels and converts to bindings.
- For AWS, Tag-based conditions require tags on buckets. Many older buckets lack tags; DS team will onboard their buckets to tagging as part of this ticket.

Next steps (owner: Luca):
- Draft Terraform skeleton and a minimal IAM policy by 2026-03-12.
- Schedule 45m sync with DS + SRE to validate tag naming and prod deny rules.

Related business context:
- Supports faster DS iteration and reduces helpdesk ticket volume. Also aligns with org audit requirement to reduce long-lived privileged credentials.

title: Customer reports output regression/drift after silent model change; needs exact model/version change history for investigation
content:
Customer reports output regression/drift after silent model change; needs exact model/version change history for investigation

Issue summary
- Customer reports model outputs changed noticeably starting 2025-10-10 ~18:30 UTC without any intentional prompt/code changes on their side.
- They are calling the model alias `rw.chat/llama-3.1-70b-instruct:stable` (not pinned to a specific model version).
- They need a definitive answer for: exactly what model/version/config changed, when it changed, and whether/why the change could affect response style and medical summarization formatting.

Customer impact
- Production: patient-message summarization and triage routing. Customer notes increased verbosity + different section headings and missing a previously reliable "Assessment" subsection.
- Reported downstream impact: higher human review load and failures in a strict JSON extraction step due to extra prefatory text.

Environment
- Dedicated cluster: lattice-dedicated-us-east-02
- Region: us-east
- API: /v1/chat.completions (streaming=false)
- Customer auth: org_id=org_lattice_2041

Steps to reproduce (customer)
1) Use same system + user prompt used for the last 2 weeks (shared privately in support thread).
2) Call alias `rw.chat/llama-3.1-70b-instruct:stable` with temperature=0.2, top_p=0.95.
3) Compare response structure from 2025-10-09 vs 2025-10-10.

Observed vs expected

title: Intermittent high inference latency during concurrent streams due to ephemeral socket exhaustion + retry bursts
content:
Intermittent high inference latency during concurrent streams due to ephemeral socket exhaustion + retry bursts

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent spikes in end-to-end inference latency and occasional timeouts during periods of high concurrent streaming traffic. Symptoms are more pronounced after short bursts of requests and persist even when the serving runtime shows healthy token throughput.

Impact: Several user-facing features at NovaScribe experienced degraded responsiveness for ~5-30s windows, leading to user timeouts and feature degradation. No model correctness regressions observed.

Environment: Customer uses Redwood Dedicated cluster in us-east, SDK v1.3.2 (Node and Python clients), requests over TLS through API gateway. Dedicated pool sized according to contract and reporting normal GPU utilization in CloudWatch dashboards.
1) Use SDK v1.3.2 with default client settings (maxConnectionsPerHost=2, aggressive retry strategy).
2) Start 30 concurrent streaming chat sessions that each send an initial prompt simultaneously.
3) Observe end-to-end latency for first token across sessions and any 504/timeout errors from the SDK.
4) Repeat with SDK config: increase pool to 8 and disable exponential retry to compare behavior.
Customer-provided SDK client logs (abridged): 
[2026-03-10T14:21:03Z] WARN request_retry: attempt=1 host=api.redwood.example.com queue_time_ms=324 context=stream-init
[2026-03-10T14:21:03Z] ERROR request_timeout: request_id=abc123 elapsed_ms=15000 status=timeout
[2026-03-10T14:21:05Z] INFO socket_status: opened=2 in_use=2 idle=0 total_attempts=18
[2026-03-10T14:21:30Z] WARN retry_backoff: backoff_ms=8000 attempts=3 jitter=0.0

Gateway logs show many simultaneous TLS handshakes followed by TCP TIME_WAIT spikes on gateway hosts during the window. Serving metrics do NOT show corresponding GPU saturation; token service QPS remains within expected range.
Initial hypothesis: problem originated in serving runtime. Validation: serving runtime metrics (latency and token throughput) stayed normal, GPUs not saturated.
Conclusion: issue likely client-side or gateway-level resource exhaustion leading to request queueing before reaching runtime.
Observed SDK defaults: maxConnectionsPerHost=2 and aggressive exponential backoff without jitter in v1.3.2. Under bursty concurrency, the SDK serialized pending requests behind the small connection pool; combined with long backoff windows and no jitter, many clients retried in lock-step (retry bursts), causing transient queueing and perceived latency spikes.
Additional contributing factor: short socket idle timeout at the gateway + high connection churn produced many sockets in TIME_WAIT, causing ephemeral port exhaustion on gateway frontends and increasing TLS handshake latency for new connections.
Reproduction verified in-house using synthetic load: with SDK default settings we reproduced 5–20s tail latencies and request timeouts; increasing pool and enabling jitter eliminated most spikes.
Telemetry: traces show requests spending majority of time in SDK-level client queueing (queued_ms) and time in TLS handshake rather than in serving runtime.
Customer applied temporary mitigations: updated SDK config to maxConnectionsPerHost=8 and reduced retry maxAttempts to 2 with randomized jitter; enabled HTTP keepalive and increased OS ephemeral port range on their gateway. This eliminated the immediate 5-30s spikes.
Recommendation to ops: add connection reuse and tune gateway TCP TIME_WAIT reuse to reduce churn until SDK patch deployed.
Root cause: combined client SDK connection pool small default and non-jittered exponential backoff produced synchronized retry bursts, which—together with gateway ephemeral socket churn—caused queuing and perceived inference latency. Serving runtime was healthy.
Fix implemented: SDK patch released in clientsdk v1.3.5 that increases default pool to 8 for dedicated-class customers, changes retry policy to use full jittered backoff by default, and exposes clear doc strings for pool/timeouts. Gateway-side guidance added to recommendations.
Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood/clientsdk/pull/3421
Customer status: NovaScribe upgraded to v1.3.5 and confirmed latency spikes resolved in production. Follow-up monitoring window of 72 hours completed with no recurrence.
Postmortem tasks: update QuickStart docs to call out pool and retry defaults for streaming workloads; add guidance to Dedicated onboarding checklist; create alert rule for SDK queue_time_ms exceeding 200ms in API gateway metrics.

[Customer - 2026-03-10] NovaScribe SRE (Erik M.): We see the problem only during bursts. Serving looks fine. Please advise whether we need to scale Dedicated pool.
[Support - 2026-03-11] Liam Chen: Initial triage suggests client connection pool defaults + retry logic. Can you temporarily increase connection pool in SDK and report back?
[Customer - 2026-03-11] Erik M.: Increased pool to 8 and enabled keepalive per instructions — spikes disappeared in our test. Waiting for your SDK patch for long-term fix.
[Eng - 2026-03-11] Priya Nair (SRE): Observed TIME_WAIT spike on gateway. Recommend tuning ephemeral port range and enabling reuse as stopgap. Filed INT-3245 to track gateway OS tuning.
[Support - 2026-03-12] Liam Chen: Released clientsdk v1.3.5 (PR #3421) with default changes and jittered backoff. NovaScribe has validated in prod. Marking as resolved after 72-hour monitoring window.

title: Clarify atomic refill and token-slicing interactions for multiplexed orchestrator causing intermittent 429s
content:
Clarify atomic refill and token-slicing interactions for multiplexed orchestrator causing intermittent 429s

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 429s from a dedicated pool while running orchestrated worker fanouts that multiplex many short-lived sessions. The customer suspects token-slicing and atomic refill semantics are causing groups of parallel workers to collide on refill boundaries.

Impact: Roughly 8–12% of requests are receiving 429s during scheduled flush windows for their background ingest and the rate spikes are correlated with their orchestrator job starts. This is causing delays in their pipeline and some time-sensitive webhook retries to fail.

Environment: MetricFlow dedicated pool in prod-us-west, traffic originates from a fleet of orchestrator workers that open ephemeral sessions and use API keys rotated every 6 minutes. Workload pattern: bursts of ~200 short sessions that call streaming start then immediately push small chunks (~1-3k tokens).

Observed behavior: 429s come in tight waves aligned to the orchestrator job start times. Throttle headers show remaining=0 and x-refill-epoch points to a refill event that applied to a group of sessions simultaneously. Customer believes refill is being computed atomically per-namespace and token-sliced windows allow momentary negative bursts.

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1) Create a dedicated pool and provision 2 workers per orchestrator shard.
2) Rotate ephemeral keys every 6 minutes and fanout 200 workers to start within a 30s window.
3) Each worker starts a streaming session and immediately emits a small payload.
4) Observe 429s concentrated within the first 90s of the job.

Request: Customer asks for an explanation of refill semantics when many short-lived sessions start together and guidance on configuration to avoid synchronized 429 waves. They also ask whether splitting refill epochs or changing token-slicing granularity will help and what recommended knob changes are safe for a dedicated pool.
2026-03-12 10:20 UTC - Received initial ticket with customer logs and sample traffic pattern (200 workers, ephemeral keys).
Checked tenant rate limiter logs: refill events recorded at epoch boundaries with batch size consistent with configured burst budget. Noted a cluster of token grants followed by immediate consumption and subsequent remaining=0 for many sessions.
Hypothesis A: Atomic refill per-tenant combined with synchronized session start leads to token allocation granularity causing short-lived sessions to contend and exhaust micro-budgets simultaneously.
Hypothesis B: Token-slicing uses coarse-grain shards (N=8) for this tenant; when many sessions map to same slice the refill appears atomic and causes seen 429 wave. Consider reducing slice size or enabling random jitter on refill mapping.
Observed metric: token_grants_per_epoch spiked from baseline 1200 to 18k during job window; per-slice utilization showed 60% of allocations hitting two slices.
Console trace: route-level latency spiked 5x during event; no 5xxs from serving runtime—rejections are explicit rate rejects.
Customer token rotation pattern (6m TTL) is causing many ephemeral keys to align with refill boundaries due to orchestrator scheduling; recommend reviewing key rotation schedule as well.
Checked linked issue SUP-3141596 for similar refill alignment cases; that ticket implemented refill jitter experiments on staging with positive results.
Action taken so far: increased customer's burst allowance temporarily by +20% for their dedicated pool to provide immediate relief while we evaluate config changes.
Telemetry snapshot saved: s3://redwood-support/telemetry/SUP-527890/epoch-snap-20260312.json (access granted to eng on request).
Priya Agarwal (2026-03-12T11:02Z): Thanks for the report. I've increased a temporary burst buffer on the dedicated pool to reduce immediate impact. Can you send a short window of request IDs and the orchestrator start timestamps so we can correlate?
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-12T11:37Z): Provided sample requestIDs and job-start timestamps for two windows (2026-03-11T23:00Z and 2026-03-12T03:00Z). Noted pattern: starts are scheduled by cron jobs in their orchestrator which align closely with system clocks across shards.
Ethan Chen (SRE) (2026-03-12T13:10Z): Observed per-slice hot-spotting. Tentative plan: run a controlled experiment to change slice_count from 8 to 32 for this tenant in staging and add random refill jitter of up to 30s to epoch boundary. Asking Product if jitter change is safe for SLA window accounting.
Product (2026-03-12T14:05Z): Jitter change acceptable at customer-level for non-critical low-latency lanes. For higher tiers would need rollout notes. Suggest start with orchestrator/background lane only.
MetricFlow - Dev (2026-03-12T15:22Z): We can stagger cron starts by introducing per-shard random delay up to 45s. But we'd prefer config guidance on the server side so we don't have to change many orchestrators across fleets.
Ethan Chen (2026-03-13T09:40Z): Deployed slice_count=32 and refill_jitter=20s in staging for a shadow of MetricFlow traffic. Early results: reduction in 429 wave amplitude by ~70% in staging shadow runs. Preparing rollout playbook.
Priya Agarwal (2026-03-14T08:12Z): Noted that customer agreed to a staged rollout: apply slice_count increase + refill jitter to background-lane only, monitor for billing/console effects, then decide on global lane changes. Will coordinate maintenance window.
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-14T12:01Z): Thank you, please proceed with background-lane change during our maintenance window 2026-03-15 02:00-03:00 UTC. We'll monitor.
Temporary burst allowance increased +20%; staging experiment with slice_count=32 and refill_jitter=20s reduced 429 wave amplitude by ~70%. Planned staged rollout to customer background lane during maintenance window. Final resolution pending production rollout and 48h monitoring.

title: Chat sessions experiencing initial emit delay after hotpatch and model repin
content:
Chat sessions experiencing initial emit delay after hotpatch and model repin

Issue summary:
Customer reports that chat completions show a pronounced delay before the first token is emitted after our runtime hotpatch and a model repin that went out 2026-03-09 02:00 UTC. The problem appears as ~1.5-4s extra TTFB on initial responses for small prompt payloads.

Impact:
- Affects Noteable Analytics (dedicated deployment).
- ~25% of chat sessions show elevated TTFB; some requests also time out after backend retries.
- User-facing: slow UI response, occasional socket disconnects when frontend gives up after 10s.

Environment:
- prod:us-east (customer-dedicated cluster noteable-prod-us-east)
1) Using Noteable Analytics workspace, start a new chat session with a short prompt (~12 tokens).
2) Trigger generation via the standard /v1/chat/completions endpoint pinned to rw-chat-medium-v1.
3) Observe that the client receives no tokens for 1.5-4s before streaming begins.
4) Repeat across multiple sessions and note percent impacted.

Observed behavior:
- Elevated TTFB (1.5-4s) on first token emission.
- Backend traces show requests queued at the serving-runtime input queue for 200-800ms and an additional ~1.2-3s spent in pre-compile/compat checks for certain kernels.

Expected behavior:
- Typical TTFB for same workloads is <500ms with small variance.

Relevant logs and traces:
- Trace IDs (sample): 34b7f2c1, 98a2c11e, d1a8b7f3.
- SLO dashboard: spike in first-token latency starting 2026-03-09 02:10 UTC and matching the hotpatch rollout window.
- Serving runtime logs: intermittent messages: "compat-layer: verifying kernel variant" followed by "alloc: delayed on device sync" for affected requests.

Temporary workaround:
- We validated that pinning the customer's route to the previous runtime bundle (runtime-2026-03-02) removes the extra TTFB.
- Routing to the dedicated fallback pool also mitigates the issue but reduces throughput capacity.

Notes:
- Customer is sensitive to latency; they have dashboards and are asking for an update within our SLA window.
Summary of preliminary findings:
- Timeline: hotpatch runtime bundle runtime-2026-03-09 was rolled out across regions 02:00-02:30 UTC 2026-03-09. At 02:10 UTC we see first-token latency increase correlated with that window.
- Kernel selection gating: New runtime adds an ABI compatibility check that performs a lightweight compile/verification step for some quantized kernels. For models rw-large-v2-onnx-quant we observed a full verification path that adds ~1-2s.
- Queueing behavior: The scheduler has a new affinity microtuning that attempts to consolidate KV-caches; this increases input queue wait when nodes are cold for a specific kernel variant (~200-800ms measured).
- Cache miss amplification: When model repin to rw-chat-medium-v1 occurs concurrently with runtime hotpatch, KV cache entries are evicted and subsequent requests pay an added compilation/verify penalty.
- Error surface: No increased 5xx rates observed in metrics, but client-level timeouts increase due to extra latency.
- Repro on staging: Reproduced by toggling the compatibility check flag and repinning model; deterministic on specific quantized variants.

Hypotheses:
1) The newly-introduced compatibility verification step in runtime-2026-03-09 causes per-request serial preflight work for certain quantized kernels, driving the 1-3s extra TTFB.
2) Affinity microtuning + on-the-fly model repin amplifies queueing and prevents warm kernel reuse, increasing overall tail.
- Short-term: keep customer's route pinned to runtime-2026-03-02 (validated). Continue routing to fallback pool while we patch.
- Medium-term: land a hotfix to skip full verification for previously-seen kernel signatures (change id: PR #2145) and deploy to a canary subset.
- Long-term: add a fast-path cache for kernel-compatibility checks and enhance rollout gating to avoid concurrent repins during hotpatch windows.
- Action owners: Marco Chen (runtime) to own hotfix; Priya Singh (scheduler) to evaluate affinity rollback; Aisha Patel (support) to coordinate with customer.
- ETA for patch: targeting 2026-03-16 canary; broader rollout after validation.

Workarounds in place: customer route pinned to previous runtime and temporary fallback cluster configured. Full resolution pending hotfix rollout (PR #2145). No permanent code rollback performed. Will update when canary metrics confirm improvement.

2026-03-10 12:03 UTC - Marco Chen (SRE): Reproduced locally by enabling compatibility_check=true. Observed ~1.6s extra in verification path for rw-large-v2-onnx-quant. Tentative root cause: verification step is not cacheable across warmups.
2026-03-11 09:45 UTC - Priya Singh (Scheduler): Noted that affinity microtuning bumped consolidation thresholds during the same window. Rolling affinity back for customer's pool reduced queueing in a quick test.
2026-03-11 13:02 UTC - Noteable Analytics (Customer): Confirmed that pinning to previous runtime removed the latency; they want ETA for permanent fix and timeline to resume standard runtime.

title: SSE streaming stalls mid-generation during priority escalation and route-swap to dedicated pool
content:
SSE streaming stalls mid-generation during priority escalation and route-swap to dedicated pool

Issue summary: Customer LexiconHealth reports server-sent events (SSE) chat streams silent-pausing mid-token when the platform performs a priority escalation and swaps the request routing to a dedicated GPU pool. Impact: Multiple in-flight streaming chats for a small percentage (~0.6%) of requests into LexiconHealth's tenant stall for 6-20s of silence followed by either resumed stream or silent close. Environment: prod, us-east-1, dedicated tenant, observed on redwood-chat-3.5-dedicated and open-llama-7b-v2. Steps to reproduce: 1) Send long-form streaming chat with chunked SSE enabled and per-request priority flag set to high. 2) Trigger autoscale/priority escalation by issuing several concurrent high-priority requests from same tenant. 3) Observe stream silence between SSE chunks during routing transition. Expected behavior: Stream should continue with minimal interruption or graceful handoff. Actual behavior: Stream pauses mid-token for many seconds without TCP FIN or SSE keepalive events; sometimes client reports connection still open but no data. Preliminary hypothesis: During priority escalation the routing layer performs an in-flight route-swap to a dedicated serving pool. The swap path currently moves the connection state asynchronously; a gap occurs where the worker continues generation but the SSE proxy stops forwarding chunks due to connection pinning with the previous router. NGINX/edge keepalive/proxy connection reuse prevents immediate reconnection, producing silent periods instead of errors. Additional factors: KV-cache pinning and staged worker eviction observed on nodes with heavy batching.
logs: router-A 2026-03-12T14:18:12.412Z request=rid:abcd1234 chunk=12 -> forwarded; router-A recorded route-swap to router-B at 14:18:12.419Z
traces: distributed trace shows worker continued generating tokens (token 13..18) but SSE proxy at router-B did not forward until 14:18:20.592Z
tcp captures: no FIN/RST during gap; keepalive pings continued on TCP connection; kernel retransmits negligible. Indicates application-layer stall rather than TCP drop.
heap/kv-cache: small eviction noted on worker node 7 around same timeframe; likely unrelated but worth investigating interaction with pinned KV state during handoff.
nginx config: connection reuse enabled via upstream keepalive; swap created a mismatch in backend connection mapping causing buffered data to sit at old proxy writer thread.
load: incident clustered around autoscale events (scale-up to dedicated pool) between 14:15-14:25 UTC; similar minor regressions seen in Canary on 2026-03-09.
attempted fixes: forced proxy flush on swap in staging removed the silent gap but introduced 1-2s latency spike; need a smoother approach.
2026-03-12 09:18 - Aisha Kumar: Customer reported ~4 distinct chats stalled yesterday during peak processing window. Provided request ids and sample traces.
2026-03-12 10:05 - Support (Liam): Requested tcpdump, client logs, and full request IDs; asked if customer is behind a corporate proxy (they are not).
2026-03-12 13:40 - Customer (LexiconHealth): Shared three request IDs and client-side timing: heartbeat frames continue but no SSE lines arrive for ~8s. No reconnect triggered by client.
2026-03-13 02:12 - SRE (Priya): Correlated request IDs to router logs. Observed route-swap events and a sequence where router A forwards first chunks then hands off to router B with no explicit proxy-level flush. Noted NGINX keepalive reuse between A and B.
2026-03-14 07:30 - Eng (Marco): Recreated in staging with controlled route-swap; observed identical silent gap when route pinning is released mid-generation. Proposed mitigation: serialize route handoff or stream proxy flush on swap.
2026-03-14 12:10 - Support (Liam): Applied temporary mitigation for LexiconHealth by disabling priority-escalation path for their tenant and forcing in-place worker processing. Customer reports no further stalls in 3 hours of monitoring.
2026-03-14 14:05 - Customer (LexiconHealth): Acknowledged mitigation and requested ETA for permanent fix and rollback plan.
Mitigation applied 2026-03-14: disabled priority-escalation route for LexiconHealth tenant and adjusted router config to avoid asynchronous connection pin release during swap. Immediate customer impact mitigated; monitoring confirms zero stalls in 4h post-mitigation. Next steps: engineering to implement atomic handoff (server-side stream relay) or graceful stream-forwarding with explicit flush on swap. Scheduler team to review autoscale handoff ordering and ensure KV-cache pin/unpin ordering. Target permanent fix in serving-runtime v1.14.2 with canary rollout 2026-03-21.

title: Commitment Hedge and Ephemeral Burst Contract (Dedicated Capacity) - PRD
content:
Commitment Hedge and Ephemeral Burst Contract (Dedicated Capacity) - PRD

Executive summary: This PRD proposes a new contract primitive for Dedicated capacity: the Commitment Hedge with Ephemeral Burst (CHEB). CHEB lets customers combine a baseline reserved commit with a transparent, short-duration burst mechanism underpinned by an escrowed credit ledger and post-burst reconciliation. The feature aims to provide predictable unit economics, safety for isolation-sensitive tenants, and a controlled runway for legitimate short spikes without expanding long-term reserved commitments.

Problem statement: Many customers want predictable latency and cost on Dedicated GPU pools, but also need to absorb short, real-world traffic spikes (marketing events, nightly batches, or ad-hoc eval runs) without overprovisioning long-lived reserved capacity. Current Dedicated semantics (hard reserves + opportunistic bursting) either force customers to buy too much capacity or rely on opaque fallback behavior that causes customer confusion and SLO surprises. Customers also want clear billing, compensatory protections for tenants adversely affected by bursts (no silent SLA degradations), and operational knobs for admins to audit and control burst behavior.

Goals: 
- Provide a contract-level primitive (CHEB) that mixes a committed baseline with an escrowed burst allowance usable for short windows (minutes to a few hours).
- Ensure transparent billing and post-burst reconciliation so customers understand cost impact and credits.
- Protect isolation guarantees for high-priority tenants via tenant-cooling windows and compensatory credits when a burst causes measurable SLI regressions.
- Expose API + Console surfaces for programmatic lease/borrow flows and operator controls.

Non-goals / out of scope: 
- Replacing primary reserved commit contracts or billing models entirely. 
- Full multi-cloud rescheduling or VM-level autoscaling (infra-level autoscale improvements are separate).
- Deep ML model-level inference optimizations (this PRD focuses on allocation, policy, and economics).

Success metrics: 
- Percentage of Dedicated customers who avoid increasing baseline reserve after using CHEB for at least three months: target >= 40%.
- Percentage reduction in overcommit churn (customers upgrading reserved tiers due to transient spikes): target 20% within 6 months.
- Mean time to reconcile (post-burst ledger settle) under 10 minutes for 95% of events.
- No customer-visible SLO regressions for P0 customers attributable to CHEB on launch (SLO regressions attributable to misconfiguration are acceptable).

Stakeholders: 
- PM: Ava Martinez (owner), 
- Eng (Serving/runtime + Orchestration): Rohit Kapoor (lead), 
- Console/UX: Maya Chen, 
- Billing/Revenue: Daniel Osei, 
- Support/Success: Priya Iyer, 
- Legal/Billing ops: Hannah Schultz.

Design principles and trade-offs: 
- Deterministic economics: CHEB must not create opaque burst charges. Using an escrow ledger (customer-funded burst credits or on-demand conversion at a transparent rate) trades short-term friction for predictability.
- Isolation-first default: High-tier customers (SLA tier A) get stronger implicit protections; default tenant-cooling windows are configurable per-contract but conservative at launch. This choice reduces risk to critical customers at cost of slightly reduced burstability.
- Simplicity of API: Expose 2 primary API calls (ReserveLease, BorrowBurst) plus a reconciliation webhook. Avoid complex per-request policy expressions at initial launch.

Requirements:
R1: Contract primitive CHEB must allow baseline commit (vGPU hours) + burst escrow (credit amount or burst-hours) to be attached to a Dedicated reservation.
R2: BorrowBurst API must atomically request ephemeral capacity for a named contract; response must include estimated cost, pre-authorized debit, and expected reconciliation timeline.
R3: Escrow ledger must be queriable via API and console with transaction-level detail and human-friendly reconciliation summaries.
R4: Tenant-cooling windows: when a burst occurs that impacts other tenants’ P0 SLOs, the system must enforce a configurable cooldown period for borrower tenant’s subsequent burst attempts and credit back compensatory credits to harmed tenants as defined by policy.
R5: Post-burst reconciliation must settle charges and credit transfers within 10 minutes for 95% of events and always within 24 hours.
R6: Console must provide a CHEB contract view, real-time escrow balance, and a timeline of burst events with per-request latency/cost deltas.
R7: Billing integration: final reconciled charges must appear in the customer invoice with a transparent line-item indicating burst consumption and compensatory credit adjustments.
R8: Admin/operator controls: operators must be able to throttle borrowing globally and per-pool, view active borrowings, and trigger manual reconciliations or rollbacks.
R9: Safety: Default contract settings must include conservative burst caps and cooldown windows; customers may opt-in to more permissive settings after an explicit intent flow.
R10: Observability: Emit events for borrow request, borrow grant, fallback invocation, reconciliation complete, and compensatory credit transfer to internal telemetry and alerting systems.
O1: Dynamic kernel selection or model-level quantization guidance; those remain separate runtime efforts.
O2: Long-term market-driven pricing model changes; CHEB uses existing per-token / per-embedding cost primitives for charge calculation.
O3: Automatic vertical scaling of physical GPU clusters; infrastructure autoscale handled by infra queue.
As an SRE for a SaaS customer, I want a way to handle surge traffic for an hourly marketing campaign without increasing my monthly commit, so I can avoid long-term cost increases.
As a Platform Admin at Redwood, I want operator controls to mute runaway burst consumers quickly, so I can protect tenant isolation and SLOs.
As a Billing owner, I want ledger-level visibility into burst usage and compensatory credits so invoices reconcile directly with events and support tickets.
As an App engineer, I want a simple API to request ephemeral capacity with an estimated cost so I can implement graceful fallbacks in my application.
POST /v1/dedicated/leases - create ReserveLease (baseline + optional escrow parameters).
POST /v1/dedicated/leases/:lease_id/borrow - BorrowBurst (duration_minutes, max_cost, tags).
GET /v1/dedicated/leases/:lease_id/escrow - return ledger balance and pending transactions.
POST /v1/dedicated/leases/:lease_id/reconcile - trigger reconciliation (internal use or webhook target).
New CHEB contract page under Dedicated -> Contracts showing baseline reservation, escrow balance, active borrows, and historical reconciliations.
Inline ‘Borrow now’ CTA with pre-checks and estimated cost modal for contract admins.
Operator dashboard with active borrow heatmap, per-pool borrow rate, and one-click mute/throttle buttons.
Primary: churn_change_reserved_commit (fraction of customers who increase baseline after CHEB use).
SLOs: post_burst_reconcile_p95_ms <= 600000 (10 minutes)
Isolation: percent_burst_events_with_comp_credit >= 95% when impact detected
Safety: operator_mute_actions_per_week (monitor for tuning default limits)
Phase 0 (internal alpha): small subset of internal teams + selected Enterprise customers, 2 weeks of synthetic spike exercises.
Phase 1 (beta): invite-only customers with support coverage and manual operator oversight for the first 6 weeks.
Phase 2 (general availability): publicly available with self-serve opt-in; provide migration guide for existing reserved customers.
Rollback plan: immediately revoke BorrowBurst grants and pause CHEB acceptance; reconciliations still processed for already-used credits.
Support playbook: runbook for investigating tenant impact, compensatory credit calculations, and customer communication templates.
AC1: Create ReserveLease and BorrowBurst calls successfully provision ephemeral capacity in the Dedicated pool and return deterministic cost estimates in 95% of requests.
AC2: Escrow ledger exposes transaction history in the Console and via API; reconciled charges appear on a test invoice line-item within the billing pipeline.
AC3: Compensatory credit transfers are performed automatically when a borrow event is correlated with a downstream P0 SLO regression (heuristic to be defined in implementation), and evidence of transfer is visible in ledger and invoice test data.
AC4: Operator controls (mute/throttle) can be exercised from Console and take effect within 30 seconds for active BorrowBurst sessions.
AC5: Load test: CHEB borrow workflow survives 10,000 concurrent borrow attempts across pools without causing controller panic or >5% increase in median P50 latency for unaffected tenants.
AC6: Documentation: PRD, API spec, Console UX spec, and support runbook published and reviewed.
Tradeoff: escrowed credits create a small UX friction on purchase but solve the core problem of predictable economics.
Operational concern: need throttles that operate at the scheduler level to avoid noisy-neighbor amplification; partner with ENG scheduling team for rate-limits.
Decision log: default cooldown windows set to 30 minutes for tier B, 10 minutes for tier A, and 60 minutes for tier C in alpha to protect critical tenants.
