title: Per-tenant Commitment: Virtual Credit Buckets and Late Adjustment Billing PRD
content:
Per-tenant Commitment: Virtual Credit Buckets and Late Adjustment Billing PRD

Implement a per-tenant "virtual credit" commitment mechanism to allow customers to pre-allocate committed compute/usage in flexible buckets that roll forward, support late adjustments, and produce clear invoice line items. This PRD defines product requirements, acceptance criteria, API contracts, billing reconciliation, migration paths for existing committed plans, and rollout controls.
Enterprise customers have asked for more flexible commitment constructs that let them prepay or reserve capacity across models and routes without rigid per-model purchase commitments. Current 'reserved capacity' and monthly credits are too coarse for teams that want: per-tenant priority routing, the ability to increase and retroactively apply extra credits for prior usage windows, and transparent invoice line items specifying applied virtual credits. We need a feature that minimizes billing disputes and supports late adjustments up to a configurable reconciliation window.
Create virtual credit buckets that map to a tenant and can be scoped to: global, per-environment, or per-route
Support time-windowed commitments (monthly/quarterly) with auto-rollforward or expire behavior
Allow admins to submit late adjustments (increase/decrease commitment) within a reconciliation window (default 30 days) which triggers invoice re-calculation or credit memo workflow
Expose APIs and Console UX for purchasing, assigning, and viewing virtual credit usage and projections
Produce explicit invoice line items and accounting-ready export for reconciliations
Replacing existing Dedicated SKU reservations (this will integrate but not deprecate)
Complex per-token micro-pricing negotiation flows (outside of standard per-credit unit price)
Automated tax calculations (will rely on billing platform integrations)
Create a VirtualCreditBucket object: id, tenant_id, name, scope (global/env/route), units_total, units_remaining, purchase_date, window_start, window_end, rollforward_policy (auto/expire), price_per_unit, refundable_flag
Tenant admin can purchase or top-up a bucket via Console or Billing API
Usage engine must debit buckets in priority order: explicitly assigned bucket -> route-scoped -> env-scoped -> global
Support soft caps with callbacks: when remaining units fall below threshold X% send webhook and Console alert
Late adjustment API: allow admin to increase or decrease units_total within 30-day default reconciliation window; decreases create credit memos; increases can be applied retroactively to close gaps
Invoice generator must emit line items: purchase, applied-usage, adjustment-credit, adjustment-debit, expiration-writeoff
Reporting: per-bucket consumption timeseries, forecast projection using trailing 7/30-day burn rates
Access controls: only billing admins or roles with 'billing.modify' can do late adjustments
Telemetry events: virtual_credit.purchase, virtual_credit.apply, virtual_credit.adjust, virtual_credit.expire, virtual_credit.topup
Migration utility: map existing committed credits and reserved capacity into initial VirtualCreditBucket(s) with mapping rules
POST /v1/billing/tenants/{tenant_id}/buckets - body: {name, scope, scope_id?, units, price_per_unit, window_start, window_end, rollforward_policy}
GET /v1/billing/tenants/{tenant_id}/buckets - list buckets with units_remaining and applied_routes
POST /v1/billing/tenants/{tenant_id}/buckets/{bucket_id}/adjust - body: {delta_units, reason, effective_date}
GET /v1/billing/tenants/{tenant_id}/buckets/{bucket_id}/usage - query: start,end,granularity
Webhook: virtual_credit.threshold_exceeded - payload includes tenant_id, bucket_id, remaining_pct
New Billing > Commitments page lists buckets with visual burn bars and projected exhaustion date
Bucket detail panel shows applied routes, burn chart (7/30/90 day), adjustment history, invoices referencing the bucket
Top-up flow: quick modal to add units with confirmation of invoice impact and proration preview
Late adjustment flow: wizard with required justification and preview of invoice delta; require 2FA for adjustments affecting >$50k
Purchases create liability line items and a bucket resource. Applied usage consumes units and generates a 'virtual_credit.apply' record tied to the usage event and invoice id. Adjustments inside the reconciliation window cause invoice updates: decreases produce credit memos applied to the most recent invoice(s) in chronological order; increases may be marked as retroactive charge and appended to the next invoice unless customer requests immediate invoice re-bill. Expired units follow rollforward_policy: auto-rollforward merges remaining units into the next window or expiration generates an 'expiration-writeoff' line item. All automatic changes must be represented in exported invoices for accounting.
AC1: Create bucket - API creates a bucket and Console shows it with correct scope and initial units; units_remaining == units_total
AC2: Consumption - when tenant sends usage with route tag, system debits appropriate bucket and emits virtual_credit.apply event; units_remaining decrements and matches usage units
AC3: Priority routing - if multiple buckets apply, debit order (route-scoped, env-scoped, global) is enforced and deterministic
AC4: Low-threshold alerting - when units_remaining < 10% for a bucket, webhook and Console alert are triggered within 60s
AC5: Late increase - increasing units_total inside reconciliation window can be applied to past usage: invoicing reflects retroactive application and finance export shows adjustment line item
AC6: Late decrease - decreasing units_total produces an immediate credit memo and invoice delta; finance export contains credit memo and explains reason
AC7: Rollforward - buckets with rollforward_policy=auto merge remaining units into next period and produce a rollforward audit record
AC8: Invoice visibility - all bucket-related line items appear in tenant invoices and CSV export; sample invoice for test tenant contains at least one purchase, one apply, and one adjustment line
AC9: Migration - migration job maps existing reserved credits into buckets and total units conserved; pilot tenant migrated with zero data loss and reconciled invoice
AC10: Access controls - attempts by non-billing-admin to call adjust API returns 403
primary: percent_of_customers_using_virtual_buckets (>10% within 3 months post-launch)
billing: count_of_late_adjustments_per_month
operations: time_between_bucket_creation_and_first_apply (median)
reliability: webhook_delivery_success_rate
finance: number_of_invoice_disputes_related_to_buckets (target <2/month after stabilization)
Dashboards: bucket burn rate heatmap, buckets near expiration, top customers by retroactive adjustments. Alerts: SLO breaches on webhook delivery, >5% mismatch between applied units and invoice applied-usage line items for any tenant for 24h.
Phase 0 (pilot): create migration job to transform reserved_capacity records for 3 pilot customers into per-tenant buckets; manual validation of invoices
Phase 1: run migration for 10% of customers who have commitments under $50k; provide a support runbook
Phase 2: open self-serve migration tool for customers to opt-in
Fallback: retain old reserved_capacity records until reconciliation window closes; ability to rollback mappings
Internal alpha: enable feature flags for platform and billing teams; endpoints only
Beta: enable for selected customers and invite-only Console controls; collect feedback
GA: public on Console and API; backfill migration tool; release billing-2025.03
Risk: Retroactive charges create billing disputes - Mitigation: conservative default (do not auto-rebill invoices unless tenant opted-in) and require invoice preview/ack for retro-bills >$5k
Risk: Complexity in reconciliation - Mitigation: create finance export schema and run parallel validation for 2 billing cycles before GA
Risk: Abuse of late adjustments - Mitigation: audit trail + approval threshold + rate limits on adjust API
All adjust endpoints require billing.modify role and 2FA for high-value adjustments. Audit logs retained for 365 days. Adjust API calls write immutable audit records including actor, justification, and IP.
Q1: What is the canonical unit for 'units' across models (tokens vs. compute_seconds vs. normalized_credit)? Decision: use normalized_credits with an exchange table maintained by ModelOnboarding team
Q2: Should we allow negative top-ups (i.e., immediate decrease) beyond reconciliation window? Decision pending finance input
Q3: How to handle refunds for expired units when refund policy is enabled? Need legal input
2025-02-20 - Ben Carter: Scoped initial MVP to purchase/top-up, consumption debit, late adjust API. Left out auto-rebills by default per finance recommendation.
2025-02-24 - Priya Shah (Finance): Need explicit credit memo schema. Added requirement for invoice line 'adjustment-credit' and 'adjustment-debit'.
2025-02-27 - Miguel Ortega (Engineering): Proposed efficient debit path in usage router; will deliver debit ordering and telemetry. ENG-2701 linked for implementation
2025-03-03 - Aisha Kumar: Updated acceptance criteria to include AC9 (migration) after pilot review. Marking security_review_required=false for MVP but will engage security for audit retention scoping.

title: Console API: create and query Shadow Experiments (CRUD, aggregates, example sampling) with RBAC
content:
Console API: create and query Shadow Experiments (CRUD, aggregates, example sampling) with RBAC

Goal
Implement the Console backend API surface for Shadow Experiments so the Console UI and SDKs can:
- Create/update/delete shadow experiments attached to routes and/or rollouts
- Query experiment status, targets, and sampling config
- Fetch aggregated quality deltas (with confidence intervals) and core health counters
- Fetch sampled examples (prompt/response pairs + score breakdown) in a cardinality-safe and privacy-safe way
- Enforce RBAC/tenant boundaries and audit relevant actions

Context
Shadow traffic duplicates a sampled subset of production requests to one or more candidate variants (“shadow targets”) while returning the control response to the user. Shadow outputs are scored asynchronously (eval-harness adapter + rubric runner) and results are surfaced in Console alongside latency/cost/error metrics.

Non-goals (this ticket)
- Implement routing/mirroring in the data plane (ENG-5402)
- Implement telemetry ingestion/event schemas (ENG-5404)
- Implement scoring pipeline mechanics (ENG-5405/ENG-5406)
- Build UI pages (ENG-5408)

API shape (v1)
Note: exact route prefix may vary based on Console gateway conventions; below uses /v1/console for clarity.

1) CRUD
- POST /v1/console/shadow-experiments
  - Creates a shadow experiment definition.
  - Required inputs:
    - tenant_id (derived from auth context)
    - display_name
    - route_id OR rollout_id (at least one)
    - control: (implicitly the live route config at time of run; stored as a snapshot ref for auditability)
    - shadow_targets: list of variant refs (model_id/model_version OR policy_variant_id depending on rollout integration)
    - sampling: percent + bucketing salt/seed policy (seed stored, salt derived from tenant + experiment id)
    - fail_open: true (hard default; can’t be disabled in v1)
    - retention_profile: default (short) or dedicated/private override (validated)
  - Validations:
    - sampling_percent must be within [0.1, 20] by default (hard cap configurable per tenant; see guardrails)
    - max shadow targets: 3 (v1)
    - cannot target same variant as control snapshot
    - must match route request type constraints (chat vs completions vs embeddings)
    - streaming requests allowed only if shadow_streaming_mode is supported for the route (see ENG-5414)

- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments
  - List experiments for a tenant.
  - Filters:
    - status (draft/running/paused/stopped)
    - route_id
    - rollout_id
    - created_by
    - updated_at range
  - Pagination:
    - cursor-based (opaque cursor) + limit (default 25, max 100)

- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Returns experiment definition + current state.

- PATCH /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Allows updates to:
    - display_name, description
    - sampling_percent (within guardrails)
    - paused flag
    - shadow_targets (restricted; requires “experiment:editTargets” permission)
  - Immutable after start:
    - route_id/rollout_id binding
    - bucketing seed

- DELETE /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Soft-delete (archival) in v1; actual artifacts are handled by retention policies.

2) Aggregates
- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}/aggregates
  - Purpose: power the “Quality deltas” and “Health” panels.
  - Query params:
    - window: 1h | 6h | 24h | 7d (default 24h)
    - segment: optional pre-defined segment key (e.g., region, request_type, route_variant_bucket). Must be from allowlist.
    - metrics: optional list of metric keys; defaults to v1 bundle.
  - Response conceptually includes:
    - sample counts (n_control, n_shadow per target)
    - pass/fail rates (format adherence, refusal rate, etc.) per target
    - deltas vs control with confidence intervals (method per Observability Standard)
    - pipeline health indicators (scoring lag p50/p95, missing score rate)
  - Cardinality guardrails:
    - only allow breakdowns on dimension allowlist (no raw prompt_id, no user_id, no customer internal ids)
    - enforce max number of series returned per request (e.g., top K + “other”)

3) Examples (sampled)
- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}/examples
  - Returns a paginated list of scored examples with a stable sampling strategy.
  - Query params:
    - shadow_target_id (required)
    - window (default 24h)
    - outcome filter (regressed | improved | neutral | missing_score | shadow_error)
    - metric_key (optional; used to sort/filter by “worst offenders”)
    - limit (default 20, max 50)
    - cursor
  - Privacy & retention:
    - response payload should return redacted prompt/response fields per retention_profile.
    - examples may include only references (artifact ids) when prompt/response storage is disabled for the tenant.
  - Ordering:
    - default sort: most recent
    - optional sort: highest absolute delta contribution (requires precomputed index; if unavailable, return 400 or fall back)

RBAC & permissions
- All endpoints scoped to tenant derived from auth token.
- Required permissions (names are placeholders; align with Console RBAC system):
  - experiment:read for list/get/aggregates/examples
  - experiment:write for create/edit/pause
  - experiment:delete for archive
  - experiment:editTargets for updating targets after creation
- Additional checks:
  - If route_id is provided, caller must have route:read (and route:write for binding changes).
  - If rollout_id is provided, caller must have rollout:read (and rollout:write if attaching to an active canary).
- Audit logging:
  - Create/update/pause/archive actions emit audit log events with experiment_id, actor, tenant, and diff summary (detailed diff stored server-side; response returns a safe summary).

Data sources / storage
- Control-plane stores experiment definitions (source of truth), but Console API will read from Console DB read model for latency.
- Aggregates are backed by analytics tables derived from shadow telemetry + scoring results (ENG-5404/5405). This ticket includes query-layer plumbing + guardrails, not pipeline creation.
- Examples use a pointer-based model:
  - metadata in analytics store
  - payload in artifact store (if enabled)
  - redaction at write-time + additional redaction at read-time based on role/tenant settings

Edge cases
- Scoring pipeline lagging: aggregates should include “incomplete” flags and missing_score_rate; UI should surface “data still processing.”
- Shadow target errors: count separately (shadow_error_rate) and do not treat as “quality regression,” but do include in health panel.
- Streaming requests: examples may contain partial captures; surface capture_status (partial/complete/timeout) and only compute certain metrics when capture_status=complete.

Acceptance criteria
- CRUD endpoints implemented with validation + proper error messages.
- Aggregates endpoint returns correct values for internal dogfood experiments (validated against notebook queries by Applied ML).
- Examples endpoint respects retention/redaction settings and does not expose raw PII fields.
- RBAC enforced at route/rollout and experiment object levels.
- Audit logs emitted for create/update/pause/archive.
- Load: endpoints remain responsive under high-cardinality tenants; enforce allowlists and series caps.
- Unit + integration tests covering:
  - pagination correctness
  - RBAC denial cases
  - sampling cap enforcement
  - dimension allowlist enforcement

References
- GitHub: sources/github/redwood/pr-24933-console-api-shadow-experiments-crud.json
- Related tickets: ENG-5408 (UI), ENG-5417 (audit logs), ENG-5410 (cardinality guardrails)
- ADRs: shadow routing architecture + telemetry data model/cardinality (Confluence ADRs)

Open questions (tracked here until resolved)
1) Do we allow attaching a shadow experiment to a route without a rollout object in beta? Proposed: yes (route_id supported), but rollout_id required for “show in rollout timeline.”
2) Example payload shape: do we return raw text (redacted) or only artifact refs by default? Proposed default: return redacted text when tenant retention allows; otherwise artifact refs.
3) Confidence intervals: computed in query-time vs precomputed. Proposed: precompute common windows; query-time only for small series counts (guarded).

2026-01-16 (Dylan Brooks): Creating as P0 for Phase 2 Console beta. UI work (ENG-5408) is blocked until we have stable endpoints + pagination + RBAC semantics. Please coordinate with Jonas/Selene on what metrics must be in aggregates v1.
2026-01-18 (Chloe Martin): Drafted initial API contract (aligning with Drive: shadow-experiments-api-contract-draft). Main concern: aggregates query must be dimension-allowlisted to prevent support escalations like the earlier cardinality incident. Will sync with Allison (Obs) on series caps.
2026-01-22 (Allison Grant): +1 on allowlist + cap. Please do NOT allow arbitrary “tags” query param in v1. We can add a small set of segment keys (region, request_type, model_family) and bucket anything else. Also: include scoring_lag_ms p50/p95 in the aggregates response so dashboards and UI can show “processing delay.”
2026-01-23 (Jonas Weber): For v1 metrics, we need at least: format_adherence_rate, refusal_rate, instruction_following_score (model-graded), safety_flag_rate, and missing_score_rate. Also include sample sizes; we’ve seen small n produce misleading deltas. Confidence intervals should follow the observability standard (Wilson for rates, bootstrap for rubric scores if precomputed).
2026-01-26 (Marcus Lin): Security review note: examples endpoint must enforce retention_profile; do not return raw prompts if the tenant disables storage. Also ensure authZ checks happen before any artifact store lookup to avoid metadata side channels.
2026-01-29 (Chloe Martin): Implemented CRUD + list/get with cursor pagination. Added hard caps: max_targets=3, limit<=100 for list, limit<=50 for examples. Drafted RBAC checks using existing Console policy engine hooks (route:read/rollout:read). Starting aggregates query implementation next; blocked on final metric key names from Applied ML.
2026-02-03 (Selene Huang): Metric keys finalized for v1 bundle: format_adherence_rate, refusal_rate, rubric_overall_score, safety_policy_violation_rate, missing_score_rate. Please expose both absolute values and delta_vs_control + ci_low/ci_high (as floats). If your response schema is strongly typed, ensure we can add new metric keys without breaking older SDKs (map/dictionary).
2026-02-04 (Chloe Martin): We can’t return a map/dictionary in our public API without committing to a schema; but this is Console API (not data plane). Proposal: return metrics as a list of rows {metric_key, control_value, shadow_value, delta, ci_low, ci_high, n}. That keeps it extensible without a map. Will confirm with Monica (SDK).
2026-02-05 (Monica Patel): List-of-rows is good for SDKs. Please ensure metric_key is a stable enum-ish string and add a display_name field in server response for UI convenience (or keep display logic in UI). Prefer not to put display strings in API long-term, but ok for beta if needed.
2026-02-07 (Chloe Martin): PR up for review: implements aggregates + examples endpoints with allowlisted segment keys and series caps. Examples endpoint supports outcome filter and uses artifact refs when payload storage disabled. Added integration tests for RBAC denial + retention gating. PR: redwood/pr-24933.
2026-02-10 (Jada Williams): Rollouts integration: if experiment is created with rollout_id, we should store rollout_phase_id (canary phase) when available so we can later pin metrics to the phase timeline. Not required for beta but please add optional field to create request and store it if present.
2026-02-11 (Chloe Martin): Added optional rollout_phase_id and validated it belongs to rollout_id. Also added audit log hooks behind feature flag (audit schema work in ENG-5417). Merged after approvals.
2026-02-12 (Dylan Brooks): Marking Done. Next: UI integration (ENG-5408) and SDK bindings (ENG-5418). Please ensure docs mention that examples may return artifact refs only depending on tenant retention.

title: Staging validation and publish playbook for Redwood-verified model performance profiles
content:
Staging validation and publish playbook for Redwood-verified model performance profiles

Problem statement:
Redwood needs a reproducible, low-friction playbook that takes a candidate model from a verified bench run to a published Redwood-verified performance profile. Current onboarding is ad-hoc across teams: engineering runs benches, PM curates results, and publishing is manual. This ticket captures a staged validation + publish workflow that can be automated and audited, includes version pinning guidance, canary rollout rules, rollback criteria, and ongoing revalidation cadence.

Goals:
- Define a deterministic staging validation pipeline that mirrors production workload slices (latency P50/P95/P99, throughput, cost/unit).
- Standardize artifacts required for publishing (bench results, sample workload traces, cost model inputs, bias/quality check links).
- Provide a pinning policy for model variants and a default canary rollout with automated metrics gates.
- Create a publish checklist + automated checks to reduce human error and make publishing auditable.
- Specify periodic revalidation cadence and drift triggers to mark profiles stale.

Success metrics:
- Reduce manual review time per profile by 60% (measured as hours spent by PM and Eng per publish).
- 95% of published profiles have full validation artifacts and pass automated gates at publish time.
- Mean time to rollback for a bad profile <= 30 minutes with automated fallback.

Acceptance criteria:
- A documented staging-to-publish playbook in Confluence (link in attachments).
- CI pipeline job (profile-staging-validation) that runs benches and outputs a canonical manifest with latency/throughput/cost and artifact links.
- Canary deployment policy template: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with automated gate at each step based on SLO/delta thresholds.
- Release checklist implemented as checklist file in repo and a lightweight UI action in the Console to trigger publish.
- Periodic revalidation job scheduled (every 30 days) and drift hooks wired to the evals pipeline.

Proposed staging validation flow (high-level):
1) Intake: model PR + model metadata (architecture, weights hash, quantization knobs) and target dataset slices.
2) Bench run: standardized bench harness executes representative workloads (chat, completion, embeddings) at multiple sequence length distributions and concurrency profiles. Outputs: token-level latency histogram, P50/P95/P99, throughput@seqLen, and cost-per-1M-tokens estimate.
3) KV/prefix caching sanity: run prefix cache microbench to verify KV cache scaling characteristics.
4) Quality smoke tests: run PM prompt set to validate basic output quality (contains sample prompts and reference metrics).
5) Artifact bundle: bench JSON, perf plots, run logs, PR link, and verified-model-manifest attached to staging job.
6) Automated gates evaluate deltas versus baseline profile(s) and check absolute thresholds. If gates pass, job creates a DraftProfile in the profile registry and notifies reviewers.
7) Manual review window (24-48 hours) for PM/Eng/Research to comment; minor issues can be remediated and bench re-run.
8) Canary publish: template rollout policy applies; profile pinned to a stable model variant ID that maps to both hosted and dedicated runtimes.

Automated gate rules (examples):
- Latency P95 must not regress >15% relative to pinned baseline for given sequence lengths.
- Throughput per GPU must be within -20% of baseline or a documented capacity tag with justification.
- Cost per 1M tokens must not exceed baseline by >25% unless explicit business justification present.
- No single microbenchmark should exceed historical max P99 by >200ms for interactive models.
- KV cache hit rate must be >70% for workloads that exercise prefix caching.

Pinning policy summary:
- All published Redwood-verified profiles must include a pinned model identifier that includes model name, semantic version, checksum (weights hash), and recommended runtime flags (quantization, kernel hints). Example: 'gpt-small-v2+q4_0+sha256:abcd1234'.
- Minor weight-only changes (same checksum) are allowed as patch updates; any checksum change requires staged revalidation and a new profile version.
- Profiles should support a backward-compatible aliasing system (stable alias vs exact pin) to allow safe rollback to an older pinned fingerprint.

Canary rollout template (automated):
- Stage 0: DraftProfile created, no traffic. Notify reviewers.
- Stage 1: Canary-1: 5% traffic for 2 hours. Gate: no P95 regression >10% and error rate unchanged.
- Stage 2: Canary-2: 25% traffic for 4 hours. Gate: P95 regression <=12% and SLI error budget consumption within expected range.
- Stage 3: Ramp to 100% after automated approval or manual signoff.
- Fallback: immediate rollback to previous pinned fingerprint if any gate fails; trigger incident alert to oncall and update profile status to "rolled_back".

Revalidation and staleness rules:
- Schedule a full revalidation every 30 days for production profiles and every 7 days for Canary profiles in active testing.
- Trigger revalidation on upstream infra changes (runtime-1.*), major kernel updates, or if the model's token distribution shifts by >20% (tracked by console histogram diffs).
- Profiles failing revalidation are marked STALE and moved to a suggested-refresh queue; customers with active usage receive an opt-in email and a 14-day grace period before autoswitching to fallback variants.

Observability / dashboard needs:
- Per-profile dashboard tile (latency histograms, throughput, cost trajectory, last validation timestamp, pinned fingerprint).
- Diff view between candidate profile and baseline with highlighted regressions and cost delta.
- Automated audit log entry for every publish/rollback with links to artifacts and reviewer approvals.

Operational checklist for publishing (short):
- [ ] Bench artifacts uploaded and manifest created.
- [ ] Automated gates green.
- [ ] PM review complete (comments resolved).
- [ ] Security & privacy checklist (data handling) verified if model used customer data.
- [ ] Canary policy applied and scheduled.
- [ ] Release note drafted and changelog entry created.

Integration and automation tasks (engineering):
- New CI job profile-staging-validation that produces canonical artifact bundle and manifest (ENG-27108).
- Console API endpoint to create DraftProfile and kick off canary (ENG-27345).
- Profile registry change to store fingerprint + alias mapping + publish metadata (ENG-26890).
- Hook evals pipeline for revalidation triggers (ENG-27910).

Risks and trade-offs:
- Tight automated thresholds may block useful model variants that are costlier but still acceptable; include a documented override flow with explicit business justification.
- Additional staging runs increase onboarding latency and infra cost; mitigate by sampling adaptive bench sizes for low-impact models.
- Pinning to exact fingerprints increases operational safety but can delay quick fixes; use aliasing and fast rollback for agility.

Owners and reviewers:
- PM owner: Jonah Patel (assignee).
- Eng owners: Performance infra (Riya Kapoor), Runtime (Marcus Li).
- Research / quality reviewer: Clara Nguyen.
- Design reviewer (Console UX): Leo Martinez.

Deliverables & timeline:
- Week 1 (2025-02-12 -> 2025-02-18): Draft playbook and automated gate definitions; prototype bench harness inputs.
- Week 2 (2025-02-19 -> 2025-02-25): Implement CI job and profile manifest; initial console endpoint stub.
- Week 3 (2025-02-26 -> 2025-03-04): Integrate canary template and audit logging; run two internal onboarding trials.
- Week 4 (2025-03-05 -> 2025-03-15): Iterate on reviewer feedback, finalize Confluence playbook, and flip publish to GA for open-model catalog.

Attachments:
- https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/PM-24321+Profile+Staging+Playbook
- https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1abcStagingBenchArtifacts
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness/pull/374
- Draft checklist: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1exampleChecklist

Notes: This ticket intentionally separates gating logic from the Console UI surface — the former must be engine-agnostic and owned by Performance infra, the latter is a thin orchestration layer owned by Console.

Next steps:
- Jonah and Riya to align on gate thresholds and signal definitions (+ meeting scheduled 2025-02-14 11:00 PST).
- ENG owners to open the CI job epic and link back to this ticket.
- Run the first internal onboarding with model 'open-translate-v1' and document learnings as comments below.
2025-02-12 10:03 - Amina Ruiz: Created initial ticket after sync with Research. Added high-level flow and success metrics. Assigned to Jonah.
2025-02-14 11:47 - Jonah Patel: Meeting notes: agreed to start gates conservative (15% latency / 25% cost), Riya to prototype bench harness. Action: ENG to spin up profile-staging CI job (ENG-27108).
2025-02-18 16:22 - Riya Kapoor: Prototype bench harness PR opened (link in attachments). Early run on open-translate-v1 shows P95 +8% but cost +30% against small baseline. Need PM decision on cost tolerance for translation models.
2025-02-20 09:05 - Clara Nguyen: Research review: quality smoke tests passed for prompts in baseline set, recommend adding semantic similarity checks (BLEU/COMET) for translation workloads.

title: Define “minimum supported” observability pack for Redwood Private (dashboards, alerts, logs) + acceptance criteria and rollout plan
content:
Define “minimum supported” observability pack for Redwood Private (dashboards, alerts, logs) + acceptance criteria and rollout plan

## Summary
We need a clear, supportable definition of the “minimum supported” observability experience for **Redwood Private** (VPC + on-prem). This ticket defines:
- What we ship by default (dashboards, alert rules, log pipeline)
- What “supported” means (and what is explicitly out of scope)
- Acceptance criteria for v1
- Rollout plan and enablement requirements (Support/SRE readiness)

This definition is used by Engineering (Telemetry/Private Deployments), SRE, Solutions/PS, and Support as the contract for Private installs.

## Background / Why now
Private customers consistently ask:
- “What do I get out of the box for monitoring?”
- “Which dashboards/alerts are supported by Redwood Support?”
- “How do I export logs to my SIEM in an air-gapped environment?”

We’ve also seen recurring support cases where:
- Dashboards are missing/blank after install or upgrade
- Prometheus scrapes fail due to NetworkPolicy changes
- Alert rules are noisy with default thresholds

We will standardize the baseline and ship it as a versioned bundle via Helm + private installer.

## Definition: Minimum Supported Observability Pack (v1)
### Supported baseline (what Redwood ships + supports)
**A) Metrics + Dashboards (Grafana)
**We ship a curated set of **versioned Grafana dashboards** under an explicit “Redwood Private / Minimum Pack” folder. The dashboards are expected to render against the shipped recording rules and bounded-cardinality metrics.

Must-have dashboards (v1):
1) **Runtime Overview (Serving runtime)**
   - Request rate (RPS) and token throughput
   - p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end + runtime processing)
   - Error rate by class (4xx/5xx, timeouts, upstream)
   - Batching/queueing indicators (queue depth, batch size, queue wait)
   - GPU utilization + memory pressure (where available)
   - KV cache indicators (hit rate / reuse where instrumented)

2) **Control Plane Health**
   - API gateway health (availability, latency)
   - Routing/policy engine health
   - Auth/RBAC integration points (error rate/timeouts)
   - Installer/upgrade controller status and recent reconciles

3) **Infrastructure / Kubernetes Signals (minimum view)**
   - Pod restarts / CrashLoopBackOff for Redwood namespaces
   - Node pressure (CPU/memory), PVC usage for Prometheus/Grafana/log collector
   - Prometheus scrape health summary (targets up/down, scrape errors)

Nice-to-have (explicitly not required for v1 support):
- Deep per-model performance breakdowns beyond bounded aggregates
- Multi-cluster federated views
- Customer-specific custom panels maintained by Redwood

**B) Alerting (Prometheus alert rules)
**We ship a minimal set of alert rules aligned to Private SLO guidance. Alerts must include:
- Severity taxonomy (page vs ticket)
- Clear annotations with “what to do first”
- Runbook link (internal + customer-facing where appropriate)

Minimum alert categories (v1):
1) **SLO / Golden signal alerts**
   - API availability SLO burn (fast + slow burn)
   - Latency SLO burn (p95 and/or p99 depending on endpoint)
   - Elevated error rate (5xx + timeouts) with suppression for planned maintenance windows

2) **Saturation / resource pressure (inference-critical)**
   - GPU saturation sustained
   - OOM kills / CUDA OOM (or container OOMKilled)
   - CPU throttling / memory pressure for runtime pods (sustained)
   - Queue depth / backpressure sustained (where available)

3) **Platform health**
   - CrashLoopBackOff/restart loops for core control plane + runtime
   - Prometheus scrape target down (Redwood services) beyond grace window
   - Prometheus TSDB disk filling / PVC high watermark
   - Grafana unhealthy (service down)

Alerting defaults:
- **Paging** only for conditions that imply customer-visible outage or imminent outage.
- Everything else defaults to **ticket / non-page** to avoid “noisy by default” installs.
- Customers can opt into more aggressive paging thresholds, but Redwood Support will treat those as customer-configured.

**C) Logs (structured, safe-by-default) + export options
**We ship a supported **log collection and forwarding configuration** for Redwood namespaces.

Log content requirements:
- Structured JSON logs for core services
- Required fields (where applicable): `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `component`, `cluster_id`, `namespace`, `pod`, `request_id`, `route` (bounded), `model` (bounded/normalized), `status_code`, `latency_ms`
- Tenant identifier must be **hashed** (no raw tenant/customer identifiers)
- **No prompt or completion payloads** in operational logs by default
- Explicit redaction rules for tokens/secrets/credentials

Supported sinks/export (v1):
- **Loki** (Grafana ecosystem)
- **Elasticsearch/OpenSearch**
- **Splunk HEC**
- **OTLP logs** export is optional for v1 (documented if low-risk; not required for GA support)

Retention defaults (v1 guidance):
- Metrics: 15 days (configurable)
- Logs: 7 days locally (configurable), with recommendation to export to customer SIEM for longer retention

### What “Supported” means (contract)
If a customer deploys Redwood Private using the installer/Helm charts with the minimum pack enabled **without unsupported modifications**, Redwood Support/SRE will:
- Troubleshoot missing dashboards and alert behavior using the shipped runbooks
- Validate data availability (scrapes, recording rules, datasource)
- Provide recommended tuning for thresholds where documented

Not supported under “minimum pack”:
- Maintaining bespoke dashboards created by the customer
- Debugging third-party Prometheus operator variants with significant customization (we can provide best-effort guidance)
- Long retention or advanced compliance configurations beyond documented knobs
- Full-fidelity distributed tracing across all internal hops (v1)

## Requirements / Non-goals
### Must-haves (v1)
- Turnkey installation via Helm/installer with sane defaults
- Works in air-gapped/on-prem packaging (dashboards + rules + images bundled/versioned)
- Bounded metrics cardinality (no unbounded `route`, `model`, `tenant_id`, `request_id` labels in Prometheus series)
- Backward-compatible upgrades OR a documented migration path (dashboards/alerts should not silently break)
- Runbooks linked directly from alert annotations
- Security review sign-off for log fields + retention guidance

### Non-goals (v1)
- Multi-cluster observability federation
- Premium features: long retention, advanced tracing sampling controls, per-customer dashboard customization
- Building a new SIEM (we export to the customer’s tools)

## Acceptance Criteria
The minimum pack is considered defined and ready for GA when all items below are true.

### Functional acceptance
1) **Dashboards render** out-of-the-box in reference environments (VPC + on-prem-like) and show non-empty panels after running basic traffic.
2) **Prometheus alerts** load successfully and fire under controlled failure injection (e.g., scrape down, pod restart loops, forced latency).
3) **Logs are collected** from Redwood namespaces and can be exported to at least one supported sink (Loki OR Splunk HEC OR Elasticsearch) using documented examples.
4) **Installer/Helm wiring**: minimum pack can be enabled/disabled with a single top-level values switch; key knobs (retention, scrape intervals, sink config) are documented.
5) **Air-gapped packaging**: offline bundle includes all required artifacts (dashboards, rules, collector config, images) with version pinning.

### Supportability acceptance
6) Every page-worthy alert includes:
   - impact statement
   - immediate checks (“what to do first”)
   - runbook URL
   - ownership (team/service)
7) Known issues documented with workarounds (dashboards blank, scrape blocked by NetworkPolicy, alert noise tuning).
8) Sizing guidance published (Prometheus/Grafana/log collector CPU/mem/PVC) for at least 3 footprint tiers.

### Security/compliance acceptance
9) Security sign-off that operational logs do not include secrets/PII by default; redaction guidance included.
10) Clear guidance on audit logs vs operational logs, with retention recommendations.

## Rollout Plan
### Phase 0 — Internal dogfood (staging/private reference)
- Enable minimum pack by default in Redwood-managed reference clusters.
- Run smoke tests on every build that touches installer/Helm/observability-pack.
- Success gate: dashboards stable across 2 upgrades + 1 rollback test.

### Phase 1 — Design partners (opt-in)
- Select 2–4 Private customers (mix of VPC + on-prem/air-gap) with Solutions involvement.
- Default remains **off** for existing installs unless explicitly enabled.
- Weekly alert noise review with SRE (tune thresholds and disable non-actionable alerts by default).
- Success gate: Support can resolve “no dashboards / scrape down / log export auth” issues using runbooks without engineering intervention in >80% of cases.

### Phase 2 — GA (supported minimum)
- Ship as “Minimum Supported Observability Pack” in release notes.
- Default **on for new installs**; existing installs prompted during upgrade with a migration note.
- Support readiness checklist complete (on-call playbooks, known issues, escalation paths).

### Phase 3 — Post-GA hardening
- Track top 5 support drivers and iterate (dashboards, alert noise, export configs).
- Evaluate OTLP logs/traces as a first-class supported sink for v2.

## Metrics of success
- Reduce time-to-triage for Private incidents (target: -30% median from support ticket open to first actionable diagnosis)
- Reduce “missing/blank dashboards” support cases (target: -50% QoQ)
- Keep alert noise within acceptable levels (page rate aligns to SLO impact; no default paging for non-outage signals)

## Open Questions
1) Do we require OTLP logs export as a supported sink for v1, or treat it as “documented best-effort”?
2) Do we ship Prometheus/Grafana (batteries included) or integrate with customer-managed Prometheus/Grafana as the primary path?
   - Current direction: ship integration + defaults; allow customer-managed as supported if they meet documented prerequisites.
3) What is the minimum set of runtime-specific recording rules needed to keep dashboards stable while bounding cardinality?

## References
- Confluence: Private minimum pack requirements: sources/confluence/product-docs/requirements/private-observability-minimum-pack-requirements.json
- Confluence: Metrics/alerting standards for Private: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/metrics-and-alerting-standards-for-private.json
- ADR-021 scope: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-021-private-observability-minimum-pack-scope.json
- ADR-022 log pipeline defaults: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-022-log-pipeline-defaults-private.json
- SLO guidance: sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/private-install-slo-guidance.json
- Kickoff notes: sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/private-deployments/private-observability-min-pack-kickoff-notes.json

## Updates
### 2025-05-22 (Vivek)
Aligned with Neha/Sean on “page vs ticket” philosophy: only SLO burn + imminent outage conditions page by default. Added explicit non-goals for premium observability.

### 2025-06-05 (Vivek)
Confirmed air-gap requirement: bundle must include dashboards/rules/config + checksums, and installer must validate presence of artifacts preflight.

### 2025-06-27 (Vivek)
Reviewed early alert noise feedback from staging: CPU/memory thresholds too tight; default rules should target sustained saturation + correlate with error rate where possible.

### 2025-07-18 (Vivek)
Definition finalized for GA readiness. Engineering work tracked in ENG sub-issues; Support enablement and known-issues doc required before default-on for new installs.

title: Proportional burst allocation and post-facto billing adjustments for Dedicated capacity
content:
Proportional burst allocation and post-facto billing adjustments for Dedicated capacity

Background: Dedicated pools expose reserved throughput (committed capacity) plus opportunistic burst capacity. When pool degradation or preemption occurs we must: 1) fairly attribute reserved vs burst usage per tenant; 2) apply SLA credits if reserved throughput was degraded; and 3) offer deterministic, auditable post-facto billing adjustments so finance and customers can reconcile invoices. Current implementation uses a best-effort leaky-bucket per-tenant counter and applies burst credits at coarse windows which leads to noisy attributions and occasional overcharges during multi-tenant pool events. This ticket designs and implements a proportional, time-sliced usage ledger and a reconciliation job that computes SLA credits and negative-balance adjustments after the fact.
Create a deterministic, time-sliced ledger for Dedicated pools that: (a) attributes reserved vs burst consumption proportionally across tenants for each time-slice; (b) computes SLA credit allocation and negative-balance protections post-facto; (c) is idempotent, auditable, and compatible with existing billing pipelines.
Introduce 1-minute time-sliced ingestion of pool-level telemetry and per-tenant request tokens. For each minute slice, compute theoretical reserved entitlement per tenant (based on their committed throughput at that minute) and classify actual tokens consumed into reserved vs burst proportions using a proportional allocator when aggregate demand > reserved capacity. Persist ledger rows per-tenant per-minute. Run a daily reconciliation job to calculate SLA credits for minutes where actual available capacity < reserved capacity and to generate post-facto adjustments (credits/debits) exposed to billing. Implement a shadow mode for 6 weeks before enabling adjustments to invoices.
Telemetry ingestion: use existing runtime metrics endpoint to emit pool.available_capacity and per-tenant.request_tokens per 10s, aggregate into 1m buckets in the ingestion service.
Allocation algorithm: for each minute M, let R = sum(reserved_capacity_i) for tenants i, A = available_capacity_observed for the pool, and T_i = tokens_consumed_by_tenant_i in M. If sum(T_i) <= R then mark consumption as reserved up to each tenant's reserved share. If sum(T_i) > R then compute reserved_share_i = min(T_i, floor(R * (reserved_capacity_i / R))) and remaining tokens are burst. When reserved_capacity floats (reassignments), use the committed reservation snapshot at minute boundary.
SLA credit calc: for minutes where A < R_expected (expected reserved pool capacity), compute an availability_ratio = A / R_expected. For each tenant, SLA_credit_minutes = (1 - availability_ratio) * reserved_share_i. Convert SLA minutes into monetary credit using the tenant's reserved unit rate at invoice time.
Ledger schema (persisted): one row per tenant per-minute with fields: timestamp_minute, tenant_key, reserved_entitled, tokens_consumed, reserved_attributed, burst_attributed, pool_id, capacity_snapshot_tag. Stored in OLAP as CSV/Parquet and exported to billing pipeline. (Persisted as flat columns; no nested blobs.)
Idempotency: reconciliation job computes adjustments by looking up ledger rows with reconciliation_tag=NULL and emits adjustments with a deterministic hash. If a run fails, it can safely retry without double-applying adjustments.
Performance: aggregation and allocation done inside a streaming job (Flink/kafka-streams) with local in-memory per-pool windowed state to operate at scale. Output to an events topic consumed by reconciliation worker.
Auditability: generate per-adjustment proof payload (ledger_rows included by id) linked in billing records and customer-facing invoice adjustments UI.
Compatibility: provide mapping from new ledger rows to existing billing pipeline fields so finance reports remain consistent. Add feature flag to toggle applying adjustments to invoices while still writing ledger rows.
Edge cases: short spikes (<1s) are captured in 1m buckets; preemption mid-minute uses capacity_snapshot_tag to ensure visibility and later correction via SLA credit logic. Pool split/merge operations include a migration mapping table to re-anchor ledger rows when pool topology changes.
Bucket granularity: 1-minute buckets are chosen as a balance between accuracy and storage/compute cost. Finer buckets (10s) increase accuracy for short preemptions but increase ingestion and storage by ~6x.
Proportional allocation fairness vs. simple first-come attribution: proportional approach is fairer for multi-tenant events but requires committed-reservation snapshots per-minute which increases complexity.
Real-time billing adjustments are avoided; we prefer batch post-facto adjustments to keep invoicing deterministic and allow dispute handling.
Shadow-mode complexity: running two parallel attribution models (current production + new ledger) doubles some compute but is necessary for confidence before switching invoice application.
Streaming ingestion emits per-pool 1m buckets with pool_capacity and per-tenant tokens_consume metrics with >=99.9% success under normal load
Allocation job produces ledger rows for 95% of tenant-minute combinations (allowing small data loss windows) and ledger row schema is exported to billing pipeline consumer test harness
Reconciliation daily job computes SLA credits deterministically and produces adjustments with a deterministic hash; two identical runs on the same input produce identical outputs
Shadow-mode comparison: after 4 weeks of shadow runs, discrepancies between old and new attribution are within expected bounds and documented; finance approves cutover criteria
System-level invariants: sum(reserved_attributed + burst_attributed) == tokens_consumed for all ledger rows, and sum(reserved_attributed) <= pool_reserved_capacity for each minute accounting for rounding tolerances
End-to-end e2e integration test that simulates a pool-wide degradation produces SLA credits visible in test-billing UI and an associated audit trail link
Phase 0: Instrumentation (2w) - ensure runtime emits per-tenant tokens and pool capacity at 10s resolution and add aggregator that writes 1m buckets to topic
Phase 1: Allocation service + ledger writer (3w) - implement proportional allocator in streaming job, write ledger to OLAP and events topic, enable feature flag to start writing rows in production (shadow)
Phase 2: Reconciliation job + billing adapter (2w) - daily job that reads ledger rows, computes SLA credits and adjustments, writes adjustments to billing microservice with idempotency keys
Phase 3: Shadow validation (6w) - run alongside existing system, produce discrepancy dashboards, run stakeholder reviews (Finance, Customer Success, Legal)
Phase 4: Controlled cutover (2w) - enable invoice application for a pilot tenant cohort, monitor closely, then full rollout
Phase 5: Backfill and audit (3w) - backfill historical ledger for rolling window (30d) as allowed by compute budget; apply agreed-upon retroactive credits only after legal/finance sign-off
Unit tests around allocation math (including edge rounding cases)
Property-based tests that assert conservation of tokens across synthetic request traces
Integration test that boots a small dedicated pool in staging and replays recorded production traces to verify ledger outputs
Chaos tests: simulate short preemptions and host-level degradation to validate SLA credit paths
Billing pipeline integration tests that consume adjustments and verify idempotency and balance preservation
Metric: fraction_of_minutes_without_ledger_row_per_pool > 0.1% -> paging alert
Metric: daily_total_adjustment_amount > threshold -> pager to finance-runbook
Dashboard: per-pool discrepancy between old_attribution and new_attribution distributions
Audit logs: reconcile_job_run_id and list of ledger row ids included; unprocessed rows metric
Start as write-only: ledger rows are produced but do not feed billing; run shadow comparisons and produce weekly reports for Finance
Pilot tenants: choose 3 mid-size tenants that represent different reservation topologies for invoice pilot
Backfill window: default to 30 days; longer backfill requires manual approval from Finance due to invoice exposure
Dispute handling: adjustments include a human-review flag and can be suppressed until manual approval for enterprise customers
Rollback: feature flag to disable automatic invoice application; ledger rows can continue to be written for forensics
Should monetary conversion for SLA minutes use the reservation rate at invoice issue date or at the minute timestamp? (Finance preference: invoice issue date to simplify accounting)
Rounding policy for fractional token attribution when many tenants share a pool — use deterministic floor-with-remainder distribution?
How to show micro-credits on customer invoices without confusing UX — condensed line items vs. aggregated monthly credit?
Policy for retroactive credits older than billing cutoff (e.g., >90 days) — require legal sign-off?
Storage and compute costs increase due to per-minute ledger rows (estimated +15% infra cost for ingestion and OLAP storage)
Finance or Legal objections during audit of historical adjustments that could delay backfill/cutover
Complexity in mapping pool topology changes (split/merge) to existing ledger rows could cause orphaned rows if mapping not recorded
Incorrect implementation could double-credit or double-debit invoices if reconciliation idempotency keys are not robust

2025-02-21 Liam Chen: Added allocator pseudocode and notes about 1m bucket choice. Suggest we evaluate 30s in stress tests.
2025-02-24 Mateo Rivera (PM): Finance wants deterministic hashes attached to each adjustment for ledger reconciliation. Added requirement.

title: FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint epic (runtime perf suite + rollout decisions)
content:
FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint epic (runtime perf suite + rollout decisions)

Epic goal
Deliver a defensible, reproducible FP8/INT8 benchmark matrix across top hosted models and primary fleet GPUs (H100, A100, plus at least one cost SKU where feasible), then translate results into concrete runtime changes: kernel auto-selection heuristics, scheduler knob defaults, and hosted-catalog quantization profile guidance. Changes must be safe to roll out via flags + perf canary with automatic rollback.

Why this sprint
We have kernel-level wins from FP8/INT8 paths that are not consistently realized end-to-end due to scheduling interactions (prefill/decode mix, batching window, backpressure) and shape-specific constraints. We also need reproducibility improvements (driver/CUDA pinning, clock locking, artifact metadata) so results are defensible internally (and selectively externally via PM).

Owners / stakeholders
- Program driver: Talia Benson
- Kernel lead: Hiro Tanaka (primary assignee)
- Scheduling lead: Sofia Ivanova
- Benchmark harness owner: Rina Kobayashi
- Perf/Evals decision owner: Jonas Weber
- Infra capacity sponsor: Neha Kapoor
- SRE canary/rollout owner: Rafael Mendes
- Observability/dashboards: Allison Grant

Scope (in)
1) Benchmark harness updates (microbench + E2E serving)
- Add FP8/INT8 modes, consistent warmup/measurement loops, standardized artifact export and metadata (git SHA, container, CUDA/driver, clocks, model hash, config).
- Add scheduler instrumentation to isolate prefill vs decode and expose queue depth/backpressure for mixed workloads.

2) Execution: benchmark matrix runs
- GPUs: H100 + A100 as required; add one cost-focused SKU (L4) if the harness supports apples-to-apples + we can reserve time.
- Models: “top hosted models” (final list captured in sprint plan / benchmark suite v3). Include realistic workloads: prompt length distributions, prefill/decode mixes, batch sizes, and concurrency profiles.

3) Analysis + decisions
- Kernel-selection heuristics: when to pick FP8 vs INT8 vs baseline by GPU arch and shape regime; include guardrails and correctness fallbacks.
- Scheduler parameter tuning: batching window / backpressure defaults tuned so end-to-end realizes kernel wins without TTFT regressions.
- Quantization policy guidance: which models eligible for FP8 vs INT8 defaults; when eval sign-off is required; calibration requirements and known risks.

4) Shipping + rollout
- Implement changes behind flags; enable per-model/per-region cohorts.
- Perf canary gates: thresholds for TTFT/TPOT/tokens/s with noise handling; automatic rollback triggers.
- Release notes + runbook updates.

Out of scope (explicit)
- Re-architecting the scheduler (we are tuning knobs + instrumentation only).
- Publishing public benchmarks. PM will decide what can be shared and with what footnotes.
- Model training changes (this is serving/runtime only).

Definition of done
- Benchmark matrix produced with p50/p95 latency, throughput, variance (error bars), and cost proxies across the agreed GPU/model/workload set.
- Reproducibility: runners pin driver/CUDA and optionally lock clocks; artifacts include required metadata; reruns on the same setup reproduce within standards variance.
- ADR-level decision captured for kernel auto-selection heuristics + guardrails + fallback.
- Scheduler tuning validated against the benchmark suite to avoid TTFT regressions (or documented trade-offs + gating).
- Perf canary thresholds implemented and dashboards live; rollback triggers tested at least once in staging or via controlled degradation.
- Runtime 1.22.0 changes merged, flagged, and rolled out via canary; release notes drafted.

Milestones / timeline (sprint-style, ~2 weeks)
- Day 1–2: Kickoff + methodology sign-off; reserve GPU capacity; finalize model/workload list.
- Day 3–4: Harness updates + calibration runs; validate measurement stability; address variance.
- Day 5–9: Full benchmark execution across matrix; daily anomaly triage.
- Day 10–11: Analysis + decisions (kernel heuristics + scheduler knobs + quant policy).
- Day 12–14: Implementation + perf canary gates; staged rollout and documentation.

- Model registry variants: sources/github/redwood-model-registry/pr-233-add-fp8-int8-variants-and-default-policy-stubs.json
- Scheduler knobs: sources/github/redwood/pr-19911-optimize-scheduler-knob-defaults-for-mixed-workloads.json
- Metrics tagging: sources/github/redwood/pr-19934-metrics-tagging-model-gpu-kernel-mode.json
- Release notes finalization: sources/github/redwood/pr-19955-update-release-notes-runtime-1-22-0.json

Milestone checklist (tracked here for the epic)
- [x] Kickoff held; methodology signed off (Claire + Jonas); list of models/workloads locked.
- [x] GPU reservations approved (Neha/Irene) and window scheduled to avoid Dedicated pool conflicts.
- [x] Harness supports FP8/INT8 toggles; measurement stability within standards on calibration runs.
- [x] Runner pins container/driver/CUDA; clocks lock option exercised for H100 variance issue.
- [x] Full H100/A100 matrix completed for top models; anomalies documented and re-runs performed.
- [x] Quality sanity suite executed for candidate defaults; model-specific caveats documented.
- [x] ADR-019 finalized; heuristics implemented + unit tests.
- [x] Perf canary thresholds deployed; dashboards verified with model/GPU/mode tags.
- [x] Canary rollout executed; one rollback event handled per runbook; follow-up hotfix merged where needed.
- [x] Runtime 1.22.0 notes updated and shared with #eng-runtime / #eng-sre.

Key decisions (summary)
- Kernel selection follows ADR-019: prefer FP8 on H100 for eligible shapes unless long-context quality risk is flagged; INT8 used primarily where matmul shapes align and quality is stable; baseline is default fallback.
- Scheduler knobs adjusted to prevent TTFT spikes under mixed workloads; batching window capped in low-concurrency regimes; backpressure thresholds tuned to avoid decode starvation.
- Quantization defaults require Applied ML sign-off for specific model families and long-context workloads; canary gating remains mandatory for default flips.

Risks + mitigations logged during sprint
- Variance on H100 due to clock drift/thermal throttling and shared-node contention → mitigate by pinning clocks where permitted, enforcing exclusive allocation in runner, and tagging artifacts with clocks + thermals.
- Correctness failures for INT8 on specific shapes → shape guardrails + runtime fallback to baseline + unit tests.
- End-to-end TTFT regressions even when kernel microbench wins → add scheduler instrumentation, tune batching/backpressure, require canary TTFT/TPOT thresholds.
- Customer impact from capacity contention during benchmark windows → reservation plan guardrails + avoid Dedicated pools + explicit SRE/Infra coordination.

Comms cadence used
- Daily 15-min triage (runtime + applied ML + SRE rep) during matrix execution.
- End-of-week readout to performance stakeholders (Jonas/Neha/Aditya/Henry) with “what we can claim” caveats.
- Rollout coordination in #eng-releases for runtime-1.22.0 RC sign-off.

Notes / updates (condensed)
- 2026-02-10: Epic created after kickoff thread; sub-issues opened for harness, kernel flags, scheduler instrumentation, and canary gates.
- 2026-02-13: Calibration run found unacceptable variance on H100; pivoted to driver/CUDA pinning + clock lock support.
- 2026-02-17: First full matrix pass complete for H100; A100 in progress; INT8 correctness failure reproduced → added shape guardrails and reran affected cells.
- 2026-02-20: ADR heuristics review converged; implemented + started canary gating integration.
- 2026-02-24: Canary detected TTFT regression in a narrow prompt regime; auto-rollback triggered; issue triaged to launch overhead + scheduler mix; hotfix landed to disable FP8 for that shape cohort pending deeper kernel work.
- 2026-02-28: Final matrix + eval summary attached in Drive; runtime-1.22.0 release notes updated; epic marked Done.

Follow-ups (not in scope for this epic, but recommended)
- Add L4 coverage and validate INT8 wins in cost SKU regimes (requires updated runner support + reservations).
- Expand quality suite to include more structured-output/tool-calling long-context prompts where FP8 showed sensitivity.
- Extend perf canary baselines per region and add automated drift detection for driver updates.

title: Private deployments: sync regional failover guidance with new trigger hierarchy + automation guardrails
content:
Private deployments: sync regional failover guidance with new trigger hierarchy + automation guardrails

## Context
We updated Hosted API + Dedicated regional failover automation (signal hierarchy, deterministic policy evaluation, rollback guardrails, dry-run/simulate tooling). Our Private deployment guidance still reflects the pre-upgrade world (manual runbooks + ad-hoc triggers), which is now out of sync and confusing for regulated / VPC / on-prem customers.

This ticket aligns Private docs with the new approach:
- Make it explicit what Redwood supports vs. what we recommend customers implement.
- Translate trigger hierarchy + anti-flap/rollback semantics into Private-friendly patterns (where customers may own routing + health evaluation).
- Ensure we are consistent with security boundaries (data residency, audit logs) and avoid implying unsupported automation.

## Goals
1) Reduce support load from ambiguous expectations (“Does Redwood automatically fail over my Private region?”).
2) Provide a clear reference architecture for Private multi-region failover using the same signal hierarchy concepts as Hosted/Dedicated.
3) Document supported integrations (Region Health Service API, audit event formats, recommended probes) and constraints (residency, KMS/HSM, customer-controlled routing).

## Non-goals
- Shipping new Private automation features in this ticket.
- Changing SLAs/contract language.
- Providing bespoke per-customer playbooks beyond the standard guidance doc.

## Primary doc(s) to update
- Confluence: sources/confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/private-region-failover-guidance.json

## References / related specs
- ADR-042: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-042-failover-trigger-signal-hierarchy.json
- ADR-043: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-043-automated-routing-policy-rollback.json
- Security boundaries: sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/failover-and-security-boundaries.json
- Region health service: sources/confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/region-health-service.json
- Hosted/Dedicated runbooks (for consistent terminology):
  - sources/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/routing-policy-failover-controller-runbook.json
  - sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/hosted-api-regional-failover-runbook.json

## What must be crystal clear in Private docs
### Supported (Redwood)
- Provide region health signals (where deployed) via Region Health Service API endpoints and/or exported metrics.
- Provide audit events for failover decisions/actions in Hosted/Dedicated; for Private, provide schema + recommended logging fields customers should record (who/what/why/evidence).
- Provide recommended signal hierarchy + default thresholds as guidance.
- Provide an operator procedure for controlled testing (staging first) and safe rollback patterns.

### Recommended (Customer)
- Customer-operated failover controller/policy evaluation (or equivalent) unless contract explicitly includes Redwood-managed routing.
- Corroboration-based trigger gating (reachability + burn-rate + capacity) with hold-down timers to avoid oscillation.
- Synthetic probes from each region (and from “client vantage points” if applicable) to distinguish internal vs external impairments.
- Explicit blast radius constraints (per-tenant/per-service) and rate limits on policy flips.

### Not supported / avoid implying
- Fully automatic cross-region failover “out of the box” for all Private deployments.
- Cross-region routing that violates data residency constraints.
- Using Redwood-controlled global anycast/DNS for customer-managed domains unless explicitly provisioned.

## Proposed content changes (outline)
1) Terminology + responsibility model
   - Define “control plane impairment” vs “regional data plane impairment” vs “partial degradation”.
   - RACI: customer-owned vs Redwood-owned components in Private.

2) Signal hierarchy (Private translation)
   - Authoritative: reachability (from multiple probe vantage points).
   - Next: 5xx burn / error budget burn.
   - Next: tail latency burn.
   - Next: capacity exhaustion / headroom gates.
   - Emphasize dampening + corroboration and missing-signal behavior (do not flip purely on missing telemetry).

3) Guardrails + rollback semantics
   - Anti-flap timers, minimum dwell time, max flips per hour.
   - Rollback triggers vs. “hold-down” semantics.
   - Auditability: record evidence signals, config version, operator approvals.

4) Data residency + security boundaries
   - Region pinning rules and when cross-region failover is disallowed.
   - KMS/HSM and secrets replication prerequisites.
   - Audit log retention expectations.

5) Controlled failover testing (“game day”) pattern
   - Pre-flight checklist (capacity headroom, probe readiness, comms, rollback owner).
   - Suggested success criteria (failover time, max error rate, p95 latency delta).
   - Post-test validation + follow-ups.

6) FAQ (must answer)
   - “Does Redwood automatically fail over Private?”
   - “How do I validate triggers without impacting customers?”
   - “What happens if the region health service is down?”
   - “How does this interact with Dedicated / Hosted if I use hybrid routing?”

## Acceptance criteria
- Updated Private failover guidance doc includes:
  - A “Supported vs Recommended vs Not Supported” section.
  - A table mapping each trigger type to: required corroboration, suggested windows, default dampening, and failure modes.
  - Explicit language on data residency constraints and examples.
  - A short runbook-style checklist for controlled failover tests.
- Reviewed by:
  - Simran Kaur (Private deployments), Miles Thornton (architecture), Victor Alvarez (network), Allison Grant (observability), and Security (via failover-and-security-boundaries doc owner).
- Support-ready: Dev Patel/Owen Phillips confirm the FAQ + phrasing matches how we want to answer customer tickets.

## Open questions
- For Private customers who run Redwood-managed routing inside a customer VPC: do we document optional integration with the failover controller (dry-run only) or keep it fully customer-owned?
- Do we want to provide a “reference implementation” snippet for policy evaluation config (non-executable) to reduce ambiguity?

## Implementation plan
- Draft doc updates in Confluence (Simran + Kira Thompson).
- Add a short “diff” note for Support/CS (what changed, what to tell customers).
- Link the updated doc from the operator-facing guide where relevant (docs PR: sources/github/redwood-docs/pr-982-regional-failover-operator-guide.json).

## Risk / pitfalls
- Over-promising automation: wording must avoid implying Redwood runs customer failover for Private.
- Security: accidental suggestion that customers can fail over across residency-restricted regions.
- Too much detail: keep thresholds as “starting points,” not commitments.

## Tracking
- Target: have updated guidance ready before expanding automation rollout beyond initial tiers/routes (see ENG-2424 quarterly cadence follow-up).

2026-01-22 (Simran Kaur): Started outline; main gap is Private doc still treats latency spikes as a primary trigger. New ADR-042 makes reachability + 5xx burn authoritative. Will update with corroboration requirement and missing-signal behavior.
2026-01-28 (Allison Grant): Please avoid listing metric labels that increase cardinality. For docs, talk about aggregation by region/service tier; do not suggest per-tenant alerting by default. Also include guidance on how to annotate events for postmortems (links to automation audit events).
2026-01-30 (Victor Alvarez): Networking section needs a clear callout: DNS TTL changes don’t guarantee fast failover due to resolver caching. Recommend including ‘expected vs best-case’ timing and mention anycast constraints for customer-managed zones. Point to cross-region DNS notes.
2026-02-03 (Miles Thornton): +1 to a ‘Supported vs Recommended’ table. Also add a warning that missing telemetry must not cause a flip (we fixed this in controller after the staging crash). Suggest wording: ‘treat missing signals as UNKNOWN; require at least one positive impairment signal + corroboration.’
2026-02-07 (Dev Patel): Please add a short customer-facing snippet (2–3 paragraphs) Support can paste into tickets for: (a) planned tests, (b) real incidents. Keep it aligned with comms playbook language.
2026-02-12 (Security reviewer via Simran Kaur): Residency section should include an explicit example: ‘EU-only tenant cannot fail over to us-east even during impairment.’ Also note audit logging requirements when changing routing policies, even if customer-operated.
2026-02-18 (Kira Thompson): Draft is in Confluence with tracked changes; requesting final technical review on trigger hierarchy table and rollback semantics. Once approved, I’ll add the Support ‘diff’ note and cross-link from operator guide PR-982.

title: Reserve allocator and autoscale safeguards: predictable reserved capacity with tenant surge isolation
content:
Reserve allocator and autoscale safeguards: predictable reserved capacity with tenant surge isolation

This PRD defines a reserve allocator and autoscale safeguard layer for Dedicated capacity aimed at providing predictable reserved throughput for tenants while protecting the cluster from noisy neighbor surges. The feature introduces per-tenant reservoirs, a configurable headroom buffer, and a graceful preemption/eviction window. It also specifies operator controls and observability to ensure safe rollouts and clear incident remediation paths.
Customers with Dedicated (reserved) capacity require strong guarantees that committed tokens/throughput remain available during normal operations while still allowing bounded, auditable transient burst behavior. Current behavior either over-allocates headroom (wasting capacity) or allows bursts to degrade other tenants' SLOs without clear eviction or fallback policies.
We already support reserved pools and some burst policies, but feedback from enterprise customers and SRE indicates the need for: 1) a deterministic allocator that reduces fragmentation across zones, 2) clear tenant-level isolation thresholds, and 3) autoscale safeguards that prevent runaway preemption during cluster-wide scale events. This PRD proposes an allocator + safeguard pattern that balances predictability and efficient utilization.
1) Guarantee reserved throughput for committed tenants within defined SLO windows. 2) Provide bounded soft-bursting with measurable grace periods that are reversible. 3) Expose operator controls to tune headroom, preemption thresholds, and eviction policies. 4) Deliver telemetry and acceptance tests for correctness and regression detection.
1) This PRD does not replace the full scheduler rewrite. 2) It does not introduce per-request billing changes. 3) It will not modify on-prem networking or KMS integrations.
As a platform customer I want my reserved capacity to sustain baseline traffic even when other tenants spike, so my production features keep latency SLOs.
As an SRE I want an autoscale safeguard that prevents mass preemption from causing cascading evictions across tenants during a rapid cluster scale-down.
As an operator I want to set and adjust a cluster headroom parameter and observe its utilization so I can tune utilization vs safety trade-offs.
As a tenant admin I want to see a clear audit trail when my burst credits are consumed and when preemption occurs, so I can justify capacity purchases to stakeholders.
R1: Introduce per-tenant reservoir objects that record committed units, ephemeral headroom, and burst credits.
R2: Allocator must allocate capacity by reservoir in a way that minimizes cross-zone fragmentation and respects tenant affinity tags.
R3: Provide a cluster-wide headroom parameter (percentage of cluster reserved for safe burst) and a tenant-level cap on burst consumption.
R4: Implement a graceful preemption window: when capacity is constrained, mark surplus ephemeral allocations as preemptible and wait N seconds before evicting to allow rollback or fallback routes.
R5: Autoscale safeguards: the autoscaler must not trigger preemptions that would drop more than M tenant baseline slots in a single minute (operator-configurable).
R6: Audit logging for reservoir events: allocation, burst debit, preemption mark, eviction executed, and rollback. Logs must include tenant, pool, zone, timestamp, reason, and correlating request IDs.
R7: Expose operator APIs and Console controls to adjust headroom, per-tenant caps, and emergency reclaim policies (with change history).
R8: Provide end-to-end regression tests and chaos scenarios that validate SLO preservation for reserved tenants under spike conditions.
AC1: In test harness, a tenant with committed 100 units should retain >=95% of baseline throughput under a synthetic cross-tenant spike for a 10-minute window when headroom configured to 10%.
AC2: Autoscaler changes that would cause >20% of committed baseline slots across tenants to become preemptible in <2 minutes are rejected by safeguard logic (configurable thresholds).
AC3: Audit logs for a simulated eviction sequence contain required fields and are queryable from Console within 30s of event emission.
AC4: Console UI displays per-tenant reservoir state (committed, used, headroom, burst_credits) with live update frequency <=15s.
AC5: Can perform controlled rollback of a headroom parameter change within 5 minutes with no more than 1% incident-level customer-impact deviation compared to baseline.
AC6: Release tests include chaos scenario where zones are partially degraded and system maintains reserved tenant baseline throughput within SLA for 90% of tenants.
AC7: Documentation and operator runbook published and linked from Console help menu prior to GA rollout.
AC8: Security review signoff (if later required) must be trackable; for initial launch security_review_required set to false but process must be documented.
POST /api/dedicated/v1/reservoirs - create reservoir (tenant_id, committed_units, burst_profile)
GET /api/dedicated/v1/reservoirs/{reservoir_id} - reservoir state (committed, used, headroom, credits, zone_allocations)
PATCH /api/dedicated/v1/reservoirs/{reservoir_id} - adjust committed_units or burst_profile
GET /api/dedicated/v1/allocator/status - cluster headroom, utilization, preemptible_count
POST /api/dedicated/v1/operator/safeguard - adjust autoscale-safeguard params (max_preemptible_rate, preemption_window_seconds)
Events: reservoir.allocated, reservoir.burst_consumed, reservoir.preempt_marked, reservoir.evicted (emitted to event bus)
New 'Reservoirs' tab under Dedicated -> Capacity showing per-tenant cards and aggregated charts.
Operator panel to adjust cluster headroom and emergency reclaim with audit trail and soft-confirm modal.
Time-series line charts for reserved baseline utilization, burst consumption, and preemptible counts with selectable windows.
Drill-down view showing last 24h of reservoir events and links to correlated logs/PRs/incidents.
metric: dedicated.reservoir.committed_units (gauge, per-tenant)
metric: dedicated.reservoir.used_units (gauge, per-tenant)
metric: dedicated.headroom.utilization (percentage, cluster)
metric: dedicated.preemptible.count (gauge, cluster/zone)
alert: headroom_utilization > 90% for 5m -> P1 ops-staff
alert: preemptible_evictions_rate > configured_threshold -> P1 ops-staff
logs: structured JSON events for audit entries available in Logstore with index on tenant_id and reservoir_id
1) Canary: enable allocator in 5% of clusters (non-production tenants) for 2 weeks and run synthetic spike tests. 2) Gradual ramp: enable for 25% of customer clusters with operator monitoring for 1 week. 3) Soft GA: opt-in release for dedicated customers with documentation and runbook. 4) GA: default enable for new Dedicated contracts and migration path for existing customers. Each stage requires signoff from SRE, Product, and Legal (if contract wording changes).
ENG-232100: allocator core implementation and zone-aware placement
ENG-233450: autoscaler safeguard integration
ENG-238122: events bus schema changes for reservoir events
DES-44100: Console UX for Reservoirs tab
SEC-1002 (optional): security audit for audit-log retention policy
1. Create reservoir records for all committed tenants using billing-backed committed_units snapshot.
2. Simulate allocations in staging with mirrored traffic and reconcile differences under a 'dry-run' allocator mode.
3. Schedule a low-risk migration window for tenants with complex multi-zone footprints; provide opt-out toggle for customers during migration.
4. After migration, monitor headroom and utilization for 72h before moving to soft GA.
5. Provide rollback instructions to revert reservoir assignment and headroom adjustments within the operator Console.
Risk: Overly conservative headroom reduces utilization and increases customer costs. Mitigation: provide default conservative value + operator tuning guide and auto-suggest based on historical utilization.
Risk: Preemption cascade inadvertently evicts high-priority tenants. Mitigation: implement max_preemptible_rate and preemption window; require canary validation and operator alerting.
Risk: Fragmentation across zones reduces scheduler efficiency. Mitigation: allocator uses zone-aware packing heuristics and periodically compacts reservoirs during low traffic windows.
Risk: Ambiguous audit logs make incident forensics slow. Mitigation: enforce structured event schema and expose a Console query template for common investigations.
Q1: Default values for cluster headroom and preemption window? Proposed 10% headroom, 60s preemption window for initial canary.
Q2: How should burst credits be priced/charged for committed customers? Discussion required with Pricing team.
Q3: Should we expose per-tenant emergency reclaim toggle to tenant admins or only operators? Security and abuse considerations.
Q4: Do we need gRPC equivalents for API endpoints above or is REST sufficient for GA?

Test harness: https://gitlab.redwood.ai/dedicated/reservation-test-harness
