title: Rollout plan + feature flag strategy for Console onboarding checklist (dogfood → cohorts → GA)
content:
Rollout plan + feature flag strategy for Console onboarding checklist (dogfood → cohorts → GA)

## Context
We are shipping a new in-Console onboarding checklist (“Guided onboarding + first production launch”) for Hosted API. This ticket defines:
- Rollout phases (internal dogfood → gradual cohort exposure → GA)
- Feature flag gating + cohort selection rules
- Kill switch criteria + operational monitoring
- Comms plan for Support/CS and internal stakeholders

Goal: de-risk launch and avoid creating new onboarding confusion or support burden while we validate step funnel instrumentation and checklist state correctness.

## Owners / stakeholders
- PM (Hosted API): Nikhil Sharma
- PM (Console): Marissa Cole
- Program sponsor: Alex Martinez
- Rollout + lifecycle messaging: Ben Carter (assignee)
- Console Eng: Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin
- Telemetry: Logan Wright
- Support enablement: Dev Patel
- SRE review: Sean Gallagher

## What we are rolling out
### User-visible
- New “Get started” checklist module in Redwood Console
- Step details drawer + deep links to Console pages and docs
- Admin/support tools (override/reset) for troubleshooting (Support-only)

### Behind the scenes
- Event emission from gateway/control plane (server-side) to progress tracker
- Progress tracker API powering checklist state
- KPI dashboard + alerts (TTFS/TTFP + funnel)

## Feature flag strategy
### Flag names / surfaces
Primary exposure flag:
- `console.onboarding_checklist.enabled`

Supporting flags (if Eng prefers split for blast-radius control):
- `console.onboarding_checklist.ui_enabled` (pure UI)
- `onboarding_progress_service.enabled` (Console reads from service)
- `onboarding_events.emit_v1` (server-side event emission)
- `onboarding_admin_override.enabled` (Support-only)

### Default behavior
- Flag OFF by default across all tenants.
- When OFF:
  - Checklist module hidden (no empty state)
  - No user-facing changes in Console nav
  - Events MAY still emit (if we choose “dark launch” for telemetry) but must be safe + PII-free.

### Cohort selection rules (MVP)
Cohorting is done at the tenant/org level (not per-user) to avoid inconsistent experiences within an account.

Proposed targeting (ordered):
1) Allowlist (internal + design partners)
   - Redwood employees (dogfood tenants)
   - Explicit external tenants selected by PM/CS (design partners)
2) Gradual ramp for self-serve Hosted API tenants
   - Hash-based percentage rollout by `tenant_id` (e.g., 5% → 15% → 35% → 70% → 100%)
   - Only for “Hosted API / self-serve” plan to start
3) Expand to all new signups
   - Option A: show checklist for all new tenants created after a cutoff date (plus a percentage of existing)
   - Option B: continue hash-based ramp only (simpler)

Exclusions initially:
- Dedicated/Private tenants (until step content is validated and Console links are correct for those flows)
- Tenants in an active incident mitigation state (if we add a suppression toggle later)

### Kill switch / rollback
- Global kill switch via `console.onboarding_checklist.enabled = false`.
- Separate kill switch for event emission if needed (`onboarding_events.emit_v1 = false`) to avoid pipeline overload or data issues.
- Rollback should be possible without data migrations.

## Rollout phases
### Phase 0 — Internal readiness (pre-dogfood)
Exit criteria:
- KPI dashboard available and updating (freshness < 30 minutes)
- State monotonicity verified (no step regression from out-of-order events) — see ENG-5866
- Support playbook draft available (how to interpret checklist state)

### Phase 1 — Dogfood (Redwood employees)
Target:
- 2–3 internal tenants used by DevEx + Console teams
- Encourage running quickstart + streaming example in at least 2 SDKs (Python/TS recommended)

Duration:
- 3–5 business days (or until no P0/P1 bugs open)

Success criteria:
- No repeated step regressions for the same tenant
- Checklist UI stable (no broken deep links)
- At least 20 complete “first success” flows recorded end-to-end

### Phase 2 — External design partners (allowlist)
Target:
- 3–10 friendly customers (Support/CS coordinated)
- Include at least one account that previously hit 401/403 and one that hit 429 issues to validate mitigations

Guardrails:
- Support and PM notified before toggling on
- Dedicated Slack channel / shared thread for issues

Success criteria:
- Qualitative feedback that step order/copy is understandable
- No measurable increase in onboarding ticket rate from these accounts

### Phase 3 — Gradual cohort rollout (self-serve Hosted API)
Ramp proposal (adjustable based on incident risk):
- Day 1: 5%
- Day 3: 15%
- Day 5: 35%
- Day 7: 70%
- Day 10: 100%

Go/no-go at each ramp gate based on monitoring (below).

### Phase 4 — GA + comms
- Enable for 100% of eligible Hosted API tenants.
- Publish release notes + docs updates.
- Support macros updated and “what changed” internal blurb shared in #support and CS enablement channels.

### Phase 5 — Existing tenants backfill / experience parity (post-GA)
- Decide whether to show checklist to older tenants who already completed key steps.
- If we do: rely on backfill job (ENG-5844) + derived completion so checklist doesn’t look “stuck at 0%” for mature users.

## Monitoring + kill switch criteria
### Primary metrics (dashboard)
- TTFS (signup → first successful 2xx request) p50/p75
- TTFP proxy (first production traffic) as defined in PM-751
- Step funnel completion rates (view checklist → API key created → first 2xx → first streaming → retries/timeouts guidance acknowledged → usage dashboard visited → quotas/budgets configured → model pinned → fallback policy set)

### Data quality / pipeline health
- Event ingestion lag and drop rate
- % of tenants with checklist enabled but no events after 24h
- Cardinality checks (no high-card fields beyond schema constraints)

### Kill switch triggers (proposed)
Immediate kill switch (same day) if any of:
- Console error rate regression attributable to checklist rendering or progress API (e.g., +1% absolute 5xx on checklist endpoints)
- Progress service error rate > 1% for > 30 minutes in cohort
- Widespread step regressions (monotonicity violation) in > 2% of enabled tenants in a 24h window
- Support reports “checklist is blocking onboarding” (e.g., broken API key flow deep link) with multiple confirmations

Pause ramp (hold at current %) if any of:
- Onboarding-related support tickets per new tenant increase by > 20% vs baseline for 48h
- Funnel drop-off increases significantly at a new step (step completion -15% relative) and correlates with a UI/link issue
- Data freshness > 60 minutes for > 2 hours (dashboard unreliable)

## Support / CS comms plan
### Before Phase 2 (design partners)
- Share Support/CS briefing doc:
  - what the checklist is
  - what tenants will see
  - how to interpret partial completion
  - how to use admin override (once available)
- Add macros: 401/403 troubleshooting, streaming disconnects, 429/rate-limit handling, usage dashboard lag explanation

### During cohort rollout
- Weekly note (or per ramp gate) in #support + #customer-success:
  - current rollout %
  - known issues
  - links to runbook + “how to disable for a tenant” instructions

### GA communications
- Release notes: `sources/confluence/product-docs/release-notes/console-guided-onboarding-checklist-2025-04.json`
- Internal FAQ:
  - “Why does checklist say incomplete if we already use the API?”
  - “Why can’t I see it?” (cohorting)
  - “How do I reset it?” (Support only)

## Open questions
1) Do we want a “dismiss” option in MVP, or only auto-hide once complete? (Design leans auto-hide; Support prefers dismiss for mature users.)
2) Dark launch events for all tenants: are we comfortable with event volume prior to UI exposure? (Telemetry review needed.)
3) Cohorting policy for enterprises on Hosted API with procurement in-flight: should they be included or only allowlist? (CS input.)

## Decisions needed (for sign-off)
- Final ramp schedule (dates) and who can approve ramp gates (PM + SRE)
- Confirm kill switch thresholds + alert routing
- Confirm eligibility rules for “Hosted API self-serve” in flag targeting

## References
- PRD: `sources/confluence/product-docs/requirements/guided-onboarding-first-production-launch-prd.json`
- UX spec: `sources/confluence/product-docs/design-specs/onboarding-checklist-console-ux-spec.json`
- KPI dashboard spec: `sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/onboarding-kpis-dashboard-spec.json`
- Support playbook: `sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/onboarding-escalation-and-triage-playbook.json`

## Updates / activity log
2025-02-14 (Ben Carter): Drafted cohorting approach (allowlist → hash ramp). Waiting on Telemetry confirmation that events are safe to emit broadly.
2025-02-24 (Marissa Cole): Asked to ensure we can disable UI while keeping events on for debugging; suggests split flags.
2025-02-27 (Dev Patel): Support requests admin override included before external rollout; otherwise Support is blind when checklist gets stuck.
2025-03-03 (Logan Wright): Data freshness alert recommended; dashboards should block ramp gate if freshness > 60m.
2025-03-05 (Sean Gallagher): SRE wants explicit kill criteria tied to progress service 5xx and Console error budget; added above.

## Acceptance criteria
- Documented rollout phases + eligibility rules are agreed by PM (Hosted + Console), Support enablement, Telemetry, and SRE.
- Feature flag(s) and cohort targeting rules are defined clearly enough for implementation (ENG-58467) and for Support to understand.
- Kill switch criteria are actionable and tied to dashboards/alerts.
- Comms plan for Support/CS exists (what/when/how) and includes a path to disable per-tenant or globally.

title: Define latency SLO tiers and acceptance gates for tiered batching perf CI/canary
content:
Define latency SLO tiers and acceptance gates for tiered batching perf CI/canary

Goal
Finalize numeric latency targets for the three customer-facing SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient) and codify pass/fail gates used by the perf suite + perf-canary so we can safely roll out workload-aware batching defaults.

Scope
- Provide concrete numeric targets (p50/p95/p99) per tier for:
  - Non-streaming requests (end-to-end latency)
  - Streaming requests (TTFT and per-token cadence; explicitly call out what we gate on)
- Define acceptance gates for:
  - Benchmark-lab suite runs (pre-merge / nightly)
  - Perf-canary (merge blocker) thresholds and baseline refresh policy
- Specify which model families/hardware/regions are in-scope for gating for runtime-1.22 launch.

Non-goals
- We are not defining customer contractual SLAs here (Product will reference these for messaging, but SRE owns SLA docs).
- We are not choosing batching knob values here (that’s the scheduler/profile work); this is the target + gating contract.

Proposed tier definitions (for runtime perf validation)
Units: milliseconds. All numbers are measured at the runtime boundary (request admitted -> response complete) for non-streaming, and at runtime boundary for streaming TTFT (request admitted -> first token emitted). Unless noted, gates are evaluated at steady-state concurrency (see “Gating workload shape”).

A) Non-streaming (end-to-end latency)
Fast tier
- p50 <= 350ms
- p95 <= 900ms
- p99 <= 1400ms
Standard tier
- p50 <= 500ms
- p95 <= 1400ms
- p99 <= 2200ms
Cost-efficient tier
- p50 <= 700ms
- p95 <= 2200ms
- p99 <= 3500ms

B) Streaming
We gate streaming on TTFT and “decode smoothness” (not strict p95 token-to-token, but a regression guard). Rationale: batching defaults mainly move queueing/prefill behavior; customers mostly feel TTFT + long stalls.

Fast tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 250ms
- TTFT p95 <= 650ms
- TTFT p99 <= 1100ms
- Stall guard: % of responses with >250ms inter-chunk gap after first token must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline (measured on streaming scenarios only).

Standard tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 350ms
- TTFT p95 <= 900ms
- TTFT p99 <= 1500ms
- Stall guard: % with >400ms inter-chunk gap must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline.

Cost-efficient tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 450ms
- TTFT p95 <= 1200ms
- TTFT p99 <= 2000ms
- Stall guard: % with >600ms inter-chunk gap must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline.

Notes / clarifications
- These are runtime targets for the tiered batching defaults feature. The platform will still enforce overload behavior (backpressure/load shed) rather than allowing unbounded tail latency. Where overload mode triggers, we treat results separately (see “Overload handling in gates”).
- If a model family cannot meet fast-tier p99 on a given hardware class without unacceptable throughput collapse, the correct path is: model-family compatibility doc marks “fast tier not supported” for that hardware (and selection logic must emit a reason code and downgrade). This ticket defines the targets and gating expectations, not the compatibility matrix.

Gating workload shape (benchmark methodology contract)
To avoid bikeshedding in each perf PR, we standardize the workload parameters used by CI/canary for these gates:
- Prompt length buckets: short (<=256 tok), medium (257–1024), long (1025–4096)
- Output length: fixed per scenario (e.g., 128 tok decode for chat, 256 for summarization) to reduce variance
- Mix for tier validation:
  - Fast: 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long; streaming-heavy (>=70% streaming)
  - Standard: 40% short, 40% medium, 20% long; mixed streaming (50/50)
  - Cost-efficient: 30% short, 45% medium, 25% long; mostly non-streaming (>=70% non-streaming)
- Concurrency ramps: evaluate at 3 points (low/target/high) per model/hardware to catch queueing thresholds (exact numbers owned by benchmark-lab but must include a “near saturation” point).

What we gate in CI vs canary
1) Pre-merge (benchmark-lab / perf suite)
- Soft gate (non-blocking initially for 2 weeks after enabling new scenarios): report deltas, create auto-ticket if exceeding thresholds.
- After warmup period: blocking gate for fast-tier TTFT p99 and non-streaming p99 only (to avoid blocking on high-variance metrics early).

2) Perf-canary (merge blocker)
Hard gates (must pass to merge for runtime-1.22 branches once enabled):
- Fast tier:
  - Streaming TTFT p99 must not regress by >7% vs baseline (per model/hardware), and must remain under the absolute target above.
  - Non-streaming p99 must not regress by >7% vs baseline and must remain under absolute target.
- Standard tier:
  - Non-streaming p95 must not regress by >8% vs baseline and must remain under absolute target.
- Cost-efficient tier:
  - Throughput guard (primary): tokens/sec must not regress by >5% vs baseline on cost-efficient scenarios.
  - Tail-latency guard (secondary): non-streaming p99 must not regress by >10% vs baseline.

Baseline policy
- Baselines are per (model family, hardware class, scenario tier, streaming flag).
- Baseline refresh requires:
  - Two consecutive nightly runs showing improvement and stable variance
  - Approval from Runtime Scheduling EM (Sofia) + SRE (Sean) to avoid “refreshing away” a regression
  - Linked internal ticket (use INT-* or ENG-18428 follow-up) documenting why refresh is safe.

Overload handling in gates
- If overload mode triggers (admission control / shedding), we do not fail solely on latency inflation; instead:
  - Verify overload mode is entered at the expected concurrency point (no earlier than baseline by >10%)
  - Verify shed rate does not increase by >1pp vs baseline for fast tier scenarios
- Any earlier-than-baseline overload triggering is treated as a regression.

In-scope for runtime-1.22 gating (initial)
Model families (top traffic):
- Llama-3.x 8B/70B chat variants (hosted)
- Mistral-family mid-size chat (hosted)
Hardware classes:
- H100 and A100 for hosted; L4 for a single “edge/cheap” lane (standard + cost-efficient only)
Regions:
- us-east-1, eu-west-1 (primary); add us-west-2 once variance is within bounds.

Deliverables
- Numbers and definitions above are mirrored into the SRE/architecture SLO tier doc:
  sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/latency-slo-tiers-definition-fast-standard-cost-efficient.json
- Perf-canary gating spec to be implemented under:
  sources/github/perf-canary/pr-489-gate-on-fast-tier-p99-and-standard-tier-p95.json
- Benchmark-lab scenarios updated under:
  sources/github/benchmark-lab/pr-612-add-mixed-workload-slo-tier-scenarios.json

Open questions (resolved in comments below)
- Whether to gate streaming on p95 TTFT or p99 TTFT for fast tier (decision: p99, with baseline % regression + absolute target).
- Whether to publish absolute numbers externally or keep as internal gates (decision: publish tier intent and ranges externally; keep p99 absolute values as internal gates initially; PM to update copy accordingly).

Acceptance criteria
- Confluence SLO tier doc updated with numeric targets and explicit measurement definitions.
- Perf-canary gate definitions agreed by Runtime + SRE and tracked for implementation.
- Any model/hardware exceptions documented as compatibility constraints (reason-code-driven downgrade) rather than silently failing fast tier.

Risks
- High variance on p99 in GPU-shared environments could cause false positives. Mitigation: baseline regression threshold + require multiple-run confirmation for baseline updates; canary runs pin to dedicated canary capacity.
- Streaming stall guard metric instrumentation is not fully baked. Mitigation: implement as “delta vs baseline only” initially and do not hard-block on it until metrics are stable.

Owners
- Primary: Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling)
- Review/approval: Sean Gallagher (SRE), Jonas Weber (Applied ML / evals), Marcus Reed (perf suite integration)

2025-11-20 (Sofia Ivanova): Drafted initial numeric targets based on recent H100/A100 traces. Pushed p99 targets slightly looser than current best-case to allow batching headroom; will rely on perf-canary regression thresholds to catch unexpected tail regressions.
2025-11-22 (Sean Gallagher): SRE feedback: we need explicit streaming definition. Customers care about TTFT and long stalls more than mean throughput. Requested stall-guard metric but ok to keep non-blocking until telemetry stabilizes.
2025-12-02 (Marcus Reed): Perf suite note: p99 is noisy unless we standardize concurrency ramps and use pinned canary capacity. Added proposal to treat overload separately (don’t fail on high latency if admission control is behaving).
2025-12-08 (Jonas Weber): Applied ML note: please ensure prompt sets include at least one code-ish workload; some models have distinct prefill characteristics that affect TTFT. OK with weighting staying mostly chat/summarization for launch.
2026-01-06 (Allison Grant): Observability constraint: tier label cardinality must be controlled; gates should be per (tier/model/hardware) but avoid per-route. Confirmed baseline keys match proposed dimensions.
2026-01-10 (Sofia Ivanova): Decision: fast tier gates on streaming TTFT p99 (not p95). Reason: tail latency protection is the core risk; p95 can look fine while p99 explodes under mixed prompt lengths.
2026-01-14 (Sean Gallagher): Final pass: targets acceptable. Added baseline refresh approval process to avoid masking regressions. Confirmed this ticket now blocks ENG-18428 enabling merge gates.
2026-01-27 (Sofia Ivanova): Marking done. Numeric targets mirrored into SLO tier doc; perf-canary and benchmark-lab PRs reference this ticket for thresholds.

title: Incidents runbook: overload behavior with tiered batching defaults (fast/standard/cost-efficient)
content:
Incidents runbook: overload behavior with tiered batching defaults (fast/standard/cost-efficient)

## Goal
Provide a single on-call runbook for diagnosing and mitigating overload-related latency regressions when tiered batching defaults are enabled (fast / standard / cost-efficient). This runbook covers:
- symptom → likely cause mapping
- immediate mitigations (no code)
- tier-specific guidance
- rollback / kill-switch procedures
- post-incident follow-ups

This is intended for Runtime + SRE on-call during staged rollout (internal canary → hosted subset → Dedicated opt-in → broader default).

---

## Definitions / mental model
**Overload** here means one (or more) of:
- arrival rate > sustainable throughput for the active tier profile
- queue growth that increases time-to-first-token (TTFT) and/or p99 end-to-end latency
- admission control/load shedding triggers (or fails to trigger)
- scheduler behavior that starves some requests under mixed prompt length / mixed streaming

**Tier expectations** (high-level):
- **fast**: protect tail latency; will sacrifice throughput earlier via tighter wait budget + admission control.
- **standard**: balanced; modest batching, modest wait; aims to be stable for general SaaS workloads.
- **cost-efficient**: maximize throughput / $ per token; can tolerate higher tail, but must not allow runaway queue depth.

**Key guarantee:** correctness must be preserved; degrade predictably under overload (backpressure, rate limiting, or load shedding) rather than silent latency collapse.

---

## When to use this runbook
Trigger when any of the following occur after enabling tiered defaults (feature flag on, or tier selection introduced):
1) **Fast tier p99 regression** (especially TTFT) vs baseline.
2) **Queue depth increasing** with p95/p99 latency increasing.
3) **Streaming endpoints** report slower TTFT or irregular chunking (perceived "stalling").
4) Increased **429/503** (load shedding / admission control) after enabling fast tier.
5) Dedicated tenant reports override not applying or unexpected effective tier.

Related tickets/threads to reference:
- Slack: fast-tier p99 regression investigation (eng-runtime/1768501140)
- Slack: overload mode behavior discussion (eng-runtime/1768664305)
- Jira: SUP-48219 p95 regression during canary
- Hotfix precedent: PR-28544 limit tier label cardinality (telemetry blow-up can masquerade as perf regression)

---

## Required dashboards / queries
1) **Tiered batching dashboard** (Observability Pack)
- latency: p50/p95/p99 by {tier, model_family, region, streaming}
- TTFT (streaming vs non-streaming)
- queue depth and time-in-queue
- batch size distribution (prefill batch tokens, decode batch tokens)
- admission control / shed counters
- cache hit rate (prefix/KV) and cache evictions

2) **Reason codes** for profile selection
Check selection reason counts over time to confirm expected behavior.
Common reason codes:
- `tier.default.fast|standard|cost_efficient`
- `tier.override.route_policy`
- `tier.override.customer` (Dedicated)
- `tier.constrained.model_limit` (model/hardware constraint clamps knobs)
- `tier.overload_mode.active` (scheduler entered overload behavior)
- `tier.fallback.compat_variant` (if applicable)

3) **Infra saturation**
- GPU utilization / SM occupancy
- HBM usage / OOM events
- CPU saturation in control plane / streaming gateway
- network egress saturation for streaming-heavy regions

---

## First 5 minutes: decision tree
### A) Is this a telemetry artifact?
- If latency histograms degrade while service-level sampling changes or metrics cardinality spikes, verify metrics ingestion health.
- Check whether tier labels exploded (known early canary issue); if so, apply telemetry hotfix / sampling controls and re-evaluate.

### B) Is the tier actually applied?
- Confirm effective tier for affected routes/tenants.
- Look at reason code mix:
  - if `tier.override.*` dominates unexpectedly → config precedence issue.
  - if `tier.constrained.model_limit` spikes → model/hardware clamp causing different behavior than expected.

### C) Is it localized?
- Compare by region/model family. If one region/model family only, suspect:
  - heterogeneous fleet hardware
  - different concurrency distribution
  - cache behavior differences
  - a single model family with prefill/decode imbalance sensitivity

### D) Is it overload vs regression under normal load?
- If queue depth and time-in-queue increase in parallel with latency → overload/backpressure problem.
- If queue depth is flat but p99 increases → scheduler/kernel regression, model-level issue, or downstream gateway.

---

## Triage steps (deeper)
1) **Identify impacted dimension(s)**
- tier (fast vs standard vs cost-efficient)
- streaming vs non-streaming
- prompt length bucket (short/medium/long)
- model family + quantization variant (if applicable)
- region

2) **Check queue dynamics**
- queue depth trend
- max wait budget usage (esp. fast tier)
- batch formation rate (are we forming too-small batches due to tight wait? or too-large due to aggressive batching?)

3) **Check for starvation under mixed workloads**
Signals:
- long prompts are consistently delayed behind short prompts (or vice versa)
- streaming requests get delayed behind large prefill batches
Mitigation options (no-code):
- shift affected route from cost-efficient → standard, or standard → fast (depending on symptom)
- temporarily cap max batch tokens / max wait via override if available (Dedicated/enterprise)

4) **Check admission control / shedding**
- Rising 429/503 with stable latency may indicate fast tier protecting tail correctly, but upstream rate limits need tuning.
- Rising latency without shedding indicates admission control not triggering when it should (regression or thresholds too lenient).

5) **Confirm cache behavior**
- If cache hit rate dropped coincident with tier change, larger batches may be increasing eviction or changing request interleaving.
- Cache issues can present as sudden prefill time increase (TTFT regression) without obvious queue growth.

---

## Tier-specific guidance
### Fast tier (protect tail latency)
Typical failure modes:
- **p99 TTFT regression** due to queueing from insufficient admission control or too much prefill work per step.
- **increased 429/503** because admission control became more aggressive than expected.

Mitigations:
1) If p99 is rising and queue depth is rising:
- enable/raise fast-tier admission control (if not already) and verify it is active.
- reduce exposure: roll back fast tier defaults for affected model/region cohort.
2) If 429/503 rose sharply but latency stayed healthy:
- validate upstream rate limiting configs; communicate expected behavior (fast tier chooses fail-fast under overload).
- consider shifting high-QPS non-critical routes to standard tier.

Escalate to Runtime if:
- starvation suspected (mixed prompt lengths) despite admission control.
- prefill/decode balancing looks off (high prefill time spikes while decode steady).


### Standard tier (balanced)
Typical failure modes:
- slow creep in p95 under sustained load due to queue depth increasing.
- mixed streaming and non-streaming contention.

Mitigations:
- if streaming routes are impacted, isolate by moving streaming routes to fast tier.
- if batch sizes are too small (low throughput), consider cost-efficient for non-latency-sensitive routes.
- if batch sizes are too large (queue blowups), temporarily clamp max batch tokens via route override (if available) or move to fast.


### Cost-efficient tier (throughput-first)
Typical failure modes:
- **queue blowup** under bursty traffic (tail latency becomes unbounded).
- **timeouts** at gateways due to slow TTFT.

Mitigations:
1) For queue blowup:
- shift impacted route(s) to standard temporarily.
- if overload mode exists, verify it is active and is reducing queue growth (not increasing).
2) For widespread impact:
- reduce rollout scope for cost-efficient tier; disable for streaming endpoints by policy.

Hard rule during incident:
- Do not recommend cost-efficient tier for customer-facing interactive streaming endpoints unless they explicitly accept TTFT risk.

---

## Rollback / kill switch procedures
### Scope options (prefer smallest blast radius first)
1) **Per-route tier override** (Console/policy): change tier for a single route.
2) **Per-tenant override** (Dedicated): enforce tier at tenant/cluster level; ensure precedence (customer override > route policy > tier default).
3) **Disable tiered defaults feature flag** for cohort (region/model family).
4) **Global kill switch**: revert to pre-1.22 manual batching behavior / previous defaults.

### Rollback checklist
- capture incident timestamp window + impacted dimensions (tier/model/region/streaming)
- snapshot key graphs: p99, TTFT, queue depth, batch size distribution, shed counters
- confirm reason codes show the expected effective tier before and after rollback
- post rollback: monitor for 30 minutes (or 2x traffic peak window) and confirm metrics return to baseline band

### Communication
- If customer-facing degradation (Hosted): notify Support + PM on-call with:
  - affected regions/models
  - mitigation (tier shift / rollback)
  - expected time to stabilize
- If Dedicated tenant: coordinate with CSM/Support; document effective tier and override precedence.

---

## Known pitfalls / lessons learned (add as we learn)
1) **Metric cardinality can look like a perf regression**
If tier labels are added without cardinality controls, ingestion pressure can create noisy dashboards and delayed data.
Reference: runtime hotfix PR-28544.

2) **Streaming requires TTFT-first thinking**
Even if end-to-end p95 is stable, TTFT regression is a user-visible incident for streaming chat.

3) **Mixed prompt lengths can induce starvation**
Watch for bimodal latency by prompt-length bucket; consider policy split by route type.

---

## Artifacts / links
- Confluence (design): workload-aware batching defaults design doc (eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling)
- Confluence (SLOs): latency SLO tiers definition fast/standard/cost-efficient
- Confluence (dashboards): batching defaults observability dashboard spec
- GitHub: PR-28480 (feature flag + kill switch plumbing)
- GitHub: PR-28473 (reason codes)
- GitHub: observability-pack PR-933 (tier dashboards)

---

## Acceptance criteria
- Runbook published and linked from:
  - SRE on-call handbook
  - runtime-1.22 launch brief
  - batching defaults rollout checklist
- Includes explicit rollback order + kill switch instructions.
- Includes tier-specific symptom→mitigation guidance.
- References dashboards and reason codes needed for validation.

---

## Follow-ups (not required for closure, but tracked)
- Add a lightweight "incident note template" to the rollout checklist (owner: Rafael Mendes)
- Add an alert annotation when overload mode toggles (owner: Allison Grant)
- Add dedicated override precedence troubleshooting snippet to support playbook (owner: Aisha Bello)

2026-03-13 (Sofia Ivanova): Please include explicit checks for starvation under mixed prompt lengths + streaming contention. We’ve seen cases where queue depth doesn’t look terrible, but certain buckets get stuck behind large prefill batches.
2026-03-14 (Allison Grant): +1. Also call out the cardinality incident we hit earlier; dashboards can mislead during ingestion pressure. Recommend first step: validate metrics pipeline health before assuming real latency regression.
2026-03-17 (Sean Gallagher): I’ll own final edit + publication. Suggest we add an ordered rollback ladder (route override → cohort flag off → global kill switch) so on-call doesn’t jump to global rollback immediately.
2026-03-20 (Omar El-Sayed): Added notes on TTFT vs end-to-end for streaming. Fast tier should be evaluated primarily via TTFT p99 + time-in-queue. If TTFT is rising with flat queue, suspect prefill/decode imbalance.
2026-03-24 (Aisha Bello): Please include the paging vs ticketing guidance: page on fast-tier p99 sustained breach + high customer impact; otherwise file ticket with dashboard snapshots. I’ll align alerts once runbook is final.

title: Dynamic scope binding and privilege resolution spec for RBAC v2
content:
Dynamic scope binding and privilege resolution spec for RBAC v2

Define a deterministic, auditable privilege resolution model for RBAC v2 that supports dynamic scope binding across resource hierarchies, integrates with SSO/SAML assertions, emits rich audit events for every decision, and provides admin controls including emergency breakglass and scoped delegation. This ticket captures design goals, concrete resolution algorithms, example matrices, migration considerations, and operational hooks for the Console and runtime.
Core idea: treat scopes as first-class, namespaced bindings that can be static (tenant-level) or dynamic (request-bound). At request time, the system builds a 'scope stack' by walking the resource hierarchy from requested resource to tenancy root, collecting explicit scope bindings and evaluating them with an ordered algorithm: 1) explicit deny at nearest scope, 2) explicit allow at nearest scope, 3) role-derived permissions (closest scope wins), 4) attribute-based grants (SAML/OIDC claim-driven) as tie-breakers, 5) global defaults. Roles are declarative sets of actions tied to resource classes; role-templates may be parameterized by scope variables (e.g., project_id). For SSO/SAML, attributes map to initial role assignments and to ephemeral request attributes (group, department, external_project). These attributes have a precedence table: direct role assignment > SAML-group assignment > SCIM-synced group > OIDC claim. Audit events must capture the fully expanded permission set and the evaluation trace (scope anchors, rules hit, deny/allow source). Breakglass is implemented as a short-lived override token issued by the Console with mandatory justification recorded; breakglass tokens are revoked automatically and emit both creation and use audit events.
A clear, unambiguous permission evaluation order that covers role inheritance, scope overrides, deny/allow precedence, and attribute-based exceptions.
Mapping rules from SAML attributes / OIDC claims to role assignments and scope anchors with deterministic precedence documented.
Audit event schema defined for: role assignment changes, resolved permissions per request, scope-binding decisions, and breakglass activations.
Admin UI wireframes and API endpoints for scoped delegation, role previews, and one-click breakglass with TTL and justification tracking.
A migration plan with compatibility mode for existing RBAC v1 tokens and a rollout checklist for Dedicated/Private clusters.
Spec review and alignment with Product and Security (1 week): finalize evaluation order and SAML claim mappings.
Schema changes: extend role binding table with 'scope_kind' and 'binding_origin' columns and add 'evaluation_trace' field to audit_events (DB migration + index plan).
Runtime: implement scope stack builder and evaluate permission engine with deterministic logging (feature-flagged).
Console: add Role Preview UI (show expanded permissions for a given user+resource), Breakglass flow, and scoped delegation controls.
E2E tests: policy fuzzing harness that generates random hierarchies and asserts deterministic outcomes; include regression suite for deny/allow precedence.
Migration: compatibility layer for RBAC v1 tokens for 8 weeks, telemetry to track mismatches, and rollback plan.
Should explicit 'deny' be globally highest precedence or scoped-nearest highest? (proposal: nearest-scope deny outranks global allow).
How to represent attribute-based ephemeral grants in audit logs without leaking sensitive attribute values? (proposal: hash attributes and store policy id).
What is the retention period for evaluation_trace in audit_events given storage costs? (proposal: 90 days hot, 365 days cold).
Do we allow nested delegation (A delegates to B, B delegates to C) and how to limit blast radius?
How does breakglass interact with external identity providers' session policies and MFA requirements?
Adopt 'nearest-scope wins' for both allows and denies; explicit deny at a closer scope overrides allows at parent scopes.
SAML/OIDC claim mapping will be configurable per customer; default mappings provided for common IdPs (Okta, Azure AD).
Evaluation trace will include policy identifiers and decision outcomes; raw claim values will be redacted and represented by stable hashes.
Incorrect precedence could accidentally grant access during the migration window; mitigated by compatibility mode and sampling telemetry.
Audit log volume will increase significantly when we log evaluation traces per request; require retention/aggregation plan.
Complex delegation chains introduce escalation paths; require approval workflows and delegation TTLs in UI.
2026-03-06 Marcus Liu: Drafted evaluation order and shared with Security. Need product sign-off on SAML attribute precedence.
2026-03-08 Priya Menon (Product): Recommend adding an explicit 'role preview' step in the Console before applying scoped delegation; this is now included.
2026-03-10 Security Review: Agreed to redact raw attribute values in logs and use SHA-256 with salt for stable hashing. Follow-up: define salt rotation policy.
2026-03-12 Marcus Liu: Added DB migration notes and flagged audit index performance as potential blocker; scheduled spike.

title: Progressive degradation exposure and adaptive throttle observability
content:
Progressive degradation exposure and adaptive throttle observability

Background: We've observed tenant-visible progressive degradation during regional congestion events where token-level latency climbs before the admit-rate controller engages. Current dashboards surface p95/p99 at request level but do not attribute degradation slices to token positions, region failovers, or per-tenant admit decisions. This ticket builds instrumentation and a dashboard layer to expose progressive degradation signals and tie them to adaptive throttling and circuit states for faster diagnosis and safer rollouts.

Scope:
- Add token-level timing histograms (position-aware) with tenant and region labels.
- Emit admit_score/admit_decision metrics at ingress and attach shard/route metadata.
- Register circuit_state transitions (OPEN/HALF_OPEN/CLOSED) per-region and per-priority-path.
- Surface derived SLO SLIs: token_p50/p95/p99 latency, token_kv_cache_hit_ratio, tenant_admit_rate, region_fallback_count, circuit_state_ratio.
- Build an operational dashboard (panels listed below) and a small synthetic harness to validate signal correctness.

Instrumentation details (implementation notes):
- Token timing: instrument the decode loop to record per-token durations into histograms bucketed at ms resolution. Label dims: tenant_id, model_family, region, shard_id, token_position_bucket (0-15,16-63,64+), route_priority. Keep cardinality low by truncating tenant_id to org_id.
- Admit metrics: emit admit_total{decision="admit"} and admit_total{decision="reject"} with tenant/org labels. Also emit admit_score gauge per request for sampling.
- KV cache: export kv_cache_requests and kv_cache_hits with model_family + region to calculate hit ratio.
- Circuit transitions: emit circuit_transitions_total{state="OPEN"|"HALF_OPEN"|"CLOSED",region=..,path=..}. Also emit circuit_active{region, path} gauge.
- Sampling: for high-volume tenants sample token histograms at 1/100 and provide full sampling for tenants flagged in .whitelist for initial validation.

Suggested example queries (PromQL-style) for dashboard panels:
- Token p95 (position 0-15): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(token_latency_bucket{token_position_bucket="0-15"}[5m])) by (le, tenant_id, region))
- KV cache hit ratio: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) by (model_family, region) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests[5m])) by (model_family, region)
- Tenant admit rate: sum(rate(admit_total{decision="admit"}[5m])) by (tenant_id) / sum(rate(admit_total{decision!=""}[5m])) by (tenant_id)
- Region fallback count: increase(region_fallback_events[1h]) by (region)

Dashboard panels to build:
1) Progressive token-latency waterfall: stacked view by token_position_bucket and tenant cohorts.
2) Tenant admit-rate heatmap sorted by traffic-weighted latency impact.
3) Circuit state timeline per-region and per-priority-path (interactive to jump to traces).
4) KV cache heatmap and its correlation with token p95 over time.
5) Synthetic-run comparison panel: baseline vs degraded run showing admit metrics and latencies.
6) SLO surface: tenant-level burn-rate with links to runbook and auto-run remediation checklist.

Acceptance criteria:
- New metrics are emitted in prod telemetry pipeline within low-cardinality constraints.
- Dashboard panels implemented in Grafana and wire up to alerting rules.
- Synthetic harness can reproduce a progressive degradation scenario and dashboards reflect expected signals (p95 climb, admit_rate drop, circuit OPEN transitions).
- On-call runbook updated with steps: interpret heatmap, trigger holdback for specific tenant, escalate to SRE and product.
- No more than 5% added ingestion cost for global telemetry (validated by telemetry budget dashboard).

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): instrument on canary region with full sampling for 5 tenants (2 days), validate correctness (owner: Marco Ruiz).
- Phase 2 (staged): enable sampled histograms globally (1/100) + admit metrics; run synthetic at peak window to validate (owner: Leah Nguyen).
- Phase 3 (GA): increase sampling for top-20 tenants gradually and enable dashboard alerts.

Risks and mitigations:
- Cardinality blowup: mitigate by truncating tenant_id and bucketing positions. Add quota guard in ingestion pipeline.
- Perf overhead: token timing is cheap but avoid nanosecond-precision across all hot paths; use sampling and efficient histograms.
- Mis-attribution during multi-region failover: ensure region and fallback_reason tags are present on fallback events.

Links & artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Progressive+Degradation+Observability (draft)
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128 (WIP)
- Dashboard prototype: https://grafana.internal.redwood.ai/d/xyz/progressive-degradation (prototype)
2026-02-28 - Aisha Patel: Scoped during reliability sync; flagged as high priority after recent tenant incident where p99 spiked ahead of admit controller engagement.
2026-03-02 - Marco Ruiz: Initial instrumentation PR opened (WIP) to add token_position_bucket label and sampled histogram. https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128
2026-03-05 - Leah Nguyen: Reviewed dashboard mockups; suggested adding a tenant burn-rate panel and a synthetic compare view.
2026-03-07 - Marco Ruiz: Canary instrumentation deployed to us-east-1 canary cluster with 5 tenants; observed expected p95 increases during synthetic injection. Follow-up: add admit_score gauge for correlated analysis.
2026-03-10 - SRE (Jonas Becker): Verified circuit transition events emitted; noted a missing 'path' label on some transitions (ticketed in sub-task ENG-824568).
1) Metrics present and queryable; 2) Dashboard panels implemented and accessible; 3) Synthetic run reproduces degradation and triggers expected alert; 4) Runbook updated and owners listed; 5) Ingestion cost within 5% of current baseline.
Follow telemetry cost guardrails; coordinate with observability infra to add buckets before full rollout. Use sample flag 'pgd_observe' during staged rollout.

title: nodeagent image digest mismatch and webhook CA skew causing post-upgrade operator crash in customer clusters
content:
nodeagent image digest mismatch and webhook CA skew causing post-upgrade operator crash in customer clusters

Multiple customer Private clusters (notably BrightBank and AeroRetail) reported operator crashloops and webhook rejections immediately after an automated Helm upgrade from runtime 1.12.0 -> 1.12.1. Root cause appears to be two simultaneous skewed conditions: (1) the nodeagent image referenced by the release manifest was removed from the upstream registry and a new digest was pushed under the same tag between CI artifact publish and chart rendering, causing ImagePullBackOff/crashloop; (2) the mutating/validating webhook CA bundle in the Helm chart was rotated independently by our release automation resulting in webhook TLS verification failures (conversion/mutation requests rejected) for existing kube objects. This ticket tracks triage, hotfix, customer coordination, and follow-up engineering work to prevent recurrence.
1) Install runtime-1.12.0 on a fresh k8s 1.27 cluster using the existing helm chart and operator image tag 'redwood/operator:1.12.0'.
2) Simulate release pipeline by publishing a new nodeagent image with the same tag but different digest and delete original digest from test registry (private test only).
3) Run helm upgrade to runtime-1.12.1 that references the moved tag; observe operator ImagePullBackOff or crashloop due to digest mismatch in environments that validate digests.
4) Separately, patch the MutatingWebhookConfiguration caBundle to an unrelated value and attempt to apply CRs to verify webhook TLS rejects requests.
03/10 09:12 UTC - Support alert: BrightBank reported multiple operator pods in CrashLoopBackOff after an automated upgrade initiated by their platform team.
03/10 09:40 UTC - Triage: reproduced in staging by forcing the release pipeline to re-publish a nodeagent tag with a different digest. Verified image referenced by helm values.yaml did not match registry state.
03/10 12:00 UTC - Discovered mutation: release tooling rotated webhook CA bundle in separate step; helm chart values shipped with new caBundle without performing a rolling restart for existing CRs, leading to immediate webhook validation failures until webhook pods reloaded with the new CA.
03/10 14:20 UTC - Confirmed two simultaneous failure modes: image digest drift + webhook CA skew. Either alone might be recoverable; together they blocked automated in-place remediation in customer clusters.
03/11 02:05 UTC - Customer-communication call run with BrightBank and AeroRetail; they requested immediate rollback and a guaranteed remediation path for remaining clusters.
Temporarily paused automated upgrades for all active Private clusters via control plane toggle (feature flag: private.auto_upgrade=false).
For impacted clusters we provided an emergency runbook: kubectl rollout undo for operator StatefulSet if previous image digest present; otherwise kubectl set image to a previously cached digest we uploaded to our customer-accessible registry mirror.
Applied a manual patch to MutatingWebhookConfiguration/ValidatingWebhookConfiguration caBundle to match the new operator server cert for clusters where webhook pods had been rotated, then restarted webhook pods where necessary.
Opened an immediate mirror in our registry for the original nodeagent digest and pushed the missing digest back into the customer-accessible mirror to unblock ImagePulls.
Create runtime-1.12.1-hotfix1 that pins nodeagent images by immutable digest in the chart templates instead of floating tags (chart change: templates/images.yaml and values.schema).
Add preflight validation in the Helm upgrade pipeline that ensures every image digest referenced in the rendered chart exists in the target registry and is reachable from the customer's cluster network (registry-check step).
Adjust release automation so webhook CA rotation is atomically coupled with a managed rolling restart of webhook deployments and a post-apply validation step for webhook readiness (fail-fast on mismatch).
Add cluster-scoped migration job for affected clusters to reconcile MutatingWebhookConfiguration caBundle safely when CA rotation is required in the future.
Build and publish runtime-1.12.1-hotfix1 images and chart artifacts to staging registry (03/11 08:00 UTC).
Create PR #7654 (runtime/charts) with chart pin and registry-check step. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7654
Smoke deploy hotfix to internal integration clusters, run automated upgrade pipeline with --dry-run checks, then a real upgrade on one non-customer cluster (03/11 12:00 UTC).
Coordinate with Customer Success and affected customers to schedule staggered hotfix upgrades during low-traffic windows. Provide an outage-free path when possible and a rollback command set if needed.
Mark release as hotfix and increment changelog; publish customer advisory after verification (03/12 target).
On a test cluster: helm upgrade --install runtime -f values-hotfix.yaml runtime-chart-1.12.1-hotfix1.tgz and verify operator Pods reach Ready state within configured PodStartupTimeout.
Run 'kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration redwood-webhook -o jsonpath="{.webhooks[*].clientConfig.caBundle}"' and compare to the operator-serving TLS cert; requests to the webhook should succeed (tested by applying a sample CR and observing admission success).
Network check: ensure registry-check step passes from a customer-like network path (simulate private registry firewall rules).
Post-upgrade monitor: 48h elevated telemetry for operator restarts, webhook 5xx rates, CR mutation errors; if any metrics exceed threshold, rollback and investigate.
03/10 15:00 UTC - Incident notification sent to BrightBank and AeroRetail with initial mitigation steps and ETA for hotfix.
03/11 19:00 UTC - Provided targeted remediation commands and offered assisted upgrade with engineering on-call present.
03/12 10:00 UTC - Customer advisory drafted for broader customer base explaining root causes, immediate mitigations, and next steps. Will schedule webinar for customers with >100 nodes.
Implement digest pin enforcement in release CI and chart linting (owner: infra-ci team, due 2026-04-01).
Add end-to-end test that simulates CA rotation + upgrade in CI integration lane (owner: operator team, due 2026-03-31).
Add registry retention policy notes and change request to prevent garbage-collection of recently-referenced digests for 14 days post-release (owner: releases team, due 2026-04-10).
Update on-prem upgrade runbook to include ordered steps for webhook CA rotation and operator redeploy to avoid split-brain conditions.
Decision made 03/11: hotfix route preferred over rolling rollback for clusters where image digest cannot be restored quickly because hotfix includes both registry-check and caBundle-handling improvements.
Engineering lead approval granted by Priya Raman 03/11 18:45 UTC for hotfix release and customer-assisted upgrades.
Security reviewed the CA rotation plan and requested additional audit logs for future rotations; security review ticket created.

title: Sandboxed executor with stream-aware result injection and recursion guardrails
content:
Sandboxed executor with stream-aware result injection and recursion guardrails

Problem: Current tool execution loop permits multi-tool chains and result injection but lacks a unified sandbox that: prevents runaway recursion, coordinates partial streaming of tool outputs with downstream injection, and gracefully supports older tool protocol versions. This ticket proposes a sandboxed executor layer that observes and enforces chain-level guardrails and provides a compatibility shim for v1/v2 tool contracts.

Goals and scope:
- Implement a lightweight "execution sandbox" that tracks per-request tool graph (call edges, timestamps, cumulative tokens) and enforces recursion/loop limits.
- Add stream-aware result injection rules: support both (A) immediate incremental injection of tool output into the LLM stream with safe markers and (B) deferred final injection once tool completes; make policy configurable per-route.
- Provide compatibility layer to translate older tool result shapes (legacy v1) to the new structured-output contract we use for function calling / structured outputs.
- Instrument traces and metrics (call depth, unique tool-chain signature, injection latency, circuit breaker triggers) for Console dashboards and rollout guardrails.

Non-goals:
- This ticket does not implement autoscaling or allocation-level throttling for Dedicated clusters (follow-up).

Design summary (high level):
1) Call graph & signature: Each request gets a short-lived call graph ID. We record ordered edges (toolA->toolB) and compute a signature hash (sha256 of ordered tool names + short params fingerprint). If a signature repeats > N times within request or across closely related requests, trigger loop prevention.
2) Recursion/loop guards: hard limits (max_call_depth=6, max_invocations=20 per top-level request) plus heuristic detection of cycles via signature repetition. When guard trips, the sandbox returns a structured error to the LLM with a stable reason code (TOO_MANY_INVOCATIONS or DETECTED_CYCLE).
3) Stream-aware injection policies: the sandbox exposes two injection modes per tool call.
   - streaming_incremental: stream tool stdout/chunks into the LLM response as they arrive, prefixed with a safe sentinel frame and with token-budget accounting. Each chunk is annotated with a provenance header so downstream tools or finalizer can sanitize.
   - deferred_final: buffer tool output and only inject a single structured value when tool completes (used for large, binary, or untrusted tools).
   A per-route config controls policy and a per-call override allows tool authors to request one mode.
4) Compatibility shim: for legacy tools that return freeform text or old JSON shapes, the sandbox will run a small transform chain (mapping rules + JSON schema validator) to produce the canonical structured-output envelope (fields: output_type, content, metadata). The shim logs warnings and attaches a compatibility_score header.
5) Circuit breakers and graceful fallback: runtime-level rate-limited breakers per tool name that trip on error-rate or latency percentiles. When tripped, the sandbox returns pre-defined fallback results or instructs the LLM to call an alternate tool variant.
6) Observability: add traces (span names: sandbox.call, sandbox.inject, sandbox.circuit_trip), metrics (sandbox.calls_total, sandbox.cycles_detected, sandbox.stream_injected_bytes), and error tags for Console dashboards and alerts.

Acceptance criteria:
- Sandbox layer prototyped and wired into executor path in staging.
- Unit tests for cycle detection heuristics and guard triggers.
- Integration tests for both streaming_incremental and deferred_final injection modes covering partial chunking, ordering, and provenance headers.
- Compatibility shim transforms 3 example legacy tools to canonical envelope with test harness.
- Console dashboard tile showing sandbox.cycles_detected and sandbox.circuit_trip rate with 1-min resolution.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (staging): feature-flagged sandbox enabled for internal canaries, collect metrics and internal evals (2 weeks).
- Phase 2 (beta): opt-in for selected customers and internal SDK examples, monitoring and escalation playbook (2 weeks).
- Phase 3 (gradual): enable by default with conservative defaults; expose per-route toggles in Console for advanced teams.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- When streaming_incremental is used, do we inject escaped partial JSON fragments (which complicates downstream parsing) or only textual chunks with provenance markers? Devs prefer textual chunks for performance; product prefers structured fragments for reliability. Proposed compromise: streaming mode emits small line-delimited envelope frames where each frame is a base64-encoded structured chunk to avoid interleaving parse issues.
- Signature hashing scope (include args/payloads?). To avoid privacy concerns, only include anonymized param fingerprints (SHA1 of length-limited prefix) in the signature.

Security review required: yes (sandbox influences injection content and structured outputs).
2025-03-13 - Arianna Patel: Kickoff notes: outlined goals and constraints. Discussed compatibility with existing function-calling API. Action: Diego to draft prototype PR and a unit test plan.
2025-03-17 - Diego Morales: Spike complete. Implemented in-memory call graph and basic cycle-detector. Found the current tool-runner lacks an easy hook for streaming byte slices; added a small shim which preserves order but requires API change to ToolResult.chunks -> BREAKING for internal tool contracts. Posting design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/STREAM-SANDBOX-PROPOSAL
2025-03-19 - Priya Kaur (Security): Reviewed and requested explicit policy for sanitization of tool output when injecting into user-visible streams. Asked for threat model doc and list of headers allowed in provenance. Marked security_review_required=true.
2025-03-22 - Diego Morales: Implemented streaming_incremental + deferred_final modes behind feature flag. Added provenance header format: sandbox-provenance: <call-graph-id>:<chunk-index>. Added unit tests for ordering and chunk reassembly. Open PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8842
2025-03-25 - Maya Chen (Product): Reviewed UX for error cases. Product wants a clear, user-facing error text when guard fires and a Console breadcrumb with example reproduction. Added to follow-ups: add example prompts & docs in SDK quickstart.
2025-03-28 - Diego Morales: Stabilized compatibility shim mapping rules for 3 legacy tools (calendar-extract-v1, pdf-ocr-old, db-query-text). Dashboard tile prototype deployed to staging. Next: add rate-limited circuit-breaker and finalize security review responses.

title: Eastern Canada 'g5x' reservation bundles: launch orchestration and partner enablement

title: Diversify probe signals and SLO-driven admission controller for regional autoscale stability
content:
Diversify probe signals and SLO-driven admission controller for regional autoscale stability

Problem: We observe periodic autoscaler instability during mixed workloads (long chat sessions + short completions) across regions. Liveness/readiness probes are overly homogeneous (single HTTP healthz and synthetic short-completion check), causing correlated probe failures and noisy scale decisions; regional failovers amplify oscillation and trigger circuit breakers too aggressively. SLOs (p99 latency and error budget burn) are at risk when autoscaling overshoots or sheds capacity too late.

Goal: Reduce correlated probe noise, enforce SLO-aware admission decisions earlier, and make autoscaling more stable across regions and workload mixes. Deliverables: (1) probe diversification (passive + targeted synthetic + KV-cache warmness checks), (2) an SLO-driven admission controller that applies token-aware request shaping and soft circuit-breaker signals to upstream routers, (3) a sliding-window SLO-enforcement policy used by autoscaler to prefer steady-state capacity over reactive ramping, and (4) simulation harness + dashboard to validate behavior before rollout.

Proposal summary:
- Probe diversification: add three orthogonal signals per instance: (A) passive latency window (quantiles from the last 30s of actual requests), (B) synthetic warmup probes that exercise long-sequence KV cache & batching (low-frequency, ramping from 1/min to 1/s per instance during canary), (C) dependency probes (eg. GPU driver/disks/KV store) that are lightweight but catch resource degradation early. Readiness becomes an AND of (A OR B) with C as a gating signal for severe infra issues instead of immediate eviction.
- Sliding-window SLO enforcement: compute burn-rate and latency violations on a 5m rolling window and expose an "autoscale bias" metric [-1.0, +1.0] that nudges scale decisions toward conservatism when transient spikes are detected. The autoscaler will use this bias to prefer smaller step changes and longer cool-downs when bias < -0.2 (indicating recent SLO risk).
- Admission controller & soft circuit breaker: implement an admission policy at the edge router that (i) classifies requests by expected cost (short vs long vs streaming), (ii) applies per-token concurrency caps and priority tiers, and (iii) emits soft circuit-breaker signals (warning states) to autoscaler and regional router so degraded capacity can be steered rather than fully rejected. Token-aware shedding reduces tail impact on short requests while allowing long-running sessions to finish with degraded throughput.
- Multi-region failover coordination: add cross-region health-weight smoothing so when a region degrades, traffic is stepped down gradually to avoid sudden worldwide influx; maintain per-region failover limits controlled by policy (eg. max 15%/minute shift).

Implementation notes: Start with a feature flag (ff:probe_diversify_slo_admission) to enable behavior per deployment. Probe agents will run in the same pod process to avoid network flakiness biasing signals. The admission controller will be implemented in the router (Go) and expose metrics via Prometheus with dedicated labels (request_class, token_estimate, admission_action).

Testing & verification:
- Simulation harness: extend ENG-68211's probe sim (see design doc) to generate mixed workloads and validate autoscaler bias effects. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1205 (WIP).
- Canary plan: enable for 5% traffic in east-us, monitor p99 latency, error budget, autoscale oscillation metric for 72h, then expand to 25%/72h and regionally to eu-west.
- Dashboards: new dashboard runtime/slo/admission with burn-rate, autoscale-bias, probe-signal-fusion, admission-drop-rate per region. Draft: https://dashboards.redwood.local/d/runtime/slo-admission (internal).

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Increasing synthetic probes increases load and could bias batching behavior; we'll keep synthetic frequency conservative and tie activation to canary windows.
- Admission controller complexity: token-estimate models must be calibrated; initial implementation will use heuristic token cost buckets derived from current payload stats.
- Backward compatibility: ensure older console components that rely on simple liveness don't break by keeping previous endpoints until rollout completes.

Rollout steps:
1) Merge probe and metric changes behind flag (runtime-1.22 branch).
2) Lab validation + sim runs (2 days).
3) Small canary in one AZ (5% traffic) for 72h.
4) Regional canary (25%) 72h.
5) Global staged rollout with monitoring gates.

Success criteria:
- 30% reduction in autoscaler step-change frequency during mixed workloads in sim.
- No increase in p99 latency > 5% in canary regions.
- Lowerized circuit-breaker hard trips (>=50% reduction) during degraded infra events in test scenarios.

Links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.internal/display/INF/Probe+Diversification+and+SLO+Admission
- Simulation harness proto: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sim-harness/compare/feature/probe-diversify
- Related Linear tickets: ENG-31877 (health telemetry pipeline), ENG-46002 (graded liveness checks)

title: Hosted API Lite Slate: PRD, Scope Clarification, Acceptance Criteria & Launch Checklist
content:
Hosted API Lite Slate: PRD, Scope Clarification, Acceptance Criteria & Launch Checklist

Purpose: Define a minimal, interoperable PRD for a 'Lite Slate' of hosted inference endpoints (chat, completions, embeddings, rerank) targeted at rapid onboarding for small/medium customers while preserving safety, observability, and predictable economics. This document clarifies requirements, enumerates scope changes vs. full-surface PRDs, and provides a concrete launch checklist with acceptance criteria and rollback gates.
- Expose compact endpoint contracts for: chat (conversational API), completions (single-shot generation), embeddings (vector encode), and rerank (similarity-based reranking).
- Streaming support for chat & completions (text-only).
- Basic tenant isolation (per-tenant API keys, usage accounting).
- Runtime defaults tuned for cost-effectiveness (presets for batching/quantization).
- Minimal observability: per-endpoint latency, error rate, token cost telemetry, and canary dashboards.
- Safety guardrails: prompt-safety filters and basic rate limits.
- No multi-protocol surface (gRPC/other) or advanced composable endpoints.
- No multi-model orchestration (mosaic routing) in initial lite slate.
- No tenant-managed private deployment package; this is hosted-only.
- No advanced KV cache controls surfaced to customers (runtime-managed only).
- No long-term retention analytics beyond 30d for the initial rollout.
Functional: Provide REST endpoints: /v1/lite/chat, /v1/lite/completions, /v1/lite/embeddings, /v1/lite/rerank with consistent authentication headers and JSON schemas.
Behavioral: Deterministic contract for input/output fields; stable schemas for customer SDKs during launch window.
Rate limits: Default per-account QPS and token caps, with simple upgrade path to higher tiers.
Defaults: Endpoint presets for latency (low-latency), cost (economy), and balanced. Customers can override via documented 'profile' parameter but not arbitrary runtime knobs.
Billing: Usage metering per token for chat/completions, per-vector for embeddings, and per-request for rerank. Integrate with existing billing pipeline.
Safety: Integrate hosted prompt-safety service; block high-risk content according to current policy version. Expose a 403 code for safety blocks with a reference code in response.
Docs: Quickstart, SDK snippet, schema examples, migration notes from existing endpoints (if any).
Latency: p95 <= 220ms for embeddings; p95 <= 400ms for short-completion (<=128 tokens); chat streaming first-byte <= 180ms for 90% of requests in supported regions.
Availability: 99.9% monthly uptime SLA for lite slate endpoints in hosted region(s).
Scalability: Autoscaling to absorb 3x baseline traffic burst without errors; throttling behavior documented.
Cost profile: Unit cost targets to be within 12% of comparable 'economy' presets from platform benchmarks.
Observability: Canary dashboard with per-route latency/error/token cost, traces linked to request-id, alerting for degradation.
Security: TLS everywhere, KMS-backed service keys for internal signing, and audit logging of admin actions.
Compliance: Initial rollout in non-EU regions; EU rollout gated on data residency clarifications and DPA updates.
API contract: All four endpoints implement the documented request and response schemas with example fixtures in the repo.
SDK tests: Official JS and Python SDK integration tests pass against a staging stack and are included in CI.
Performance: Benchmarks meeting NFR latency targets in staging under synthetic traffic (see bench artifacts link).
Reliability: Canary run for 72 hours with error rate <= 0.5% and no sustained latency regression >20% vs baseline.
Safety: Prompt-safety integration active; at least one block example tested and an error code returned as specified.
Billing: Usage events for these endpoints flow through billing pipeline end-to-end and invoices reflect test usage in sandbox accounts.
Docs & Guides: Quickstart, migration notes, and troubleshooting guide published in Confluence/Docs with review approval from Developer Experience.
Operational Runbook: On-call playbook, rollback plan, and escalation matrix documented and linked to pager duty schedules.
Security Review: Completed and signed off by security with required mitigations tracked as issues.
Launch Signoff: Cross-functional signoff (PM, Eng, DX, Security, SRE) recorded in the release ticket before cutover.
Region gating: EU/UK rollout gating tasks created; initial global rollout excludes EU until gating closed.
Alpha: Internal alpha with 3 partner accounts in staging (2w).
Canary: 5% traffic to lite-slates in us-west for 72h with active monitoring and rollback gate (2w).
Gradual: 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 weeks with automated traffic ramp if canary metrics stable.
Documentation: Publish quickstart & migration docs at canary start.
Billing: Enable billing in parallel for canary tenants; verify metering.

title: Deadline-aware microburst packer for streaming chat to reduce tail latency and GPU memory churn
content:
Deadline-aware microburst packer for streaming chat to reduce tail latency and GPU memory churn

Problem: Streaming chat workloads show microbursts of short requests interleaved with longer generations. Our current continuous batcher either (a) dispatches immediately and pays heavy tail latency during high contention, or (b) waits too long to coalesce and harms P50. Additionally, KV cache allocation and slab reserves jitter under bursty arrivals, causing opportunistic GPU OOMs and frequent small evictions that hurt throughput.

Goal: Implement a deadline-aware microburst packing heuristic that: (1) respects per-request streaming latency budgets, (2) opportunistically coalesces short windows of arrivals into low-jitter microbatches, (3) stabilizes KV slab reservations and eviction patterns to reduce memory churn, and (4) preserves fairness across sessions/tenants. Target SLO: P95 generation token latency <= 160ms for short-turn chat completions under 95th-percentile load, and reduce small-eviction frequency by >= 40% on stress traces.

Approach summary:
- Introduce soft-deadlines per incoming chunk derived from client-declared latency preference (fast/standard) and historical session pacing.
- Maintain a short lookahead buffer (configurable 2-15ms) and a microburst aggregator that holds requests until either the soft-deadline expires or the microbatch reaches a size heuristic.
- Use a deadline-weighted packing score to rank coalescing candidates: score = alpha*(remaining_deadline_ms) + beta*(predicted_token_length) + gamma*(session_priority). Lower score -> higher packing priority.
- For KV cache: implement slot pre-reservation for requests expected to touch KV (chat continuations) and a slab smoothing policy that increments reserves in small deltas instead of immediate full expansion. This reduces transient OOMs and evictions.
- GPU memory policy: maintain a headroom watermark per GPU (configurable, default 12%) and evaluate speculative quantized execution (int8 fallback) when headroom is low and request can tolerate small quality delta.
- Fairness: ensure that long-running, greedy sessions cannot starve microburst aggregation by capping per-session tokens-in-flight used for batch decisioning.

Why unique: This ticket focuses on deadline-first packing for streaming chat (not purely latency-first or throughput-first) and couples the batch formation heuristic with KV reservation smoothing and GPU headroom-aware fallbacks — a coordinated cross-layer strategy rather than independent knobs.

Risks/Unknowns:
- Client-declared latency preferences may be missing or abused; need conservative defaults and rate limits.
- Predicted token-length model needs training/tuning on production traces to avoid mispack.
- Interaction with distributed routing: when routing across capacity tiers we must preserve deadlines or risk inter-region tail spikes.

Success metrics (see acceptance_criteria): P95/P99 latency, small-eviction frequency, GPU OOM incidence, throughput impact.
P95 generation token latency for short completions (<= 8 tokens) under 95th-percentile arrival trace <= 160ms
Small-eviction events (slab < 4MB triggers) reduced by >= 40% on replay of 2026-02 production bursts
No increase in overall cost-per-token > 5% compared to baseline simulated load
Feature gated and can be rolled back at runtime; config flags for lookahead_ms and headroom_pct
Integration tests that simulate interleaved microbursts and long sessions with assertions on batch sizes and reservation deltas
High-level algorithm (prototype):
1) On chunk arrival, attach a computed soft_deadline_ms = client_latency_pref_ms * deadline_scale(session_history).
2) Insert into microburst_buffer indexed by affinity_key (model + tenant + session_shard).
3) Periodically (every scheduler_tick_ms = 1ms) consider buffer: compute packing_score for candidate set and attempt to form microbatch up to gpu_token_budget or until any candidate's soft_deadline <= tick_slack_ms.
4) Before dispatch, call kv_pre_reserve(batch) which calculates incremental slab growth: delta = min(max_delta_bytes, predicted_kv_bytes - current_reserve). Apply in small increments; if global_mem_headroom < headroom_pct, mark requests with speculative_quantize=true.
5) Dispatch: update per-session tokens-in-flight counters and start per-request deadline timers; collect runtime telemetry for observed latency and kv_eviction events.

Notes on parameters to tune: lookahead_ms ∈ [2,15], alpha/beta/gamma weight grid search, headroom_pct default 12%, max_delta_bytes default 8MB.

Prototype artifacts: initial simulator (python) generates synthetic traces of short microbursts + long sessions. Use replay harness to drive dedicated dev cluster with small-scale GPUs to validate eviction frequency changes.
2026-03-10: Triage and spec by Maya. Decided to scope initial rollout to hosted API paths for streaming chat only (no private runtime yet).
2026-03-11: Simulator prototype finished (python harness). Ran 5k trace replays; microburst packing reduced average batch creation events by ~28% in synthetic load. Logged simulator code in /confluence/runtime/2026/deadline-microburst/simulator and added sample traces to drive-tests bucket.
2026-03-12: Implemented microburst_buffer and packing_score in batcher-v2 branch. Initial CI unit tests green. Hooked kv_pre_reserve stub; added feature flag runtime.deadline_microburst = false by default.
2026-03-13: Benchmarked on dev-gpu-4 (A10x4) with replay trace; observed P95 drop for short completions from 220ms -> 150ms, small-eviction delta -36% (below target but promising). Identified jitter in slab growth under heavy concurrent demands.
2026-03-14: Updated slab smoothing to use additive-increase cap and introduced per-tenant reserve ceiling to avoid noisy neighbor expansion. Preparing PR for internal review (see prs).

title: Rosetta: Precision Embed Quality Harness and Drift Ops
content:
Rosetta: Precision Embed Quality Harness and Drift Ops

Background:
We need a repeatable, production-ready evaluation harness that measures embedding accuracy and reranker fidelity across model variants and operating conditions. Existing nightly runs are ad-hoc and focus on signal-level drift; Rosetta centralizes reference corpora, multi-metric scoring, and operational alerts so product teams can trust quality over time.

Goals:
- Create a curated reference corpus ("Rosetta set") covering 12 production verticals and a stratified sample of heavy, medium, and tail queries.
- Implement an offline runner that computes per-model and per-route metrics nightly: recall@1/5/10, MAP@10, average cosine drift, embedding norm stability, interquartile distance, and rerank NDCG@10.
- Surface regression alerts with severity (info/warn/critical) tied to user-visible thresholds and deliverable runbook links.
- Keep compute cost under budget by sampling and adaptive evaluation windows while preserving statistical power for drift detection.

Scope and non-goals:
In scope: corpus curation process, nightly pipeline, metric definitions, alerting integration with PagerDuty/Grafana, dashboards, and a simple UI for inspecting counterexamples.
Out of scope: automatic model rollback; that will be handled by rollout policies in a follow-up ticket.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Reference set vs. continuous sampling: we'll maintain a small, human-curated Rosetta reference + larger synthetic perturbation set used for sensitivity probes. The curated set provides low-noise regressions; synthetic probes stress edge cases.
- Metrics: prefer ranking-aware metrics (NDCG, MAP) plus distributional drift stats rather than only mean cosine change. This better correlates with user-facing quality regressions.
- Sampling cadence: nightly full-run on Rosetta set and weekly aggregated checks on production-sampled logs. This balances timeliness with cost.
- Alert thresholds: use dynamic baselines (28-day rolling median) with absolute minimum thresholds to avoid alerting on natural variance.

Data & Golden/reference curation process:
- Pull 20k labeled Q-A pairs from product teams (see linked Confluence doc). Labeling rubric includes relevance tiers and known duplicates.
- Augment with 40k synthetic perturbations (noise, paraphrase, truncation) to probe robustness.
- Store reference vectors and metadata encrypted at rest in the eval datastore (access controlled).

Pipeline and infra:
- Runner implemented as a k8s CronJob in the infra repo; runs on dedicated CPU nodes with optional GPU acceleration for batched rerank scoring.
- Uses Redwood Embed API (hosted) and the internal rerank simulator to compute logits and ranking metrics.
- Outputs JSON artifacts per run: per-route metric bundle and counterexample list. Artifacts uploaded to S3 and indexed in the evaluation catalog.

Telemetry & alerting:
- Instrument per-token timing and per-request end-to-end latency for embeddings and rerank passes.
- Send metrics to Grafana/Loki; alerts wired to Slack channel #embed-quality and PagerDuty for critical regressions.
- Alert logic examples: NDCG@10 drop >5% vs 28d baseline (warn), drop >12% (critical). Cosine drift above historical 99th percentile -> investigate.

Rollout & operational playbook:
- Run harness against candidate model prior to any rollout. If critical regression, block rollout and create evaluation ticket with artifacts.
- On alert, on-call follows runbook: reproduce locally, triage root cause (model change vs data shift), and if model is culprit, coordinate with model-ops for immediate rollback.

Acceptance criteria:
- Nightly run completes within 3 hours and publishes metrics to Grafana and S3.
- Alerts trigger correctly for injected synthetic regressions in canary tests.
- Dashboards show stable baselines for control models and clear signal for introduced perturbations.
- Documentation and runbook published and reviewed by PM and SRE.

Risks and mitigation:
- False positives from natural traffic drift -> mitigate with 28-day dynamic baselines and minimum effect size thresholds.
- Cost overruns from large-scale rerank simulation -> cap full rerank runs to weekends and rely on sampled checks during weekdays.

Next steps (milestones):
- 2025-11-10: Finalize Rosetta set selection and labeling rubric (owner: UX/PM).
- 2025-11-21: Implement nightly runner prototype and basic metrics (owner: Eng).
- 2025-12-01: Integrate alerts + dashboard and run synthetic regression smoke tests (owner: Eng + SRE).
- 2025-12-15: Documentation, runbook sign-off, and handoff to product teams.

Notes on cross-team reviews and dependencies:
- PM review requested: Riley Thompson (product) — please validate vertical coverage and thresholds.
- Security: encryption and access audit to be reviewed by Security (ticket to be created if needed).
- Depends on embedding throughput improvements in ENG-341900 and the evaluation catalog work in ENG-32456.

Artifacts and example outputs:
- Sample run JSON: https://s3.redwood.ai/eval/rosetta/2025-11-04/metrics.json
- Counterexample viewer: https://internal.redwood.ai/rosetta/viewer?run=2025-11-04

2025-11-11: Design review with PM/Design. Request to add more tail queries for enterprise customers — accepted.
Action: expand Rosetta set by 4k enterprise queries (assigned to UX).
