title: Streaming Chat connector patterns and migration guide for Python SDK
content:
Streaming Chat connector patterns and migration guide for Python SDK

Problem: multiple consumer patterns in the Python SDK (callback hooks, iterator-based, and low-level SSE adapters) have led to repeated user confusion and brittle integrations when applications attempt to add telemetry, retries, or partial-resume. Goal: introduce a connector pattern + migration guide that provides a small, typed consumer facade (ConsumerConnector) and a set of adapter recipes so existing customers can migrate incrementally. The connector must support: resumable checkpoints, typed event signals (message, meta, error, watermark), prioritized soft-retries, and clear telemetry hooks. This ticket covers design, reference implementation, migration docs, and 2 integration examples (FastAPI webhook and a serverless consumer).
Spec: a one-page event contract + connector API published in docs and linked from SDK README
Reference implementation added to python/sdk/connectors with unit tests covering resume/replay and retry semantics
Migration guide with code snippets for callback -> iterator -> connector flows
Two example apps updated: examples/fastapi-chat-consumer and examples/serverless-stream-consumer
Bench: latency regression < 5% for typical 16-token responses in CI microbench compared to current iterator baseline
Telemetry: connector emits token-level counters and persisted resume checkpoints to SDK tracing hooks
Connector API: class SyncConnector(consumer_callable) and AsyncConnector(async_consumer_callable) with methods: start(), pause(), resume(checkpoint), close()
Event contract: 'type' in {message, meta, error, watermark, checkpoint}; payload schema versioned (v1); include optional 'id' and 'seq' on message events
Retries: connector will expose soft_retry(retry_policy) hook; default policy = exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency by event id
Resume semantics: checkpoint = {cursor, last_seq, model_variant, kv_cache_snapshot_id}; SDK will persist checkpoint to configured storage adapter (in-memory for examples; external store optional)
Telemetry: emit connector.resume, connector.pause, connector.error, connector.message spans; add counters for tokens_emitted and resume_attempts
Migration helpers: callback_to_connector adapter and iterator_to_connector shim provided; examples in the migration guide
Testing: unit tests + integration playback harness that feeds recorded event streams from /tests/fixtures/streams
Risk: breaking existing integrators who depend on low-level SSE shapes. Mitigation: provide adapter layer and keep old APIs for at least 2 releases with deprecation warnings.
Risk: performance regression from extra event wrapping. Mitigation: microbench target <5% regression; inline event object to reduce allocation pressure.
Risk: incorrect resume leading to duplicate token emissions. Mitigation: add seq-based dedupe in connector and test against recorded streams and race conditions.
Finish PR fixes for cache leak and merge feature-flagged connector to canary branch
Add migration snippets to README + full migration guide in docs
Run CI microbench and smoke tests across macOS/ubuntu py3.11 and publish results
Schedule follow-up tickets for TypeScript and Go adapters after stabilization

title: Attribution Lens — Per‑Route Cost Drift Inspector (UX Prototype)
content:
Attribution Lens — Per‑Route Cost Drift Inspector (UX Prototype)

Design and prototype an Attribution Lens — a focused Console view that surfaces per-route and per-model cost drift over time, with interactive decomposition and exportable artifacts. This ticket covers the UX copy, wireframes, prototype links, and initial review notes for the first iteration. The feature helps platform and product engineers quickly surface anomalous cost increases, attribute them to model variants / prompt patterns / request routing, and export a trace for audit or billing reconciliation.
Primary goals: 1) Make cost drift visible at route-level (small multiples + sparkline anomaly badges) 2) Provide fast root-cause slicing (model, quantization, batch, prefix cache hit/miss, token types) 3) Enable one-click trace export (CSV/JSON) for downstream billing or incident handoff. Core UI patterns: timeline slider to focus windows, progressive decomposition panel, role-aware toggles (dev vs finance), and inline suggestions for remediation (e.g., pin cheaper variant, enable prefix cache).
Figma: https://www.figma.com/file/REDACTED/attribution-lens-proto
Prototype (InVision): https://invis.io/REDACTED/attribution-lens
Clickable HTML prototype: https://redwood-internal.builds/attribution-lens/2025-02
Show per-route small multiples (top 12 routes by spend) on page load to surface hotspots quickly.
Default time window = 14 days with fast presets (24h, 7d, 14d, 30d).
Anomaly detection is client-side thresholding at design time (visual flags only). Product will wire server-side anomaly signals later.
Export formats: CSV for finance, JSON trace for engineering replay. Include provenance metadata (model version, route id, request id samples).
Progressive disclosure: show aggregated cost bars by default; expand to token-level token-type breakdown on demand to avoid cognitive overload.
Complexity vs clarity: Showing token-level breakdowns in-line makes cards dense; we chose expandable drilldowns to keep the overview scannable.
Performance: live decomposition for many routes is expensive. We will lazy-load detailed slices when users expand a route or adjust the slider.
Privacy: including request ids aids debugging but must honor PII/data policies. We will mask full payloads and include 'sampled request id' only with appropriate role permission.
Test with PMs and 3 engineering on-call users to validate that the anomaly badges correlate with real incidents.
Validate that export contains stable keys for join back to logs (route_id, model_version, timestamp window).
Onboarding micro-copy: 'How to use' tooltip outlining steps to go from hotspot -> slice -> export.
Prototype exists in Figma with interactive timeline and expandable route cards.
Design review completed with Eng and PM; feedback items captured as separate sub-issues.
Export spec documented (CSV & JSON schema) and linked in PRD.
Accessibility check: color contrast for anomaly badges meets AA; keyboard navigation for slider and expand controls follows patterns.
Mock data demonstrates a clear cost drift case and a resolved remediated case for QA validation.
Incorporate engineering feedback from 2025-02-24 review and update Figma prototypes.
Create ENG subtask to implement API for aggregated slices (ENG-XXXXXX) and include example payloads.
Run 2 moderated usability sessions w/ platform engineers and finance analyst (schedule in Cycle 42).
Finalize export schema and add to console docs (docs: Console > Cost > Attribution Lens).

title: Stuck canary state and version pinning: timeline, root cause, and remediation
content:
Stuck canary state and version pinning: timeline, root cause, and remediation

A model rollout entered a stuck canary state due to an interplay between version pinning and the rollback handler; resulting in residual traffic to the canary and degraded throughput for pinned customers. This ticket tracks the timeline, root cause analysis, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence.
Between 2026-03-02 07:40 and 2026-03-02 09:20 UTC ~15% of production requests to the europe-west1 region were routed to a pinned canary variant that had degraded tokenization performance. Observed effects: 5-10% tail latency increase for affected tenants, error rates for long-sequence generation increased from 0.2% to 1.6%. Two enterprise customers reported degraded response times; no data exfiltration or model output integrity issues identified.
2026-03-02 07:36 UTC - Automated rollout to model-v2-canary begins
2026-03-02 07:40 UTC - Canary healthcheck shows elevated decode latency (alerts fired to SRE)
2026-03-02 07:48 UTC - Rollout controller observes metric regressions and initiates automated rollback
2026-03-02 07:49 UTC - Rollback API call returns 202 accepted but subsequent routing update fails intermittently due to rate-limited control-plane write (cp-worker-3)
2026-03-02 07:50-08:05 UTC - Partial rollback: control-plane applied routing table update for 80% of nodes; remaining 20% retained pin flag in canary_state table
2026-03-02 08:08 UTC - Autoscaler sees unusual connection patterns and scales pools conservatively, amplifying degraded tail latency
2026-03-02 08:18 UTC - On-call manually forces canary unpin (routing-matrix v2 API) and triggers a cleanup job; traffic returns to expected distribution by 08:22 UTC
2026-03-02 09:00 UTC - Post-incident triage call; decision to open this follow-up ticket for long-term fixes
Two contributing defects aligned: 1) The version-pin API writes were not fully idempotent under partial failures: rollback flow assumed the routing-matrix update would be atomic across control-plane shards but control-plane uses eventual convergence and the cp-worker component was rate-limited, leaving stale entries in the canary_state table. 2) The rollout guardrails did not validate global route convergence post-rollback: the canary lived in a half-committed state with pin=true in ~20% of nodes which continued to accept A/B routing binds. The combination allowed residual client sessions and sticky routing to persist to the degraded canary.
Alerts: infra.alerts#latency-tail, rollout.alerts#canary-regression. Customer reports via support noting slow responses. Grafana anomaly detection flagged increased 95th/99th percentile decode time for model-v2-canary. Incident created from paging and support escalation.
Immediate mitigations performed: 1) Manual unpin via routing-matrix v2 API and forced sync job (control-plane job cp-20260302-07) to reconcile canary_state across shards. 2) Temporarily increased capacity in europe-west1 to absorb backlog and reduce tail latency. 3) Short-term rollout freeze for model-v2 variants until follow-ups are implemented.
OWNER: Diego Morales - Implement a post-rollback convergence check that verifies routing-matrix entries across all control-plane shards before marking rollback complete. ETA: 2026-03-18
OWNER: Claire Ng - Add end-to-end test to the rollout pipeline that simulates partial control-plane failures and validates idempotent unpin semantics. ETA: 2026-03-15
OWNER: SRE Team - Add Grafana dashboard panel (rollout.convergence) that shows live shard-level pin counts and a Prometheus metric for 'stale_pin_count'. ETA: 2026-03-12
OWNER: Diego Morales - Rate-limit backoff: make rollback writes use exponential backoff with bounded retries and produce a safety stop if >X% of shards report pending state. ETA: 2026-03-20
OWNER: Product/Platform - Update rollout runbook to include explicit manual unpin steps and verification checklist (who can execute, required logs). ETA: 2026-03-10
OWNER: Security - Verify that canary unpin workflow continues to meet RBAC expectations when executed manually; document audit steps. ETA: 2026-03-22
PM review (Liam O'Rourke): prioritize preflight checks for pin operations in the rollout pipeline.
Design feedback (Nora Blake): consider UX guardrail in Console that surfaces 'stuck canary' state and blocks new rollouts until resolved.
SRE comment: add incident-specific runbook snippet to avoid repeated manual fixes; automate reconcile-job and run as a controlled cron until fixed.
Primary focus is on making rollback and pin/unpin operations observable and strongly consistent from the caller's perspective. Secondary work items include improving Console UX and adding automated reconciliation that only runs under a safe rate-limited mode. We'll re-check incident metrics after completing the first three action items and close this ticket when the convergence check is merged, end-to-end test added, and dashboard live.
No customer data exposure detected. Audit logs for pin/unpin operations retained for 90 days per platform retention policy. Manual unpin steps were performed by SRE and recorded in audit trail cp-audit-20260302-9.

title: Automated scenario-based retention composer and attested evidence workflow for prompt/response/log/metric artifacts
content:
Automated scenario-based retention composer and attested evidence workflow for prompt/response/log/metric artifacts

Problem: Customers need clear, auditable retention controls for the four primary artifact classes (prompts, responses, request logs, metrics) that can be composed into scenario presets (e.g., 'Regulated PII flow', 'GDPR minimize', 'Audit-ready full retention'). Current retention UI and APIs require manual per-route configuration and produce brittle evidence exports that are hard for legal/compliance teams to validate.

Goal: Deliver a scenario-driven Retention Composer that: (1) lets operators pick or author scenario presets which map to per-tenant/per-route retention rules across artifact classes; (2) produces tamper-evident attested evidence bundles (signed metadata + chained hashes) suitable for audits; (3) enables residency-aware retention rules (region pinning + cross-region export); and (4) provides a preview/simulator to estimate storage impact and evidence size.

Scope: UX + API for editor and presets, backend policy engine to translate scenarios into per-route TTLs and sampling rules, evidence exporter format and signer integration (KMS/HSM), residency-aware routing hooks for exports, and CI gating to ensure no scenario rollback breaks SLOs. Excludes: automatic legal approval workflows (out of scope for initial release).
Retention Composer UI: create/edit/save scenario presets that set TTLs and sampling rates for prompts, responses, request logs, metrics
API: POST/GET endpoints for scenario presets and per-tenant binding; changes are versioned and immutable once released
Evidence Bundles: exported bundles contain signed manifest, chained SHA-256 digests for artifact shards, and a human-readable audit summary
Residency: scenario can require region pinning for stored artifacts and the system prevents cross-region exports unless explicitly authorized
Preview Simulator: shows estimated monthly storage, expected export bundle size, and sample evidence timeline for a sample traffic profile
Security: evidence signing uses customer KMS when available; fallback to Redwood attestation; security sign-off obtained
Backward Compatibility: existing per-route TTLs remain honored; binding a scenario should not silently change per-route settings without a preview and confirmation
Operational: rollout supports canary binding (10% of routes) and automatic rollback on retention-export errors
Design note: composer should support both policy-first (RPEL-like) and template-first workflows — operators choose which UI path to use
Implementation idea: translate scenario presets into a small set of primitive rules (TTL, sample_rate, residency_region, export_schedule) which the runtime can enforce without expensive lookups
Evidence format: ZIP with manifest.json, artifacts/*.ndjson (sharded), chainlinks.txt (hash chain), signature.sig; manifest must include per-shard offsets and schema version
KMS integration: prefer EKM/HSM customer keys; when unavailable include a Redwood-produced attestation header and key-rotation metadata
Telemetry: emit retention-affecting config change events to audit log with actor, diff, and before/after preview
Edgecases: handling deleted/retained metrics derived from aggregated counters vs raw time-series—documented in runbook

title: Prober-driven schema gate with probabilistic function-call diff thresholds and staged unwind
content:
Prober-driven schema gate with probabilistic function-call diff thresholds and staged unwind

Goal: Add a lightweight probing layer that runs parallel (shadow/prober) requests during canaries and A/B slices to detect structured-output and function-call incompatibilities earlier, and automatically trigger a staged unwind when mismatch rates exceed probabilistic thresholds.

Success criteria:
- Detect schema or function-call argument divergence with >90% precision and <2% false positive rate in production-like traffic within first 10k probe events.
- Auto-unwind (canary -> rollback) initiates within configured hysteresis window when the 1-minute rolling mismatch probability exceeds threshold.
- No measurable end-user latency increase for primary traffic (probe traffic is shadowed).

Design overview:
1) Prober agents: small, deterministic probe variants that exercise edge-shaped prompts and typical tool-calling surfaces. Probers run as shadow requests (non-blocking) at a configurable sample rate per route (default 2%).
2) Differential comparator: lightweight sawtooth comparator that computes three signals per invocation: schema-structure-diff (shape/type mismatch), named-arg-diff (missing/extra keys), and semantics-fail (function invoked unexpectedly). Each signal is boolean per probe.
3) Probabilistic gate: instead of hard counts, we maintain exponentially-weighted mismatch probability per route and model-variant; the gate trips when P(mismatch) > configured threshold (default 0.015) sustained for N windows (default 3).
4) Staged unwind actions: on trip, first reduce rollout percentage by 50% and notify canary watchers; if sustained, fully revert to last stable variant and execute incident runbook.

Telemetry & monitoring:
- Metrics: probe.invocations, probe.mismatch.{schema,args,semantics}, probe.mismatch_probability, probe.rollback_trigger_count, probe.latency_p95_shadow.
- Dashboards: canary-compatibility (per-route, per-variant) with a drilldown to failed probes (payload hashes + example diffs).
- Alerts: Pager alert when rollback_trigger_count > 0 for a paid customer route and severity is high. Slack notification to #rollouts for non-prod.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Probabilistic thresholding reduces noisy rollbacks from low-count random divergences but requires careful tuning to avoid delayed detection for high-latency bugs. We prefer EWMA-based probability over fixed counts to adapt across traffic profiles.
- Shadow probes avoid user-facing latency but increase egress and runtime cost; we scope probes to 2% by default and allow burst budgets.
- Comparator must be conservative on schema (type/shape) but aggressive on required named args for tool-calling safety.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for comparator logic + fuzz harness that generates pairwise function-call variants.
- Integration: run prober against model-variants in staging with a replay of production prompt corpus (dataset: canary-prober-replay-2026-02).
- Canary: enable shadow probes at 2% for first 24h then evaluate mismatch_probability; ramp to 5% for second 24h.

Rollout strategy:
- Feature flag gated (canary-compat-prober) plus per-customer opt-out.
- Initial alpha on internal routes and selected non-prod customers.
- Ramp plan: internal -> sandbox customers -> small set of production routes (low-risk) -> global.

Runbook excerpt (automated portion):
1) Gate trips => reduce rollout_pct *= 0.5, send automated Slack message and create a temporary incident channel.
2) If sustained for 3 windows => revert variant, annotate rollout with reason and attach failing probe sample.
3) Post-mortem triggers if rollback happened on >1 route within 24 hours.

Open implementation notes & blockers:
- Need a compact canonical diff format to store probe failures in telemetry without PII; blocked by privacy review (SEC-PRIV-41).
- Runtime integration: lightweight comparator must run in serving path's shadow pipeline; avoid allocating large objects to not perturb GC in host process.
- Edge case: cached responses (KV cache) can mask mismatches for some probes; we're adding a probe header to force no-cache for probe traffic.

Artifacts & references:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/PROBER-GATE-2026
- GitHub sketch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1782 (prober scaffolding)
- Telemetry dashboard (Datadog): https://app.datadog.com/dashboard/canary-compat-2026
- Probe corpus (internal GCS): gs://redwood-canary/probes/2026-02-replay.jsonl

Next steps (this sprint):
- Complete comparator C implementation and land PR for shadow pipeline integration.
- Finalize canonical diff schema with security & product.
- Add alerting rules and dashboard panels for first-run alpha.

Acceptance criteria for this ticket:
- Shadow probe pipeline lives in runtime and can be toggled by per-route config.
- Comparator produces telemetry metrics and example diff payloads (sanitized).
- Automated staged unwind executes on simulated trip in integration tests.

title: Consistent dense mode and scroll-snap behavior for data grids and overlays
content:
Consistent dense mode and scroll-snap behavior for data grids and overlays

Goal: unify dense-list/table spacing, and normalize scroll snapping and overlay (modal/popover) interactions across browsers for dashboard pages. This ticket covers design decisions, a small prototype, cross-browser quirks inventory, and acceptance criteria for handoff to engineering. Scope: table row density toggles, compact card lists on cost/dashboards, sticky column headers, in-panel charts with scroll-snap behavior, and modal/overlay stacking + scroll locking behavior on mobile and desktop.
Dense mode toggle applies consistent vertical rhythm to tables and cards across Chrome, Firefox, Safari (desktop + iOS Safari); no visual clipping at typical breakpoints (320px -> 1920px)
Virtualized table headers remain visually sticky and aligned with columns when scroll anchoring or GPU transforms are present (no header drift)
Chart panels that use horizontal scroll snap present predictable snap points and accessible keyboard focus order
Overlays (modals, confirmation popovers) lock body scroll on iOS and Desktop without breaking underlying sticky headers or causing layout shift
Design spec includes CSS fallbacks and a developer test matrix with repro steps for at least 6 browser/os combos
1) Introduce a 'dense' spacing token set that reduces row/card padding and line-height; update layout token map and component variants. 2) For data grids, use overflow: auto on a single scroll container with position: sticky headers and avoid transform() on ancestors; where transforms are necessary, provide a sticky fallback by moving header out of the transformed wrapper via portal. 3) Implement scroll-snap for horizontal chart lists using scroll-snap-type: x mandatory and explicit scroll-snap-align on children; pair with tabindex and aria-roledescription for keyboard users. 4) For overlays, use a robust scroll-lock strategy: apply fixed positioning to body with saved scroll offset for desktop and -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch + overflow-anchor adjustments for iOS; add focus trap and restore focus on close. 5) Provide feature-detection helpers and CSS fallbacks for Firefox/Safari behaviors and document them in the dev spec.
Dense tokens: token.dense.* (spacing, minHeight, icon sizes) — used by TableRow, ListCard, CostRow
Virtualization: ensure row height is consistent between DOM and virtual engine; include header height accounting in measurement hooks
Sticky + transforms: Safari refuses to honor position:sticky if any ancestor uses transform; plan two patterns: portal header or remove transform; recommend avoiding transform for non-animated containers
Scroll snapping pitfalls: fractional pixel rounding can cause off-by-1 px gaps on Safari; use exact pixel widths where possible or a small margin-tolerance in JS snap helpers
Accessibility: snap containers must not trap keyboard users; allow arrow and PageLeft/PageRight navigation and expose current index via aria-live if content is dynamic
Portal-ing sticky headers simplifies cross-browser consistency but increases DOM complexity and may complicate virtualization boundaries. Heavy reliance on JS for scroll corrections closes gaps in older browsers but increases runtime complexity and test surface. We prioritize predictable production UX; where necessary, accept small JS polyfills for non-critical animations.
Should dense mode be global user preference (persisted in profile) or per-route control?
Engineering preference: portal header pattern vs removing transforms from layout containers — which has lower engineering and performance cost in runtime?
How to handle third-party embedded charts that introduce their own scroll containers and transforms?

title: Deprecation orchestration: guided rollforward, compatibility shims, and staged notice flow
content:
Deprecation orchestration: guided rollforward, compatibility shims, and staged notice flow

Problem statement: We need a repeatable, low-friction deprecation workflow for old model versions that reduces customer outages and support load, preserves production latency/cost characteristics, and gives clear migration paths. Current gaps: sparse automated notices, no standard compatibility shim, inconsistent SDK warnings, and limited telemetry that ties regressions to specific deprecation stages. This ticket defines a pragmatic orchestration pattern we can implement across hosted, dedicated, and private customers: (1) early advisory + performance profile snapshot, (2) soft-warning in SDKs and console, (3) automated rollforward recommenders and compatibility shims for minor API/response changes, (4) staged traffic shadowing and canary deferrals, (5) final sunset with archive/readonly and migration runbook. Deliverables: notice templates, console UI treatment, SDK warning release, backend APIs for pinning+rollforward, compatibility-shim prototype, telemetry events and dashboards, and a customer-facing migration guide. Links: Confluence spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ML/PM-20456+Deprecation+Orchestration, Draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/7851, Example migration guide draft: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folder/0B-migration-guides
Notice templates for 90/60/30/14/7/0 day windows drafted and available in Confluence
Console UI mockups showing deprecation state and recommended replacement completed and approved by Design
SDKs emit non-blocking warnings at 60/30/7 days with links to migration guide (major languages: python, js, go)
Backend APIs to record pinned versions and rollforward recommendations implemented and integration-tested
Compatibility shim prototype that maps legacy response shapes to new model variant for simple breaking changes (eg. renamed fields) completed and validated against two sample models
Telemetry events emitted for each deprecation lifecycle action and dashboards created (customer-level signal of attempted pin, migration, and regression rate)
Customer migration guide published and linked from deprecation notices
Runbook for escalations and manual pin extensions available to CS/Support
SLOs and rollback triggers defined for staged sunset (shadowing, canary, cutoff)
Trade-offs: full backward-compatibility shim for arbitrary model changes is infeasible; limit shims to structural/field-level adapters and content-preserving normalizations.
We should prioritize hosted API and Dedicated customers first; Private deployments will get the notice + runbook but require packaged tooling for on-prem installs.
Consider a short-lived 'compat-mode' header that clients opt into; this can be used to route to compatibility runtime that applies light transforms.
Telemetry must include a fingerprint of the model perf profile snapshot (hash) so we can compare pre/post quality and latency regressions tied to a deprecation.
Legal/Compliance: check disclosure requirements for GDPR customers before sending automated notices; coordinate with Legal on language.

title: Secure SDK flows: API key rotation, SSO token lifetimes, and ergonomic patterns
content:
Secure SDK flows: API key rotation, SSO token lifetimes, and ergonomic patterns

Problem: Customers and platform teams repeatedly ask for clearer guidance and built-in helpers for secure API key rotation, SSO token handling for enterprise orgs, and concrete examples across Python/TypeScript/Go. Current SDKs have fragmented patterns: some expose low-level token objects, others hide refresh entirely, and none include a recommended rotation rollout workflow or examples for ephemeral credentials (short-lived API keys backed by KMS/HSM).
Deliver a cross-language set of SDK primitives and docs that: (1) make rotating keys straightforward for customers without breaking in-flight requests, (2) provide a standardized SSO token refresh/validation pattern for enterprise flows, (3) offer prescriptive secret-handling guidance (env vars, file perms, CI secrets), and (4) ship example migration guides and sample apps in Python/TS/Go.
SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) expose a single opinionated helper for injecting credentials that supports hot-swap rotation without restarting the process
Documentation includes a step-by-step key rotation playbook and an enterprise SSO token lifecycle example (OIDC refresh and short-lived session tokens)
E2E tests covering: rotating a key while concurrent streaming/generation requests are in-flight; token refresh failure and graceful fallback; and automated CI secret rotation integration
Security review sign-off recorded in the ticket and confluence doc
Migration example repos (one per language) added to /examples/sdk-key-rotation with readme and scripts
Technical approach: introduce CredentialProvider interface (language-specific name) that supports get(), refresh(), and on_rotate(callback). SDK internals will call get() for token fetch and subscribe to on_rotate to atomically swap live credentials for new ones.
Rotation model: recommend short-lived signing keys (T=1h) with automated server-side rotation + stable verification keychain. Provide example of issuing ephemeral API key via KMS-signed JWT exchange.
SSO guidance: document OIDC refresh best practices, recommended clamp on refresh attempts (exponential backoff), and how to escalate to interactive reauth in CLI apps.
Secret handling: enforce / recommend env var names (REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_SSO_TOKEN), avoid storing long-lived secrets in repo, recommend secrets manager integrations (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault) with code snippets.
Streaming ergonomics: ensure in-flight streaming requests continue using previous credential until a safe boundary (end-of-stream or token expiry threshold) then switch. Provide cancellation semantics for forced immediate rotate.
Backward compatibility: provide adapter shims for existing SDK users; deprecation plan documented in CHANGELOG and migration guide.
Week 1: Merge provider interfaces into beta branch; add feature flags for rotation helpers
Week 2: Land language idiomatic implementations and minimal examples; run E2E on staging cluster
Week 3: Internal dogfood — enable auto-rotation for a small set of internal customers and monitor metrics
Week 4: Publish docs, example repos, and SDK minor releases; announce breaking changes/migration path
Post-release: 2-week observability window and iterate on edge cases reported by customers
New telemetry: rotation_success, rotation_failure, rotation_latency (ms), active_credential_version
SLOs: rotation success >= 99.9% within configured window
Alert: >1% rotation failures across requests for 10m triggers P1 ops runbook
Atomic swap semantics for streaming: chosen approach keeps old token valid for in-flight streams. Risk: longer-lived token exposure for a short window versus risk of breaking in-progress calls.
Auto-rotate default: enabled for Dedicated/Private customers on new SDKs; default off for hosted in case customers rely on sticky long-lived keys. This divergence needs clear docs to avoid confusion.

title: Tokenizer + Chat-Template Fuzz Suite and Pin Validation Runbook
content:
Tokenizer + Chat-Template Fuzz Suite and Pin Validation Runbook

Build and integrate a deterministic fuzz-testing suite and a pin-validation runner that exercises tokenizer and chat-template permutations during model onboarding. The goal is to catch tokenization drift, role-marker/escape regressions, and template alignment regressions early and to gate performance-profile publishing until a set of compatibility checks pass. Deliverables: (1) fuzz suite that generates edge-case prompts (control chars, long prefix/suffix, mixed encodings, RK/role escapes), (2) a pin-validation runner that verifies pinned model bundles against the golden template contract, (3) a runbook that maps failure classes to automated remediation or required engineer actions, (4) dashboards and alerts for gating failures prior to profile publish.
Fuzz suite integrated into onboarding CI and runs within 12m for nightly smoke
Pin-validation runner produces a pass/fail artifact with token-level diff and example repro prompts
Performance-profile publishing is prevented by a gating flag when compatibility failures are present
Coverage: role marker normalization, multibyte char splitting, KV-cache prefix preservation, template delimiter collision
On-failure runbook links to exact repro PR and a suggested mitigation (shim, template fallback, or pin update)
Aggressive fuzz rules can produce false positives that block publishing. Conservative thresholds reduce noise but may miss subtle regressions. We will start with strict detection but soft-fail for non-blocking classes (label: informational) for two cycles, then tighten to block publishing after operator review. Running full corpus on every onboarding would increase CI cost; we will tier runs (fast smoke in CI, full corpus in nightly and pre-publish).
- Implement generator that composes message envelopes varying role tokens, unicode sequences, and delimiter sequences.
- Token-diff output must include byte offsets and tokenizer variant used (bpe/byte-level, model-specific vocab fingerprint).
- Pin-validation runner will exercise pinned model bundle via local runtime shim; if runtime unavailable, fall back to a lightweight tokenizer-only check.
- Collect throughput and tokenization-time telemetry during runner to detect pathological cases that might skew performance profiles.

title: Usage Signal Runbook: automated triage + mitigation for cost/latency anomalies
content:
Usage Signal Runbook: automated triage + mitigation for cost/latency anomalies

Deliver a pragmatic, automatable runbook and triage playbook for the console backend usage analytics pipeline that covers detection, classification, and automated mitigations for anomalies in usage/cost/latency metrics. This ticket includes: (1) canonical list of signals and dimensionality for detection, (2) detection algorithms and thresholds per signal, (3) automated classification rules that map alerts to likely root causes, (4) immediate mitigation playbook actions that can be executed automatically or by on-call, and (5) integration points (Grafana dashboards, Dataflow/Beam jobs, BigQuery queries, PagerDuty, Slack, Console Incident View). The goal is to reduce mean time to detection (MTTD) and mean time to mitigation (MTTM) for incidents where customer bill or latency spikes exceed normal bounds or threaten SLOs.
Runbook covering at least: cost-per-minute, p95/p99 latency by route/model, token ingestion rate, queued requests, batch size distribution, and KV cache hit rate
Automated detectors deployed to staging that produce synthetic alerts for 3 fault modes: sudden traffic surge, regression in batching/kv-cache, and a model quantization misconfiguration
Alert -> classification mapping that correctly tags >=80% of synthetic incidents with root_cause labels: traffic_spike, batching_regression, cache_eviction, pricing_leak, hardware_degradation
Playbook steps include exact queries/commands, 1-click mitigation links (scale up pool, force-fallback to cheaper model, enable token rate-cap), and validated PagerDuty escalation mapping

title: Attention Kernel Symmetry Mapper + Prefill Heuristics
content:
Attention Kernel Symmetry Mapper + Prefill Heuristics

Background: As we onboard more FlashAttention v3 variants we see sporadic decoding jitter and rollout reverts for tenants whose workloads exercise uncommon shape/precision combinations. Past tickets addressed gating, warmup and fallback shims, but we lack a compact mapping that describes when two kernels (v2 vs v3 or different tilings/precision) are functionally equivalent for a given request profile.

Goal: Build a small "Symmetry Mapper" and a set of runtime prefill heuristics that together let the runtime classify an incoming request and choose a kernel variant with reduced oscillation and predictable latency. The mapper produces a lightweight compatibility table (shape ranges, precision tolerance, workspace delta, expected latency delta) and the heuristics use that table plus short telemetry probes and tenant history to select the runtime kernel for prefill vs decode phases.

Acceptance criteria:
- Symmetry Mapper can produce compatibility entries for a model within an automated profiling run (CI job) in under 30 minutes.
- For the canary tenant set, prefill latency p95 regression against baseline is <= +6% and decode p95 <= +8% while tail error rate (OOMs / kernel fallbacks) is reduced by >= 30%.
- Mapper output serialized to a compact JSON that can be consumed by runtime (<= 16KB per model) and included in model-catalog metadata.
- Rollout strategy and staged canary documented and validated via smoke tests and telemetry dashboards.

Plan / Implementation steps:
1) Design mapper schema (shape_range, qtype_compat, min_workspace_bytes, latency_est_ms, probe_signatures). Deliverable: mapper-schema.md in design docs.
2) Implement automated profiler harness (benchmarks/attn_mapper) that runs a matrix of key shapes and precisions on v2 and v3 kernels, captures latency / memory and produces compatibility score.
3) Build a small compressor that folds similar entries and outputs the compact JSON artifact.
4) Integrate mapper artifact ingestion in the model onboarding flow (model-catalog + runtime config).
5) Implement runtime prefill heuristic: (a) if exact match in mapper -> select recommended kernel; (b) if near-match -> attempt a short optimistic probe (one short prefill) and record result in tenant cache; (c) if unknown -> fall back to conservative kernel with safe workspace margin.
6) Add telemetry: probe success rate, selection delta, kernel oscillation metric (switches per 10k requests), per-tenant rollback counter.
7) Canary rollout: 5 tenants initially -> 50 -> broad with automatic rollback thresholds.

Telemetry & Experiments planned:
- Synthetic profile run against llama-13B and mix of 8B/70B shapes to populate mapper.
- Real-traffic canary on four internal customers (chat, summarization, search) for 72 hours.
- Collect: prefills/sec, average/kernelswitches, p50/p95/p99 latencies for prefill and decode, OOMs, fallback counts.

Risks & Mitigations:
- Risk: Mapper may miss rare shape outliers causing unexpected OOMs. Mitigation: default to conservative kernel with workspace guard and add rate-limited warmup fallbacks.
- Risk: Probing adds small overhead to cold tenants. Mitigation: limit probes per tenant per hour and use cached probes.
- Risk: Mapper JSON drift across model versions. Mitigation: tie mapper artifact to model-version hash and invalidate on new upload.

Rollout plan & SLO thresholds:
- Canary acceptance checks run hourly in CI and require no more than 2 rollbacks in 72h window.
- Auto-rollback if kernel oscillation > 30 switches per 10k requests or if OOMs increase by > 50% vs baseline.

Open questions:
- Should the mapper include explicit per-layer compatibility or only per-shape aggregated summaries? (Design doc will recommend aggregated summaries initially with optional layer-level expansion.)
- Where to persist tenant probe cache (local node vs central KV) for rapid reads during scheduling?

Follow-ups after initial rollout:
- Add quantized-precision delta cost model to suggest fallbacks to lower-precision kernels when quality delta is acceptable.
- Expose a diagnostic route in the Console that shows the mapper decisions for a request-id for debugging.

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RT/attn-symmetry-mapper (draft)
- Profiler repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/attn_mapper (WIP branch)

title: Capacity Assurance: service-level spec and degradation notice protocol
content:
Capacity Assurance: service-level spec and degradation notice protocol

Purpose: Define a compact, measurable SLA and associated error-budget/credit computation for Dedicated capacity customers that (a) ties to observable throughput and availability metrics, (b) integrates with autoscaling/fleet controls, and (c) specifies customer-facing notice and remediation language.

Scope: This ticket covers: the SLA objective definition (metrics, quantiles, aggregation windows), error budget math (how credits are computed and applied), a degradation corridor concept for phased remediation, autoscaling interactions (grace windows and burst entitlements), and contract/legal phrasing for notices, credits, and termination triggers. Non-goals: detailed billing invoice UX and backend billing integration (tracked in PM-155120).

Key proposals (summary):
1) SLA objective: "Committed Throughput" defined as a daily 95th-percentile of per-minute served throughput measured in tokens/second per GPU pool. Degradation threshold triggered when 24-hour rolling Committed Throughput falls below the committed rate for more than 30 continuous minutes.
2) Error budget: Measured as the percentage of minutes in a rolling 30-day window where Committed Throughput < committed rate. Credits are proportional: Credit% = min(100, (CommittedRate - ObservedRate)/CommittedRate * AllocationFactor) applied to the monthly reserved capacity fee. AllocationFactor defaults to 0.8 to reflect partial operator responsibility for transient congestion.
3) Degradation corridor: Introduce two remediation bands: "Notice Band" (5-15% below committed rate) with automated notification and accelerated autoscale; "Remediation Band" (>15% below) where credits accrue and manual escalation to ops is triggered.
4) Autoscale interplay: Customers may opt into an "Autoscale Assist" mode where Redwood will automatically provision burst capacity for short excursions. Burst capacity is limited to 2x baseline for up to 20 minutes per day without crediting. Longer bursts reduce the AllocationFactor for that day.
5) Fleet controls & failover: Committed Throughput is AZ-aware. If Redwood fails over customer traffic to a secondary AZ due to infrastructure outage, we consider served throughput equivalent for credit computation, but not if the customer requested failover.
6) Notice & remediation language: 72-hour window for formal notice before a contractual remediation or termination clause can be invoked; immediate temporary credits may be applied pending root cause analysis.

Measurement & instrumentation details:
- Primary metric: served_tokens_per_minute_per_pool (derived from token emissions and request counts).
- Aggregation: per-minute measurements, compute percentiles over 24h and 30d rolling windows.
- SLO alerting: fire at 10% error budget burn in 24h and at 50% in 7 days.
- Auditability: all raw minute-level data retained for 90 days accessible via console report and exportable CSV for contract disputes.

Credit computation worked example (illustrative):
- Committed rate: 1,000 tokens/s sustained (baseline).
- Observed 30-day rolling avg: 900 tokens/s -> shortfall 100 tokens/s -> shortfall fraction 10%.
- AllocationFactor: 0.8 -> Credit% = 10% * 0.8 = 8% -> Customer receives 8% credit on reserved capacity line item for the affected billing period.

Open questions for Legal/Finance:
- Cap on cumulative credits per year (proposed cap = 30% of annual reserved fee).
- Whether credits should be applied as invoice adjustments or as account credits in the Console.

Acceptance criteria:
- Draft SLA language ready for legal review and inclusion in Dedicated contract templates.
- Instrumentation and dashboard mock (console) showing committed throughput, error budget burn, and ledger of applied credits.
- Autoscale Assist config exposed in Console and documented in docs.

Deliverables:
- Contract paragraph (customer-facing) + internal playbook for ops.
- Data pipeline query and sample dashboard tiles.
- Runbook for customer notifications and escalations.

2025-02-11 - Luca Moreno: Initial write-up complete; flagged two measurement edge-cases: cold-start warming (first 10 minutes of a new pool) and KV cache priming. Asking SRE for instrumentation guidance.
2025-02-12 - Nadia Patel (Legal): High-level OK, need to limit ambiguous terms like 'sustained' and define whether token accounting includes retries. Also asked for cap on credits — proposing 25-35% band.
2025-02-12 - Owen Brooks (SRE): Suggested treating the first 15 minutes after a pool launch as 'warm-up' and exclude from rolling 24h windows. Recommended adding 'opportunity to remediate' clause of 60 minutes before applying credit when autoscale is in progress.
2025-02-13 - Maya Chen: Updated draft to add 'warm-up' exclusion and 60-minute remediation opportunity. Added AllocationFactor defaulting to 0.8 per Ops feedback. Sent for Legal quick review.
2025-02-14 - Legal review note (Nadia): Acceptable to proceed with 0.8 AllocationFactor and 30% annual cap recommended. Please add example contract clause for notice and cure periods.
Adopt 'Committed Throughput' measured as 95th-percentile per-minute throughput over 24h as the primary SLA signal.
Introduce a two-band degradation corridor (Notice Band and Remediation Band) with differentiated actions.
Default AllocationFactor set to 0.8; Finance to confirm cap on annual cumulative credits (proposed 30%).
Ensure Console exposes both raw minute-level metrics and summarized SLO views. Autoscale Assist is opt-in and requires clear billing/credit implications in the UI.

title: Deferred-ack protocol and delivery safeguards for audit/residency events
content:
Deferred-ack protocol and delivery safeguards for audit/residency events

Design and implement a deferred-ack delivery protocol + runtime safeguards for audit, retention, and residency events exported from Redwood. Goal is to provide guaranteed-at-least-once delivery semantics without overwhelming downstream subscribers, support residency-anchored delivery rules, and produce machine-readable evidence for audit trails.
Several recent customer audits and a postmortem highlighted two recurring problems: (1) spikes in evidence export load cause downstream webhook receivers to return transient 5xxs and time out, which cascades into retries that overload the event pipeline; (2) residency and retention assertions need a signed/verifiable handoff and must be stored with the correct region metadata before final ack. Current shipper acks on enqueue which provides weak guarantees for end-to-end delivery and leaves little room for backpressure management.
Provide a deferred-ack handshake that only acknowledges events once residency and retention preconditions are durably recorded
Implement bounded retry/backoff and circuit-breaking to avoid cascading overload during receiver outages
Attach verifiable residency assertions and signing metadata to each delivered payload
Expose observable signals (per-route lag, retry rates, and drop counts) in Console for on-call and PMs
Preserve idempotency for consumers with a clear deduplication token contract
End-to-end evidence delivery SLO: 99.9% within 30 minutes for non-batch events under normal load
Retry storms reduced: peak retry concurrency to subscribers down by >= 70% in synthetic outage tests
Evidence payloads include residency-assertion and signed-proof headers in >= 99% of deliveries
Zero incidents caused by undelivered retention-delete-notices in the next quarter
1) Define wire contract: headers, idempotency token, residency-tag, signed-assertion format (JWS), and deferred-ack status codes. 2) Implement a delivery shim in the shipper that persists a 'delivery intent' record in regional ledger before attempting external delivery; only then returns success to upstream systems. 3) Add a delivery queue with backpressure-aware concurrency limits per-subscriber route and global circuit-breaker. 4) Implement deterministic dedupe using consumer-visible idempotency_token and server side dedupe window (configurable TTL). 5) Integrate KMS rotation & signing service and include a verification endpoint for auditors. 6) Add metrics/tracing and expose Console dashboards and incident runbooks.
Phase 1: Contract + small PoC (wire schema, JWS signing, per-route concurrency control)
Phase 2: Durable delivery-intent ledger + deferred ack server changes, limited rollout to low-risk partners
Phase 3: Autoscaling knobs and circuit-breaker tuning, full rollout, Console dashboards and runbook
Phase 4: Hardening: developer docs, security review, key-rotation automation, disaster recovery playbook
Spec doc reviewed and approved by PM and Security (Confluence link in artifacts)
End-to-end PoC sends 10k events with simulated 50% receiver failure and demonstrates no retry storm
Observability: Grafana dashboard shows per-route queue depth, retry rate, last-success timestamp
Automated integration tests covering idempotency and signed-assertion verification
API docs and sample consumer verification client published
Trade-offs: deferred-ack increases upstream latency and storage footprint (delivery-intent records). We mitigate via TTL compaction and per-tenant retention policies.
Consider an opt-in mode for partners that cannot verify signatures; fallback to unsigned but marked "unsigned" in header and routed to a lower-trust ingest path.
We should avoid changing existing webhook contract headers for older integrations; provide an opt-in new 'v2' header and route.
We will reuse existing KMS integration but need a short-lived signing token mechanism to minimize blast radius on key compromise. Ops to own rotation cadence.
2026-03-11: Kickoff w/ PM and Security. Agreed JWS (compact) for signed-assertion and 'X-RW-Residency' header format.
2026-03-12: PoC of signing flow complete (local KMS emulator). Basic delivery-intent ledger schema drafted; reviewed by infra team.
2026-03-12: Identified dependency on pubsub consumer checkpointing; opened follow-up ENG-83450 to add consumer visibility into dedupe window.
2026-03-13: Design review feedback: Security asks for encrypted payload-at-rest for delivery-intent ledger in non-US regions; added to acceptance criteria.

title: eng-platform
content:
eng-platform

Nina Petrova: looping in eng-platform folks — we need to nail down the integration points between the new VPC terraform modules and platform/installer config. Today we’re doing a lot of “paste subnet ids here” in pilots and it’s brittle.

Victor Alvarez: +1. main question from my side: what outputs do we want to be part of the “contract” for alpha? if we change names/shape every PR it’ll be chaos.

Irene Choi: yep. for alpha I’d like a minimal stable set that redwood-private-installer can consume (either flags or a config file). optional extras can be “best effort” outputs.

Bruno Silva: current modules output the basics (vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, public_subnet_ids, nat_gw_ids) but we haven’t standardized endpoint outputs. also log sinks.

Sean Gallagher: from SRE standpoint: the only things we *must* know to validate networking before we start are: subnets for nodes, cluster SGs, and whether required VPC endpoints exist + private DNS enabled where expected. (we’re adding preflight checks in installer; it needs something deterministic).

Allison Grant: observability angle: we need to know where to send/expect logs. at minimum: cloudwatch log group names/arns for flow logs (if enabled) and any S3 bucket used as sink (flow logs / access logs). plus tags so we can discover.

Rafael Mendes: +1 on deterministic. installer preflight should not scrape AWS too much without inputs; but we can also do discovery if we have VPC ID and region and explicit “I expect endpoints ON”.

Nina Petrova: what’s the preferred format? terraform output -json can be consumed by installer? or we want the terraform to render a yaml file?

Irene Choi: preference: don’t generate files in terraform for alpha. keep it as outputs, then docs say: `terraform output -json > networking.json` and pass to installer.

Victor Alvarez: okay so define a single composite output? e.g. `redwood_private_networking` containing everything.

Bruno Silva: we can, but then we have to keep object shape stable. also some people want individual outputs for reuse.

Sean Gallagher: composite is fine as long as it’s additive-only in alpha. but note: in terraform output -json you’ll get nested structures. installer can parse that.

Allison Grant: I’m fine w nested, but we should keep the “leaf values” as IDs/ARNs/strings. no giant lists of objects unless needed.

Simran Kaur: from RA review: docs should clearly map outputs -> installer flags/values. a table would help. also call out which are required vs optional.

Victor Alvarez: concrete proposal for v0.1 contract:
- required:
  - aws_region
  - vpc_id
  - private_subnet_ids (list)
  - cluster_node_security_group_id (or sg_ids list if pattern module returns multiple)
  - vpc_endpoints_required (map service->endpoint_id?)
- optional:
  - public_subnet_ids
  - nat_gateway_ids
  - flow_logs: enabled + destination (cw log group arn OR s3 bucket arn)
  - interface_endpoint_security_group_id
  - resolver / private hosted zone info (if we ever create)

Bruno Silva: we don’t currently create cluster SG in the VPC module; that’s in SG patterns module. but we can wire outputs through example.

Nina Petrova: for EKS private control plane constraints: installer/cluster will need the endpoint access pattern too. do we need to output whether EKS endpoint private/public is allowed? (or is that out-of-scope since modules aren’t creating EKS)

Irene Choi: out of scope for modules, but we should include “assumptions” in outputs/docs. i.e. “private subnets have route to NAT or endpoints for ECR/S3/Logs”.

Rafael Mendes: installer needs to know ecr endpoints specifically. we already have PR to detect + warn when missing.

Sean Gallagher: yeah PR-19110 is exactly this. it currently checks:
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api`
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr`
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.s3` (gateway)
plus `logs` and `sts` depending on mode.
We should align the terraform endpoints module defaults to match what the installer expects, then output “expected endpoints list” so preflight error messages can be explicit.

Victor Alvarez: re: “expected endpoints list” — do we output actual endpoint IDs or just booleans?

Bruno Silva: actual IDs are useful for debug. but installer can also query by service name + VPC ID.

Irene Choi: I’d like both: output the service names we *intend* to have and whether private DNS is enabled for each interface endpoint. then installer can cross-check reality.

Allison Grant: +1. private DNS misconfig is a common pilot issue (ECR). if we output the intended `private_dns_enabled=true` for ecr endpoints, that maps nicely to a preflight message.

Nina Petrova: can we keep it simple like:

```
output "redwood_network" {
  value = {
    region = var.region
    vpc_id = aws_vpc.this.id
    private_subnet_ids = module.subnets.private_ids
    public_subnet_ids  = module.subnets.public_ids
    endpoints = {
      ecr_api = { service = "ecr.api", endpoint_id = module.endpoints.ecr_api_id, private_dns = true }
      ecr_dkr = { service = "ecr.dkr", endpoint_id = module.endpoints.ecr_dkr_id, private_dns = true }
      logs    = { service = "logs",    endpoint_id = module.endpoints.logs_id,    private_dns = true }
      sts     = { service = "sts",     endpoint_id = module.endpoints.sts_id,     private_dns = true }
      s3      = { service = "s3",      endpoint_id = module.endpoints.s3_gateway_id, private_dns = "n/a" }
    }
    flow_logs = {
      enabled = var.flow_logs_enabled
      destination = var.flow_logs_destination
      cw_log_group_arn = try(aws_cloudwatch_log_group.flow.arn, null)
      s3_bucket_arn    = try(aws_s3_bucket.flow.arn, null)
    }
  }
}
```

Victor Alvarez: yes-ish. minor: service names should be full AWS service strings or standardized keys? i’d prefer full: `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.api` to avoid ambiguity.

Bruno Silva: agreed. and keep `endpoint_type` too (Interface/Gateway) so installer messaging can be better.

Rafael Mendes: re: `private_dns = "n/a"` — better to omit or set null. :)

Allison Grant: for log sink naming: can we output a “recommended log group name” even when not created? (customers sometimes bring their own). maybe:
- `flow_logs.destination_type` = `cloudwatch|s3|none`
- `flow_logs.log_group_name` OR `flow_logs.s3_bucket_name`

Irene Choi: careful: we shouldn’t output customer-provided values in a way that looks like Redwood-managed. but if it’s an input and we just echo it, that’s fine.

Sean Gallagher: also add `tags` output? not required but helps SRE inventory.

Victor Alvarez: tags in terraform output can be noisy. i’d skip for alpha contract.

Simran Kaur: +1 skip tags, but doc should say we tag everything with `redwood:component` etc.

Nina Petrova: question: should installer accept `--networking-json` path? or will it be `--terraform-outputs-json`? naming matters.

Rafael Mendes: i vote `--networking-outputs` or `--network-config`. `terraform-outputs-json` sounds too terraform-y.

Sean Gallagher: installer side can accept a JSON file with just the subset we need. but docs can recommend generating it with terraform output.

Bruno Silva: we can add an example script in the repo:

```
terraform output -json redwood_network > redwood-network.json
redwood-private-installer install --network-config ./redwood-network.json
```

Irene Choi: this is good. action items:
1) Victor/Bruno: standardize a `redwood_network` (or `redwood_private_network`) output in the examples (not necessarily in every module) with: region, vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, endpoints (service_name + endpoint_id + private_dns_enabled + endpoint_type), flow_logs destination info.
2) Sean/Rafael: confirm which fields installer will read in alpha and what’s optional; we can update preflight messaging to reference service names.
3) Allison: provide the minimal log sink fields SRE wants surfaced (cw log group arn/name and/or s3 bucket).
4) Simran: update RA/deployment guide mapping table outputs -> installer inputs.

Victor Alvarez: works. i’ll post a proposed schema in the PR description when we wire it.

Sean Gallagher: please also make sure endpoint keys match installer checks. we’ve been bitten by “logs” vs “cloudwatch-logs” naming.

Bruno Silva: noted. i’ll align to full service names:
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.api`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.dkr`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.logs`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.sts`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.s3` (gateway)

Allison Grant: for flow logs, if destination is CloudWatch we should output retention days too (defaults matter for security/compliance). if it’s customer-owned log group, we can output “unknown”.

Irene Choi: ok but keep it optional. don’t block alpha on it.

Rafael Mendes: :thumbsup: once we agree schema, we should freeze names for v0.x and only add fields. breaking changes require bump and release note callout.

Nina Petrova: +1. also if we can, add a “schema_version”: "0.1" in the output so installer can warn if incompatible.

Victor Alvarez: good call. we can set `schema_version = "0.1"` at top-level.

Sean Gallagher: :+1: that will save us in pilots.

Irene Choi: cool. let’s do it. please link the PR here when ready.

14:02:11 WARN retryer taskId=rt-9845 governor=embed-retryer-3 retry=1 role=embed-retryer-role

```

Jenna: that trace shows automated role action immediately after repeated failures. Looks like svc-deploy-bot invoked a remediation which mis-applied an ACL.

Dave: mapped keys -> customers: preliminary mapping shows some customer-owned keys (customer ids: cu_1123, cu_7809) present in redwood-temp-cache. Need to validate if those keys contain raw PII or only embeddings.

Arun: Jenna, can you confirm the type of data stored for those keys? Embeddings are derived but we treat embeddings as potentially sensitive per policy.

Jenna: right. For this cohort, mappings indicate embeddings + metadata (filename, minimal prompts). We need a quick data classification: run `s3select` to inspect a small sample; do not download more than necessary.

Mike: running selective s3select sampling for cu_1123 and cu_7809 (only 10 objects each) now.

Mike: sample results: objects contain embedding vectors + metadata: original filename, customer-annotated tag. No raw free-text prompt bodies in sample.

Jenna: ok that lowers risk but still qualifies as potentially sensitive under our privacy policy. Notify customers as potential exposure of derived embeddings and metadata.

Arun: Sara, can you draft the short customer alert? Keep it concise, explain what we know, actions we've taken, and next steps. Example draft below — use plain language and include contact link and mitigation advice.

Sara: Draft v1 for potentially affected customers:
"Hi — we’re reaching out to let you know we’re investigating a potential exposure involving a subset of embedding data stored in our temporary cache. We have isolated the automation that caused the change, blocked further access, and are performing a scope assessment. At this time we have no evidence of exfiltration. We will provide an update within 60 minutes and will follow up with a detailed notice if your data is confirmed affected. If you have urgent concerns, contact security@redwood.ai."

Jenna: tweak: add data types and timeframe.

Sara: Draft v2 (with tweaks):
"Hi — we’re investigating an incident that may have exposed embedding vectors and metadata for a small set of customers between 2026-04-27 14:00–14:10 UTC. We have isolated the process, disabled the automation, and begun a targeted review. No confirmed data access by third parties at this time. We will update you within 60 minutes and notify you if your account is confirmed affected. For immediate questions, email security@redwood.ai."

Legal-Bot: For customer outbound, avoid language implying actual exposure until confirmed. Use 'potentially affected' and include required data elements per our breach notification checklist: incident id, timeframe, data types, mitigation steps, contact, next update ETA.

Jenna: also preserve logs for audit and regulator timelines. Add retention note.

Arun: agree. Mike, ensure immutable log snapshots saved to secure-storage with chain-of-custody metadata.

Mike: snapshots saved: s3://secure-audit/INC-2026-0427/snap-1769204512.tar.gz (read-only).

Dave: CS-led inbound: please route any customer replies that look for further detail to me and do not speculate. We’ll coordinate with security to draft follow-ups.

Sara: I'll hold the two drafts. Which segment do we send to cu_1123 and cu_7809 now? Short or longer?

Jenna: short alert is fine now; follow with full notice if confirmed. Keep record of sent messages.

Arun: agreed. Mike post the status page update now (include ETA). Sara send short email to the two customers with cc to security and support. Jenna coordinate on the wording.

Mike: Status page posted. Link: https://status.redwood.ai/incidents/INC-2026-0427 (interim). Note: ETA next update 60 minutes.

Sara: Sending emails. Using templated subject: "Security notice - Potential impact to embedding data (INC-2026-0427)". Copy below:

--- email body start ---
Hi <Customer>,

We’re contacting you about an ongoing investigation that may involve embedding data and related metadata for a small number of customers between 2026-04-27 14:00–14:10 UTC. We have temporarily isolated the process and blocked further access. At this time we have no evidence of unauthorized access outside our systems.

What we’re doing: targeted review, preserving logs, and preparing a full notification if your data is confirmed affected.

When we’ll follow up: within 60 minutes with an update or sooner if we confirm scope.

Contact: security@redwood.ai
--- email body end ---

Sara: sent to cu_1123 and cu_7809 at 14:17 UTC.

Dave: note: customer cu_7809 replied asking if their raw files were included. I forwarded to Jenna.

Jenna: replied to Dave for the customer: "At this time our sample shows only embeddings + minimal metadata; no raw files seen in the sampled objects. We’re completing full verification and will notify within timeline."

Arun: brief incoming update on scope scan?

Mike: full mapping complete. Affected objects count: 28 for cu_1123, 11 for cu_7809. Data types: embeddings + file name metadata + small tag fields. No raw text blobs found.

Jenna: based on classification, this is a limited exposure of derived vectors + metadata. Regulatory risk moderate — depends on customer vertical. Recommend final customer notice and opt-in to offer extended monitoring.

Legal-Bot: Confirmed: if embeddings are not reversible to raw PII per our tech assessment, we still must notify customers under contractual terms. Regulatory notification not required at this time but escalate if requests from regulators.
